en: Preface to the *Jīnglù yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of the Sūtras and Vinaya),
Volume One, compiled by the Liang dynasty śramaṇas Sengmin, Baochang, and others.
The Tathāgata follows his traces to respond to conditions and expounds the teachings according to the capacities of beings,
extending his grace even to dragons and spirits.
Not only did he transform the heavens and men,
awakening Kauṇḍinya at the beginning;
his Way was perfected with Subhadra at the end.
The texts accumulated by the tens of millions and the scrolls piled up to the size of a great chiliocosm;
from west to east, it is truly difficult to exhaustively investigate them all.
As for Liu Xiang’s collation of the books—
The profound words had long been stored away;
when Emperor Ming of the Han was moved by a dream,
the spiritual verification became even more manifest.
From that time onward, translations were transmitted one after another.
Although the profound scriptures of the Tripitaka have been largely and comprehensively translated,
the miscellaneous discourses of the nine divisions have not yet been systematically collected.
The Emperor, whose realization is equal to that of the Samyak-saṃbuddhas and whose virtue rivals that of the All-Knowing One,
has extensively propagated the sūtras and teachings, benefiting both the Dharma and the secular world.
He has widely summoned those of profound antiquity and gathered together scattered texts from all quarters.
Thereupon, verses and prose passages were scattered and emerged from time to time;
what has now been obtained is indeed considerable.
Your Majesty’s intention is as follows:
In the final years of the Liang dynasty, faith and devotion gradually declined;
the texts were vast and sprawling, making them difficult to comprehend in their entirety.
In the seventh year of the Tianjian era, [...]
The Emperor issued an edict to Shi Sengmin and others,
instructing them to compile a comprehensive abridgment of the various scriptures to elucidate profound texts and bring forth the essential principles of the divine tradition.
The phrasing is concise yet the meaning is clear;
for those who investigate and seek it, this already provides more than half the benefit.
However, rare and extraordinary characteristics remain scattered throughout various sections.
The rare and secret teachings had not yet been formally promulgated;
furthermore, at the end of the fifteenth year,
he issued an imperial decree for Baochang to extract essential matters from the sutras and vinayas.
He ensured that all items were grouped according to their kind so that readers might easily understand them;
he also issued an edict to Śramaṇa Seng-hao of Xin’an Temple.
Shi Fasheng and others of Xinghuang Monastery assisted him in collating and reading the texts; thereupon,
he comprehensively mastered the scriptures and classics, selecting and extracting their most profound essentials.
The Emperor consulted the divine insights and adopted established precedents as his model,
resulting in fifty volumes in total,
with an additional five volumes comprising the catalog.
It is divided into five sections and titled *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Diverse Phenomena of Sūtra and Vinaya).
For future students, it serves as...

One may thus attain broad knowledge without toil. **Section on Heaven and Earth, Part 1: Section on Heaven, Upper (I)** **I. The Three Realms of Heavens** 1. The Formation and Destruction of the Three Realms 2. The Length of the Kalpas 3. The Sun, Moon, and Five Planets 4. Thunder 5. Lightning 6. Clouds 7. Wind 8. Rain **1. The Heavens of the Three Realms** **First: The Desire Realm** 1. The Form Realm 2. The Formless Realm **First: The Six Heavens of the Desire Realm** 1. The Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) 2. The Trāyastriṃśa (Heaven of the Thirty-three) 3. The Yāma (Yama Heaven) 4. The Tuṣita (Joyous Heaven) 5. The Nirmāṇarati (Heaven of Delighting in Emanations) 6. The Paranirmitavaśavartin (Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations) 7. The Māra Heaven **First: The Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings** The Four Heavenly Kings dwell upon the four terraces of Mount Sumeru.
All are forty-two thousand yojanas high. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that on each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru there is a mountain, all of which are named Yugandhara;
each is forty-two thousand yojanas high.
The Four Heavenly Kings govern and transform the regions above them.
The Heavenly King of the East is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
his city is called Uṣitaviśeṣa.
The Heavenly King of the South is named Virūḍhaka;
his city is called Sudarśana.
The Heavenly King of the western quarter is named Virūpākṣa;
his city is called Cakravāḍa, or alternatively Cakrapura— the latter being uncertain as to which is correct.
The Heavenly King of the North is named Vaiśravaṇa;
he resides in three cities.
The first name was Bhīṣma;
the second was Devapūjita;
the third was Gaṇasaṃmata.
The bodies of the four kings are each half a yojana in height;
their robes are one yojana in length and half a yojana in width.
Its weight is two parts.
The lifespan of its gods is five hundred years,
with few exceeding it and many falling short.
Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the gods;
likewise, thirty such days constitute one month.

Twelve months constitute one year; five hundred such years equal ninety thousand years of the human realm. They consume pure *kavaḍīkāra* food (edible morsels), and bathing and clothing serve as their food of smoothness (*ślakṣṇa*).
The male marries and the female weddeth; their physical acts of yin and yang are identical to those of humans.
Because of the wholesome karma of the three actions (*trikarma*) in a former life, they were born as devas.
They manifest spontaneously through transformation, appearing upon the lap of a celestial being.
Regarding their physical size, it is as that of human children two years old;
according to a separate record, the male sits upon his father’s knee and the female sits upon her mother’s knee. Not long after birth, the child naturally knows hunger.
Exquisite vessels made of the seven precious gems were filled with food of a hundred flavors;
according to one's merit, the color of the rice would naturally appear white for those with great merit, and blue for those with middling merit.
If one’s merit is meager, the color of the rice turns naturally red.
When the child eats it and it is digested, if they feel thirsty afterward,
the nectar in the precious vessel appears with the same color as the food.
The drink consumed did not remain in his body, like clarified butter cast into a fire;
his body grew long and became equal in stature to the heavens,
whereupon he entered the pond to bathe and approached a fragrant tree whose branches hung down in curves.
There are trees that produce fragrances for anointing the body, garments, ornaments, flower garlands,
precious vessels, fruits, and musical instruments; one goes to each of these and takes whatever one desires,
as described in the *Loutan jing* (Sutra on the Staircase of Jewels).

The descriptions are largely the same with minor variations, so they are not recorded here in full; however, in the various gardens, countless celestial maidens play music, sing, and converse with one another, causing deep attachment to arise.
Looking west, they forget the east.
In the midst of their play and pleasure, they forget the thoughts, perceptions, and knowledge they possessed at birth.

Having inherited the virtues of previous lives, they are born in the heavens; as described in the *Loutan jing*, these realms are roughly like clear, limpid ponds where flowers and fruits flourish in abundance.
The city has seven tiers, each six thousand yojanas wide.
The railings, lattices, palace walls, and rows of trees are all likewise sevenfold.
King Vaiśravaṇa [resides there].
There are always five great spirits:
the first is named Naṭarūpa,
and the second is named Dantura.
The third was named Haimavata;
the fourth, Traiśaṇḍaka;
and the fifth, Tārkṣyapa.
He constantly attended upon him,
observing the three fasts during the half-month on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days.
On the eighth day of every month, the Four Heavenly Kings constantly command their messengers:
"Go forth and patrol the world to observe the people:
whether they are filial toward their parents, and respectful toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders."
When those who observe the precepts and practice giving sent messengers to report their deeds—both good and evil—the messenger respectfully presented the full account.
Upon hearing of evil, he was displeased; upon hearing of good, he rejoiced.
On the fourteenth day, the Four Great Kings constantly dispatch their crown princes to inspect the world;
on the fifteenth day, the Four Heavenly Kings themselves travel through it in person.
Thereafter, they proceed to the Sudharmā Hall and report everything in detail to Śakra.
Hearing of evil brings sorrow, while hearing of good brings joy.

[The Buddha] spoke a verse in praise of those who uphold the precepts of the fast and walk the same path as he. This is recorded in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* and also appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Loutan jing*.
2. The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa, resides at the summit of Mount Sumeru.
There are thirty-three celestial palaces there.
Its king is named Śakra Devendra (in the Liang language, "The Heavenly King Who Can Act"); his body is one yojana in height, and his robes are two yojanas in length.
The garments are two yojanas wide and weigh six zhu.
Their lifespan is one thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
When they are about to die, five signs appear.
First, their garments are soiled and greasy;
second, the flowers upon their heads have withered;
third, their bodies are foul and stinking.
Fourth, sweat flows from beneath his armpits.
Fifth, he finds no joy in his original seat.
When he perceives these five signs, his mind is greatly afflicted with suffering, as if it were the suffering of hell.
Eating, drinking, marriage, and procreation are like the Four Heavenly Kings.

When bodies draw near, they form yin and yang through their breath. The *Chushifa du jing* (Sūtra on the Threefold Dharma Measure) says: "If one indulges in desire with body, speech, and mind as wholesome acts, one will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
By natural transformation, he appeared on the lap of a deva like a three-year-old child;
the deva immediately recognized him, saying,
"This is my son" or "This is my daughter."
They themselves recognize their previous lives of practicing generosity and maintaining the precepts.
Desiring food and drink, they receive vessels filled with gold according to their merit;
for as the blessings are deep or shallow, so too are the foods superior or inferior.
As with the Heaven of the Four Great Kings,
the city measures eighty thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth;
the *Loutan jing* (Sūtra on the Burning of the City) states that it is three million two hundred thousand *li* in width and length, and its city walls are sevenfold.
There are nine hundred and ninety-nine gates,
each guarded by sixty blue-clad yakṣas; the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that they are sixty yojanas high.
Five hundred yojanas apart, there is a gate;
at each gate, five hundred spirits stand guard over the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There are golden walls with silver gates and silver walls with golden gates.
Thus, these seven treasures served as the gates for one another,
with multi-storied pavilions and towers surrounding them on all sides;
gardens, groves, bathing pools, and precious flowers were interspersed throughout.
Rows of precious trees were lined up, their flowers and fruits lush and abundant;
fragrant breezes arose from all sides, gladdening the hearts of men,
while countless birds of diverse species sang in harmonious chorus.
Within each of those four gardens, there are two stone mounds, each fifty yojanas in length and breadth, composed of the seven precious substances and as soft as celestial robes.

As described in the *Loutan jing* (Sutra on the Burning House), the text is largely similar [to other accounts], though it is not recorded here in full due to its prolixity. Between the gardens of Roughness and Delight lies the Nanda Pond.
Extending for a hundred yojanas in both length and breadth, its waters are clear and limpid.
Sevenfold jeweled moats grow with four kinds of flowers:
blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and variegated hues.
Its fragrance permeates everywhere for a distance of one yojana.
Its roots are like the hubs of chariot wheels, its sap is white as milk, and its taste is sweet as honey.
Furthermore, there are various gardens, including the Great Garden of Joy.
In the middle there is a tree named Jambu,
seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height,
with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions.
Its fragrance extends against the wind for a hundred yojanas within.
To the south of the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa gods,
there is another tree named Pārijātaka.
It is four thousand li in height;
its branches and leaves extend for two thousand li.
When the wind blows, the fragrance of its flowers travels against the wind and can be smelled for two thousand li.
When the trees are in bloom, the devas sit together beneath them to enjoy themselves.
They spend one hundred and twenty days wandering about.
Śakra has thirty-two ministers.
Therefore, they are called the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Each has its own palace, all situated within the city.
They sport in the gardens for exactly seven days.
As for those who are coarse and rough, when they enter this garden, their bodies become coarse and rough.
As for those who are painted, when they enter this garden,
their bodies naturally take on various painted colors, with which they find mutual delight.
As for "mixed," it refers to the practice where, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of every month,
he releases his court ladies to roam and play together with the devas;
because he remains alone in one place with Śacī, it is called "mixed."
"When one of great joy enters this garden, the mind experiences immense rapture. This is from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 20;
it also appears in the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The Avataṃsaka and the Nirvāṇa. 3.
Yāma Heaven: the third Yāma Heaven; in the Liang language, "the Heaven of Timely [Delights] Palace."
Supported by the wind-circle, it abides in the midst of space.
Its king is named Śubhakāla; according to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, his body is two yojanas tall, and his garment is four yojanas long and two yojanas wide.
Their garments, weighing three *zhu*, emerge from the trees;
they are bright, pure, and radiant, possessing various colors.
Their bodies emit such brilliance that they have no need for the sun or moon.
Through goodness of body, speech, and mind,
or by giving offerings such as lamps, candles, and bright jewels,
and through the karma of observing the precepts and practicing meditative concentration, one is born in the Yāma Heaven.
The lifespan in that heaven is two thousand years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.

Their food, drink, marriage, and desires are like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The *Sāndhābhāṣya-sūtra* (San-fa-du-jing) states: "One fulfills desire by embracing with a mind of defiled attachment; if there is no deep attachment, there is no pleasure. At birth, their form is like that of a four-year-old human.

The radiance of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven cannot reach it. [This is] from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 20; also from the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra?), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
4. Tuṣita Heaven: The fourth heaven, Tuṣita, which in the Liang language means "Heaven of Contentment" (*Tuṣita-deva-loka*). Its celestial palace is the abode of the gods.
Supported by the wind-wheel, it abides in the midst of space.
Its king is named Subhūṣita.
Bodhisattvas in their final existence are mostly born in this heaven.

Because those in the lower heavens are dissolute and those in the higher heavens are dull-witted, one is born in this heaven. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa*) in the lower stages are thick and turbid;
the fetters and afflictions in the upper stages are sharp."
Only in Tuṣita Heaven is there neither excess nor deficiency; there,
wisdom is secure and at peace.
Furthermore, when those in the lower realms reach the end of their short lives before a Buddha has appeared in the world,
or when those in the higher realms have not yet exhausted their long lifespans as the Buddha has already passed away from Tuṣita Heaven, their lifespans are equal.
Furthermore, the Buddha constantly dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, which is the middle among the six heavens; his body is four yojanas in height,
his robe is eight yojanas in length,
and four yojanas in width.
Their garments weigh one and a half *zhū*.
Their lifespan is four thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
Their food is the same as that of the lower heavens.
There are also those who marry and fulfill their desires by holding hands.
When these devas are first born, they are like five-year-old humans;
they naturally know of the deeds they performed in their previous lives, such as practicing generosity and observing the precepts.
They partake of natural food and drink, wear crowns, and engage in song and dance;

their bodies possess a radiance superior to that of Yama. This is recorded in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, as well as in the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Lokadhātu* (or *Ratnakūṭa*), and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

5. The Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati). The palace of the fifth heaven, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, is likewise supported by a wind-wheel and situated in the midst of space.
Its king is named Sunirmita.
They manifest the five sensory objects by their own power to amuse themselves.
Their bodies are eight yojanas in height,
and their garments are sixteen yojanas in length.
It is eight yojanas wide;
the garments weigh one zhu;
and the lifespan is eight thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The rules for eating are the same as those below.
There are also three methods regarding marriage and sexual intercourse: looking at one another while cooking, and the fulfillment of desire; as the *Sanfadu jing* (Sūtra on the Three Methods) states:
"With a deeply defiled mind..."
If one engages in sexual desire with celestial maidens, it is not accomplished if one is free from defilement;
it is merely pleasure. When that deity is first born, he is like a six-year-old human.
His own radiance is exceptionally superior. [This is] from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, twentieth fascicle, on the departure from Tuṣita.
Furthermore, the *Loutan jing* and the *Huayan jing* state: "The sixth heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven,
is also supported by a wind-wheel and abides in the midst of space."
The king is named Īśvara.
He gathers those he has transformed to amuse himself; they are called the gods who cherish their own bodies (Ātmabhāva-rati-deva).
He alone attains mastery within the desire realm;
his body is sixteen yojanas in height,
and his robe is thirty-two yojanas in length.
It is sixteen yojanas in extent;
the garments weigh half a zhu;
the lifespan is sixteen thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
Their food is like that of the heavens below.
They also have marriage; by merely looking at one another for a moment, desire is fulfilled. The *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) says:
"By mere thought, it is accomplished. The *Sanfadu jing* (Tridharmaka-sūtra) says: [The same].
When the male and female deities become deeply attached to one another and gaze at each other, desire is fulfilled;
if only one is not so attached, it does not constitute fulfillment, being merely a pleasure like that of humans embracing one another.

Because they perceive the emanations of others as if seeing them, they are called "Those Who Delight in the Emanations of Others" (Paranirmita-vaśavartin). When these gods are first born, they resemble seven-year-old humans and possess knowledge of their own past lives.

Because they have abandoned evil through generosity and the observance of precepts, their natural provision of food, drink, clothing, and celestial maidens is identical to what was described previously.
Their radiance is superior, and this describes the Heaven of Delight in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati-deva*). This is from the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
and the *Loutan jing* state:
"The seventh Māra Heaven, the Māra-deva Heaven, is located between the two realms of desire and form."
Māra is like a stone mill;
he grinds away one's meritorious virtues.
It is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
The palace walls are sevenfold,
and all their adornments are like those of the lower heavens;
they possess ten common characteristics.
First, flying away in infinite numbers;
second, flying back in infinite numbers;
third, moving without obstruction.
Fourth, they come without obstruction.
Fifth, their celestial bodies possess no skin, bone, marrow, sinews, veins, blood, or flesh.
Sixth, their bodies are free from impurities such as excrement and urine.
Seventh, the body is free from exhaustion;
eighth, the celestial maidens do not give birth;
ninth, the celestial eyes do not blink.

Tenth, their bodies appear according to their will: if they wish for them to be blue, they appear beautifully blue; if yellow, beautifully yellow; if red, white, or any other color, they manifest as they desire.
These are the ten qualities of the devas.
Furthermore, there are those who maintain these ten matters.
First, the infinity of flying;
second, the infinity of coming and going;
third, the absence of thieves among the various devas.
Fourth, one does not speak of the bodily virtues of others,
nor does one speak of the faults of others.
Fifth, there is no mutual encroachment.
Sixth, the teeth of all devas are even and aligned.
Seventh, his hair is deep blue-black, glossy, and eight zhang long.
Eighth, among the gods and humans, his hair is of this deep blue color.
The body is also blue.
Ninth, if one desires it to be white, the body immediately becomes white.

Tenth, if one desires it to be black, the body immediately becomes black. This is from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle eighteen (or thirty), and also appears in the *Loutan jing* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

2. The Twenty-three Heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). The twenty-three heavens of the Form Realm are as follows: 1. The Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (*brahmakāyika*); 2. The Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (*brahmapurohita*); 3. The Heaven of the Brahma Assembly (*brahmapārṣadya*); 4. The Great Brahma Heaven (*mahābrahmā*); 5. The Heaven of Light (*ābhāsvara*); 6. The Heaven of Limited Light (*parīttābhā*); 7. The Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*apramāṇābhā*); 8. The Heaven of Radiant Sound (*ābhāsvara*); 9. The Pure Heaven (*śubha*); 10. The Heaven of Limited Purity (*parīttaśubhā*); 11. The Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*apramāṇaśubhā*); 12. The Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsnā*); 13. The Adorned Heaven (*bṛhatphala*); 14. The Heaven of Limited Adornment (*parīttaśubha*); 15. The Heaven of Immeasurable Adornment (*apramāṇaśubha*); 16. The Heaven of the Fruit of Adornment (*śubhakṛtsna*); 17. The Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*); 18. The Heaven Free from Affliction (*abṛha*); 19. The Heaven Free from Heat (*atapa*); 20. The Heaven of Good Vision (*sudṛśa*); 21. The Heaven of Great Good Vision (*sudarśana*); 22. The Heaven of the Ultimate Form (*akaniṣṭha*); 23. The Heaven of Maheśvara (*maheśvara*). 1. The Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (*brahmakāyika*). Regarding the first, the palace of the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue: [text continues]
The palace was made of pure gold;
his body was the color of white silver, and all the realms of the form realm were likewise so.
He wore robes of golden hue, practiced dhyāna to become free from desire, and cultivated the fire-light samādhi.
Therefore, their bodies emit a wondrous light surpassing that of the sun and moon;
they are neither male nor female,
and they take the joy of dhyāna as their food.
Their lifespan is one kalpa, though some may have less;
their height is half a yojana, and their lifespan is half a kalpa. (From the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 20.)

2. The Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita). Regarding the second heaven, the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā, its numerical designation is *pūrvakl* (or *purukla*), which is the same as the preceding heaven.
If one cultivates the intermediate dhyāna (*madhyama-dhyāna*), this is the birthplace of the noble Brahmās.
A body one *yojana* in height and a lifespan of one *kalpa*, as recorded in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
3. The Brahmakāyika Heaven; the third [heaven] is the Brahmakāyika Heaven.
It is the same as the previous day.
If one cultivates the lower dhyānas and is born in the various minor Brahma realms,
the body length is one and a half yojanas.
His lifespan is one and a half kalpas; this is recorded in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
4. Mahābrahmā: The fourth [level] is the Great Brahmā King, named Śikhin (translated in the Liang language as "Fire"). He is identical to the aforementioned deity.
If one cultivates the higher dhyānas, one is born here.
Amidst the assembly of the Brahmakāyika devas, one utters a great sound such that there is no one among the entire multitude who does not know it.
The various devas of the Brahma-body each thought to themselves:
"The Great Brahma King converses only with me and does not engage others;
thus, I naturally obtain that which no one else can inherit."
I possess supreme sovereignty over a thousand worlds;
I am wealthy and abundant, capable of creating all things.
I am the father and mother of all sentient beings.
Later, among all the Brahmās, he was the most honored;
his countenance was like that of a youth,
and thus he was named Kumāra (The Youth).
Holding a rooster, bearing a bell, and grasping a red banner while riding upon a peacock—
this is called the Brahmakāyika [Heaven] of the First Dhyāna.
Its palaces are situated distant from the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Palace.

One *yojana* [is the measure] for each successive level. According to the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Huayan*, *Loutan*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are seventeen abodes in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). The lower three *dhyānas* each have three heavens, while the fourth *dhyāna* has nine heavens; thus, there should be eighteen. However, the lowest heaven of the first *dhyāna* is not counted because its inhabitants are the "slaves of the Brahmās. Furthermore, the first *dhyāna* lacks the "Brahma-body," the second lacks "light," and the third lacks "purity."
5. Ābhāsvara Heaven: The fifth heaven is Ābhāsvara.
They take the flavor of dhyāna as their food.
Their lifespan is two kalpas, though some may have less; this is from the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
6. The Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhā devāḥ). Regarding the sixth heaven, Limited Light, it is briefly the same as before.
As stated in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, in the "Chapter on the Vipaśyin Buddha," it says: "When speaking, a slight light issues from the mouth."
7. The Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābhā-deva*). Regarding the seventh heaven, the Heaven of Immeasurable Light, it is largely the same as described previously.
As stated in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, in the "Chapter on Relying" (*Niśraya-varga*), it says: "When they speak, light issues forth from their mouths."

8. The Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven). Regarding the eighth heaven, the Ābhāsvara, the *Yizhipin* (Chapter on the Basis) states: "The deities of the Ābhāsvara Heaven emit pure light from their mouths as they speak; they are called the Infinite Kings. The *Lèguānglóuchán jīng* (Sutra of the Light-Sound Tower and Charcoal) states: "The deities of the Abhāsvara [Heaven] are also called Bodhisattvas, or alternatively, Light-Mind (*Prabhāsmṛti*), or alternatively, Light-Sound (*Prabhāśabda*). They observe the foul odors and noxious vapors of Jambudvīpa."
It perfumes upward for seventy million *li*.

Therefore, Bodhisattvas are not born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; as the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "From a distance of one hundred *yojana* in the heavens, one can smell odors even more acutely than those from a latrine. The Second Dhyāna is collectively named Ābhāsvara (Light-Sound).

There is a palace located one *yojana* away from the Brahmakāyika palace; this is recorded in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, as well as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and the *Bodhisattva Garbhāvakrānti Sūtra*.
9. Śubhakṛtsna Heaven. This is the ninth heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna.
They take the bliss of dhyāna as their food.
Their lifespan is three kalpas, though some may be less. [Cited from] the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 20.
10. The Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttābha). The tenth heaven is the Heaven of Limited Purity. Briefly, it is the same as the preceding [heavens].

According to the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, in the "Chapter on Reliance" (*Niśraya-varga*), it says: "The three heavens collectively practice the dhyāna associated with the bliss of being free from affliction; thus they are born into these three kinds of heavens. By means of a minor degree of application in the dhyāna associated with that [bliss], one is born into the Heaven of Limited Purity, where the bliss experienced is likewise limited."
11. The Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha). The eleventh [heaven], the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity, is briefly the same as the preceding one.
As stated in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, in the "Chapter on Reliance" (*Āśraya-varga*), it says: "By means of intermediate skillful means, one is born in this heaven."

12. Śubhakṛtsna Heaven. Regarding the twelfth heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna, the Sanskrit term is *veśeṣya*. According to the *Yi-pin* (依品), it is said that by means of superior skillful means one is born here; the king of this heaven is named *Jñānaśuddha* (淨智).
Four-armed, holding implements and bearing a wheel,
he rides upon a garuḍa.
The third dhyāna is collectively named "Universal Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna).
It is also called Śuddhāvāsa.

There is a palace located one yojana above the Ābhāsvara Palace. This is recorded in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* and also appears in the *Loutan jing* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
13. Śubhakṛtsna Heaven (The Thirteenth). The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven takes the joy of dhyāna as its sustenance;
its lifespan is forty thousand kalpas, though some may be less. [From the *Dīrgha Āgama*, Scroll 20.]
14. The Heaven of Few Adornments (Parīttābha). The fourteenth heaven, the Heaven of Few Adornments, is roughly the same as the preceding one;
it is excerpted from the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
15. The Heaven of Immeasurable Adornments (Aparimitavyūha-deva). The fifteenth heaven, Immeasurable Adornments, is largely identical to the preceding one;
it is excerpted from the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
16. The Deva Realm of Adorned Fruits. The sixteenth is the Deva Realm of Adorned Fruits.
Its king is named Dharmapadmaprabha. The four dhyānas are collectively termed "fruits."
There is a palace located one *yojana* away from the Palace of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*). This is cited from the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* and also from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Section 17: The Heaven of Non-conception (*Asaṃjñisattva-deva*). Regarding the seventeenth heaven, the *Loutan jing* (Kāraṇḍavyūha-sūtra or similar compendium) states: "In this heaven there is no perception of persons; they take the bliss of meditative concentration as their sustenance."
Their lifespan is five hundred kalpas,
though some may be less,
according to the reckoning of the Form Realm.
The radiance surpasses that of the fruit.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) claim this to be nirvāṇa; as stated in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, in the "Chapter on Reliance" (*Āśrayavarga*), it says: "When perception ceases and non-perception arises, there is only the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and a small portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). When the perception of birth arises, one dies immediately."

18. The Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha), the Eighteenth. Regarding the Heaven of No Affliction, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that there is no creation; the *Lòután jīng* (Ratna-kūṭa Sūtra) states that they are called "Abibei" (Avṛha) because they take the bliss of dhyāna as their food.
Their lifespan is one thousand kalpas, though some may be less;
their radiance surpasses that of those who have emerged from the state of non-conception (asaṃjñisamāpatti). — *Dīrgha Āgama*, Fascicle 20.
19. The Heaven of No Heat (Atapa). In the nineteenth heaven, the Heaven of No Heat, the bodies of the devas are four thousand yojanas in height;
they are so delicate and soft that they lie prostrate upon the ground and cannot stand upright on their own.
If those of lower faculties see the Buddha manifesting in a coarse form and take meditative absorption as their sustenance,
their heavenly lifespan is two thousand kalpas.

There are some who maintain that there is a reduction [in size]. Regarding the fact that the radiance is superior to that of the Avṛha Heaven, it is stated in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

As for the Sudarśana Heaven (the twentieth heaven), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* refers to it as the Sudarśana Heaven, while the *Loutan Jing* states that the bodies of the Sudarśanas are four thousand *yojanas* in height.
They also take the joy of dhyāna as their sustenance.
Their lifespan is three thousand kalpas; according to the *Sanchuan mingshu jing* (Saṃghāṭasūtra), it is four thousand kalpas, though some accounts state it may be less.
Their radiance surpasses that of the Avīci hell; this is recorded in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

21. Mahāsudarśana Heaven. Regarding the Mahāsudarśana Heaven, the twenty-first [chapter], the *Sudarśana-avaivartika-sūtra* states: "The *Loutan jing* says that the height of the Sumeru-candana [deities] is eight thousand yojanas."
They also take the bliss of dhyāna as their sustenance.
Their lifespan is four thousand kalpas; according to the *Sāṃkhyā-nāma-sūtra* of the Triyāna, it is eight thousand kalpas, though there may be some reductions.
Regarding the excellence of their radiance, the *Bhadraśrī-vyūha* appears in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

22. Akaniṣṭha Heaven. Regarding the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the twenty-second [chapter], the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states in the same passage as the *Loutan jing*: "The body of the Akaniṣṭha devas is sixteen thousand yojanas in height."
They also take the bliss of dhyāna as their sustenance.
Their lifespan is five thousand kalpas; according to the *Saṃyuktāgama*, it is sixteen thousand kalpas, though some accounts state it may be less.
These five heavens are collectively known as the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes).
The dwelling place of the various Anāgāmins.

The *Mahāvaipulya-dīrgha-āgama*, fascicle 20, also states that it is the Abode of Light (*Ābhāsvara*). Furthermore, the *Loutan jing* (Kāraṇḍavyūha-sūtra), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* state:
23. The Heaven of Maheśvara. The Heaven of Maheśvara, number twenty-three. Maheśvara; in the Liang language, "Great Sovereign" (*Maheśvara*), also called the Pure Abodes (*Śuddhāvāsa*).
Beyond the five Pure Abodes there are eight realms, all of which are utterly empty and tranquil;
these are the dwelling places of the Mahāsattvas of the ten stages.
Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-cloud stage often act as the kings of these heavens.
His form has eight arms and three eyes, and he rides a great white ox.
Great clouds pour down rain upon the great trichiliocosm;
no sentient beings are able to know its measure.

Only this Heavenly King alone is able to know this. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If a person makes offerings to Maheśvara, one should know that this person has already made offerings to all the devas. The *Loutan Jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) states: "Above the Ābhāsvara Heaven, no king appears. This is recorded in the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
3. The Four Formless Heavens: The third of the four formless heavens is the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana), also called the Heaven of the Wisdom of the Sphere of Space;
its lifespan is ten thousand kalpas.
Some versions slightly abbreviate this, while the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and the *Loutan jing* refer to it as the "Deva of Space-Wisdom" (*ākāśa-jñāna-deva*).
The *Vibhaṅga* refers to it as the "Sphere of Infinite Consciousness" (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), or alternatively as the "Deva of Consciousness-Sphere-Wisdom."
The lifespan in that heaven is twenty-one thousand kalpas;
it may be slightly less. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* and the *Loutan jing* state: "One cognizes the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)."
Some call it the Heaven of the Knowledge of Nothingness;
others call it the Sphere of Nothingness.
Therein is the Utrāsaṇa [Heaven].
Without receiving the Buddha’s transformation, he passed away of his own accord.
The Buddha prophesied that this person would be born in the Place of Non-Action (āsaṃjñika).
Furthermore, if he were to cast off his body and become a king in a borderland who harms the people...
Thereafter, one is born within the hells.
The lifespan of the gods is forty-two thousand kalpas;
some may be slightly less. According to the *Chang-a-han jing* (Dīrgha Āgama) and the *Lou-tan jing* (Lokānuvartana Sūtra), they are called the Ajakāvana devas.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
alternatively called the heaven of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Therein dwells the Brahmakāyika deity.
Without receiving the Buddha’s transformation, he met his end;
the Buddha prophesied that he would be reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception,
but later he would again become a winged, malicious wildcat.
No flying or running beast can escape it;
at the end of life, one is reborn in hell for eighty-four thousand kalpas of celestial lifespan.

Some accounts slightly reduce this number, adding one or two more Āgamas; the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) states: "Above there is a heaven named 'Non-existence,' where there is neither perception nor non-perception."

2. The Formation and Destruction of the Three Realms (Triloka-saṃvarta-vivarta). Chapter Two. I. The Three Minor Calamities (Tṛṇi kṣudra-vipattayaḥ), also known as the Three Minor Kalpas (Tṛṇi kṣudra-kalpāḥ) or the Three Intermediate Kalpas (Tṛṇi antarakalpāḥ). II. The Three Major Calamities (Tṛṇi mahā-vipattayaḥ), also known as the Three Major Kalpas (Tṛṇi mahā-kalpāḥ). 1. The Three Minor Calamities. Regarding the first minor calamity: at the beginning of the kalpa, the lifespan of humans is forty thousand years.
Thereafter, the lifespan gradually decreases until it stops at one hundred years;

eventually, it declines further until it reaches ten years. According to the *Jiaoxin tongxiaojie jing chao* (Excerpts from the Sūtra on the Intermediate Kalpa of Mixed Minds), girls as young as twelve years old and five months are already married off.
The period of ten years is called a "small kalpa" (antarakalpa).
The three calamities are: first, weapons;
second, famine resulting from the depletion of flesh; and third, disease. As stated in the *Dīrgha Āgama*: "Grain becomes expensive [during the famine]."
Regarding the kalpa of weapons:
when people are largely greedy and practice the ten unwholesome deeds,
if anyone performs even a single act of goodness, the multitude will collectively mock and deride them.
They will be deemed foolish and will conspire together to oppress and destroy one another;
they will learn from each other to do evil until not a single person is virtuous.
The five grains will no longer produce fine flavors, and all things will be consumed and destroyed.
Silks, fine fabrics, and cotton cloths will naturally vanish;
they will eat only tares and weeds, and weave grasses for clothing.
The seven treasures will sink away, and sand and stones will fill the land.
The ground sprouts thorns, and both the large and small branches and leaves are all swords; arched wooden structures collapse and fall.
The earth is entirely covered with ditches and pits, with surging waves and crumbling banks.
Rivers and streams gradually widen, while level ground steadily diminishes.
When the calamity of weapons arises for seven days, even the grasses,
trees, tiles, and stones held in their hands will all turn into swords and blades.
They will plunder one another in mutual strife, trembling with fear and desiring only to kill each other.
It is like a hunter who encounters a herd of deer;
among them, one who is wise hides far away in a mountain valley where no humans dwell, subsisting on fruit and drinking water for ten years.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that those who kill one another during the seven days of the *Īśvara-kalpa* when they emerge again into the human world will be reborn in hell.
This is called the kalpa of weapons.
As for the kalpa of famine,
many people act contrary to the Dharma, being ignorant and holding false views.
Driven by stinginess, greed, and envy, they hoard their wealth and do not practice charity.
Rain and drought are irregular, and the crops fail to yield.
As rice and grain are exhausted, the price of even a single morsel of food becomes startlingly high.
They were ordered by Maudgalyāyana to sweep away the chaff and the fallen leaves from the streets and alleys;
once the chaff and leaves were exhausted, they began digging underground to eat the roots of plants and trees.
Those who were unable to keep up died first.
They carve and dismember dead people, then eat them together;
as they devour them, the corpses at the slaughterhouses are completely exhausted,
until they must go so far as to gather various skeletal remains from among the graves.
They boil the broth and drink it to sustain themselves;
those who die of hunger are reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta),
which is called a minor kalpa of famine.
Regarding the kalpa of disease:
all people possess right view and practice the ten wholesome deeds;
although diseases are numerous, they have no other recourse, and medicine is scarce.
Although they have practiced various virtues, they cannot ward off adversity;
because their merit is meager, they die as soon as they fall ill.
Their spirits then come together to harass them, beating and striking them with staves and whips.
They cause their minds to become distracted and seize their vital spirits to kill them and depart.
Once their lives have ended, these people are all reborn in the heavens;
this is called the Kalpa of Disease.
If one can observe the precept against killing for a single day and night,
one will never be born during the kalpa of weapons.
If one gives even a single harītakī fruit as an offering to the Sangha, [one shall not fall into the hells].
One will never be born during an eon of pestilence;
if one gives a single meal to the Sangha,
one will never be born during an eon of famine.
In this Jambudvīpa, the calamities of the degenerate age arise alternately, whereas in other regions they are few;
when the calamity of weapons arises here, there is only intense hatred in those places;
when the calamity of pestilence arises here, there is only physical weakness and debility in those places.
"In this world, an eon of famine arises;

there, however, there is only slight thirst and exhaustion. (Cited from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 22; also cited from the *Saṃkṣipta-tri-saṃvartanī-sūtra*; also cited from the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, fascicle 14).
2. The Three Great Calamities. Second: The Beginning and End of Heaven and Earth is called one *kalpa*.
When the *kalpa* ends and is destroyed, the calamity of fire is about to arise.
All the people turn their backs on the right and face toward the wrong, vying with one another to practice the ten non-virtuous deeds.
Because it has not rained for a long time, what was sown does not grow;
all springs and sources of water,
even the four great swift rivers, have completely dried up.
After a long period of time, the wind enters the ocean floor and seizes the great city of the sun, placing it upon the side of Mount Sumeru within its original course.

Regarding this, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states that at the time of the kalpa’s destruction, seven solar disks remain on Mount Yugandhara and emerge from there; furthermore, it is said that one day is divided into seven days. It is also taught that these emerge from the Avīci Hell due to the karmic power of sentient beings. When a single day emerges:
All the hundred grasses and trees wither and fall at once.
When two suns appear,
the waters of the four great oceans recede by a hundred yojanas.
Even within a distance of seven hundred yojanas,
the water naturally dries up.
When three suns appear, [the same occurs].
The waters of the four great oceans,
within a range of one thousand yojanas up to seven thousand yojanas,
gradually dry up and vanish.
When four suns appear,
the four great oceans, which are one thousand yojanas deep, [dry up].
When five suns appear, [the oceans dry up completely].
The four great oceans, measuring more than seven hundred yojanas in extent,
will eventually be completely exhausted when the six suns appear.
This earth, sixty-eight thousand yojanas thick, all emits smoke,
extending from Mount Sumeru as far as the trichiliocosm.
And the eight hells were all incinerated until not even smoke or ash remained;
when the people’s lives ended, they all took refuge upon Mount Sumeru.
The five classes of devas:
the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma heaven,
and so on, up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven.
All have reached the end of their lives, and the palaces are entirely empty;
all things are impermanent and cannot endure for long.
When the seven suns appear, [the world shall be consumed].
The great earth and Mount Sumeru gradually crumble and collapse;
for a hundred yojanas, nothing remains.
All things such as gold, silver, copper, and iron are completely melted away.
As it was consumed, it dried up completely; the mountains were all set ablaze.
The various jewels burst and shattered with a thunderous roar, and the smoke and flames shook as far as the Brahma Heaven.
All the evil realms and the asuras were entirely swept away.
Those whose sins have ended and whose merit has arrived all gather in the fifteenth heaven;
those from the fourteenth heaven downward all become flaming ink.
The newly born deva-son, having never before seen this, is filled with universal fear.
The long-established devas each came to console him, saying:
"Do not give rise to fear; you shall never come to such a state as this.
When people’s lives end, they are reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, where they take thought as their sustenance."
They illuminate themselves with light and travel through the air by means of supernatural power;
they may be reborn in other lands or in the hells,
and once their karmic retribution in hell is exhausted, they are reborn in the heavens.
Even if their retribution is not yet exhausted, they may be reborn in the heavens.
If their retribution is still not finished, they are further transferred to another realm where there is neither sun, moon, nor stars, and no day or night;
there is only great darkness, known as the fire-kalpa conflagration.
Due to the retribution of causes and conditions, this destruction occurs.
When the kalpa is about to be formed, the fire naturally extinguishes itself.
Then, great clouds arise again, gradually releasing heavy rain with drops as large as axle-trees.
At that time, this trichiliocosm is filled with water reaching up to the Brahma-heaven.

The *Miśrakābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states that it is destroyed by the calamity of water; the water falls from the third dhyāna down to the second dhyāna. It is further explained that the water-wheel emerges, which is called the "water kalpa" or the "calamity of water."
Furthermore, there are four winds that sustain the water so that it does not disperse:
the first is named Abiding,
and the second is called Assisting.
The third is called Immovable;
the fourth is called Firm.
This lasts for many thousands of billions of years.
The foam upon the water transforms into the celestial palaces of the Four Great Kings, numbering one thousand, all composed of various jewels.
As the waters gradually recede and are driven by the winds,
they successively transform into the palaces of the various devas of the world, as well as those of the sun and the moon.
Next, one visualizes a thousand Mount Sumerus,
proceeding in sequence until a thousand sets of four continents, with their mountains,
rivers, cities, and moats, and the waters all pure and clear.
When the celestial palaces were first created, they were composed of various jewels;
their radiance was most supreme, but it gradually diminished and grew turbid.
The light of the seven-jeweled palaces of the devas likewise gradually descended and became inferior.
When the earth was exposed, the waters and sands flowed with great force;
rushing downward and competing to flow together, they eventually formed rivers that entered the ocean, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep.

Its breadth is boundless; the *Loutan jing* states that it is eight hundred and forty thousand *yojanas* deep, and Mount Sumeru stands within the ocean, rising eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the sea.
The taste of the water was salty and bitter.
At the time when the kalpa first formed, clouds arose spontaneously reaching as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
raining down everywhere to wash the celestial palaces.
It washes away all impurities from the myriad things;
flowing downward into the ocean, it makes it salty and bitter.
Furthermore, there is a great seer (maharṣi).
Through incantations, it is made salty and bitter so that people will not drink it.
Furthermore, various kinds of sentient beings dwell therein;
because they void their excrement within it, it becomes salty and bitter.

This refers to the wind-aeon and the calamity of wind; the *Miśrakābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states that what is destroyed by the calamity of wind reaches up to the third dhyāna. When ten billion sets of the four continents are simultaneously destroyed, these three [calamities] along with the earth constitute the four calamities and the four aeons.
Excluding the earth element, the remaining three are said to constitute a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
As for the kalpa that transcends the earth element,
it refers to the extent of the kalpa’s destruction.
Only those who have not yet reached the fourth dhyāna can be reborn among the Śuddhāvāsa deities;
there is no higher stage from which such a birth can occur.
He attains parinirvāṇa in that very place and does not descend again;
because the aeon has not yet diminished, it transforms into heaven and earth.
Heaven and earth begin anew, vast and utterly empty.
It was utterly devoid of anything, and there were neither sun nor moon.
From the earth, sweet springs welled up, their flavor like ghee and honey.
At that time, the devas of Ābhāsvara [descended].
Some, their merit exhausted, come to be born there;
others, delighting in new lands and being by nature flighty and impulsive, taste it with their fingers.
Thus, after doing so two or three times, they come to know its flavor.
As they ate this incessantly, their coarse flesh gradually grew;
they lost their celestial beauty, their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and their radiant light, falling into a profound and total darkness.
Subsequently, a great black wind blew upon the waters of the ocean, casting forth the sun and the moon.
Placed at the edge of Mount Sumeru and situated within the path of the sun, it circles Mount Sumeru to illuminate the four continents.
At that time, when people see it emerge, they rejoice; when they see it enter, they are struck with fear.
From this point onward, the cycles of day and night,
the new and full moon, the seasons,
and the years suddenly began anew.
Those who ate much were reborn with ugly countenances,
while those who ate little still retained their exquisite beauty; thus,
distinctions between the beautiful and the ugly gradually arose.
Arrogance and envy arise in succession;
anger, resentment, contention, and rivalry continue without interruption.
The sweet spring dries up of its own accord, and manure grows upon the earth.
Its flavor was fragrant and exquisite, as if it were nectar (*amṛta*).
At that time, the sentient beings again ate it together;
those who ate much of it suddenly lost their majestic radiance, and their flesh was replaced by bone.
Those who eat little have light bodies and no burdens, such that they can even fly;
those who are heavy, upon seeing them, all wail and weep loudly,
crying out, "I am in dire straits, dwelling in this world!"
Contentious disputes and litigation became twice as severe as under the previous laws.
They subsisted on the essence of the earth and observed one another’s complexions;
those with excessive lustful desires were transformed into women.
Becoming mutually attached, they subsequently engaged in sexual desire; thus it spread.
The other gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven saw that all the sons of heaven had fallen.
They came together and reviled them, saying,
"Why do you practice impure conduct?
The earth's fertility has entered into the soil, and wild rice grows of its own accord."
It was fresh, pure, and skinless, both fragrant and delicious;
those who ate it became plump and fair-skinned. When harvested in the morning, it grew back by evening.
As people gradually became indolent, they began to harvest it for many days at once.
They indulged their passions and desires to the utmost, regardless of the proper seasons;
when women became pregnant and gave birth to sentient beings,
others would see them and immediately drive them away or banish them.
He was sent outside the city for three months, after which he was permitted to return.
Having realized his shame and remorse, he consulted with others on a suitable course of action;
they gathered various grasses and trees and constructed a palace and dwellings.
They concealed their bodies so that others would not see them;
as they indulged in sexual desire, it increased further and further,
and they gathered large quantities of grain to serve as provisions.
When the rice plants exhibit such signs of decay and become overgrown with weeds,
and the husks and chaff begin to grow so that the grain no longer sprouts after being harvested,
sentient beings see this and their minds are filled with great distress.
When great calamities befell the world and the non-glutinous rice was no longer as it had been,
each thought to themselves:
"When I was first born, I took mindfulness as my food."
Possessing the supernormal power of flight, they were self-illuminated with light;
yet, remaining in this state of indolence until the present day,
they again said to one another:
Now, the land was divided and boundary markers were established separately;
thus did the demarcation of borders begin.
From that time on, people began to hide their own portions and steal the grain and rice of others.
The rice owner saw him and said, "I now pardon your offense; do not do it again.
Thus, as [the offenses] increased, he rebuked him with ever-increasing severity.
Rebuking him incessantly, he seized him with his hand and announced to the crowd,
"This man is a thief."
The thief spoke again, saying,
"This man struck me.
When the crowd saw this, they were filled with sorrow and distress.
They all gathered together and deliberated, saying:
"Sentient beings are turning toward evil; this is the source of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Through afflictions and the retribution of suffering, they fall into the three evil realms."
"Because of these fields, this dispute has arisen.
Now, it would be best for us to collectively appoint one person of intelligence and high talent as our leader,
so that he may protect those who ought to be protected according to the principles of the Dharma."
Those who deserve reprimand shall be reprimanded;
those who should be sent away shall be sent away.
We must gather rice together to provide for one another.
They chose one who was wise, of upright form,
and possessed of majestic virtue, and said to him: "Be our impartial lord."
With these kind words of consolation, the assembly was filled with joy,
and they all exclaimed together:
"Excellent, Great King!"
One who governs the people by means of the True Dharma is called a Kṣatriya;
this is entirely the ancient law.
Later, when people encroached upon the property of others, they were immediately punished.
When such offenses were committed repeatedly, guards and wardens were established.
Even with whips and staves, the transgressions could not be stopped; thus, prisons, swords, and clubs were further created.
Reflecting on the slaughter and killings in Chu, he was filled with fear.
At that time, there was a man who thought of his household as being full of afflictions, like poisonous thorns;
he abandoned his wife and children and dwelt alone in the mountain forests.
They would arise and dwell in grass huts to quiet their wills and cultivate the holy life; these were called *brāhmaṇas*.
Later, among the *brāhmaṇas*, there were those who did not delight in seclusion, sitting in meditation, or contemplation.
He then entered among human beings, making the recitation and study of scriptures his primary occupation.
Furthermore, he declared of himself:
"I am one who does not practice dhyāna."
Consequently, the people of the world called them "non-meditating brahmins.
At that time, among sentient beings, there were those who delighted in managing household affairs and accumulated much wealth and treasure; they were called "householders" (gṛhapati).
Furthermore, there are many who possess great skill and ingenuity,
known as śūdras; and there are others who,
out of self-loathing for the ways of the world, shave their hair and beards, don religious robes, and cultivate the Way.
They were called śramaṇas;
at that time, people harbored thoughts of killing and stealing,
and furthermore, they lost their non-glutinous rice.
Five types of seeds are established:
first, root-seeds; second, leaf-seeds.
Third, those produced from flowers;
fourth, those produced from fruits;
fifth, those produced from stems and other types of seeds.
These are called the five kinds of seeds;
they are all seeds from other lands blown here by the wind to save the sentient beings of this country.
Such are these auspicious omens.
There is birth, old age, sickness, and death;
there are the five aggregates of clinging,
and one does not reach the end of suffering.
At the end of the kalpa of water, the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven enter the water to bathe.
The vital essence of the four great elements enters their bodies;
physical pleasure arises within them as the vital fluid flows into the water.
Swept away by the eight winds, she fell into the mud.
There, she spontaneously became an egg which remained for eight thousand years before finally opening to give birth to a woman.
Its form is blue-black, like muddy silt.
It has nine hundred and ninety-nine heads,
a thousand eyes, and nine hundred and ninety-nine mouths.
In each mouth he has four fangs from which fire issues forth like thunderbolts;
his twenty-four hands all grasp every kind of weapon;
his body is as tall and massive as Mount Sumeru.
She entered the great ocean and took delight in splashing the water.
A whirlwind blew upon the waters of the great ocean,
and as the water-essence entered her body, she immediately became pregnant.
After eight thousand years had passed, a son was born.
His body was four times taller and more magnificent than his mother's;
the boy had nine heads, each with a thousand eyes, and fire issued from his mouths.
He had nine hundred and ninety-nine hands and eight feet;
in the midst of the ocean waters,
he proclaimed himself, "I am Vemacitra, the King of the Asuras."
They subsist only on mud and lotus roots.

Such was the transformation at the beginning of the kalpa; this appears in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 32, as well as in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 6, the *Kṣudrakavastu-kalpa*, and the second fascicle of the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi*. When the kalpa is consumed by fire, everything becomes empty.
By the power of the causes and conditions of the merit of sentient beings,
winds from the ten directions arrive and follow one after another, able to sustain the great waters.
Above [the waters] is a being with a thousand heads and two thousand hands and feet.
The one named Viśvabhu has a thousand-petaled golden lotus flower grow from his navel;
its light is brilliantly radiant like ten thousand suns shining,
and within the flower sits a person in the full lotus posture.
This person further possesses immeasurable light,
known as the Brahmā King.
He has just fathered eight sons.
The eight sons gave birth to heaven, earth, and the people;
this is the Brahmā Heavenly King,
whose lust and anger are already exhausted, sitting upon a lotus flower.
The Buddhas, conforming to worldly custom,
appear seated cross-legged upon precious lotus flowers and preach the six pāramitās.

Suppose there were a city measuring one hundred yojanas on each side, filled with mustard seeds.
A long-lived person, reaching a hundred years of age,
were to take out a single mustard seed every hundred years until all were exhausted.
The kalpa would still not be exhausted.
Furthermore, it is like a stone measuring one hundred yojanas in each dimension,
which one might wrap in the light and soft cloth of Kāśī.
If one were to sweep this rock once every hundred years until it was completely worn away, the kalpa would still not have ended;
this is what is called a *mahākalpa*.
Furthermore, it is said:
It is one yojana square, and its height and depth are likewise.
A single iron city is filled with mustard seeds;
taking out one seed every hundred years until they are all exhausted constitutes one kalpa.
Furthermore, suppose there were a rocky mountain one yojana in extent,
and a man were to brush it once every hundred years with a cloth from Kāśī;
by brushing it incessantly, that rocky mountain would eventually be worn away entirely.
The kalpa has not yet ended;
one thought-moment out of sixty thought-moments is called a *paramāṇu-kalpa* (extremely small kalpa).
This is cited from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 36; also from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 31; also from [the same], fascicle 28; and also from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 34.
4. Every day for four days, he built city walls.
They were square, measuring two thousand forty li on each side, and their height was likewise.
When its light strikes the human eye, it appears as a circle.
The palace city is made of pure gold and the seven treasures, brilliant and exquisite, free from all blemish.
It is sustained by five winds.
First, upholding;
second, nurturing;
third, receiving.
There are four revolutions and five adjustments.
The square of the sun-king’s throne measures twenty *li*.
From his body issued forth a radiance that illuminated the palace;
the light of the palace shone upon the city walls;
and the light from the city walls descended upon the lands below.
Countless devas preceded and followed him as attendants,
providing entertainment with music that never ceased;
the groves, pavilions, and bathing pools were like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The lifespan of the gods there is five hundred years;
their descendants succeed one another until the end of a kalpa.
The city of the sun revolves around Mount Sumeru.
In the east, the sun rises;
in the south, it is midday;
in the west, it is midnight.
In the north, the sun sets;
thus, by revolving to the right, it constitutes day and night,
which further vary in length.
As the sun moves slightly southward, the southern [hemisphere] gradually lengthens;
after traveling sixty *li*,
over the course of one hundred and eighty days, the northern [hemisphere] gradually shortens.
Furthermore, as the sun moves slightly northward, the northern day becomes slightly longer;

for one hundred and eighty days it is thus, while the southern day becomes slightly shorter. This is recorded in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* and also appears in the *Loutan jing*.
The city of Yueyue is located five months' journey away.
It is one thousand nine hundred and sixty li in width and length;
its height is likewise the same.
It is solemn and square, and because it sees afar, it is circular.
Two parts are made of heavenly silver and one part of lapis lazuli;
it is pure and transparent inside and out, with its brilliant light shining far and wide.
Supported by five winds,
the Moon King sits within a square palace of seven precious jewels measuring twenty li.
It is preceded and followed by the radiance of immeasurable devas and the sounds of music and dance.
His gardens, ponds, and other amusements were like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
his celestial lifespan was five hundred years,
and his descendants succeeded one another until the end of an eon.
The moon undergoes waning and waxing.
When it is deficient, one corner moves through the night, gradually becoming obscured and tilted; therefore, it appears diminished.
Furthermore, it is said:
Beside the city wall of the moon there is a deity whose complexion is pure blue and whose garments are also blue;
because the blue light from his face shines upon the city, it is thus diminished and incomplete.
When full, the moon’s course gradually turns toward the right.
Furthermore, on the fifteenth day, the blue-colored deity enters the lunar city and meets with the King.
Moreover, to the south of Mount Sumeru, there is a great tree.
The tree is named Jambūdvīpa;

it is four thousand *li* high, with branches and foliage covering two thousand *li*, and its reflection appears within the moon. This is recorded in the second volume of the *Dīrgha Āgama* (*Cháng āhán jīng*) and also in the *Lóutàn jīng*.
During solar and lunar eclipses, there is an asura king named Rāhu.
His body is twenty-eight thousand li in height;
on the fifteenth day of the month, he stands in the center of the ocean.
The seawater rose only to his navel.
He lowered his head and gazed upon Mount Sumeru, the Jewel Mountain,
which stands as a sovereign over the four directions above.
If one were to cover the sun and moon with their fingers, the world would become dark and gloomy;
or by covering the sun, day would be turned into night.
This refers to the time of solar and lunar eclipses when the brilliant light is obscured. (From the *Loutan jing*, scroll five.)
6. The Six Star Constellations are the city-walls of the celestial deities' abodes.
They have crystal for their walls and the seven treasures for their palaces.
Suspended in mid-air, it is held by great winds like a floating cloud;
it moves along with the sun and is visible to the eye.
The largest is seven hundred li in circumference.
The middle [size] is five hundred *li*, and the smallest is one hundred and twenty *li*.
Their palaces, halls, gardens, and ponds are like those of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and their lifespans are likewise.
This is from the sixth fascicle of the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra), and also appears in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
7. Regarding the seventh [element], thunder in the midst of the clouds of space:
at times the earth element comes into contact with water;
at times it comes into contact with the great elements of fire, wind, and so forth.
The great elements of water, fire, and wind strike against one another, all producing the sound of thunder within the clouds of empty space; this is from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 20.
8. Lightning: There are four kinds of lightning.
In the east is named Kāyaprabha; in the south, Durdharṣa;
and in the west, Jvālāprabha.
In the north, it is named "Stable Radiance.
Why is there this lightning-light within the clouds of space?
Furthermore, the lightnings of the four directions strike against one another.
This light arises from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 20.
9. Clouds: There are four kinds of clouds.
First, white.
Second, black;
third, crimson;
fourth, red.
The white [color] indicates that the earth element is predominant;
the black [color] indicates that the water element is predominant;
the red [color] indicates that the fire element is predominant.
Those that are red have a predominance of the wind element;
they are located ten, twenty, or thirty *li* above the earth.
Extending even for forty *li*.

With the exception of the beginning of the kalpa, when [clouds] rise as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven, they appear in four colors, as stated in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*: first, blue; second, yellow;
third, red; and fourth, white.
Second, red;
third, yellow-white;
fourth, black.
That which is blue has a predominance of the water element within it;
that which is red has a predominance of the fire element within it;
and that which is yellowish-white has a predominance of the earth element within it.
Regarding the black [clouds], the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra), fascicle four, states that the breath of the dragons forms clouds. From the *Cháng āhán jīng* (Dīrgha-āgama), Sūtra 10, "The Winds":
When the ten worlds are destroyed by wind, a great wind arises named "Destruction and Scattering."
It is capable of blowing apart, destroying, and annihilating the great trichiliocosm,
as well as all things such as the vajra-circled mountains (cakravāḍa).
At that time, outside the great trichiliocosm...
Furthermore, there is a wind named "Obstructing Dispersion" (*āvaraṇa-vināśana*) which can block the wind-disaster so that it reaches other regions; were it not for this obstructing wind,
[the disaster would otherwise prevail].
In the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, there is none that does not disperse and perish. This concludes the thirtieth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
11. Rain and the Eleven Signs of Rain; the Master Divines the Rain.
There are five causes and conditions that cannot be definitively known,
which cause diviners to be confused.
First, when clouds are accompanied by thunder and lightning, the diviner predicts that it will rain.
First, because the fire is excessive, it burns the clouds so that they do not rain.
Second, when there are thunder and lightning in the clouds, divination also predicts rain;
however, a great wind arises and blows the clouds apart, scattering them into the midst of the mountains.
Third, when clouds are accompanied by thunder and lightning, divination likewise predicts rain;
at such times, the asuras seize the floating clouds and place them within the great ocean.
Fourth, when clouds are accompanied by thunder and lightning, divination likewise predicts rain.
Yet the Rain Master was arrogant and licentious, and ultimately failed to send down rain.
Fifth, when clouds are accompanied by thunder and lightning, diviners likewise predict rain;
yet the sentient beings of the world act contrary to the Dharma with reckless abandon, defiling pure conduct.
Because of stinginess, greed, jealousy, and inverted views, the heavens are caused not to send down rain.
These five matters are known through their varying characteristics; they appear in the twentieth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* and are identical to those in the *Loutan jing*.
The Dragon King Anavatapta raised a vast and heavy cloud that filled Jambudvīpa, and a great rain fell everywhere,
causing all the hundred grains, grasses, and trees to flourish and grow.
The rivers, streams, and marshes were all completely filled.
This great rainwater issued from the body and mind of the Dragon King, benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.
The Dragon King Mānasvin was about to let fall the rain.
First, heavy clouds arose and completely covered the void;
out of compassion, they remained suspended for seven days,
first allowing sentient beings to bring all their karmic actions to completion.
A gentle rain gradually falls, universally moistening the great earth. *Dīrgha Āgama*, Volume 20. *Scriptures and Vinaya:

Section on Devas (2). The Dharma of King Śakra Receiving the Precepts from a Jackal. 1. King Śakra Receiving the Precept of Non-Retaliation.

1. Asuras attack [the heavens] followed by the five bonds; the two Śakras are reborn as donkeys, perish from the womb, and return to their original forms. 2. The Trisittiri deva-putra’s previous life of giving; the Four Sun and Moon Kings inquire about their past conduct. 3. The life of the Trāyastriṃśa devas nearing its end; seven omens appear, and meeting the Buddha, they attain birth among humans. 4. A celestial maiden’s hand produces sweet water to save five hundred merchants. 5. A deva-putra of the Thirty-three Heavens was destined for rebirth as a pig, but turned instead toward the human path. 6. A celestial maiden sits upon a flower; all the necessities of life emerge from the flower. 7. A precious maiden speaks in secret. 8. Ten celestial maidens hear a deer and an ox playing the lute; they descend and all sing and dance. 9. Śakra receives the precepts from a jackal. **Śakra Receives the Precepts from a Jackal (1)** Once, in the kingdom of Pimā, on Mount Tuo, there was a jackal. It said to Śakra: "O Great King, you have long enjoyed the pleasures of the heavens, yet you have not yet received the precepts. You must now receive them. Śakra replied: "I am a king of the gods; how can I receive the precepts from a beast? The jackal said: "If you do not receive them from me, you shall fall from the heavens and be reborn as a dog. Śakra then asked: "What is the method for receiving the precepts? The jackal replied: "First, one must abandon the ten unwholesome paths of action. Second, one must practice the ten wholesome paths of action. Third, one must cultivate the four immeasurable minds. Fourth, one must practice the six perfections. Fifth, one must seek the three jewels. Sixth, one must respect one's parents. Seventh, one must honor teachers and elders. Eighth, one must give alms to the poor. Ninth, one must protect the Dharma. Tenth, one must maintain a mind of compassion. Śakra then accepted these teachings and received the precepts from the jackal. Having received the precepts, he returned to the heavens and ruled over the gods with righteousness. Because of this, his lifespan increased and his merit grew. Thus, one should know that even a lowly beast can bestow the precepts; how much more so a Buddha or a noble person! Therefore, one should always respect and uphold the precepts. This is called "Śakra Receives the Precepts from a Jackal. Chased by a lion, he fell into a lonely well in the wilderness.
Having already been there for three days, his heart was exposed and he was on the verge of death.
He spoke these verses himself:
All things are impermanent; it is a regret that one did not feed the lion.
Alas for this body of karmic retribution! To crave life in vain and die in vain is already regrettable;
furthermore, it defiles the waters of the human realm.
I repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions; May they deign to illumine my mind.
All evil karma from past lives, I now repay so that it may be entirely exhausted.
From this point on, meeting with enlightened teachers, I shall practice until all become Buddhas.
When Śakra heard this, he followed the eighty thousand devas to search for their location, flying to the side of the well and saying:
"We have not heard the holy teachings for a long time; it has been dark and we have had no guide."
"You have just spoken words that are not those of ordinary men; I pray you will proclaim the teachings of the Dharma.
He replied, "Devendra, there are no such instructions."
He was greatly ignorant of propriety;
while the Dharma Master remained below, he placed himself above him and did not initially offer any respect.
He then asked for the essentials of the Dharma.
Śakra lowered a celestial robe to receive him; the jackal prostrated itself and repented.
The Heavenly Emperor said:
I recall that in the past, when I saw people of the world wishing to hear the True Dharma,
they would first prepare a high seat, adorning it with purity, and then invite the Dharma Master. Thereupon,
the various devas would each remove their celestial jewel robes and pile them up to form a high seat.
The jackal ascended the seat and said:
"There are two great causes and conditions:
first, because preaching the Dharma to transform and enlighten devas and humans brings forth immeasurable merit."
"Secondly, because it would be a repayment for the kindness of being given food, how could one not speak?
The Heavenly Lord said:
'The merit and retribution for escaping the calamity of the well are indeed great.'"
Why is it that repaying the kindness of preaching the Dharma does not equal this?
The answer is:
such is the proper way of life and death.
Each has its own people: some crave life,
while others delight in death.
There are foolish people who do not know that one is reborn after death;
they remain far removed from the Buddha-dharma.
Failing to encounter an enlightened teacher,
they commit killing, stealing, sexual misconduct,
and deception, yielding only to evil.
Such a person craves life and fears death;
upon dying, they fall into hell.
A person of wisdom serves the Triple Gem and encounters an enlightened teacher.
Abandoning evil and cultivating goodness;
filially supporting one's parents;
and reverently serving one's teachers and elders.
His retinue is harmonious and compliant;
he is humble and respectful toward all things. Such a person as this—
He took pleasure in death and feared life;
upon his death, he was reborn in the heavens. Śakra said:
As Your Reverence has instructed,
I shall preserve my life and limb;
there is no need for further effort.
"I wish to hear about the giving of food and the giving of the Dharma.
The jackal replied,
"As for the giving of food and drink..."
By providing precious objects, one relieves the lack of a single lifetime; by providing them for a day,
one relieves the need for a single day.
Increasing birth and death,
and through the causes and conditions of bondage,
he preaches the Dharma to teach and transform beings.
This is called the gift of Dharma.
It enables sentient beings to enter the supramundane path;
first, they attain arhatship.
Second, the pratyekabuddhas;

These are the three types of people who delight in [this].
All [attain this] by hearing the Dharma and practicing according to what has been taught.
Furthermore, all sentient beings...
To escape the three evil realms and receive the blessings and joys of humans and devas—

Therefore, the Buddha said:
"The merit of giving the Dharma as a gift is immeasurable."
The Heavenly Emperor said,

"Is it a response-body or an emanation-body? He replied,
