"It is not a manifestation through transformation. The deva said,

This Bodhisattva, a holy being who manifests to save sentient beings,
has only now heard of the fruits of his transgressions;
he does not yet know the reason for this.
"I wish to hear the causes and conditions.
The jackal said,
"In the past, I was born in the city of Padmāvatī in Vārāṇasī."
He was the son of a poor family,
born of the Kṣatriya caste;
from his youth, he possessed keen intelligence.
He was exceptionally fond of learning.
By the time he reached the age of twelve,
he followed a learned master.
Remaining in the deep mountains,
he served [the Buddha] with hardship and toil,
remaining diligent and untiring.
The teacher also, day and night,
refined and instructed him,

Over the course of fifty years,
he mastered ninety-six types of scriptures, prophecies, and treatises.
Medical prescriptions and incantations;
divining good and bad fortune through physiognomy;
and portending calamities, anomalies, misfortunes, and blessings.
There was nowhere he did not penetrate;

He then reflected to himself:

The merit [of this] is difficult to repay;

I subsist by begging for alms;

"Is the merit of his teaching not sufficient to repay my kindness? Having said this,
he remained in the mountains.
He sustained himself by begging for alms.
Not long after, the king passed away.
The ministers assembled more than five hundred scholars from within the kingdom.
They debated for seven days;
the victor was to become king,
yet he was the son of a poor family.
He enjoyed the royal throne and,

Later, the kingdom of Andhra and the kingdom of Mālava waged mutual warfare for many years,

King Andhra summoned his ministers and asked,

He reached the country of Mālava.
The ministers replied,

The king was born into a humble and lowly station;

Although there were palace women,

Young, handsome, and able to please the heart,

He immediately followed the minister’s plan and presented everything at once.
The king was greatly delighted.

Only then did he realize it was superior;

He was indulgent in luxury, lewdness, and pleasure,
neglecting the affairs of state; thus, the hundred officials and the various ministers [were left without direction].
They joined together in rebellion;
the sons of virtuous commoners were plundered and made into slaves.
Wind and rain do not come at their proper times;
hunger fills the roads;
and hostile enemies from foreign lands [arise].
They subsequently came to invade and plunder;

Born into the hells,
they undergo manifold agonies; yet,

He personally recollected his past lives;

In a brief moment, his life ended and he was reborn among the hungry ghosts;
he then further offered repentance and prostrations.
Having cultivated mindfulness of the ten wholesome actions,
he relinquished his life in an instant and received the body of a jackal.
Still mindful of his former conditions,
he again practiced the ten wholesome deeds;
then he encountered a lion.
Having fallen into this well,
his heart was torn apart and he was on the verge of death;

Because you received me,
my original vow has been violated;
only now am I undergoing this hardship.
"When shall I be delivered?
For this reason I say:
you have saved my life."
"It required no effort.
The reason I was able to enter the robe and emerge from it is simply that I did not violate my heavenly vow."
When one's aspirations are not fulfilled,
one gives rise to great suffering and distress,
and inflicts suffering and distress upon others.
First, wherever they are born, their prayers and aspirations remain unfulfilled;
second, they desire to hear the Dharma from the various devas.
If a person is stingy with the Dharma,
in every life they are born deaf, blind, or mute.
Their faculties are obstructed;
they are born in the borderlands,
dull-witted and ignorant.
Even if one is born in a favorable realm,
if one's faculties and consciousness are dull and obtuse,
what one studies will not be accomplished.
First, they bring about suffering and affliction for themselves;
second, they act as a medium for the transformation through the Dharma,
awakening devas and humans.
This is itself the gift of Dharma.
The benefit of the gift of Dharma is that it enables sentient beings to know that death gives rise to birth.
By performing good, one obtains blessings;
by committing evil, one suffers calamity;
by cultivating the Way, one attains the Way.
Born from the turning [of the wheel],
their wisdom is clear and lucid,
and they constantly know their past lives.
If born in the heavens,
one becomes a teacher for the devas;
if born among humans, [one becomes a teacher for humanity].
He becomes a Golden Wheel-turning King,
transforming the world through the ten virtuous paths.
The light of his wisdom gradually increases.
They accomplish the bodhisattva practices and reach the stage of the patience of non-arising;
their giving of material wealth is like a lamp.
It merely clarifies the small chamber;
the Dharma-gift is like the sun shining afar upon the world.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with eighty thousand devas, received the ten wholesome dharmas.
First, one should subdue the various faculties by means of the ten skillful methods—
namely, the six pāramitās and loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
At that time, a deity asked:
"Now I am returning to the celestial palace.

The jackal replied:

Furthermore, he recollected his past lives and practiced the ten paths of wholesome action;

4. The Former Life of the Devaputra Śveta: The Former Life of the Devaputra Śveta’s Generosity. At four times, the Devaputra Śveta addressed the Buddha, saying:
In a past life, I was a king named Śivirī.
I bestowed gifts everywhere at the four city gates to cultivate merit,
and I also gave alms at every crossroads within the city.
Then the first wife said, "The King has performed great meritorious deeds, yet I was there before him. The King replied,
"Whatever merit you have gained through giving and performing meritorious acts outside the eastern gate of the city all belongs to you."
The sons spoke again, saying,
"Whatever merit was produced by acts of giving outside the southern gate of the city all belongs to you.
At that time, a high minister addressed the king once more, saying:
"The merit from the acts of giving performed outside the western city gate all belongs to you.
Then the generals and soldiers spoke again to the king, saying,
"We shall share [the merit] together outside the northern city gate."
Then the common people spoke again to the king.
The king replied,
"The merit from the acts of giving performed at the crossroads within this city belongs entirely to you."
At that time, the king, his queen, the ministers, the soldiers, and the common people all practiced giving.
Regarding all the merits previously performed by me,
my merit from giving has now been exhausted here.
At that time, those who had performed meritorious deeds under my direction returned to me, prostrated before me, and addressed me, saying: "Great King,
you should know that among those who cultivate merit— whether they be queens, princes, ministers, military officers, or commoners— "
Each person, occupying their respective place, performed acts of giving and cultivated merit;
thus, the Great King’s giving was brought to an end here.
At that time, I replied:
"The annual tribute due from all quarters should be brought in.
Of my portion, half shall enter the treasury and half shall be bestowed as alms there.
In this way, through such long-term giving, I have always obtained desirable and pleasing karmic rewards."
They constantly experience happiness without end.
By means of the retribution of this meritorious karma, they enter the great mass of merit,
just as the five great rivers merge into a single current.
It is said that no one can measure the Ganges River;
its volume of water, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of *dou* and *ji*,
and the karmic fruits and rewards of its merit are likewise beyond measure.
They all attained entry into the great mass of merit.

At that time, the devaputra Siviṃli, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, prostrated at his feet, and immediately vanished from sight. This concludes the *Siviṃli-devaputra-buddhagāthā-sūtra*.

On the fifth day, the Heavenly King of the Sun and Moon asked about their movements; on the fifth day, the Heavenly King of the Sun and Moon, accompanied by countless devas, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, and said:
By what conduct does one become the Sun Deity who illuminates the four continents?
Furthermore, by what conditions does one become the Moon Deity who illuminates and dispels the darkness of night?
The Buddha said:
There are four matters:
first, always delighting in giving;
second, cultivating the person and being careful in conduct.
Third, reverently upholding the precepts without transgression.
Fourth, lighting lamps in Buddhist temples;
by doing so for one's parents, śramaṇas, or other practitioners of the Way, one plants the seeds of radiance.
Furthermore, one practices the ten wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, such as non-killing and so forth.
The Buddha said:
"Moreover, there are four matters by which one becomes a King of the Moon."
First, practicing generosity toward those who are destitute;
second, upholding the five precepts;
third, reverently serving the Three Honored Ones.
4. Lighting Lamps for the Ruler, Father, Teacher, and Monastery from the *Chao riming sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Transcending Solar Radiance), Scroll Lower.

6. The Seven Omens Appearing When a Deva of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is about to End His Life; Encountering the Buddha and Attaining Birth among Humans. Part Six: Once, in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there was a certain deva.
When one's lifespan is nearing its end, there are seven kinds of omens:
first, the light from the nape of the neck fades;
second, the flowers upon the head wither.
Third, the complexion of the face changes;
fourth, dust appears upon the robes;
fifth, sweat breaks out from beneath the armpits.
Sixth, his physical form underwent transformation;
seventh, he left his original seat and immediately reflected within himself.
After his life ended, he was reborn in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, becoming a pig within the womb of a leperess;
he was filled with great anxiety and suffering, not knowing what plan to make for himself.
A deity spoke these words:
"The Buddha is currently here preaching the sutra for his mother;
only the Buddha can deliver you from your transgressions."
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in salutation, and had not yet begun to ask his question when the Buddha addressed the devaputra:
"All things in the universe ultimately return to impermanence."
"Why do you grieve over that which you have long known?
The deva explained this fully to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"Those who wish to leave their porcine bodies should recite the Three Refuges.
Do this three times each day.
Thus, following the Buddha’s teaching, the devas took refuge morning and night.
Seven days hence, his life will come to an end in heaven,
and he will descend to be born in the kingdom of Vaiśālī as the son of an elder;
while in his mother’s womb, he will take refuge [in the Triple Gem] three times each day.
As soon as he was born and fell to the ground, he knelt and took refuge [in the Buddha].
His mother straightened her body, and there were no impure secretions.
The maidservants attending his mother were terrified and fled.
The mother also found this deeply strange;
as soon as he fell to the ground, he spoke,
and she thought he was the planet Mars (Ketu) and intended to kill him.
Withdrawing, he thought to himself:

if I kill this child, my son's father will surely hold me guilty."
Xu Bai said to the elder, "It will not be too late to kill him.
His mother immediately took her son and went to inform the elder.
As soon as the boy was born and fell to the ground, he knelt down, joined his palms, and took refuge in the Triple Gem.
The entire family marveled at this, calling it a "confusing delusion.
Their father said,
"Stop, stop!"
"This child is no ordinary person.
Among the people of this world, there are those who do not understand the need to take refuge in the Triple Gem even after a hundred years;
how much more so this one, who was able to utter 'Namo Buddha' as soon as he fell to the ground."
He was raised with careful attention, ensuring he was never treated with negligence or contempt.
The boy eventually grew up until he was nearly seven years old,
when he was playing with his peers by the side of the road.
He encountered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana;
the child went before them and prostrated. The assembly of sages were astonished and marveled that one so young could perform such a salutation.
The child said:
The practitioner no longer recognized him.
[The man] explained in detail how he had met the Buddha again in the heavens and been recognized there.
"Originally, while I was in the heavens, I should have been reborn in the evil realms."
Because he encountered the Buddha’s compassionate instruction to take refuge, he was able to become a human being.
The bhikṣu then offered a prayer of blessing, saying:
"Cullapiṇḍola spoke to Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra."
I pray that you will convey my words to the World-Honored One, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, and all of you gentlemen:
please accept this request and return to inform your parents,
entreating them to prepare the offerings so that they may be complete and delicious.
His parents loved him and followed whatever he said;
they marveled at his precocity as a youth and were struck by his profound insights.
Furthermore, they were amazed by his deeds, for he possessed the knowledge of past lives.
These were of the utmost rarity and excellence, possessing all the renowned flavors of the world;
the ritual implements were so refined that they surpassed the boy's expectations.
Then the Buddha and the assembly of monks each manifested their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and came to the boy’s house for a meal.

The Buddha preached a sutra for them, and the child, his parents, and all their internal and external relatives all attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) through the Sutra on Subduing Arhats. 7. The Heavenly Being’s Hand Produces Sweet Water to Save Five Hundred Merchants. In ancient times, there was a guide. He led five hundred merchants across a vast desert. After traveling for many days, they encountered a great expanse of waterless sand. The merchants were terrified and distressed; they could not advance and feared they would perish. The guide, seeing their plight, felt great compassion and pity. He then extended his hand toward the sky, and from it there issued forth sweet water, which he used to provide for the merchants. Because of this, the merchants were able to cross the desert and reach safety. The guide then said to the merchants: "I have now saved you from this perilous place. You must all repay my kindness by practicing the Way. The merchants replied: "We are deeply grateful for your benevolence. We shall surely follow your instructions. At that time, the guide was none other than the present Śākyamuni Buddha. The five hundred merchants were the present five hundred arhats. It is because of this causal connection that the Buddha has now attained supreme enlightenment and, out of compassion, saves sentient beings. This is why the Buddha’s hand can produce sweet dew and nectar, and why the Buddha’s tongue can cover his face. It is because he has practiced such deeds throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Therefore, one should know that the Buddha is truly the World-Honored One who is worthy of offerings. If one hears of the Buddha’s virtues and gives rise to a single thought of faith, one will attain immeasurable merit. How much more so for those who take refuge in the Buddha, uphold his precepts, and practice the Way! Those who do so will surely attain the fruit of the Path. One should never doubt this. Thus it is said: "The Buddha’s hand produces sweet water, Saving five hundred merchants; Because of this causal connection, He attains supreme enlightenment. His tongue can cover his face, And his body emits light; Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, He has practiced these deeds. Therefore, know that the Buddha Is truly the World-Honored One. If one hears of his virtues And gives rise to a thought of faith, One will attain immeasurable merit; How much more so for those who take refuge! Thus ends the seventh chapter, "The Heavenly Being’s Hand Produces Sweet Water to Save Five Hundred Merchants. From the *Sutra on the Definitive Subjugation of Arhats*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Volume Two. Chapter Eight: The Story of the Elder’s Daughter. The Elder’s Daughter Attains the Way and Manifests Miracles. The Elder’s Daughter Attains the Way and Manifests Miracles. At that time, the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī at the Jetavana Monastery in the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, there was an elder in the city of Śrāvastī named Mahānāman. He had a daughter named Śrīmatī. She was beautiful and possessed of excellent qualities; she was well-versed in the arts and skilled in all crafts. She was wise and eloquent, and her conduct was pure and upright. She took pleasure in giving alms and was devoted to the Three Jewels. She always maintained the eightfold precepts and observed the fast days. She was diligent in making offerings to the Sangha and never neglected the recitation of the scriptures. She was respected by the community of monks and nuns, and she was beloved by the laypeople. Her father, the elder, was also very fond of her. He provided her with all necessities and ensured she lacked nothing. Once, the elder went to visit the Buddha. Seeing his daughter, he said to her: "My daughter, go to the Buddha and listen to the Dharma. The daughter replied: "Father, I am already well-versed in the Dharma. There is no need for me to go. The elder said: "Even so, you should go to pay your respects to the World-Honored One. The daughter then took her leave and went to the monastery. Upon arriving, she prostrated herself before the Buddha and sat to one side. The Buddha, knowing her thoughts, preached the Dharma to her. She listened with rapt attention and attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. Having attained this realization, she rose from her seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed. As she was leaving, she manifested various miraculous powers: she walked upon the water without sinking, passed through walls without obstruction, and ascended into the air. She performed these wonders to demonstrate her attainment of the Way. When she returned home, her father asked her: "Daughter, did you see the Buddha? Did you hear the Dharma? The daughter replied: "Father, I saw the Buddha and heard the Dharma. I have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. I have manifested various miraculous powers to demonstrate my attainment of the Way. The father was amazed and said: "It is wonderful how you have attained such a high state in such a short time! The daughter then explained to her father the meaning of the Dharma she had heard. The father, hearing her words, also gave rise to a heart of faith and attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. From that time forward, the entire family practiced the Way and became disciples of the Buddha. Thus it is said: "The Elder’s Daughter Attains the Way, Manifesting Miracles; She Walks Upon the Water, Passes Through Walls, and Ascends into the Air. Her Father Sees These Wonders And Gives Rise to Faith; Together they practice the Way, Becoming Disciples of the Buddha. Thus ends the eighth chapter, "The Elder’s Daughter Attains the Way and Manifests Miracles," from the *Sutra on the Definitive Subjugation of Arhats*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Volume Two. Chapter Nine: The Story of the Woman Who Offered Food. The Woman Who Offered Food Attains the Way. The Woman Who Offered Food Attains the Way. At that time, the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha. There was a woman in the city named Sujātā. She was wealthy and virtuous, and she took pleasure in giving alms. She heard that the Buddha was dwelling in the city and that he was preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings. She felt great joy and decided to offer food to the Buddha. She prepared a great feast and invited the Buddha and his disciples. On the day of the offering, she rose early and set out for the monastery. Upon arriving, she prostrated herself before the Buddha and offered the food. The Buddha accepted her offering and preached the Dharma to her. She listened with rapt attention and attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. Having attained this realization, she rose from her seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed. She then returned home and shared the Dharma she had heard with her family. Her family members also gave rise to hearts of faith and attained the fruits of the Path. Thus it is said: "The Woman Who Offered Food Attains the Way; She Listens to the Dharma And Attains the Fruit of *Srotāpanna*. She Shares the Dharma with Her Family, And They All Attain Realization; Because of this causal connection, They are all born in the Pure Land. Thus ends the ninth chapter, "The Woman Who Offered Food Attains the Way," from the *Sutra on the Definitive Subjugation of Arhats*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Volume Two. Chapter Ten: The Story of the Sick Monk. The Sick Monk Is Cured by the Buddha’s Power. The Sick Monk Is Cured by the Buddha’s Power. At that time, the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī. There was a monk in the city who was suffering from a severe illness. His condition was grave, and he was in great pain. He heard that the Buddha was dwelling nearby and that he possessed great compassionate power. He wished to see the Buddha, but his strength failed him. The Buddha, knowing his thoughts through his divine power, sent a disciple to visit him. The disciple arrived at the monk's room and asked after his health. The monk told the disciple of his suffering and requested that the Buddha come to see him. The disciple returned and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha, moved by compassion, went to the monk's room. Upon seeing the Buddha, the monk felt a surge of joy. The Buddha touched the monk’s head with his hand, and immediately the monk’s pain vanished. His body was restored to health, and he was able to rise from his bed. The monk was filled with gratitude and followed the Buddha back to the monastery. The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, and he attained the fruit of *arhatship*. Thus it is said: "The Sick Monk Is Cured By the Buddha’s Power; Upon Seeing the Buddha, His Pain Vanishes.
Traveling together with five hundred merchants on a trading journey,
they reached a vast wilderness where they were utterly exhausted by hunger and thirst.
Taking refuge in the World-Honored One, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, they were struck with terror and had no other recourse.
At that time, the Master of the Way climbed to a high vantage point and looked afar.
Seeing a grove of trees where birds were flying toward it, he hoped there must be water there.
Together they ran forward, and before long they arrived.
Seeing only trees surrounding him with grass growing all around and the ground being clean, the guide said to the merchants:
"Let us all dig into the earth together to seek water; it must surely be obtainable."
Just as they had finished their consultation,
a celestial being, observing from afar in the heavens that this leader and his five hundred followers were exhausted for lack of water and food,
arrived at the place where they stayed atop a tree in the time it takes to stretch out one's arm.
Extending his right hand, he caused eight kinds of sweet and delicious water to flow from between his five fingers,
offering it to the Teacher and the five hundred people.
Each took what they needed without end, and all were fully satisfied.

using exquisite sandalwood as fragrant plaster;
there were one thousand two hundred separate chambers for his residence.
Having struck the *gandī* at all one hundred and twenty locations,
he addressed the King:
"I pray only that Your Majesty will dispatch a messenger to invite the Buddha."
The king immediately dispatched a messenger to Rājagṛha to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha, saying,
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will deign to visit Śrāvastī.
The Buddha, surrounded by the fourfold assembly in front and behind, set out.
He emitted a great radiance that shook heaven and earth, reaching as far as Śrāvastī.
At every guesthouse he passed, he stayed for a time;
along the way, he delivered countless people to liberation.
Gradually approaching the vicinity of Śrāvastī,
the entire great assembly, bearing various offerings, went out to welcome the World-Honored One.
Upon his arrival at the city, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance that illuminated the trichiliocosm.
As he pressed the ground with his toes,
the earth shook everywhere;
the musical instruments within the city sounded of their own accord without being struck.
The blind saw, the deaf heard, the mute spoke, and those who were hunched straightened themselves;
those with chronic ailments, deformities, or physical constraints all attained full physical integrity.
All the people—men and women, great and small—beheld this auspicious response.
Filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they came to where the Buddha was;
eighteen billion people gathered there in total.
At that time, the World-Honored One, administering medicine according to their ailments, preached the sublime Dharma for them.

Each attained the stage of the Path; this is found in the tenth fascicle of the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra on the Wise and the Foolish), the *Saṃyuktāgama*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Madhyamāgama*, the *Buddhacarita*, and various Vinayas, all of which are largely identical.

3. Regarding the mountains: among the three Kunlun Jewel Mountains where five hundred arhats dwell, there are ten great mountain kings. There are eight causes for the earth to quake. 1. Regarding the Kunlun Jewel Mountain where five hundred arhats reside: as for the Kunlun Mountain, it is the dwelling place of five hundred arhats. As for the Kunlun Jewel Mountain where five hundred arhats reside—this Kunlun Mountain is...
It is the very center of Jambudvīpa. The mountains are all composed of precious gems,
and they are surrounded by five hundred caves.
The caves are all made of gold.
Five hundred arhats constantly reside there.
Outside the surrounding mountains lies the great Anavatapta Spring.
In the midst of this level ground within the mountains lies a river;
at its banks are four golden animal heads from whose mouths water flows forth.
Each circled once and returned to its respective quarter, where they entered the four great oceans.
That which issued from the mouths of the elephants was the Yellow River.
The spring is twenty-five yojanas square and twenty-one li deep;
within the spring is a golden terrace.
The terrace is one yojana square.
Upon the terrace is a golden lotus flower,
with its stem made of the seven precious gems.
The Tathāgata, together with five hundred arhats, would regularly recite the precepts on the fifteenth day of the month; this is from the first fascicle of the *Cīvarotpatti-sūtra*.
2. The Ten Great Mountains of Jambudvīpa: Within the two great earths, there are ten great mountain kings.
First, the King of Mountains, Himavat;
second, the King of Mountains, Gandhamādana;
third, the King of Mountains, Kailāsa.
Fourth is the mountain king Catur-ṛṣi;
fifth is the mountain king Yugandhara;
sixth is the mountain king Aśvakarṇa.
Seventh is King Nimiṃdhara; eighth is King Khadiraka;
ninth is King Īṣādhara.
The Ten Sumeru Kings appear in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. 3.

Regarding the eight causes for the great trembling of the earth: there are eight causes for the great trembling of the earth. Once, when the Three Buddhas were in Śrāvastī, they addressed the bhikṣus.
There are eight causes and conditions by which the earth-element quakes.
This earth is sixty-eight thousand yojanas deep and is supported by water.
Water depends upon space;
or again, at that time, when the wind moves within space, the water also moves,
and as the water moves, the earth then shakes violently.
This is the first movement.
If a bhikṣu has attained the supernormal powers (ṛddhi) and possesses mastery over his desires,
he can perceive the earth as if it were the palm of his hand and cause the great earth to tremble violently.
These two are movements.
Furthermore, if there are devas who possess great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) and great majesty,
they are able to cause the earth to tremble.
This is the third earthquake.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva is in the Tuṣita Heaven and desires to descend in spirit to be born, at that time the earth shakes.
These are the four movements.
When the Bodhisattva himself knows that he is in the stage of being in the mother’s womb,
this is the fifth movement.
If a bodhisattva knows that when ten months are complete he shall emerge from his mother’s womb, the earth shakes greatly;
this is the sixth shaking.
If the bodhisattva leaves the household life and sits at the site of enlightenment, [the earth shakes].
Having subdued the hosts of Māra and attained ultimate perfect enlightenment,
the earth shook greatly;
this was the seventh movement.
If the Tathāgata were to enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder,
this would constitute one of the eight disturbances; see the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

In each of the four thousand light-radiating trees, the sound of the Dharma issues forth: first, the tree of divine medicine; second, the tree of great medicine; third, the great tree that benefits beings with five faces; fourth, the elephant-treasury incense; fifth, ox-head sandalwood; sixth, the southern tree of Mount Sumeru; seventh, the poisonous tree; eighth, the tree of the thousand-light-radiating country from which the sound of the Dharma issues forth. In the thousand-light-radiating country, the sound of the Dharma issues forth from the trees. In the past, there was a Buddha named Siṃhanāda-dundubhisvara-rāja (Lion’s Roar Drum-Sound King).
The name of the land is Thousand Radiances.
Its trees are composed of the seven treasures,
and from these trees issue forth the teachings of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-existence, and the absence of grasping at signs.
Thus, from these sounds of all dharmas, the *Sarvadharmācāra-sūtra* emerges.
2. Regarding the medicinal tree spirits: there are two medicinal trees, named Mātangi and Jayanti.
The world was then so poisonous that one could not move about at will.
There was a great divine serpent, its body one hundred and twenty zhang long;
it moved along, seeking food.
There was a black-headed insect five zhang in length.
While traveling along its path, it encountered a snake;
just as it raised its head, it was about to sever the large beast in front of it.
Upon smelling the fragrance of the medicine, the snake bent its head and attempted to flee;
however, its body became entangled in the medicinal tree, and it was immediately severed in two.
The head has lived for half its life,
yet the tail is already putrid and rotting.
When all the various venomous creatures smell the stench of this snake, [they flee].
All evil poisonous vapors are extinguished. From the *Shanxin jing* (Sutra on Good Faith), Scroll Lower, Chapter 3:
The Great Medicine Tree. Upon the summit of the three snow mountains, there is a king of medicinal trees.
It is called "not born from the sense-faculties" and yet "not not born from them.
It extends six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
reaching down as far as the adamantine foundation.
When this tree produces roots,
all the roots of the trees of Jambudvīpa are produced;
likewise when it produces stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
In Jambudvīpa, all the trees produce branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits;
the roots of these trees can produce stems,
and the stems can produce roots.
For this reason, it is said that it does not arise from roots, yet it is not the case that it does not arise from roots;
it is able to grow and flourish in all places,
with the sole exception of the deep pits of hell.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle thirty, that [beings] cannot grow within the water-circle, nor can ears produce flowers.
4. The Five-Faced Tree That Benefits Beings. Regarding the Five-Faced Tree That Benefits Beings: Long ago, there was a king.
The king’s name was Wuliè; in his kingdom there was a tree named Xiūbótíhuán.
Its circumference was five hundred and sixty *li*, and its roots spread out for eight hundred and forty *li* at their base.
It is four thousand li in height;
its branches spread in the four directions for two thousand li.
The tree bears five kinds of fruit.
The road has five sections.
In one section, the King of Chi and his palace courtesans partake of its fruit together.
In the second section, the ministers and hundreds of officials all partake of it together.
That which has three faces is eaten by the common people together.
That which has four faces is eaten together by all the śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way.
That which has five faces is eaten together by flying birds, insects, and beasts.
The fruits are all like two-dou measures of jars;
their flavor is like honey.
There is no one to guard the trees.
The fruits of their labor were not encroached upon by others.
At that time, people all lived for eighty-four thousand years.
During that period, people suffered from nine kinds of diseases.
First is cold; second is heat;
third is hunger.
Fourth is thirst;
fifth is excrement; sixth is urine.
Seventh is lustful desire;
eighth is overeating;
ninth is old age.
Women reach the age of five hundred years before they marry.
This concludes the *Ānanda-ānusmṛti-sūtra*.
5. The Great Elephant Treasury Incense: Among the five types of people, there is incense.
It is named the Great Elephant Treasury;
it was produced from the battle of dragons.
If one burns a single pellet, [it will produce immeasurable fragrance].
A great cloud of fine light arose and covered it from above;
its flavor was like nectar.
For seven days and seven nights, a rain of fragrant water fell.
If it touches the body, the body becomes golden;
if it touches clothing, palaces, or multi-storied towers,
they too all become golden.
If there are sentient beings who catch the scent of this incense,
they shall experience joy and delight for seven days and seven nights;
all their illnesses will be extinguished, and no calamities or untimely deaths shall befall them.
Having distanced themselves from hearts of fear and harm,
they are single-mindedly oriented toward great compassion and universal mindfulness of sentient beings;
knowing them thus, I preach the Dharma for them.
Causing immeasurable sentient beings to attain non-retrogression from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Forty-two.
6. Gośīrṣa-candana (Ox-head Sandalwood Incense). Gośīrṣa-candana, six [types of] Gośīrṣa-candana.
It is produced from Mount Vigatamala.
If it is applied to the body, fire cannot burn it. (From the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 42)
7. Southern Tree of Mount Sumeru: To the south of Mount Sumeru there is a great tree, four thousand *li* in height, upon which various *parrot* birds (*pattraka*) constantly dwell.
The tree remained forever motionless.
There was a small bird there,
its form resembling that of a quail or a sparrow.
As he stood upon it,
the tree shook and stirred.
The *pāṣa* asked the tree deity, saying:
"You are ignorant.
My body is heavy and large, yet it does not move of its own accord;
when small birds come, it shakes and trembles instead."
The deity said:
"Although this bird is small,
it has swallowed a vajra from the bottom of the ocean."
Diamond is a substance that, wherever it falls, nothing remains unshattered.
This is why one cannot remain at ease when confronted by great terror. (From the *Daśottara-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Seven).
8. Poisonous Trees. In the kingdom of Śrāvastī there was a royal garden where a poisonous tree grew.
Men and women would go there for recreation and rest beneath it.
Some experience headaches as if their heads were about to split;
some suffer pain in their waists and spines;
or they pass away beneath trees.
The gardener gave him a long-handled axe,
more than ten feet in length.
He struck it from afar and cut it away;
yet before ten days had passed,
the tree had already returned to its former state.
Thus there are many faults;
the branches and leaves follow after,
remaining as they were before in their original circularity.
The most exquisite among trees;
all who behold it cannot help but rejoice.
Not knowing what to avoid or refrain from,
they all came to meet this fate.
The gardener and his kinsmen—
Craving the shade of the tree,
they all died there;
the gardener stood alone.
Day and night he was filled with sorrow and anxiety;
wailing in grief, he wandered about.
When someone questioned him:
The wise man said to him,
"You must eradicate its roots.
Just as he was about to dig up the roots, [the tree fell].
Fearing further that he would surely die,
he proceeded to reflect once more:
"I shall leave the household life to study the Way."
The Buddha said:
"If one cuts down a tree but does not exhaust its roots, though it has been cut, it will grow back again.
If one cuts through craving but does not exhaust its source, suffering will arise again and again."

Awakening his mind and reproaching himself, he immediately attained the first fruit [of the path]. This is from the *Kṣuradhāra-viṣavṛkṣa-nirgama Sūtra*. 5. The one hundred and twenty-third of the four great rivers
From Lake Anavatapta, two rivers flow toward the great ocean:
the first is named Gaṅgā,
and the second is named Sindhu.
The third is called Puṣya;
the fourth is called Sthira.
That Gaṅgā flows forth from the mouth of the golden elephant.
Circling the lake once, it flows toward the eastern ocean.
That Sindhu river issues from the mouth of the silver ox;
circling the lake once, it flows toward the southern ocean.
The Puṣkariṇī river issues from the mouth of the lapis lazuli horse,
circles the lake once, and flows toward the western ocean.
The Sītā river issues from the mouth of the crystal lion, circles the lake once, and flows toward the northern ocean.
Each of those four great rivers has four tributary rivers as its retinue; here,
only those that are vast and possess specific names are mentioned.
However, each of those four rivers has five hundred tributaries;
together there are two thousand rivers that ultimately flow toward the great ocean. (From the second fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā*).
2. Regarding the five great rivers: of the two that flow westward, one is named Gaṅgā;
the one that flows southward is named Yamunā;
and those that flow eastward are two.
One is named Śālukī; one is named Airāvatī;
that which flows northward is named Mṛttikāvatī.
All flow and pour into the sea.
Since the establishment of heaven and earth, the rain that falls and the rivers that pour have neither increased nor decreased.
Their former names are now set aside.
Combined, they form the waters of a single ocean. From the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Eight Virtues of the Ocean):
"The great ocean possesses eight virtues. Regarding the eight virtues of the great ocean: the Three Buddhas once traveled to the country of Anabhibhūta (Unconquerable).
On the fifteenth day as usual,
he sat down to recite the precepts for the śramaṇas;
the Buddha remained silent and spoke no word.
Ānanda said, "They are seated.
Then the World-Honored One spoke.
Among all śramaṇas, there are those whose minds follow wrong conduct and oppose [the Dharma];
such things are not within the capacity of those who are lowly or base to carry out.
The pure and the turbid are mutually contradictory; I do not speak of them.
Maudgalyāyana entered meditative concentration and beheld them with his vision.
He said to him, "Rise!
This is not a place where you, a worldly person, ought to sit.
When he refused to rise, [the Buddha] took him by the arm and led him out, saying, "You possess no supreme virtue."
With a mind harboring the six perversions,
how would I dare to occupy this throne of celestial fragrance with this foul and defiled body?
"You are a person who has abandoned [the path]; you are not a śramaṇa.
Thus spoke the Buddha to the śramaṇa.
Contemplate that great ocean as possessing eight qualities:
its vastness is a boundless expanse,
and its depth is such that its bottom cannot be measured.
Entering slightly further and becoming increasingly deep, one encounters no obstacles as before;
this is the first virtue.
The tide does not exceed its appointed time.
These are the two virtues.
Just as the ocean contains all manner of treasures, encompassing everything within its embrace,
it cannot tolerate a putrid and decayed corpse.
These are the three virtues.
The ocean harbors all manner of treasures;
there is nothing one seeks that cannot be obtained.
These are the four virtues.
Beneath the heavens, there are five great rivers that flow into the sea.
All former names are discarded and merged into a single ocean;
this is the fifth virtue.
The five rivers and ten thousand streams fall like rain and flow constantly;
yet the water in the ocean remains as it was, never increasing or decreasing.
This is the sixth virtue.
In the ocean there are many fish whose bodies are immense.
The first fish is four thousand li in length;
the second fish is eight thousand li in length.
The third fish is twelve thousand li in length;
the fourth fish is sixteen thousand li in length;
the fifth fish is twenty thousand li in length.
The sixth fish is twenty-four thousand li in length;
the seventh fish is twenty-eight thousand li in length.
These are the seven virtues.
The seawater is uniformly salty from its edges to its center; such is the eighth of its eight qualities. This is from the *Bāguǎn jīng* (Sutra on the Eight Qualities of the Sea).

6. Precious Jewels: 1. Moonlight *maṇi* jewel. 2. Great Ocean-born Jewel. 3. Radiant Great Jewel. 4. Moonlight *maṇi* jewel. 5. Moonlight *maṇi* jewel. 6. Moonlight *maṇi* jewel. [Note: The text repeats "Moonlight *maṇi* jewel" three times.]
It is mostly found within the *kakkola*.
If sentient beings possess merit,
they will naturally obtain it.
It is just like the hells,
where instruments for punishing transgressors arise spontaneously;
this jewel is also called the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
It constantly produces all manner of precious objects—
clothing, food, and drink— according to one's every wish.
Whoever obtains this jewel...
Poisons cannot harm them;
fire cannot burn them.
Or it is said:
This was held by Śakra;
when he fought with the asuras,
it shattered and fell into Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The śarīra of all Buddhas of the distant past,
once the Dharma has completely perished,"
It transforms into this jewel for the sake of benefiting others; this is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 59.
2. Regarding the "Born Jewel" (*jātaratna*): within the two great oceans, there are four types of precious jewels.
All manner of precious jewels arise from these;
were it not for these four jewels,
all precious objects would gradually perish and vanish.
The various minor dragon spirits are unable to see it;
only the Dragon King Sāgara places it within a secret, deep treasury.
This deep treasury has four names.
First is named Accumulation of All Jewels;
second is named Inexhaustible Treasury of Jewels; third is named Far-Reaching Radiance;
fourth is named Source of All Adornments. These are from the thirtieth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Within the three great oceans of the Great Jewel of Radiance,
there are four blazing Great Jewels of Radiance:
the first is named the Great Jewel of Radiance of the Sun-Treasury (Sūryagarbha).
The second is named the Great Jewel of Light Free from Aridity;
the third is named the Great Jewel of Fire-Bead Light;
the fourth is named the Great Jewel of Ultimate Light Without Remainder.
If these four treasures did not exist within the great ocean,
then the four continents, the world-system, the Vajra-encircling mountains,
and even the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception would all be submerged and swept away.
The Radiance of the Sun-Treasury can transform the waters of the ocean into curd;
it is the Radiance of Parting from Drying Up.
One can transform the milk of the ocean into ghee;
the radiance of the fire-jewel can ignite the ghee of the ocean.
The ultimate, peerless, great jewel of light, which can burn the ocean of ghee until it is forever exhausted without remainder, emerges from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Forty. Seven:

The Differences in the Quantity of Milk Consumed by Humans and Their Physical Lifespans. Regarding the differences in the quantity of milk consumed by humans and their physical lifespans: [there are] seven Jambudvīpas.
From the moment the child was born and fell to the ground until he reached the age of three,
how much milk did he drink from his mother’s breast?
Maitreya replied,
"I drank one hundred and eighty hu of milk,
excluding the four parts consumed while in my mother's womb."
In Pūrvavideha, from the time a child is born and falls to the ground until they reach the age of three, [they are able to speak].
They drink eighteen hundred *khu* of milk.

The Buddha joined his palms and rose;

You have condescended to come here from afar.
Such is the nature of all conditioned phenomena;

Although Ānanda suppressed his feelings and endured himself,

"Sentient beings of future generations will surely question me."
As the Buddha was approaching his final passing, what further did he say? How did he answer?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
You should answer:
"The Buddha has already entered nirvana;
Lady Māyā has descended."
For the sake of sentient beings who may later become unfilial,

and spoke the aforementioned verses of reverence.
This sutra is titled *The Sutra on the Buddha’s Encounter with His Mother at the Time of His Parinirvāṇa*.
It is thus received and upheld from the lower fascicle of the *Māyā-sūtra*.
From the *Sutra-lakṣaṇa-vibhāga* (Distinguishing Characteristics of Sutras and Vinaya), Fascicle Four.

"This cessation is bliss.

According to the dharma of the brahmins,

He was told to take it himself.
He took a pinch of it away.

The accumulation [of his merit] did not diminish.
Knowing that this king’s past merit made him ready for deliverance,
the Buddha transformed himself into a brahmin and went to his kingdom.
The king came out to meet him;
having paid his respects and inquired after his well-being,
he asked, "What is it that you seek?"
"Do not harbor self-doubt.
The brahmin replied,

"I wish to beg for precious jewels to use as a dwelling.
The king said, "Very well," and he took a heavy handful himself and departed.

furthermore, I must take a wife."
Fearing it would not suffice for use,

Thus spoke the King.
He took another three handfuls;
the brahmin immediately took them,
walked seven steps, and then returned to his original place.
The king asked, "Why? He replied,
"This [wealth] is sufficient to take a wife."
Furthermore, he possesses no fields, lands, slaves, servants, oxen, or horses;
for this reason, his mind is at rest.
The King said:
He took seven more handfuls;
the brahmin immediately took them,
walked seven paces, and returned to his original place.
The king asked,
"For what further reason?
The brahmin replied:
If there are men and women who ought to marry,
the expenses for auspicious and inauspicious rites would be calculated as insufficient;

The king said,
"I offer all my accumulated treasures to you.

The king found this very strange and questioned him again regarding the reason for his intention.
The brahmin replied:
Originally, I sought alms merely for the sake of sustaining my life;
yet, reflecting deeply, I realize that human life in this world is but brief.
All things are impermanent, and it is difficult to preserve them even from morning until evening.
Consequently, his anxieties and sufferings grew ever more profound;
though he accumulated treasures like mountains, they were of no benefit to himself.
Driven by greed and scheming, he labored in vain.
"It would be better to quiet the mind and seek the Way of Non-action;
therefore, I do not accept [this gift].
With his mind thus opened and enlightened, the King accepted the teaching.

Though one may acquire accumulated treasures so vast they reach the heights of heaven and fill the entire world,

one who is unwholesome appearing as if wholesome, and whose craving resembles the absence of craving.
Taking suffering for pleasure is what the madman detests;
yet the King beheld the Buddha’s radiance and heard this verse.
The king and his ministers immediately received the five precepts and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
This concludes the first chapter of the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*.
