From Rājagṛha to that city, when the Nirgranthas heard that I intended to go there,
they immediately thought this:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama comes here,
these people will surely abandon me and no longer provide for me.
He thus addressed the people of that city.
"The śramaṇa Gautama now wishes to come here.
Yet that śramaṇa has abandoned his parents to wander hither and thither."
Wherever they go, they cause the five grains not to ripen in that land;
the people suffer from famine and many die, with no peace or happiness at all.
Upon hearing this, those people immediately conceived fear.
He addressed him, saying,
"Great Master,
what plan should be devised?"
The Nirgrantha replied,
"Śramaṇa Gautama, by nature you delight in groves, flowing springs, and clear waters."
"Whatever exists outside should be destroyed.
You all must go together out of the city to cut down the forest trees,
leaving nothing remaining— not even flowing springs, wells, or ponds."
They filled it with foul filth and firmly closed the city gates,
each man strictly prepared his weapons.
One should guard the walls and diligently fortify oneself;
even if they should come, [one remains secure].
"Do not let him advance.
We shall also employ various stratagems to cause that Gautama to turn back on his path."
Those people reverently honored and practiced [the teachings]. At that time,
I went to those cities and towns.
Having seen this, he immediately gave rise to compassion and directed a heart of loving-kindness toward them.
All the trees grew back as they were before, beyond measure;
the rivers, ponds, wells, and springs were filled with pure water,
as clear as blue lapis lazuli.
Various kinds of flowers grew there, covering it completely.
He transformed the city walls into deep blue lapis lazuli,
so that the people within the city were all able to see me and the great assembly clearly.
The gates opened of their own accord, and none were able to restrain them;
the weapons they had arrayed transformed into various flowers,
with the elder Lu-zhi as their leader.
Accompanied by his people, he came to where I was;
I then expounded for him various essential teachings of the Dharma.
Causing all those people to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. From the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen. 9.
Manifesting as Śramaṇas to Deliver the Five Bhikṣus. Regarding the manifestation as Śramaṇas to deliver the five bhikṣus: Long ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a mountain.
Forty or fifty *li* from the city,
there were five śramaṇas dwelling in the mountains to study the Way.
At dawn he would leave the mountain to beg for food among the people;
having finished his meal, he would return to the mountain, arriving only at dusk.
Exhausted from the journey there and back, he was unable to engage in seated meditation.
He practiced right concentration in this manner for many years,
yet he was unable to attain the Way.
The Buddha took pity on him.
Toiling without any gain,
he transformed himself into a practitioner and went to where [the man] was.
He asked the various practitioners,
"I trust you have not grown weary in your secluded cultivation of the Way?
The śramaṇas replied:
"We are here, yet we are very far from the city.
This body composed of the four great elements must have food."
Traveling back and forth day after day,
they grew weary over the years and were unable to practice the Way.
One should simply conclude one's life in this very manner.
A practitioner of the Way said:
"For one who cultivates the Way, the precepts are the foundation."
He took the gathering of the mind as his practice;
he held the physical form in contempt and prized the Truth,
even to the point of casting away his body and life.
One takes food merely to sustain the body;
one guards the mind in right concentration and internally cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā.
By extinguishing the mind one attains the Way;
by nourishing the body and following its passions,
how can one escape suffering?
"I pray that you, venerable practitioners,
do not travel tomorrow.
I shall provide for your needs."
The various practitioners rested for one day.
At that time, the five śramaṇas were filled with great joy,
marveling at this unprecedented occurrence.
With a settled mind and composed intent,
he no longer worried about his conduct.
The next day, this transformed practitioner of the Way brought food for him.
When they had finished eating, their minds were peaceful and harmonious, and their spirits were tranquil.
After the man who transforms people through the Way had finished reciting the verses for them, he manifested the physical form and radiant countenance of a Buddha.
At this, the five śramaṇas were struck with awe and their spirits trembled.

They all contemplated the precepts and immediately attained the path of Arhatship. This concludes the third chapter of the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, titled "Attaining the Path of Arhatship through Contemplating the Precepts.

10. Manifesting as a Śramaṇa to Transform a Miserly Couple. In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a poor household. A husband and wife were both stingy and greedy. [The Buddha] manifested as a śramaṇa to transform them. Chapter Ten: Manifesting as a Śramaṇa to Transform a Miserly Couple. In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a destitute family.
The husband and wife were stingy and greedy, having no faith in the Way and its virtue.
Out of compassion for their folly, the Buddha manifested as a śramaṇa and went to their gate to beg for alms.
At that time, her husband was away;
his wife reviled him with words devoid of reason.
The śramaṇa said,
"I am a seeker of the Way;
I live by begging for alms."
"You must not revile me;
I look for nothing but a single meal.
The wife said:
If you were standing at the point of death,
it would be difficult even to obtain food;
how much less so now that you are healthy and strong, yet desire my food?
"It is merely a matter of timing; it would have been better to leave sooner.
Thereupon, the śramaṇa stood before him.
With eyes staring upward and vital energy dissipated,
one immediately manifests as standing dead;
the body swells, and worms emerge from the nose and mouth.
His abdomen burst open and his intestines were rotten, with impurities flowing out.
When the woman saw this, she was struck with terror, lost her voice, and fled.
Thereupon, the practitioner...
Suddenly he abandoned his departure and went several li from the house,
where he sat beneath a tree to rest.
When her husband returned home,
he saw his wife on the road;
he marveled at her state of alarm and terror.
His wife spoke to her husband,
recounting the matter in detail;
the husband became greatly enraged.
He asked where she was.
The wife replied,
"She has already gone."
Not long after he had this thought,
he took up his bow and girded on his sword, following the tracks to pursue him.
Drawing his bow and unsheathing his sword, he ran straight forward.
He wished to strike down the practitioner.
The practitioner immediately manifested a small city of lapis lazuli to surround himself several times over; [the man] was unable to enter.
He immediately asked the practitioner,
"Why have you not opened the door?
The practitioner replied:
He wished to make the gate open and told him to cast away his bow and sword.
The man thought to himself,
"I shall follow his words."
When he was about to take hold of the hand-rolled bolt to apply it,
he immediately cast aside his bow and sword;
yet the gate would not open.
He spoke again to the gatekeeper:
"I have already cast away my bow and sword;
why is the gate not opened?"
The practitioner said again,
"I have caused you to discard the bow and sword of evil intent within your mind;
I did not mean the bow and sword in your hands."
Thereupon, that man’s heart was startled and his body trembled,
for the practitioner was divine and holy.
He then realized the Master’s mind and immediately prostrated himself, repenting his transgressions and reproaching himself.
He addressed the Master, saying:
I have a wretched wife who does not recognize the True Man;
she incites me toward evil.
I pray that you will deign to show me a small measure of compassion.
"Do not abandon me so easily.
I wish to take you along now to exhort you to practice the Way.
Having said this, he immediately rose and returned home.
His wife asked, "Where is the śramaṇa?
Her husband then gave a detailed account of the śramaṇa's miraculous virtues.
"He is there now;
you should go yourself to repent and extinguish your transgressions."
Thereupon, the husband and wife went to the place where the practitioner was;
prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they repented of their transgressions and vowed to become his disciples.
I ask concerning the city of Vaiḍūrya:
it is firm and stable beyond comparison;
its resolve is clear and its mind is settled.
"Forever free from sorrow and affliction—
by what virtue has one reached such divine and wondrous excellence?
The practitioner replied:
I have studied extensively without weariness;
I have served the Dharma without slackening;
and I have practiced with diligence in upholding the precepts.
The mind is not negligent;
by relying on this, one attains the Way and personally reaches Nirvana. From the *Dharmapada*, Chapter Three.
11. Converting the Butchers and the Brahmins so that they Attain the Fruit of the Path. Once upon a time, there were five hundred brahmins.
They constantly sought opportunities to find fault with the Buddha, desiring to slander him;
they deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Let me have a butcher slaughter a living being to invite the Buddha and the assembly of monks;
the Buddha will certainly accept the invitation."
They praised a butcher,
whereupon we went forward and collectively reviled him.
The Buddha then accepted our invitation.
He said to the butcher:
"When fruit is ripe, it falls of its own accord;
when merit is ripe, one is delivered of its own accord."
The butcher returned home and prepared food and drink.
The Buddha, leading his disciples, arrived at the butcher's village and went to the house of the donor.
The brahmins, both great and small, all rejoiced together, thinking,
"Today we have finally found an opportunity against the Buddha.
If he praises merit, [we shall refute it].
They use the fact that he previously committed the sin of killing to revile him.
If one were to speak of the origins of his transgressions, [it would be as follows].
One should challenge him with the merit of this very day;
between these two options, one now has the opportunity.
When the Buddha arrived, he sat down immediately.
They proceeded toward the water to eat.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One observed the minds of the assembly.
For those who were to be saved,
he extended his tongue so that it covered his face and licked his ears;
he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire city.
He then spoke a verse of benediction in a Brahma-like voice, as taught by the True Man:
"Living one's life through the Way, the fool envies it and acts wickedly upon seeing it.
By practicing evil, one obtains evil, just like sowing bitter seeds."
Evil brings its own retribution; goodness brings its own reward. Each must ripen for itself and cannot be substituted by another.
By practicing good, one obtains good—just as when the five hundred Brahmins planted sweet seeds, their minds were spontaneously awakened and liberated.
He immediately prostrated himself before the Buddha,
casting his body to the ground in the five-limbed obeisance,
seeking to fully comprehend the Sage’s instructions.
"May you have compassion for us and nurture us so that we may become śramaṇas.
The Buddha immediately granted them permission,
and they all became śramaṇas.
The villagers, both young and old,
beheld the Buddha’s miraculous transformations;
there was none among them who did not rejoice.
All attained the fruit of the Path;
it was called the "Village of the Wise.
No longer was there anyone bearing the name of a butcher. (From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume One).
12. Transforming the Faithless on the Banks of the Great River. To the southeast of Śrāvastī, there was a great river.
It was both deep and wide;
more than five hundred households lived along its banks,
yet they had not heard of the practice of the Way and Virtue that transcends the world.
They were habituated to violence and devoted themselves to deception;
greedy for profit, they indulged themselves, following their own whims and desires to the utmost.
The Buddha knew that this family possessed the merit to be saved and should be delivered.
He went to the edge of the water and sat beneath a tree.
When the villagers saw the Buddha’s extraordinary radiance, they were struck with wonder.
There was no one who was not struck with awe and solemnity;
they all went to pay their respects, some prostrating and others bowing, inquiring after his well-being.
The Buddha bade them sit and preached the Dharma for them.
When the multitude heard this, their hearts still did not believe it.
The Buddha then manifested a person who came from south of the Yangtze River.
He walked upon the water,
with his ankles barely submerged,
until he arrived before the Buddha, where he bowed his head to the ground in prostration.
When the multitude saw this, there was none who was not struck with wonder and astonishment.
They asked the transformed man, saying,
"Our ancestors have lived by this river for generations."
"I have never heard of anyone walking upon water.
Who are you? What spiritual art do you possess that allows you to tread on water without sinking?"
The transformed person replied,
"I am a simple and straightforward man from south of the Yangtze River.
Hearing that the Buddha was here,"
Delighting in the path of virtue,
he reached the southern bank,
yet was unable to cross at that time.
He asked the man on the other shore about the depth of the water.
That man looked at him and said:
"The water may reach up to the ankles.
Trusting his words,
I have thus come across.
"There is no other method.
The Buddha praised him, saying, 'Excellent!
Indeed, by holding fast to faith, one can truly cross the abyss of birth and death.'"
"A river of only a few *li*— how could it be considered extraordinary?
Upon hearing this, the villagers' minds were opened and their faith became firm.

All received the five precepts and became lay devotees (*upāsaka*). This concludes the third chapter of the *Dharmapada*, titled "The Deliverance of Five Hundred Robbers from the Household Life and Their Attainment of the Way.
13. The Deliverance of Five Hundred Robbers from the Household Life and Their Attainment of the Way. Thirteen. At that time, [the Buddha was] in Śrāvastī or Vaiśālī.
The two countries harbored mutual resentment and engaged in plundering and warfare.
The King of Śrāvastī thought to himself:
I am a king; it is my duty to repel enemies and bring peace to the people.
Why then do I allow bandits to plunder the property of others?
He immediately commanded his officers and soldiers:
"I entrust you with the pursuit;
you must ensure that he is captured."
At that time, the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī, having completed their summer retreat,
wished to travel to Vaiśālī;
however, the bhikṣus lost their way.
He fell among those robbers.
Then the bhikṣu asked him,
"Householder, where do you wish to go?"
He replied, "To Vaiśālī. The bhikṣu spoke again.
"We should become companions," he said; they replied,
"We are bandits."
We have traversed thickets and forests;
we traveled without choosing our path.
You are a virtuous person.
"How shall I follow you?
the bhikṣu asked again, requesting,
"I pray that you will take me with you."
Before he had finished speaking,
the pursuers arrived and seized the bhikṣu together with him.
As they were about to reach the king’s presence,
[the king saw] that these were a band of thieves. The king said:
First, bring the bhikṣu.
The king said,
"You are a renunciant."
"How did you commit the theft?
He replied, "I am not a thief."
"Why are you following him?
The bhikṣu reported all the aforementioned matters to the king in detail.
The king said, "Let him go."
The king asked the thief,
"Is this renunciant your companion?
He replied:
"He is a companion.
The king said,
"Take the thief away and summon the bhikṣu again."
The king asked,
"Monk, you have lied and deceived the official;
the bandits claimed that you were their accomplice."
"Why do you say it is not?
The bhikṣu answered as he had before.
The king immediately ordered that the thief be released and dealt with according to the law.
Five hundred thieves were seized,
adorned with garlands of *kapila* flowers, and paraded through the city to the beat of drums as a public proclamation.
He intended to kill him.
The bandit wept bitterly.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked him:
There was the sound of many people.
The bhikṣu replied,
“World-Honored One.”
These are the sounds made by five hundred thieves who have been ordered by the king to be executed.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Go and say to the king:
'You are a king of men.'"
"One should love the people as one's own children;
how could one kill five hundred people at once?
Ānanda received these instructions.
He immediately went to the king's presence and related the Buddha’s words in full.
The king said:
Venerable sir,
I know this matter:
the offense of killing one person is great.
How much more so for five hundred;
they merely destroy villages and plunder the people.
"The World-Honored One can ensure that he will not become a thief again;
he should be released and allowed to live.
Ānanda returned and reported this fully to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Tell the king simply to release him;
I shall ensure that this man shall not commit further theft from this day forward."
Ānanda received the instruction and went first to the place of execution,
where he spoke to the executioners, saying:
These sinners have already been saved by the World-Honored One;
they must not yet be put to death.
He went again to where the king was.
The World-Honored One said to the king,
"I can cause this man not to commit robbery ever again."
The king immediately granted him his life;
without yet untying his bonds,
he sent him to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
wishing to deliver that person,
sat in the open air.
When the bandits saw the Buddha from afar,
their bonds fell away of their own accord,
and they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet.
They stood to one side.
The Buddha, observing their conditions,
taught the Dharma accordingly.
The retribution for the practices of giving and maintaining the precepts,
and the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths— suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path— at that very moment.
They attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
He then asked them,
"Do you wish to leave the household life?"
They replied,
"World-Honored One,
had we gone forth earlier, we would not have encountered this suffering."
"I only pray that you will now ordain me as a renunciant.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣu."
At that time, the five hundred bandits had their entire bodies and garments transformed into the three robes;
they spontaneously possessed alms bowls and displayed dignified deportment with such orderliness that they resembled veteran bhikṣus of a hundred years' standing.
All became Arhats. (*From the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume 19). 14.

Blowing the medicinal incense of Mount Gandhamādana into the eyes of five hundred blind bandits, they regained their clear vision. (Blowing the medicinal incense of Mount Gandhamādana into the eyes of five hundred blind bandits, they regained their clear vision. 14. The Kingdom of Kośala.
There were five hundred bandits whom King Prasenajit found troublesome for their lawlessness and violence.
He dispatched soldiers to lie in wait and capture him; having seized him,
they gouged out his eyes and drove him away to the depths of a dark, dense forest.
These bandits had already planted many roots of virtue under previous Buddhas;
now that they have lost their eyes, they undergo great suffering and distress.
Each of them spoke these words:
"Namo Buddhāya. At that time, I was residing at the Jeta Grove Monastery.
Upon hearing their voices,
he immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness;
at that moment, a cool breeze arose.
He filled his eye sockets with various fragrant medicines from Mount Cīrṇa; immediately,
his eyes were restored to their original state, no different than before.
As soon as the bandits opened their eyes,
they saw the Tathāgata standing before them, preaching the Dharma to them.
Having heard the Dharma, the bandits...

The fourteenth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, titled "Generating the Mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," is largely identical to the seventh fascicle of the *Mahā-upāya-buddha-pratyupakāra-sūtra*.
15. In the city of Vaiśālī, he manifested as the son of a Brahmin obsessed with worldly attachments, causing his parents to regain their original minds. [End of] Fifteen. In the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
There was a brahmin who clung to false views and had no offspring.
Fearing he might suddenly pass away,
his wealth and goods were forfeited to the government,
while offerings were maintained for the various mountains.
The tree spirits also perceived that the wife was pregnant;
when the months were complete, she gave birth to a son.
The child was handsome;
his parents loved him dearly,
and he reached the age of twelve.
While traveling abroad for sightseeing,
he encountered a drunken elephant on the road;
the elephant trampled him, and he died instantly.
The parents were filled with anguish;
their minds became deranged and deluded,
and they ran about naked.
The Tathāgata, out of compassionate concern,
manifested himself as the child;
the parents then took him into their arms.
He experienced immeasurable joy;
his madness and delusion were immediately extinguished,
and he regained his original mind.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, whereupon he immediately gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. This concludes the fourth fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Great Expedient Means for Repaying the Buddha’s Kindness*.
16. Transforming a Courtesan to Cause Her to Feel Aversion for Suffering. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
In the past, during my summer retreat in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī,
there was a courtesan.
His name was Wondrous Intention (Miyi).
He had a karmic affinity with the Buddha.
The Buddha [was accompanied] by Nanda.
"I am going to the courtesan's house;
I have been begging for alms there every day,
yet this woman has never shown me respect."
However, she conceived a particular attachment for Nanda.
After seven days had passed,
the girl thought to herself:
"Śramaṇa Gautama,
if you can send Nanda and Ānanda to fulfill my wish."
"I shall provide various offerings.
The Buddha said to Ānanda and Nanda,
"From this day forward, do not go to that village."
The World-Honored One went alone to the women’s quarters;
from one day until the third day,
he emitted a golden light.
He transformed the devas and humans,
yet this woman did not awaken.
Later, on another day, the World-Honored One...
Furthermore, he took Ānanda and Nanda and walked beneath the trees;
because the courtesan felt love and reverence for these two bhikṣus, she [accompanied them].
From afar, he scattered many flowers over the Buddha and the two bhikṣus.
Ānanda said to him,
"You may pay homage to the Buddha."
The woman loved Ānanda;
she paid him homage at that moment.
The Buddha then manifested three youths.
They were all fifteen years of age,
with handsome and upright features;
when the girl saw them, she was filled with joy.
To convert the youth,
he prostrated himself on the ground in reverence and said to him:
"Good sir, this house of mine is like the goddess Puṇyavatī;
it is powerful, wealthy, sovereign,
and adorned with all manner of jewels."
I now offer my own body, as well as my male and female servants,
to you, O Great Man, to serve as your attendants for sweeping and cleaning.
If you would deign to accept this,
I shall provide for all your needs according to my wishes, withholding nothing.
The emanated person sat upon the couch.
Before even a meal’s time had passed,
the woman approached him and spoke.
May my wish be fulfilled;
may you transform others without fail,
and for one day and one night, may your mind never grow weary or fatigued.
When the second day arrived, his compassionate heart gradually subsided.
When the third day arrived,
he spoke, saying:
"The husband may rise to eat and drink.
The transformed person immediately rose,
yet they continued to embrace each other without ceasing.
The woman felt regret and remorse,
saying, "My husband,
you are truly a most extraordinary man."
The transformed man said:
"According to the laws of my former lives,
whenever one has sexual intercourse with a woman..."
After twelve days had passed, they finally rested.
When the woman heard these words,
she was like a person choking on food.
Being unable to vomit it up and unable to swallow it down,
his body was racked with pain.
It is as if being pounded by a pestle;
when the fourth watch arrives,
it is as if being crushed under the wheels of a chariot.
On the fifth day, it is as if iron balls have entered the body;
on the sixth day, [it is even more so].
Her limbs were all in pain,
as if arrows had pierced her heart.
The woman thought to herself:
"I have heard that the Prince of Śuddhodana is always present to rescue those in distress;
why does he not come today to save me?"
Having formed this thought,
he was filled with remorse and reproached himself:
"From this day forth until the end of my life..."
One should not crave sensual desires;
it would be better to dwell in the same room as tigers, wolves, lions, and other fierce beasts.
"I shall not endure this suffering.
Having spoken these words,
he rose again to eat and drink.
Whether walking or sitting together, there was nothing that could be done;
the transformed person also became angry and spat, saying,
"You wicked woman!"
"You have ruined my livelihood.
Now I shall merge my body with yours into one place."
"It would be better to die early.
If my parents and kinsmen come searching for me,"
Where could I hide myself?
I would rather hang myself than endure such shame.
The woman said,
"I have no use for such wretched things.
You may die as you please."
The conjured man took a knife and stabbed his own neck;
blood stained the woman's body,
and he collapsed on the ground in a faint.
The woman could not prevail;
she was likewise unable to escape death.
After two days had passed, her body became livid, foul-smelling, and blackened.
On the third day, it swells; on the fourth day,
it becomes putrid and溃 (festered/ruptured),
with the discharge of feces and urine.
And various evil insects [emerge],
with splashing blood and pus smeared all over the woman's body.
The woman felt extreme loathing and aversion, yet she could not escape;
by the fifth day, her skin and flesh were gradually rotting away.
By the sixth day, the flesh had completely fallen away.
By the seventh day, [the bones were exposed].
There is only stinking bone,
as sticky as glue or lacquer,
adhering to the woman's body.
The woman made this vow:
"If the various devas and the rishis..."
"The Prince of Śuddhodana can deliver me from this suffering;
I shall offer him this house."
When he gives away all precious treasures as alms,
he forms this thought:
The Buddha was preceded by Ānanda, Nanda, and Śakra,
who held a precious incense burner and burned priceless incense.
The Brahma King followed behind,
holding a great precious parasol,
while immeasurable devas performed music and dance.
The Buddha emitted his constant light, illuminating heaven and earth.
The entire great assembly all beheld the Tathāgata as he proceeded to this woman’s tower.
At that time, when the woman saw the Buddha,
she felt shame and remorse;
having no place to hide her bones, she was at a loss.
He took various white cotton cloths and immeasurable quantities of incense to wrap the stinking bones,
yet the power of the stench remained as it was before.
It could not be concealed.
When the woman saw the World-Honored One,
she immediately paid him homage.
Because of her sense of shame and remorse,
her body became transparent down to the bones;
suddenly, a stinking skeleton appeared upon the woman's back.
The woman wept and said,
"The Tathāgata’s merit and compassion are immeasurable.
If you can enable me to be free from this suffering..."
"May the resolve of this disciple never falter.
By the power of the Buddha's spiritual authority,
the stinking bone did not appear.
The woman was greatly rejoiced;
she prostrated herself before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"Bhagavān, all that I now hold dear I offer as a gift to the Buddha.
May the Buddha bestow his blessing upon it, and may his Brahma-voice flow forth in harmony."
Upon hearing this, the woman was filled with joy.
At that very moment, she attained the stage of Srotāpanna. This concludes the seventh fascicle of the *Buddhasamādhi-sūtra*.
Chapter Seventeen: Manifesting Five Fingers as Five Lions. "Good sons, [the Buddha] manifested five fingers as five lions."
I entered the great city of Rājagṛha and went on my alms-round in due order. Devadatta—
He instructed King Ajātaśatru to immediately release the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla,
intending to cause harm to me and my disciples.
At that time, I immediately entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and extended my hand to show him;
from the five fingers, there appeared five lions.
Upon seeing this elephant, his heart was filled with terror;
he lost control of his bowels and bladder and threw his entire body to the ground.
"Prostrate at my feet.
Good son, at that time, my fingers truly had no lions."

This is due to the power of the roots of goodness cultivated through compassion. It causes them to be subdued and emerge into Great Nirvana. (From the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Volume 14). 18. Scattering a Massive Rock with a Toe. Furthermore, son of good family: [The Buddha said: "Furthermore, son of good family, in the past, immeasurable, incalculable, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *kalpas* ago, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. At that time, there was a king named Mahādeva who ruled over Jambudvīpa. He possessed great wealth and vast resources, and his territory was as expansive as the four continents. His life span was eighty-four thousand years. He had a son named Mahāpraṇāda, who was handsome, upright, and possessed of great strength. His physical form was like that of a *Nārāyaṇa*, and he could lift up Mount Sumeru with one hand. At that time, King Mahādeva, having heard that the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū had appeared in the world, went out to meet him with a retinue of eighty-four thousand people. Having seen the Buddha, he prostrated at his feet and circumambulated him three times before sitting to one side. Then, the World-Honored One, knowing the king’s thoughts, preached the Dharma for him extensively. Having heard the Dharma, the king and his retinue attained the stage of non-retrogression. After the king had left, the prince Mahāpraṇāda went to the Buddha’s place. Having seen the Buddha, he prostrated at his feet and sat to one side. The Buddha then preached the Dharma for him extensively. Having heard the Dharma, the prince attained the stage of non-retrogression. At that time, the prince thought to himself: ‘I have now obtained this supreme human body; I must practice the path with diligence so that I may not waste it. Thinking thus, he took off his upper garment, placed it on his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, I now wish to renounce my home and follow the Buddha to study the Way. May the World-Honored One grant me permission. The Buddha said: ‘Son of good family, you may go according to your wish. Then the prince Mahāpraṇāda, having received the Buddha’s permission, immediately shaved his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and followed the Buddha.

The Buddha then taught him the various methods of meditation and concentration. After practicing diligently for seven days, he attained the fruit of Arhatship. At that time, King Mahādeva heard that his son had become a monk and attained Arhatship. He felt deep resentment and anger, thinking: ‘My son has abandoned me and gone to join those shaven-headed ones. I shall go and destroy their Dharma. With this thought, he gathered a great army of eighty-four thousand men and set out toward the Buddha’s location. When the Arhat Mahāpraṇāda learned of this, he thought: ‘If I do not manifest some supernatural power, the king will surely destroy the Buddha’s Dharma. Thinking thus, he rose from his seat, went to the king, and stood before him. The king then asked: ‘Who are you? The Arhat replied: ‘I am your son, Mahāpraṇāda. The king said: ‘I have no such son. You must be a demon or a ghost who has come to deceive me. The Arhat said: ‘I am truly your son. Why do you not believe me? Then the Arhat extended his right hand and stroked the king’s head. At that moment, the king remembered his past lives and realized: ‘This is indeed my son. He wept and said: ‘My son, why did you abandon me? I have committed many evil deeds; I pray you, teach me how to repent. The Arhat then preached the Dharma for him extensively. Having heard the Dharma, the king and his retinue all attained the stage of non-retrogression. At that time, the Arhat Mahāpraṇāda thought: ‘The king has already been tamed. I should now return to the Buddha’s presence. He then returned to where the Buddha was. Seeing the Buddha, he prostrated at his feet and sat to one side. The Buddha then praised him, saying: ‘Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you have well performed this work of taming sentient beings. [The Buddha continued: “Furthermore, son of good family, in the past, immeasurable, incalculable, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *kalpas* ago, there was a Buddha named Ratnaśikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha... [The text continues with further accounts of the Buddha’s past lives and miraculous powers, including the scattering of a massive rock with a toe. ... when the multitude wished to lift and move it,

At that time, out of compassion,
I immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness;
those Mallas then saw it at once.
With the big toe of my foot,

He then received it with his hand,
placed it upon his right palm,

He then rejoined them,
causing that wrestler’s arrogant mind to subside;
he immediately expounded for him in brief the various essential points of the Dharma.

Buddha Section (6) 1. Devas, Humans, and Nāgas Divide the Relics and Erect Stūpas.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Malla clansmen of the city of Pāvā—known in the Liang language as *Lìshì* (Wrestlers)—and the Vṛji clansmen of the city of Allakappa, [gathered together].
The Koliya assembly in the kingdom of Rāmagrāma;
the Brahmin assembly in the kingdom of Vaiśālī;
and the Śākya assembly in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
The Licchavi assembly of the kingdom of Vaiśālī;

King Ajātaśatru of the kingdom of Magadha—according to the *Tāi jīng* (Garbha-sūtra), he is called King Youtian, King Dingsheng, King Esheng, King Ajātaśatru, King Zuibingmazu, King Rongyanbingmazu, King Chishengbingmazu, and King Jinggangbingmazu—each with his fourfold army, dispatched the Brahmin Xiangxing (Gautama); according to the *Shisong lü* (Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya), he is called Yinxing, while the *Tāi jīng* calls him Upajīvika, who addressed the Mallas of Kuśinagara, saying:
"The Buddha is my teacher and my supreme honor.
Since he has entered parinirvāṇa within your kingdom,
I have come from afar to request a portion of his relics so that I may return to my own country and erect a stūpa."
"If you would share it with me, I shall take all the national treasures and share them with you.
The Malla replied,
"The World-Honored One descended to this land and attained parinirvāṇa here."
"The people and officials within our own borders should naturally provide for them;
it is not possible to trouble you all from afar.
Thus the various kings deliberated together.
Having spoken humbly and sought peace, since he was not granted [his request],
I shall take it by force, even at the cost of my own life.
The King of Mallas said:
If one wishes to mobilize military forces to oppose him,
it will ultimately be impossible to do so.
The Brahmin of the Gandhāra clan raised his voice and proclaimed among the eight assemblies:
The Buddha has cultivated the patience of goodness for immeasurable eons.
You all should likewise hear and further praise forbearance;
why then raise armies to mutually oppress and seize one another?
"This is not a respectful treatment.
Since the śarīra is now present, it should simply be divided into eight portions so that the people in every place may all be able to make offerings."
"You all have likewise received the Buddha's precepts and recite his words;
why then do you contend over the śarīra and proceed to harm one another?
The Mallas replied:
"I respectfully follow your proposal.
Thereupon, the brahmin Dhūma divided [the property] into eight portions.
Then Śakra-devānām-indra immediately manifested himself as a human being and said to the kings:
"We gods also have our share. If we contend by force together, there will be victory and defeat."
"It would be fortunate if you would grant it to us; there is no need for such difficulty.
Then the Dragon King Anavatapta, the Dragon King Vāsuki, and the Dragon King Elāpattra said to the eight kings:
"We, too, should have a share of the relics."
When he did not see that they were being subdued by his superior strength, Upagika said,
"Gentlemen, stop! You should divide it among yourselves."
He then divided it into three portions:
one portion he gave to the devas,
and one portion he gave to the nāga kings.
One portion belongs to the Eight Kings.
They measure it using a jar smeared with honey;
having received their respective portions, the devas return to the heavens and erect stupas made of the seven precious substances.
The various nāgas each received their portions and returned to their nāga palaces, where they also erected jeweled stūpas.
King Aśoka together with them counted the portions, and each obtained eighty-four thousand śarīras.
There remained a single morsel from the Buddha’s own mouth that no one dared to take;
because King Ajātaśatru had initially sought the relics with such profound sincerity—throwing himself to the ground and fainting from exhaustion—they all held it together and gave it to him.
King Ajātaśatru was filled with joy, and as the drums and music shook the heavens,
the Nanda Dragon King encountered him midway and said,
"The Buddha has left behind his relics; take one portion and give it to me."
The king said,
"It cannot be obtained.
The dragon said:
"I am Nandaśi. I can lift up your kingdom and hurl it eighty thousand li away, grinding it into dust.
The king was immediately struck with terror and gave him the Buddha’s hair.
The dragon erected a stupa at the foot of Mount Sumeru,
eighty-four thousand li in height,
a towering crystal and lapis lazuli structure.
When King Ajātaśatru passed away,
Aśoka obtained his kingdom.
At that time, a high minister said to King Aśoka:
Nanda showed the dragon first, and Ajātaśatru seized and took away the Buddha’s bowl.
When Aśoka heard of this,
he immediately commanded the king of the spirits to create an iron net and an iron basket.
He placed Mount Sumeru beneath the waters, intending to bind and capture the Dragon King.
The Dragon King was greatly terrified and, consulting with his ministers, said:
"Aśoka serves the Buddha; while he is fast asleep, we shall seize his palace and transport it to the waters beneath Mount Sumeru."
If he goes beneath the Crystal Stūpa and meets him in person to recount the full details from beginning to end, his anger will surely subside.
He then dispatched a dragon to carry away Aśoka’s palace;
when [Aśoka] awoke from sleep, he did not know where it was.
He saw a crystal stupa eighty-four thousand *li* high;
with joy and fear mingled in his heart,
Nandō revealed himself as a dragon, emerged, and took his leave with words of thanks.
"King Ajātaśatru himself gave these to me; I did not take them by force.
In the past, Śākyamuni Tathāgata made a covenant with me, saying:
'After my parinirvāṇa, at the time when the kalpa is nearing its end, all the sūtras, vinayas, as well as the kashāyas and alms bowls, shall be taken and stored within this stūpa.'"
When Maitreya descends, he shall once again bring it forth.
The dragon delivered it to the royal palace and placed it in its original location.
Then, the Brahmin Dhūma said:
The *Śāriputra-buddhavaṃśa-uttaratantra-sūtra* states: "I shall return to the village of Kuṇḍalavana and erect a stūpa for the jar.
The Mallas shall grant it to me;
then, with both the jar and the śarīra contained within the jar, we shall together erect a precious stūpa."
The brahmin and householder Pārayana spoke again, saying,
"Give me the charcoal from where the Buddha was cremated;
I shall return to my own country and erect a charcoal stūpa."
The master of the Way from the country of Xing traveled abroad seeking earth and ashes, which he brought back to his own country to erect a stūpa.
The same was done by the Mallas.
Furthermore, there were those who erected precious stūpas at the sites where the cremation took place.
There were forty-nine hu of ash, charcoal, and earth,
and forty-nine jeweled stupas were erected;

in each were placed tall pillars, Dharma wheels, silk banners, and two scrolls of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-nidāna*, the *Bodhisattvagarbha-sūtra*, and the *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra*.
2. King Aśoka Constructs Eighty-four Thousand Stūpas. King Aśoka constructed eighty-four thousand stūpas. [The second section:
King Aśoka arrayed his fourfold army and went to open seven stūpas in order to take the relics; only the Nāga stūpa remained.
The Dragon General entered the palace and said, "I have made offerings to this stūpa; I pray that you will allow me to keep it.
The King immediately granted his permission.
Upon returning to his kingdom, he fashioned eighty-four thousand precious caskets and distributed the relics throughout them.
He further created eighty-four thousand precious vases, as well as various banners and canopies.
He entrusted the yakṣas with the task of erecting stūpas everywhere throughout Jambudvīpa, from all lands to the great oceans.
First, he consulted the arhat Yaśas, saying:
"I wish to erect eighty-four thousand stūpas within a single day and a single thought-moment, so that they may all be completed simultaneously."
The Arhat Yaśas praised them with great admiration.
Later, the King compared their merits with those of the dragon,
weighing both images on a scale.
The dragon was heavy while the king was light.
The king extensively invited the assembly of monks to cultivate merit without ceasing;
later, they weighed them again together.
Balancing lightness and gravity,
the king further cultivated this practice and came to know that his merits increased day by day.
He raised an army to go and subdue [the region].
As he first set out upon the road,
the dragon kings, both great and small, all came forward to welcome him.
One stupa containing the śarīra was also respectfully presented to the King.

Subsequently, stupas were constructed wherever the Buddha attained the Way or converted beings; according to the first fascicle of the *Aśokarāja-sūtra* and the first fascicle of the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*, there were one thousand two hundred monasteries within the King’s domain.
He also had one thousand two hundred banners made of woven golden threads;
furthermore, he intended to personally suspend and scatter a thousand-petaled golden lotus flower,
but while he was just preparing for this, he fell gravely ill.
Fearing that he might deviate from his original intention, [the King] wept with tears falling.
The śramaṇa said to the King,
"The merit you have cultivated is beyond calculation."
Since your mind is now set right, why indulge in grief?
Simply maintain single-minded concentration;
I shall cause the King to attain his desired fruit.
The śramaṇa then used his supernatural powers to cause one thousand two hundred temples to appear before the king;
the suffering of his illness was immediately extinguished,
and he wished to fasten the various banners.
All the various *kṣetras* bowed their heads to the King’s hand, fulfilling his original vows.
His life was extended by twenty-five years. This is recorded in the *Kāśyapa-sūtra*, as well as the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*. Furthermore, for twenty years, he promoted meritorious deeds.
At the time of death,
one should maintain mindfulness of the Triple Gem with an uninterrupted mind,
giving up all that is held dear to fully accomplish Bodhi. (From the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Volume 25).

3. The Causes of the Eighty-four Thousand Stūpas. Regarding the causes of the eighty-four thousand stūpas, Ānanda asked the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what prior causes and conditions led to their construction? Ānanda addressed the Buddha thus.
He caused eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas to arise for the distributed relics of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a king named Prasenajit who ruled over eighty-four thousand kingdoms in Jambudvīpa."
At that time, there was a Buddha in the world named Puṣya.
The king, together with his ministers and subjects, made offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
Then the king thought to himself:
In a remote borderland kingdom, where the location was secluded and the people had no means to cultivate merit,
[the king] immediately summoned a painter to depict an image of the Buddha.
He distributed these throughout distant lands so that all might obtain the opportunity for making offerings.
At that time, the painters examined the Buddha’s marks and signs;
having managed to complete one part, they forgot the rest and were unable to finish it.
Then King Prasenajit—
He blended various pigments and painted a portrait with his own hand to serve as a model;
other masters copied and studied it, producing eighty-four thousand images which were distributed throughout eighty-four thousand small kingdoms.
All the minor kings received my offerings;
King Prasenajit was none other than I myself.
By virtue of this merit, my body came to possess the thirty-two marks of a great man.
After the Parinirvāṇa, eighty-four thousand stupas were further established; from the *Xiányújīng* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish), Volume Four.
4. King Puṣyamitra destroys the eighty-four thousand stupas. Regarding King Puṣyamitra’s destruction of the eighty-four thousand stupas: after King Aśoka passed away...
The ministers wished to establish the crown prince to succeed to the royal throne.
Among them was a great minister named Anurādha.
He said:
"The Great King Aśoka vowed to relinquish a full ten trillion pieces of gold."
Although he performed various meritorious deeds,
he was still short by four hundred million;
the Prince sealed them away and would not give them.
The king relinquished the land of Jambudvīpa to bestow it upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
desiring thereby to fulfill [his vow].
"Today the entire earth belongs to the Triple Gem.
How can we simply make the Prince the king?
The ministers then prepared four hundred million pieces of gold and sent them to the temple, after which they installed him together.
Knowing him to be the fourth king of the world, named Puṣyamitra,
he asked his ministers:
"What should I do so that my name and deeds may endure for a long time?
A minister then addressed the king, saying:
The former king Aśoka constructed eighty-four thousand stūpas for the Tathāgata and restored various kinds of offerings.
Their fame and virtue have been handed down through generations without interruption.
The king said,
"The former kings possessed great majestic power."
"He can accomplish this task; I cannot do it.
Let me consider another matter."
A certain minister said,
"There are two kinds of dharmas whose names are transmitted without perishing."
First is the performance of good;
second is the performance of evil.
The former kings constructed stupas.
"Now, if Your Majesty destroys the stupa,
both [the merit and the offense] will remain imperishable.
The King then followed his advice.
He immediately mobilized the fourfold army and proceeded toward the monastery.
First, he arrived before the middle gate of the Kukkuṭārāma,
where there was a stone lion.
He immediately let out a lion's roar.
Upon hearing it, the king was struck with terror and retreated back into the city.
Thus he asked a second and a third time,
calling out to the bhikṣus and questioning them:
"Between destroying a stūpa and destroying a dwelling, which would be better?"

and the second was named Viśuddhanetra.
These two sons possessed great supernormal powers.
Cultivating the bodhisattva path through merit and wisdom,
the Buddha, wishing to guide King Subhavyūha and out of compassion for sentient beings, preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. At that time,
Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra addressed their mother, saying:
"I pray that you, Mother, will go to the Buddha Cloud-Thunder Sound King of Hosts of Flowers and Wisdom.
We, too, shall follow as attendants to offer worship and pay our respects.
His mother said to her sons:
"Your father believes in and accepts the teachings of non-Buddhists and is deeply attached to the Brahmanical dharma.
You should go and inform him so that we may go together.
The mother spoke again, saying:
"You should remember that your father witnessed these divine transformations.
Thereupon, the two sons leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and manifested the eighteen miraculous powers.
Seeing their supernatural might, the father was filled with great joy; joining his palms toward his sons, he said:
"Who is your teacher? The two sons replied,
"The Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom is currently seated upon the Dharma throne beneath a bodhi tree made of the seven precious gems, preaching the Lotus Sutra."
"He is our teacher.
The father said to his son,
"I wish to see him now."
The two sons descended from the sky and said to their mother, "Our father the king has now attained faith and understanding and has resolved to attain bodhicitta.
We have already performed the work of a Buddha for our father;
we pray that you will grant us your permission."
He went forth from home to practice the path under that Buddha.
His mother said, "I grant you permission,
for a Buddha is difficult to encounter."
Thereupon, the two sons said to their parents,
"We pray that you will go at once to the place where the Buddha is to behold him in person and make offerings.
Then, King Subhavyūha, together with his ministers and retinue, [set out].
Lady Śuddhāśaya, together with the ladies-in-waiting of the inner palace and her two sons— totaling forty-two thousand people—
went to the Buddha at once.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.
The king was greatly delighted.
At that time, the king and his consort immediately untied a necklace of genuine pearls from their necks and scattered it over the Buddha.
In the midst of the void, there appeared a transformed jeweled terrace supported by four pillars.
Within it was a great jeweled couch spread with hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial garments.
Upon it sat a Buddha in the full lotus posture, emitting a great radiance.
At that time, the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Abiding-King-Flower-Wisdom addressed the fourfold assembly, saying:
"Do you see this King Subhavyūha standing before me with palms joined?"
This king shall become a bhikṣu within my Dharma and, through diligent cultivation of the dharmas that assist the path to buddhahood, shall attain buddhahood under the name Śālarājā.
His land shall be named Mahāprabha, and his eon shall be named Mahocchrayarāja.
The king immediately entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother.
Together with his consort, two sons, and all his attendants, he left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma.
Having gone forth, for eighty-four thousand years he constantly practiced with diligence the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
After this, he attained the Samādhi Adorned with All Pure Merits and ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees.
This King Wondrous Adornment is none other than the present Bodhisattva Flower Virtue (*Puṣpaśrī*).
The Lady Pure Virtue (Śuddhaguṇā) was the Bodhisattva Radiant Adornment Mark (Prabhāsa-vyūha-lakṣaṇa).
Her two sons were the present-day Bodhisattvas Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja) and Medicine Superior (Bhaiṣajyasamudgata). This is from the seventh fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

4. Kṣāntivādin Residing in the Mountains Encounters the King’s Men Who Cut Him to Pieces. Once, in a former life when he was a bodhisattva, he was a brahmin named Kṣāntivādin who dwelt in the mountains.

Dwelling beneath trees, subsisting on fruits and spring water, his internal defilements were completely eliminated; he attained the six supernormal powers and the wisdom that knows all things exhaustively.
His sublime fragrance wafted everywhere, reaching throughout the eight directions, above, and below.
Sages and commoners alike will sigh in praise and protect the nation.
Wind and rain will follow their proper seasons, the five grains will ripen in abundance, and calamities and poisons will be extinguished.
The king’s name shall be Kāli.
He entered the mountains to hunt,
pursuing the deer and following their tracks until he passed before the Bodhisattva.
The king questioned him about this.
The Bodhisattva remained silent.
The king said, "I am a beggar who is about to die; I am the most honored person in my entire kingdom."
The questioner replied, "I have been following the tracks of this beast for some time now, yet you pretend to look down; my power is such that I can slay you.
The Bodhisattva said:
"I shall listen to you, O King.
[The king] asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a man of forbearance."
The king, enraged, drew his sword and severed his right arm.
The Bodhisattva said, "My resolve is set upon the Unsurpassed Way; I do not contend with the times."
"If even this king can practice patience toward me, how much more so should the common people?
I vow that when I attain Buddhahood, I shall deliver him first,
so as not to allow sentient beings to emulate his evil deeds."
The king asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"I am a person who practices patience.
Furthermore, my left hand was severed, as were both my feet, ears, and nose;
the blood flowed like a spring, and the pain was immeasurable."
Heaven and earth shook, and the sun and moon lost their brilliance.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings all arrived together and, with one voice, spoke in indignation:
"This king is cruel and tyrannical."
He said to the Daoist practitioners,
"We shall execute him along with his wife and children,
and annihilate the entire state to manifest his evil."
The Daoist replied, "What words are these?
This is because in my previous lives I did not honor the Buddhist teachings and instead inflicted poison upon others."
When evil is committed, calamity follows, just as a shadow is bound to a form.
When the common people witnessed these transformations, they rushed to confess their transgressions, crying out with one voice:
"It is because the Daoist masters dwell here that disasters are warded off and misfortunes extinguished."
Your foolish majesty does not distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy, nor do you know when to withdraw or advance.
You have brought evil upon the Original Sage.
We only pray that the Holy One will not report us to the Supreme Deity.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Your Majesty has treated me with cruelty and harshness, yet my heart feels compassion for you as a mother thinks of her infant.
What fault have the common people committed that they should not be spared? Please do not harbor such doubts."
The Bodhisattva had a younger brother living on a different mountain.
Observing with his divine eye,
he saw that at that time the devas and nāgas were deliberating upon the king’s wickedness, and there was none among them who did not harbor resentment.
Fearing that his brother might harbor thoughts detrimental to his virtue,
he used his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) to come to his brother's side,
took off the severed hands, feet, ears, and nose, and restored them to their original places.
The younger brother returned and continued it, whereupon it was restored to its original state.
The elder brother said,
"My faith in universal compassion has now been manifested."
The heavenly deities and terrestrial spirits were all moved by both grief and joy;
they bowed their heads in reverence, praised him, exhorted one another, received his admonitions, and withdrew.
The one named Kṣāntivādin was my own self.
The younger brother was Maitreya;
the king was Kauṇḍinya. (From the *Chudujiwuji ji*, fascicle five). 5.
Receiving Celestial Precepts through Silence and Attaining the Four Dhyānas by Contemplating the Meaning. Five times, in the city of Rājagṛha, the general Siṃha produced a son in his household.
At the time of his birth, the devas of the void spoke these words:
"The youth constantly contemplates the Dharma and reflects upon the Dharma; in whatever he speaks, let him not speak of worldly affairs."
One should always proclaim the supramundane Dharma;
one should always guard the mouth, be cautious in speech, and speak little.
One must not give rise to various discursive thoughts regarding worldly affairs.
"One should rely on the meaning and not rely on the words.
At that time, having heard this, the boy no longer wept and was free from the characteristics of an infant;
for seven days his countenance remained serene and joyful, he brought delight to those who saw him, and his eyes never blinked.
At that time, someone said to his parents, "This child is inauspicious; he should not be raised.
His parents replied:
Although this child is silent,
his physical faculties are complete;
you should know that this child must possess merit and fortune, and is not the cause of any misfortune.
He was given the name Wuyan (Silent).
In time, the youth Wuyan gradually grew up to the likeness of an eight-year-old child,
whom all people delighted to behold.
Wherever the Dharma was being taught and the wheel of Dharma was being turned,
he delighted in hearing and receiving the Dharma without uttering a word.
At that time, he remained silent together with his parents, retinue, and kinsmen.
Traveling between the realms of form and desire, he went into the midst of the Jewel Monastery.
Seeing the Buddha and the bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions, he gave rise to a heart of great joy.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
as for the son born to General Siṃha,
who possesses all his physical faculties yet is unable to speak— by what karma was this brought about?”
The Buddha said,
"One should not disparage this youth. Why is that?"
Such a person is indeed a great bodhisattva.
Having planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas,
they have not regressed from the path to enlightenment.
When this child was born, many devas came as before to exhort him;
following their instructions, he reflected in silence and attained the four dhyānas.
By manifesting such a body, he is able to subdue immeasurable sentient beings.
By the power of his vows and his supernormal powers,
he caused the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly to each see a great lotus flower upon his right hand, as large as a chariot wheel,
perfect in color and fragrance, and of the most exquisite beauty.
It was a sight that all people delighted to behold.
Upon each flower pedestal sat a bodhisattva in the full lotus posture, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence.
Seeing this great power of supernatural manifestation, they remained silent,
bowed their heads, joined their palms, and cried out, "Namo Buddhāya.
Within all the flower pedestals, all the bodhisattvas likewise spoke these words.
The worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shook in six ways.
The devas in the void offered worship to the Buddha with exquisite incense, flowers, and various kinds of music.
At that time, Wu-yen (Avalokiteśvara) and the various bodhisattvas leaped up into the air to a height of seven tala trees and spoke verses in praise of the Buddha;
this is from the seventeenth fascicle of the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra.

6. Changbei Eastward in Search of the Dharma Encounters the Buddha Who Shows the Way. Changbei Eastward in Search of the Dharma Encounters the Buddha Who Shows the Way. Six Groups of Benefactors: Long ago, he was a bodhisattva.
He was named Constant Compassion (Sadāśoka).
He beheld the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha of the world; yet he also saw that the world was defiled and turbid.
Turning one's back on the correct path and heading toward the heterodox, with flowery pretenses and a pursuit of profit,
is like a moth delighting in a flame.
One should instead take the four immeasurables and the six perfections as the dwelling place of eternal peace.
Yet the world abandons the Buddha and pursues those dangerous calamities, thereby destroying itself.
The Bodhisattva is constantly filled with sorrow, desolation, and lamentation.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Jingfa Wuhui (Stainless Radiant Dharma).
Not long after his parinirvāṇa,
the sūtras and the Dharma were completely exhausted;
yet he constantly wept as he saw that Buddha in his dreams preaching the Dharma for him.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva’s mental defilements were eliminated and he entered a state of pure concentration.
He immediately abandoned his wife and children to enter the seclusion of the mountains,
where he sustained himself naturally with fruits and water.
Beating my breast, I wailed in grief:
"I have failed to meet the Buddha, nor have I seen the Dharma or the Sangha.
As the Great Way reached its ultimate limit, my lamentation finally ceased.
The celestial deity descended and said,
"O wise one, do not lament any longer.
The Buddha possesses a Great Dharma called the Radiance of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā)."
All Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained realization through this alone.
You should seek it out, recite and study its text, contemplate and master its meaning,
and reverently put it into practice.
"You shall certainly attain Buddhahood.
He then gazed up with constant sorrowful longing and said,
"From whom shall I hear this sublime Dharma?"
By what means shall you go to which land, and what will be the name of your teacher’s clan?
The celestial being replied:
"Proceed straight toward the east."
There is no mindfulness of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
The mind severs all worldly aspirations and remains unswerving in its resolve.
I instruct you to behold this sublime scripture of the Perfection of Wisdom.
Changbei said, "Yes," and from beginning to end he kept it hidden.
The celestial being spoke again:
He applied himself with diligence to preserve it,
but suddenly it vanished.
Following the instructions, the Bodhisattva traveled eastward to search for it.
After several days, it ceased.
He reflected deeply within himself, saying:
"I have meager merit from my past lives."
The sovereign and his ministers were in a state of confusion;
none among them knew of the Buddha,
save for our venerable teacher who dispels darkness.
"How many *li* is it from here?
[The deity replied: "To the utmost limit of sincerity and devotion, one may move the Buddha of the Upper Realm to appear before them, with the various devas attending as his retinue."
He praised the Bodhisattva, saying, "Excellent, excellent! Such a thing is rare in this world.
Seeing the Buddha, the Bodhisattva was both joyful and sorrowful;
he prostrated himself and spoke.
"I pray that the Buddha will take pity on me and preach the sūtra for my sake.
The Buddha told him:
"The three realms are all empty."
"Indeed, existence is necessarily non-existence; the myriad things are like illusions, arising and ceasing like waves upon water. Behold the world as such, and do not forget this.
Thereupon, he traveled eastward for twenty thousand li.
There is a land named Gandhāva,
the city of all bodhisattvas.
Within this single country, there are only superior beings and no ordinary people.
I wish to describe to you the virtues of a bodhisattva.
Though the number of kalpas has already come to an end, his virtues remain inexhaustible.
This bodhisattva is named Dharmāgata.
Among those noble ones, he was like the moon among the stars;
cherishing the various sūtras, he taught others by reciting them repeatedly,
while the bodhisattvas received, recited, copied, and read them.
The originator of this sutra will surely be your teacher; you should be encouraged to approach him, for he shall explain it to you.
Constantly weeping, whether in meditation or awake, he looked around to his left and right, but no longer beheld the Buddha.
His heart was filled with grief and he shed tears. He said:
"From where have the numinous radiances of the Buddhas come, and now they pass away? (From the *Chududu Wujiji*, Volume 7). 7.

Shanxin Travels Eastward in Search of Half a Gāthā; He Treads Mud Without Sinking. In a world devoid of the True Dharma, the Bodhisattva Shanxin traveled eastward in search of half a gāthā. A voice from the sky said: "Tread upon the mud, yet you shall not sink. (From the *Shanxin Pusa*).
To the east of here, ten thousand yojanas away, there is a king named Supratiṣṭhita.
Long ago, a Tathāgata appeared in the world and has long since passed into parinirvāṇa.
During the decline of the Semblance Dharma,
there was a woman who was born into a state of extreme lowliness and whose appearance was so hideous as to be without peer in the world;
yet, she was somehow able to recognize half a phrase or a single verse.
He manifested that there was something transmitted, so that one might go and inquire about his doubts.
There was a mire extending ten thousand li in both length and breadth; anyone who stepped upon it would sink immediately.
It was such that even a bird flying over it could not pass, nor could a single hair bear its weight.
"You are now exhausted and afflicted, with your hands and feet torn and split; how can you advance further?
Hearing this, I leaped up with joy and ran eastward to the place of the mire."
I shall sacrifice my life and body by casting myself down, intending to sink into the depths.
When I throw my body,
whatever my body may touch—
A small path emerged,
pure white and straight;
as I trod upon it, there were no longer any further hardships.
He proceeded directly to that country and entered the city of Suvilīta.
Lamenting and reproaching himself for not having beheld the World-Honored One,
he saw this woman dwelling in a lowly and humble state.
The dwelling was dilapidated and full of holes,
and the person’s appearance was coarse and vulgar;
yet I regarded him with reverence, perceiving him as a Buddha.
They paid homage, prostrated, circumambulated, and offered praise;
they looked up to her with reverence, requesting that she serve as their Great Teacher,
and prayed that she would grant them instruction so that they might fulfill their deep faith.
The woman replied, "The sublime Dharma of the Buddhas is immeasurable and boundless; that which I have heard is but a single half-verse.
If you wish to hear it, I shall speak it now."
"Commit no evil; practice all that is good.
When I heard these words, my body and mind became cool and refreshed, my faculties were stilled, and I was naturally subdued.
As I recited and practiced them, contemplating their meaning, I thoroughly penetrated this profound principle.
He immediately attained supernormal powers and flew back to his own country, where he proclaimed this verse everywhere.
By virtue of this merit, I have attained firm faith in the Buddha-dharma that cannot be destroyed.
The multitudes of Māras were subdued and all turned to conversion.
There has never been such a faith as this: "I am always within birth and death;

for the sake of sentient beings, I reveal this faith so that they may practice it and attain deliverance. This concludes the first fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-niyata-caryā-uttara* (The Supreme Practice of the Bodhisattva’s Definitive Course).

8. Throughout all the world, there is the case of one who, though beloved by his teacher’s wife, suffers for disobeying her commands. In Śrāvastī, not far from the northern part of the city, there was a village named Sana. There lived a poor Brahmin woman.
Her name was Bhadrā.
A son was born from her womb,
named Sarvalokābhyudgata.
He lost his father when he was young;
at the age of twelve,
his physical appearance, vitality, and human characteristics were foremost among all.
He was intelligent, eloquent, wise, and skilled in explaining subtle words.
Furthermore, there was another village named Phalakaśī,
where there lived an elder Brahmin teacher.
His name was Maṇibhadra.
He was thoroughly proficient in the four Vedas,
and all those in the world currently received instruction from him.
Humble and reverent, he served with all his heart; his faculties were pure and refined, and he maintained whatever he received.
When the Teacher accepted the King’s invitation, he left behind Ānanda to remain and guard the dwelling before departing.
The Brahmin’s wife was young and beautiful;
seeing her, he conceived a deep sense of passion in his heart.
Suddenly forgetting his decorum and shame, he reached out and seized her garment.
At that time, the world appeared bright.
"O Noble One, you are now my mother;
how can you act contrary to the Dharma?"
Feeling inward shame and trepidation, he cast off his robe and fled far away.
The teacher’s wife, her passions aroused, wept as she thought of him, saying:
"Alas, I see that our union has been severed; he does not follow my will."
Thinking, "He will certainly not comply, and he must take my life," she immediately tore at her own body with her fingernails and,
adopting the deceptive adornments of a woman, embellished her person.
She tied herself with a rope so that her feet did not leave the ground.
When her husband returned, he saw his wife cutting the rope with a knife;
he raised a loud cry and asked why she was doing this.
The wife replied,
"In this world, there are those who, being powerful, see fit to oppress others and commit such acts.
Her husband then reflected and said:
On the day he was first born into the world, all the swords and blades belonging to the kṣatriyas spontaneously drew themselves from their scabbards;
their sharp points all curled inward and fell to the ground.
At that time, all the kṣatriyas were seized with great terror.
One should know that on the day of his birth there were such signs as these;
this person possesses the power of great virtue,
which is manifested to the world.
"You are an evil person who has insulted those worthy of honor.
You are no longer a true Brahmin;
you must kill a thousand people to expiate your sin."
In this world, people naturally revere and follow the instructions of their respected teachers.
Thus, he addressed his teacher, saying:
"Alas, Upādhyāya! To kill a thousand people is not something that I ought to do."
The teacher then said to him,
"Are you such an evil person that you do not wish to be reborn in heaven as a brahmin?
He replied:
The Upādhyāya said, "Excellent! He received the command and immediately killed a thousand people, returning to prostrate at the teacher's feet.
Upon hearing and seeing this, the teacher gave rise to a sense of wonder and said, "You are a person of great evil; why have you not yet died?"
He further thought to himself, "I shall now cause them to die," and addressed them, saying,
"Kill one person and take a finger from each."
Having killed a thousand people, he took their fingers to fashion a garland which he placed upon his head before returning;
only then did he attain the status of a brahmin.
For this reason, he was named Aṅgulimāla.
He then said to his teacher, "Excellent, Preceptor; I shall follow your instruction.
He then killed one thousand people, yet he was still short by one.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla’s mother, thinking her son would be hungry,
personally took four kinds of fine food and went to give it to him.
Upon seeing his mother, the son reflected thus:
"May my mother be reborn in the heavens.
He then took up his sword and advanced, intending to take her life,
coming to within one zhang less than ten yojanas from Śrāvastī.
There was a tree there named Aśoka.
At that time, the Buddha approached like an elephant king with his all-encompassing wisdom.
Having seen the World-Honored One, Aṅgulimāla grasped his sword and rushed toward him.
He thought to himself,
"I shall now kill this śramaṇa," but the World-Honored One manifested himself as having already departed.
Aṅgulimāla spoke these verses:
"Stop, stop, great śramaṇa! I am Aṅgulimāla, the prince of King Śuddhodana;
Now you must pay the tax of one finger."
The World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Stop, stop, Aṅgulimāla! You should abide in pure precepts;
I am the Samyaksaṃbuddha, And I grant you the tribute of the sword of wisdom."
At that time, the mother saw the Buddha and Aṅgulimāla engaging in this profound exchange of difficult discourse.
Her mind was subdued, and as she cast her thoughts upon him, she spoke these verses:
"The precious treasury lost long ago is now regained; The eyes ruined by dust and defilement are now purified."
Alas, my son, your mind is deluded; you constantly smear your body with human blood, and a most sharp sword is always in your hand.
Having killed many people, you have formed a heap of corpses.
You must cause this son to follow me; now I respectfully bow my head to the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Many people saw him and reviled him, making it difficult to hear;
thus did your son reprimand me. From the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, Volume One.

9. The Auspicious Vow of Radiant Conduct: Encountering a Woman and Retiring from Family Affairs. The Auspicious Vow of Radiant Conduct: Encountering a Woman and Retiring from Family Affairs. Nine: In the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a seeker of the Way.
His name was Jyotiṣprabha.
Dwelling in forest thickets, he practiced auspicious vows for four million two hundred thousand years, cultivating unimpeded conduct.
Upon entering the kingdom of Śāketa, he encountered the daughter of a potter.
Seeing that this seeker of the Way possessed a beautiful and handsome countenance,
her desire for him grew intense, and she immediately cast herself upon him.
Śaikṣa replied, "I have no desire.
The girl said:
"If it were otherwise, I would destroy myself.
Yaśas thought to himself: 'I have guarded the prohibitions and precepts;
if I were now to violate them, it would not be auspicious.'"
After departing seven paces, she then gave rise to compassion and pity. [She thought:
"If I were to violate the prohibitions and precepts, I would fall into the sin of hell;
if I do not act thus, this woman will destroy herself."
"I would rather let this woman attain peace and security;
I shall endure the pains of hell myself.
Thereupon, the blazing light returned and complied with the woman's wish.
He retired from his family business and practiced for twelve years;
after his life ended, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha said:
If you wish to know who that student of the Dharma, Radiant Light (Jyotirasa), was at that time, could he have been anyone other than myself?
And the potter’s daughter was Gopī. This is recorded in the first fascicle of the *Huishang pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Prajñottara).

10. Regarding the two Tiqilanaletis who disputed and caused five days of darkness: In the past, there were two bodhisattvas whose aspirations were pure and whose conduct was stainless. They fell into a dispute, and because of this contention, they caused five days of darkness. Ten. Long ago, there were two bodhisattvas whose wills were clear and whose practices were pure.
Internally tranquil and free from desire, his outward appearance was like celestial gold.
He carved a dwelling out of rock to dwell in seclusion with a serene mind;
he wore coarse grass for clothing and sat upon grass mats, subsisting on water and drinking from mountain springs.
Pure and unconditioned, his resolve was like empty space.
Fully perfected in the four dhyānas, he attained the wisdom of the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
All the sages of the Śākya clan, the holy ones, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits bowed their heads in reverence to him.
He dwelt in the mountains and marshes for over sixty years,
out of compassion for sentient beings, reverently serving the Triple Gem. His name was Tigrā.
The second was named Nanda.
While Tiṣya was reciting the sūtras, he became so exhausted that he fell asleep and emerged from his place.
At that time, Nanda was also reciting the sūtras; he mistakenly stepped upon Tiṣya’s head.
He wrote a poem titled "Spontaneous Verse upon Seeing an Old Man," saying:
"Whoever treads upon my head,
at dawn when the sun rises, I shall split your head into seven pieces!"
Narada said, "How grave is this oath that you have sworn for the sake of a mere trifle?
Even among common objects there may be accidental contact;
how much more so when people dwell together for years without ever failing to notice one another?"
"You said that if you tried it tomorrow morning, my head would surely shatter.
I shall restrain the sun so that it does not emerge.
Consequently, the sun did not rise for five days, and the entire kingdom was plunged into darkness.
As torches and candles were sought one after another and the various officials failed to attend to their duties, the ruler and his subjects were filled with alarm and confusion.
They assembled all the subordinate officers and invited various Daoist masters.
The King said:
"Wherein lies the fault that the sun does not emerge?
A practitioner among the Daoists replied, "Among the Daoists in the mountains there have been two who engaged in a subtle dispute; they have restrained it so as not to let the sun come forth."
The King asked, "What should be done? He replied,
"If Your Majesty leads your officials and the people, great and small alike, to that place and prostrates yourself to seek reconciliation, they will surely respond with compassion and harmony."
The king immediately issued a decree for them to go to the mountain marshes, where they prostrated themselves, saying:
"The abundance of the realm and the peace of the people are due to the grace of your two venerable selves.
Yet now, being in discord, the entire land has lost its proper course."
"The fault lies with me; my people are without transgression.
I pray that you will compassionately pardon them. Nalāi replied:
