He then pressed his two feet together, causing the seawater to gush forth and be cast beyond the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven said:
In the past, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I heard of his vow:
"I shall certainly become a World-Honored One and deliver sentient beings such as ourselves.
Thereupon, I descended to assist him by clearing away eight-tenths of the water.
The Sea God said in fear,
"This water is exhausted;
my dwelling will be destroyed."
He immediately returned the pearl and proceeded along the road to give alms;
in every country he passed through, there were no longer any impoverished people.
In every place, the various kings reformed their conduct;
they established the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions as the laws of their kingdoms and opened the prisons for a great amnesty.
"Rūṇa reached all sentient beings and eventually attained Buddhahood; he was none other than I.
The father was King Śuddhodana."
The mother was none other than my own mother, Śrīmatī;
the female ascetic at that time was the present-day Jyotiṣkā;
and the deity in the Silver City was the present-day Ānanda.
The deva of the Golden City was Maudgalyāyana;

the deva of the Lapis Lazuli City was Śāriputra. This is from the first fascicle of the *Chutudu Wujie Ji* (Collection on the Infinite Deliverance), as well as the *Xianyu Jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish).
7. King Ghoṣila’s association with women was censured by Ānanda; King Ghoṣila’s association with women was censured by Ānanda. Seven. Ānanda addressed the Buddha.
I recall that in the past, when I entered the city of Śrāvastī,
I saw the Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta on the same bed with a woman.
I thought he had committed an act of impurity and wondered if he were not an extraordinary person.
When those training in the holy life do not give rise to views, perceptions, thoughts, or mental constructions regarding the teaching of the Tathāgata,
at the moment they utter these words, the trichiliocosm shakes in six ways.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Weighty Victory immediately leaped up into the air and remained suspended four zhang and nine chi above the ground,
addressing Ānanda, saying:
"How could one who has committed such forbidden and defiling acts leap into the air and stay suspended in the void?
Before the Tathāgata,
Ānanda threw himself down and immediately repented his transgression.
"How can you harbor such biased views as to seek out the faults of the Great Dragon?
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"As for that woman..."
In a past life, she was the consort of King Bhūmipati for a hundred lifetimes;
her lingering attachment remained unextinguished, and out of greed for the king's countenance, she uttered this vow:
"If King Bhūmipati grants me this wish, I shall follow his instructions.
At that time, King Bhūmipati knew her thoughts in his heart;
he dressed himself properly in the early morning and entered her chamber.
Then he spoke in verse:
"I was foolish and rebellious toward desire, That which all Buddhas do not praise;
But one who can eliminate affection and craving Attains Buddhahood, the highest among men."
At that time, the woman was filled with joy;
she rose from her seat, threw herself upon the ground, and, taking refuge [in the Buddha],
reproached herself, prostrated in submission, and repented her transgressions.
For the sake of the Honored King, he uttered this eulogy:
"I have already departed from all desires; The World-Honored One has praised the virtue of ceasing attachment to affection.
I pray that the Buddha may attain the unsurpassed Way."
Regarding what was previously conceived by the mind, she now confesses her transgressions and feels compassion for all living beings, ultimately resolving to seek the Way.
At that time, King Cūḍāmaṇi bestowed the secret instructions upon her.
After transmigrating through ninety-nine kalpas following this female body, she shall attain Buddhahood,
titled the Tathāgata Free from Countless Hundreds of Thousands of Receptions, Supreme Wisdom Emergence Bodhisattva Sūtra, Volume One.

8. Mahāsattva Who Sacrificed His Life to Save the Multitude When the Sea-Vessel Was Wrecked. When Śākyamuni Buddha was a bodhisattva, he sacrificed his own life to save the multitude when their sea-vessel was wrecked. This is the eighth [tale]. When Śākyamuni Buddha was practicing the path as a bodhisattva...
He was named Mahāsattva.
While crossing the great ocean, his ship was wrecked by a violent wind;
he said to the merchants, "Seize my hair, head, hands, and feet, and I shall carry you across."
Everyone, having seized them, committed suicide with knives.
It is the nature of the waters of the great ocean not to retain corpses;
immediately, a swift wind blew them to the shore. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle Four).

9. The Bodhisattva sits upright in the mountains; a bird’s nest rests upon his head. Though its young are not yet able to fly, he does not leave them. The Bodhisattva sits upright in the mountains; a bird’s nest rests upon his head. Though its young are not yet able to fly, he does not leave them. [This is] the ninth [chapter]: The Bodhisattva in the Mountains.
Sitting upright with a mind of loving-kindness, he remained in contemplation without moving.
When the bird felt its young on its head, it realized they were atop its crown;
fearing the eggs might fall, it did not shift or shake its body.
He abandoned his body and went to that place; though he remained motionless and the bird grew wings, as long as it was still unable to fly, he would not leave.
Thus, knowing this for himself, he spoke this verse:
If one can accomplish this task, being able to remain untainted by the afflictions among those who are gods among gods—
since no virtue surpasses this, that Blessed One is the foremost deity.
Therefore, at the site of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, all merits are fully perfected.
(From the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*, Volume One). 10.

Entering the Sea to Gather Pearls to Relieve Poverty and Suffering. Entering the Sea to Gather Pearls to Relieve Poverty and Suffering. Ten: Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have sought the Way with diligent effort.
From the very beginning, without ceasing for a moment, I brought myself to the attainment of Buddhahood;
I transcended nine kalpas and emerged before Maitreya.
I recall that in times past, when the people of the land were impoverished, I gave rise to a heart of compassion.
He then desired to enter the sea to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
A great assembly of people gathered, hoisting their sails at the mere sight of the wind,
and went before the Sea Dragon King to request the wish-fulfilling jewel from his head.
Upon hearing that he wished to assist the destitute man, the Dragon King immediately gave him the pearl.
Then the merchants each gathered their treasures until they were fully supplied, and they set sail on their ships to return home.
The various nāgas and spirits within the ocean all deliberated together, saying,
"This wish-fulfilling pearl is a supreme treasure of the sea;
it is not something that should be obtained by worldly people."
"How can it be that the ocean is diminished while Jambudvīpa is enriched?
This is truly lamentable.
We must devise a plan to reclaim those jewels; they must not be lost."
At that time, various nāgas and spirits surrounded him day and night, desiring to seize his pearl;
yet, because the power of the wish-fulfilling gem was derived from the venerable virtue of the guide, they were unable to take it away.
Having thus completed the crossing of the sea, [he arrived].
The Bodhisattva leaped for joy and stood by the seashore;
bowing his head and lowering his hands, he offered a prayer of blessing to the Sea God and fastened the jewel around his neck.
At that time, the Sea Dragon King, seizing an opportunity through various causes and conditions, caused the pearl to fall back into the sea.
The leader was deeply moved, thinking, "I traveled into the sea,
braving hardships upon my ship with immeasurable toil and suffering, only to obtain this treasure."
"While I was intended to rescue those who were destitute,
the deity of the sea has instead caused me to fall into the ocean.
He then commanded his attendant at his side to bring a vessel.
"I shall roll back the waters of the ocean until I reach the mud at its bottom;
I will never rest or grow weary until I have obtained the jewel.
Thus, he immediately rolls back the waters, disregarding even his own life.
The water naturally flowed and entered all the vessels.
When the nāgas and devas of the various oceans saw this,
they were filled with fear at the power and vigor of this man’s diligence.
"Truly, such a thing does not exist in this world.
The water will not dry up for long.
He then took the pearl, apologized, and returned it.
"We have just now tested you and did not realize that the power of your diligence was such as this.
In the heavens above and the world below, none can surpass you.
O Guide, having obtained the treasure, you shall carry it back to your kingdom."
He caused it to rain down the seven treasures to provide for all under heaven, so that none remained in insecurity.
The one who was the guide at that time was myself; this is the first fascicle of the *Shengsheng jing* (Sutra on the Birth).
11. Saving the Merchants While Seated in the Sea. Once upon a time, the Bodhisattva entered the sea with five hundred merchants to gather treasures.
Having spent several months at sea, he obtained a heavy cargo of treasures.
As he was about to return to his native land, he encountered a tempestuous wind;
thunder and lightning shook the earth, and water deities gathered like clouds.
Surrounded on all sides like a city, with fire erupting from their eyes and surging waves flooding the mountains,
the multitude cried out,
"We are going to die!"
Terrified and his complexion turning pale, he looked up to heaven seeking mercy.
The Bodhisattva was moved with compassion and thought to himself:
"My quest for Buddhahood is solely for the sake of sentient beings."
A corpse is detested by the Sea God; yet,
for the sake of endangering one's own life to save the multitude,
this is precisely the noble undertaking of a Bodhisattva.
"I shall not pour my own blood into the sea, for I loathe the intent of the sea deity; otherwise, the sailors would never reach the shore.
He said this to the multitude.
"You all must join hands and support my body.
The multitude obeyed his command,
and the Bodhisattva immediately drew his sword and took his own life.
The Sea God took pity on him and drifted his boat onto the shore,
whereby all the people were saved.
The boatmen embraced the corpse and wailed, saying:
"This must surely be a bodhisattva, no ordinary person.
He leaps and dances, crying out to Heaven:
'I would rather let my life perish here.'"
There was no superior man of lost virtue.
His words were so sincere that they moved the heavens above;
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, beheld the Bodhisattva’s vast compassion.
Śakra descended and said,
"This Bodhisattva of supreme virtue is destined to become a Holy Hero;
I shall now restore him to life."
He poured divine medicinal herbs into the corpse’s mouth and also smeared them over its entire body.
The Bodhisattva immediately revived, suddenly rose to his feet, and exchanged greetings with the assembly.
Śakra filled his boat with famous jewels,
a thousandfold more than before;
he then returned to his native land, where all his nine kinsmen beheld him with mutual joy and delight.
He provided relief to the destitute and succor to the needy, extending his kindness to all sentient beings.
He proclaimed the Buddhist scriptures to enlighten the ignorant and deluded.
The king, moved by the Bodhisattva’s virtue, came to receive his pure transformation.
The ruler is benevolent and the ministers are loyal; throughout the land, the precepts are observed, and every household has filial sons.
The nation is prosperous and poison is extinguished;
the common people rejoice, and they shall dwell forever in the heavens, eternally free from all suffering.
The Bodhisattva practiced with unremitting diligence over many kalpas until he finally attained Buddhahood.
He who sacrificed his own body to save the multitude was none other than myself;
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was Maitreya.

The five hundred merchants are these five hundred *saṃyaksambuddhas* (true ones) currently seated in this assembly; this is recorded in the *Sūtra on Sacrificing One’s Body to Rescue Merchants* and the *Collection on the Infinite Deliverance*.
12. From the Earth, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms within a thousand worlds appear, leaping forth from the earth and manifesting the mark of the long tongue.
Emerging from the earth, they joined their palms with single-minded devotion, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we..."
Wherever the World-Honored One’s emanated bodies may be in various lands and places of parinirvāṇa, this sutra should be extensively preached there.
We, too, desire to obtain this truly pure Great Dharma for ourselves, to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and make offerings to it.

At that time, the World-Honored One was before a multitude of all beings—countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas who had long resided in the Sahā world, such as Mañjuśrī, as well as śrāvakas, humans, non-humans, and others.
He extended his broad and long tongue until it reached the Brahma-world,
and from all his pores he emitted rays of light of immeasurable colors,
which completely illuminated the worlds of the ten directions.
The Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jewel trees were likewise so; this concludes the sixth fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

13. The Cowherd Boy Skillfully Explaining the Meaning of Prajñā and Propagating the Vast Mahāyāna. In the past, there was a bhikṣu who was diligent in upholding the precepts and never transgressed them.
Dwelling in a vihāra,
he recited this Prajñāpāramitā; there was no one who,
upon hearing the sound of this bhikṣu’s voice, did not rejoice.
There was a young boy, only seven years of age, who was herding cattle outside the city.
Hearing from afar the sound of a bhikṣu reciting and expounding the sūtras, he followed the sound to the monastery; upon hearing it, he immediately understood.
Appearing greatly delighted, he then questioned the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu’s answer was not to his liking;
the boy, on the contrary, explained its meaning as being most wonderful, something he had rarely heard before.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu marveled at the child, thinking, "He possesses such wisdom; he is no ordinary man.
At that moment, the child immediately departed and returned to where the oxen were.
The calves he was tending scattered and fled into the mountains;
the boy followed their tracks and encountered a tiger, whereupon he was killed.
He was then reborn as the son of the chief consort of a householder.
The lady, while pregnant, was able to recite the Prajñāpāramitā from morning until evening without ceasing for even a moment. Previously,
the household of that elder had not followed the Dharma.
People marveled at this lady, calling her a liar and claiming she had been possessed by a ghost;
though they sought divinations and consulted exorcists, none could discern the cause.
All within and without the household were filled with anxiety and alarm.
At that time, a bhikṣu entered the city for alms and approached the gate of an elder's house.
Hearing from afar the sound of the sutra being recited, his heart was filled with great joy.
He immediately asked the elder, "Who within this house is reciting the profound sutra, the sound of which is so subtle and exquisite?"
The elder replied, "My wife has been afflicted by a demonic illness;
she speaks falsely day and night, her mouth never ceasing."
The bhikṣu replied,
"This is not a demonic affliction;
it is simply that you have spoken a profound sūtra which possesses great meaning and principle."
Suspecting that the child conceived by this lady was a disciple of the Buddha,
the elder understood her intention and immediately invited the bhikṣu to stay, providing him with food and drink.
When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son;
moreover, there was no foul discharge.
As soon as the boy was born, he joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and recited the Prajñāpāramitā.
Once the lady had given birth, she returned to her original state, just as one who has awakened from a dream finds nothing at all of it remaining.
The elder gathered the assembly; upon seeing the child, he preached the sutra without any obstruction whatsoever.
At that time, the members of the Sangha each focused their minds on observing this child.
The elder asked, "What kind of being is this?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“I am truly a disciple of the Buddha;
pray, do not be alarmed or doubtful.”
"Raise him well. This child shall later become a teacher for all people;
we shall all receive his instruction."
By the age of seven, he fully understood all subtle and profound matters;
his wisdom was transcendent beyond the masses, reaching the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
and all the bhikṣus followed him to receive instruction.
There were errors, omissions, and deficiencies within the sutras;
all of these have been revised and finalized to fulfill what was lacking.
Whenever the child went out or entered [the city], wherever he stopped, [he would recite them].
He immediately transformed others, causing them to resolve upon the Mahāyāna.
Within the house of the elder, five hundred people— both men and women, great and small—
all followed the boy’s example and resolved their minds on the Mahāyāna, practicing all the deeds of a Buddha.
Among those he taught in the cities, towns, and marketplaces,
there were eighty-four thousand who were inspired to conceive the aspiration for the unsurpassed Way,
and five hundred who became his ordained disciples.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus attained understanding; with their minds set on seeking the Mahāyāna, they all attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "The child at that time was none other than myself."
The bhikṣu at that time was Kāśyapa Buddha. A small child emerged and, upon hearing the Dharma, immediately understood the sūtras.
*Xiàngyì jīnglù* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya), Scroll Nine;
