14. The Prince Gives His Own Blood to the Sick. Section Ten: Bodhisattvas Manifesting Bodies According to Circumstances.
1. Śākyamuni as Śakra Devendra Saving His Former Friend. One bodhisattva was Śakra Devendra. He manifested as the Lord of the Devas to deliver his former friend.
Their resolve is set upon suffering, emptiness, and the signlessness of the non-self;
they contemplate while seated and transform others through their teachings while traveling.
Compassionate toward the ignorant and loving toward the wise, he exerted himself without ceasing.
He saw that his former friend had received a female body and was being deluded by wealth and beauty as the wife of a wealthy man.
Unaware of impermanence, he sat at a stall in the marketplace;
Śakra transformed himself into a merchant,
and a woman invited him to sit.
The merchant gazed at her intently and smiled;
the woman then found this strange.
Beside them was a young boy scattering grain and leaping about in play.
The merchant laughed again.
Someone else had a father who was ill, so his son sacrificed an ox for him;
the merchant laughed at that as well.
There was a woman carrying her child;
as the child scraped his mother’s cheek, blood flowed down until it mingled on their necks.
The merchant laughed again.
The wife of that wealthy family asked,
"You stand before me with an unceasing smile;
why do you laugh at me as I am holding my child?"
The merchant replied, "You were my good friend; have you now forgotten me?
The woman was despondent, her heart becoming even more displeased.
The strange merchant spoke;
the merchant further said,
"The reason I laughed at those who would seize the child was this:"
"This child was your father in a former life;
his spirit has now become your son.
If one cannot recognize one's father within a single lifetime, how much less so over the course of eternity?"
The boy Pāṭaliputra was originally born as an ox;
when the ox died, it returned to become his son.
His family used the ox-hide to tie this child.
This child now beats [the father] without recognizing his true nature;
to use an ox for sacrifice while the father’s illness is not yet cured is like taking poison to treat a disease.
His father ended up as an ox, slaughtered for generations;
now this sacrificial ox has returned to receive a human body.
The mother is scraped away, yet the child remains.
The son was originally the concubine’s child,
while the mother was the legitimate wife.
Driven by jealousy and envy, the daughter constantly treated her with extreme cruelty.
The concubine harbors resentment;
yet the wife ultimately becomes the principal wife, and her children become the legitimate sons.
Because their faces are struck and their bodies are wounded, they do not dare to resent it.
The mind has no constancy;
what was once loathed may now be loved—how can there be any permanence?
If one does not understand this within a single lifetime, how much less so across successive kalpas.
The Sūtra says:
"Those who obstruct themselves with form are blind to the Great Way;
those who focus exclusively on deviant sounds do not hear the Buddha’s voice."
This is why I laugh at them.
Worldly glory is like a flash of lightning; it vanishes in an instant.
You should realize that all things are impermanent and not associate with the foolish.
"I honor the six perfections;
I shall now go before you tomorrow and surely visit your gate.
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
The wife returned home dejected;
with a purified mind, she gazed toward him in reverence.
Later, he was indeed at her gate.
His appearance was ugly and his clothes were tattered.
[The man] said, "My friend is inside;
call him out to come here."
The disciples entered and reported the matter in full detail.
The woman came out and said,
"You are not my friends."
Śākyamuni smiled and said,
"If you do not yet recognize me when I have changed my form and altered my clothing,
how much less so in another world?"
The Master replied:
"You have diligently served the Buddha;
indeed, a Buddha is difficult to encounter in this world."
"A bhikṣu of high conduct is difficult to provide offerings for;
his life hangs by a thread, lest he fall into worldly delusions.
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
The entire nation rejoiced and sighed in admiration,
each upholding the sublime and wondrous practices of the six perfections.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
The woman was Maitreya; the Heavenly Lord Śakra was my own self. This is from the *Maitreya-as-a-Woman-Born-Sutra*. 2.

When the Buddha of Benevolence (Śākyamuni) was in the body of a courtesan, he transformed his body to become a king and gave food to birds and beasts. [This occurred] twice in past lives in the kingdom of Uppalavanna. When the Buddha of Benevolence was in the body of a courtesan, he transformed his body to become a king and gave food to birds and beasts. This happened on two occasions in past times in the kingdom of Uppalavanna.
The five grains ripened in abundance and the population was vast.
Within the kingdom there was a king named Pāra.
Previously, there had been a courtesan of exquisite beauty and loveliness.
While traveling to another house, she encountered a man who had given birth to a son and intended to eat it;
the courtesan questioned him,
and he replied, "I am hungry."
The courtesan said,
"Wait a moment while I seek food for you.
He replied:
I am in urgent hunger.
If you do not leave the gate, I shall die of starvation;
how could I wait for you?
The courtesan thought to herself:
"If I take the child away, the mother will starve to death;
if I leave him here, she will devour him. I must find a way to save them both."
The courtesan cut off both her breasts and gave them to him to eat;
her mother then ate them.
The courtesan asked:
"Have you had enough?
he asked. She replied, "I am full.
The courtesan then returned home.
A certain man went to the courtesan’s house;
upon seeing her, he said,
"Who has cut off your breasts?"
Thereupon, a sense of compassion arose within her and she no longer gave rise to desire. The man asked,
"Sister, you should manifest this sincerity for my sake."
The courtesan said,
"If you are truly sincere, let my breasts be restored.
Instantly, both breasts were restored as they had been before.
Śakra Devānām Indra, seeing the merit of this courtesan’s act of giving and fearing that she might usurp his throne,
took the form of a brāhmaṇa and went to her house.
The courtesan then took a golden bowl, filled it with rice, and gave it to the brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa declined and refused to accept it.
The woman asked the practitioner, "Why do you not accept it?"
He replied,
"I do not need food.
Have you truly heard that you are giving milk as an act of alms?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The brāhmaṇa asked,
"When you took this milk to offer as a gift, did you have any regrets?"
The woman said,
"If my sincerity in holding this milk as an act of giving is unwavering,
may I, upon changing this body, be reborn as a man."
Having finished speaking, he immediately turned [the wheel]. At that time,
King Uparāja had already ruled the kingdom for fifty years.
When his life span was exhausted and he passed away,
the attendants and those around him heard that the lustful woman had been transformed into a man,
and they thought to themselves:
Just as he was being established as king,
they all requested his enthronement together;
once he was established, he took great delight in practicing generosity.
He provided for all their needs according to what was required.
He taught the entire realm to observe the eightfold precepts of the fast.
Thus, the state was well-governed, the people were joyful, and their lifespans were prolonged.
The king then thought to himself:
"Although I have practiced giving, I have not yet given my own body.
To give one's own body is indeed difficult."
At that time, the king immediately smeared his body with ghee and incense,
then entered an empty mountain and lay upon a rock.
All manner of birds came and began to devour him alive.
After his life ended, he was reborn into a brahmin family;
he was handsome and attractive,
and when he reached adulthood, he secretly went out toward the marketplace.
Seeing those who were selling themselves as poor beggars, he spoke with words of sorrow:
"If these people were wealthy and happy, they would not sell themselves.
He then hurried to inform his parents and requested to become a śramaṇa.
His parents did not permit it,
so he fasted for five days.
His relatives and acquaintances came and all exhorted him with counsel.
The youth did not consent.
His relatives exhorted his parents to allow him to study the Way;
the parents looked at one another and, weeping with grief, granted their permission.
After raising his parents for six or seven days,
he circumambulated them three times, paid his respects, and departed.
Upon reaching a thicket of trees, he saw two practitioners of the Way.
Having attained the five supernormal powers, he sat exposed to the elements,
contemplating the Way and performing arduous ascetic practices for the sake of the people.
Thereupon, the youth sat beneath a grove of trees.
Through meditative contemplation and ascetic practices, he immediately attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
His diligence and valor surpassed those of the two practitioners.
According to the dharma of the practitioners, when the fruit fell from the tree of its own accord, they would take it and eat it, rather than plucking it from the tree.
While the practitioners were traveling together in search of various fruits and melons,
they saw a pregnant tigress.
The young practitioner spoke to the two other practitioners.
"The tigress will soon give birth;
having been hungry for days, she fears she will devour her own cubs.
Who can offer their own bodies as food for her?"
Maitreya said, "I shall carry my body and eat it.
Having returned from gathering fruit, he saw that the tiger had already given birth.
Being extremely hungry, she wished to eat her own child.
The young man, a practitioner of the Way, said to the two practitioners:
"The tigress has already given birth; being famished, she wishes to devour her offspring."
Who could sustain their bodies to rescue them from the suffering of hunger and go together to where the tiger was?
The tiger opened its eyes and gaped its mouth toward the two practitioners;
the practitioners, struck with fear, immediately flew into the void.
One person said, "Is your utmost sincerity truly such as this?
Your body was just now being eaten by tigers; why is it flying now?"
One of the practitioners was moved by compassion and shed tears;
looking around him, he saw that there was nothing at all.
The young practitioner then took a sharp knife and pierced his own arm until it bled.
In this way, with blood from seven places entering the tiger’s mouth, he drank it; he threw himself before the tiger and fed his body to the beast.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"If you wish to know, the courtesan at that time, the one who was established as king, and the son of the brahmin who threw himself to feed the tiger—these were all my own self."
The practitioner at that time was none other than the two Bodhisattvas Kāśyapa and Maitreya.
Through diligent application of energy over sixty kalpas, I gave my own body as alms;
thereby I transcended nine kalpas and attained Buddhahood before Maitreya. This is recorded in the *Sutra of the Three Turnings of the Wheel from Previous Lives*.

3. Śākyamuni as King Sarvadatta Cuts His Own Flesh to Exchange for a Hawk. In the past, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was the king of a great nation. He cut his own flesh to trade for a hawk. Part three. Long ago, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was a great king.
He was named Sarvadatta.
He universally bestowed gifts upon sentient beings, granting them whatever they sought and compassionately rescuing them from calamities and hardships.
The devas, spirits, and nāgas all spoke in unison, saying:
The position of the Heavenly Emperor is honorable, yet there is never one who holds it permanently;
when one’s conduct is known to be lofty, their compassion and wisdom profound, and their merit abundant,
they shall succeed him upon death.
Fearing that the king might usurp his celestial throne, Śakra went to test him in order to discern the true from the false.
Śakra manifested himself and commanded a bordering king, saying:
"Now that this human king’s compassionate moisture flows profusely and his merit and virtue are most majestic,"
Fearing that his ambition was to usurp his imperial throne,
he immediately transformed himself into a hawk,
while the border king became a pigeon.
The pigeon approached the king’s feet in terror and said, "Great King, how tragic! My life is at its end.
The king said:
"Do not fear; I shall now save you.
The hawk soon arrived and said, "My pigeon has just come here."
"The pigeon is my food; I pray that Your Majesty will return it to me.
The King said, "The pigeon has come to sustain my life; I shall never go back on my word."
"If you truly wish to obtain meat that is a hundred times heavier," the hawk said,
"I only wish to have this pigeon; I do not need any other meat."
The king asked,
"By what means can you cause this hawk to release the pigeon so that it may depart in joy?
The hawk replied:
"If Your Majesty, out of compassion and kindness, will surely take pity on this creature, then I shall joyfully accept it even if you must cut from your own flesh to exchange for the dove.
The King was then greatly delighted;
he personally cut the flesh from his thigh, weighed it against the dove, and continued until it equaled the weight of the bird.
The pigeon grew increasingly heavy as it exhausted its body flesh;
thus, it was still unable to equal the king’s immeasurable pain from the wound.
Out of compassionate forbearance, the king again commanded his close minister, saying:
"You have killed me so that you might claim my marrow to equal the weight of the pigeon.
I, however, uphold the grave injunctions of the Buddha to rescue the world from peril and distress.
Though I endure these manifold afflictions, they are like a gentle breeze; how could they possibly move Mount Tai?"
The King of the Hawk and the King of the Owl each returned to their original forms.
Prostrating themselves upon the ground, they said,
"Great King, what is your aspiration that causes you such distress and suffering?"
He said, "I do not aspire to the status of Śakra, Lord of Devas, nor to that of a Cakravartin Emperor.
I observe sentient beings submerged in blinding darkness, failing to behold the Triple Gem;
they act wantonly in evil and calamity, casting themselves into the Avīci Hell."
Filled with compassion,
he made a vow to seek Buddhahood,
to deliver all sentient beings, and enable them to attain Nirvana.
The Heavenly Lord said in alarm, "I thought the Great King wished to seize my throne;
that is why I disturbed you. How can this be rectified?"
The king said,
"I shall restore my body's sores to their former state and remain constant in my vow to practice giving.
Then Śakra sent a celestial physician to apply divine medicine upon him.
His wounds were immediately healed and his physical strength and complexion surpassed those of before.
Śakra bowed his head, circumambulated the king three times, and departed with joy. (From the *Duchu wuji ji*, Volume One).
4. Mañjuśrī Manifests as a Youth to Transform Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī: Mañjuśrī manifests as a youth to transform the girl Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī. The four Buddhas travel to Rājagṛha.
There was a woman of noble family named Jyotīrasāśirṣā, who was upright,
beautiful, and possessed a complexion like that of refined purple-gold.
The king, crown prince, ministers, elders, and others gave rise to thoughts of passionate attachment; wherever he went, they followed him.
Men and women, both great and small, all pursued his tracks.
Then, on another day, Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī,
together with the merchant’s son Bhayadarśin, went to the market to purchase goods.
Having presented these as offerings and prepared a fine meal, they went together to the pleasure grove.
At that time, Mañjuśrī emerged from his private chamber and,
giving rise to great compassion for all living beings, reflected:
"Which person might I be able to inspire and transform so as to cause them to set their minds upon the Mahāyāna?"
Seeing that Suvarṇottamaśrī was traveling in a single carriage with the elder’s son Bhayadarśana toward the pleasure grove where those ready for conversion were to be reached,
Mañjuśrī immediately transformed his body into that of a youth.
His countenance was upright and exquisite, surpassing that of the gods, bringing joy to all who beheld him.
His robes radiated light for forty li.
He observed the path where the Licchavi girl Mahāprajāpatī was traveling and stood before her.
The son of the elder and Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī, with their carriages, horses,
and garments, when compared to Mañjuśrī,
were like a mass of ink set beside a bright pearl.
When Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī saw that Mañjuśrī’s countenance was as magnificent and exquisite as that of a celestial son,
and his bodily radiance was so brilliant as to be difficult to surpass,
she became covetous of the splendor of his robes.
The mind thought to itself:
"I now wish to abandon this son of the elder;
I shall descend from my carriage, leave him behind, and take pleasure with this man."
Having obtained these robes and having formed this thought,
Mañjuśrī established his majestic spiritual power to cause their minds to be stilled.
The Heavenly King transformed himself into a man and said to her, "Stop, stop!"
This is done to arouse a mind free from indolence. Why is this?
Because such a person does not set their will upon sensual desires.
The woman asked, "For what reason?
The Heavenly King replied,
"This person is named the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī."
They are all able to fully satisfy the wishes of all people;
seeing that sentient beings have things they seek, they do not oppose the intentions of others.
The woman thought to herself:
"Since you have heard this now, you must surely bestow upon me fine and exquisite garments.
He descended from his carriage and said,
"O Benevolent One!"
"I pray that you would graciously bestow this robe upon me. Mañjuśrī replied,
"Sister," and so on.
"If you can resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path,
I shall then bestow this robe upon you as a gift.
The girl replied, "So be it."
He immediately resolved his mind upon the unsurpassed path and upheld the five precepts.
From the *Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of Great Purity*, Chapter Five: "The Story of Sarvadarśin, Son of Blind Parents, Who Was Shot by a King While Hunting. (Five times in past lives.)
In the kingdom of Kāśī, there was an elder who had no son;
both husband and wife had lost their sight.
With the aspiration to enter the mountains to seek supreme resolve,
he cultivated pure intent and took delight in solitude.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Sarvavairocana.
The mind formed this thought:
"This person’s resolve is subtle and his vision is without sight;
if he enters the mountains, he will surely encounter harm."
When the Bodhisattva’s life came to an end, he made a vow to be reborn into the family of a wealthy elder and was named Śyāma.
He was profoundly filial, benevolent, and compassionate, practicing the ten wholesome actions.
Day and night, he applied himself with diligence to serve his parents.
Just as one serves Heaven, Śyāma,
having reached the age of ten,
knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed his parents.
I originally conceived the great intention to enter the deep mountains to seek the aspiration for emptiness, stillness, and unsurpassed, true,
and correct enlightenment. How could I abandon my fundamental vow on account of you?
Human beings in this world face the hundredfold changes of impermanence;
life is not of stone or metal, and its end approaches without fixed date.
I pray that you will fulfill your original intention and, while the opportune time remains, enter the mountains for pure cultivation.
I myself shall provide offerings without missing the proper seasons.
Thereupon, his parents entered the mountains,
and Śyāma bestowed all the household wealth upon the poor and destitute within the kingdom.
He then entered the mountains together with his parents.
Once Śyāma reached the mountains, he made a hut of *p'u* grass and prepared beds and mats; it was neither cold nor hot, always being perfectly suited to their needs.
Having entered the mountains for one year, the various fruits were abundant and delicious, their fragrance sweet and pleasing.
Springs gushed forth, clear and cool;
within the ponds, lotuses of five colors bloomed with brilliant clarity.
The various sandalwood trees emitted a fragrance twice as intense as usual.
Birds of diverse species produced the sounds of music.
As for the lions, bears, brown bears, tigers, wolves, and venomous beasts—
They faced one another with hearts of loving-kindness, no longer harboring any intent to harm.
They ate grass and fruit without feeling fear.
Śāṇa was so profoundly filial and compassionate that he feared the ground would be pained by his footsteps.
The heavenly deities and mountain spirits constantly assumed human forms to comfort him day and night.
While Śyāma wore a deer-skin garment and carried a pitcher to fetch water,
the deer, wild animals, and birds also went there to drink, feeling no fear or apprehension toward one another.
At that time, the King of Kāśī entered the mountains to hunt.
Seeing a flock of birds and deer by the water’s edge, the king drew his bow and shot at them;
by mistake, the arrow struck Śyāma in the chest.
Śyāma was struck by a poisoned arrow;
raising his voice, he cried out loudly,
"Who has shot and killed three practitioners of the Way with a single arrow?"
Upon hearing the sound of human voices, the king immediately dismounted his horse and went before Śyāma.
Śyāma said to the king,
"The elephant died because of its tusks."
The rhinoceros dies for its horn;
the pheasant dies for its feathers;
the elk and the deer die for their hide and flesh.
"What kind of death am I currently facing as I sit here?
The King asked Śyāma,
"What sort of person are you?"
Wearing a deer-skin garment, he was no different from a hunter.
Śyāma said, "I am a man from the kingdom of the King."
For more than twenty years, I have come here with my blind parents to study the Way,
and never once have I been harmed by tigers, wolves, or venomous insects.
Yet now, I have been shot and killed by the king.
At that moment, a violent wind suddenly arose in the mountains, blowing and breaking the trees;
the hundred birds cried out in lamentation, and the lions, bears, brown bears, and beasts of prey all let out great roars.
The sun lost its brilliant radiance, flowing springs ran dry,
and various flowers withered and died; as thunder shook the earth,
the blind parents rose in alarm and said to one another:
Śāṇa had been gone for a long time fetching water and had not yet returned;
could it be that he had been harmed by venomous insects?
The cries and calls of the beasts and birds were no longer as they usually were.
Winds arose from all four directions, and the trees were broken and shattered.
There must surely be some calamitous anomaly.
At that time, the King was struck with fear and deeply reproached himself.
"What I have done is unfathomable.
Originally, I was shooting a deer;
by mistake, my arrow struck and killed a practitioner of the Way. This sin is extremely grave."
By coveting a small piece of meat, he has incurred a heavy calamity.
I shall now use the treasures and storehouses of the entire kingdom,
as well as my palaces, female musicians, villages, hamlets, and cities, to save my son's life.
Then the king stepped forward and pulled at the arrow in Śyāma’s chest with his hand,
but it was so deep that it could not be extracted.
Birds and beasts gathered from all directions like clouds, wailing in a way that shook the mountains.
The king became even more terrified;
his three hundred and sixty joints all trembled.
Śyāma said to the king:
"This is not the fault of the King, but is caused by my own past karma.
I do not begrudge my body or life;
I only feel pity."
"My blind parents are already advanced in years and both eyes are blind;
were I to suddenly pass away, they would also come to their end with no one to look after them.
For this reason, I am filled with self-reproach and distress.
"It is not merely for the sake of ending my pain.
The King spoke again with renewed earnestness:
"I would rather enter the hells and suffer punishment there for a hundred kalpas than allow Śyāma to live."
Kneeling for a long time, he turned toward Śyāma and repented his transgressions, saying:

"If your life should come to an end, I shall no longer return to my kingdom, but will remain in these mountains to provide for your parents just as I did when you were here; do not harbor any further concerns."
"May all the devas, nāgas, and spirits bear witness that I shall not fail this vow.
Upon hearing the king’s oath, Śyāma felt joy and gladness in his heart;
though he was pierced by a poisoned arrow, he had no regrets even in death.
"I entrust my parents to Your Majesty.
By making offerings to these practitioners of the Way, their present-life offenses will be extinguished and they shall obtain immeasurable merit.
The King said:
"You must tell my parents where you are and speak to them before you die so that they may know.
Śyāma then pointed out the way:
"From here, walk forward; it is not far from here."
"You shall see for yourself a grass hut where my parents reside. Your Majesty,
proceed slowly so as not to cause my parents alarm or distress."
Using skillful means and expedient methods, he understood their intent and said,
"Please convey my thanks to my parents on my behalf:
the impermanent has now arrived, and I must depart for the next world."
"I do not begrudge my own life, but I think only of my parents who are aged and both blind;
were I to die suddenly, they would have no one to rely upon.
It is for this reason that I am so distressed and torment myself."
Death is the natural lot, brought about by the consequences of past transgressions;
there is no escaping it. Now, I personally repent before my parents for all the various evils I have committed since time immemorial.
In this, may my transgressions be extinguished and merit arise.
May I and my parents meet with one another in every lifetime and never be separated.
May my parents preserve their longevity until the end and remain free from all sorrow and affliction.
Devas, nāgas, and spirits constantly followed and protected him, causing calamities and harms to be extinguished.
The king then took several attendants and went to his parents' residence.
After the king had departed,
Śyāma suddenly passed away;
birds and beasts wailed and circled above his corpse.
He licked the blood from Śyāma’s chest with his mouth.
Upon hearing this sound, the blind parents became even more terrified.
As the king traveled swiftly, he brushed against the grasses and trees, producing a rustling sound like the voice of a person.
The parents said in astonishment, "Who is this? This is not the conduct of our son.
The king replied, "I am the King of Kāśī."
Hearing that a man was practicing the Way in the mountains, he came to provide offerings.
His parents said,
"It is well that the Great King has come."
We are honored by Your Majesty’s deigning to travel so far from your majesty to visit this humble wilderness.
Is your person in good health?
Are the palace ladies, the crown prince, the officials, and the citizens all well and at peace?
"The winds and rains are harmonious, the five grains are abundant, and neighboring states do not harm one another.
The King replied to the practitioner,
saying, "By virtue of your grace, O practitioner, all is peaceful and secure."
The king inquired after his blind parents, asking:
"You have come to this mountain, enduring toil and hardship;
amidst these trees, are there no predatory birds or wild beasts to harm you, O practitioner of the Way?"
"Does it not grow cold or hot in the mountains according to the seasons? Is the world at peace?
The blind parents replied, "By the profound grace of Your Majesty, we have always been at peace."
"I have a filial son named Śyāma.
He constantly gathers fruits and melons for me, and the spring water is always abundant.
The winds and rains in the mountains are harmonious and well-regulated, so that nothing is lacking."
"I have grass mats upon which you may sit and wild fruits and melons whereof you may eat.
Śyāma has gone to fetch water and intends to return shortly.
When the king heard this, his heart was grieved and tears fell from his eyes.
Furthermore, he said:
"I, a man of wicked and shameless conduct, entered the mountains to hunt.
Seeing a herd of deer by the water's edge, I drew my bow and shot at them."
"A stray arrow has struck Śyāma; therefore, I have come to inform you.
Upon hearing this, the parents threw themselves to the ground, their bodies collapsing like a great mountain falling, causing the earth itself to tremble.
The King then stepped forward to support and pull them up.
The parents wailed and wept, looking up to heaven and saying of themselves, "Our son was filial and compassionate;
he stepped upon the ground in fear of causing it pain.
What kind of crime has he committed that you have shot and killed him?"
Just now, the wind arose and the trees shook as the hundred birds wailed;
suspecting my son was dead,
his parents wept and wailed aloud.
The father said, "Stop for now.
Birth is inevitably followed by death; it cannot be avoided."
Now, let me ask the King:
where was Śyāma shot, and is he now dead or alive?
When the King spoke of Śyāma’s words, his parents were moved to utter despair.
"Once I am without a son, we both shall surely die.
I pray that Your Majesty will lead us two to stand over the corpse.
The King then led the blind parents to the side of the corpse.
The father held his feet and the mother held his head as they looked up to heaven and cried out.
The mother then licked the wound on Śyāma’s chest with her tongue,
vowing, "May the poison enter my mouth."
"I am already old;
my eyes can see nothing.
I shall substitute my own body for that of my son."
"Śyāma lives and I die;
in my death, I have no regret.
If Śyāma’s supreme filial piety is known to Heaven and Earth," [then let this happen].
"The arrow must be extracted, the poison must be removed, and Śyāma must be restored to life.
Thereupon, the seat of the second King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven immediately shook.
With his divine eye, he saw two practitioners of the Way embracing their son and wailing.
Then the various celestial palaces of the fourth Tuṣita Heaven were all shaken; Śakra,
Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings immediately followed the Fourth Heavenly King.
In the time it takes for a person to bend or extend their arm, he descended before Śyāma.
He poured divine medicine into Śyāma’s mouth;
as the medicine entered his mouth, the arrow was drawn out by itself, and he was restored to life as before.
The parents were struck with both alarm and joy;
seeing that Śyāma, though already dead, had returned to life with both eyes open,
the birds and beasts all rejoiced greatly.
The wind subsided and the clouds dispersed, so that the sun shone with renewed brilliance.
Springs gushed forth, and the various flowers of five colors and the trees flourished twice as luxuriantly as usual.
The King was filled with great joy, unable to contain himself.
Having paid homage to Śakra Devendra, he then paid homage to his parents and to his son, Śyāma.
He wished to offer the wealth of the kingdom to the practitioners of the Way. Śyāma said:
If the King wishes to repay his debt of gratitude,
let him first return to comfort the people and cause them all to uphold the precepts.
Let the King no longer engage in hunting or shooting, thereby sparing the lives of insects and beasts.
In this present life, the body is not at ease, and when one's lifespan is exhausted, one shall enter the hells.
When people dwell in the world, affection and love are but temporary;
separation lasts for a long time and cannot be maintained forever.
"Your Majesty, it is because you possessed merit in the past that you have now become king.
Do not, on account of having attained sovereignty, indulge in self-indulgence.
Thus the king reproached himself.
"From this day forward, we shall follow Śyāma’s instructions.
Several hundred followers were filled with great joy and received and upheld the five precepts.
The king then ordered that throughout the kingdom, all those whose parents were blind, such as Śyāma’s, should be provided for.
"All should provide offerings and must not abandon him;
those who violate this shall now incur heavy punishment.
Thereupon, the people of the kingdom, because Śyāma had been restored to life, [honored him].
Those who, from the highest to the lowest, instruct one another to reverently practice the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions will,
upon death, attain rebirth in the heavens and none shall enter the three evil realms.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
The one who was Śyāma in his past life was my own self.
The blind father was King Śuddhodana, my father, in this life.
The blind mother was Queen Māyā.
The King of Kāśī was Ānanda; the Heavenly King Śakra at that time was Maitreya.
It was he who enabled me to swiftly attain the prediction of supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.
All of this is due to the compassionate and benevolent grace of one's parents' support;
it moves the heavens, dragons, spirits, and deities,
and arises from the profound debt of parental kindness fulfilled by a filial son.
That I have now attained Buddhahood and am able to deliver the people of this land is entirely due to filial piety and the practice of virtue. (From the *Śyāma-sūtra*).
6. In the Wilderness and Elsewhere, Manifesting Various Forms to Transform Diverse Beings. At that time, the Bodhisattva of the Wilderness manifested himself in the form of a ghost.
The Bodhisattva Saṃjñeya manifests in the form of a deer;
the Bodhisattva Prajñāolkā manifests in the form of a monkey;
the Bodhisattva Vigatarāga manifests in the form of a black sheep.
The Bodhisattva Kṣīṇāsrava manifested the body of a king of geese.
In this manner, these five hundred bodhisattvas each manifested and assumed various kinds of bodies.
From their bodies issued forth great fragrant light;
each and every bodhisattva held a lamp in their hand,
desiring to make offerings to all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Saṃśayacitta observed the five hundred people and immediately knew that they were all bodhisattvas.
He then spoke to the wilderness spirit.
"Good sons, for what reason do you manifest such bodies to make offerings to the Buddhas?
The wilderness spirits replied:
"Good son, in the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha,
a World-Honored One, named Vipaśyin."
At that time, I, together with those such as these—
sharing the same parents and being brothers— upheld the five precepts and gave rise to the bodhicitta,
desiring to subdue all sentient beings.
They also made offerings to the Buddhas Śikhin, Viśvabhū, and Krakucchanda.
Before those Buddhas, the Great Being Saṃjñeya established a great vow, saying:
"In a future age, may I teach and transform sentient beings by means of the body of a ghost-spirit."
If there are wicked and evil ghosts,
I shall preach the Three Vehicles for them to subdue them;
only then shall I attain the path of Bodhi.
There were also twelve thousand great spirits who made great vows in this world to discipline sentient beings;
they further made great vows.
If there are evil spirits who wish to destroy the True Dharma,
I shall subdue them. For this reason,
I accept such a ghostly body to tame and transform them, causing them to abide in the Three Vehicles.
If there are sentient beings who distance themselves from wholesome dharmas and perform unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind,
their bodies will already have been born within the three evil realms.
Because there are those who receive the bodies of ghosts due to mixed karma of good and evil,
evil ghosts are numerous while benevolent ghosts are few;
I wish to subdue them by manifesting this body.
It also causes the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras to remain far removed from evil thoughts. Good son,
there is a Vajra-mallet mantra that prevents all malevolent spirits from doing harm to those of the four castes.
Even down to the birds and beasts, all shall give rise to wholesome minds and remain far removed from all evil and fear.
I have made a great vow to proclaim this mantra; it is found in the twenty-first fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.
7. When Vāsava was in the body of a rishi, he saved six million two hundred thousand merchants. The seven Buddhas of the past formerly resided in the Tuṣita Heaven.
At that time, the seer Vasu was in Jambudvīpa.
Together with six million two hundred thousand merchants, he constantly served as their caravan leader as they entered the sea to gather treasures.
Riding upon a great ship, they were about to return to his native country.
In the midst of that journey, they encountered the perils of makara fish, great storms, and yakṣas.
Thus, six million two hundred thousand people immediately each made a vow to the god Maheśvara.
Each person offered one sacrificial victim;
thus they were freed from the four perils and returned safely to their own country.
Each prepared a sheep,
intending to go to the temple of the gods.
At that time, Vasu thought silently to himself:
"How can I now instruct these merchants to perform unwholesome deeds?
I must employ skillful means.
He then immediately manifested two persons.
First, there were those who had gone forth as śramaṇas;
second, there were householders who were brāhmaṇas. At that time, a brāhmaṇa made this proclamation among the multitude:
"The Lord of Devas, together with six million two hundred thousand people, intends to go to the celestial temple."
At that time, while on his way, the śramaṇa saw this brahmin from afar and asked him,
"With such a great multitude, where do you intend to stay?"
The layperson said,
"I went to a celestial temple to seek great benefit.
The śramaṇa replied:
I observe that you wish to obtain great decline;
what is the great benefit?
Your disputes and litigation do not cease.
At that time, the crowd asked the brahmin,
"Who is this person? His appearance is such as this."
The brahmin said, "This one is called a śramaṇa. The people asked:
"What do you say, śramaṇa? He replied,
"To kill living beings to sacrifice to the heavens shall result in great sin."
The crowd said, "What use is this talk for this foolish śramaṇa?
Go quickly to the celestial shrine; there you will obtain great benefit."
Then the brahmins said, "Our Great Teacher is currently at the temple; there is nothing he does not master. Let us go together and consult him.
They all replied, "Excellent!"
The śramaṇas, brahmins, and various other people went to the place where the Great Seer was.
At that time, the śramaṇas asked the Great Seer:
"If one kills living beings to sacrifice to the gods, will they be reborn in heaven or fall into hell?"
The Great Sage replied,
"O deluded śramaṇa, one who kills living beings to sacrifice to the gods will surely fall into hell. Vasu said:
"No," said the śramaṇa. "If it does not fall, you should bear witness to this."
At that moment, Vasu immediately sank into the Avīci Hell.
When the people saw this, they cried out, "Alas, what a calamity! Such a thing has occurred;
the Great Sage, so wise and intelligent, has now been utterly destroyed."
"How much more so for us— how could we avoid falling into hell?
At that time, the multitude each released their sheep and fled in the four directions,
seeking the sages among the various mountains.
Having attained the state of immortals, they received the immortal teachings.
After twenty-one years, each passed away and was reborn in Jambudvīpa.
At that time, I descended from Tuṣita Heaven to be born in the house of King Śuddhodana in Jambudvīpa.
At that time, six million two hundred thousand people were born in the kingdom of Śrāvastī and attained human bodies.
In the past, when I first arrived in Śrāvastī, I subdued these six million two hundred thousand people, causing them to leave the household life and resolve upon Bodhicitta.
"He was none other than the merchant of old. Good son,
the seer Vasu possessed such majestic spiritual power."
Having thus transformed these people, they came to my presence. [From] the *Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, Volume One, Chapter Eight:
The Wheel-Turning King’s Body Vows on Generosity; The Wheel-Turning King’s Body Vows on Generosity. Eight: In the past, in the eastern Jambudvīpa, there was a bodhisattva named Lupo-luo.
By the power of his vows, he was born therein as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) who ruled over the four continents,
named Ākāśaviśuddha.
He addressed all sentient beings:
"Abide in the ten wholesome paths of action and the three vehicles;
during that time, practice giving everything without any discrimination."
The beggars were not satisfied even with immeasurable treasures;
he then questioned his great ministers:
"From where do such treasures arise?"
The minister replied,
"Although the Dragon King possesses [these offerings], they are intended solely for the Holy King;
however, the afflictions in this age of five corruptions are thick and heavy."
When the human lifespan is one hundred years, he will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He will manifest as a great nāga king, displaying various treasuries of jewels within worlds characterized by manifold evils.
In every location throughout the four continents, within each continent,
he undergoes rebirth seven times; in each of those bodies,
he manifests immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of treasuries of precious jewels.

In this manner, proceeding in succession throughout the ten directions, during the era of the five turbidities and evil world, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of devas and humans in the void rained down flowers, praising him as "Excellent" and exclaiming, "It is according to our wishes! while the great assembly heard these sounds.
The gods of the Pure Space King realm bestowed upon him the name "Giver of All.
At that time, each of the people individually begged the king for his wives, concubines, and children.
The king gave everything to him.
There was a beggar named Qing Guangming (Light of Blue Radiance) who observed the precepts of a dog and begged from the king for the entirety of Jambudvīpa.
The king, filled with joy, conferred upon him the consecration of perfumed water to succeed to the holy throne of kingship.
Furthermore, the people came to serve and honor this king,
and his lifespan remained no different from before.
"When I attain the Way of Buddhahood, you shall receive a prediction [of enlightenment] as one who is in his final birth before becoming a Buddha.
The Brahmin Luzhi begged for both his feet,
and the Brahmin Yabalu requested his two eyes.
The Brahmin Śuddhadṛḍha begged for both ears;
the Nirgrantha thought he would beg for the male organ;
and the Brahmin Madhurāsvāda begged for both hands.
He immediately cut them off and gouged them out, bestowing them as alms at that very moment.
Then all the minor kings and great ministers said, "Alas! What a fool!"
How much is the remaining flesh worth that I cut from myself?
I shall cast it away into the wilderness so that insects, beasts, vultures, and eagles may all come and devour it.
If my vow is to be fulfilled, [may this happen].
I shall cause this body to become a great mountain of flesh;
may all sentient beings who drink blood and eat flesh come here and eat and drink at their will, so that my body grows ever greater.
By the power of my vow, the tongue-organ I have relinquished [shall remain].
May I, in a future life, obtain a broad and long tongue.
When my life here in Jambudvīpa comes to an end, may I,
by the power of my original vow, be reborn as a dragon king.
His name was Śaṅkhadarśana-ratnagarbha.
On the very night of his birth, he manifested hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of various kinds of treasure-treasuries from within himself.
He issued a proclamation stating that all manner of rare treasures, even up to mani-jewels,
were to be used as one wished; furthermore,
he enjoined them to fully practice the ten virtuous deeds.
He gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
In this manner, he received a body seven times,
with a lifespan in each instance of seventy-seven thousand *koṭi-nayuta* hundred-thousand years.
The *Sūtra on the Selection of Various Evil Worlds in the Future*, from the *Infinite Treasuries*, is likewise thus.

Chapter Nine: Being a King’s Body, Giving One’s Eyes to a Sick Person. The Buddha spoke to the worthy Ānanda: [Being a King’s Body, Giving One’s Eyes to a Sick Person] (Chapter Nine) The Buddha addressed the worthy Ānanda: [...]
In the distant past, there was a king named Candrasūryaprabha (Moon-Sun Radiance).
He was handsome and beautiful, with a majestic and towering spiritual power.
Emerging from the palace, he saw on the road a blind man,
destitute and famished, begging along the way;
he then proceeded toward the king’s presence.
He addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty alone is honored, noble, secure, and happy;
I alone am impoverished and, moreover, blind."
When the king saw him, he took pity on him and asked the blind man, "What medicine can cure your ailment?
The blind man replied,
"Only the king's eye can heal my eyes."
At that time, the king personally plucked out both his eyes and bestowed them as a gift upon the blind man;
his mind was pure and serene, without a single thought of regret.
King Candraprabha was none other than my own self.

The Buddha said: "One might still be able to know the weight of Mount Sumeru, but the merit of giving away one's eyes is incalculable. [From the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, Chapter 10:

"Acting as a King to Punish a Brahmin. Once upon a time, the Bodhisattva was a great king. Acting as a king, he punished a Brahmin for his crimes. 10. Acting as a King to Punish a Brahmin for His Crimes. Ten: In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king.
They take refuge in the Triple Gem and fully observe the ten wholesome paths of action.
Weapons are not employed, and there are no prisons.
Wind and rain fall in their proper seasons, crops are abundant, and the people are wealthy.
The *Huáiwéi xiǎoshū* was silenced throughout the land;
yet the *Liùdù zhēnhuà* was recited by everyone.
At that time, there was a Brahmin who maintained pure and aloof conduct, dwelling in seclusion among the mountains and forests, remaining uninvolved with worldly customs.
Thirsty while traveling at night,
he mistakenly drank water from a lotus pond planted by the people of the country;
having finished drinking, his mind became awakened.
He went to the authorities and confessed, saying, "I have committed theft;
I only pray that Your Majesty will punish me according to the law.
The King said:
"This water is natural and insubstantial; what crime could there be in it?
He replied, "I drank it without being informed."
"Is this not theft? I pray that Your Majesty will pass judgment upon it.
The King said, "State affairs are many and pressing; sit here in the garden for now."
The Crown Prince ordered him to stay deep within the park;
the King, preoccupied with many affairs, forgot about him for six days.
Suddenly, he was awakened from his forgetfulness and said:
"Where is the brahmin?
Call out to him quickly to come!
The brahmin has observed his precepts for six days, enduring hunger and thirst."
His body became emaciated and scarred; as he rose, his feet stumbled upon the ground.
When the King saw this, he wept and said, "My transgressions are too heavy."
The Queen laughed at him.
The King sent men to bathe him and prepared a feast, personally making offerings while prostrating himself to repent for his transgressions.
From that time until he attained Buddhahood, he transmigrated through the cycle of birth and death without end; even when he was on the verge of attaining enlightenment, he did not eat for six years.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the king was my own self; the lady was Gopī."
The Crown Prince was Rāhula.
Because the King had forgotten the ascetic, the latter suffered for six days of hunger and endured six years of retribution.
Only when the famine had subsided did the King personally provide offerings on the sixth day thereafter.
"Therefore, now that the calamities of six years have ended, the Way has been perfected.
Jīvaka laughed at this. [He replied:
"Now, while Rāhula was suffering from a grave illness for six years, the Crown Prince, out of his deep attachment as a brahmin, remained within the garden."
Therefore, he dwelt in darkness for six years; this is from the *Jingquewang jing* (Sūtra on the King Who Released the Sparrows).
11. For the sake of a king’s body, he renounced his kingdom, city, wife, and children. Eleven: Once upon a time, the Bodhisattva was a great king.
He governed the people with compassion, traveling on circuit every month.
For the poor, the destitute, widowers, and widows, he provided medicinal gruel for their illnesses.
Whenever he went on inspection tours, he would command his attendants to load the necessary clothing and medicines onto the rear carriage.
When he died, he was buried there;
his fame spread throughout the ten directions.
Śakra, seeing his virtuous conduct, feared it would usurp his own position and sought to destroy him.
He transformed himself into an old brahmin and begged the king for one thousand silver coins.
The king immediately granted them to him, saying, "I dwell in a cramped place and fear that someone might steal them; I wish to entrust them to the king's care."
The king said, "In my country, there are no thieves; one may accept a heavy trust immediately.
He then transformed himself into a brahmin.
He went again to the palace gate,
whereupon the king appeared before him.
The brahmin sighed in admiration, saying:
"Great King, your name is Pūṣa, and your virtuous conduct is rare and marvelous.
Born among the common people, I long for noble honor and wish to beg for this kingdom.
The King said, "Very well."
He immediately took his wife and children and departed on a light vehicle.
The Lord of Devas then transformed himself into another brahmin and begged the king for the carriage.
He bestowed chariots and horses upon him as gifts.
Accompanied by his wife and children, he proceeded on foot and took up residence by the mountains.
There was a Daoist master of the Five Powers who was a friend of the king.
Suddenly, he recalled the King’s virtue and, seeing that [the King] had lost his kingdom, he stilled his mind and entered meditative rest.

Seeing that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was emaciated and haggard from greed and jealousy over the loss of his realm, the Daoist suddenly transported himself by means of his supernormal power to the King's presence and asked, "What do you seek that you labor your will in this way? The King replied:
"You already fully know what my intentions are.
The Daoist then transformed himself into a single-axle chariot to escort the King.
A celestial Brahmā then appeared as a wandering ascetic and begged for the chariot.
Before he had yet reached that country, which was several thousand li away,
the deity again transformed himself into the aforementioned brahmin and came to demand the silver coins.
The king said:
"I have bestowed the kingdom's bounty upon others and inadvertently forgotten your money.
The king immediately used his wife and children as collateral to obtain one thousand coins, which he returned to the brahmin.
The wife had originally been staying at the house of the one who held the collateral.
While the woman was bathing and had stripped off her pearls, jewels, and various ornaments,
a deity transformed into a hawk and snatched away her clothes and treasures.
The husband, suspecting his wife of theft, seized her and cast her into prison.
The boy lay down to sleep with the son of a collateral relative.
During the night, [a deity] killed the relative's son.
The family took their own son and delivered him to prison.
Mother and son were imprisoned;
ravaged by famine and deformed by suffering, they wailed for help in vain.
Weeping all day long, their crime was finalized and they were abandoned at the marketplace to die.
The king hired himself out for one thousand silver coins to ransom his wife and children;
as he passed through the marketplace, he beheld them.
He immediately called to mind the Buddhas and repented his transgressions, saying:
"Was it through the necessity of my past karma that I have come to this?
Calming my mind, I entered into clarity and beheld the workings of Heaven."
A voice from the sky said,
"Why do you not kill him immediately?
The king replied:

"I have heard that Śakra universally rescues sentient beings with a heart of sincere compassion, nurturing them more than a loving mother; among all creatures that possess blood, there are none who do not receive his blessings.
You, having no evil karma, have obtained the position of Emperor."
Having cast off the heavy poison of his mind, his evil karma ripened and his transgressions were completed;
he was reborn and entered Mount Tai.
Among devas, humans, dragons, and ghosts, there were none who did not acclaim this as virtuous.
The King of the Land immediately pardoned the offenses of his wife and children.
When the two kings met, they inquired into the origins of the matter;
from the highest officials to the commoners, there was no one who did not shed tears.
The King, Lord of the Land, divided the kingdom to rule over it.
Consequently, the ministers and subjects of the nations sought out the king’s location, and the entire realm came forward to welcome him.
Thus, the inhabitants of the two kingdoms were respectively in mourning and in joy.
At that time, the king was I myself;
the queen was Jīvī; and the prince was Rāhula.
The Heavenly Lord was Devadatta;
the brahmin in the mountains was Śāriputra;
and the king of that country was Maitreya. This is from the first fascicle of the *Chutudu Wujide Ji* (Collection on the Infinite Perfection of Deliverance).

12. Manifesting as the Body of a King to Transform and Rescue Those in Peril. The Buddha was in Śrāvastī and addressed the bhikṣus: "Manifesting as the body of a king to transform and rescue those in peril. (Twelfth) [Sūtra]. The Buddha was in Śrāvastī and told the bhikṣus: [The following].
In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king named Samantaprabha.
His light of compassion and benevolence shone throughout the ten directions, and he was celebrated in song for his excellence.
The people longed for his rest, just as a filial son desires the peace of his parents.
In a neighboring state there was a king named Aqun.
The method of governance is through rectitude.
His strength is like that of a lion pouncing or a soaring eagle;
when the butcher seeks meat, he rushes to the market at dawn to search for it.
While traveling, he saw a freshly killed corpse and took it for its delicious flavor, eating it alongside domestic meat.
On a subsequent day, when he prepared a meal, it was not as sweet as before.
The King reprimanded the Chief Cook.
The cook returned in sincerity, prostrating himself and confessing his crime.
The king felt ashamed at heart and said,
"Is human flesh truly sweet?"
He then appointed the cook to serve as his regular attendant.
Therefore it is said:
"Those who are excessive in their pursuit of flavors are thin in the Way of benevolence."
When the Way of benevolence thins, the hearts of jackals and wolves arise.
Indeed, wolves and dogs crave the flavor of meat and thus plunder the lives of creatures.
Consequently, the world held him in enmity.
The cook received the command and silently went to kill a person to provide food for the King.
The subjects and citizens cried out in distress, uniting their hearts and voices to pursue him.
The king fled into the mountains, where he lay in wait for the other kings to emerge;
then the *Vṛtra* host seized him,
just as hawks and falcons snatch away swallows and sparrows.
He captured ninety-nine kings. At that time,
King Samantaprabha went out to inspect the suffering and happiness of his people,
and on the road he encountered a brahmin.
He said, "Your Majesty, do not go out.
The King replied, "Once a mandate has been issued, I must go; it is difficult to go back on one's word."
He then emerged from it and was captured by Aqun.
The King said:
"I do not fear losing my life; I only regret that it would damage my integrity.
Aqun asked, "What do you mean?"
The king related this in detail.
Upon seeing it, the Daoist emerged and spoke with a solemn admonition:
"I pray that you will behold it once more and receive its grave warning."
He put this into practice and died shortly thereafter without regret.
Aqun released him, allowing him to return for a short time.
Having seen the Daoist bestow gold coins upon him, he accepted them with a smile and went to where Āqún was.
He asked, "Your life is in peril this very day; why are you joyful and smiling?"
He replied,
"The words of the World-Honored One are rarely heard within the triple world.
Now that I cherish them in my heart, what kingdom or life could be more precious?"
Aqun spoke again, saying,
"I pray to hear your venerable teaching.
The King took it and handed it to him.
Aqun was both surprised and delighted, saying:
"How majestic is the World-Honored One, proclaiming the four signs of impermanence!
Indeed, not to hear or see this would be called perverse madness."
He immediately released the hundred kings, each ordering them to return to their own kingdoms.
Aqun repented his errors and renewed himself, dwelling beneath a tree while daily reciting four gāthās.
When his life ended and his spirit departed, he was reborn as the crown prince of a great king.
When he took a wife who was not male, the King was deeply concerned;
he therefore recruited women from the kingdom to transform her into a man.
Later, she became dissolute and abandoned the path of chastity.
The king had him torn apart at a crossroads and commanded the passersby, saying,
"Strike his head with your fingers; thus shall you humiliate him."
When he had just reached ninety-nine people, the Crown Prince passed away.
His spirit underwent transformation and transmigrated without end until,
encountering the Buddha while he was in the world, he was born in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Having lost his father at an early age, he lived alone with his mother and served a Brahmin teacher.
By nature, he was sincere and his word was trustworthy; he possessed the courage and strength of one who could subdue an elephant.
His teacher loved him and his friends respected him, such that he was praised as a man of virtue by those both near and far.
Every time the Master went on a tour, he would entrust [the community] to him for his residence.
His wife, harboring lewd intentions, reached out her hand and attempted to seduce him with licentious words.
Aqun declined, saying:
Among all the elderly people in the world,
men are my fathers and women are my mothers.
How much less so for the teacher’s wife?
Even if one were to follow [the teacher] by burning one's own body, one would not dare to violate this command.
The teacher’s wife disapproved of this; as he was about to retreat from the Way, she reflected upon the change of circumstances.

The man said to his wife, "Did your sighing not sufficiently reveal that he was a worthy man? I have fully described his transgressions; you were a female demon appearing as a true Brahmin, and the master has indeed believed you.
He then told Āgnya, "Do you wish to become an immortal?"
He replied, "Yes.
[The Emperor] commanded that one hundred people be executed and their fingers severed,
hoping thereby to attain the state of an immortal.
Having received orders to engage in swordsmanship, he killed whomever he encountered.
He obtained ninety-nine fingers,
which caused the masses to flee and the state to tremble.
Seeing his mother, he said joyfully, "Mother, since our years have reached their full measure, I am now an immortal.
The Buddha thought, "The heterodox paths delude the masses; throughout the heavens, they offer prayers for this very reason."
He transformed himself into a śramaṇa walking ahead of them and said,
"The number of people is sufficient;
those who follow behind cannot keep up."
He said, "Śramaṇa, you should stop.
He replied, "I have stopped;
it is you who have not stopped."
He said, "The mind of Aqun has opened wide like clouds being cleared away.
Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he bowed his head in repentance for his transgressions.
Joining his palms, he followed [the monk] back to the vihāra immediately and became a śramaṇa.
The Buddha explained his past conduct to him, whereupon he realized the four marks of impermanence and attained the stage of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
When the king intended to punish him, he heard of this and sighed; he then addressed the Buddha, expressing his desire to see him. The Buddha said:
"A person of superior virtue and wisdom may be granted a single glance;
let us do so up to three times.
He replied:
"The radiance of my eyes is so brilliant that it is difficult to withstand.
The King bowed his head and said, "Tomorrow I shall prepare a modest meal; I pray that you will deign to look upon me."
He replied,
"I go to the latrine,
but not to the palace."
The king said,
"I shall do as you command.
Upon his return, he tore open the latrine and dug up the ground.
They used fresh *candana*, *sāla*, and *ci* wood for the pillars and beams;
they sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground, mixing *candana*, *sugandha*, and *uragasāra* with various other perfumes to form a paste;
and they used *kambala* wool and various silks to make seats and mats.
It was adorned with carvings and engravings, made beautiful by various jewels;
it shone brilliantly, surpassing even palaces.
On the following day, the king himself held a fragrant incense burner and welcomed it.
Aqun took his seat. The King bared his clothes,
crawled on his knees, and having completed the offerings,
immediately spoke this sutra:
"The latrine from the previous day is filthy;
how could one eat above it? He replied, "No. "Would it be acceptable now? [The Master said: "No."
He replied, "It may be done. Aqun said,
"Before I had seen the Buddha, I used to defecate in that latrine."
Relying on the grace of past merit, I was born to encounter the age of a Buddha;
bathed in pure transformation, I have cast off foulness and embraced fragrance,
becoming inwardly and outwardly pure like a celestial mani-jewel.
While traveling through the marketplace, he heard that there was a woman who had given birth prematurely and whose life hung by a thread.
He returned and reported the matter exactly as it was.
The Buddha said,
"Go and assist her in giving birth.
Aqun received his instructions and went to proclaim the Buddha's grace.
Mother and son were born together.
The Buddha told Aqun:
"The day one receives the Way may be called one's true birth."
"One who has not yet beheld the Three Honored Ones and has not received the weighty precepts is like a child in the womb; though they possess ears and eyes, how can they hear or see?
It is because they have not yet been born."
Aqun’s mind was opened and he immediately attained the path of Arhatship (*arhat*).
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The King Puming at that time was my own self."
"In a previous life, I bestowed upon him four verses.
By saving a hundred kings, he has now attained the Way and shall no longer undergo manifold sins."
In a previous life, Aqun was once a bhikṣu.
He carried one hu of rice to a monastery and offered a knife to the Buddha.
Rejoicing and praising the Honored One, they bowed their heads and departed.
By carrying rice, one gains great strength;
by ascending the blade, one obtains many treasures.
Through joy one obtains an upright appearance;
by praising the Honored One one obtains kingship;
and because of performing prostrations, one becomes honored by the multitude throughout the land.
Ninety-nine people chipped away at his head until they lost their own lives;
therefore, he killed his former enemy and cut off his finger.
When the next person wished to chip it, he saw that [the head] had already perished.
Furthermore, seeing that the śramaṇa still possessed a compassionate heart,
the person who was later his mother first conceived an evil intention; therefore, Ajita also became wicked.
Because one perceives the śramaṇa as even more compassionate, seeing the Buddha is itself filial piety. One reaps what one sows:
if one sows purity, one obtains purity;
if one sows mixture, one obtains mixture.
When good and evil enemies have already bestowed their blessings or calamities, these follow immediately;
like shadows pursuing forms or echoes responding to sounds, all have their causes.
They do not arise spontaneously. —From the *Pumingwang jing* (Sūtra of King Universal Radiance).
13. As the crown prince of King Padma, he gave his marrow to a sick person; as the crown prince of King Padma, he gave his marrow to a sick person—this was the thirteenth, Ānanda.
In a past age, there was a prince named King Lotus.
Handsome, beautiful, and of towering majesty,
he went out onto the road and saw a man whose body was afflicted with leprosy.
Having seen him, he felt compassion and asked the patient, "What medicine can cure this?
The patient replied:
"Only by obtaining the marrow from the king's body to anoint my own can my illness be cured.
At that time, the prince immediately broke his own bones and marrow to bestow them joyfully upon the sick man, his heart free of regret.
"At that time, the crown prince was none other than myself.
One might as well measure the waters of the great ocean with a peck;
the marrow of my body given in alms cannot be reckoned. This is from the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*.

14. For the sake of a king’s crown prince, he drew blood from his own body to give as an offering to a sick person; for the sake of a king’s crown prince, he drew blood from his own body to give as an offering to a sick person—this is the fourteenth.
Ānanda, when I was originally seeking the Way, I underwent immeasurable hardships and suffering.
In a past life, he was the crown prince of a king,
named Khyāpayan (Manifesting to the Multitudes).
His appearance was upright, dignified, and most beautiful.
Emerging from the park and garden,
he saw a man on the road who was afflicted with a grave and terminal illness.
Seeing him, he asked the sick man,
"With what medicine shall I treat your illness?
The patient replied:
"Only the blood from the King’s own body can cure my illness.
The Prince immediately pierced his body with a sharp blade and gave his blood to the sick man;
he bestowed it with a sincere heart, his mind free of regret.
The Crown Prince was none other than myself.
Ānanda, the waters of the four great oceans might yet be measured with a peck.
The blood from my own body given as an offering is beyond measure.
For the sake of seeking perfect enlightenment, I have brought forth this *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*.
(From the *Sūtra-lakṣaṇa-vibhaṅga*, Volume 10)
*Jīnglù yìxiàng*, Scroll Eleven, Section on Manifesting Bodies According to Circumstances, Part Four: Bodhisattvas.
Compiled by the Liang Dynasty Śramaṇas Sengmin, Baoshang, and others.
First, he bestowed [the teachings] upon the four *ṛṣis*; later, he became a king in a future world. One.
1. Because the intentions of his paternal uncles and himself were different, his conduct and standing became distinct from theirs.
2. He manifested as a mountain of flesh to give it away to sentient beings. 3. As the son of a great householder, he saved a turtle, a snake, and a fox.

4. He manifested as a lion and became a close friend to a monkey. 5. He manifested as a white elephant to benefit all things. 6. Formerly, as a dragon, he exhorted his companions to practice patience.
Seventh, he took the body of a bear to rescue a lost traveler; eighth, he took the body of a deer king to undergo death in place of one who was pregnant;
ninth, he took the body of a majestic deer king and, having fallen into a net, was released by a hunter; tenth, he took the body of a nine-colored deer to save a drowning man;
eleventh, he took the body of a goose king, and when a hunter captured him, he was released so that the king might repay his kindness.
12. Appearing as a parrot to extinguish a mountain fire in order to repay a debt of gratitude;
13. Appearing as a king of sparrows to extract a bone from a tiger’s mouth; 14. Appearing as a great fish to relieve hunger and thirst; 15.
Appearing as a king of turtles to transform his fellow creatures and save a multitude of merchants; 16. Section on Bodhisattvas Manifesting Bodies According to Circumstances.
(1) First, having previously given [alms] to the four *ṛṣis*, he later became a king in a future life.
First, having previously given [alms] to the four *ṛṣis*, he later became a king in a future life. A long time ago, incalculable *kalpas* past.
There were five rishis dwelling in mountain thickets;
four of them served as leaders.
A certain person attended and served him without ever losing his composure, gathering fruits and drawing water to offer at the proper times.
One day, while gathering fruits for juice, he grew weary and fell asleep.
They did not return at the appointed time;
by then the sun had already passed its zenith,
and the four men lost their meal.
Harboring resentment can lead to malevolent incantations.
Upon hearing this, the attendant withdrew to the foot of a tree and reflected with self-reproach upon his long years of diligent service.
Now, having violated the four sages' provision of food at the proper time,
he has lost the Way of the Teachings and failed to follow the Four Immeasurables;
consequently, he has perished through his own karma.
His feet were always clad in sandals made of the seven precious gems.
He sat with one foot raised,
and the gem-encrusted sandal on that foot fell into the water and was lost.
After his life ended, he was immediately reborn as a follower of external paths (tīrthika),
becoming the son of a practitioner of malevolent incantations.
He was over ten years of age.
He was playing with his peers by the side of the road when a brahmin happened to see the boy playing.
As the number of people was vast,
he observed them all and saw that the son of the malevolent sorcerer possessed the unique marks of a nobleman and should become a king.
His countenance was exceptionally distinguished, surpassing that of all men.
A brahmin addressed him, saying, "You possess the marks of a king; it is not fitting for you to wander among the common multitude."
The youth replied, "I am a son of an evil incantation; how could I possess the marks of a king?
The brahmin spoke again:
If the appearance and physical form [of this person] accord with our own scriptures and match the prophetic texts,
then you should respond accordingly.
"When the king of this country passes away, you shall surely succeed him to the throne.
The youth replied, "I shall do so;
as for those like you who have shown such sincerity, I must surely keep your great kindness in mind."
When the brahmin had finished speaking,
he immediately fled and went abroad to travel through other lands.
Not long thereafter,
the king passed away without an heir.
The state sought out a man of virtue to serve as the royal successor.
The messengers dispersed in the four directions.
From afar, they beheld this youth possessing the extraordinary bearing of a man of distinction;
they immediately dispatched others back to inform the ministers.
Only the solemn imperial carriage arrived in search of him to welcome him;
among the ministers and all the officials, there were none who did not leap for joy.
He bathed in fragrant water and donned his court robes for the five periods of the day.
Wearing a jeweled crown and sword-belt, he ascended the throne in the palace and proclaimed his imperial authority facing south;
the realm was peaceful and secure, and the common people rejoiced exultantly.
At that time, the brahmin looked upward at the celestial phenomena and downward at the terrestrial features; having understood [the signs],
he knew that his son had been established as the successor.
He immediately went to the palace gate to seek an audience with the king.
The brahmin performed divinations and offered thanks,
pronouncing these words of blessing:
"It is as you have sworn, most earnestly.
The King said,
"Truly so!"
"You may have whatever you desire.
The brahmin replied,
"I seek only two boons."
The first is that his food and drink, movements and halts, clothing, and rising and reclining are equal to those of the king.
The second is:
"In matters of state, you must consult with those who have reached a consensus; do not act on your own authority.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The king governed with the True Dharma and did not wrong the myriad people;
however, the brahmin was arrogant and self-indulgent, treating his high ministers with contempt. Consequently, the assembly of ministers became resentful and incensed.
They all advanced together to remonstrate, saying:
"The King’s honorable position is high;
it is fitting that you consult with the elder ministers of the state."
By placing undue trust in mendicants,
you have allowed them to act with arrogance and insolence, insulting the various offices of state.
When neighboring countries hear of this, they will surely mock you, leading to the onset of invasions and calamities.
The king said, "I have made a vow with him; how can it be broken?
Though his ministers remonstrated without ceasing, when it was time for the king to eat, he [the monk] arrived.
"Do not associate with him;
then he will surely reform.
The King then agreed to this.
Whenever the brahmin went out, [the Buddha] would eat first.
The brahmin, filled with resentment, said:
"What was our original agreement? Why do you eat alone before me?"
He rebuked him, saying,
"Shame on you, you wretched sorcerer!
Simply provide him with provisions and drive him out of the country."
Traveling alone along a distant road, braving cold and heat,
he reached another country utterly exhausted and emaciated,
where he went to the home of a non-Brahmin (vānaprastha) with whom he had long been acquainted.
He asked again: "From where have you come, and what have you studied?
Which scriptures do you master, and which can you recite from memory?"
He replied,
"I have come from afar and am oppressed by hunger and cold;
I have forgotten what I had practiced and recited."
The brahmin thought to himself:
"This man is incapable of doing anything else;
I shall have him perform field labor."
He immediately provided him with slaves, oxen for plowing, and farming implements.
The Brahmin engaged the slaves in the arduous labor of tilling and sowing,
cruelly ordering them to level the ground and dispatching them here and there.
The servant was despondent;
wishing to throw himself into the water,
he went to the riverbank and there found a pair of sandals made of the seven precious gems.
He thought to himself:
"This brahmin has exhausted me with his baseless demands;
I shall now comply with him."
"If you offer these wooden clogs to him, you may obtain his pardon.
He immediately took the clogs back and presented them to the king.
The Brahmin was filled with joy and thought to himself:
"The value of these sandals made of the seven precious gems is beyond reproach.
By offering them to the King against his will,
my transgression may be resolved."
He soon returned to the kingdom and presented his wooden clogs to the king,
deeply confessing and repenting for his previous transgressions and offenses.
"I pray that you will grant me your pardon.
The King said,
"Excellent!"
He immediately ushered him inside the inner curtain,
led him to a seat,
and assembled his various ministers.
The Emperor issued an edict, saying: "Have you all seen that former brahmin?
They replied: "We have."
"I do not see it.
The King asked, "If you were to see it, what would you do?"
Everyone said,
"One should treat this with the five poisons.
The King then brought out his precious sandals to show them to his ministers.
He commanded the brahmin to come forth and meet with his ministers,
saying, "Since this extraordinary treasure has been brought here, we should investigate its origin together. The ministers replied:
"The offenses of this brahmin are like mountains and oceans;
offering a single sandal provides no remedy or repair.
Only by obtaining a pair could his transgressions be expiated."
The king agreed to this.
He again pursued the brahmin,

The brahmin, filled with distress, returned to his former master and asked the slave boy:
"From where did you originally obtain those precious sandals?"

The servant then abandoned them and departed.
The brahmin thought,
"These sandals must have come floating down from upstream," and he immediately began traveling upstream against the current.
He saw a great lotus flower floating amidst the swirling currents, held in the mouth of a fish;
the flower had more than a thousand petals.
The brahmin thought to himself:
"Although I do not have sandals, I can offer these flowers to him.
Perhaps he will forgive my transgression and restore me to his former favor."
He then took up a flower and saw four seers sitting beneath a tree.
The seers said:
"From where have you come, sir?
He replied,
"I have lost the King's favor."
Although offering a single sandal was insufficient to atone for his transgression,
he followed the current upstream to seek it but did not find it.
The rishi said to him:
"You, as a student, ought to know when to advance and when to retreat.
That king is my disciple; we share a bond of service, affection, and respect, sitting together and eating from the same vessel."
"Why did you suddenly revile him as the son of an evil incantation?
Your sin has led to this execution and harm.
Now, instead of questioning me, point out the tree beneath which he lies."
The King had previously served as my attendant;
he passed away with one leg raised,
and a single jeweled sandal fell into the water, remaining upon his foot.
The brahmin took the sandals, bowed his head in apology for his transgression,
and returned to his own country where he continued to offer them to the king.
The king was immediately filled with joy, and the great minister’s mind was liberated.
He was restored to his former position of honor.
The Buddha said,
"The king was none other than myself."
As for the four sages:
Krakucchanda Buddha and Kanakamuni Buddha.
Kāśyapa Buddha and Maitreya Buddha are they;
that brahmin was Devadatta. This is from the *Pañcārṣa-sūtra*.

"Upon entering a country, one should adapt to its customs and observe its protocols."

"How can you go about naked and destroy our ancient rites?

From the beginning, Shi both criticized and praised the greatness of the provisional path (upāya).
Consequently, they went together to that place. Bo said:
