the Earl said,
"You must certainly follow the customary rites."

they smear their heads with sesame oil and paint their bodies with white earth.

the people of the land rejoiced and sighed in admiration,

Boer rode in a carriage into the state and said that the enforcement of strict laws would invariably run counter to the hearts of the people.
The king, enraged by the people's insolence and having confiscated their wealth, sentenced them to flogging.
When the younger brother pleaded on their behalf, they were released.
Together they returned to their own country.
Those who saw off their uncle were reviled on the road, while those who saw off their elder brother covered their ears.
The elder brother felt ashamed and angry, saying,
"What kinship do they have with you?"
"What enmity do you have with me?
You have bestowed a favor upon me, yet you now seize it; is this not slander?
He then made a solemn oath with his uncle, saying:
"From this day forward, for generation after generation, we shall persecute you and never pardon you.
The Bodhisattva, moved with deep sorrow, shed tears and vowed:
"May I, in every lifetime, encounter the Buddhas, behold the Dharma, and personally serve the śramaṇas."
The fourfold kindness universally covers and moistens all sentient beings;
having received [the teachings] from the Elder, I shall not violate this vow.
From this time forward...
Boche oppressed his uncle, but Shu Chang rescued him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the uncle was my own self."
The Bodhisattva Tiyue appeared in the *Peacock King Sūtra* and also in the fifth fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Collection of the Infinite*.
Third, he fashioned a mountain of flesh to give as a gift to sentient beings; he fashioned a mountain of flesh to give as a gift to sentient beings three incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past.
At that time, this world-realm was named Vimala-Meru;
the human lifespan was one hundred years,
and a Buddha appeared in the world.
His name shall be Fragrant Lotus.
After his parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, at that time, I—
He became a Cakravartin King of great power,
known as Hard to Overcome,
and ruled over Jambudvīpa.
I have fully exhorted and transformed his thousand sons,
causing them all to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
I wish to leave the household life and cultivate the Way during the Semblance Dharma,
so as to ardently increase and propagate the Bequeathed Teachings of the Buddha;
with the sole exception of my six sons.
Unwilling to leave the household life and resolve upon bodhicitta,
he would ultimately not go forth despite my speaking with kind words.
I questioned them again,
seeking to inspire in them the aspiration for the unsurpassed path;
the six sons replied:
"If you can grant me Jambudvīpa,
then I shall resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having heard this, my heart was filled with joy.
He thought to himself:
"I have now converted the people of Jambudvīpa;
I shall now divide this Jambudvīpa."
He divided it into six portions and gave them to these six sons,
causing them to give rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed path.
"Only then shall I renounce the world to practice the Way.
He immediately divided Jambudvīpa into six parts and bestowed them upon his six sons,
whereupon he promptly went forth into homelessness.
At that time, the six sons were each at variance with one another, plundering and attacking;
meanwhile, throughout the entire Jambudvīpa, [the people suffered].
The crops failed to ripen and the people suffered from famine;
rain and water did not fall in their proper seasons, and all the trees withered away,
failing to produce flowers or fruit.
The birds and beasts were all hungry,
and their bodies were burning with heat;
at that time, I gave up my own body— its skin, flesh, and blood.
In order to give to sentient beings so as to satisfy them,
at that time I cast my own body.
By the power of his vow, it immediately became a mountain of flesh,
one yojana in height,
with its length and breadth being exactly equal.
At that time, the people,
flying birds, and wild beasts all began from this very moment.
Devouring flesh and drinking blood,
by virtue of their original vows,
they increased and expanded their bodies within that place.
It is even a thousand yojanas in height,
and its length and breadth are likewise exactly a thousand yojanas;
on its perimeter, human heads naturally emerge.
Their hair, body hairs, eyes, ears, noses, mouths, lips,
and tongues were all fully formed. Within each of those heads,
there was a voice that uttered these words:
All sentient beings,
each according to their own desire and will, took and used them as they pleased,
drinking blood and eating flesh.
He takes their eyes, ears, noses, tongues, teeth, and so forth, providing them all with what they lack;
thereafter, he causes them all to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
or else to resolve upon the mind of a *śrāvaka* or a *pratyekabuddha*.
Or, seeking the wealth and happiness of the heavens or among humans,
by virtue of their original vows, their bodies shall suffer no diminution for as long as ten thousand years.
Within Jambudvīpa,
humans, various ghosts and spirits,
flying birds, and beasts.
All were fully satisfied.
You should now know that during my past ten thousand years, I...
He gave away immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodies,
providing his flesh and blood as alms to immeasurable, boundless beings until they were all fully satisfied; yet,
not even for a single moment did he give rise to a mind of regret.
In this manner, he successively filled Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
giving away his own body’s flesh and blood, he bestowed them upon sentient beings, causing them all to be fully satisfied.

This constitutes the Dānapāramitā; it is largely identical to the ninth fascicle of the *Beihua jing* (Sutra of the Compassionate Flower), specifically the section on the "Past World of Fragrant Lotus Buddha," with the sole exception that the bodhisattvas are not mentioned therein.
4. To save the tortoises, snakes, and foxes while serving as a high official. Once in the past, the Bodhisattva served as a high official.
He accumulated wealth amounting to billions,
yet he constantly made offerings to the Triple Gem and extended compassion toward all sentient beings.
He went to the market to watch a performance and immediately saw a turtle; his heart was moved with compassion for it,
and he asked what its price was.

The turtle-master knew that the Bodhisattva possessed the virtue of universal compassion, constantly rescuing sentient beings; his wealth was beyond counting, and he showed no partiality toward the noble or the lowly.
He replied, "One million."
"If you can take it, that is well; if not, I shall devour you.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Excellent! Take the turtle home, bathe it, and protect it so that it is not harmed.
When you release it by the water, watch as it floats away."
With compassion and joy, he made this vow:
"May the beings of the realm of hungry ghosts in Mount Tai and those in the prisons of worldly rulers be swiftly delivered from their hardships."
May your body be at ease and your life preserved, just as it is now.
Bowing my head to the ten directions with palms joined, I pray:
"Sentient beings are in turmoil, their suffering immeasurable."
I shall act as earth; I shall provide moisture for the drought-stricken;
I shall provide rafts for those in the marshes.
For the hungry, food; for the thirsty, drink;
for those cold, clothing; for those in heat, coolness;
acting as physicians for the sick and as light for the darkness.
"If there should be a time of turbidity and perversion in the world,
I shall become a Buddha therein to deliver those sentient beings.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions have approved this vow.
He praised him, saying: "Excellent!
You shall surely attain your aspiration."
That night, a turtle came and gnawed at his gate;
finding the gate making a noise,
he sent someone out to look and saw the turtle.
He returned and reported the matter exactly as it had happened.
The Bodhisattva looked at the turtle and it immediately spoke in human speech, saying:
"I have received profound kindness; my life has been preserved."
There was no way to express my gratitude.
Creatures that dwell in water know the ebb and flow of the waters;
when the floodwaters were about to arrive, they knew it would surely cause great harm.
"I pray that you will quickly prepare a boat to come and welcome me when the time arrives.
He replied, "Very well."
At dawn the next morning, he went to the palace gate and reported the matter to the king.
The king said,
"The Bodhisattva has long possessed a reputation for goodness."
Believing his words, he moved from the low ground to a high place.
At that time, Shi Bie came and said,
"The great flood is arriving!"
"You may quickly mount and follow where I am going;
you will surely obtain freedom from harm."
The boat followed after it.
A snake approached the boat,
and the Bodhisattva said:
He took it.
The turtle said,
"Excellent!"
Furthermore, they saw a floating fox and said, "Let us take it.
The turtle also said, "Excellent."
Furthermore, he saw a person being swept away,
striking his cheeks and crying out to Heaven, lamenting for his life. He said:
He reached out to seize it.
The turtle said,
"Be careful not to seize it!"
The hearts of ordinary people are full of deceit and falsehood;
few ever maintain constant faithfulness.
They turn their backs on kindness and pursue power.
"Regarding those who are good, evil, or cruel and rebellious," the Bodhisattva said,
"I shall deliver all classes of sentient beings."
"To further abandon them to seek others—
how could that be benevolent?
I cannot bear to do such a thing."
Thereupon he took it.
The turtle said, "Alas, what a regret! Go instead to fertile soil."
The turtle declined, saying,
"Now that my debt of gratitude has been repaid, I beg to withdraw.
He replied:
"When I have attained the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
I shall certainly deliver you.
The turtle said:
"Excellent! The turtle withdrew;
the snake and the fox each departed.
A fox made its dwelling in a burrow and discovered an ancient hidden treasure of one hundred catties of purple-polished gold.
Rejoicing, it said:
"I must repay that kindness.
He hurried back and reported,
"The small insect received my moisture and was saved from its precarious life."
An insect, a creature that dwells in burrows, sought a hole for its own security and obtained a hundred catties of gold.
This hole was not dug by cultivation, nor was it a home;
it was not seized by force, nor stolen by theft.
"This is the result of my sincere devotion;
I wish to offer it to you as a tribute to your worthiness.
The Bodhisattva reflected deeply and did not accept it.
To let it go to waste would be of no benefit to the poor;
would it not be well to take it and bestow it as alms upon sentient beings so that they may obtain relief?
He searched for and took it.
The man who had been adrift saw this and said, "Give me half."
The Bodhisattva then gave him ten *jin* [of gold].
The man adrift said,
"You have dug up and unearthed the gold of a robber."
"What shall be done with this crime?
Do not divide it in half;
I shall certainly inform the authorities."
He replied,
"I wish to give impartially to the poor and the distressed; you, however,
desire to monopolize it for yourself."
"Is this not also partial?
The drifting man then reported the matter to the authorities.
When the Bodhisattva was seen and detained, he had no one to whom he could appeal.
I take refuge solely in the Triple Gem, repenting my transgressions and reproaching myself.
I pray with compassion that all sentient beings may soon be freed from the eight difficulties,
and that none may harbor enmity as I do now.
The snake and the fox met and said,
"What shall we do about this matter?
The snake replied:
"I shall rescue him. He then took excellent medicine in his mouth, opened the gate, and entered the prison.
Seeing the Bodhisattva’s appearance, his countenance was impaired; he was moved with deep sorrow and grief at heart.
He said to the Bodhisattva,
"Take this medicine with you;
I shall soon bite the Prince."
The poison was so extreme that none could provide relief;
yet, when the worthy man applied his medicine to himself, he was immediately cured.
The Bodhisattva remained silent.
The snake was as had been said.
As the prince was about to perish,
the king commanded:
If there is one capable of rescuing this state,
I shall enfeoff him as Chancellor and inform him that he shall participate in the governance.
When the Bodhisattva heard this, he applied it and [the king] was immediately cured.
The king, filled with joy, asked how this had come about;
the Bodhisattva then related the matter from beginning to end.
The king, filled with regret and blaming himself,
immediately executed the man who had drifted ashore and issued a general amnesty throughout his kingdom.
He was enfeoffed as Chancellor of the State.
[The Emperor] took his hand and entered the palace;
they sat side by side and said:
What scriptures does the Sage expound?
What Way does he cherish?
And how does he manifest the benevolence and grace of the Two Polarities?
"Does this apply to sentient beings? He replied,
"It refers to those who expound the Buddhist scriptures and cherish the Buddha-way."
He asked,
"Does the Buddha have an essential secret instruction? He replied:
It exists. The Buddha taught the four impermanences;
those who preserve them will have their manifold blessings flourish.
The King said,
"Excellent! I pray that I may obtain its fruit."
The Bodhisattva spoke thus.
The King said,
"Excellent!"
The Buddha taught that there is no self, and my mind has faith in this.
If even the body cannot be preserved,
how much less so the realm?
How tragic it is for the former kings that they did not hear the teaching of the Unsurpassed, Right, True, and Perfectly Awakened One— that all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
These kings immediately became treasuries of emptiness, bestowing their wealth upon the poor and destitute.
He treated widowers, widows, orphans, and children with compassion as if they were his own sons.
The entire nation was filled with joy, walking about with smiles upon their faces.
Looking up to heaven, he sighed and said:
The bodhisattva’s spiritual transformations reached such an extent that the four quarters praised his virtue, leading to a state of great peace.
The Buddha then addressed the śramaṇas:
The Bodhisattva was my own self; the king was Maitreya;
and the tortoise was Ānanda.
The fox was Qiuluzi; the snake was Maudgalyāyana;
and the drifting man was Devadatta—this is recorded in the *Boshishudu wujijing* (Sutra on the Perfection of Giving).

After the lion had awakened,
he sought the young monkey but could not find him;

He then addressed the vulture, saying,
"I received two children as a trust from a monkey;
I have failed to guard them with sufficient care."
I have allowed you to depart,
thereby betraying my word and my trust;
I now demand restitution from you.
I am the king among beasts,
and you are the lord among birds;
our noble status and power are equal.
"It is fitting that you return it.
The vulture said,
"You do not know the proper time."
"I am now hungry and exhausted; what need is there to discuss similarities or differences?
The lion, knowing it was impossible to obtain [the meat], used his own sharp claws.
He tore the flesh from his own flanks to trade for the monkey.
Furthermore, in a past life...
The people were afflicted by many diseases;
they suffered from jaundice and impotence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva took the form of a red fish.
He personally gave his own flesh as an offering to various sick people in order to save them from their illnesses.
Furthermore, in the past, the Bodhisattva...

He saw a man who had entered deep water;
in a place not frequented by humans, he was caught in a snare set by a water spirit.
The water deity’s noose-bindings are such that they cannot be untied; however,
if one can reach Mount Gandhamādana, [they may be released].
He took a medicinal herb and placed it upon his snare;
the cord immediately rotted away, and the man was able to escape.
Such are his immeasurable *jātaka* tales.
The *Jātaka-sūtra*, which contains many accounts of saving others, appears in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
6. Manifesting as the body of a white elephant to benefit beings; manifesting as the body of a white elephant to benefit beings. Part Six: Subhūti’s Questions.
The Bodhisattva has perfected his roots of goodness.
Why, then, is he born as an elephant or a horse?
The Buddha said:
Bodhisattvas truly possess merit and have perfected their roots of goodness;
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they assume the forms of animals.
There is no sin of being an animal.
When a bodhisattva is among animals,
he feels compassion for his enemies and plunderers.
This is something that Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas do not possess.
When Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are harmed by the arrival of enemies and thieves, [they are unable to prevent it].
Although they do not repay [his kindness],
they are unable to love, cherish, provide for,
or support him as the Bodhisattva did in his previous lives.
He manifested as a six-tusked white elephant.
A hunter struck him in the chest with a poisoned arrow;
at that moment, the Bodhisattva elephant embraced the hunter with his trunk.
He did not allow other elephants to harm him,
and he said to the female elephant,
"You shall be the wife of a Bodhisattva."
For what reason did he give rise to an evil mind?
The hunter’s fault lies in his afflictions;
it is not the fault of the non-human being.
"When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall extinguish their afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is like a sorcerer who treats a person possessed by a ghost; he treats the ghost, yet does not see the person."
He questioned the hunter slowly:
"Why did you shoot me?
The hunter replied:
"I require your tusks.
The elephant immediately approached a rock, pulled out his tusks, and gave them to him;
though both flesh and blood gushed forth, he felt no pain.
Providing food and drink, showing the way,
and such acts of compassion are things that Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas do not possess.
Question: Why does he not assume a human body to preach the Dharma,
but instead takes on this animal form?
The answer is:
There are times when sentient beings do not believe or accept [the teaching] upon seeing a human body;
therefore, one preaches the Dharma while manifesting in the body of an animal.
Then they will give rise to faith and joy,
and receive his transformative teaching,
O Bodhisattva.
Desiring to fulfill the mind of great compassion and desiring to practice its actual deeds,
sentient beings who see him are filled with joy and wonder, and all attain entry into the Way. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, scroll 93).
7. Formerly, as a Dragon, He Exhorted His Companions to Practice Patience. Once upon a time, the Bodhisattva was together with Ānanda;
their karmic retributions were now complete.
Each transformed into the body of a dragon.
One of the dragons said,
"I alone shall dwell with you together within the ocean."
"There is nothing I do not see.
May we now ascend together to the dry land to play?
He replied:
The land-dweller became enraged; encountering such an extraordinary occurrence, he could not escape.
Another dragon said, "Transform yourself into a small snake."
"If there are no people on the road, we shall play along the great path;
whenever we encounter someone, we will hide—what have we to worry about?
Thereupon, they agreed.
They ascended together to travel and observe.
Not long after emerging from the water,
they encountered venomous snakes and vipers on the way.
When the viper saw the two snakes, its malevolent intent to harm them arose,
and it spat out poisonous foam.
One of the snakes then sought to kill the venomous viper.
One serpent, out of compassion and patience, admonished him to stop,
saying: "Now,
one who acts as a noble person should forgive the many who are ignorant."
To endure what is unbearable is the instruction of the sages.
He then spoke in verse:
Greed makes a man mad; no one possesses a heart of righteousness.
Envy leads to the desire to harm and to heedlessness; only silent forbearance brings peace.
Thus the snake praised patience.
One snake respectfully accepted this and consequently did not harm the viper.
Another snake said,
"Let us return to the sea."
They then departed together,
manifesting their majestic spiritual power,
which shook the heavens and made the earth tremble.
Clouds rose and rain fell;
both humans and spirits were struck with alarm,
while the viper was filled with terror.
The corpse appeared lifeless;
for seven days it had been without the desire for food.
This was the dragon Aṇḍa, who later became Ānanda.
The one who spoke of patience as being his own self was I;
the venomous serpent was Devadatta. This is from the fifth fascicle of the *Dazhidu wuji ji* (Collection on the Immeasurable Perfection of Wisdom).
8. Saving the Lost Traveler by Assuming the Form of a Bear. There were eight people.
Entering the forest to fell timber,
he became disoriented and lost his way;
at that time, a heavy rain fell.
At twilight, overcome by hunger and cold,
and threatened by predatory insects and venomous beasts,
this person enters a stone cave.
There was a large bear;
seeing him, it came out in fear.
The bear said to him:
"Do not be afraid.
This house is warm; you may stay the night within it.
At that time, it rained continuously for seven days.
He constantly provided this man with sweet fruits and fine water.
After seven days, the rain ceased,
and the bear led the man and showed him the path.
The bear spoke to the man, saying:
"I am a body of sin, and you are my enemy.
If anyone asks about this," [he said].
"Do not say you have seen me.
The person replied, "I have.
Then that man went forward.
He saw some hunters.
The hunters asked him,
"Where have you come from?"
"Do you see any wild beasts?
He replied,
"I see a large bear."
"He has been kind to me;
I cannot reveal him to you.
The hunter said:
"You belong to the human faction;
viewing things from the perspective of human characteristics,
why do you begrudge the bear?"
Now that I have once lost my way,
when shall I come again? Show me the path.
"I will give you most of it.
This man's mind changed;
he then showed the hunter the bear's location.
The hunter killed the bear and gave him the greater portion.
The man extended his hand to take the meat.
Both his arms fell off.
The hunter asked,
"What crime have you committed?"
He replied,
"This bear looked upon me as a father gazes upon his son."
I have now repaid his kindness with ingratitude;
may this karmic retribution bring terror to hunters.
He did not dare eat meat,
but instead took it and offered it to the assembly of monks.
The presiding elder was an Arhat endowed with the six supernormal powers.
He said to the junior monks,
"This is a bodhisattva;
in a future age he shall become a Buddha."
"Do not eat this meat.
He immediately erected a stūpa to make offerings to it.
When the king heard of this matter, [he was moved].
An imperial edict was issued throughout the realm:
"Let no person who betrays their gratitude dwell here.
For various reasons, people [acted accordingly].
This praise of those who recognize kindness extracts essential matters from various sūtras.
9. Acting as a Deer King to Take the Death of One Carrying a Fetus. Long ago, when the Buddha was in the country of Vārāṇasī, at the Ṛṣipatana Deer Park, [he told this story].
The seers possessing the five supernatural powers all travel and study in this country;
it is not a place where ordinary worldlings dwell.
The king went out on a hunting expedition and encountered a herd of a thousand deer that had all fallen into a net.
The king deployed his infantry to surround them in a single circle.
The herd of deer was terrified;
some let out cries and rushed headlong into the thicket, while others prostrated themselves on the ground to hide their forms. Śākyamuni Buddha—
In the past, when he was a bodhisattva,
he was the king of a herd of deer.
The Buddha himself addressed the herd of deer, saying:
"Set your minds at ease and do not fear further.
I shall employ skillful means;
by entreating the king with compassion, we will surely save our lives."
Each was without another.
The deer king came toward the human king, knelt down, and begged for mercy.
The human king saw him from afar.
The king issued a decree to his attendants, saying, "Do not harm the deer.
The deer said,
"Now I observe the King's intention."
"I wish to kill a thousand deer to provide for the kitchen for one day.
It is currently very hot;
the meat cannot be kept for long."
"I pray that Your Majesty will take pity on me;
let me kill one deer each day to provide for the kitchen,
so as not to trouble Your Majesty's messengers."
"The deer shall go of its own accord to the kitchen to meet its death; thus,
the supply of meat for offerings will never cease."
The deer became numerous.
The king asked a deer,
"Are you the largest among the herd?"
He replied, "It is so.
The king then questioned the deer again.
"Is this truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The king immediately abandoned the deer, withdrew his forces, and entered the city.
At that time, the Bodhisattva led five hundred deer,
and Devadatta likewise led five hundred deer.
Every day a deer was sent to the king’s kitchen for his provisions.
On this occasion, it was the turn of Devadatta to dispatch a deer to the king.
It happened that a doe, who had been pregnant for several months and was next in line to be provided to the kitchen,
addressed the king, saying:
"Now she is about to give birth;
it is my turn to go next,
though my son's turn has not yet arrived."
"I wish to see you ranked and seated; let me wait behind for a moment.
Devadatta said in anger, "Why do you not go quickly?"
"Who can die before you to take your place?
The mother deer wept piteously, wailing and crying out,
immediately approaching the Bodhisattva to present her plea in this manner.
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant me forgiveness and allow me to follow behind.
The Bodhisattva then questioned the deer.
"Does your master allow you to speak for yourself?
He replied, "My master does not grant me permission."
The Bodhisattva comforted the deer,
saying, "Do not fear;
I shall now take your place."
To provide for the kitchen,
the Bodhisattva Deer King immediately summoned a thousand deer.
I earnestly exhort you:
do not harbor indolence or arrogance,
nor must you encroach upon the king’s autumn harvests and grain.
Devadatta became angry with Mṛgāramātā and said, "It is your turn; what do you have to say?
The Bodhisattva spoke to Devadatta.
"Stop, stop! Do not speak such words.
While it is indeed true that the mother deer should die next, she must not die yet for the sake of her unborn fetus."
"I shall take their place to save their lives.
The herd of deer spoke of themselves, saying,
"We wish to take the King's place and undergo death in his stead."
"As long as I remain alive, Your Majesty,
you shall have access to water and grass;
you may roam at your pleasure."
Free from fear or hesitation,
the king then proceeded to the kitchen;
the herd of deer followed him in pursuit all the way to the royal palace.
The deer king went to the kitchen and sought to offer himself for slaughter.
When the cook saw the deer king,
he immediately went to inform the king.
"The deer king has entered the kitchen;
he is next in line for slaughter.
I do not know, Great King."
"Is he fit to be killed?
The king commanded his ministers,
"Bring the deer king here at once."
The king asked the deer,
"Are the thousand deer all gone? Why have you come?"
The deer said to the king:
"A thousand heads have been born and nursed, forming a great herd that increases day by day."
There was no omission; he recounted the preceding events in full detail,
and the king reproached himself with earnest sincerity.
I lament my own inadequacy;
as a beast, I could not distinguish between the true and the false,
and have thus wrongly killed living beings.
Upon arriving there,
the king addressed his ministers,
ordering them throughout the realm that anyone who went hunting and killed deer should be punished.
"You must seize and execute him.
He then dispatched the deer king back,
ordering that no one within the kingdom was permitted to eat deer meat.
"Whoever eats meat shall have their head struck off as a warning.
It was for this reason that the place was named Mṛgadāva (Deer Park). *Chūyào jīng* (Udānavarga), Scroll 9.

10. Regarding the body of the majestic deer king that fell into a net and was released by a hunter; regarding the body of the majestic deer king that fell into a net and was released by a hunter. The Buddha said:
In a past life, near the foot of the Snowy Mountains,
there was a king of deer named Vīryaśrī.
He became the leader of five hundred deer.
At that time, there was a hunter who set out grain and laid snares.
The leader of the deer walked forward;
his right foot fell into a hair-net.
The king of the deer thought to himself:
"If I manifest my form,
then the deer will not dare to eat the grain;
they must finish eating all the grain."
Thereupon he manifested his feet;
at that time, all the deer departed,
but one female deer remained.
He spoke in verse, saying:
"Great King, you should know that this hunter has come; I pray you, exert yourself with skillful means to escape from these snares. At that time, the Deer King replied in verse:
"I have exerted myself with diligent skillful means until my strength was exhausted; the snare of hair has tightened further, and I cannot escape.
When the female deer saw that the hunter had arrived, [she spoke thus].
He spoke these verses:
"O hunter, first kill my body with a sharp blade, and only then may you release the king of deer to go. Upon hearing this, the hunter...
Giving rise to a heart of compassion,
he replied in verse:
"I shall never kill you, nor shall I kill the king of deer."
"I release you and the king of the deer; go wherever you wish.
The hunter immediately released the king of the deer.
The Buddha said:
The Deer King of old was my present self;
the five hundred deer were the five hundred bhikṣus. [This is from] the first fascicle of the *Saṃyukta-varga* of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
11. Regarding the Nine-Colored Deer who saved a drowning man: Regarding the Nine-Colored Deer who saved a drowning man, number eleven. Long ago, the Bodhisattva...
He was a nine-colored deer;
its fur was of nine different colors,
and its horns were as white as snow.
While he was eating grass and drinking water by the side of the Ganges River,
he had always been on friendly terms with a crow.
At that time, there was a drowning man in the water.
Carried along by the current,
they were swept downstream; now emerging, now submerging,
they looked up toward the heavens and cried out.
"O mountain deities, tree deities, and all the devas and nāgas,
why do you not have pity on me?
Hearing these words as he descended into the water, the deer spoke.
"You may mount my back and grasp my horns;
I shall carry you out onto the shore and set you down on the ground."
He circumambulated the deer three times,
bowed his head to it,
and begged to become the Great Officer’s slave.
He ordered his attendants to gather water plants,
but the deer said, "There is no need for that;
let us each depart on our own way."
Those who wish to repay my kindness,
do not say that I am here;
people covet my hide and horns.
"He will surely come to kill me.
At that time, the king's consort saw a nine-colored deer in a dream during the night.
He then feigned illness and did not rise.
When the king asked why, he replied:
Last night, I saw in a dream an extraordinary deer;
its fur was of nine different colors,
and its antlers were white as snow.
"I wish to obtain its hide to make a seat-mat and its horns to make a fly-whisk handle;
Your Majesty should procure these for me."
"If Your Majesty does not obtain me, I shall die.
The king issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom:
"If there is anyone who can obtain him, I shall share the kingdom with him and grant him authority over it."
He was granted a golden bowl filled with silver grain and a silver bowl filled with golden grain. Upon hearing this,
the man who had drowned desired to obtain such wealth and honor.
He thought to himself:
"The deer is an animal;
what does it matter whether it lives or dies?"
He went to the king and informed him of the deer's location.
The king was greatly delighted and said,
"If you can obtain its hide and antlers and bring them here..."
He offered half his kingdom in recompense.
On the face of the man who had drowned him, leprosy immediately broke out.
The man who had been drowned said:
"Great King, although this deer is a beast, it possesses great majesty and power;
Your Majesty should dispatch many men and soldiers, and only then can it be captured.
The King immediately sent forth a vast multitude of people.
When they reached the banks of the Ganges, a crow perched atop a tree.
Seeing the king’s army approaching, it called out to the deer, saying, "Friend, arise! The king is coming."
Because the deer was lying so deeply asleep, he did not wake up.
A crow descended and pecked at his ear;
only then did the deer startle awake and look in all four directions, yet he no longer made any effort to flee.
He then proceeded toward the side of the king’s chariot.
As a courtier was about to shoot at him,
the king said:
"Do not shoot!
This deer is no ordinary one;
it must be a celestial deity."
The deer said,
"Great King,
please do not shoot me."
"I previously saved one person in the king's realm.
The deer then knelt again and asked the king,
"Who said I was here?"
The king then pointed out,
"It is the man with the leper’s face by the chariot.
The deer immediately raised its head.
Looking upon this person's face,
tears welled up in his eyes;
he could not restrain himself.
"This person was previously drowning in the water;
I did not spare my own body or life,
but threw myself into the water."
Carry this person out;
agree not to speak of it to one another.
There is no returning or reciprocating that is not like a piece of floating wood emerging from the water.
The king felt ashamed.
He counted his people three times over:
"You have received his grace."
How can you instead wish to kill it?
Immediately descend into the kingdom;
if there are those who drive away this deer, [punish them].
When he was about to execute five clans,
several thousand deer all came to seek refuge with him;
they fed on water and grass, never encroaching upon the crops.
The winds and rains fall in their proper seasons, the five grains ripen in abundance,
people are free from illness,
and the world is at peace.
At that time, the nine-colored deer was my own self;
the crow was Ānanda;
and the king was my father, King Śuddhodana.
The king’s consort at that time was none other than the present Sundarī;
the person who drowned at that time was Devadatta.
Although I directed a virtuous mind toward him, [he did not respond].
Therefore, they sought to harm me.
Ānanda, with sincere intent, produced the *Sūtra of the Nine-Colored Deer*.

12. [As] the King of Geese, he was captured by a hunter but released; seeking to repay the king’s kindness, he became the King of Geese again. The hunter captured him once more and released him, seeking to repay the king’s kindness. (Twelfth: In a past life.)
There was a city named Vārāṇasī.
Beside the city was a pond,
and the pond was named Varṣākāra.
In this pond there were many fish, turtles, geese, wild geese, ducks,
and so forth. Among them was a king of geese named Rāṣṭrapāla.
He became the leader of five hundred geese.
At that time, there was a hunter who had previously set out a snare of hair.
The king of geese went forward;
his right foot was caught in the snare,
and he thought to himself:
"If I extend this leg of the snare,
the other geese will not dare to eat the grain;
once they have finished eating, I shall immediately reveal my legs."
The flock of geese flew away,
leaving behind only a single goose named Suma.
He did not leave the king.
The king said to the great minister,
"I shall grant you the office of king."
He went before the geese.
They replied,
"We cannot."
He asked, "For what reason has this come to pass?
At that time, the great minister...
He replied in verse:
"I vow to follow Your Majesty through death and birth, never changing;
It would be better to die with you than to live apart from you. Great King, you should know that this fowler has arrived."
"Only through diligent skillful means shall we seek liberation from this snare.
At that time, the king of geese replied in verse:
"I have exerted myself with diligent skillful means, yet my strength is now exhausted;
the snare of hair has tightened further and I cannot escape.
Then, the minister Soma saw the snare-maker arrive.
He spoke these verses:
"O Great King, my hair, fat, and flesh are no different from yours;
if you kill me with a blade, I shall release you without harming you."
At that time, the fowler said to the minister,
"I will not kill you."
"I release you and the king;
go wherever you please.
The hunter then untied the goose king.
The two geese departed together and said to one another,
"This hunter has performed a most extraordinary feat."
"You have given us our lives;
we shall repay you handsomely for the means of our livelihood. The hunter asked:
"You are a beast; what means of livelihood do you have with which to repay me?
The two geese replied:
"The King of Vārāṇasī is named Brahmadatta.
Take me and deliver me to the hunter;
take the geese and place them upon both your shoulders."
Upon arriving in the city streets,
the goose was so upright and handsome that all the people delighted in seeing it.
Some gave him five coins, ten coins, or twenty coins,
all saying, "Do not kill him.
By the time this man reached the royal palace, [he was accompanied by these offerings].
Having obtained great wealth,
the hunter arrived at the gate of the royal palace and set the wild goose down upon the ground.
The king of geese said to the gatekeeper,
"Inform King Brahmadatta that the king of geese who governs the kingdom is now standing outside the gate."
He then went and informed the king.
The king immediately granted him entry and provided him with a golden couch.
The minister Soma exchanged greetings with him as was appropriate,
and then took his seat.
He addressed King Brahmadatta with a verse of inquiry:
Is the King’s person secure and at ease? Is the realm abundant and prosperous?
Does he transform the people according to the Dharma? Does he govern the kingdom with an impartial mind?
At that time, King Brahmadatta—
He replied in verse:
"I am always personally secure; I transform the people and the nation with the Dharma, so that the land is forever abundant and peaceful, and my mind is impartial, free from favoritism."
In this manner, he replied with five hundred verses.
At that time, the minister Soma remained silent.
King Brahmadatta said,
"Why do you remain silent?
The minister replied:
"You are a king of men, a sovereign of a kingdom;
this goose-king is the sovereign of a marshland.
When two kings converse together, how can you dare to interrupt?"
The king said,
"I have a beautiful garden;
can you dwell there?"
He replied, "I cannot.
The king asked.
"Why is that? the goose said.
"The king might wake up."
I forgot and did not purify myself;
I ordered that wild goose meat be prepared.
If the butcher was unable to obtain any more wild geese, [he would have to use other meat].
"Or they may kill us to provide for the king's kitchen.
King Haṃsa, while governing the kingdom, entered the royal palace;
the geese followed him from the rain-formed pond and emerged above the palace.
They paced back and forth, crying out in grief;
their wings were wet, and water dripped from them, defiling the palace.
The king asked:
"What is this? The king of geese replied,
"These are my attendants."
The king said,
"Do you wish to go?
He replied, "I do."
He wished to depart.
The king said,
"What do you require?"
He replied,
"I was captured by a hunter;
he has done us a great favor."
"Grant us our lives.
If one were killed first and then another were killed afterward, who could prevent it?
The king said:
"How should we repay him?
The two geese replied,
"By giving him gold, silver, musāragalva, agate, clothing, food, and drink."
Having spoken these words, he flew up into the void.
The Buddha said,
"The king of geese was none other than my own self."
The five hundred geese were these five hundred bhikṣus;
the hunter was this elephant, Dhana-pāla.
King Brahmadatta was none other than King Śuddhodana;
the minister Soma was Ānanda. (From the first fascicle of the *Saṃyukta-āgama* of the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*).
13. Saving the Mountain Fire by Manifesting as a Parrot to Repay Kindness. Once, in the past, the Bodhisattva...
He was currently a parrot dwelling constantly in a tree.
When the wind blew against that tree, the branches rubbed against one another,
and fire immediately emerged.
The fire gradually grew more intense until it consumed an entire mountain.
The parrot reflected:
It is just as when a flying bird alights upon a tree;
therefore, one should repeatedly give rise to a mind of gratitude.
How much more so for those who have dwelt with me throughout the long night!
Unable to extinguish the fire,
he immediately went to the ocean and took up water from the great sea with both his wings.
He went up onto that fire and sprinkled water upon it,
or else he sprinkled it with his mouth while running hither and thither.
At that time, there was a benevolent deity.
Moved by his diligent perseverance, [the Buddha] immediately extinguished the fire and brought forth the first fascicle of the *Saṃgharakṣa-sūtra*.

14. As the Body of the King of Sparrows, He Extracted the Bone from the Tiger’s Mouth. Once upon a time, the Bodhisattva was the body of a king of sparrows. When he was trapped in the mouth of a tiger, he extracted the bone [from the tiger’s jaw]. This is the fourteenth [chapter]. Formerly, the Bodhisattva took the form of a king of sparrows.
Out of compassion, he rescued the multitude by protecting his own body from wounds.
There was a tiger that had been eating an animal; its teeth were caught in the bone, and it was suffering from illness and nearing death.
The sparrow enters its mouth and pecks at the bone day after day in this manner.
The sparrow’s mouth develops sores and its body becomes emaciated and scarred.
Only when the bone emerges from the tiger’s mouth [is it released].
A sparrow flew up and perched upon a tree.
It recited a Buddhist scripture, saying:
"Killing is a calamity; its evil is beyond compare."
Upon hearing the sparrow’s admonition,
the tiger became suddenly enraged and said,
"You have only just escaped from my mouth!"
Yet he dared to speak so much.
Seeing that he could not be transformed,
the sparrow immediately flew away in haste.
The Buddha said:
"The sparrow was my own body;
the tiger was Devadatta. This is from the *Jingquewang jing* (Sutra on the Sparrow King).
15. Taking the Form of a Great Fish to Relieve Hunger and Thirst. Fifteenth: In the past, the Bodhisattva was poor and destitute.
He traveled together with a group of merchants to another country.
The Bodhisattva beheld the fish in the sea, both large and small, devouring one another.
He sacrificed his own body to save the smaller ones, granting them a moment’s life.
He then threw himself into the sea; the large fish were satiated, and the small ones were saved.
His spirit was transformed into the king of whales,
with a body several *li* in length. At that time,
the coastal kingdom suffered from drought, and the people were afflicted by famine.
They prey upon one another;
the fish that tosses its body about the kingdom survives while those that devour it perish.
He carried the meat for several months, yet the fish remained alive.
A celestial deity descended and said, "You have practiced such benevolence; can you truly endure this suffering?"
"Why do you not prolong your life to escape this agony?
The fish replied, "My spirit has departed; my body is rotting."
"The people will later suffer from famine and will surely devour one another;
I cannot bear to witness this."
The deity said:
"You shall certainly attain Buddhahood and deliver suffering sentient beings.
However, when someone takes its head, the fish will die."
His spirit became that of a prince,
possessing the brilliance of a supreme sage;
his fourfold kindness and vast compassion moistened all things like the two polarities of heaven and earth.
He took pity on the people's poverty and distress;
speaking of it, his voice was choked with emotion.
Yet, the country was still suffering from drought.
With a tranquil mind, I maintain solemn reverence;
I withdraw from my meals and cease all offerings.
With my head bowed, I repent for my transgressions, saying:
The people’s lack of goodness is the fault of my own person.
I pray that I may lose my life to benefit the people with timely rain and dew.
Month after month he was filled with grief and lamentation,
for as a son of supreme filial piety, he had encountered the loss of a sage father;
his sincerity was renowned far and wide.
The Buddha arrived at the borders of that kingdom with five hundred followers.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy;
he went out to welcome them, prostrating himself with his head to the ground and weeping.
With a defiled mind and turbid conduct,
he failed to accord with the teachings of the Triple Gem and the Four Debts of Gratitude,
and he oppressed the people with cruel severity.
Drought has persisted for many years;
the common people suffer from famine,
their resentment and grief wounding their hearts.
"I pray that you remove the calamities of the people and cast this misfortune upon my own transgressions.
The Buddhas replied,
"You are the sovereign of men."
Your compassion and benevolence are equal to those of Śakra;
all Buddhas know this fully and cause you,
O King, to receive blessings— be careful not to grieve.
The Emperor commanded the people to sow grain;
there was no household that did not cultivate it,
and the rice grew in abundance.
The King said,
"It must ripen;
let the grain cover the land."
All of them contained unhusked rice;
each could hold several *hu* (measures).
The fragrance of the rice was so exquisite that the entire nation rejoiced.
They praised and extolled the King’s virtues;
throughout the land, all maintained the precepts and took refuge in the Triple Gem.

The king, his ministers, and the common people, upon the end of their lives, were reborn in heaven. At that time, the poor man was my own self. This concludes the first fascicle of the *Collection on the Infinite Deliverance*. 16. As the King of Turtles, He Transformed His Fellow Beings and Saved a Multitude of Merchants. In the past, the Bodhisattva—once he had perfected the practice of giving and attained mastery over his mind—was born as the king of turtles.

There was once a great merchant who, together with five hundred other merchants, set out to sea to seek precious treasures. Having traveled for many days, they encountered a violent storm; the waves surged high, and the ship was tossed about by the wind and waves. The merchants were terrified and cried out in distress. At that moment, the king of turtles, perceiving their peril, transformed himself into a human being and approached the ship. He asked the merchants, "Why are you so distressed? The merchants replied, "We have encountered a fierce storm; our ship is about to sink, and we fear we shall all perish. The turtle-king said, "Do not fear. I shall save you. He then transformed his body into a massive mountain, rising high above the water. He told the merchants, "Climb onto my back and I will carry you to safety. The merchants, filled with joy, climbed onto his back. The turtle-king then plunged into the depths of the ocean, carrying them through the vast expanse until they reached the shore. He was once a king of turtles.

That ocean was deep and vast, its limits difficult to fathom.

He then devised a skillful stratagem and entered a shallow part of the water;

In the past, while I was in the deep mountains,

To dream of lying upon the great ocean means that your body is immediately within the great ocean of birth and death.

Emerging from birth and death, one attains the mark of nirvana.
As for the dream of all sentient beings entering within one's own body in the midst of a great ocean,
it signifies that within the great ocean of birth and death, [one shall attain liberation].

to dream of holding the sun in one's hand signifies that the light of wisdom universally illumines the entire Dharma-realm.
The dream of grasping the moon signifies that by means of skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*),

"Ganges" refers to rivers, streams, ponds, and lakes extending to the great ocean,

The Buddha said:
In the past, after the parinirvāṇa of Buddha Vipaśyin,
there was a bandit who, while traveling through a monastery with plundered goods,

At that time, the lamp before the Buddha was about to go out, and in the darkness nothing could be seen.
The bandits straightened the wick of the lamp with their arrows so that the lamp would shine brightly.
Seeing his majestic radiance, which dazzled the eyes and caused his hair to stand on end,

"How could I steal? he thought, and he immediately departed.

Tiṣya heard that a man had appeared in a dream, clad in armor and holding a vajra,

"Although all external objects may be used for giving, they are not what I require.

If you do not refuse me, it should be granted."
Upon hearing these words, the king leaped for joy beyond measure.
The brahmin said, "When will you give me your head?"
The king said,
"Seven days hence, I shall give you my head.
At that time, the great minister brought seven heads made of the seven precious jewels.
He spoke again to the brahmin:
"This king's head is a composite of flesh, bone, and blood—an impure thing—yet you seek it for this purpose.
Now, take these heads made of the seven treasures and trade them for it."
"You may take it; by trading it extensively, you will surely obtain enough wealth to sustain you for the rest of your life.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I have no need for this;
I desire the king's head to fulfill my vow.
At that time, the Great Moon Minister exhorted him with various arguments, but [the king] never turned back; his heart was so consumed by rage that it split into seven pieces, and he died.
The King previously issued a command:
"My subjects, mount an elephant that travels eight thousand *li* and proclaim throughout all lands:
'In seven days from now, Great King Candraprabha shall offer his own head as alms to a Brahmin.'"
"If you wish to come, go quickly by carriage.
At that time, eighty-four thousand kings arrived by rapid relay;
they all saw the Great King prostrating himself before the King with his belly pressed to the ground.
"The people of Jambudvīpa rely upon the King's benevolence and grace.
Why, for the sake of a single person, would you forever abandon the multitude and no longer show them compassion?
We only pray that you will take pity on us and not give away your head."
Ten thousand ministers all threw themselves to the ground, striking their bellies against the king’s feet, saying only: "Have mercy and compassion upon us;
do not give away your head.
Twenty thousand ladies likewise threw themselves to the ground and looked up, addressing the king:
"Do not forget us or abandon us; please grant us your compassionate protection.
If you give your head to us, what will we have left to rely upon?
Thus the five hundred princes wept before the king.
"We are but infants; to whom shall we turn for refuge?
We pray that you take pity on us and do not offer your head, so that you may raise us up and bring us to the level of human beings."
Thereupon, the Great King addressed his ministers, subjects, consorts, and crown prince:
"Consider that since I first received this body,
I have traversed the cycle of birth and death for a very long time."
If one is in the three miserable realms, even if one's head is severed and one dies only to be born again,
though such occurrences may happen countless times, there will be no karmic reward.
If one is born among humans, one will quarrel over wealth and sensual pleasures.
Driven by greed, hatred, and delusion, one constantly kills many bodies, yet never performs meritorious deeds before casting off this life.
Now, this body of mine, composed of various impurities, must inevitably be abandoned; it cannot endure for long.
"Since I am giving up this foul head to exchange it for a great benefit, how could I not grant it?
I shall offer this head to the Brahmin;
by this merit, I vow to seek the path of Buddhahood and deliver you from suffering."
"Now my resolve for giving is on the verge of fulfillment;
pray do not obstruct my aspiration for the unsurpassed path.
When all the kings, ministers, subjects, ladies, and crown princes heard the king's words, they remained silent and spoke no word.
At that time, the Great King said to the brahmin,
"If you wish to take my head, now is the very moment.
The brahmin replied:
"Now, the King is surrounded by his ministers, subjects, and a great multitude.
I am all alone, my strength and power being meager and weak; I cannot endure to strike off the King's head here amidst this crowd.
If you wish to give it to me, you should come to the rear garden."
At that time, the Great King addressed the minor kings, princes, ministers,
and citizens: "If you all truly love and revere me,
take care not to harm this brahmin."
Having spoken these words,
he entered the rear garden together with the brahmin.
At that time, the brahmin spoke again to the king, saying:
"You possess the strength of a powerful athlete in your prime;
yet if you suffer the pain of being cut, you may well regret it later.
Only if you take your own hair and tie it firmly to a tree can you endure being cut."
Then the king said to the linguist Brahmin,
"Cut off my head and let it fall into my hands before you take it away.
I now offer this head as a gift, seeking the unsurpassed, perfect, and true Way, vowing to deliver all living beings."
At that time, the brāhmaṇa raised his sword, intending to strike.
Seeing this, the tree deity was deeply distressed, thinking:
"How can one wish to kill such a person?"
He immediately seized the Brahmin by the ear with his hand;
the man's head was turned backward and his limbs were completely contorted.
He dropped his knife to the ground and was unable to move.
At that time, the Great King looked up and spoke to the tree deity: "Since the distant past,
I have offered nine hundred and ninety-nine heads as alms beneath this very tree."
"Now, by giving up this head, I shall complete the thousand;
having given up this head, I will fulfill my practice of generosity.
Do not obstruct my resolve for the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the tree deity heard these words from the king and restored the brahmin to his former state;
the brahmin then rose up from the ground.
He took up his sword once more and struck off the king’s head; the head fell into his hands.
At that moment, heaven and earth shook in six ways, and the palaces of the devas trembled uneasily.
Each harbored fear and wondered at the reason for this;
they soon saw that the Bodhisattva, for the sake of all beings, had relinquished his head as an act of giving.
They all descended from their positions, moved by his extraordinary deed, and wept with tears like rain.
They spoke in praise together, saying:
"The Great King Candraprabha has now fulfilled the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) by bestowing his own head as an offering."
The sound spread everywhere.
When King Vemacitrin heard these words, he was so overcome with joy,
leaping and trembling in astonishment that his heart burst asunder and he died.
At that time, the brahmin carried away the king’s head.
The kings, ministers, subjects, queens, and crown princes,
having already seen the king’s head, threw themselves upon the ground.
They cried out in unison with piteous wails, fainting and then reviving.
At that time, the brahmin, loathing the stench of the king's head, immediately cast it to the ground, kicked it away, and departed.
Or again, there were some people who spoke to the brahmin.
"Your cruelty and malice are indeed extreme.
Since it is of no use, why did you seek it?
At that time, the Brahmin proceeded on his way and departed.
People who saw him immediately rebuked those who did not provide him with food;
he was so emaciated by hunger and so utterly exhausted that it reached the limit of human suffering.
Along the way, a person asked him for news of himself.
Knowing that King Vemacitrin had already passed away and that his hopes were lost,
as well as knowing that Raudrākṣa had also passed away and that both had fallen into the Avīci hell.
Furthermore, among the other subjects and citizens who died from the grief and longing they felt for the King’s kindness, all were reborn in the heavens.
It was thus, Ānanda.
If you wish to know who that King Candraprabha was at that time:
I am that very person now.
King Vemacitrin is now Pāpīyan.
The great minister Mahācandra is now Śāriputra.
At that time, unable to bear seeing me die, he passed away before me;
even until today, unable to bear seeing me enter into *nirvāṇa*, he has entered extinction first.

This is found in the fifth fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányú jīng*), and it is largely the same as, though with minor differences from, the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Expedient Means* (*Fāngbiàn fó bào'ēn jīng*).

9. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Compete in Manifesting Supernatural Powers. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Compete in Manifesting Supernatural Powers, Nine: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, on the fifteenth day, the World-Honored One was reciting the precepts.

Then the community of bhikṣus and the assembly of five hundred bhikṣus—whom the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to as five hundred great arhats—departed from the Jetavana Grove and proceeded to Lake Anavatapta.
Then the Dragon King Anavatapta went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Observing the countenance of the Tathāgata and that of the bhikṣus,
he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Observe that within this assembly all is empty and nothing exists.
Now, the bhikṣu Śāriputra has no seat here.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Go quickly to Śāriputra; I am calling him by voice.
Having received these instructions, Maudgalyāyana went to the city of Śrāvastī and said to Śāriputra:
The Buddha called for you, saying, "O Dragon King Anavatapta, I wish to see you.
Śāriputra then untied his own saṃkakṣikā robe and placed it before Maudgalyāyana, saying to him:
"You possess supernormal powers; lift this cloth-belt and the Jambūdvīpa tree.
Maudgalyāyana grasped the belt but could not move it;
he exerted all his strength to lift it, and the entire earth shook violently.
Śāriputra then feared that Maudgalyāyana would go to Pūrvavideha;
he also used his supernatural power to encircle Mount Sumeru,
whereupon Maudgalyāyana lifted and moved Mount Sumeru.
Śāriputra then wrapped this sash around the seat of the Tathāgata.
Maudgalyāyana was consequently unable to move it; he set aside the sash and returned to the place of the Nāga King.
From afar, he saw that Śāriputra had already arrived there before him.
Sitting cross-legged with his body straight and his mind upright, he focused his mindfulness before him.
Upon reaching the World-Honored One, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and said,
"Have I not lost my supernormal powers?"
Why is this? I vanished from before the Jeta Grove and did not appear until I arrived at this pond;
Śāriputra vanished after me and did not appear until he arrived and sat down first.
The World-Honored One has always declared me to be foremost; why have you arrived so late?
The Buddha replied, "Śāriputra, the bhikṣu, possesses great wisdom and does not regress."
When the assembly returned to Śrāvastī, they also gave rise to doubt.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Many bhikṣus lack a mind of reverence toward you, saying that Śāriputra’s supernormal power is superior to yours."
"You may manifest your majestic power within this assembly.
He replied, "I accept your instruction," and immediately rose from his seat and went to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
With one foot he stepped upon the summit of Mount Sumeru;
lifting his other foot, he placed it upon the Brahma Heaven.
He kicked Mount Sumeru, causing the earth to tremble in six ways.
At that time, he spoke these verses in a Brahma-like voice:
"One should swiftly seek skillful means; within this Buddha-dharma and Sangha, one should eliminate the afflictions of birth and death, just as an elephant eats bamboo leaves."
If, within this Buddha-dharma, one has cultivated various practices free from desire and eliminated all defilements, exhausting even their very source and root—
at such a time, the bhikṣus will exclaim, "This is unprecedented!"

When Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke this verse, sixty bhikṣus, on account of it, attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind; [this is recorded] in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle twenty-seven.

10. Maudgalyāyana causes the waters of the Ajiravatī River to swell and transforms a jeweled bridge to ferry the Buddha across. At a great assembly in Śrāvastī, the people exhorted him to convert others.
He provided ninety-six kinds of rice for the renunciants,
and further invited King Prasenajit, the crown prince, the ministers, the heads of various villages,
long-established elders, and caravan leaders.
On the day before, they gathered on the bank of the Ajiravatī River.
Maudgalyāyana arrived first and took the seat of the elder;
he caused the river water to swell suddenly so that foam covered the banks.
The various non-Buddhists vied with one another to bind rafts and floats,
intending to cross first and claim the foremost seat; however,
the current surged violently, overturning them and drifting them back.
Having spent the entire night in exhaustion and suffering, his raft was shattered and he was submerged in freezing waters.
He climbed onto the bank and crouched there, facing the sun.
At that time, at the Jetavana Monastery, someone invited the Sangha for a meal.
The Buddha remained waiting for the proper time.
A young bhikṣu said, "The World-Honored One has come out late; I fear the non-Buddhists will obtain the seat of honor and depart."
The Buddha, knowing that the time had come,
went to the riverbank together with the great assembly, their deportment composed and dignified.
The various non-Buddhists said:
"We are unable to cross over.
What plan should these śramaṇas devise?
Maudgalyāyana then manifested a precious bridge, adorned with various ornaments, flowers, incense, and music.
The various non-Buddhist practitioners each said, "The śramaṇa has come late; we shall cross first.
As they stepped onto the bridge, they fell into the water, soaking their bodies and robes, and the army lay prostrate, carried along by the current.
By the Buddha’s supernormal power, no one died.
The Buddha and the bhikṣus proceeded with solemn dignity;
as they advanced step by step in orderly succession, the precious bridge vanished at each place they stepped upon.
Maudgalyāyana withdrew his supernormal power,
and the ground returned to its former state,
allowing all the non-Buddhist practitioners to proceed.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having first reached this shore, one has already crossed the ocean of birth and death;
the swift current cannot sweep one away. This is called the one of right wisdom. —From the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll Six.
11. Maudgalyāyana Constructs a Basin for His Mother. Regarding the eleventh [section], "Maudgalyāyana Constructs a Basin for His Mother":
Having first attained the Way, Maudgalyāyana desired to deliver his parents to repay the kindness of their nursing him.
He saw his deceased mother reborn among the hungry ghosts;
she was seen without food or drink, her skin and bones joined together.
Maudgalyāyana was filled with sorrow and grief.
He immediately filled his alms-bowl with rice and went to offer it to his mother.
When his mother received the bowl of rice, before it had even entered her mouth, it transformed into glowing embers.
Maudgalyāyana hurried back and reported this matter in detail.
The Buddha said,
"Your mother's roots of sin are deeply entrenched;
this is not something that can be remedied by your power alone."
One must rely on the majestic spiritual power of the Sangha to attain liberation.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
one may [perform rites] for the sake of parents through seven generations who are in distress and calamity.
Providing the Sangha with offerings of all that is sweet and exquisite in the world— prepared meals, the five fruits, water jars, basins and vessels, fragrant oil, incense sticks,

candles, couches, mats, and bedding— on that day, the noble ones— the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas endowed with the six supernormal powers— manifested themselves as bhikṣus within the great assembly.
All are of one mind, having received the *pātra-bharaṇa* and being endowed with pure precepts.
For those who make offerings to such monks,
their parents of seven generations and their five kinds of relatives [shall likewise receive benefit].
They attained liberation from the three miserable realms immediately, and clothing and food appeared spontaneously.
The Buddha then commanded the assembly of monks to perform rites on behalf of the parents of seven generations for the sake of the donors' families.
12. Maudgalyāyana Harassed by Māra: Maudgalyāyana was harassed by Māra while walking at night. He practiced meditative concentration before partaking of his meal;
this is from the *Ullambana Sūtra*. Maudgalyāyana was harassed by Māra. Maudgalyāyana was harassed by Māra. Twelve: Maudgalyāyana walked at night.
The evil Māra transformed himself into a transparent shadow and entered Maudgalyāyana’s belly.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself,
"Why does my belly rumble like the sound of hunger when carrying a heavy load?"
Entering into meditative concentration,
he observed and saw him, and immediately said:
"Evil Māra, depart at once!"
"Do not disturb the Tathāgata and his disciples. Māra was immediately terrified.
[This concludes] the *Bie mo shi mulian jing* (The Scripture on the Evil Māra Testing Maudgalyāyana), in which the transformed phantom emerges from the shadows and stands before his body.
13. *Mulian quan di shi bing shi bao chu* (Maudgalyāyana Exhorting His Brother to Give and Indicating the Place of Retribution). Part 13: Maudgalyāyana had a younger brother born of the same parents.
He possessed abundant wealth, and his treasuries were filled with many jewels;
his servants and slaves were beyond counting.
Maudgalyāyana said to his younger brother:
"I have heard that you are stingy and envious, and do not delight in giving.
The Buddha has always proclaimed that when a noble person practices generosity, they obtain immeasurable rewards.
Your younger brother, having heard your instruction, opened the treasury to practice giving."
Having established a new storehouse with the desire to receive its rewards,
before even ten days had passed,
his wealth and treasures were completely exhausted; thus the old storehouse was entirely empty and the new storehouse yielded no reward.
His heart was filled with distress, and he said to his elder brother:
"Previously, when you instructed me that giving yields great rewards,
I did not dare disobey your teaching and exhausted my treasury in acts of charity."
"Among all those who have been impoverished in the past and will be so in the future, there are none whom we have not reached.
Our treasures and goods are exhausted, and the new stores yield no returns.
Could it be that you, my elder brother, have led us astray through some error?"
Maudgalyāyana said, "Stop, stop! Do not utter such words.
Let it not be heard by those of other schools or those with heterodox views."
If merit were to have a physical form,
even the realm of empty space would not be able to contain it.
I now provisionally manifest this subtle retribution for you to show.
"If you wish to see him, follow me. Then,
by means of his supernatural powers, Maudgalyāyana took his younger brother in his hands and transported him to the sixth heaven.
He possesses palaces composed of the seven treasures,
with bathing pools before and behind from which fragrant breezes spread afar;
his treasuries and storehouses are filled to overflowing beyond all calculation.
The retinue of these jade maidens numbered many tens of millions;
they were exclusively women with no men and no husbands.
The younger brother questioned Maudgalyāyana.
"Why is this palace so exceedingly majestic?
No men are to be seen; it consists entirely of women.
Maudgalyāyana said to his younger brother:
"Go yourself and ask," he said.
"What palace is this? The goddess replied:
Within Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Kapila,
there was a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha endowed with supernatural powers named Maudgalyāyana.
"There is a younger brother of yours who is very wealthy and delights in giving alms to relieve the destitute and assist the needy.
After his life ends, he shall come to be born here to become our husband.
Upon hearing this, the man was filled with joy, and a virtuous mind arose within him.
Returning to his elder brother’s place, he was filled with great shame and remorse;

bowing his head to the ground, he repented. He then returned to the world and practiced extensive giving without weariness. This concludes the *Sutra on Maudgalyāyana’s Younger Brother’s Hope for Immediate Retribution for His Almsgiving*.
14. Maudgalyāyana Subdues the Arrogance of Bodhisattvas. Chapter Fourteen: Maudgalyāyana, having received the holy command of the Buddha, [was told that] there is a world in the western direction.
The land is named Radiant Banner;
the Buddha is named King of Radiance,
who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.
When Maudgalyāyana arrived there to listen to the Buddha’s words,
his body was four thousand li in height,
while the bodies of the various bodhisattvas were two thousand li in height.
The alms bowls used by those bodhisattvas were one *li* in height;
Maudgalyāyana walked upon the rim of their bowls.
At that time, the bodhisattvas addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, O Great Sage,
from where did these insects come?"
Wearing the robes of a śramaṇa,
he walked upon the edge of the alms-bowl.
At that time, that Buddha said:
Sons of good family, you must be careful not to give rise to thoughts of contempt for this worthy one. Why is this?
This youth is now named Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
He was the foremost in supernormal powers among the śrāvaka disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhāsa-rāja said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"In my land, the bodhisattvas and all the śrāvakas—"
"Seeing that your body was small, everyone felt a sense of contempt.
You, O Benevolent One, should now manifest the power of your spiritual feet to uphold the majestic virtue of Śākyamuni.
Maudgalyāyana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and then stood before the Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "I wish now to sit cross-legged upon this spot; would it be permissible?
The Buddha said:
According to his wish,
Mahāmaudgalyāyana then leaped into the air to a height of hundreds of millions of fathoms;
there, within that precious city, he fashioned a couch.
He sat cross-legged,
and from his seat hung billions of precious jewels; from each and every jewel,
hundreds of thousands of rays of light issued forth.
Each ray of light contains a lotus flower,
and upon every lotus appears the body of Śākyamuni seated;
his speech is exactly like that of Śākyamuni.
The resonance was pure as he proclaimed the sutras with equal consistency.
Having displayed his supernormal powers,
Maudgalyāyana stood once more before the Buddha.
At that time, the bodhisattvas marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"For what reason has Maudgalyāyana come to this world?"
The World-Honored One said:
"They have come to this land because they wish to test how far the resonance of Śākyamuni Buddha’s voice can reach.
At that time, the Buddha King of Radiance told Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Virtuous one, you should not test the resonance of the Tathāgata.
The resonance of the Tathāgata is neither distant nor near; it is vast, immeasurable, and beyond all analogy.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana threw himself at the Buddha's feet and repented his transgression.
"So be it, World-Honored One.
My own person is not quick-witted;
though the Buddha's voice is immeasurable, I have rashly conceived the desire to know its limits."
That King of Radiance said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Although you have come from afar to this buddha-field," and he further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods, we are exceedingly far away;
our bodies are utterly exhausted and we cannot return to our own land.
The World-Honored One said:
"How did you come to this world by means of your supernatural power?
It is established by the majestic authority of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha.
You should now pay homage from afar, bowing your head in prostration to Śākyamuni Buddha."
"You shall surely arrive.
Even if you, sir, were to use your own supernormal powers to return to your native land, you would not reach it even in an eon.
Then Maudgalyāyana knelt with his right knee on the ground, turned toward the east where the Buddha Śākyamuni was, and joined his palms in self-surrender.
In the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, he immediately arrived at the *Madhuvāsiṣṭha-vajrapuruṣa-sūtra*, Volume Three.

15. Maudgalyāyana Subdues a Brahmin through Supernatural Power. [The Buddha] said to Maudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, use your supernatural power to subdue and convert this brahmin. 15. Maudgalyāyana Subdues a Brahmin through Supernatural Power. Fifteen. The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: [...]
There was a great kingdom located eight thousand *yojanas* from here on the frontier;
they did not behold the Triple Gem and practiced perverted views.
The king, along with his ministers and subjects, served the brahmin.
Five hundred of them attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*),
enabling them to move mountains, arrest the flow of rivers, and manifest various transformations by dividing their bodies.
In the kingdom there was a great mountain that blocked the paths of the people; the entire nation suffered from it.
The king spoke of this to the brahmins, and the brahmins immediately sat down encircling the mountain.
Each focused their mind with the power of meditative concentration, attempting to move the mountain that had arisen.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Go to that land and manifest spiritual transformations to bring about the long-term salvation of the brahmins, the king, and the people."
He caused them to distance themselves from the three miserable realms and dwell eternally in halls of merit.
Maudgalyāyana emitted light that eclipsed the sun and moon as he stood suspended in mid-air;
even when he reached the summit of the mountain, the mountain remained immovable.
The brahmin was startled and said, "This mountain has already risen; who could suppress it?
The sun lacks its brilliant radiance; there must be a reason for this."
Among them was one who possessed clarity of vision; observing the assembly of disciples, he saw that some were defiled and turbid, which caused the mountain not to move.
Looking up, he beheld a śramaṇa standing upon the summit of the mountain.
The brahmins all said,
"This was surely done by a disciple of Gautama.
The brahmins called out:
The King has commanded us to remove the suffering of the people;
you must restrain him.
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"I have suspended myself in the void; who can suppress your mountain?
The Brahmin exhausted his ascetic powers three times in an attempt to move the mountain, but the mountain descended three times, finally becoming level ground.
The brahmins looked at one another and said,
"He who possesses clear understanding and has deeply penetrated the Way and its Virtue is our teacher. They all rose,
adjusted their robes with propriety, and bowed their heads to the ground in respectful salutation.
"I wish to be your disciple;
please reveal to me your supreme spiritual power.
Maudgalyāyana said:
If you wish to leave the darkness for the light, it is well.
I have a venerable teacher,
titled the Unsurpassed, Truly Real One, the God among Gods.
"He is the All-Knowing One.
You all should go to where the Buddha is.
The brahmins said:
"Is the Buddha’s transformation through the Way not superior to that of the Teacher?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"The virtue of the Buddha is like Mount Sumeru."
We are like mustard seeds;
you should follow after us and,
upon reaching the presence of the Buddha, report our situation in full detail.
Both internally and externally pure,
we only pray that the World-Honored One will wash away these subtle defilements and cause us to attain true purity.
The Brahmin saw the Buddha; his mind opened and his understanding was resolved, and he became a śramaṇa. This concludes the *Buddha-spoken Sūtra on the Resolute Mind*, number sixteen.

[Chapter] 16: Maudgalyāyana Converts Various Ghosts and Spirits; the Spirits Themselves Speak of Their Previous Evil Deeds. In the past, Maudgalyāyana went into the Snow Mountains. There, he converted various ghosts and spirits, who themselves spoke of their previous evil deeds. (Sixteen.)
He transformed various ghosts, spirits, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, and others.
At that time, there was a gandharva deity.
Dwelling in a palace of the seven treasures, he excelled all others;
his physical form was upright and handsome, and he was exceptionally intelligent and distinguished.
Nevertheless, he had a human body with the head of a dog.
Maudgalyāyana asked in wonder,
"Why is it thus? He replied:
I was a wealthy elder during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin.
I delighted in providing meals for bhikṣus and brahmins and supplying the needy;
however, I was quick-tempered and irritable by nature.
They utter coarse words and insults directly, showing no regard for whether one is old or young.
If guests or visitors do not take their fancy even slightly regarding food and drink, they immediately say,

Long ago, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha...

9. Cūḍapanthaka Recites a Single Verse and Is Able to Understand Its Meaning; Furthermore, by Supernatural Power, a Bowl Is Bestowed Upon Him. Cūḍapanthaka recites a single verse and is able to understand its meaning; furthermore, by supernatural power, a bowl is bestowed upon him. Nine: The Buddhas were in Śrāvastī.
