"Guard the mouth, restrain the mind, and let not the body transgress."
Thus the practitioner attains transcendence of the world.
Upatiṣya (Pāṇṭaka), moved by the Buddha’s compassionate grace,

This is not to be considered extraordinary;

It arises from one [path] of the mind, four of the body, and three of speech.
Observe its arising and examine its cessation; through this,

By means of this one falls into the abyss, and by means of this one attains the Way.
Nirvana is spontaneous;

Suddenly his mind was opened and he attained the path of an Arhat.

therefore, he extended his arm and offered me his bowl.

The King said to the Buddha,

"By what means is the Way attained?
The Buddha told the King:

The worthy Panta understood the meaning of a single verse;
its refined principle entered the divine,

"Though a person may study much, if they do not practice it, they merely waste their consciousness and perceptions;

Thereupon, the World-Honored One—
Then he spoke in verse:

It is not as good as a single principle; through hearing and practicing it, one may attain liberation. Though one may recite many sutras, what benefit is there if one does not understand them?
To understand even a single verse of the Dharma and practice accordingly, one can attain the Way—just as those who heard this verse did.
Two hundred bhikṣus attained the path of arhatship.
The king, his ministers, ladies, and the crown prince were all filled with joy. [Excerpted from] the *Dharmapada*, Volume One.

11. Madhuvāsiṣṭha and others possess residual habitual tendencies (vāsanā). Regarding those who possess residual habitual tendencies, such as Madhuvāsiṣṭha and others, there are some individuals who, although they have severed all afflictions (kleśa), [still possess these tendencies].
The body and speech also possess the marks of afflictions;
when ordinary people see or hear them, they give rise to impure thoughts,
as was the case with the Arhat Madhuvāsiṣṭha.
For five hundred lifetimes he remained among the monkeys;
though he has now attained the Way, he still leaps and bounds upon trees.

Furthermore, the Arhat Pilindavatsa had been born among the Brahmins for five hundred lifetimes,

"Little maid, stop your flow."
The deity Gaṅgā became enraged and went to the Buddha to lodge her grievance;

One should know that the Buddha has exhausted the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of affliction;

They will certainly attain understanding.

the Buddha saw the four men from afar and smiled, emitting light of five colors.
The four men prostrated before the Buddha and said,
"We are foolish and deluded;
we pray that the Buddha will explain this to us."
He caused them no longer to contend. In the past,
there was a king named Vīra.
The body was afflicted with illness;
a physician was summoned to examine it,
and it was determined that medicine should be prepared using lion’s milk.
The king immediately issued a proclamation for his recruitment. To whoever captured him,
he would grant a fief and bestow his younger daughter as a wife.
At that time, a poor man petitioned him,
and the king granted his request.
The man, being skillful, first sought out the location of the lion.
He then slaughtered a sheep and prepared several *hu* of grape wine;
he went to that mountain and waited for the lion to go out.
He then slaughtered a sheep and placed it along with grape wine at the lion's dwelling.
Upon seeing the wine and meat, the lion immediately began to eat and drink until he was deeply intoxicated and lay down.
Having taken the milk, he returned with joy;
before reaching his own country,
he stayed overnight in a village.
There was an arhat who, while staying overnight,
joined this man in pursuing a lion through a perilous path.
While his body was in the state of deep sleep,
he was entirely without consciousness;
yet the practitioner perceived the six consciousnesses within his body.
Each claimed credit for their own merit. The god Zu said,
"It was by relying on my actions that we reached this place and obtained the milk."
The hand-deity spoke again:
"It is thanks to my hand that [it] was seized.
The eye-deity spoke again: [It is thanks to my eye that it was seen].
"It is thanks to me that you have seen it," the ear-spirit said again.
"It is thanks to me that you heard the king seeking milk and brought you here."
The deity of the tongue then spoke:
"You all have debated in vain;
this merit belongs to me."
"Now, whether he lives or dies rests with me alone.
This man, carrying the milk, went to the king's presence and said:
"Now that the lion's milk has already been obtained and is outside," the king said,
"do not merely present it."
When the king saw the milk,
his tongue immediately spoke:
"This is not lion's milk."
"It is merely donkey's milk.
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly incensed and said,
"I sent you to fetch lion's milk!"
He then used donkey's milk and was about to kill him. At that time,
there was a fellow practitioner who had stayed with him overnight.
Immediately, by means of his supernormal power,
he went before the king and reported, saying,
"This letter contains the lion's milk."
At that time, while staying together with this person in a village settlement,
I saw within his body six physical constituents competing with one another for their own merit and diligence.
The tongue spoke:
"I shall act contrary to you all.
Now, the result is indeed as such.
"Your Majesty, simply mix the medicine with milk and the illness will surely be cured.
The King then placed his trust in the words of the Arhat.
He prepared a medicinal compound with milk and gave it to him as a wife,
along with conferring titles and lands according to their original agreement.
The practitioner then said to the king:
If even one person’s own body and consciousness are mutually contradictory,
how much more so for another?
At that time, those who take milk—
Having received the grace of the Way-attainer,
he sought to become a śramaṇa;
through the liberation of his mind, he attained the path of arhatship.
At that time, the king also received the five precepts with joy and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Upon hearing this, the four men were liberated in mind.
He then followed the Buddha and requested to become a bhikṣu.
The Buddha remained silent and stroked his head with his hand;
his hair fell away and the kāṣāya robe was placed upon his body.
Their fetters were untied and their defilements removed. Ānanda asked,
"What fundamental merits did these four people possess?"
Now, upon hearing this sutra, he immediately understood and swiftly attained arhatship.
The Buddha said:
In the past, during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, Śāriputra was a bhikṣu,
and these four individuals were merchants.
Together they offered a single *kāṣāya* robe to Śāriputra.
Śāriputra then offered a prayer of blessing, saying:
"May you all, in future lives, quickly attain liberation."
Now, from Śāriputra, one attains liberation through the *Vyūharāja-siṃhakṣīropama-sūtra*. 13.

Constantly serving the community of monks with food, drink, clothing, and robes leads to the attainment of the Way. [Section 13]: There was a man who constantly served the community of monks with food, drink, clothing, and robes, and thereby attained the Way. There was a man.
Having gone forth in the True Dharma,
he was able to perform services for the bhikṣus in whatever monastery he visited.
He was made to serve them,
but later he became utterly exhausted and thought to himself:
"Who can preach the Dharma for me and provide instruction?
He heard that in the kingdom of Mathurā there was Upagupta.
This was prophesied by the Buddha:
that he would be the foremost among his future disciples.
[The Buddha] went before him, paid homage with palms joined, and said:
"Venerable One,
perform the Buddha's work and preach the Dharma for me. Upagupta said:
"If you can follow my instructions, I shall preach the Dharma for you.
He replied, "I can.
[The Buddha] asked:
"At the Nadapada Monastery,
how many monks are there?
You should continue to serve the community of monks."
The answer is:
There are eighteen thousand arhats,
and twice as many practitioners still in training.
There were countless ordinary persons who were diligent.
At that time, that bhikṣu [acted] for the sake of the entire community of monks.
He served as an attendant so that all the monks could devote themselves exclusively to their spiritual practice. Then,
the attendant bhikṣu rose early in the morning.
Having donned his robes and taken up his alms bowl, he entered the country of Mathurā.
There, he encountered an elder who had gone out in the morning.
The elder thought to himself:
"I have never seen this before;
now that I see it, I prostrate my head at his feet and ask."
"Venerable sir,
from how far or near have you come, and for what purpose?
He replied:
Coming from the eastern land,
he went to the place of Upagupta,
desiring to hear the Dharma.
Furthermore, Upagupta appointed me as an attendant to the Saṃgha;
I do not yet know which among the people of Mathurā are diligent and which are not.
The elder said,
"You need not worry about this matter now;
I shall take your place in providing the community of monks with all their food, drink, clothing, and medicine."
I shall provide everything for the bhikṣus and the elder;
together we will take food, drink,
and other provisions to make offerings to the Saṃgha.
During the three-month rains retreat, the bhikṣus, through this offering, cultivated practice and attained the fruits of the Path.
14. Seeing a Rākṣasa Ordain and Attain the Path; Seeing a Rākṣasa Ordain and Attain the Path (14). Mathurā Country.
There was a man who requested his parents for permission to renounce the household life and went to the place of Upagupta.
Having paid homage with reverence, he said:
"Venerable Sir,
may I become a bhikṣu?"
Seeing that he was bound to his body by craving,
Upagupta said, "Welcome."
"I shall grant you the going forth.
He joyfully prostrated at his feet and requested permission to return home for a short while first.
While traveling along the road,
he reflected: "If I reach home,
there may be obstacles."
That evening, he stayed overnight at a shrine along the way. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Upagupta manifested two rākṣasīs in an empty house:
one holding a corpse and the other with empty hands.
They both entered the temple together;
each claimed, "I have found it," and they disputed with one another without reaching a decision.
He then asked this person,
"Who brought the corpse here?
This person reflected.
"You must not speak falsely;
you must speak the truth.
As soon as he spoke thus, the empty-coming ghost seized his arm and drew it toward its mouth, intending to devour him.
The ghosts that attend corpses assisted in the dismemberment;
thus, those with inferior physical traits were spared. After a long while, the sun eventually rose.
After two days had passed, he returned to Guptā’s place,
left the household life to pursue the Way,
and practiced with diligent vigor.
Attaining the Fruit of Arhatship: *The Sutra of King Aśoka*, Scroll Nine; also appearing in *The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom*, Scroll Twelve.
15. Some People Fleeing Calamity Leave Home and See the Buddha Attain Enlightenment. Fifteen: In the past, there was a group of people.
On the banks of the river,
they were harmed by the waters;
the people suffered without limit.
Among those who attain liberation, one in ten thousand does so;
such a person who attains liberation in the deep waters went to where the Buddha was.
He requested to become a śramaṇa;
the Buddha then granted his consent, allowing him to join the ranks of the Path.
Within himself, he did not contemplate that this would mean being freed from distress.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, exhorting him to practice the Path.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt inward shame and remorse;
he came to understand that all phenomena are impermanent.
With his mind opened and his will liberated, he became serene and free from thought. There, before the Buddha,
he attained arhatship and emerged to preach the *Śramaṇa-sūtra*.
16. The Arhat and the Elephant: Their Previous Lives as Brothers Who Differed in Practicing Goodness. Sixteenth: During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, [there were two brothers].
There were two brothers who both became śramaṇas.
The elder brother maintained the precepts and practiced dhyāna with single-minded devotion, seeking the Way.
He did not practice giving,
whereas his younger brother practiced giving and cultivated merit,
yet delighted in breaking the precepts.
The elder brother left the household life with Śākyamuni and attained the path of an arhat;
yet his robes were insufficient and his food was constantly inadequate.
The younger brother was born as an elephant.
Because elephants possess great strength,
they can repel enemies and are thus beloved by kings.
Adorned his body with gold, silver, rare jewels, and necklaces;
he granted him several hundred households as a fief to provide for this elephant.
According to his needs,
at that time, the elder brother bhikṣu encountered a period of great famine;
he traveled about begging for food for seven days without obtaining any.
At the very end, he obtained only a small amount of coarse food and barely managed to survive.
He then realized that this elephant had been his younger brother in a previous life.
He then went to the elephant,
grasped its ear with his hand,
and spoke to it, saying:
"In the past, I and you both committed offenses," said the bhikṣu Hastiśrī;
immediately, he recognized his past lives.
Seeing the causes and conditions of his previous lives,
he became sorrowful and ceased eating;
the elephant cub was likewise filled with fear.
He then went to inform the king, saying,
"The elephant will neither eat nor drink;
I do not know what its intention is."
The king asked the elephant’s son,
"Has anyone ever previously violated this elephant?
The elephant’s son replied:
There was no other person;
only a single śramaṇa came to the side of the elephant and departed after a brief moment.
The king immediately dispatched men to find the śramaṇa and asked him,
"By which path did you go to my elephant?"
The śramaṇa replied,
"I say to you, elephant:
both you and I are indeed guilty."
The śramaṇa recounted the matter to the king exactly as it had occurred above.
The king’s mind was immediately enlightened,
and he released the śramaṇa at once.
Return to their respective dwellings. *The Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables*, Volume Four. 17.
Five Hundred Blind Boys Traverse the Rough Terrain, See the Buddha, Their Eyes Are Cleared, and They Realize the Path. [Section] Seventeen: The Kingdom of Vaiśālī.
There were five hundred blind men who sustained themselves by begging. At that time,
they heard that a Buddha had appeared in the world.
Those who behold it shall all have their chronic ailments and hundredfold maladies cured;
to the poor, they shall give food and clothing.
It can completely resolve and exempt one from sorrow, anxiety, suffering, and calamity.
Thus, the blind men deliberated together.
"Our accumulated sins and the poisons of our suffering are especially severe;
if we were to encounter the Buddha, we would surely receive his salvation.
Thus, they went together to beg for alms.
Each person was given one gold coin,
which was sufficient to hire laborers for the journey to that place.
During the time spent begging on the way, each person obtained one coin.
He called out to those on his left and right, "Who will take me to Śrāvastī?
and offered five hundred gold coins as wages for their labor.
At that time, a man came forward.
He gave them money for their shared labor and told the blind men to lead one another by turns.
Leading the way with sovereign ease,
as he was about to reach Magadha,
he abandoned all those who were blind.
They were placed in a desolate marsh; not knowing which country they were in,
the blind men grasped one another's hands and trampled upon the fields of others.
The sprouts and grain were trampled and shattered.
When the owner of the field saw this, he became violently enraged and said,
"I will give you a painful beating with my hand."
The beggar entreated him piteously, recounting the aforementioned circumstances.
The elder took pity on him and ordered an attendant to lead him to Śrāvastī.
Upon arriving in that country,
he heard that the World-Honored One had already departed for the kingdom of Magadha;
he then dispatched messengers to lead the way toward the kingdom of Magadha.
The blind man revered the Buddha with all his heart, desiring to see him.
Although his physical eyes were closed, his mental eye had already beheld him;
filled with joy, he resolved his mind and was unaware of his exhaustion.
Having already arrived in Magadha,
he heard that the World-Honored One had returned to Śrāvastī;
thus he pursued him, traveling back and forth a total of seven times.
At that time, the Tathāgata, observing that the roots of goodness of the blind men had ripened,
remained there waiting for them.
The Buddha’s light touched their bodies.
Instantly, his two eyes were opened and cleared;
he then beheld the Tathāgata surrounded by the fourfold assembly,
his body radiant and brilliant like a mountain of purple gold.
They approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground,
paid homage to the Buddha,
and spoke with one voice.
They addressed the Buddha together, saying,
"We only pray that you will show us compassion and grant us permission to join the ranks of those on the Path."
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣus. Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, and the Dharma robes were upon their bodies.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him once more.
He attained arhatship. [From] the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Six.
18. The Son of a Caṇḍāla Attains Enlightenment through the Buddha’s Compassionate Transformation. 18. Within the city of Śrāvastī...
There was a son of a *caṇḍāla* named Niti; the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish) says he supported himself by clearing away refuse.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city to beg for alms and arrived at his house.
The guest who was clearing away the filth immediately moved aside to another alley.
The Tathāgata went toward him.
The man thought to himself:
"I am carrying impure excrement;
how could I possibly have an audience with the World-Honored One today?
He then went to another marsh.
The Buddha called out from afar,
saying, "I have come for you. The man replied:
We did not dare to draw near.
We do not understand what the World-Honored One’s instruction was,
such that you were able to show compassion and speak with these offenders.
The World-Honored One said,
"I wish to ordain you as a śramaṇa.
The man addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Can those in the hells and the animal realm also attain the Way?
The Buddha said,
"I have now appeared in the world."
Precisely for the sake of their sinful suffering,
he grasps those people with his hand and ascends into the void.
He went to the banks of the Ganges River,
bathed his body, and then returned to the Jetavana Monastery.
The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to ordain him as a śramaṇa;
thereafter, he exhorted himself with diligence, improving daily.
Within less than ten days, he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and proceeded up to the fruit of *arhat*.
His six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) became pure and penetrating, and he could emerge from and submerge into them with complete mastery.
He went to a large square rock and sat upon its center, mending his old robes with patches.
When the king heard that the Buddha had ordained the son of a caṇḍāla,
he reflected that the Buddha had come from a noble family of the Śākya clan.
The disciples on both sides were all from the four castes;
they entered the palace chambers to receive offerings and acts of faith.
Prostrating with his five limbs touching the ground,
he joined his palms at the Buddha's feet in worship and said,
"I have now heard that the Tathāgata has delivered the Caṇḍāla."
"What is this salutation?
I shall now go to reprimand the Tathāgata.
Before he had yet arrived—
He saw the bhikṣu sitting on a large square stone,
surrounded by five hundred gods from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven who were paying him homage.
The king approached and said to him:
"I venture to inform the World-Honored One that King Prasenajit wishes to visit the World-Honored One.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu immediately sank into the stone.
Emerging from the vihāra, he went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "The time is right.
The bhikṣu then emerged from the rock.
He said to the king,
"The Tathāgata has an instruction:
first ask this bhikṣu how he was able to enter this hard, adamantine stone."
Moving up and down with complete ease,
he approached the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet,
and sat to one side.
He then addressed the Buddha,
saying, "What is the name of that bhikṣu who was just here?"
He possesses such supernormal power.
The Buddha said to the king,
"This is a guest scavenger."
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One spoke these two verses:
"Just as a field is defiled and foul,
with deep ditches and pits,"
A fragrant and pure lotus flower has grown there.
Great King, would a person with sight take this flower or not?
The king said,
"World-Honored One,
the flowers are exceedingly fragrant and pure."
One should take up the impurities as ornaments and contemplate the mother’s womb; within that womb, the flower of merit is born.
At that time, the king addressed the Buddha.
That person has gained a most excellent benefit that is inconceivable.
From this day forward.
Please this bhikṣu.
[This is from] the *Candālaputra-parivarta-sūtra*, Chapter 19:
"The Hunter Who Abandoned His Home to Study the Path. Chapter 19: The Story of the Hunter Who Abandoned His Home to Study the Path. Long ago, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Magadha...
In the sweet pear grove,
within a stone chamber cave to the north of the city,
there were many hunters.
He entered the mountains to hunt,
spreading out nets extensively and killing countless deer.
He returned to the mountain once more.
At that time, there was a deer that had fallen into that pit.
They raised a great shout;
having heard it, the hunters each fled in haste.
They fell back into the pit themselves,
harming and injuring the people in numbers beyond reckoning.
Although they did not die, their wounds were so severe that the pain was beyond description;
they supported one another.
The man of inferior capacity then went to his home,
sought some medicinal ointment,
and applied it to the wound.
The members of the household and the five types of relatives each received the corpse and returned to perform the funeral rites;
among them were sentient beings who had been afflicted by wounds.
Knowing for himself that his wound had healed,
he grew weary of hunting; it was his past karmic conditions that it was time for him to be delivered.
Having planted various roots of goodness,
he then left his home to study the Way and became a śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
Surrounded before and behind by countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings,
he preached the Dharma for them.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
wishing to uproot those sentient beings and establish them in merit, acted accordingly.
Manifesting the teaching and precepts,
they forever leave birth and death behind and dwell eternally in the Hall of Blessings amidst the great assembly.
And he spoke this verse:
"Just as one who fashions an arrow Harms his own body with it, So too is the arrow of craving: It wounds sentient beings."
At that time, although that hunter had become a śramaṇa,
he was not aware that the Tathāgata was there today.
Proving ourselves to be hunters,
we felt inward shame and remorse.
Reflecting upon one's own fundamental transgressions,
one should dwell in a secluded and tranquil place and contemplate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
He fixes his mind without distraction.
For this reason, sons of noble family shave off their hair and beard, don the three dharma robes,
leave the household life to study the Way, and cultivate the unsurpassed holy life.
Realizing this for oneself, one dwells in its enjoyment;
birth and death have been exhausted, the holy life has been established,
what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further undergoing of birth and death.
He knew them as they truly are.
At that time, all the bhikṣus attained arhatship.
The six supernormal powers are pure and transparent, without any obstruction;
therefore, this verse is spoken.

One who is able to awaken to this—where craving and suffering arise together with existence, yet there is neither desire nor the perception of existence—that bhikṣu, with single-minded mindfulness, crosses over; he has abandoned the hunter’s life to study the Way.
*Jingjing lü yixiang*, Scroll Seventeen.

22. Fearing the attainment of the Way, twenty-two bhikṣus were playing with women; having incurred a bad reputation, they committed suicide, but a heavenly deity enlightened them so that they attained the Way through diligent practice.
23. Twenty-three bhikṣus had harmed their mothers while still laypeople; they were converted by the Bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna, left the household life, and attained the Way.
24. A poor old man was on the verge of death; the Buddha spoke of his past deeds and granted him [the Dharma].

29. A śramaṇa smeared his hands with food while wiping a pillar, causing the pillar to split asunder. 30. A śramaṇa urinated without snapping his fingers, and the urine splashed onto the face of a spirit.
31. When a śramaṇa opened a door, fire issued from his five fingers. 32. A man of the "double surname" (Chongxing) was swallowed by a fish but did not die;
he left the household life and awakened to the Way. 33. A man of the "double surname" (Chongxing) was swallowed by a fish but did not die; he left the household life and awakened to the Way.
The Way says: In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a wealthy elder whose riches were immeasurable;
yet, having no offspring, he was constantly filled with melancholy and longing.
Through their prayers and supplications with sincere and profound devotion,
the wife gave birth to a son who was exceptionally handsome and rare;
his parents and kinsmen [were filled with joy].
At that time, they gathered together for a banquet and went to the banks of a great river to enjoy themselves with food and drink.
Their parents took their child and went to that place of assembly.
Out of affection for this child, she carried him on her shoulders while dancing from her seat.
When the father had finished his dance,
the mother took him up again.
While enjoying himself in pleasure,
his mind suddenly became distracted as he reached the riverbank;
unable to hold the child firmly, he lost him, and the child fell into the water.
They searched for him at once, but in the end were unable to find him.
His parents, filled with pity and deep affection, were overcome with grief;
yet, by virtue of their son’s merit, he did not die.
Floating and sinking with the current, he was swallowed by a fish;
though within the fish’s belly, he still did not die.
Downstream in a village, there was a wealthy household.
Furthermore, he had no son;
though he sought one in various ways, he was unable to obtain one despite his efforts.
That wealthy family, however, constantly employed a slave whose occupation it was to capture living creatures.
"It is worth swallowing this small fish;
by cutting it open, one finds a child.
Let me give it to everyone."
Everyone reflected upon this and spoke with self-congratulation, saying: "For generations,
our family has offered prayers and sacrifices to the gods and spirits."
Seeking offspring with sincere devotion, she received a response from the heavens;
thus, Heaven granted her a child,
whom she immediately rubbed and cleansed, nursing and raising him.
When the parents of the upper village heard that the child had been found in the belly of a fish by the elder of the lower village,
they immediately went to his place and sought him out, saying:
"This is my son. I lost this child in that river;
now you have found him."
"I pray that you will return it.
Then that householder replied to him, "In my family,
we have long offered prayers and sacrifices in search of a son."
"Now, through divine retribution, you have granted me a son.
Your deceased child has finally been found.
As this matter remains unresolved amidst such confusion, I have come to the King to seek a judgment."
Thereupon, each of the two families cited their own reasoning.
The child’s parents said, "This is my son;
I lost him in the river at such-and-such a time."
Furthermore, that elder spoke again, saying:
"I found him in the belly of a fish in the river.
He is truly my son and was not born of you."
Upon hearing their accounts, the king did not know how to proceed;
he therefore adjudicated the matter impartially for both families,
decreeing that each of you, O two elders, shall name this child.
Now, it would be unreasonable to give [the child] to only one;
therefore, we shall provide for him together until he has grown up.
He provided each with a wife and settled them in their respective households; thus,
they lived separately in two different places.
The son born to this wife belongs to this family;
the son born to that wife belongs to that family.
Then the two elders each followed the king’s instructions;
when their sons had grown up, they married them both off,
providing all their necessities so that they lacked for nothing.
The boy said to his two parents, "Since my birth, I have encountered many hardships and sufferings.
Once I fell into the water and was about to be swallowed by a fish; I was on the verge of death before I was rescued."
"Now my heart's desire is to leave the household life;
I only pray that my parents will grant me their permission.
At that time, his two parents loved this son dearly.
Unable to refuse or oppose him,
he immediately granted permission.
He then went to where the Buddha was.
Seeking to enter the Path, he said, "Welcome."
His hair fell off of its own accord and he immediately became a śramaṇa;
his name was Ghoṣila.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him.
Having brought all suffering to an end, he became an Arhat.
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One."
Named Vipaśyin, he gathered a great assembly and preached the sublime Dharma for them.
At that time, an elder came to the assembly.
Hearing the discourse on the merit of the great Dharma-giving and the precepts,
he gave rise to a mind of faith and reverence,
received the three refuges and the precept against killing.
Furthermore, he offered a single coin as alms to that Buddha;
consequently, in birth after birth, he received blessings and his wealth and treasures never failed.
The son of the elder was none other than the present Bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka.
Because he offered a single coin to the Buddha,
for ninety-one kalpas he was constantly wealthy in money and goods;
even in this present life, the parents of both families provided him with all his necessities.
Having received the precept against killing, even when falling into water and being swallowed by a fish, he could not be made to die;
because he had taken the Three Refuges, he attained Arhatship—thus it is told in the fifth fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.
2. The Great Excess of Vigor of Viśrutasvara. Two Buddhas were staying at the side of the Thunder-Sound Pond in the kingdom of Campā.
The Venerable Viśrutasvara was staying in a secluded place;
practicing the foundations of the Dharma himself and not abandoning the dhūta ascetic practices,
he practiced walking meditation day and night.
Wherever he walked, his footprints were like streams of flowing blood;
though he constantly exerted himself with self-discipline,
his mind was not liberated from the outflows (*āsrava*).
At that time, Viśvantara (Twenty-Ears) thought to himself:
"In asceticism and diligence, I am foremost;
yet my mind remains defiled and has not attained liberation."
Furthermore, my family estate possesses abundant wealth and many treasures;
it would be fitting for you to cast off these robes and return to the life of a layman,
using your wealth to practice extensive giving.
The Buddha, knowing this in his mind, went to that place.
The Buddha said to Viśvantara:
"In your former life as a householder, you were skilled at playing the lute."
"If the strings of a lute are extremely tight, can the sounds be heard as even and harmonious?
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "If the strings of a lute are extremely loose, can they still be heard?"
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Is the sound neither too hurried nor too slow easy to listen to?"
"So it is, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Even one of extreme diligence is like a playful child."
If one is indolent, this constitutes falling into false views;
if one can remain within this [middle way],
this is the supreme practice.
"In this way, before long,
you shall become free from outflows.
Having heard these words, Twenty-Ear-Billion (Viṃśati-karṇa-koṭi) [and his followers] were moved.
Returning to the side of the Thunder-Sound Pond,
he contemplated the Buddha’s teachings and attained arhatship; this is recorded in the eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
3. Ratha was entreated by his father; Ratha was entreated by his father three times. The Brahmin Ratha sought to go forth as a monk under the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
He first took leave of his parents,
but they would not grant him permission.
Rata lay upon the ground for many days, refusing to eat.
His parents consoled him,
yet he remained silent until the end;
they then took pity on his resolve.
He immediately granted his permission;
[the youth] left the household life, received full ordination, and became an Arhat.
Ten years later, he returned to the village.
He went on his alms-round in sequential order.
His father, not recognizing him, scolded him and refused to give anything.
A maidservant took his bowl, filled it with discarded, rotten food, and gave it to him.
He returned and informed his parents,
"Rattha has returned.
His father immediately went out to look.
Question:
Why did you not return to my door?
Answer: [He] said:
Having already arrived and received abuse,
the father led him into the room and prepared various kinds of fine food.
An elephant carrying gold and silver stood in the middle of the courtyard,
rising higher than a man;
the money and goods were beyond counting.
"You may return to lay life.
His mother then instructed her daughter-in-law to adorn herself and go to Rāṣṭrapāla's location,
where the relatives together exhorted him repeatedly.
Rattha wished to offer food; why wait for him to be disturbed?
[This is from] the Madhyama Āgama, Volume 28, Sūtra 4, "The Wealthy One" (*Suvarṇavipra*).
The Wealthy One offered two coins to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, and in this life his hands hold gold coins. In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder.
The wife gave birth to a son named Suvarṇadhana,
who was exceptionally handsome and distinguished.
The child’s hands were clenched into fists;
his parents were struck with alarm and fear,
and they immediately opened both of his hands.
He saw two gold coins in the child's hand;
he joyfully took them, yet they immediately grew back again.
Thus he diligently gathered until the storehouse was full and could not be exhausted.
As his son grew older,
he addressed his parents, requesting permission to leave the household life and become a renunciant.
Even though he heard this,
he went to the place where the Buddha was, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the kāṣāya robes, and,
upon reaching the required age, received full ordination.
The assembly of monks at the altar shall perform prostrations in successive order,
according to the places where they are to be paid homage.
At that time, he pressed both hands against the ground,
and from each there emerged two gold coins.
Having thus completed his reception of the precepts.
Through diligent cultivation, he attained the path of Arhatship.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"This Bhikṣu Suvarṇadhana..."
"What merit did he previously create to hold gold coins in his hand?
The Buddha said,
"Ninety-one eons ago."
There was a Buddha named Vipaśyin who appeared in the world and traveled through the various realms together with the assembly of monks.
At that time, various elders prepared offerings for the Buddha and his disciples.
At that moment, a certain poor man was gathering firewood to sell.
At that time, he obtained two coins.
Seeing the Buddha, he was filled with joy and immediately offered the two coins to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Because that poor man gave two coins as an offering to the Buddha and the Sangha,
for ninety-one kalpas he constantly held gold coins in his hand.
Wealth and treasures appeared spontaneously.
The poor man of that time was the bhikṣu Suvarṇadatta. (From the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Two.)

5. In a previous life, Puṣpadeva gathered flowers as an offering; therefore, the heavens now rain down those flowers for him. Because Puṣpadeva gathered flowers as an offering in a previous life, the heavens now rain down those flowers for him. Fifth, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a wealthy and noble householder.
A son was born, with a countenance and features that were upright and handsome;
the heavens rained down various flowers, which filled the interior of the house.
He was thus named Puṣpaketu,
meaning "Flower-Deity Son. As he grew older,
he went to the place where the Buddha was.
He thought to himself,
"I have appeared in this world and encountered the Holy Honored One.
He then stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
I only pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of monks will deign to visit my humble home tomorrow and accept a modest offering of vegetarian food.
The Buddha accepted the invitation.
The Flower-God returned and transformed himself into jeweled couches that filled the entire interior of the house.
The preparations were duly made with solemn adornment;
the Buddha and the assembly of monks then took their seats upon those thrones.
The Flower Deity provided the food and drink through his own merit.
After the Buddha and the Sangha had finished their meal,
he extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the Flower Deity.
The Flower Deity and his entire household attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Huatian immediately took leave of his parents and sought to leave the secular world;
his parents granted him their permission.
The Buddha said, "Welcome.
His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, the saṃghāṭī robe was donned upon his body,
and by practicing in accordance with the Buddha's teachings, he attained arhatship.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What merit did the Flower Deity possess to attain such a state?"
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin."
Having appeared in the world to deliver sentient beings,
he was then honored and supported by all the noble clans.
At that time, there was a poor man.
Seeing the monks, he was filled with joy;
he immediately gathered various wild flowers from the marshes and scattered them over the great assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The poor man at that time was none other than the bhikṣu Puṣpadanta."
By the merit of scattering flowers,
for ninety-one kalpas his body was upright and handsome,
and whatever he required from his mind was provided.
"Arriving as soon as one thinks of it," from the *Xiányújīng* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish), Volume Two.

6. Because the former life of the Jewel-God (*Ratnadeva*) had once thrown a handful of stones at monks in place of pearls, when he was born, the heavens rained down the seven kinds of jewels. In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was an elder.
A son was born; at that very moment,
the heavens rained down the seven treasures.
It pervaded the entire interior of the house.
When the physiognomist saw this,
he addressed the elder, saying:
The boy’s features were exceptionally distinguished;
at his birth there were auspicious omens, and he was named Lènnàtípió (in the Liáng language, "Precious Heaven"). As the boy grew older, [his virtues increased].
His talents and arts were widely mastered;
having heard that the Buddha was divine and sagely,
his heart was filled with deep veneration and longing.
He took leave of his parents and went to where the Buddha was,
addressing the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you will allow me to leave the household life."
The Buddha said, "Welcome.
His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the Dharma robes appeared upon his body.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma for him.
He immediately attained arhatship.
When Vipaśyin Buddha appeared in the world,
there were several lay devotees.
They invited the assembly of monks and made various offerings.
At that time, there was a poor man.
Although he harbored a joyful heart, he lacked any articles for making offerings;
thus, using a handful of white pebbles as if they were beads,
he scattered them over the assembly of monks.
He made a great vow.
The poor man was none other than this Bhikṣu Ratnadeva;
he has enjoyed immeasurable merit for as long as ninety-one kalpas.
Abounding in wealth and treasures, with food, clothing, and drink provided spontaneously,
he now encounters my world and attains the realization of the fruits of the Path. (From the *Xianyu jing*, Volume Two).

7. The Bhikṣu of Few Desires and Contentment Attains the Way upon Hearing the Dharma; The Bhikṣu of Few Desires and Contentment Attains the Way upon Hearing the Dharma. At the seventh watch, there was a man from South India.
He went forth in the True Dharma;
having few desires and being content, he did not delight in honor or renown,
nor did he anoint his body with ghee or oil.
They do not bathe with warm water,
they do not consume ghee or oil,
and they are constantly fearful of birth and death, their four great elements being devoid of strength.
Failing to attain the Noble Path,
he immediately gave rise to this thought:
"Only Upagupta [can help me]."
"May you be able to preach the Dharma for me.
He then proceeded to the kingdom of Mathurā,
where he joined his palms in reverent salutation.
Upagupta beheld his future existence and became terrified of birth and death.
He never took pleasure in coarseness or wickedness,
nor did he desire worldly glory. Upagupta said:
"Simply follow my instructions and I shall explain it for you.
He replied, "Yes."
Upagupta instructed the various donors to prepare various kinds of food and drink and provide baths for the assembly of monks;
he also spoke to the young śramaṇas.
"You may bathe this bhikṣu with warm water,
anoint his body with ghee and oil,
and provide him with various kinds of fine food."
After this bhikṣu had eaten for several days, his body regained its strength.
Upon hearing the sublime Dharma spoken by Guptā just once, he applied himself with diligence and attained the fruit of arhatship. (From the ninth fascicle of the Aśokarāja-sūtra.)
8. A Craftsman Bhikṣu Attains Enlightenment through Contemplation. Regarding the craftsman bhikṣu attaining enlightenment through contemplation:
there was a certain man who went forth into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma.
He was highly skilled in the arts;
wherever he went, all the monastic communities...
He ordered the construction of monasteries and dwellings to continue day after day without ceasing;
becoming greatly fatigued,
he then thought to himself:
"I shall sit in meditation and reflect.
When the Buddha was formerly in the world,
he taught that all bhikṣus should sit in meditation and cultivate the Path."
Not being able to remain at ease,
he went immediately to Upagupta,
prostrated, joined his palms, and said:
The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa;
O Venerable One, you now perform the work of a Buddha.
We pray that you will preach the Dharma for us.
At that time, Upagupta saw that although his future rebirth was imminent, the causes and conditions for his fear of the suffering of birth and death were not yet exhausted;
thus he became a craftsman once more,
and again observed him becoming weary and exhausted.
"It cannot be done again.
Upagupta said, "If you follow my instructions..."
"I shall preach the Dharma for you.
He replied, "So be it. Upagupta said:
If there is a site where no monastery has yet been built, you should build one there;
the Buddha has said in the past that such an act gains the merit of Brahma.
He replied,
"Venerable sir,
I am from the country of Mathurā."
[The Buddha] did not know who was diligent and who was not. Guptā said,
"Are you able to rise early, put on your robes, take up your bowl, and enter the city?"
He replied,
"I was able to enter the city early in the morning and encountered an elder who was coming out."
"Never before have we seen such a thing; yet now we see this bhikṣu.
They immediately paid him homage and asked:
"Venerable sir,
from where have you come— far or near?
The bhikṣu replied:
"He has come from the eastern land.
He was asked again what his business was,
and he replied, "It is as follows."
The householder said,
"Venerable sir,
there is no need for further deliberation now."
"I shall become a bhikṣu.
Having thus prepared various requisites,
the bhikṣu then [joined] with the elder.
He took up his measuring line to find a suitable location;
before the line had even reached the ground,
he reflected within himself.
The merit thus performed eliminates all afflictions and leads to the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship. (From the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*, Scroll Nine.)
9. The Robber Who Became a Bhikṣu Meets the Buddha and Attains Enlightenment. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kośala...
King Prasenajit issued an edict to the jailers:
"Any thieves whose crimes warrant execution according to the law shall be taken to the marketplace and put to death.
At that time, there was a certain thief among the great crowd.
Having escaped by means of theft,
he outwardly assumed the dharma robes and privately became a śramaṇa.
However, within, they do not reflect,
thinking that they have forever escaped the perils of distress and no longer fear harm.
In a secluded and quiet place,
one does not contemplate the Way and its Virtue,
nor does one practice the sutras and precepts.
Although they follow the path of discipline, meditation, and recitation,
they have not yet attained the fruits of realization,
nor do they diligently seek such realization.
The Buddha told that person:
"Since you have already escaped the calamity of the bandits of birth and death,
there remains some lingering fear."
The body of the five aggregates of clinging revolves through the five destinies;
lacking understanding,
it is harmed by the various fetters and afflictions.
They will then fall into the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.
At that time, that bhikṣu dwells in a secluded and quiet place.
Reflecting and deliberating,
he reproached himself within and understood that all phenomena are entirely impermanent.
Once born, one does not remain long;
all things ultimately return to extinction.
Such is the transformation of rise and fall.
Having come here for a long time,
he immediately repented and reproached himself before the Buddha.
Attaining the Path of Arhatship and Speaking on Secretly Becoming a Śramaṇa.
10. The Bhikṣu Greedy for Food Attains the Path through Contemplation. At the ten watches, in the kingdom of Mathurā, there was a man.
Having left secular life and become a renunciant under Upagupta,
he was unable to attain the Way because of his greed for food.
Guptā said, "I shall give you food tomorrow.
When the time arrived, she filled a bowl with gruel using a single vessel.
Furthermore, he placed another empty vessel before him and said to him,
"You may take food and empty this vessel."
Furthermore, it was said,
"Wait for it to cool and eat it little by little.
However, this bhikṣu’s greedy mind was thick and heavy.
He then blew on it to cool it,
and said to his preceptor,
"It is now cold; let us eat it together."
Guptā said, "Though the milk-rice is cold,
your heart remains hot."
Furthermore, one should cool it;
one should use the contemplation of impurity as water to remove this heat of the mind.
If one views food and drink as being like taking medicine,
a bhikṣu may, upon finishing his meal,
immediately vomit it up.
The vessel was filled to the brim.
Guptā said, "You may eat more."
The bhikṣu said,
"How could that which is impure be eaten again?
He further said:
"Observe all phenomena as being like mucus or spittle," he said,
and for that reason he taught the Dharma.
The bhikṣu applied himself with diligence, reflecting and observing.
Attaining the Fruit of Arhatship, from the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*, Volume Nine. 11.

The Bhikṣu Beggar Manifests Supernatural Powers and Enters Prince Jeta’s Palace. Regarding the eleventh [chapter], "The Bhikṣu Beggar Manifests Supernatural Powers and Enters Prince Jeta’s Palace": Prince Jeta dispatched a messenger.
He invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal on the following day,
but did not invite the bhikṣu who was a beggar.
When the beggar bhikṣu arrived, he followed the Buddha and the Saṃgha into the palace to eat.
The beggar-monk,
by means of his supernormal powers, went to Uttarakuru in the north and took naturally grown non-glutinous rice.
Each maintaining their majestic deportment, they descended through the air and entered the Prince’s palace, where they took their seats in order.
Upon seeing them, the Prince marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
He asked the Buddha,
"From where have these worthy sages come?
The Buddha said:
These were none other than the five hundred beggars who became śramaṇas.

This is recorded in the fifth fascicle of the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish), titled "The Four Bhikṣus Speak of Suffering and Attain the Way upon Meeting the Buddha. 12. The Four Bhikṣus Speak of Suffering and Attain the Way upon Meeting the Buddha. At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī.
Four bhikṣus were sitting beneath a tree when they asked one another:
"What is the most painful thing in all the world?"
One person said,
"Of all the sufferings in the world, none exceeds sensual desire.
Another person said:
There is no suffering in the world greater than hunger and thirst.
Another person said:
"There is no suffering in the world greater than anger."
One person said,
"Among all the sufferings in the world, none surpasses fear and terror.
They continued to dispute the meaning of suffering, and why would it not cease?
The Buddha, knowing their words,
went to where they were and asked about the subject of their discussion.
He immediately informed the Buddha of these matters, saying:
"What you have discussed does not exhaustively investigate the meaning of suffering.
Among all the sufferings in the world, none surpasses having a body."
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, fear, desire, and calamity—all arise from the body.
Indeed, the body is the root of manifold sufferings and a vessel for misfortune;
it exhausts the mind and strains the intellect with myriad forms of anxiety and dread.
The wriggling beings of the three realms prey upon one another;
bound by the attachment to a self, they do not cease from birth and death—
all of which arises from the body.
One who wishes to leave behind the suffering of the world should seek nirvāṇa.
By concentrating the mind, maintaining rectitude, and remaining tranquil and free from discursive thought, one may attain nirvāṇa.
"This is the supreme bliss.
The Buddha spoke these verses to inform the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, incalculable eons ago..."
There was a bhikṣu possessing the five supernormal powers named Vīryabala,
who sought the Way in the seclusion beneath a tree in the mountains.
At that time, there were four birds that stayed by his side, always remaining safe and secure:
first, a pigeon;
second, a crow.
Third, venomous snakes;
fourth, deer. These are the four types of wild animals.
They went out during the day to seek food and returned to roost at night; thus,
these four birds spent one night together.
They asked one another:
"Of the sufferings of the world, which is the heaviest?
The crow said:
In times of hunger and thirst, the body becomes emaciated and the vision darkens, such that the consciousness finds no peace.
One casts oneself into nets and disregards sharp blades;
it is invariably because of this that we lose our lives.
Speaking thus, he said,
"Hunger and thirst are suffering.
The pigeon replied:
When sensual desire blazes intensely, one has no regard for anything;
there is nothing that does not lead to the endangerment of the body and the extinction of life.
The venomous snake said:
Once a thought of anger arises, one does not distinguish between kin and stranger;
it can kill others and can likewise lead to one's own suicide.
The deer said:
In the forest, my mind was constantly filled with anxiety and alarm;
fearing hunters and various tigers and wolves,
I heard what seemed like a sound and rushed toward the edge of a pit.
Mother and son abandoned each other, their livers and gallbladders grieving and trembling with alarm.
From this it may be seen that fear and terror constitute suffering.
Then Viryabala replied, "What you have discussed is merely superficial;
it does not investigate the root of suffering."
In all the world, there is no suffering greater than conditioned existence (*saṃskāra*).
This is a vessel of suffering, with immeasurable grief and fear.
For this reason, I have abandoned the secular life to study the Way.
Extinguish the mind and sever conceptualization;
do not crave the four great elements.
Desiring to cut off the source of suffering, set your will upon Nirvana.
The path to Nirvana is quiescent and formless; there,
all anxieties and afflictions are forever ended,
and one attains ultimate peace.
Upon hearing this, the four birds’ minds were immediately opened and liberated.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
At that time, the bhikṣu with five supernatural powers was none other than myself.
The four birds were these four people.
In a previous life, they had already heard the meaning of the root of suffering.
"How is it that only today do you speak thus again?
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu felt shame and reproached himself;
he immediately attained the path of an arhat before the Buddha. Excerpted from the *Dharmapada-avadāna*, Volume Four.

13. The Four Monks Who Spoke of Pleasure: The Buddha Taught that This is Suffering; Awakening to the Path through Suffering. Thirteen: The Buddha was at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī. The four monks spoke of pleasure, but the Buddha taught that this is suffering; they awakened to the path through the realization of suffering. (13) The Buddha was at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were four newly ordained bhikṣus who went beneath a *nālikera* tree to sit in meditation and cultivate the Way.
The *nālikera* flowers were in full bloom, beautiful in color and fragrant.
The companions said to one another,
"Of all the myriad things in this world, what is truly worth enjoying?
One person said:
In the second month of spring, the hundred plants flourish and bloom.
To roam and play upon the plains and fields is the greatest pleasure.
One person said:
At this auspicious gathering of kinsmen, cups and goblets were passed back and forth;
music, song, and dance—this was the height of joy.
Then one person said:
Having accumulated vast wealth and treasures, he obtained whatever he desired.
His carriages, horses, and attire were superior to those of others;
wherever he entered or exited, his radiance was so brilliant that all passersby turned their eyes toward him.
"This is the greatest pleasure.
Another person said,
"A wife and concubines who are beautiful and dressed in bright, colorful garments."
The fragrance of the incense was rich and pervasive, allowing them to indulge their desires to their heart's content;
this was their greatest pleasure.
The Buddha knew they were ready to be transformed.
I shall now explain for you that which is the most grievous:
it is said that in the past there was a king.
His name was Pujian (Universal Peace).
He shared a close friendship with the four kings of neighboring kingdoms and invited these four kings to a banquet for one month.
While enjoying food, drink,
and entertainment, on the day of their departure, Prince Puan asked:
When people dwell in this world,
what do they take to be happiness?
This is the question posed by the Four Heavenly Kings.
"It is no different from yours.
At that time, King Puxian (Universal Peace) became the embodiment [of the truth].
Upon hearing this, the Four Kings rejoiced, placing their faith and understanding it.
At that time, King Puhuan was none other than myself.
The four kings at that time were you four people.
I have already discussed this previously, yet you still do not understand it now.
"How can this long cycle of birth and death be brought to rest?
At that time, the four bhikṣus,
having heard this teaching again, felt shame and remorse for their transgressions.
The Mind Awakened and Attaining the Path of Arhatship, from the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Four. 14.
The Bhikṣu Who Rescued His Mother from the Suffering of Hell. 14. Once upon a time, there was a man.
Having bid farewell to his kin to study the Way, he attained the state of an Arhat.
Having fulfilled all his obligations of gratitude, he practiced universal salvation;
then, observing that his mother was within the Avīci hell, [he resolved to save her].
He extensively sought expedient means, desiring to liberate his mother from her suffering.
He saw that at the border there was a king who had killed his father and usurped the kingdom,
and whose life would end in seven days.
The place where he was to undergo punishment was the same as that of his mother.
At night, he went to the king’s quarters and manifested his upper body from within the wall.
The king, seeing this, was struck with terror;
he drew his sword and struck at his own neck,
and his head immediately fell to the ground.
The bhikṣu remained unmoved.
Only then did the king’s mind open,
and he prostrated himself, apologizing for his transgression.
The bhikṣu said to the king,
"Did you not kill your father and seize the kingdom?
He replied:
"It is indeed so," [the Buddha] said. "Seven days remain of your life;
you shall enter hell."
"I have therefore come to speak with you.
The king immediately sought his mercy,
and the bhikṣu said:
"Performing great meritorious deeds may not suffice;
Your Majesty need only recite 'Namo Buddha' without ceasing for seven days, and you shall be freed from your transgression."
The king then single-mindedly recited "Namo Buddha" for seven days without ceasing.
At the end of his life, his spiritual consciousness still remembered entering the gates of hell.
Therefore, they uttered "Namo Buddha," and the niraya immediately became cool;
all the people within the city were able to escape.
The bhikṣu then preached the Dharma for them;
the bhikṣu’s mother, the king, and those among the inhabitants of hell all attained liberation and deliverance. (From the *Daśavastuka-avadāna-sūtra*, Scroll 2).

15. A Bhikṣu Attains the Path through the Teacher’s Instruction. In the southern region of India, there was a man who left the household life to join the Buddha’s Dharma. He attained the Path through the instruction of his teacher. Thus ends the fifteenth [chapter].
Bound by craving, they anoint their bodies with ghee and oil,
and further bathe them with warm water.
Provided with various kinds of food and drink,
his body was bound by craving so that he could not attain the Noble Path;
he then went to the place of Upagupta in the kingdom of Mathurā.
He prostrated at his feet and said,
"I wish to hear the essentials of the Dharma.
Upagupta saw that his future life was bound by craving.
"Language. Young man,
if you can receive my instruction, I shall speak for you."
He replied, "I can.
Upagupta led him into the mountains and,
by means of his supernormal powers, manifested a great tree.
He said, "You should climb this great tree.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately climbed the tree.
Furthermore, beneath the tree, he manifested a great pit,
a thousand cubits deep and wide.
He then spoke again.
"I release your two legs.
He immediately released his legs.
[The king] then ordered him to release one hand.
He then released one hand,
and then released the other hand.
The bhikṣu replied:
"If you let go of my hand again, you will fall into the pit and die.
Upagupta said, "I have previously agreed with you that I shall obey all your instructions."
"How is it that you do not accept it?
At that moment, his bodily craving was immediately extinguished;
he let go of his hand, and [the body] fell.
Not seeing the tree pit, Guptā preached the Dharma;
through diligent contemplation, she attained the fruit of Arhatship. (From the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*, Scroll Ten).
16. The Bhikṣu Entering the Path through the Contemplation of White Bones. In the kingdom of Mathurā, there was a man who left the household life to become a monk under Upagupta.
Having heard the teachings on the contemplation of impurity and so forth,
they suppress the afflictions through the contemplation of impurity,
thinking, "I have already accomplished what was to be done."
Guptā said, "You should be diligent; do not harbor thoughts of indolence.
He replied:
He replied, "I have already attained arhatship. Guptā said,
"Have you seen the woman who sells wine by overturning the *Gandhāra* country?"
This woman claims for herself that she has attained the Way;
she is no different from you.
To claim that one has severed the afflictions when they have not yet been severed is overweening pride.
Do you now observe whether this woman has attained the Way or not?
He replied,
"I have not yet seen it;
I wish to go to that land."
The Master then granted his permission.
At that time, the bhikṣu went to the kingdom of Gandhāra.
A report from the Tsuchi-ji Temple in Jichi:
Rising early, I donned my robes and took up my alms bowl to enter the village for alms.
At that time, a wine-seller took some food and wished to give it to me.
When the bhikṣu saw the woman,
a mind of lustful desire arose within him, and he took the parched grain and curd from his bowl and gave it to her.
When the woman saw him, her mind was likewise transformed by lustful desire; she bared her teeth and smiled.
The bhikṣu immediately entered the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā).
...up to contemplating the body as a white bone.
From this contemplation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship. (From the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*, scroll ten). 17.

A Bhikṣu Attains the Way through the Pravāraṇā and Upasaṃpadā: Seventeen Buddhas were in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. A bhikṣu attained the Way through the pravāraṇā ceremony and the reception of the upasaṃpadā. (Seventeen. Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
After residing there for three months,
until the arrival of the new year,
he addressed Ānanda, saying:
Strike the ghaṇṭā;
the sound of the ghaṇṭā shall pervade an entire buddha-field,
[relieving] all the sufferings of illness among those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals.
Upon hearing these sounds, all afflictions were entirely removed and they all attained peace and security.
At that time, the Buddha said,
"Bhikṣus, you should arise and distribute śalākā-voting sticks."
Each person, facing the others, repents and reproaches themselves;
they apologize for the various faults and transgressions of the assembly that were contrary to the Dharma,
and each, with patience and harmony, purifies their body, speech, and mind.
"May there be no further impurity.
Then the bhikṣus accepted the Buddha’s instruction;
having completed the task, they returned to their seats.
At that time, the Buddha,
out of compassion, rose from his seat and turned toward the bhikṣus.
With palms joined, he said:
"Although the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Most Perfectly Awakened One, is without fault,
these matters should nevertheless be put into practice as a lesson for instruction."
Then the Buddha paused, offering his apologies to the assembly of noble ones;
out of compassion for all beings, he returned to his grass mat.
As soon as the Buddha sat down again, the assembly of noble ones did likewise.
Each returned to their former positions.
At that time, ten thousand bhikṣus attained the fruit of the path, and eight thousand bhikṣus attained arhatship.
They then performed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony with full clarity and received the *varṣa* (rainy-season) ordination; this is recorded in the *Navasūtra* (Sutra on the New Year).

18. The Eighteenth Buddha, Delighting in Sleep and Joyful in Abiding Practice, Attained the Way. The Eighteenth Buddha, Delighting in Sleep and Joyful in Abiding Practice, Attained the Way. The Buddhas were at the Jeta Grove Monastery.
"O bhikṣus, diligently cultivate the work of the path and cast off the hindrances (āvaraṇa).
There was once a bhikṣu..."
Having eaten their fill, they enter their rooms and sleep quietly in seclusion;
receiving the body with pleasure, they do not contemplate impermanence,
and for them there is no further distinction between day and night.
Seven days hence, his life will come to an end.
The Buddha, moved by compassion for him,
immediately entered his room and awakened him by snapping his fingers.
He spoke for him a sublime verse, which caused him to be startled into awakening; he prostrated himself in homage.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu: "This was your former destiny."
During the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, he once attained renunciation;
however, being greedy for his own body and material gain, he did not contemplate the sutras or the precepts.
Having eaten his fill, he would fall back asleep, failing to reflect upon impermanence.
When their life ends, their spirits are reborn among the *wēng* worms,
where they remain for fifty thousand years.
When their lifespan is exhausted, they are again born as conch and clam worms, or as wood-boring insects within trees.
Each lives for fifty thousand years.
These four types of worms grow and dwell in darkness,
greedily clinging to their bodies and cherishing their lives.
They delight in dwelling in secluded and hidden places as their home and take no pleasure in light.
When they sleep, they awaken only after a hundred years.
Entangled in continuous nets, they do not seek the essential way of deliverance.
Now that your transgressions have finally come to an end and you have been able to become a śramaṇa,
how can you sleep and remain ignorant of the need for contentment?
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu felt shame and fear, reproaching himself;
the five hindrances were immediately eliminated, and he attained arhatship. This concludes the third fascicle of the *Dharmapada-avadāna*.

19. A bhikṣu fond of sleep saw a deep pit manifested by a transformation; terrified, he attained the Way. A bhikṣu fond of sleep saw a deep pit manifested by a transformation; terrified, he attained the Way. (19) Mathurā Country.
There was a man who,
having gone forth under Upagupta,
was constantly fond of sleep.

even when instructed to practice meditation under a tree, he again fell asleep.
Guptaka, by means of his supernormal powers...
On its four sides, he manifested deep pits one thousand cubits deep. Then,
when the bhikṣu awoke from his sleep,
he was immediately struck with terror.
Then Upagupta again manifested a path by transformation so that the bhikṣu could travel upon it.
At that time, this bhikṣu...
He departed along the road and went to where Upagupta was;
Upagupta then sent him away once more.
The bhikṣu replied,
"There is a deep pit there. Upagupta said:
This deep pit is minor birth and death;
the deep pit that is great is what is called birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
If a person does not know the Four Noble Truths, [they fall into this pit].
He then fell into that state.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu went back beneath the tree and sat down cross-legged.
In his mind, he constantly contemplated the fear of falling into a deep pit; he no longer slept,
and out of dread, he applied himself with diligent reflection.
Having eliminated all afflictions,
he attained the fruit of arhatship.
This is from the ninth fascicle of the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*.
20. A bhikṣu who eats much attained the path of arhatship; a bhikṣu who eats much attained the path of arhatship. There were twenty-one female elephants, one of whom was named Mata.
He carried the Buddha’s śarīra to the kingdom of Kaśmīra.

having left the household life, attained the fruit of arhatship.
Having consumed one *droṇa* of rice, he entered *parinirvāṇa*.

The bhikṣuṇīs did not believe her words.
She spoke to them again, saying,
"Do not harbor such lack of faith."
In a previous life, he was a female elephant.
Having cast off that elephant body, he immediately obtained this present body,
which is capable of eating one hu and five dou of rice.
Yet he eats one *śata* (a measure of grain).
This is explained at length,
and although such instances involve eating much, [it is not considered a transgression].
Yet it is easy to satisfy.
I have heard that King Prasenajit once consumed two bushels of cooked rice.
By virtue of those meritorious causes and conditions,
[he obtained sustenance] from a single grain of non-glutinous rice and a single stalk of sugarcane.
Day by day he grew older and,
because he consumed such a quantity of food, his body became stout.
With this large body, he went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha asked,
"Great King,
as your body is so stout and large, do you not feel weary?"
At that time, King Prasenajit felt shame and remorse.
He related everything to the Buddha, and the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"A person should maintain right mindfulness and know moderation in eating."
Nor will they encounter painful sensations; [these ailments] are easily eliminated, and their lifespan increases.
When King Prasenajit heard what the Buddha had said, he was moved.

He gradually reduced his food intake until, at a later time, he consumed only a single *lì* (升). [From the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 22]. 21. A Bhikṣu who had been long ill was washed by the Buddha;

having heard the Dharma, he passed away and attained *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. [The twenty-first case]: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. A bhikṣu had been suffering from a chronic illness for a long time. The Buddha personally washed him and taught him the Dharma; upon hearing it, the bhikṣu relinquished his life and attained *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. This is the twenty-first [case]. The Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
There was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha;
at that time, the bhikṣus went there.
The Tathāgata does not go there;
rather, he sends a messenger to fetch food for two reasons.
First, he wished to preach the Dharma to the devas;
second, he wished to attend to the sick.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the bhikṣus all around.
They all accepted the invitation;
he then took the key and opened the door of one room,
where he saw a bhikṣu.
His illness became suddenly grave; he lay prostrate, unable to turn over as he was soiled by his own excrement and urine.
The World-Honored One asked him, "What ailment do you have?"
The bhikṣu said,
"My nature is dull-witted and I have always harbored indolence and pride;
from the beginning, I never encouraged others to look after anyone else."
Therefore, today there is no one to look after me;
I am truly solitary and destitute, with nowhere to rely upon.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
With compassionate pity, he personally embraced [the child], removed the impurities,
and washed the sitting mat.
He washed his body,
provided him with new clothes,
and spread out a fresh sitting mat.
He returned it to the room and personally massaged it himself,
then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
If you do not apply yourself with diligence to seek the supreme Dharma,
after death you shall undergo even more intense suffering.
Gradually he preached the Dharma to him, exhorting him to be courageous and resolute.
He then addressed the monks: "O bhikṣus,
you have no parents or brothers."
Furthermore, there are no sisters or kinsmen to look after one another; this is not fitting.
In my Dharma, all things are aligned and upright, and those above and below follow one another in harmony.
From this day forward,
disciples shall serve their teachers as they would serve their own parents,
never abandoning them until death.
The teacher regards his disciples as his own breath;
he nurtures them according to the times, never abandoning them until death.
This mutual compassion between teacher and disciple shall flow through eternal kalpas.
All personal belongings shall be distributed equally;
if there are no belongings, one should extensively seek alms.
If there is anyone to attend to me while I am ill, let them attend to my body.
The merit obtained was likewise without distinction.
At that time, the sick bhikṣu reflected within himself and immediately relinquished his physical life.
The Sūtra on Attaining Nirvana Without Remainder through the Buddha’s Visiting a Bhikṣu’s Illness and Refusing the Elder’s Invitation, 22.
A Bhikṣu Attains the Way Due to Fear. Twenty-second: At that time, in the kingdom of Mathurā.
There was a man who went forth as a monk under Upagupta;
he was very fond of sleep.
Guptā transformed herself into a ghost with seven heads;
holding a tree branch in her hand, she suspended her body in mid-air.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu was immediately startled awake;
seized by great terror,
he returned to his original place.
Guptā said, "Return to the place where you practice meditation.
The bhikṣu replied:
"Upādhyāya, in that forest there was a ghost with seven heads who stood before me,
grasping a tree branch and suspended in mid-air."
"It is truly terrifying. Guptā said,
"This ghost is not worth fearing."
Sleep is most fearsome.
If a bhikṣu is killed by this ghost,
he will certainly not enter the cycle of birth and death.
"If one is slain by sleep,
then birth and death will be without end.
The bhikṣu then returned to his place for seated meditation.
Furthermore, he saw this ghost;
out of fear of this ghost, he did not dare to sleep.
At that time, the bhikṣu applied himself with diligence and contemplation.
