A Bhikṣu who Engaged in Lecherous Play with a Woman, Incurred a Bad Reputation, Commited Suicide, and Was Awakened by a Deva; Through Diligence, He Attained the Way. Twenty-three: The Buddha Resided in Śrāvastī. [The story of] a bhikṣu who engaged in lecherous play with a woman, incurred a bad reputation, and committed suicide, was awakened by a deva; through diligence, he attained the Way. Twenty-three: The Buddha resided in Śrāvastī.
There was a certain bhikṣu living in a forest grove among the people of Kosala.
A bhikṣu was sporting with the wife of a householder,
which gave rise to an evil reputation.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I shall now take my own life.
There was a deva in the forest who transformed herself into the body of an elder's daughter.
He said to the bhikṣu,
"The people of the world are falsely attributing the name of evil to me and to you."
I have associated closely with you and committed improper acts; thus,
an evil reputation has already arisen.
"You may return to lay life and enjoy yourselves together.
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have heard such a report."
I shall now take my own life.
Then, manifesting a divine body,
he spoke these verses:
Though one has many ill repute, the practitioner should endure it; he should neither harm himself nor give rise to vexation.
The bhikṣu attains awakening, applying himself with diligence to contemplation to sever the afflictions.
Having attained arhatship, he emerges from his seclusion. This concludes the Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Who Avoided the Ill Repute of Women and Intended to Commit Suicide.

24. A bhikṣu who, while still a layman, had killed his mother, was converted by the Bodhisattva Samantamukha, left the household life, and attained the Way. There was once a man on the road... [The twenty-fourth case: a bhikṣu who, while still a layman, had killed his mother, was converted by the Bodhisattva Samantamukha, left the household life, and attained the Way. There was once a man on the road.
The mother who gave birth to the one who causes harm dwells beneath a tree,
weeping and distressed.
He cried out in lamentation,
reproaching himself for his lack of virtue in committing such a great rebellion; he said,
"I have brought harm upon my own mother and shall surely fall into hell."
Although that person is thus, they should cultivate the practice of the Vinaya.
Bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna sees that they should attain deliverance in the present.
He transformed himself into another person and,
taking his parents with him, went to the place where the woman who had harmed his mother was;
not far from it, he stopped midway along the road.
The parents said to their son, "This is the correct path," but the son said it was not correct;
they then proceeded to dispute and debate with one another.
The son manifested a state of wrath and killed his transformed parents;
having done so, he wept with such bitter anguish that he could not restrain himself,
and went to the place where the mother was.
He said, "I have killed my parents; I shall surely fall into hell.
Wailing, he cried out, "Alas! What is to be done?"
"What plan should be devised?
The one who had killed his mother thought to himself,
"This man who has come here is one who has harmed both his parents."
"I have merely endangered my mother;
that person's delusion and darkness constitute a sin greater than mine.
My act of rebellion is still less grave than his."
Knowing that their punishment was still light compared to his own,
those people were overcome with grief and bitter anguish, and they cried out in unison:
"We shall go to the abode of the Buddha Śākyamuni."
For those who have no refuge, the Buddha provides a refuge;
for those who are terrified, the Buddha is able to comfort and dispel their fear.
As the Buddha has taught me, I shall reverently practice accordingly.
At that time, the transformed person proceeded along the road, walking ahead of him.
The mother-killer followed closely behind,
thinking, "Just as he repents his transgression, so shall I do."
"My transgression is slight, while that person's is extremely grave.
The transformed man went to the Buddha, prostrated himself upon the ground,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes, World-Honored One.
I have committed a great transgression by harming my parents;
I have incurred this grave offense."
The Buddha said to the transformed person:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have been most sincere and without deception; your words and actions correspond with one another as you approach before the Tathāgata."
One's speech is sincere;
one does not engage in double-tongued talk,
nor does one harm oneself.
One should personally examine the nature of the mind:
by what state of mind does one endanger one's two parents?
Is it by means of the past mind, the future mind, or the present mind?
That past mind has already ceased.
The present mind departs immediately;
it has no location and no direction.
I do not know where it dwells.
As for the future mind,
that has not yet arrived.
There is no place of accumulation;
no returning has been seen,
nor is there any coming or going.
You should know this:
the mind does not abide within the body,
nor does it arise from without, nor does it possess any objective realm.
He does not abide in the two extremes, nor can he be found in the middle; as this passage is extensive, it cannot be recorded in full. The transformed person sighed, saying:
"It is unprecedented!
The Tathāgata has attained supreme perfect enlightenment."
One understands that the dharma-realm has no agent,
nor is there any recipient, no one who is born,
and no one who attains parinirvāṇa.
Having no one to rely upon,
he wished to leave the household life;
through the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he was able to become a śramaṇa.
He received full ordination.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikṣu."
At that time, the transformed person appeared before him as a śramaṇa and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One."
"I have attained supernatural powers and now wish to enter parinirvāṇa.
Through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, that transformed person was raised forty-nine feet above the ground,
and there in mid-air he entered parinirvāṇa.
Fire issued from within his body and burned his own frame;
the wayward son saw this.

"That man became a śramaṇa and immediately attained nirvāṇa;

He went to where the Buddha was,

Being of utmost sincerity and free from any deception,

Thereupon, the fires of the Hell of the Rebellious issued forth from the pores of his body.

"I am now being consumed by fire;

When placed upon a person's head,

With various marks and signs of excellence,
his bodily pains were stilled,
and he attained peace and security.
Again, he addressed the Buddha,

the Buddha immediately granted his permission.
He immediately ordained him as a renunciant and taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; the man heard it.
Distant from dust and free from defilement, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye;
practicing according to the teachings of the Dharma,
he reached the stage of "returning" (anāgāmin).
Having realized arhatship,
he further addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I wish to enter parinirvāṇa."
The Buddha said, "As you wish.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu leaped into the air to a height of four zhang and nine chi above the ground.
He himself emitted fire from his body,
which returned to burn his own form; meanwhile,
hundreds of thousands of devas and humans were in the midst of the void.
They came to make offerings.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata has bestowed the grace of the Vinaya as he has taught it."
Thus, those who go against the current are enabled to cross over;
only the Tathāgata and the great Bodhisattvas can perceive the fundamental source of all living beings.
He followed and delivered them;
this is not the realm of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Sutra on the Original Purity of the Mind that Emerges*.

25. The Buddha’s Discourse on Past Deeds Regarding the Ordination of a Poor Elderly Monk Who Was on the Verge of Death; The Twenty-Fifth [Chapter]: Śrāvastī. Śrāvastī.
There was an impoverished old man,
over two hundred years of age,
whose eyebrows grew with fine hair and whose ears protruded from his head.
His teeth were like even shells;
his hands extended past his knees;
and when one looked at his appearance, it seemed as though he possessed the marks of a great man.
Yet they were impoverished and suffering;
their clothing did not cover their bodies, leaving their five limbs bare,

The husband spoke in a loud voice, saying,

Desiring to inquire about transgressions and blessings,

With no way forward or backward,

The Buddha said:

In a previous life, you were born into the family of a wise and sagacious king of a powerful and great nation;

Proud and noble beyond the ordinary,

Using this, they act with unrestrained arrogance toward others,

Though their wealth and treasures amount to hundreds of millions, these are all the property of the people.
The common people were impoverished and all lived by means of taxation and corvée;

At that time, there was a humble śramaṇa.
His name is Jingzhi (Śāntamati).
Having come from a distant land,
he has therefore come to your presence with but few requests.
"It is merely a Dharma robe;
you should certainly not touch it.
It is extremely foul."
Since he would neither accept the robe nor take food,
and furthermore refused to allow him to sit empty-handed before departing, [the monk] went away.
For seven days and nights,
he was deprived of water and food,
yet he showed signs of life.
He was filled with great joy;
he gathered the multitude to behold it,
regarding it as the ultimate delight.

"The śramaṇa is compassionate and respectful;
his virtue and wisdom are fully perfected within."
Freezing him does not make him cold;

Since you have not granted it,

I beg you to let him go.
"Do not incur this transgression.

"Let us try to distress him slightly;

When the bandits saw the Prince, they all bowed their heads in repentance and apologized for their offenses.
They released the śramaṇas and let them go.
At that time, the śramaṇas were none other than Maitreya.
Therefore, you, O Minister, must now undergo this retribution of poverty;
it is because of your stinginess and greed.
This is why Changshou saved the life of the śramaṇa; thus, offenses and blessings correspond to one another like shadows and echoes.
The husband said,
"I have finished with my affairs;
I wish for them to conclude now."
I beg that my life, which is like one about to sink,
may be granted so that I may become a śramaṇa;
thereafter, in birth after birth throughout all future lives, may I always attend by the Buddha’s side.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
At that moment, the old man's beard and hair fell to the ground."
With the Dharma robes upon his body,

he entered the gate of samādhi and praised the Buddha with verses.
Having paid homage, they withdrew.
In the past, when I was a beloved son, I did not recognize the principles of benevolence and righteousness;
arrogant and noble, I gave myself over to license. At that time, I was a great king.
Believing oneself to be free from both sin and merit, one thought this would ensure eternal security;

Having fallen through sin, one has again received blessings, and thus beholds the God among Gods.
Liberated from past transgressions, He enters the gateway of the Dharma at the end of his life;
Forever free from the mind of stinginess and greed, He eternally receives the root of wisdom.
In every lifetime he remains not far from the Buddha, Sustaining himself through ten thousand kalpas. —From the *Sutra on the Elder Escaping Poverty* (Chū-p’in-k’ung-lao-kung-ching).

26. A bhikṣu saw a srotāpanna who had formerly served as a *karmadāna* and was now receiving bitter retribution; out of fear of this, he attained the Way. (26) In the kingdom of Mathurā, there was a man.

and the bhikṣu applied himself with diligence in contemplation.
Having attained the fruit of srotāpanna,
through non-negligence, they are liberated from the fear of the evil realms and are reborn seven times in the heavens.

they will experience the joys of gods and humans,
and shall then enter nirvana.
Guptā perceived his intention,
and they entered the kingdom of Mathurā together;
proceeding on their almsround, they eventually arrived at the house of a caṇḍāla.

yet his body was afflicted with a foul disease.
"The entire body is being devoured by worms,

I had left the household life.

as he scratched himself, it made a noise.

"Go and enter the chamber of a candāla.

this present child is that very person.
They dragged the arhat out;
he has now been born in the station of a caṇḍāla,
receiving this retribution.
"A bhikṣu who practices with diligence out of fear [of saṃsāra] immediately attains the fruit of arhatship. (*A-yü-wáng-jīng*, Scroll 10, Section 27:

"The Two Bhikṣus Whose Practices Differed and Whose Rewards Were Also Different"). Twenty-seven: In the past, there were two bhikṣus whose practices differed and whose rewards were likewise different. There once were two bhikṣus.
Equal in their observance of the precepts and wisdom,
both attained the stage of Srotāpanna;
yet one bhikṣu subsisted solely on alms.
He used it for almsgiving,
providing meals for the community of bhikṣus and for the poor;
yet one bhikṣu merely sat in meditation, guarding himself.
This refers to those who practice begging and giving alms, saying:
"Why do you not sit in meditation?
You merely keep yourself empty and toil in vain."
A certain bhikṣu replied,
"Venerable sir,
the Buddha said:"
"One should also practice giving while being a bhikṣu;
otherwise, one will be poor in future lives.
Subsequently, both bhikṣus attained arhatship.
The son of the householder became a śramaṇa.
Having practiced begging in previous lives,
he has now attained self-restraint among the multitude.
He personally provided them with food and clothing every day.
That one bhikṣu, who in his previous life had merely looked after himself alone,
has now become the son of a maidservant.
Having become a śramaṇa and begging for alms,
there is no one who gives;
because one is constantly suffering from great hunger and thirst, one should maintain the precepts and practice giving.
"One should not remain self-contained. This appears in the third fascicle of the *Daśādhyāya-avadāna-sūtra* (譬喻經). 28.

A Śramaṇa Sitting Beneath a Tree Whose Greedy Thoughts Were Not Eliminated Attains Arhatship through the Buddha’s Emanation Preaching the Dharma. The Buddha manifested an emanation body to preach the Dharma, whereby [the śramaṇa] attained the path of an arhat.

though his body remained still, his mind roamed about without a moment’s rest.

however, the tortoise withdrew its head, tail, and four legs,

This enables the water-dogs to find no advantage.

23. A practitioner of the Way converted a hunter. 24. 1. Elīśa, a member of the four castes, was stingy and greedy; he was converted by Śakra, Lord of the Devas.

(Elīśa, a member of the four castes, was stingy and greedy; he was converted by Śakra, Lord of the Devas. 1. (Note: The repetition "Elīśa, a member of the four castes, was stingy and greedy; he was converted by Śakra, Lord of the Devas" appears twice in the source text.)
In the past, there was a person of the four castes named Elisa,
whose wealth was beyond measure.
He was stingy with his food and clothing.
There lived a poor old man nearby.
Every day he indulged himself,
consuming food, drink, fish, and meat,
with guests never ceasing to arrive.
The four castes thought to themselves,
"Our wealth is immeasurable, yet we are no match for this old man.
They then killed a chicken.

placed it upon his carriage, and traveled to a secluded place.

The Heavenly Lord transformed himself into a dog and came;
he looked up and down at him and spoke to the dog, saying:
"If you hang yourself upside down in mid-air,
shall I give it to you? The dog then immediately hung itself upside down in mid-air.
The four castes were seized with great terror and said,
"If you let your eyes fall to the ground, shall we not give them to you?
The dog's two eyes fell to the ground.
The four castes then departed.
The Lord of Devas transformed himself into the bodies of the four castes and,
riding in a carriage back to his home, gave these instructions.
A stranger falsely claiming to be of the four castes was driven away and beaten.
When a member of the four castes returned late, [he encountered them].
The disciples reviled him and drove him away.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, took all his wealth and gave it away as great alms.
Thus, the four castes were likewise unable to return.
When his wealth was completely exhausted, he went mad.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, assumed the form of a man and asked him, "Why are you grieving? He replied:
"My wealth and possessions are completely exhausted.
The Lord of Devas said, "Indeed,
the possession of precious treasures causes a person much anxiety."
Those who amass wealth without a fixed purpose for the five families and do not practice giving will become hungry ghosts after death,
perpetually lacking food and clothing.
Even if you are released from this state and become human,
you will always fall into low and base conditions;
you fail to perceive impermanence.
Though wealthy, he was miserly;
being greedily stingy, he would not eat.
What did he hope for?
The Heavenly Emperor expounded the Four Noble Truths for them;
the four castes attained understanding in their minds.
Thereupon, the Heavenly Emperor transformed himself and departed.
The four castes returned and repented of their former thoughts;
they gave with all their hearts until their wealth was exhausted, and thereby attained the Way. Excerpted from the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Five.

Having thus sent away the visiting brahmin, she said:
Just as he was about to depart,
he spoke this verse: "Having no kin,
you wander to other lands, deceiving the people of the world."
Coarse food is the constant rule; why then do you find fault with eating?
Now I give you this verse.
If he is angry and finds fault with the poor quality of the food at that time:
Then, standing at his side with his back turned, he recited it in a low voice so that the other could hear it.
Having given these instructions, he—
He then returned to his own country.
After Yaśodatta had sent his master away, [he remained].
Every time it was mealtime,
he would again become angry;
his wife then attempted to recite that verse in his presence.
When the husband heard these verses, his heart immediately became displeased,
and he thought to himself:
"Alas, this old woman!"
He exposed my private affairs;
from that time forward, he always spoke with gentle words,
fearing that his wife might tell others of his secrets.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī,
there was a brahmin named Bhāradvāja."
Could this have been anyone else?
It was none other than myself.
As for that slave named Karaha at that time—
This is the bhikṣu Cchanda here now. At that time,
he already relied upon me to treat others with contempt.
Now it is likewise so;
relying on my own power, they treat others with contempt. (From the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume Eight).

8. The Two Mahallakas Living Together in Harmony and Marriage: The Buddha Speaks of Their Past Deeds. The Two Mahallakas Living Together in Harmony and Marriage: The Buddha Speaks of Their Past Deeds. Section Eight. In the city of Śrāvastī, there were two mahallakas.
They both abandoned their wives and children to leave the household life and pursue the Way.
After traveling extensively among the people for a long time,
they returned together to Śrāvastī.
They lived together in one room,
each reflecting on his own thoughts:
he wished to return home for a moment to see his wife and children.
He immediately arrived at his own home.
When his wife saw him, she spoke with anger, saying, "You man of meager virtue and no auspicious marks! Why did you abandon your home to study the Way?"
"The girl has grown up and cannot be married off;
now we shall use her to break your leg.
At that time, the junior mahallaka—
He immediately returned to his room, filled with sorrow and distress.
At that time, the Great Mahallaka was also driven out;
they returned together to the room.
He asked his small companion,
"Why are you so sorrowful and distressed?
The companion replied:
"Why need you ask? He asked again, "We two— "
Though we dwell in the same room,
we do not know each other's good or evil deeds,
nor does he speak of them to me.
"To whom else should I speak?
He then related the matter in detail.
At that time, the Great Mahallaka said:
"Why should this be a cause for grief?
My family is likewise.
Your son and my daughter may become a match for one another."
He replied, "So be it.
Then the young mahallaka returned and said to his wife,
"I have found a husband for our daughter."
The wife replied, "Very well.
The elder brother returned and informed his wife, saying:
I have found a wife for my son.
He asked, "Who is she? and I replied, "She is the daughter of such-and-such."
At that time, the two mahallakas entered into marriage;
each rejoiced as if a poor man had found treasure,
and they cherished and respected one another.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These two mahallakas did not only perform such deeds today;
in the past, in the kingdom of Kāśī,"
There was a brahmin who lived in Masaducchen for a long time; he boiled [grain],
but it would not cook.
His goods remained unsold.
Furthermore, there was a household that kept a single stubborn donkey;
even when it was offered for sale, it would not leave.
The bean-master thought to himself,
"I can now exchange these beans for that donkey.
He then went to speak with him.
The owner of the donkey thought again,
"I shall trade this ill-behaved donkey for those beans," and he replied, "So be it."
Everyone was filled with joy.
The owner of the beans recited this verse:
"The Dharma of the Brahmins is skilled at trade; For sixteen kalpas, these dusty ice-beans have been stored."
"Though you exhaust all your firewood, it will not cook; only then shall I break the teeth of everyone in your household, large and small.
At that time, the owner of the donkey again composed a verse, saying:

O Brahmin, what do you find so pleasing? Though he has four legs, possesses fine woolly hair, and is capable of carrying heavy loads over long distances—let this make you understand: when pricked by a needle or burned by fire, he remains utterly unmoving.
At that time, [the Buddha] addressed the Lord of Beans.
Again, he spoke in verse:
A single-stemmed staff of a thousand years’ growth, With a four-inch spike at its head, can subdue a donkey of depraved nature; Why worry that it cannot be cured?
Then the donkey said to its master,
speaking again in verse:
"Planting down the two front feet, Fly up with both hind hooves."
I shall break off your front teeth; only then will you know for yourself.
The Master of Beans also called the donkey "Verse" (頌), saying:
When gadflies, mosquitoes, and venomous insects sting me, I rely solely on my tail to defend myself.
I shall cut off your tail and make you know the bitterness of hardship.
The donkey replied again:
"From my ancestors until now, we have practiced this stubborn way;
now that I have inherited and followed it, I shall die rather than ever abandon it.
At that time, the Lord of Māṣa...
Knowing that he was wicked and could not be addressed with harsh words, [the Buddha] then praised him in verse, saying:
"Your voice is clear and resonant; your face is as white as jade or snow."
"I shall find a wife for you, and we shall roam together through the forests and marshes.
Hearing these affectionate words,
the donkey immediately spoke this verse:
"I can carry eight *shu* and travel six hundred *li* in a day;
O Brahmin, you should know that upon hearing this of my wife, my heart was filled with joy.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The two individuals at that time were the two mahallakas of today;
the donkey was [the third].

In the past, there was a Buddha named Jinsheng (Jin-jie-sheng).
He had two bhikṣus.
The first was named Ajita,
and the second was named Nityapramudita.
The bhikṣu Ajita possessed the six supernormal powers and the divine foot.
The bhikṣu Nityapramudita had not yet eliminated his fetters (saṃyojana).
There was a householder named Mahāprema.
The woman’s name was Shan-huan (Good Illusion).
She was peerlessly beautiful and served as the patron (*dānapati*) for these two bhikṣus.
The skillful illusory wife made offerings to Ajita;
she managed every matter without deficiency,
yet she was always joyful, though her own resources were extremely meager.
The monk Saṃgharakṣita constantly gave rise to jealousy and slander, saying:
"The bhikṣu Aniruddha has consorted with a skilled illusionist;
he receives offerings only because of his own affection."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Do you know who Constant Joy is?
It is none other than myself."
The woman skilled in illusion was none other than the Brahmin girl Cañcā;
it was she who at that time slandered the Arhat Aniruddha.
Having remained in hell for countless thousands of years,
although she has now attained Buddhahood, due to the lingering residue of her past karma,
the young girl with many tongues dances upon a wooden basin and causes her abdomen to swell.
He came before me and said,
"Śramaṇa, why do you not speak of household matters,
but instead speak of other things?"
"You now enjoy yourself alone, unaware of my suffering.
Previously, when we were together and I was pregnant,
you required ghee and oil for the sake of the impending month."
"Whatever you have raised for your young child,
you must give it all to me.
At that time, the entire assembly lowered their heads and remained silent.
Śakra Devānām Indra was attending behind the Buddha, fanning him;
he transformed himself into a mouse and entered into the lining of his robe.
The wooden bowl fell to the ground.

At that time, the disciples of the fourfold assembly and the six heretical teachers raised their voices in celebration and rejoiced immeasurably, all shouting in unison: [They said: "The Buddha’s bowl has fallen to the ground! This is truly a great marvel! They laughed heartily and cried out in derision.
"You are an object deserving of death for your act of slandering the Unsurpassed, Right,
and True [Dharma]. This ground is ignorant."
It was able to contain such an evil thing.
The earth then split asunder and fierce flames surged forth;
the woman immediately fell into the great niraya hell.
When the great assembly saw this,
King Ajātaśatru was so terrified that his hair stood on end;
he immediately rose and said:
"Where is this woman now?
The Buddha replied,
"Great King."
"The place where this woman has fallen is named Avīci Niraya.
The king asked the Buddha again.
"This woman did not commit killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, or lying,
yet she has fallen into Avīci," the Buddha said to the Great King.
"The Dharma I teach involves superior,
middling, and inferior modes of conduct of body, speech, and mind.
The King then questioned the Buddha further.
What constitutes the superior, what the middling,
and what the inferior?
The Buddha said to King Ajātaśatru:
"Mental action is the most serious;
verbal action is intermediate."
From the *Xingqixing jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Conduct), Scroll Lower, Section 10:
"The Causes and Conditions for Rebirth in Heaven through Firm Adherence to the Precepts. In the Kingdom of Kośala, there were two bhikṣus.
One person had violated the precepts, while the other upheld them;
they both wished to go together to see the Buddha.
While on the road, they encountered water containing insects.
One who had broken the precepts said to one who maintained the precepts,
"We may drink this water together."
The observer of the precepts said,
"There are insects in the water;
how can it be drunk?"
The transgressor said:
"If I do not drink, I shall die;
I will not be able to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or [meet] the Saṃgha."
The one who maintains the precepts does not drink even unto death.
At that time, the one who violates the precepts drinks.
The one who maintains the precepts dies because he does not drink.
He was immediately reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
where he obtained a complete celestial body.
He went first to the place where the Buddha was and prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet.
Standing to one side,
the Buddha taught him various dharmas, whereby he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
He immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
"I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṃgha.
For as long as life lasts, I am an upāsaka.
After the Buddha had further preached the Dharma for him, he remained silent.
When the deva had finished prostrating before the Buddha,
he suddenly vanished. Subsequently,
the one who had been drinking water arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
While the Buddha was surrounded by an immeasurable multitude preaching the Dharma, he saw the bhikṣu approaching.
The Buddha immediately opened his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and revealed his golden-hued hand.
"You foolish person who wishes to see my physical body—
would it not be better for you to first see my Dharma-body by upholding the precepts?"
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"With a mind that does not observe well, one sees without discernment;
foolish like a moth leaping into a flame, one greedily gazes upon my body."
The physical body is nothing but impurity; what is there for you to desire to see?
Within it are fat, blood, and flesh, covered on the outside by a thin skin.
Yet, being consumed by thirst, it still practices the precepts with reverence.
"Until death, they shall protect my teaching; they see me, not you.
Having spoken this verse, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus.
From now on, it is not permitted to travel without carrying a water-strainer;
if one does not carry one, one commits an offense.
There is no offense if there is clear, flowing water.
Whether it be a great river or a spring,
if one travels from this monastery to that monastery within a distance of twenty *li*, there is no offense; this is from the third fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-saṃyukta*.

11. Pūrṇamanoratha Questions the Hungry Ghost Regarding the Length of Time His Husband Has Been in the City, and the Response Concerning the Sevenfold Rise and Fall of the Riverbank; [Section] Eleven: Kāla Country. Pūrṇamanoratha questioned the hungry ghost concerning how long his husband had been in the city, and received an answer regarding the sevenfold destruction and formation of the riverbank. [Section] Eleven: Kāla Country.
At that time, there was a hungry ghost standing leaning against the city gate.
The bhikṣu Pūrṇamanaḥ asked the hungry ghost:
"What do you seek here now?
The ghost said,
"Do you see me now?"
The bhikṣu said, "I have seen him.
The ghost said,
"My husband entered the city and has not yet returned."
Therefore, I have established this here merely to wait for her husband to emerge.
The bhikṣu asked:
"What does your husband seek when he enters the city?"
Then the ghost replied,
"In this city there is a great elder who has suffered from a carbuncle for a long time."
"Today it shall burst open;
thick blood will flow and overflow.
This man has been carrying it all along."
The two of them ate together to sustain their lives.
The bhikṣu asked again,
"How much time has passed since your husband entered the city?"
The city walls were close to the rivers.
He pointed his finger at the city and said to the bhikṣu:
Since this city was first established on both its eastern and western banks,
this is now the seventh time it has been rebuilt.
My husband has been inside the city for as long as that.

The Bhikṣu Who Mistook One Another for Ghosts at Night. In a mountain range there was a Buddhist monastery (*buddhāyatana*). The horse said to its offspring:
"You must be careful not to harbor such thoughts as to envy that parched barley.
Before long, you shall witness the proof for yourselves."
As the time for the seasonal festival drew near and the New Year was about to arrive,
every household bound a pig and cast it into a cauldron of boiling water;
it let out a loud, wailing cry.
The mare said to her foals,
"Do you remember the parched barley?
If you wish for proof, you may go and look for it."
When the young colts realized this with certainty,
they finally understood the nuances of being trained and guided;
even while grazing on grass, they encountered barley.
He protected it and did not eat it.
The Buddha spoke this verse:
"The plantain perishes because of its fruit; The bamboo and the reed are likewise."

Devadatta was wicked and dangerous;
he recklessly offered praise and admiration.
The bhikṣu Kokālika likewise extolled Devadatta.
Devadatta likewise reviled Kokālika.
Those two men were devoid of righteousness and reason.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they [reported it].
"Indeed, O Great Sage,
observe the bhikṣu Kokālika,
who for a long time has relied upon and depended on the authentic scriptures, the Vinaya, and the teachings of the Dharma."
Having left the household life out of faith,
he indiscriminately praised Devadatta;
Devadatta, in turn, extolled Kokālika.
They take what is not right to be right,
and what is right to be wrong.
The Buddha said:
These people are foolish and ignorant;
they were likewise so in their previous lives.
During past ages, it was the same.
When the eunuch passed away, he was discarded among the *chū* trees;
at that time, insects, foxes, crows, and birds came together to devour his flesh,
praising one another.
The bird said:
"Your body is like a lion; your head is like that of a seer or a deer-king.
How excellent! You are like a beautiful flower."
The Gū-hu (Ox-Fox) praised him, saying:
"Only the Honored One dwells upon the tree; His wisdom is foremost, most supreme, Brilliantly illuminating the ten directions, Like a mass of purple-polished gold."
Thus they went back and forth.
Then the Great Seer said, "You have praised me in vain; there is no reality in what you say."
The *Gū-hu* (poisonous fox) was Devadatta;
the bird was Kokālika; and the seer was the Bodhisattva.
This is from the *Buddha-spoken Gū-hu-āo-jīng* (*Buddhabhāṣita-gūhu-bird-sūtra*).

5. Devadatta approached the Buddha to request the community of followers, but failing to obtain them, he instead lost his own circle of kinsmen and followers. This is the fifth instance concerning Devadatta.
He went to where the World-Honored One was,
prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
As I observe the Tathāgata,
his complexion has changed and his faculties have matured;
he has passed beyond youth and vigor, and is now approaching decay and decrepitude.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will close his private chamber and delight himself in meditative concentration;
I wish for the fourfold assembly to be entrusted with the transmission.
"I shall instruct and admonish you no differently than the Buddha;
at all times, I shall provide the four requisites for your support without fail.
The Buddha said:
"Alas, you foolish man!
You do not consider the calamities that will follow.
[Even] the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—"
Since [the teaching] is not even entrusted to those [already mentioned], how much less could it be bestowed upon a person as indolent and depraved as you?
It must be transmitted to the Noble Assembly.
Devadatta felt envy and jealousy arise within him;
upon hearing the World-Honored One’s words,
his anger redoubled.
Today the Tathāgata has praised the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana,
yet he treats his minor disciples with contempt;
we must certainly seek an opportunity to bring about the destruction of the Master and his followers.
"May the sentient beings within this realm neither behold his form nor hear his voice.
At that time, the bhikṣu Devadatta rose from his seat,
prostrated at [the Buddha's] feet, and withdrew.
Everywhere they were restless and agitated, using clever words and false rhetoric to deceive worldly people;
having enticed dozens of followers, they exhorted one another at every turn.
To state the essentials:
while the Buddha was preaching the Dharma surrounded by a great assembly,
Devadatta addressed his own disciples, saying:
"Do not listen to what Gautama says; it does not accord with the True Dharma.
I have various profound sutras and excellent meanings;
I shall teach them to you."
He sought only through expedient means to destroy the noble assembly.
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop, Devadatta!"
Be careful not to give rise to thoughts that would disrupt the Sangha of the Noble Ones;
later you will undergo retribution whose pain will be difficult to endure.
Devadatta was stubborn and would not change, for his intent was set upon [wrongdoing].
The Buddha contemplated the past causes and conditions and their karmic retributions, knowing that they could not be averted.
Devadatta was leading five hundred disciples,
and the Tathāgata was likewise leading five hundred disciples.
They traveled together to the side of Mount Ratnākara.
The Bodhisattva’s disciples were broad-minded, benevolent, and gentle;
he instructed them with the True Dharma.
In practicing the precepts, his every movement— whether entering or exiting, advancing or halting— never transgressed its proper order. In contrast,
the followers of Devadatta spoke with coarse and vulgar language,
and anger would invariably arise whenever they spoke.
He spoke to his disciples as if they were enemies in a quarrel or a lawsuit;
the disciples grew weary and distressed, and all together abandoned him to go instead to the Bodhisattva.
He also claimed for himself, saying,
"I have a thousand disciples who are fully endowed with all virtues."
He was so far removed from the world that no one could equal him.
Devadatta, filled with rage,
immediately made a vow.
"This man today has enticed my disciples and ruined my followers;
even if he should attain Buddhahood, I shall still destroy his assembly."
It is no different now.
The Tathāgata perceives and knows that Devadatta will certainly destroy the noble Saṃgha; of this there is no doubt.
The Tathāgata then rose from his seat and departed from the assembly for five reasons.
One knows that one cannot cause dissension within the Sangha for four reasons:
first, because the Tathāgata is before one's eyes;
second, because the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power does not abandon his original vow.
Second, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa,
suppose there were someone who said:
"I have now attained Buddhahood and reached supreme perfect enlightenment."
You should ask him: "Where were you when Śākyamuni Buddha was in the world?
Third, there has never been such a time of evil.
Fourth, the bhikṣus do not compete for gain and offerings.
Fifth, the disciples of wisdom and supernormal powers are in harmony.
Thus does the Tathāgata observe with his knowledge of past lives.
Knowing for certain that Devadatta would bring about the schism and disruption of the Saṃgha,
the Tathāgata immediately departed.
Devadatta remained behind and preached the Dharma to the assembly.
If there are sentient beings who serve me as their honored teacher and receive my instructions and precepts, they should practice five dharmas.
(The text of these five dharmas is extensive and not recorded here. Any bhikṣus who cultivate these five dharmas [shall attain success].
"Having already attained liberation, exhausted all out-flows (āsrava), and become free from out-flows (anāsrava),
why should we rely on the eightfold upright conduct of Gautama?
He then spoke to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
"I have attained the great benefit of becoming the Honored One of the Three Realms, the Tathāgata.
He then addressed Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"I suffer from back pain and wish to rest for a short while."
"You two, together with the noble assembly, should preach the Dharma.
Devadatta lay on his right side, wishing to sleep;
the devas forced him onto his left side. The devas were further weary of his deceitful speech and snoring, which manifested outwardly as a foul stench that reached far and wide.
By means of his supernormal powers,
Maudgalyāyana soared through the void and performed the eighteen transformations;
he sat, lay down, walked, emerged, and submerged with complete ease and mastery.
Śāriputra addressed the assembly:
"The physical and spiritual virtues of the Tathāgata are immeasurable;
he is fully endowed with all-encompassing wisdom."
It reaches forward to infinity and reaches back to the ultimate limit.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata yields the fruit of happiness in the present life and is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is what the wise cultivate and study;
it is not the practice of the foolish.
Such is the noble assembly of the Tathāgata.
The fivefold Dharma-body is fully perfected;
it is worthy of reverence and esteem, and should be served and honored.
It serves as a field of merit for the well-being and benefit of all sentient beings.
At that time, the bhikṣus each gave rise to this thought:
"We have been foolish and deluded, failing to recognize what is true and correct.
We have abandoned the real for the ornamental, forsaking the root to pursue the branches."
"Beholding now what these two worthies have said, it is rare indeed in this world.
Would it not be most delightful for us to abandon this Devadatta and join the assembly of the Tathāgata?"
Śāriputra, knowing their thoughts,
immediately rose from his seat;
five hundred bhikṣus likewise followed him.
Maudgalyāyana followed behind him.
The bhikṣu Kokālika then stepped on Devadatta with his right foot and said:
"You wicked Devadatta, why do you indulge in sleep?
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have taken all of your disciples away."

Upon waking from his sleep, Devadatta was filled with profound sorrow and distress. He went out and questioned the Buddha regarding his facial complexion; this account is roughly the same as that found in the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya.
6. Devadatta’s Former Life as a Wild Fox. Long ago, in times past, Devadatta’s former life was that of a wild fox. Six. Long ago, in times past...
There was a māṇava— translated into Chinese as a "seer"— who was reciting the Kṣatriya scriptures within a mountain cave.
A wild fox approached his side and listened intently to the recitation, gaining an understanding of its meaning.
He thought to himself:
"According to my understanding of the words in this letter,
it is sufficient to make me the king among all beasts."
He then set out on his travels and encountered a gaunt wild fox,
which he immediately intended to kill.
He asked, "Why do you kill me?
and [the lion] replied,
"I am the king of beasts."
"You do not submit to me.
He replied, "I pray that you will not kill me."
"I shall follow you.
Thereupon, the two foxes traveled together,
and they encountered another fox.
The questions and answers were as above.
In this manner, they successively subdued all the foxes,
and then used the pack of subdued foxes to subdue all the elephants.
Furthermore, he used various elephants to subdue all tigers;
he then used various tigers to subdue all lions,
and thus he was temporarily able to act as the king among beasts.
Again, he thought to himself:
"I am the king of beasts;
it is not fitting that I should take a beast as my wife."
He then mounted a white elephant and caused a multitude of wild beasts to surround the kingdom of Kāśī for several hundred thousand circuits.
The king dispatched a messenger to inquire,
"For what reason is it thus?
The wild fox replied:
"I am the king of beasts.
You ought to give me your daughter; if you do not, I shall destroy your kingdom."
The envoy returned and reported to the king.
The king assembled his ministers for consultation,
with the exception of one minister alone.
Everyone said, "It should be given.
The kingdom relies solely upon its elephants and horses;
we have elephants and horses, while they have lions.
When elephants and horses catch their scent, they crouch in terror upon the ground;
in battle, they will surely be defeated.
Why begrudge a single woman and lose an entire kingdom?
At that time, a certain great minister, sharp-witted and possessed of far-reaching strategic insight,
addressed the king, saying:
"In my observation of the past and present, I have never heard of nor seen it that the daughter of a human king should consort with a lowly beast."
"Though I am weak and dull-witted,
I shall certainly kill this fox so that the other beasts scatter and flee.
The King then questioned him.
The minister replied,
"Your Majesty, simply dispatch a messenger to set a date for the day of battle and request one boon from him."
He intended to have the lion fight first and roar afterward;
he thought that if he were afraid, the lion would surely roar first and fight afterward.
When the day of battle arrived, the king...
"You must order everyone within the city to plug their ears.
The king followed his advice and then set out with his army.
Just as the battle lines were about to engage, [the sound occurred].
The wild fox tried to make the lion roar first;
upon hearing this, its heart split into seven pieces,
and it fell from atop the elephant to the ground.
The herd of beasts scattered and fled.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"The wild fox’s arrogance is rampant; He seeks to gather his own retinue."
Having traveled to the city of Kāśī, he proclaimed himself the King of Beasts;
likewise, those who are arrogant among men act in this way.
Manifesting as one who leads a multitude, he dwells in the kingdom of Magadha, calling himself the Lord of Dharma.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"At that time, King Kāśī was I;
the wise and sharp minister was Śāriputra."
The Wild Fox King was Devadatta; the account of his seeking the kingship among wild foxes appears in the fourth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
7. Devadatta’s Attempt to Violate Gopikā and His Descent into Hell. Section Seven: Devadatta was in Rājagṛha.
He conceived a malicious intent to cause harm.
Later, when the matter was exposed, King Ajātaśatru...
He said to Devadatta,
"It would be best for you to leave this country and not remain here;
there is no one among the sixteen great nations who does not know of this."
Devadatta committed evil acts directed toward the Tathāgata;
having heard of this, he harbored grief and distress within his heart,
and returned to his native land, bound by the fetters of resentment.
He abruptly entered the Bodhisattva’s inner quarters and said to Gopī,
"I wish to appoint you as my first lady."
"I wonder, Noble Lady, would it be acceptable? Gopī replied,
"I wish to take hold of your right hand."
Devadatta extended his hand to seize him by the neck;
the bones of Devadatta’s wrist shattered and blood flowed from his five fingers.
At that moment, he became dazed and unconscious, regaining consciousness only after a long while.
At that time, Devadatta proceeded further into the palace and sat upon the Bodhisattva’s bed;
when the palace women saw him, they seized him and threw him down from the bed.
His left hip was immediately injured such that he could no longer walk;
he was carried back to his own house.
All the Śākyas were indignant and came to inform him.
"You should now go to the Buddha and repent.
Upon hearing this, Devadatta privately devised a crafty deception.
He secretly fashioned iron claws and smeared them with poisonous venom;
his outward appearance was gentle and mild, yet within he harbored malice and rage.
At that time, Devadatta recalled what the Buddha had said:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama constantly declares this:
'One who possesses a body but has no sores will not be harmed by poison.'"
Poison is powerless against a scab;
there is no evil, nor anything created.
I shall now go there and feign repentance.
He clawed and tore at his own feet with his nails;
as the poisonous vapors overflowed, he was certain to die of himself.
Then the people carried him on a litter to visit the World-Honored One.
Having descended thirty-seven *ren*, he said to those around him, "Lower me to the ground; I wish to go on foot.
He then immediately descended to the ground.
At that time, a fierce fire boiled up and enveloped his body.
This concludes the *Sūtra on Devadatta Entering Hell Alive*. 8.

Devadatta’s Former Life as a Jackal Who Lost His Life by Breaking a Jar. When the Eight Buddhas were residing in Rājagṛha, Devadatta was formerly a jackal who lost his life by breaking a jar. When the Eight Buddhas were residing in Rājagṛha...
At that time, Devadatta sought to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha;
though the bhikṣus admonished him three times, he still did not desist.
The Buddha said:
"In a past age, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī."
There was a brahmin who constructed a charitable well in the wilderness to provide for travelers.
The sun was already setting.
A pack of jackals came to drink the remaining water.
There was a king of the jackals who did not drink the water from the ground.
He then thrust his head into the jar to drink the water;
having drunk, he lifted the jar high and dashed it to pieces.
Although the various jackals tried to speak kindly to him, he would not accept their words.
In this manner, he broke fourteen jars one after another.
At that time, the brahmin observed the jackal and consequently fashioned wooden jars so sturdy they were difficult to break.
It was easy to enter but difficult to emerge; he remained by the well, grasping his staff and waiting.
A pack of jackals gathered there.
The king, as before, finished drinking;
he struck it against the ground but could not break it.
Then the brahmin took up his staff and came out.
The jackal that was beaten to death at that time is now Devadatta.
The pack of jackals at that time are now these bhikṣus who admonished Devadatta; this is recorded in the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. 9.
Devadatta Formerly as a Monkey Attempts to Retrieve the Moon from a Well: When the nine Buddhas resided in Rājagṛha, Devadatta was formerly a monkey who attempted to retrieve the moon from a well.
At that time, the bhikṣus performed the formal act of censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) against Devadatta;
the group of six bhikṣus then associated with Devadatta, sharing his speech and his views.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, in a secluded place..."
There were five hundred monkeys wandering in a forest who came upon a nyagrodha tree.
Beneath the tree was a well, and in the well there was the reflection of the moon.
At that time, the monkey king saw this reflection of the moon and said to his companions,
"The moon has now died and fallen; it is right here in the well."
"We must all work together to bring him out; let us not leave the world in the long night of darkness.
They deliberated together, saying, "How can we get him out?
Then the monkey king said:
"I know the way out.
You must grasp my tail while I grasp a tree branch;
by holding onto one another in succession, we shall be able to escape."
Then the monkeys followed the king’s words;
as they grasped one another in succession, before the last had reached the water,
the weight of the monkeys caused the weak branch of the tree to snap, and all the monkeys fell into the well.
The monkey king at that time was none other than Devadatta; as for the other monkeys of that time, they were [the present ones].
The present account of the six groups of bhikṣus is from the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
10. Devadatta’s Previous Life Killing a Golden Lion. Devadatta’s Previous Life Killing a Golden Lion. Ten. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
If there are sentient beings who give rise to a single evil thought toward the Buddhas of the three periods of time,
or toward pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and those who are shramanas wearing dyed robes.
One incurs immeasurable transgression.
Why is this? Because dyed robes are the insignia of the noble ones and the sages.
If one can resolve to generate a mind of reverence for those who wear dyed robes,
the merit obtained will be immeasurable.
It was through my own faith and veneration that I attained Buddhahood.
Ānanda said: "What was the nature of that act performed long ago with a heart of reverence?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a great kingdom in this Jambudvīpa; according to the *Bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness), the king of Vārāṇasī was named Ti-pi and ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kings.
In a world where the Buddha-dharma did not exist,
there was a pratyekabuddha dwelling among the mountains, practicing meditation and cultivating the Path.
At that time, all the wild beasts came to him in submission and affection.
There was a lion named Kālapin, which in the language of Liang means "Firm Vow"; his body was golden in color, and its radiant marks were brilliantly resplendent.
He ate fruits and chewed grass, never harming any living beings.
At that time, there was a hunter who shaved his head and donned the *kāṣāya*.
Wearing a bow and arrows at his waist, he was traveling through a marsh when he saw a lion sleeping.

The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states that [the lion] licked the bhikṣu’s feet, whereupon he shot it with a poisoned arrow. The lion woke up in alarm and was about to charge and harm him, but seeing that he was wearing the kāṣāya, it thought to itself: "This one in dyed robes bears the outward mark of a virtuous person."
"If I were to harm him,
I would be harboring an evil mind toward the noble sages;
thus, my thoughts ceased."
With the poison of the arrow circulating within him, his life was not long for him to remain;
