The son replied:
"I shall now follow this man of the Way as my guide, whether for good or for ill.
The Buddha then led him to the Jeta Grove,
where he beheld the majestic deportment and the disciplined regulations of the bhikṣus.
His mind was deeply delighted by this,
and he addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I wish to request ordination as a bhikṣu."
The Buddha immediately granted his consent;
he stroked the man’s head with his hand,
whereupon his hair fell away of its own accord and the *kāṣāya* robe was established upon his body.
Named Sūda, he maintained the precepts with diligence and his mind was free from indolence;
after seven days had passed, he attained the path of Arhatship.
The Buddha said to Sūta,
"You should go and convert King Caṇḍa.
Sūta then went there.
The king said, "My heart is filled with great anxiety; what should I do?
The practitioner replied:
"What is there to worry about?
The king said,
"I am already advanced in years."
As his time passed without an heir, the king became filled with grief and anxiety.
When the practitioner heard the king’s words,
he did not respond at first, but merely smiled alone.
The king then spoke with indignation:
"I have been conversing with this man of the Way,
yet from the beginning he has not answered me."
Instead, he alone laughed.
[The King] then intended to kill him.
Sūdarśana perceived his intention.
He then rose lightly and flew upward, remaining suspended in mid-air;
he manifested his body in many forms and entered and exited without obstruction.
Upon witnessing this divine transformation, the king immediately repented and said:
I am truly ignorant and unable to distinguish the true from the false.
I only pray that you, Great Deity, will return once more,
so that I may take refuge in you.
Sudatta immediately descended from the air and stood before the king,
saying to him, "It would be most excellent if you could take refuge for yourself."
One should take refuge in the Buddha;
the Buddha is my teacher,
the Honored One of the three realms who delivers all sentient beings.
In the time it takes to stretch out an arm,
Sudatta led the king and the people together to the place where the Buddha was.
He took refuge in the Triple Gem and requested to receive the five precepts to become an upāsaka.
The Buddha explained it in detail: "Sudā was a prince."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words,
the king became even more terrified and could not restrain himself.
The Buddha said:
In the past, during the era of the Buddha Kūṣṭhila,
there was a king named Puṣyada.
All the people within his realm made offerings to the Triple Gem.
At that time, there was an ordinary man living in poverty with no means of livelihood.
He was constantly employed by the wealthy and noble of the kingdom to hire out his labor for herding several hundred oxen.
Seeing the king and the people making offerings to the community of bhikṣus,
he immediately asked, "What are you all doing?"
The people replied,
"We make offerings to the Triple Gem; thereafter,
we shall always abide in peace and happiness, honored and noble, free from toil and suffering."
He then thought to himself:
"I am poor; I can only boil cow's milk to make curd and butter.
Let it be for the sake of the pure-minded Bhikṣu Upāli."
The community of bhikṣus offered a prayer of blessing, saying:
"May you obtain merit in every lifetime;
thereafter, as you pass through the cycle of birth and death again and again,"
They immediately receive its blessings;
some are reborn above as devas,
while others are reborn below as kings or lords.
When the king went out on a hunting expedition,
he saw a fine cow carrying a calf and killed it.
The queen spoke to the king.
"Do not kill its calf.
At that time, the owner of the cow broke it open, took out the calf, and raised it.
The owner spoke in anger:
"May the King become like this ox.
Thereafter, his spirit became the king's son;
at that time, he had not yet been born.
The mother who was killed by the king was Sūta;
Sūta’s mother was the king’s consort at that time;
and the brahmin was Govinda.
He was born from within a *śūdra* cemetery;
half of his mother's body remained incorruptible,
and he was able to drink her breast milk.
As for his growing up to such a stature,
it was because in a previous life he had offered curd and clarified butter to the community of bhikṣus;
upon hearing this, the king’s mind was liberated.
The Sūtra on Attaining the Stage of Srotāpanna and Leaving the Kingdom of Caṇḍālava;
3. The Ordination of the Śrāmaṇera Cunda and the Causes and Conditions of His Previous Lives. Three Buddhas were in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra,
observing with his divine eye three times during the day and night,
would go forth to deliver whoever was ready for liberation.

At that time, there were merchants wishing to travel to another country. The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states that between the two countries of Māthura and [the other], there were five hundred merchants; these various traders took a dog with them—the *Bao'en jing* describes it as a white dog—and upon reaching the middle of their journey, they encountered [an event].
The merchants suddenly stopped, and the dog immediately stole the meat.
Thereupon, the people beat the dog together,
broke its leg, cast it away in the wilderness, and departed.
At that time, Śāriputra saw with his divine eye a dog hunched on the ground,
emaciated and on the verge of death from hunger;
he flew to where the dog was and bestowed food upon it as alms.
The dog was deeply delighted that its life had been saved.
At that time, Śāriputra immediately preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for this dog.
The dog then passed away and was reborn in a brahmin family in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Śāriputra...
He was walking alone on his almsround.
A brahmin saw him and asked, "Venerable sir, why do you walk alone? Do you have no śrāmaṇera?"
Śāriputra said, "I have no śrāmaṇera.
I have heard that you have a son."
"I shall give it upon seeing [you].
The brāhmaṇa said, "I have a son."
His name was Kuntī.
Since he was still a mere infant,
he was not yet capable of being commanded.
"Once we have grown up, we ought to support one another.
At that time, Śāriputra took these words to heart.
When he reached the age of seven, he came again to seek [ordination].
At that time, the Brahmin allowed his son to leave the household life.
Śāriputra took him to the Jetavana.

He gradually preached the Dharma for him, whereby his mind was opened and understood, and he attained the fruit of Arhatship. The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Repaying Kindness) records that the Buddha said, "Welcome! whereupon his hair and beard fell away naturally and the kāṣāya robe appeared upon his body; thus did the śrāmaṇera Cunda first attain the Way.
Using his own power of wisdom, he observed his past lives and saw that in a previous existence he had been a starving dog;
through the grace of his preceptor, he has now attained a human body.
Having simultaneously attained the fruits of the Path, joy arose within him,
and he thought to himself:
"Having received the Master’s grace, I have been liberated from all sufferings.
I shall now serve you with my whole being, providing whatever is required, and remain forever as a śrāmaṇera.
This was back in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
There were some bhikṣus gathered in one place.
At that time, a young bhikṣu possessed a clear and elegant voice and was skilled in chanting praises.
There was a bhikṣu who was advanced in years and elderly; his voice was muddled and dull,
and he was unable to chant the scriptures.
Every time he made a sound, he would amuse himself with it.
At that time, an elderly bhikṣu who had already attained arhatship rebuked the young bhikṣu, saying:
"Now, Elder, your voice sounds like the barking of a dog.
Then the old bhikṣu called out to the young man.
"Do you recognize me?
The youth replied,
"I certainly recognize you."
"You were the senior monk among the bhikṣus during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
He replied,
"I have now attained arhatship."
The youth was filled with fear and remorse, repenting for his transgressions;
yet, because he had left the household life and maintained the pure precepts, he continued to receive the body of a dog for five hundred lifetimes.
"Now I have been able to see you and have attained liberation. From the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Twelve. 4.

The Śrāmaṇera Saves Ants, Extends His Life through Diligence, and Attains the Way. Regarding the Śrāmaṇera who saves ants, extends his life through diligence, and attains the Way: Once, there was a small kingdom.
Not far from the city, there was a fine grove where five practitioners of the Way were training. Among them,
one bhikṣu had attained the six supernormal powers.
There was a śrāmaṇera, eight years of age,
who was staying together with [the elder] in the mountains;
they sat facing each other, contemplating the Way of the Sūtras.
The Master knew that the śrāmaṇera had only seven days remaining in his life.
His parents, who were staying there, said to him,
"Your care for us has been unpleasant, and it has caused our death."
Harboring resentment in his heart,
he spoke to the śrāmaṇera:
"Your parents are longing for you."
"You may return home and come back early on the eighth day.
The śrāmaṇera, filled with joy, bowed his head and departed.
On the way, he encountered a heavy rain, and the floodwaters flowed in torrents.
On the ground there was an anthill hole into which flowing water was about to enter.
The śrāmaṇera thought to himself:
"I am a disciple of the Buddha."
First was a compassionate heart;
second was the desire to save living beings.
He then immediately dammed up the earth to divert the water so that it would flow away.
The śrāmaṇera returned home without any other incident occurring.
On the morning of the eighth day, he came back;
his teacher saw him from afar.
He wondered at the reason for this:
"In seven days he was due to pass away;
by what causes and conditions is this now?"
"Could it be that a spirit or deity has manifested here?
He immediately entered samādhi and saw that the one who had saved the ants had appeared in this world to extend his lifespan.
The śrāmaṇera arrived,
prostrated himself in salutation, and sat to one side.
The master said to him:
"You have performed great merit;
do you know this for yourself?
The śrāmaṇera said:
"For seven days you remained at home without performing any other meritorious deeds;
the Teacher said that your life should have come to an end."
Because he saved the ants yesterday,
his lifespan increased by over eighty years in this present life.
The novice monk rejoiced, believing that good deeds are indeed rewarded.
He immediately redoubled his diligent cultivation with tireless vigor.
He obtained the *Arhat-niṣkramaṇapuṇyavipāka-sūtra* and also the seventh fascicle of the ten-fascicle *Avadāna-sūtra*.

5. The Śrāmaṇera Who Pushed His Teacher to the Ground and Died, Yet Attained the Way through Vigor Without Malice. In the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elderly man. [The story continues: A śrāmaṇera pushed his teacher so that he fell to the ground and died; yet, because he lacked malice and applied himself with vigor, he attained the Way. There were five [versions of this tale]. In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was an old man...
He lost his wife early and lived alone with his son; being destitute,
he possessed no wealth or treasures.
Realizing that the world is impermanent,
he left the household life to follow the Buddha;
his son was still young at the time.
He was also a śrāmaṇera who,
together with his father, went out to beg for food;
they were about to return at the close of day.
The father walked slowly;
the son, fearing venomous beasts,
hurriedly supported his father and pushed him forward along the path.
Holding him not firmly, he pushed his father down to the ground; the father died instantly upon touching the earth.
[The son] went alone to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the bhikṣus rebuked the śrāmaṇera and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha told them:
Although he had killed his teacher, he did not harbor ill will;
he immediately asked the śrāmaṇera,
"Did you kill your teacher?"
He replied,
"I indeed pushed him away,
but not with malicious intent."
The Buddha said,
"I know that your mind is free from evil intent;
it was likewise so in past lives."
There was no malicious intent to kill one another.
Long ago, a father and son lived together in one place.
At that time, the father fell gravely ill.
At that time, while he was sleeping,
many silk flies came and repeatedly disturbed him;
his father ordered his son to drive the flies away.
He hoped for a peaceful sleep,
but the child hurriedly swatted at a fly that would not leave him alone;
the child then became angry.

He then took up a large staff and waited to kill the fly; the *Śāriputraparipṛcchā-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya) states that while he was holding a large stone against a mosquito, various silk flies gathered in competition upon his father’s forehead.
He struck them with the staff, and his father died immediately.
The father was this very śrāmaṇera;
the son at that time was the deceased bhikṣu.
This was because he lacked malice and did not harbor ill intent.
Nor was he killed intentionally.
The śrāmaṇera practiced diligently without slackening and subsequently attained the path of arhatship. This is from the tenth fascicle of the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish).

6. A novice monk died young and was reborn in heaven; grieving over having lost his virtuous teachers and friends, he went to the Buddha and attained the discernment of the Noble Truths. The Buddha was traveling in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. A novice monk died young and was reborn in heaven; grieving over having lost his virtuous teachers and friends, he went to the Buddha and attained the discernment of the Noble Truths. (6) The Buddha was traveling in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was another bhikṣu who had a disciple whose disposition was mild and elegant, whose mind and conduct were benevolent and virtuous,
and who constantly attended upon his preceptor with sincerity, prudence, and diligence.
Respectfully following the Dharma teachings and not disobeying the preceptor’s commands,
his life was short and he passed away while still young;
he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he beheld the celestial realm.
I see only a great fire;
my original aspirations cannot be fulfilled as I wish,
and I am unable to remain together with my virtuous friends.
Now, having abandoned the virtuous teacher and followed after evil companions,
he has thereby distanced himself from the most venerable Upādhyāya as well as the Ācāryas and the assembly.
All those of similar kind who practice the holy life—
the fourfold assembly of disciples—
possess omniscience.
He is titled "Tathāgata.
Now, all such [beings] have become distant;
throughout incalculable kalpas, they are difficult to encounter and difficult to behold.
Having appeared in the world, he has never before spoken of the subtle and profound teachings of the sūtras; yet,
he now brings peace and security through his transformation of beings, explaining all dependent origination so that each may understand the causes from which things arise.
That which had never before been seen or heard throughout incalculable kalpas has all been resolved by encountering this sutra and its vinaya.
Having abandoned the household life to pursue the Way,
that which one ought to establish has not been brought to completion;
now, on the contrary, one is negligent and indolent.
He first went before the World-Honored One and prostrated at his feet.
The Buddha perceived his mind:
it was truly set upon the Way, with pure and earnest devotion fixed upon the Dharma.
When he preached the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path,
[the disciple] immediately saw the Truths.
His preceptor, overcome with grief and anxiety, wept with tears falling like rain.
The Buddha called him and asked,
"Why are you so distressed? He replied:
When the disciple passed away,
the Buddha asked,
"For what reason are you grieving?"
He replied,
"My śrāmaṇera disciple was most virtuous and excellent.
Before reaching the ultimate goal, he passed away prematurely."
Therefore, he was filled with grief and could not comfort himself.
The Buddha said, "Do not grieve;
you have already reached the ultimate goal."
They shall be reborn in the heavens.
This very night at midnight, having distinguished the Noble Truths, the Bhikṣu shall no longer weep; he has delivered the Discourse on the Life Span of the Disciples.

7. Pureṇa the Śrāmaṇera was honored by ghosts; Subhadra the non-Buddhist was naturally subdued. Pureṇa the Śrāmaṇera was honored by ghosts; Subhadra the non-Buddhist was naturally subdued. Seven. Śāriputra had a śrāmaṇera.
His name was Cūḍapanthaka.
At the age of eight, he attained the six supernormal powers and flew through the air to the Anavatapta Spring.
There was a brahmin possessing the five supernormal powers named Subhadra,
who also went to that spring.
At that time, there was a blue-clad yakṣa guarding the spring who drove away the five-foldly-empowered brahmin.
They hurled tiles and stones so as not to allow him to approach the Divine Spring.
The novice Śuddhipanthaka arrived traveling through the air;
the several hundred ghostly attendants in blue robes all came forward to meet and welcome him.
Some had already gathered up their robes;
some were holding pure water to wash their hands and feet;
and some were using clean towels to wipe their heads and faces.
When some bathed his body with fragrant water,
the brahmin Subāhu cried out at the top of his voice,
"I have now attained the five supernormal powers and immeasurable divine virtues!"
His power was such that he could move mountains, arrest flowing waters,
and turn heaven and earth as easily as one turns a bead upon the palm of the hand.
Since he first began his study of the Way more than one hundred and twenty years ago, [he has remained thus].
Exhausting the body and toiling the flesh until both form and spirit are utterly fatigued;
some devote themselves to the five sciences,
maintaining fires at four locations.
The sunlight shines down upon them;
some lie amidst ashes and excrement,
while others lie among thorns and treacherous difficulties.
There is no Way that is not learned through study.
Yet, you have driven him away so that he cannot reach the spring.
Such is this young child in black robes.
At seven or eight years of age,
he had not yet weaned from nursing;
his body was foul-smelling, yet he expected excessive respect.
For what reason? At that time, the blue-clad spirit said to the brahmin:
"This scholar here..."
"Although his physical form and years are small, his conduct transcends the three realms, and he has attained the eightfold path of the noble ones.
You do not possess these qualities now; therefore, you do not arouse reverence."
There was a brahmin named Yakṣa who established a monastery.
He was also called a yakṣa.
He constantly provided ghee and oil for the temple lamps.
At that time, there was a brahmin from a distant region.

He arrived at that monastery and heard that there was a yakṣa and a brahmin of great talent and eminent virtue who were particularly devoted to the Buddha-dharma and had established a shrine; he went to meet them.
At that time, there was a śrāmaṇera who came to fetch oil and ghee to provide for the lighting of lamps in the monastery.
A great multitude of brahmins said to the yakṣa-brāhmaṇa:
"Did you truly pay homage just now to that person dressed in dyed robes?"
Before he had finished speaking, the śrāmaṇera arrived;
[the king] immediately prostrated before him once more.
There were many brahmins present.
He said to this brahmin:
"You are one who has emerged from the four castes with talents surpassing others;
there is no aspect of astronomy or geography that you have not studied and mastered."
The divine mantra evokes spiritual efficacy such that there is no undertaking it does not accomplish.
Now, those who wear these colored robes come from many different clans.
Your lineage is not authentic.
Why do you contravene your own fundamental dharma to pay respectful homage?
Furthermore, you, O Brahmin, maintain a life of pure conduct.
He personally cultivated the Inner Treasury, the Prophecies, and the Secret Records.
By practicing the Way and accomplishing merit, there was no wish that he did not fulfill.
Regarding characters, texts, seals, and insignia, there was nothing he did not master thoroughly.
The Buddha’s conduct was sparse and simple; what is there in it that is noble?
To abandon the root and grasp at the branches is what I find most grievous.
I have heard that śramaṇas are cold and lowly.
Deceit and guile proliferate, deluding and confusing the world;
their conduct is short-sighted, seeking only the glory of a single lifetime,
unable to extend or bring forth the merit of Brahma.
"Even if we were to meet him face-to-face, it would be appropriate merely to hold up our joined palms;
why then do you prostrate yourself with your five limbs touching the ground in respectful salutation?
We have witnessed this personally and find its reason most strange."
"How much less could the Great Man, whom you previously studied under,
ever forgive you for this transgression?
The yakṣa then addressed the many brahmins, saying:
All you people, listen silently to what I say:
The virtues of the noble ones are immeasurable; The Eightfold Straight Path is the unsurpassed way.
This is the Brahmin and the Śramaṇa, as proclaimed from the mouth of the Tathāgata.
Beholding this form, though small, because it has realized the path of the noble ones,
I now take refuge; O Brahmin, why do you deride one who has attained ultimate perfection?
The Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin are able to sever the fetters, the envelopments, and the aggregates of the sense bases belonging to the desire realm;
therefore it is said that those who are "heading toward attainment" are able to exhaust the source of Māra.
One who enters meditative absorption and practices seated dhyāna delights in dwelling in seclusion and tranquility, holding fast to a single-minded resolve.
Calculating the inhalations and exhalations, they maintain firm control over their thoughts.
One who enters meditative concentration is able to sever the bonds of Māra and bind Māra himself.

One can command spirits and deities so that they arrive at will. One should seek skillful means to sever the firm bonds of Māra and emerge [from suffering]. *Chūchāoyào jīng* (The Sutra on Emerging and Shining), Volume Five. 8.

A Śrāmaṇera Follows His Holy Master into the Mountains and Attains the Fourfold Knowledge; He Is Deeply Missed by His Five Mothers. Regarding the eighth [section]: "A Śrāmaṇera Follows His Holy Master into the Mountains and Attains the Fourfold Knowledge; He Is Deeply Missed by His Five Mothers. Long ago, there was a young boy.
At the age of seven,
he took a great liking to the Buddha-way and became a śrāmaṇera.
He followed his arhat teacher to study in the mountains.
He practiced with diligent perseverance;
by the time he was eight years old,
he had attained the four supernormal powers.
First, the power of seeing through with the eyes;
second, the power of hearing through with the ears;
third, the power of flying and transforming.
Fourth, he knows his own past lives and their origins.
Sitting in contemplation,
he immediately perceives all that was undergone in his previous existences.
The five mothers acted as his children,
whereupon he immediately turned and laughed at himself.
His teacher asked, "Why do you laugh?"
The śrāmaṇera said,
"How would I dare to laugh at my teacher?
When I look at myself, I have five mothers."
Weeping and wailing day and night, he was moved by grief and tormented by sorrow;
he constantly said,
"I think of my son and have never forgotten him for a moment."
I thought to myself:
"A single body must endure the suffering and poison of five households;
that is why I smile."
When I was a child of my first mother,
there was a neighbor born at the same time as I.
After I died, those born on the same day as me continued their daily activities and movements.
When my mother saw this, she said, "If my son were here,
he too would enter and exit, walk about, and move in such a manner.
She was immediately filled with sorrow and grief, thinking of me.
Furthermore, he became the son of a second mother;
not long after his birth, he died again.
My mother saw others who nourished their sons with milk.
She then felt pained and thought of me;
she grieved, wept, and cried out.
I was again made a son by a third mother.
Before long, he died again.
As my mother was about to eat, tears fell from her eyes as she thought of me, saying:
"If you, my son, were here, you would eat with me."
They abandoned me and died.
I then became the son of a fourth mother,
but before long, I died again.
At that time, my peers were all getting married.
My mother thought to herself again,
"If my son does not die, he too shall marry a wife."
"I am the son born of my fifth mother, and thus I still exist today.
Having left home to study the Way,
my mother weeps daily, crying out:"
"My son has perished;
I do not know where he is. Starving and cold, we shall no longer see one another in this life or the next."
They were all filled with profound grief and sorrow;
now that these five mothers have gathered together,
each speaks of her deceased son as they face one another.
"He weeps and laments for me alone;
that is why I smile.
People of the world do not know that there is rebirth in future lives."
One simply says that there is death.
A person who performs good deeds obtains blessings; one who commits evil incurs calamity.
While in the world, people naturally fear their own good and evil deeds.
Those who harbor fearlessness toward evil will suffer pain and agony in the future;
once they have entered the evil realms, it will be too late for regret.
Because I am weary of the world, I have taken leave of my kin to seek the Way.
When I behold those in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the destitute,
I feel their terror on their behalf.
Having received the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts through the grace of my teacher, I [strive to alleviate their suffering].
Now, through this deliverance,
I reflect upon my five mothers;
they were unable to attain liberation.
Repetition: The Sutra on My Five Sons Leaving Home. 9.
The Śrāmaṇera Protecting the Precepts and Sacrificing His Beloved Body. The Śrāmaṇera Protecting the Precepts and Sacrificing His Beloved Body. Ninth: There was once a bhikṣu.
Having few desires and being content,
there was at that time a lay follower (upāsaka) in the country of Ānanda who,
with reverent faith in the Triple Gem, made offerings throughout his entire life.
They were dispatched day after day.
In that country, there was an elder who had fathered a son.
Wishing to cause him to leave the household life, she sought out a virtuous teacher.
She immediately went to the bhikṣu and said,
"I wish for this one son of mine to be ordained as a monk."
"I only pray that the Venerable One will compassionately accept me and deliver me.
At that time, the bhikṣu observed with his eye of the Path that this person,
having left the household life, would be able to maintain the pure precepts.
When Du was a śrāmaṇera, there was a householder who was a close friend of his as an upāsaka.
On the morning before a guest-gathering the following day,
he thought to himself:
"Now we must gather together; who shall stay behind to guard the house?
The daughter then said to her parents, "I only wish that my parents would allow me to go along with the servants."
"But you should go and invite me; I am capable of guarding [the site] afterwards.
The father said, "Very well.
The entire family then went together.
The woman then closed the door and remained alone within the house.
On that day, the lay follower was in such a hurry that he forgot to send food.
At that time, the Venerable One thought to himself:
As evening approached and laypeople had many affairs,
he immediately sent a śrāmaṇera to go and fetch it.
He properly maintained his dignified demeanor as the Buddha had taught.
The śrāmaṇera knocked on the door,
and the woman asked, "Who is it?"
He replied,
"The śrāmaṇera went out to meet the teacher with food;
he immediately opened the door for him."
This woman was upright and her countenance was exquisite;
she was sixteen years of age and consumed by the fire of lustful desire.
Before the śrāmaṇera, she—
She displayed all manner of seductive charms and manifested signs of intense desire.
Upon seeing her, the śrāmaṇera thought to himself,
"Does this woman suffer from epilepsy?"
"Could it be that the fetters of desire have driven me to seek to destroy your pure conduct?
He maintained his dignified deportment with unwavering composure.
The woman then prostrated herself on the ground and addressed the śrāmaṇera, saying:

I wish to hear a single vow.
He replied:
"Very well.
If you give rise to an evil thought, it shall perish along with my mindfulness.
Having said this, he departed.
Having arrived at that town,
he was burdened with heavy levies for many years; consequently,
his longing for his wife grew ever deeper.
"If I were to commit sexual misconduct, I would betray my original vow;
taking another wife for a separate chamber does not constitute a violation of my faith.
Thereupon, he searched and by chance encountered a woman.
Her countenance was elegant and exquisite, and her gaze was never unsteady;
they held one another in profound respect and affection,
so he went to propose marriage.
The father, recognizing his talent, wisdom, and great wealth,
joyfully granted it to him.
Once the collection of debts was completed, he was about to return to his own country.
He stayed in a separate residence before returning home;
he went out in the morning and returned in the evening, which was unlike his usual routine.
The Lotus King marveled at this and secretly questioned his attendants;
the attendants replied.
There was a young woman whose husband returned in the evening.
Utpalavarṇā asked her:
"You have a new chamber;
for what reason do you conceal it and not allow me to see it?
He replied:
"I fear that you might harbor resentment toward me, and for this reason I have remained outside.
The wife said,
"I have no jealousy or ill will."
"The deities oversee and recognize this;
you may simply call them back to assist you in managing affairs."
Even though she was returned,

when mother and child met, they did not recognize one another.
Later, while washing his hair, he observed her physical features closely and suspected she was a woman;

Formerly she shared a husband with her mother;

Having arrived at the gate of the Jeta Grove,

At that time, the World-Honored One...

Thereupon, while sitting on that very seat, she became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Having attained the fruit,
he stood with his palms joined in single-minded devotion facing the Buddha.
After the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, [he departed].
The assembly each returned to their respective places.
At that time, Utpalavarṇā approached, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and said:
"I pray that within the Buddha's Dharma, I may obtain ordination as a renunciant."
The Buddha immediately granted his permission and said to the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī:
"You may now ordain this girl to follow the Path."
He was immediately ordained, received full ordination,
and through diligent and energetic practice attained the state of an Arhat,
endowed with the eight liberations.
His countenance was radiant and twice as magnificent as it had been before.
As he entered the city to beg for alms,
a certain brāhmaṇa saw him and conceived a sense of attachment and desire.
He thought to himself:
"This bhikṣuṇī cannot be caught now;
I must seek out her dwelling place and devise a stratagem to deal with her."
Later, when she went out again to beg for alms,
that brahmin fled and hid beneath her bed.
On that day, the bhikṣuṇīs...

Returning to his room, he lay on his back and fell into a deep sleep.
Thereupon, the brahmin emerged from beneath the bed.
While they were engaged in unchaste conduct, the bhikṣuṇī immediately leaped up into the air.
At that moment, the brahmin was born alive into hell upon his bed. (From the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Volume Five)

5. When the courtesan Padmā saw the transformed person and heard the Dharma teaching, her mind was liberated. While the five Buddhas were at Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, the courtesan Padmā saw the transformed person and heard the Dharma teaching, whereby her mind was liberated.
There was a courtesan named Padmā who,
as a virtuous mind arose within her spontaneously, renounced worldly affairs.
Having become a bhikṣuṇī,
she immediately went into the mountains and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
Before she had reached the midpoint of her journey, there was a flowing spring.
The woman, having drunk water and washed her hands, looked at herself;
she saw that the features of her face were incomparably beautiful,
and she immediately thought to herself:
"Why do you abandon yourself to become a śramaṇa?
For a short while, let me satisfy my private desires;
then you may return home immediately."
The Buddha, knowing that Padma was ready to be delivered,
manifested as a woman of such exquisite beauty that she surpassed the daughter Padma.
He came along the road,
and when Padmā saw him, her heart was filled with great love and reverence.
She immediately asked the transformed person:
"From where have you come?
Where are your husband and those within and without his household?"
"How is it that you travel alone without any attendants?
The transformed person replied,
"I have come from within the city and am now returning home."
"Though we do not know one another, let us both return together to the spring.
Puṇḍarīka said, "Very well.
The two of them returned together to the spring.
Expressing his intentions with full sincerity,

In a mere moment, his life suddenly came to an end.
His body became bloated, putrid, and rotten; worms emerged from his belly, his teeth fell out, his hair dropped away, and his flesh and limbs fell apart.
When Padmā saw this, her heart was struck with great terror and fear:
"How is it that such a good person has suddenly passed away?
If even this man is thus, how could I possibly endure for long?"
Fearing this, he resolved to approach the Buddha and diligently train in the Path.
He immediately went to the Buddha’s dwelling,

The Buddha told Padma:
"There are four things concerning women that cannot be relied upon."
First, youth and vigor must inevitably give way to old age.
Second, physical strength and health must inevitably give way to death.
Third, the joyful gatherings of one's six kin must inevitably end in separation.
Fourth, accumulated wealth and treasures must inevitably be dispersed.
Upon hearing the Dharma, Padmāvatī joyfully attained liberation and became an Arhat. This is recorded in the *Padmāvatī-sūtra*.

Who is able to choose and seek that which is true?

Thereupon, the World-Honored One—
Then he spoke these verses:
Who is able to choose the ground, Abandoning the mirror to take up the heavens?

The Flower of Severing Mara Blooms; neither death nor birth is seen.
Upon hearing this verse, the women vowed to study the True Way and become bhikṣuṇīs.
His hair fell away of its own accord and his dharma robes were fully provided;
contemplating in tranquil concentration, he immediately attained the path of Arhatship. (From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Three).
7. A Brahmin Woman Invites Udāyin; Out of Pride He Does Not Listen to the Dharma. A Brahmin Woman Invites Udāyin; Out of Pride He Does Not Listen to the Dharma. Seven: Udāyin.

Again, he says that suffering and pleasure are created by both self and other;

The sister Arhat said, "Suffering and pleasure are distinct from the ordinary person.
She was asked again.
What is the meaning of this?

those various forms of suffering and pleasure arise from causes and conditions.

"Is there an eye?

He replied, "There is.

When the Venerable One had spoken this Dharma,

She rose from her seat, adjusted her robes, and [stood before him].
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"Today I have entered into certainty.
From this day forth, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
The *Udāyin-sūtra on Sitting Beneath a Tree in Silent Subduing*, based upon the Three Jewels for the duration of one’s life.
8. *Carmaphuṣpa Meets a Violent Man and Is Saved by Having His Eyes Poked Out*. Once, in the city of Śrāvastī...
It was named the kingdom of Kośala.

At that time, among the bhikṣuṇīs in the kingdom,

she was the foremost in wisdom among the bhikṣuṇīs.
The one named Kṣema was foremost in supernormal powers;

Each possessed virtuous conduct and majestic spiritual power.

When the wicked crowd saw her from afar, they immediately conceived evil thoughts;

Just as he had removed his garments and entered the water to bathe,

intending to violate him by force.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī was moved with compassion for him;
she then removed both her eyes and placed them in his palms to show them to the various offenders.
"You love me, but you love only my facial complexion;
now that I am blind and without eyes, [you no longer care]."
"What is there that is desirable? he asked,
and further showed him the stomach and intestines,
as well as the five internal organs and limbs, each distinct from one another.
They cast it aside to one side and said to the assembly of the inauspicious:
"Where is that which you call 'good'?"
Seeing this, the rebellious and wicked were suddenly struck with terror;
they realized that the world is impermanent and that the three realms are but a temporary lodging.
His body transformed into impure bone and blood,
such that there was nothing left to which one could cling;
he then immediately returned his robes and garments.
I prostrate and repent for my improper conduct;
having acted with rebellion and without righteousness, I pray that you may absolve me of this calamity.
Kneeling long and joining my palms, I shall each receive the five precepts.
As he was about to reach the Buddha's dwelling,
he prostrated himself upon the ground,

9. Vidiśā: The Formerly Miserly and Greedy Vidiśā Receives Transformation and Awakens to the Way through the Buddha. Vidiśā: The Formerly Miserly and Greedy Vidiśā Receives Transformation and Awakens to the Way through the Buddha. The Elder Sudatta had an old mother.
His name was Vidiḷa.
He was diligent and careful in his household affairs; the stewardship of the treasury and all matters were entrusted to him by the elder Sudatta.
She invited the Buddha and the Sangha to provide them with all their necessities.
However, because the bhikṣu who tended to her illness made many requests,
the old woman became stingy and greedy, and she gave rise to anger toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
And he spoke these words:
"The elder of my house is foolish and deluded;
he has adopted the arts of the śramaṇas and begs without satiety—what kind of path is this?"
Having spoken these words, he further made an evil vow:
"When shall I reach a time where I do not even hear the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
When Queen Mallikā heard this, she [was deeply moved].
And he spoke these words:
"How is it that Sudatta is like a beautiful lotus flower,
yet stands upon four venomous snakes?"
He immediately commanded Sudatta,
"Send your wife here. When the wife arrived, [the Buddha said:]
He spoke thus:
"That old servant-woman of your house speaks with such foul mouth and slanders others; why do you not expel her?"
The wife said,
"The Buddha’s appearance in the world brings such vast benefit and nourishment;
how much more so for an old slave girl like me."
When the lady heard this, her heart was filled with great joy.
"I wish to invite the Buddha;
please send a maidservant to come."
The next day, when the Buddha arrived,
the elder sent a maidservant carrying a full jar of gold and mani-jewel covers.
She exhorted the royal family to provide offerings to the assembly of monks.
At that time, as the Buddha entered the gate,
the old maidservant saw him and felt displeasure arise in her heart.
Immediately, as he wished to retreat and exit through a dog-hole,
the dog-hole and the narrow alleys in the four directions were all simultaneously blocked;
only the main road remained open.
The old woman covered her face with a fan;
the Buddha stood before her,
causing the fan to become like a mirror, without any obstruction.
Turning her head and looking around, she saw Buddhas everywhere.
She bowed her head to the ground, and her ten fingers were all transformed into Buddhas.
The old woman beheld these Buddhas and various other similes.
Excluding eight hundred trillion [kalpas],
even if one does not give rise to faith, one can still eliminate the sins of birth and death.
The Buddha perceives that their physical bodies are distinct.
The maidservant ran back home and entered a wooden cage;
she wrapped her head in white cotton cloth, fearing she would see the Buddha again.
The Buddha said:
"This maidservant has committed a grave offense and lacks the conditions for connection with the Buddha;
however, Rāhula shares a great affinity with her,
so you should cause him to transform her."
At that time, Rāhula, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power,
entered the *samādhi* of sovereign mastery (*rddhi*) and manifested a transformation body as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
The twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus were transformed into a thousand sons;
Ānanda became the minister of the treasury,
and Nanda the minister of the army.
The seven treasures and the fourfold army were all fully provided.
At that time, the precious golden wheel was in the midst of the void,
mounted upon a lotus pedestal.
He went directly to the house of the great elder Sudatta,
where the yakṣa proclaimed:
"A Holy King has appeared in the world!"
He expelled those who were evil and proclaimed the sublime Dharma.
Upon hearing this, the old woman was filled with great joy.
When a Holy King appears, he possesses the wish-fulfilling jewel;
there is nothing he need seek or strive for—this is what may be said.
At that time, the Holy King strikes the bell and beats the drum, and mounts his great precious carriage.
He arrived at the house of Sudatta.
Upon seeing him, the old mother was filled with great joy, thinking:
"A holy king has appeared in the world; he brings vast benefit and is certain to distinguish between good and evil."
The one deluded by the śramaṇas emerged from the wooden cage and paid homage to the Holy King.
The Holy King immediately dispatched his minister in charge of the treasury of jewels.
He went to where the woman was and said,
"Sister, you possess the merit of past lives;
you bear the marks of a king, a holy monarch."
"Now you wish to take my sister as the Jewel of the Jade Woman.
The old mother replied,
"My person is lowly and base, like excrement and filth."
The sage-king’s advisors were filled with immeasurable joy and said,
"Who is capable and fit to be the Woman-Jewel?
If you would favor us, [please let us know]."
I entreat my lord to release me and grant me freedom;
the favors you have bestowed upon me are already many.
At that time, the Holy King said to Sudatta:
"The old woman of your household possesses majestic and sublime physical marks."
"I now wish to take her as my Jewel of the Woman (strī-ratna). Sudatta replied,
"I shall obey your command."
"I pray that you report this to the Great King.
Upon hearing she was to be released, the old maidservant’s joy was beyond measure.
The Holy King then immediately used the wish-fulfilling jewel to illuminate the girl's face, enabling her to see for herself.
Like the precious jade woman,
he was filled with redoubled joy and spoke these words:
These śramaṇas and others engage in lofty talk and grand pronouncements,
yet they claim to possess the Way while failing to produce even a single sign of efficacy.
When a Holy King appears in the world, his vast benefits reach many.
"May I become as aged and decrepit as the Jewel of the Woman.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground to pay homage to the Holy King.
At that time, the Minister in Charge of the Treasury...
King Xuān issued a gracious edict,
opening the way for the ten wholesome dharmas.
Upon hearing of these ten wholesome dharmas, the woman’s heart was filled with great joy.
He then spoke these words:
"What the Holy King has said is entirely virtuous in meaning."
He prostrated before the king, repented, and reproached himself.
Once his mind was thus subdued,
Rāhula returned to his original form.
The old woman raised her head and, seeing one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, spoke these words:
"The Buddha-dharma is pure; it does not abandon sentient beings."
"Even one as wretched and evil as I can still be transformed and delivered.
Having spoken these words,
he requested to receive the five precepts.
At that time, Rāhula taught her the dharma of taking the three refuges and receiving the five precepts;
his mother heard this teaching.
Before he had even raised his head, she became a srotāpanna.
Then Rāhula took this old woman with him and went to the Jeta Grove.
Having arrived, he saw the Buddha;
with joy, he joined his palms, paid homage, and repented,
then requested the Buddha for ordination.
The Buddha said to Rāhula, "Take this mother and go to Gautamī.
Before he had reached her, Rāhula—
He preached for her the Dharma of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self,
and so forth. Upon hearing this,
the old woman’s hair fell out of its own accord, and she became a bhikṣuṇī.
He possessed the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā [were his patrons].
With great joy in his heart, he said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One,
such as this old mother..."
What transgressions did he commit in his past lives,

that he attained the path of an Arhat?
The Buddha told him:
"Great King,
in a past kalpa..."

named Ratnacchatradīparāja.
After that Buddha had passed into extinction, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there appeared...

He sought to leave the household life.

He accepted him as a disciple.

"May my ācārya’s wisdom and eloquence serve as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for me in this life.

10. Vāseṭṭhī: The Mother of Vāseṭṭha Loses Her Son and Goes Mad; Upon Hearing the Dharma, She Attains the Path. There was once a Brahmin named Vāseṭṭha. His mother lost her son and went mad. Having heard the Dharma, she attained the Path. (This is the tenth. There was a Brahmin named Vāseṭṭha.

As they died one after another, she became insane with grief for her children;
naked and with disheveled hair, she ran along the road.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he immediately regained his original mind.
Filled with shame and remorse, he drew himself up and crouched down.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Take your *uttarāsaṅga* robe and put it on so that you may listen to the Dharma.
Ānanda gave him the robe and he put it on;
then, having gone before the Buddha, he prostrated himself and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening her.

Holding her husband's hand, she questioned him with a verse, saying:

"The long night has passed away; so it is for me and you as well.
In whatever place we are born, we shall again devour one another."
If one knows the essential nature of birth, why should one feel any further anxiety?
I have already recognized the way out; therefore, I am no longer troubled by such talk.
Where can one hear the True Dharma Without grieving over the words of children and wives?
It teaches suffering,

all the vows I have made in the past have been fully accomplished.
Throughout great kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
he has constantly acted as the supreme caravan leader,
raining down various kinds of jewels upon the five turbidities and evil worlds, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Within a single day, it rains seven times, causing [the world] to become fully satisfied;
thereafter, he exhorts and transforms beings, leading them to abide in the Three Vehicles. This is from the *Past Sutra of the Buddha Fragrant Lotus World*.
5. Indeed, there is great benefit in serving a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin). Indeed, there is great benefit in serving a Wheel-Turning King. Five:
In the past, in Jambudvīpa, there were four river-systems and two great kings.
One Brahmin named Deva (translated in the Liang language as "Brahma") alone possessed three rivers;
his people were numerous and prosperous, yet they were weak and feeble.
Another king named Puṣyaketu (translated in the Liang language as "Vajrasamcaya") possessed only one river.
Although the population was small, all the people of that country were brave and robust.
At that time, Vajrasena was in the main hall,
and the king thought to himself:
"The troops are brave and fierce, yet the water they have obtained is meager.
That kingdom is weak and fragile, yet it alone holds sway over the Three Rivers.
We must now dispatch an envoy to demand one river back."
If you grant me this, we shall become close allies:
we shall exchange fine goods from our respective lands as gifts,
and should either face hardship or peril, we shall come to each other's rescue.
"If he does not grant it, we shall take it by force.
He then dispatched an envoy to the realm of Brahmā to convey the king's intent in full detail.
The Brahma King said,
"My country is prosperous and its population is vast;
moreover, this realm belongs to my father, the King."
He turned it over and gave it to me.
When I strove with him by force and would not yield to him,
he replied:
"This kingdom was bestowed upon me by my father;
my power has not diminished. If you wish to decide this by force," [he said].
"I do not fear you. When the messenger returned and reported this fully to the king,
the king immediately assembled his army and attacked the kingdom of Brahmādeva.
After one engagement in battle, the army of Brahmā was destroyed.
He pursued them on horseback and reached the edge of the city;
the people there were cowed with fear and did not dare to come out again.
The ministers gathered together and went to the Brahmā King,
addressing the Great King, saying:
"The military forces of the foreign kingdom are powerful, while our own country is weak."
"It is a pity that a single river has now brought about this ruin.
If things continue like this, I fear we shall lose our kingdom before long.
I only pray that you will open your mind and grant him one river."
By forming a close and intimate alliance, they will attain security.
The king dispatched an envoy with a river of water and further promised his daughter to be the queen.
The kingdom possessed rare treasures which they presented as gifts to one another;
when faced with urgent distress or peril, they would all come together to rescue one another.
At that time, Vajrasena immediately welcomed his daughter and honored her as his consort.
Each made peace with the enemy, withdrew their troops, and returned to their own country.
After several days had passed, the king’s consort perceived that she was pregnant.
Following her conception—
A great canopy made of the seven natural treasures is always spontaneously present above his body; whether sitting,
lying down, walking, or standing, it is never far from him.
When the ten months were complete, he gave birth to a son whose body was the color of purple gold and whose hair was deep blue-black;
his radiant marks were so brilliant that they were rarely equaled in the world.
The infant was born with a canopy spread over him.
The king summoned various physiognomists and ordered them to examine the child.
The physiognomists addressed the king, saying:
The Prince’s marks of virtue were rare in the world;
the King and his ministers could not contain their joy and immediately conferred a name upon him.
His name was Kṣemaka; in the Liang language, it means "Covering Affairs.
When he reached adulthood, his parents passed away.
The ministers and citizens together installed Kṣemaka as the minor king.
After several years of governing, he went abroad for an excursion and observed the common people laboring at their plowing and sowing.
He asked his attendants:
"What does this person do?
He replied, "A state takes its people as its foundation; the people take grain as their life."
"If it were not so, the lives of the people would not be preserved;
if the lives of the people are not preserved, the state will perish.
The King then said:
"If my merit is such that I am to be a king,
may my subjects obtain grain spontaneously. As soon as he had finished speaking these words, [it came to pass].
The people’s granaries and baskets were filled with various kinds of grain, all available as they desired.
Later, he went out for a stroll and saw people drawing water, pounding grain, grinding it, and performing manual labor.
He further questioned his ministers, saying,
"Why have these people acted thus?
The ministers replied to the king, saying:
Having received the King’s bounty, we have obtained grain that grows spontaneously.
As it must be brought to maturity,
the common people have prepared this food offering.
The king spoke again, saying:
"If my merit is such that I ought to be a king,
let all the people within my realm have food provided spontaneously."
As soon as he had finished speaking,
everyone throughout the entire realm obtained food that appeared spontaneously.
Thereafter, he went out on a journey once more.
Seeing people engaged in weaving and preparing garments,
he asked them,
"For what purpose are these people performing this work?"
The minister said,
"I have prepared the garments.
The king said:
"If my merit is such that I am destined to be a king,
let all the trees within my realm produce garments spontaneously. As soon as he had uttered these words, [the trees did so].
The various trees within the city all produced exquisite garments—
extremely fine and soft, in blue, yellow, red, and white, according to what people desired.
Later, he went out on a tour once more.
Seeing the people vying with one another to make musical instruments,
the king again asked his ministers,
"For what reason is this so?"
The minister said,
"I am repairing the musical instruments.
The king said:
"If I possess the merit to become a king,
let musical instruments grow upon the trees within my kingdom, appearing exactly as I desire.
Furthermore, after a short time had passed:
All the kings, ministers, and subjects came to offer their salutations and congratulations.
As they encountered the king at his mealtime, he set aside food and drink for them.
At that time, the various ministers...
Having obtained the king’s food and drink, complete with a hundred flavors,
they all together addressed the king, saying,
"The food and drink in our own homes are thin and meager in flavor."
"Now we have obtained the King’s food, which is of exquisite flavor and unlike anything ordinary.
The King said to them, "O you,
my ministers and subjects..."
If you wish to always obtain food such as mine,
those who eat at the time I eat shall all obtain food like this.
He immediately commanded his attendants:
"When my mealtime arrives, always sound the great drum so that all the people may hear and know."
"When I am employed, you shall receive the most exquisite offerings of a hundred flavors.
From this time forward, the drum shall sound at mealtime;
all the people, hearing its sound, shall think of food."
A hundred flavors of exquisite food appeared spontaneously before him,
and the people enjoyed great happiness.
At that time, King Brahmā sent an envoy.
They came to the kingdom of Ghaṭīkāra and said to him,
"When your father was alive..."
"I gave the river water to your father;
now that your father has passed away, it should be returned to me.
Then King Kapphiṇa replied to the messenger:
These territories and rivers of mine were not obtained through the force of my own power; rather,
as a king, I have acquired them without taxing the people or their resources.
"Wait for a moment; I shall meet with the king later.
The messenger returned and informed the king, who approved of his proposal.
They fixed a date for their meeting.
The two kings advanced together, surrounded by their respective armies,
and each established a great camp on one side of the river.
The two kings met upon their boats in the river.
At that time, King Brahmā first beheld the sight of the parasol;
his physical form was radiant and brilliant, like a mountain of purple gold.
His hair shone brilliantly like deep blue lapis lazuli;
his eyes were wide and long, such as are rarely found among men.
A reverent heart arose within him, and he thought, "This must be Brahmā."
Upon arriving, they exchanged greetings and sat down together;
there they conversed about their respective lands and discussed the matter of seeking water.
Gai replied, saying:
The desires of our people are spontaneous,
and they are free from the toil of taxation and royal corvée labor.
Before he had finished speaking, the time for the meal arrived.
When King Muṇḍa’s army beat their drums and prepared to eat him,
Brahmā, fearing he would be killed, arose in alarm and apologized for his offense.
He spread out four sheepskins and prostrated himself with his belly pressed against the ground.
He then personally rose from his seat, pulled [the king] back,
and made him sit down again, saying to him:
"Great King, why are you so terrified?"
When my army eats, the drums always sound of their own accord.
The reason for this is that because we eat at the proper time, everyone obtains the offering of a hundred-flavored, supreme delicacies.
Brahmā rose again and spoke regarding the white parasol, saying:
"I only pray, Great King,
that you will universally extend your protection over me and the people of this land."
May they all submit and come under his rule,
so that all the common people may receive his gracious favor;
thus he shall govern the continent of Jambudvīpa.
All the people attained complete peace and happiness.
After ascending the throne, he sat in the main hall,
while his various ministers and officials stood in attendance as guards.
When the sun first rises, the precious wheel-treasure (cakraratna) comes from the east.
Thus, these seven treasures arrive in succession, and he governs the four continents under heaven.
All sentient beings receive the sovereign’s benevolence and virtue, and their desires are fulfilled at will.
The king instructed them all to practice the ten wholesome deeds,
and after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"King Kṣemakāri was my own self; King Daśagrīva, whom the king punished, is now my father, the King;
and the mother was Māyā. This is from the eighth fascicle of the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*.

6. The Universal Monarch Carved His Body and Lit a Thousand Lamps for Half a Stanza. The Universal Monarch, during the six periods of the day, carved his body and lit a thousand lamps for half a stanza.
Seeking the Buddha-dharma, he traveled throughout Jambudvīpa, inquiring of all:
"Who understands the Buddha-dharma?
The Great Wheel-Turning King wishes to study and practice it."
At that time, everyone said:
"In a certain small country of the boundless [world],
there was a brahmin."
Understanding and knowing the Buddha-dharma,
he immediately invited [the teacher] into the palace to explain it for him.
The brāhmaṇa said,
"The king is truly foolish.
I studied the Buddha-dharma for a long time and underwent diligent hardships before finally achieving success."
"Now, how may I simply hear it?
The king said to the teacher,
"What things do you require?"
The brāhmaṇa said,
"Give me an offering.
The king said:
"What are the offerings required?
The brahmin replied,
"If you could carve a thousand sores upon the king's body."
"Since you have filled [the vessel] with fragrant oil and provided a wick for a lamp as an offering,
I shall explain the Buddha-dharma to you.
Before the King could reply, [the Blessed One] immediately descended from his high seat.
At that time, the Great King immediately stepped forward, embraced him, and replied,
"Please remain for a short while longer; you must reflect upon this yourself, and then I shall offer you my service and offerings."
At that time, the Great King immediately entered the palace and informed his consorts:
"I now part from you all."
"I wish to carve my own body to create a thousand lamps as an offering to the Great Master.
The lady said, "In all the world,
nothing is more precious than one's own body."
"What is meant by 'causing harm'?
The King replied:
'It is because one desires to seek the Buddha-dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.'"
Kindle the lamp of wisdom within this great chamber of darkness;
it shall illuminate the black gloom of ignorance regarding birth and death for you,
severing all fetters and afflictions so that you may attain nirvana.
"You all, why do you now act in opposition to my will?
At that time, the ladies remained silent and did not respond.
His heart was choked with sorrowful distress.
The King took his leave of all those inside and outside the palace,
returned to the upper story of the hall, and went to the place where the Great Master was.
Having removed his necklaces and bodily ornaments, he sat upright with his body composed and addressed the multitude, saying,
"Who among you can carve a thousand sores upon my body?"
They all replied together,
"We would rather gouge out our own two eyes than ever,
with our hands, reach up to gouge the King's body."
There was a caṇḍāla of a wicked nature who,
upon hearing the sound, went toward them and said to the princes,
"Do not grieve; I have a skillful means."
This will cause the Great King’s undertaking to fail,
so that he shall return to his kingdom just as it was before, without change.
When the princes heard this, they rejoiced.
Then the caṇḍāla said,
"I am able to perform the act of gouging out [the flesh] from my own body.
The king said:
"You are now my peerless companion on the path.
At that time, the caṇḍāla took up a cow-tongue-shaped blade and approached the king's body.
In the blink of an eye, he was gouged until a full thousand sores were formed.
Thinking that the king’s resolve had wavered, he threw down his blade and fled;
[the executioners] then filled [the wounds] with molten oil and used fine cotton wool as wicks.
Then the brahmin said to the king:
"Such diligence is difficult to perform, yet you have been able to do it;
you have practiced these ascetic austerities."
In order to hear the Buddha-dharma, he immediately recited half a verse:
"All that is born must die; this cessation is bliss. The king said:
Those who have compassion for me should remember and uphold this Dharma,
and proclaim the King’s command throughout all lands where people dwell.
O people, you should know that when a great wheel-turning monarch sees sentient beings submerged in the ocean of suffering, he [acts].
Unable to escape from this essential point, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion;
he carved lamps into his own body a thousand times to seek this half-verse.
You all should now transcribe this verse.
They recite, study, contemplate its meaning, and practice according to the teaching.
All the people, with one voice and in unison, praised the Great King, saying:
"Excellent, O Great King!"
The True Compassionate Father has practiced these ascetic austerities for the sake of all sentient beings;
we ought to go quickly and transcribe them.
Whether on paper or silk, or upon stone; whether on trees,
tiles, rubble, grass, or leaves— even at mountain paths, crossroads,
or places frequented by many people— they shall likewise write it down.
All who saw or heard him gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
The king lit a thousand lamps as an offering to the Great Master;
their light shone afar, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
From within that light, sounds also emerged, reciting this half-verse.
All who heard the Dharma gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
That light shone upward as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Palace,
eclipsing the celestial radiance. Thereupon,
the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven immediately thought to himself:
By what cause and condition does this radiance exist?
He then observed the world with his divine eye and saw that the Wheel-Turning King had cultivated his mind with great compassion.
"For the sake of sentient beings, he has carved his body to provide a thousand lamps as an offering to the Great Teacher in order to deliver them;
we should go to encourage, admonish, and assist him."
He immediately descended into the world and manifested as an ordinary person.
He went to the king's presence and asked the Great King,
"Why do you perform this ascetic practice of carving lamps from your own body?"
"What have you done for the sake of seeking this half-verse?
He replied,
"O son of good family."
"I have acted for the sake of sentient beings to cause them to resolve upon the path to enlightenment.
At that time, the emanated person immediately resumed his form as Śakra and replied:
Having made such offerings, did he pray to become a Heavenly King, a Māra King, or a Brahmā King?
He replied: "No."
I do not seek this. I seek only enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings,
so that those who are not at peace may find peace.
To liberate those who have not yet been liberated; to deliver those who have not yet been delivered;
and to cause those who have not yet attained the Way to attain the Way.
The Deva King Śakra said,
"Great King,
are you not being foolish now?"
Those who seek Bodhi must undergo diligent toil for a long time before they can achieve it.
How is it that you wish to seek the unsurpassed path?
He replied to Śakra, King of Devas:
"Even if a glowing iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of my head,
I would never, because of such suffering, retreat from the mind set on the unsurpassed path."
"Although you have spoken these words, I will never believe them.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King stood before Śakra, the Heavenly King, and made this vow:
If you do not truly seek supreme enlightenment and instead deceive Śakra, the King of Devas,
may I suffer from a thousand sores that shall never heal.
"If it were not so, the blood would turn to milk and the thousand wounds would heal.
As he spoke these words, the wounds were restored to their original state.
Śakra, King of Devas, said:
"Excellent, Great King!
You are truly one of great compassion."
"By practicing such austerities, you shall before long attain unsurpassed bodhi.
When you have attained bodhi, you must first deliver me.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, [spoke thus].
A great radiance was emitted, illuminating the body of the King.
One hundred thousand devas resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta.
Upon seeing that the sores on his father the king’s body had healed, five hundred princes were filled with immeasurable joy and resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta.
Twenty thousand queens and hundreds of thousands of court ladies did likewise. [End of] Volume Three of the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Great Expedient Means*.
7. King Māndhātṛ, the Golden-Wheel-Turning Monarch, Renounces His Kingdom to Study the Path. Seven: Once upon a time, there was a king.
His name was Māndhātṛ;
at that time he was known as the King of Cakravartin,
ruling over the four continents.
He governs by means of the True Dharma and does not wrong the people;
he constantly practices compassion, regarding his subjects as his own infants.
The lifespan of humans is eighty thousand years.
The king possessed the seven treasures and had a thousand sons;
he did not need to employ the whip or the staff.
The people were free from litigation;
there was none who did not undergo transformation.
When the King wished to travel in the four directions, he arrived wherever he desired at will.
Tens of millions of people followed behind him as he flew,
without carrying any weapons;
both the people and the spirits were filled with joy.
He said to his attendant,
"Inform me when my hair and beard have turned white.
The attendant replied, "They have turned white."
The king summoned the crown prince and said to him,
"White hair has grown upon my head and old age is approaching;
I now establish you as king."
"The four continents all belong to you.
Later, you too should grow weary of worldly pleasures and set out to seek the Way.
The king then abandoned his kingdom, shaved his head, and studied the Way.
At that time, all the ministers and citizens wept bitterly.
The descendants of Māndhātṛ successively inherited the governance of the kingdom;
when one hundred and eighty-four kings had reached old age with white hair, they studied the Way.
After one hundred and eighty-four generations of King Mādhava,
there appeared another person who resumed the royal succession;
his name was Nam.
Furthermore, upholding the True Dharma,
he immediately issued an edict to the ladies of the inner palace and all the nobility,
commanding them to observe the eight precepts and practice the six fast days each month.
The subjects, both men and women, likewise uphold [these precepts].
To the śramaṇas and practitioners who lack food and clothing,
they provide all manner of offerings, even including medicine.
The Heavenly Lord spoke these words:
"Would you like to see the various heavenly kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
King Nán immediately replied.
He desired to see him. Śakra said,
"I shall dispatch a chariot yoked with a thousand horses to welcome the King."
The chariot was named Caitraratha;
the king’s fame spread far and wide, reaching even up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
where he was held in high esteem by the various heavenly kings, who desired to meet him.
Seeing the chariot, he was startled and said,
"This is not of this world.
My King has bestowed upon me a celestial chariot to welcome him."
The King of Namban boarded his carriage;
both the carriage and the horses flew through the air.
He then addressed the charioteer:
"You have passed through two paths;
I wish to see the path of the wicked person,
and I also wish to see the path of the virtuous person."
Māra said, "Liu,
I shall immediately take you to see the places in the Niraya hells where those who have committed evil are tortured and interrogated;
then we shall ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to observe the pleasures of the celestial realms."
When the King arrived at the palace of the Śākyas,
the Lord of Devas spoke again:
"The various kings of the heavens greatly desire to see you."
King Nán constantly spoke of the merits of the Way;
he then stepped forward, took [the other's] arm, and sat together with him.
King Nán transformed his body so that it resembled the form of a celestial being.
It no longer smelled as it did in the world of mortals.
Celestial music was performed and flowers were scattered along with the burning of incense.
Then Śakra addressed King Nami, saying:
"Do not worry or grieve.
The various performers here can provide entertainment together;
this will be sufficient to dispel your sorrow."
King Nanda did not take delight in the celestial music.
King Nanda then said to Śakra:
"Just as when one borrows an object, it must be returned."
Because of his original vow, he did not take pleasure in celestial arts.
The King Nāma at that time was my own self; this is from the *Moyidiao Wang Jing* (Sūtra of King Moyidiao). 8.

The Golden-Wheel-Turning King Araṇemin Invites the Buddha and the Saṃgha. Regarding the eight bodhisattvas of the past kalpa: [The Golden-Wheel-Turning King Araṇemin Invites the Buddha and the Saṃgha]. During a past kalpa, there were eight bodhisattvas.
This Buddha-world is named Nadīraṇa;
the eon is named Supratiṣṭhita;
there was a wheel-turning monarch named Araṇemin.
He ruled over the four continents.
He had a minister named Ratnasāgara,
who was of the brahmin caste.
Skilled in the art of physiognomy,
she then gave birth to a son who possessed the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence.
His marks were perfected by a hundred merits, and his constant radiance extended one fathom.
A hundred thousand devas came together to make offerings to him,
and for this reason he was given the name Ratnagarbha (Treasure Store).
Thereafter, having grown up,
he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma-robes, left the household life, and attained perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
He was again named Ratnagarbha, fully endowed with the ten epithets.
He immediately turned the Wheel of Dharma,
causing all sentient beings to be reborn in the heavens;
they all received the benefit of liberation, bringing welfare to both devas and humans.
Surrounded by a respectful assembly of śrāvakas, he stayed at the city of Anzhoulo,
which was the place governed by the noble king.
Not far from the city, there was a park.
It was named Jambū.
At that time, the Buddha and his great assembly of śrāvakas were staying in this forest.
When the king heard of this, he [went there].
Accompanied by an immeasurable great assembly, he went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Buddha then expounded the True Dharma for the king,
using various skillful means to instruct, benefit, and gladden him.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata and the assembly of noble ones will accept my offerings of robes,
food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the duration of three months.
At that time, the Buddha remained silent.
Having prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and circumambulated him three times,
he returned and instructed the minor kings, ministers, citizens, and retinue to prepare various offerings.
At that time, the minister in charge of treasures...
In the Jambū forest, the ground was made of pure gold.
Upon that ground, he constructed a pavilion of the seven treasures;
the four gates of that pavilion were likewise composed of the seven treasures.
The rows of trees made of the seven treasures all had precious robes and necklaces suspended from them,
as well as various pearl canopies and various precious vessels;
furthermore, various fragrant flowers were scattered about.
Fine silks and cotton down were used to make bedding;
silk banners and a golden wheel were suspended from the pavilion at a height of seven feet above the ground.
The Woman-Jewel held a parasol and placed mani-jewels side by side before the Buddha;
the two lights from the jewel-wheels constantly illuminated the grove, making no difference between day and night.
He prepared couches and seats of ox-head sandalwood,
with tables and benches made of white elephants;
various precious trees provided manifold adornments before and behind the Buddha and the Sangha.
The Jewel-Woman Treasure held a canopy of seven maṇi jewels before the Buddha,
scattering gośīrṣa sandalwood and black aloeswood as an offering.
Various musical performances were played.
The perimeter of the garden was surrounded on all sides by the fourfold army treasure.
When the king arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated himself, circumambulated him three times to the right, and paid his respects.
He personally provided water for washing and served the exquisite delicacies with his own hands to the Buddha and the Sangha. When the meal was finished,
he set aside the bowls, provided water for rinsing, and offered water for cleansing the mouth.
The king held a precious fan and fanned the Tathāgata and each of the śrāvakas.
At that time, the king’s thousand sons and eighty-four thousand minor kings all made offerings to each of the śrāvakas.
Just like a wheel-turning monarch,
immediately after his meal,
immeasurable multitudes entered the forest to listen to the Dharma.
The various devas scattered flowers and performed celestial music as an offering to the Buddha.
In the void, there were celestial robes, necklaces, and various jeweled canopies.
They turned back of their own accord.
Forty thousand blue-clad yakṣas took gośīrṣa sandalwood to prepare food for the assembly.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King lit hundreds of thousands of immeasurable billions of nayutas of lamps before the assembly during the night;
the king himself wore a single lamp upon his crown.
He carries two lamps upon his shoulders;
in his left and right hands he holds four lamps,
and upon each of his two knees he places one lamp.
Upon each of his two feet there was likewise one lamp;
he made offerings day and night,
yet by the Buddha’s spiritual power, his body never experienced fatigue.
Just as one enters the third dhyāna,
so too was the pleasure experienced by the Wheel-Turning Sage King;
it lasted for a full three months.
The treasurer, as a minister, presented to the Tathāgata eighty-four thousand necklaces of Jambūnada gold fashioned in the shape of dragon heads,
as well as the precious wheel, the white elephant, the dark-blue horse, the maṇi jewels, and exquisite fire-jewels.
The Treasure of the Minister of the Treasury, the Treasure of the Minister of the Military,
and the various minor kings resided in the city of Anucala and its various small towns and villages,
adorned with garments of the seven treasures, flowers of the seven treasures, heaps of precious jewels, and exquisite canopies.
Flower garlands, necklaces, precious chariots, and precious staffs;
heads and eyes interlaced with the seven treasures, as well as various jeweled nets;
Jambūnada gold chains and strings of genuine pearls.
Exquisite sandals, cushions, and rugs;
subtle and wondrous stools and benches, along with vessels made of the seven precious gems;
bells, drums, musical instruments, jeweled bells, and conch shells.
Gardens, groves, banners, streamers, vases, jars, lamps, and candles;
birds and beasts made of the seven precious substances interspersed with exquisite fans;
various medicinal herbs, and other such items.
Each [set] numbered eighty-four thousand;
having offered these to the Buddha and the Sangha,
he performed this act of giving.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,
