2. King Vimalakīrti Nails His Body with Nails to Request a Single Verse. Regarding "King Vimalakīrti nails his body with nails to request a single verse": Long ago, in Jambudvīpa...
There was a great king named Vilepana,
whose heart delighted in the sublime Dharma.
There was a brahmin named Raudrakṣa who went to the palace gate and said:
"I am able to preach the Dharma;
however, if you can nail your body with a thousand spikes,
I shall then preach it for you."
The King said:
"Within the cycle of birth and death, I have killed my body countless times.
For the sake of the three poisons, I have accumulated white bones higher than Mount Sumeru, shed blood exceeding that of the Five Lakes, and wept tears more copious than the vast ocean."
"In the past, I have squandered my life and body without ever acting for the sake of the Dharma;
now, I shall seek the Way by driving in stakes.
When I later attain Buddhahood,"
"I shall use the sword of wisdom to sever your fetters;
take care not to obstruct my aspiration for the unsurpassed path.
The great assembly remained silent.
Then Rādhagupta spoke this verse himself:
"All things are impermanent; Whatever is born is suffering.
All phenomena are empty and unarisen; In truth, they do not belong to a self."
He immediately drove nails through his body and made this vow, saying:
"If I never feel regret, [may my body be restored]."
He was restored to his former state, his body becoming as it originally was. This is from the first fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.
3. King Mahāprabha’s Sacrifice of His Head to a Brahmin. Regarding King Mahāprabha’s Sacrifice of His Head to a Brahmin: Long ago, there was a kingdom.
It was named Vārāṇasī.
The king’s name was Mahāprabha;
his heart was compassionate toward all, and he never acted contrary to the wishes of others.
There was a minor king who constantly harbored rebellious and malevolent intentions.
On the day of the monthly fast,
the Great King loaded five hundred great elephants with precious treasures, clothing, and food.
He entered the great marketplace and the four city gates to give alms to all.
At that time, the enemies of a rival kingdom heard of this.
The king bestowed gifts upon those before him according to their wishes;
consequently, jealousy arose in his heart,
and he immediately assembled his ministers.
"Who can beg for the head of King Mahāprabha?
A reward of a thousand pieces of gold shall be given.
A certain brāhmaṇa said, "I am able to do it."
The king immediately provided him with the necessary provisions.
When the brahmin arrived at the border of the territory,
the earth shook in six ways.
Birds and beasts scattered in all directions; the sun and moon lost their brilliance;
the constellations deviated from their courses; red, black, and white rainbows appeared constantly by day and night;
meteors fell in showers; and within that kingdom, all springs and bathing pools became parched and dry.
The brahmin went to the city gate.
At that time, the deity guarding the gate said to the gatekeeper,
"This man is extremely wicked."
"An individual has come from afar wishing to beg for the Great King’s head;
do not allow him to enter.
At that time, the brahmin remained there for seven days, unable to advance further.
He said to the gatekeeper,
"I have come from afar wishing to see the Great King. Thereupon,
the gatekeeper immediately entered and informed the King.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately went out to welcome him;
as a son meets his father, he prostrated before him, inquiring from where he had come and whether he had encountered any fatigue from traveling the roads.
The brahmin said,
"I have heard in another land that Your Majesty’s generosity never goes against the wishes of others."
"His fame has spread far and wide, reaching upward to the azure heavens and downward to the Yellow Springs.
Therefore, we have come from afar desiring to obtain something.
The King said:
"I am one who gives all; if there is anything you seek, do not hesitate or doubt.
The brāhmaṇa said, "Is this truly so?"
"I have no need for other things;
I now wish to perform a great sacrifice and beg a head from the King."
The king reflected to himself:
"Since beginningless time, I have never acted for the sake of the Dharma;
in vain I have undergone birth and death, exhausting my spirit."
Now that I possess this body, I seek bodhi and vow to reach all sentient beings.
If I do not give it now, I would contradict my original resolve;
for what reason then could I ever attain unsurpassed bodhi?
The king said, "Very well.
Wait while I attend to the matters of entrusting the sovereignty of the kingdom to my wife and crown prince;
after seven days have passed, I shall bestow it upon you."
At that time, the Great King entered the palace and addressed the ladies, saying,
"There is a brahmin."
"I have already granted my head to him who asks for it.
Upon hearing these words, the Queen and the Prince threw themselves to the ground, wailing aloud with raised voices; they tore out their hair and rent their garments.
And he spoke these words:
"Great King, there is nothing in the world as precious as one's own body.
Why do you now offer it as a gift to another?"
Then the five hundred ministers said to the brahmin,
"What use have you for this head, stinking, putrid, and filled with pus and blood?
The brahmin replied:
"I have come as a beggar to question you.
The minister said,
"When you enter my country, I shall question you, and you shall answer me."
At that time, the brahmin,
wishing to answer truthfully, felt fear in his heart, fearing for his life.
Then the minister said:
"We now grant you fearlessness for the sake of the Great King.
O poor Brahmin, what use have we five hundred for this head?"
"Suppose every person were to create a head made of the seven precious jewels and offer it for trade along with whatever else was required.
The Brahmin said:
"I do not need it.
At that time, the ministers failed to achieve their desire;
they raised their voices in mournful wailing and addressed the Great King.
"How can you bear to abandon the kingdom, the queen, and the crown prince,
to cast us forever aside and turn our backs for the sake of a single Brahmin?
The king said:
"Now, for the sake of all beings, I shall sacrifice this body.
When the chief minister heard the king's firm resolve,
he reflected within himself:
"How can I now witness the Great King abandoning this life?
Thinking thus, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and took his own life with a blade.
At that time, the Great King—
He then entered the rear garden and called for the brahmin, saying:
"You have asked me for my head;
out of compassion for you, I shall not refuse your wish."
"May I, in a future life, obtain the head of wisdom to bestow upon you.
Having spoken these words, he immediately rose, joined his palms,
and paid homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, saying:
"May the majestic spiritual power and protection of all the Buddhas and honored Bodhisattvas of the ten directions cause this matter of mine to be successfully accomplished.
Tell the Brahmin: 'Take it with you as you wish.'"
Then the brahmin said, "The king possesses the strength of a great athlete; should he experience sudden pain at that moment, he might change his mind and repent, or even turn against and harm me.
If the king can truly do so, why not bind your own hair to the branch of a tree?"
Upon hearing these words, the king felt compassion in his heart, thinking:
"If this Brahmin, being both old and frail, should be unable to cut off my head, I shall lose a great benefit."
He then followed those words and bound his hair to the tree,
saying to the brahmin,
"Cut off my head and place it back into my hands."
"I shall give it to you with my own hand.
At that time, the brahmin stepped forward grasping the sword.
Thereupon, the tree deity struck the brahmin with her hand, causing him to fall to the ground in a swoon.
At that time, King Mahāprabha said to the tree deity, "You do not assist me;
on the contrary, you have arisen as an obstacle.
Upon hearing this, the tree deity felt pain in her heart.
He immediately cried out, "Alas for suffering!
Whereupon blood rained from a cloudless sky,
heaven and earth shook violently, and the sun lost its brilliance.
Then the brahmin immediately severed the king’s head and carried it back to his own country.
At that time, the five hundred princes and the various ministers gathered the remaining bodily relics of the great king, erected a stūpa, and made offerings to them.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The chief minister of that time, who heard that King Mahāprabha had given his head as alms and,

At that time, King Mahāprabha was Śākyamuni. (From the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Great Expedient Means*, Volume Four).

The king replied:
"What food do you require?
I have made a vow that any sentient beings who come to me for refuge shall certainly be protected by me.
Whatever food you require, I shall also provide it to you."
The hawk said,
"I must have fresh, warm meat.
The king thought to himself:
"Such a rare opportunity as this cannot be obtained except by taking life; how else could I obtain it?
I must kill one to give to the other.
Having thus resolved, he said:
"The flesh of my body constantly belongs to old age, sickness, and death; before long it shall become putrid and rot.
To anyone who needs it, I shall give it. Having reflected thus, he called a man, took a knife, and cut the flesh from his own thigh to give to the hawk.
The hawk said to the king:
"Although you have given me this warm flesh,
I shall employ a method so that the weight of the flesh may be equal to that of the pigeon."
The king said,
"Bring the scale and weigh the flesh against the pigeon.
He cut his own flesh until it was entirely exhausted, yet it only then equaled the weight of the pigeon.
He reproached himself, saying:
"You must remain firm and not fall into confusion or despondency;
you have vowed to ferry across all sentient beings who have fallen into the great ocean of suffering."
"Why are you weary and despondent? This suffering is very slight compared to the sufferings of hell.
If even I, who possess wisdom, diligence, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, still suffer from this, how much more so for those in hell who lack wisdom?"
When his mind was concentrated, the earth and heavens shook in six ways;
the great ocean surged with waves, withered trees blossomed with flowers,
and the heavens rained down fragrant showers and scattered famous blooms.
The celestial maiden sang praises, saying that he would surely attain Buddhahood.
Śakra addressed the king,
"As you cut your own flesh with such hardship, does your mind not feel distress or despondency?"
The king said, "My heart is joyful; it is neither afflicted nor submerged. Śakra said:
"Who would believe you?
At that time, the king made this vow:
"If, as I cut my own flesh and blood flows, I remain without anger or vexation, and with single-minded resolve do not falter in my quest for Buddhahood."
"May my body be restored to its original state immediately.
This is from the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
5. King Prajñāpradīpa’s Love of Giving and His Sacrifice of Body, Flesh, and Blood. In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a separate dwelling place.
The ground was exceedingly level and vast.
At that time, the Buddha went there and sat down,
as did Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
The various human kings, such as King Bimbisāra and others,
each addressed the Buddha, saying,
"We wish to prepare a high seat for the World-Honored One to occupy."
The Buddha said, "Cease for now; I myself know the proper time.
At that time, there were some lay devotees among the householders who placed their faith in non-Buddhist teachers.
Each was provided with a seat worth hundreds of thousands [of gold pieces].
Furthermore, there were those who, with faith and joy,
made offerings to the Buddha from the first day of the month until the fifteenth.
King Bimbisāra of Magadha further prepared offerings;
in the center of the various seats, a lion throne made of the seven treasures appeared spontaneously,
and the Tathāgata sat upon it.
Then they all took their seats.
At that time, there was a donor who,
on the following day, prepared an offering and presented a willow branch to the Buddha.
After the World-Honored One had chewed it, he cast it behind him;
it immediately became a great tree with roots, trunk, branches, and leaves spreading out in lush abundance.
At that time, the great assembly, beholding the Buddha’s supernatural power, rejoiced and praised it, having never before experienced such a thing.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
used countless skillful means and various teachings to bring them to joy.
Then, on that very seat, hundreds of thousands of people became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Thus, he manifested various kinds of supernatural transformations until the fifteenth day.
When the great assembly witnessed the Buddha’s miraculous power and transformations, they were all filled with great joy.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha,
on the fifteenth day, provided a meal for the Buddha and the Saṃgha,
as well as for King Prasenajit, King Udayana, and King Brahmadatta.
King Prasenajit, Queen Mallikā, the householder Liśāda-dapūrṇa, and the entire assembly all provided offerings of food;
once they were fully satisfied, they set aside their bowls and performed the ritual of washing the hands.
King Bimbisāra took a lower seat and sat before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One broke his cross-legged posture and stretched out his feet upon a footstool.
At that time, the earth shook in six ways and eighteen manners.
At that time, beneath the Buddha’s feet, the wheels of his marks (cakras) possessed a thousand spokes, with complete rims and fully perfected wheel-signs.
A brilliant radiance shone forth, illuminating the three thousandfold world-system.
At that time, King Magadha, seeing this,
immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and said:
“World-Honored One,
what merit did you perform in the past to obtain these marks and signs?
The Buddha told Bimbisāra:
In a past age, on the land of Jambudvīpa,
there was a king named Benefactor of Sentient Beings (Li Zhongsheng).
At that time, the country was abundant and the population was flourishing.
He governed eighty-four thousand cities and five billion five hundred million villages.
The city where the king resided was named Prajñāprabha.
The king’s principal consort was named Prajñākāryā.
Originally she had no children;
seeking to ensure the continuation of her lineage, she performed rites for the various heavens, rivers, mountains, spirits, and deities, praying everywhere.
Later, she became pregnant.
She addressed the king, saying,
"I am now pregnant.
The king then redoubled his provision of food, drink, clothing, and medicine for her service.
Later, he gave birth to a son of handsome and upright countenance.
On the day the boy was born,
eighty-four thousand treasure troves spontaneously welled up from the earth, arranged in rows according to their contents.
The king said to his mother,
"Name the child Huideng (Wisdom Lamp).
Later, the king passed away.
When the Prince was eight or nine years old,
his mother taught him the arts, writing, arithmetic, and horsemanship;
by the time he reached the age of fifteen—
At that time, the ministers addressed him, saying, "The Great King has passed away; it is now your turn to ascend the throne.
The Prince replied:
In a previous life, I served as a king for six years;
subsequently, I fell into hell for sixty thousand years.
For this reason, I cannot be a king.
The ministers said,
"Is there any expedient means by which one might become king?
He replied:
"If all people of Jambudvīpa—whether men or women, and all who are capable of speech—practice the ten wholesome deeds, I shall become their king.
At that time, the ministers and the people heard the prince's command.
He immediately issued proclamations in the four directions,
and the people of Jambudvīpa all practiced the ten virtuous deeds and refrained from taking life.
The ministers reported these matters in full to the Crown Prince.
"Now you may ascend the throne.
Thereupon, the Crown Prince himself succeeded him and ascended the throne.
The ministers addressed the King, saying:
"When the King was first born,
eighty-four thousand hidden treasures spontaneously emerged;
they may now be taken and brought into the royal treasury."
The King said,
"There is no need to enter the treasury.
He immediately issued an edict that, at every crossroads where [the goods] emerged, [a station] should be established.
He gave alms to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the orphaned, and the elderly.
At that time, the ministers, following the king’s command,
went to wherever the treasuries were located.
At the four crossroads of the eighty-four thousand city gates,
he gave them away as alms.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed himself into a man and said to his companions:
The king commanded me to commit the ten unwholesome deeds.
A high minister asked the king,
"Is there such an edict?"
The king replied,
"I have previously issued a decree to all sentient beings capable of speech within Jambudvīpa."
They all practiced the ten wholesome deeds and never spoke such words.
He then mounted his precious elephant and went to where they were.
The king asked:
"You say that the Lamp of Wisdom taught you to practice the ten unwholesome deeds?
The conjured person replied, "Indeed it is so.
The king asked again:
"Are you able to practice the ten wholesome actions?
He replied,
"If one wishes to accomplish the path of a bodhisattva,"
"I shall first eat his flesh raw and drink his blood raw;
only then will I practice the ten wholesome deeds.
The king had this thought.
"Since beginningless time, I have experienced manifold sufferings, transmigrating through the five realms and undergoing every form of slaughter.
I shall now take a knife and cut the flesh from my own thigh; place it in a vessel, and give me your blood. Thus he spoke.
"Man, you may eat meat and drink blood,
provided you practice the ten wholesome deeds.
Having said this, the transformed man immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
He then manifested in the form of Śakra and questioned him, saying,
"Does your giving concern one world or four worlds? The King replied,
"It is for the sake of seeking the Unsurpassed Way to deliver those who have not yet been delivered."
Śakra poured celestial ambrosia upon him, and his wound was immediately healed, benefiting all sentient beings.
The father-king of that time was my father-king;
the first lady was my mother.
The King Pradīpa was my own self; this is from the second fascicle of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*. 6.

King Mahābala, who delighted in giving without begrudging even his own flesh and body. Regarding King Mahābala, who delighted in giving without begrudging even his own flesh and body: In the past, there was a king.
He was named Mahābala.
Possessing great roots of goodness,
he lavishly provided offerings at assemblies, granting whatever anyone desired.
He gave food to those who needed food, and even elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, fields, and property— all were given to him.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana said,
"You are one of great generosity."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed himself into a brahmin and went to the king’s palace, saying:
"The King performs such a great act of giving."
"I now require a portion of the king's body.
The king thought to himself,
"This brahmin does not need material wealth."
Now he has come specifically to disrupt my great act of giving.
If I do not give him a portion of my own body,
I shall be the one who ruins this great assembly of offerings.
Having formed this thought, he said to the brahmin,
"I shall cut off a portion of my body and give it to you to take away;
however, there are currently many beggars gathered from all directions."
"I should cause all of them to attain complete fulfillment.
The brahmin said, "Even for me,
as a single person, there is still not enough."
Saying nothing more of the others,
the king immediately cut off his own arm with a sword and gave it to the brahmin without any regret.
With single-minded devotion he practiced giving, relinquishing all his possessions; his arm was restored to its former state.
Because Śakra created obstacles as a causal condition, his celestial merit was immediately exhausted, and he fell into the Avīci Hell.
"I am that very King Mahābala; Śakra was Devadatta.
This is from the lower fascicle of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*. 7.
King Maitrībala Pierces His Own Blood and Gives It to Five Yakṣas. The Seven Buddhas were in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, after the midday meal, Ānanda was practicing dhyāna in the forest. He thought:
"Since the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, all classes of sentient beings have received peace and happiness."
Furthermore, what roots of goodness had Kauṇḍinya and the others planted that they were the first to enter when the Dharma-gate was first opened?
[The assembly] reported this to the Buddha based on their reflections.
The Buddha told them:
"Kauṇḍinya and the others,
in a distant kalpa of the past, in this Jambudvīpa..."
There was a great king named Mīla (in the language of Liang, "Compassionate Power"), who had twenty thousand consorts and ten thousand ministers.
The king possessed the four immeasurables and never grew weary or indolent.
He instructed the people in the ten wholesome actions, and the four quarters admired him with longing; the land was peaceful and happy.
Previously, various pestilential spirits constantly devoured human blood, but at that time, the people restrained their body, speech, and mind, and earnestly practiced the ten wholesome actions.
"May pestilence not dare to invade those who are emaciated by hunger and exhausted by poverty.
At that time, five yakṣas came to the king's presence and said,
"We rely upon the blood and vital energy of humans to sustain our lives."
"By the King's instruction, we all uphold the ten wholesome actions.
Yet we are tormented by hunger and thirst, with no way to survive.
O Great King, out of your compassion, will you not take pity on us?"
The king, harboring deep sorrow,
immediately bled himself by piercing five places on his body.
At that time, the five yakṣas received the blood and drank it, feeling immeasurable joy.
The King said, "Since you have cultivated the ten wholesome paths of action, I shall now relieve your hunger and thirst with the blood of my own body.
When you later attain Buddhahood, you shall use the blood of the Dharma-body— namely, morality, concentration, and wisdom— to eliminate your three poisons and establish you in the abode of Nirvana."
The King Maitrībala at that time was my own self;
the five yakṣas were Kāuṇḍinya and the others.
My vow in life after life was to be the first to deliver them. (From the *Xiányújīng*, Scroll Two).

8. King Śūdrāśoka was carried off by King Mṛgāra; he was permitted to return and complete his acts of giving, after which he was released. King Śūdrāśoka was carried off by King Mṛgāra; he was permitted to return and complete his acts of giving, after which he was released. Long ago, there was a King Śūdrāśoka.
This king was diligent in maintaining his precepts and always relied upon truthful speech.
In the early morning, he mounted his carriage and, accompanied by his court ladies, entered the garden for recreation.
As he was leaving the city gate, a brahmin came to beg.
The king said, "I grant it," and honored him according to his request.
While I had gone out to enter the garden for bathing and amusement,
there was a two-winged king named Mṛgapāda who flew through the air,
seized the king from among his court ladies, and carried him away.
The women wailed and lamented, causing the entire kingdom to tremble; both inside and outside the city were in turmoil, filled with grief and terror.
Ruru carried the king through the air to his mountain abode and placed him among the ninety-nine other kings.
King Sutasoma shed tears like falling rain.
Mṛgāra said to him,
"O Great Kṣatriya King!"
"Why do you weep like a small child?
Birth is followed by death; meeting is followed by parting.
King Sudassuma replied:
I do not fear death; I only regret having failed to keep my word.
Since the time of my birth, I have never spoken a falsehood.
This morning, when I stepped out my door—
There was a brahmin who came to beg from me;
at that time, I promised him that I would give him alms later,
yet I did not consider impermanence and failed to fulfill his expectations.
"I weep because I have brought upon myself the sin of deception. King Mṛgāra said,
"You fear telling a lie."
"I permit you to return.
Once you have finished giving alms to the brahmins for seven days, you must come back immediately.
If you do not return within seven days, I shall take you; for though I possess wings, it would not be difficult for me to seize you."
King Susudhāma was able to return to his own country,
where he practiced giving as he pleased;
he then installed his crown prince as king.
This is the statement of repentance and gratitude addressed to the great assembly of people:
"My wisdom is not all-encompassing and my governance has not accorded with the Dharma;
you should look upon me with loyalty and forgiveness. As for my person today, it is no longer my own; I shall now truly depart."

The people of the entire kingdom and all their kinsmen prostrated themselves to entreat him to stay, saying, "We pray that Your Majesty will take heed to shelter this country; do not harbor further anxiety regarding the ghost-king Ruru."
"You should deploy the *ayaḥśarīra* (iron-bodied) vanguard troops;
even though Mṛgāra is divine, he will not fear them.
The King said:
"It must not be so. Then he spoke this verse:
"Truthful speech is the foremost precept; truthful speech is the ladder for ascending to heaven."
The person of small virtue speaks truth; the liar enters hell.
Now I shall guard my truthful speech; even if I must abandon my body and life, my mind shall have no regret. Having reflected thus:
The king immediately set out and went to the place where King Mṛgāra was.
Seeing him from afar, Mṛgāra spoke with joy:
"You are a person of truthful speech; you do not violate the bond of your promise."
"However, all people cherish their lives;
that you have escaped death and returned to fulfill your promise shows that you are a great man.
At that time, King Sutasoma praised his truthful speech.
Truthful speech is human; untruthful speech is not human.
In this way, various kinds of praise for truthful speech and condemnation of false speech [are expressed].
Upon hearing this, Mṛgāra’s faith became pure and clear.
He spoke to King Sudāsa, saying, "I now release you;
let the ninety-nine kings also return to their own countries."
This concludes the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, on the fulfillment of the Śīla-pāramitā.

9. King Śaśāda Gives His Body to a Brahmin to Serve as a Slave. Once upon a time, there was a king named Śaśāda. He gave his own body to a Brahmin to serve as a slave. 9. King Śaśāda Gives His Body to a Brahmin to Serve as a Slave. In the past, there was a king.
His title was Sāvadatta (in the Liang language, "All-Giver"); whatever was requested of him, he never refused anyone's wishes.
The king’s name resounded throughout the eight directions.
Mañjuśrī wished to go and test him.
He transformed himself into a young Brahmin who came from a foreign land to the gate of the royal palace.
The king was greatly delighted;
he immediately went out to welcome him and inquired after his well-being, asking, "From where have you come, O man of the Way?"
The brahmin said, "I have come to see you because I have heard of your majesty's virtues; now I wish to beg for alms.
The king replied, "Excellent!"
"Do not hesitate or find it difficult regarding what you wish to obtain.
The brāhmaṇa said,
"I desire to have the king's own body serve as my slave."
When the king’s consort became my servant,
the king was greatly delighted and replied, "Excellent!"
"Now this body of mine may certainly be obtained;
I wish to offer it to the man of the Way for his service and commands.
As for my wife, she is the daughter of a great king."
"I shall go and question him.
At that time, the king entered and spoke to his consort;
thereupon, the consort followed the king out.
The practitioner of the Way said,
"I wish to offer my own body as service to you,
O practitioner. The Brahmin said:
"You must follow me;
you shall all go barefoot and must not wear shoes,
in accordance with the manner of slaves."
They all replied, "We shall obey and follow the instructions of our master," and they immediately took the slaves along the road and departed.
They then used their transformative powers to take the place of the king and the queen.
He managed the affairs of state as they had been before.
His wife, however, had long resided within the deep palace and had not experienced such toil;
moreover, she was heavily pregnant for several months.
As he followed behind the master on foot, his entire body was in pain and the soles of his feet were wounded and torn;
unable to proceed further, he lagged behind, utterly exhausted.
At that time, the Brahmin looked back and reviled him, saying:
"Now that you have become a maidservant, you must act according to the conduct of a maidservant;
you must not maintain the manner you had when you were formerly a lady.
The lady knelt and said, "I dare not be negligent or arrogant."
"I am merely exhausted and have stopped here to rest.
Call out and come quickly;
follow closely behind me as we proceed to the marketplace of the kingdom."
The male and female slaves were sold separately, each to a different owner,
at a distance of several li from one another.
At that time, there was an elder who purchased this slave and employed him to guard this house.
"Those who bury the dead shall be made to collect taxes, but they must not levy taxes arbitrarily.
At that time, the mistress to whom the maidservant belonged was extremely jealous;
she compelled her to work from dawn until night without ever ceasing.
Several months later,
the maidservant gave birth to a son.
The lady spoke with resentment, saying:
"You are but a servant; how could you have this child?
Seize him and kill him!
Following her master's command, she immediately killed the child.
He buried it while maintaining his practice.
When he went to where the slave was and they met,
they did not speak of their hardships, and each harbored no resentment toward the other.
After these words were spoken,
in an instant he was as if in a daze, like a dream;
he returned to his own country and sat upon the main throne hall, no different than before.
The various ministers, the ladies of the inner palace, and the court maidservants were all restored to their former states,
and the newborn prince was also spontaneously restored to life.
The king and his queen felt doubt within their hearts as to what karmic conditions had brought this about.
Mañjuśrī sat upon a precious lotus flower in mid-air, manifested his physical form and features, and praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
"Now your generosity is so sincere," [the Buddha said].
The King and his consort leaped for joy and immediately came forward to pay their respects.
Mañjuśrī expounded the Dharma for them,
causing all three thousandfold world systems to tremble;
the entire nation was covered [in grace], and all conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
The king and his consort simultaneously attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"The king at that time was none other than myself."

The lady at that time was the present Gopī; the crown prince at that time was the present Rāhula. (From the *Sahṣvada-rāja-sūtra*). 10. King Kuruṣa Abandons His Beloved Wife and Son Upon Hearing a Single Verse. In the past, there was a great king in Jambudvīpa. He possessed a wife and a son whom he cherished deeply.

One day, while traveling through the countryside, he heard a single verse from a wandering mendicant. Upon hearing it, he immediately abandoned his beloved wife and son. [The verse he heard: "Even if one were to give away all the gold, silver, and precious jewels in the world, And even if one were to offer up one's own body as a gift, It would not equal a sixteenth part of the merit gained by hearing this Dharma. Having heard this, the king felt a profound sense of renunciation. He returned to his capital, summoned his ministers, and declared: "I shall now abandon my kingdom, my wife, and my son to seek the path of liberation. He then distributed his vast wealth and treasures among the poor and the destitute, and departed for the forest to practice asceticism. His wife and son, though grieving, could not dissuade him. Thus, for the sake of a single verse, King Kuruṣa sacrificed everything he held dear.
He was named Kuru-pa;
he governed eighty-four thousand minor kingdoms and nurtured all people and things.
He thought to himself:
"I have merely provided for all with wealth and goods;
I have never taught them the Way. This is truly my fault."
He issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom, saying: "Whoever among you possesses the Dharma and can explain it to me, I shall provide whatever they require.
Then, King Vaiśravaṇa transformed himself into a yakṣa and came to the palace gate.
"Whoever wishes to hear the Dharma, I shall preach it for them.
The King personally went out to meet him and paid his respects;
he first assembled his ministers and requested that they hear the True Dharma.
The yakṣa said, "The practice of the Dharma is difficult;
it requires the king's beloved wife and children."
"Give me some of it to eat.
The king immediately ordered his queen and crown prince to provide food for the yakṣa,
while the ministers all wept.
The king’s mind did not turn back.
The yakṣa ate him entirely and then spoke this verse:

All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; that which is born is subject to suffering. The five aggregates are empty, signless, and without self or what belongs to a self. O King, may your heart rejoice without regret! I proclaim this to gods and humans, that they all may recite and uphold it.
King Vaiśravaṇa returned to his original form,
and the queen and the crown prince remained as dignified and composed as before;
they marveled at the King’s extraordinary nature.

The Buddha said: "The king at that time was my own self in a previous life. (From the *Xiányújīng*, Volume One, Chapter Eleven: "King Śunakṣatra’s Fondness for Giving and His Commanding of the Ghost King to Change His Belief").

Eleven: Once there was a man-eating ghost. King Śunakṣatra was fond of giving, and he commanded the ghost king to change his belief. [End of Chapter Eleven]. In the past, there was a man-eating ghost. King Śunakṣatra, who delighted in charity, commanded the ghost king to alter his convictions. Chapter Eleven. Formerly, there was a ghost who devoured humans.
He became a king among men,
constantly consuming human flesh as his culinary fare.
Through military expeditions against neighboring states, he captured ninety-nine kings.
The ninety-nine kings said to the rākṣasa king:
"There is a king in a neighboring country named Sunakṣatra."
He delights in practicing charity and cultivating the virtues of a bodhisattva; when anyone makes a request, he never opposes their wishes.
Great King, if you are able to capture him, we would willingly accept death without resentment.
At that time, the Rākṣasa king immediately raised an army of spirits and went to watch for an opportunity.
It happened that Sunakṣatra was wandering in an outer garden, observing a bathing pool.
There was a brahmin who took leave of his family to study abroad.
According to the custom of the brahmins, when it was time to depart,
he addressed his parents, saying:
"I have now left my home to pursue studies with my companions;
as for the day of my return, there is as yet no fixed date.
Should my wealth and goods be exhausted, I shall borrow from the King."
"I shall surely repay them.
That person, having completed his studies and attained mastery, returned home;
however, he saw only an empty house and no people.
He immediately asked his neighbor,
"Where now are my parents, brothers, sisters, and siblings of this life?
The neighbor replied:
"After you finished your studies, you could not repay the king's wealth with anything;
consequently, you were imprisoned by the king and are now in jail.
The man thought to himself:
My family is impoverished and my affairs are few; I possess no wealth or treasures.
If I were to go to the prison to visit my parents, I too would be seized and detained, sharing in their suffering and unable to escape the king’s law.
"It would be best for you now to change your appearance and disguise yourself while remaining outside, seeking [the goods] in secret.
Only after you have fully repaid the government property will you be permitted to leave.
The man thought again:
In a neighboring kingdom there was a king named Śobhanakṣetra,
who practiced the Way and its Virtue, never ceasing his mind of giving.
"You should go there and entreat him with utmost sincerity;
he will surely not refuse you, and you shall fully repay the King's property.
Thereupon, [the man] went to that place and begged from him according to the King's instructions.
The king said, "Excellent.
I shall provide for you.
Wait until my bathing is completed."
"I shall surely grant you a favor;
wait a moment and do not worry that I will fail to keep my word.
The king went to the bathing pool and was captured by the ghost soldiers.
The king immediately turned back to look, his grief so profound that tears fell in profusion.
The king of ghosts asked,
"We have heard that Your Majesty is benevolent and compassionate, loving all extensively so that there is none whom you do not provide for."
"Though I have encountered such hardship and distress, why should I grieve?
The king replied to the spirit,
"In my life, I have practiced giving with generosity, never once having regret."
"Previously, there was a brahmin outside begging for alms;
I promised him but did not give it to him.
That is why I am grieving."
The King of Ghosts said to the king:
"Your Majesty has long maintained your sincerity and faith, never wavering from them.
Now, when you have finished bestowing these gifts, you shall know the king's heart upon his return."
The king returned to his palace,
opened the treasuries, and bestowed gifts upon others to their heart’s content.
He then immediately returned to the place of faith and went to the abode of the king of ghosts.
The King of Ghosts said,
"Are you not afraid of me?
Why have you come here to face death?"
Sunaḥśepa replied in verse:
"By performing merit and refraining from evil, One follows the dharma of past deeds;
In the end, one does not fear the path of death, Just as a boat crosses the current."
Upon hearing this, the King of Ghosts felt deep shame within his heart;
he reformed his mind and changed his conduct, resolving to cultivate the roots of goodness.
He then addressed the King Śunakṣatra, saying:
What you have now spoken is rare among men.
I shall now release ninety-nine kings;
I relinquish this position.
"I pray that Your Majesty will govern and transform my realm with the Dharma; I shall lead my host of ghosts back to our lairs.
If you remain in accordance with the Dharma, we shall surely visit you from time to time.
Having spoken thus, they parted ways and each returned to their respective abodes.
The myriad people celebrated with joy as the realm became pure and peaceful;
together they practiced the ten wholesome deeds and refrained from cultivating evil karma,
their virtuous accumulation of practice never ceasing.
Later, he attained Buddhahood.
Under the King of Trees, he again recited the aforementioned verse. *Chūyào jīng* (Sūtra on the Exalted Utterances), Volume 16;

It was named Vārāṇasī;
situated on the frontier, it had not yet witnessed the transformation of the Noble Ones.
It served non-Buddhist teachers, and the entire nation held false beliefs.
The King’s mother was bedridden with illness; he performed animal sacrifices to pray for her recovery,
seeking out various physicians and deities for many years,
yet she did not recover.
He further summoned two hundred brahmins from within the kingdom and addressed them, saying,
"My chief consort has been afflicted by illness for a long time; I do not know the cause."
The brahmins said, "It is because the stars and constellations are disordered and the yin and yang are out of harmony that this has occurred.
The king said:
"What method should be employed so that he may be cured?
The Brahmin replied,
"One should prepare a level and clean place outside the city."
For the suburban sacrifices to the four mountains, the sun, the moon, and the stellar constellations,
one must obtain a hundred head of livestock of various species as well as a small child, killing them to offer in sacrifice to Heaven.
Only after the King himself leads his mother there to kneel, prostrate, and beg for their lives will they be spared.
The king immediately obeyed the command.
He drove forth people, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and all manner of creatures;
as they followed along the road, their mournful cries shook heaven and earth.
"Upon exiting through the eastern gate, he was to be led to the sacrificial altar to be slaughtered as an offering to Heaven.
The Buddha, harboring great compassion for the king’s stubborn ignorance,
immediately led his assembly toward that kingdom.
From afar, the king saw the Buddha,
appearing like the sun first rising or the full moon, his radiant marks blazing with brilliance;
among the people who beheld him, there was none who did not feel love and reverence.
All the implements for the sacrificial offerings were intended to seek deliverance.
The king paid homage to the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt down, and inquired after his well-being, saying:
"My mother has been ill for a long time; there is no skilled physician or deity to whom we have not turned."
"Now I wish to perform a ritual of expiation for the constellations, the four mountains, and the five sacred peaks,
seeking to prolong my mother's life and hoping she may recover from her illness.
The Buddha said:
If you wish to obtain grain for food, you should practice cultivation and sowing.
If you wish to attain great wealth, you should practice giving.
If you wish to attain long life, you should practice great compassion.
If one wishes to attain wisdom, one should practice learning and inquiry.
By practicing these four matters, one reaps the fruits according to what has been sown.
To perform sacrifices while indulging in lustful disorder, taking the perverse to be the correct—this is the way of the foolish.
To seek life through killing is to distance oneself far from the path of life.
He then spoke this verse:
If a person lives for a hundred years, Diligently serving the gods of the world,
Using elephants and horses for sacrifices is not as good as practicing a single act of compassion;
the Buddha emits a brilliant light that shines fiercely upon heaven and earth,
so that all beings in the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties do not fail to rejoice.
Upon hearing the Dharma and beholding the light, the King immediately attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
His mother, hearing this, felt joy in her heart and was cured of her ailment.

The two hundred Brahmins, filled with shame and remorse for their transgressions, all became śramaṇas. [From] the *Ciren Faju Piyu Jing* (Sutra of Parables on Compassionate and Benevolent Dharma Verses), Volume Two. Also from the *Mahāyānopāya Sūtra*, Upper Volume: Thereafter, the King loved his people as if they were his own children.
The five grains will ripen in abundance, and throughout the entire land there will be no calamities or toxic influences.
The lifespan of humans will reach eighty thousand years, and they will protect all sentient beings with compassion, like Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
With faith and reverence for the Triple Gem, they will constantly practice the ten wholesome deeds and lead and transform all the people of the four quarters.
At that time, there was a poor man who stole another's property.
When the owner caught him,
the king asked why he had stolen it.
He replied,
"I am poor and lack the means to support myself, which causes me to contravene the Noble Dharma.
The King said with regret:
Those among the people who were hungry, I left them to starve;
those who were cold, I left them naked.
Although my power was such that I could have ensured there were no poor people in the state, I did not do so.
"The happiness and suffering of the people depend on me alone.
He immediately issued a general amnesty throughout the realm and distributed treasures from the treasury as alms to those suffering from hunger and cold.
Carriages, horses, medicinal decoctions, and other necessities were taken as one desired;
the King bestowed these upon birds, beasts, and even down to insects and fish.
Subsequently, the nation became abundant and the people wealthy, and they followed one another in accordance with the Way.
The names of the ten evil deeds shall not exist;
spirits and deities will assist with joy and protect the nation.
The five grains will flourish in abundance, and every household will have surplus wealth.
One immediately obtains five blessings: first, longevity;
second, a more beautiful complexion.
Third, one’s virtue moves throughout the eight directions.
Fourth, one is free from illness and strength increases.
Fifth, the realm within one’s borders is peaceful and secure, and the mind is constantly joyful. [From] the *Sūtra on the Collection of the Infinite Deliverances*, Volume Three.
2. Two kings offered their *kāṣāya* robes to the Buddha and thereby attained the stage of non-retrogression. Long ago, there were two kings.
He offered his *kāṣāya* robe to the Buddha and,
because of this, conceived the aspiration for supreme, impartial liberation.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he cremated his own body.
The *kāṣāya* is not so;
one takes the Buddha’s *śarīra* to erect a stūpa,
and even when the *śarīra* has been extinguished, the *kāṣāya* remains.
Later, when the turning of the Wheel ceased and there were no longer offerings made at the stupas,
the monastic robes accumulated for many years,
and the Dharma of the Buddha was no longer heard.
On every fast day, the king,
ministers, and countless people made offerings of incense,
flowers, banners, and canopies to the *kāṣāya*.
This succession was transmitted from one to another, with each following the example of the previous, never ceasing.
Later, there was a king who thought to himself:
"The former kings and I have respectfully served this robe.
What merit shall we obtain?
What kind of robe is it?"
No one knew [of this].
A man from the land of the Buddha came there for trade and business,
and he said to the king:
In our country there is a king named Śuddhodana,
who has fathered a holy son named Siddhārtha.
Having left the household life to study the Way, he is named Buddha.
His body possesses the thirty-two marks,
and he wears this robe correctly.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy.
He dispatched a messenger to invite the Buddha,
and the merchant said:
If one invites the Buddha, one should simply burn incense and invite him from afar with prostrations;
that is, burning incense and invoking the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha will come tomorrow."
Exerting his spiritual energy,
he offered incense and circumambulated the Buddha seven times;
immediately, it transformed in the void into a floral canopy.
At that time, the Buddha smiled;
the radiance from his breath illuminated countless lands and ascended into the void, merging with the incense.
The composite flower-canopy all returned and entered [the Buddha's] crown.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From what direction does this incense smoke come?"
The Buddha informed Ānanda in full,
and at that moment the trichiliocosm shook violently;
the city gates of that land all became made of gold.
The *konghou* lute played music spontaneously without being struck;
the pearl rings of the women all chimed;
and even a hundred-year-old withered tree sprouted anew.
The king was seized with great terror and called out to ask his people,
"What calamity or anomaly is this that causes my kingdom to tremble?"
The merchant said to the king:
"Wherever the World-Honored One goes, auspicious signs appear beforehand;
all this is brought about by the merit of Your Majesty."
The king immediately leaped for joy and proclaimed to his ministers and subjects:
"Burn incense and welcome the Buddha."
The king made this aspiration in his heart:
"May I become like the World-Honored One’s attendant arhat.
The king then offered a *kāṣāya* robe to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha could not overcome it;
it sank down into the earth until it reached countless Buddha-fields in the nadir,
whereupon it suspended itself in mid-air.
The bodhisattvas from the lower lands addressed that Buddha, saying,
"From where does this kāṣāya come?
It does not even fall to the ground."
The Buddha said,
"In a brief moment, there shall naturally be a response from Śākyamuni Buddha."
The Buddha instructed five hundred disciples, including Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, to go and fetch the *kāṣāya* robes;
each exhausted his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), yet none were able to bring them.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī to go and fetch them, but he likewise was unable to lift them.
The Buddha said,
"This kāṣāya was worn by those of previous generations as they served the Buddhas of the past."
He resolved his mind upon the Great Way.
After incalculable ages had passed,
he was once again born into the service of a king.
Now he has again approached me,
desiring to attain realization;
may he become a śrāvaka.
For this reason, the weight of the *kāṣāya* cannot be overcome.
Why is this? If one’s prior intention is one of reverence, then the *kāṣāya* becomes light.
Later, because his mind was set on the Lesser Vehicle, his kashaya robe became heavy.
Upon hearing the Buddha's teaching, the king immediately repented,
saying, "I am a king."
I do not wish for the people within my realm to desire to occupy my position;
if such a thought arises,
I consider it rebellion.
The Buddha is the World-Honored One;
therefore, [the king] did not dare to aspire to the fruit of Buddhahood.
The king, his ministers, and the people all gave rise to the supreme, impartial resolve for universal deliverance.
The *kāṣāya* robe spontaneously emerged from the earth;
the king lifted the robe and held it up to offer it to the Buddha.
I pray that you will accept this kāṣāya for the sake of all wriggling creatures throughout the ten directions,
and then preach the sutra for them.
The King and his ministers all established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression; this concludes the *Sutra on Subduing Arhats*. 3.

King Śatadatta Gives Away His Kingdom and Later Returns as King. In the third past eon, there was a great king named Śatadatta (translated into Chinese as "All-Giver"). He gave to all śramaṇas and to all people, never opposing their wishes.
In another country, there was the son of a brāhmaṇa who lost his father at a young age.
He lived alone with his mother and sister; they were in a state of extreme poverty and hardship. His mother said:
"Now we are destitute and have nothing with which to provide for ourselves;
we may go to King Sāhvada to beg for alms.
The son replied to his mother, saying:
"I have not yet attained any knowledge;
I must first study and inquire, and only then shall I act.
His mother did not permit it.
The son first borrowed one *liang* of gold,
which was sufficient to provide for a year’s provisions;
he then left home to pursue his studies and returned after one year.
When his mother saw him, she asked him in opposition:
"Where are you going, son? The son replied to his mother again: "I am going to King Śatānīka."
"If what you have studied has not yet been mastered, you must study further.
His mother said,
"The gold from before has already been exhausted."
He then went back to the house where he had previously borrowed money and borrowed one *liang* of gold.
The owner of the gold said to his son:
"Since you previously took gold and have not yet returned it to me,
if you wish to reclaim it,
you must bring both your mother and your sister along with this bond; only then can you obtain it."
When the time arrived, as they had not yet been fully paid off,
he took them back as his own slaves, gave them to their mother,
and then left the household life to study.
After another year had passed,
having acquired a general mastery of what was to be known,
he wished to return; he went to King Sāhvada.
On the way, he was seized by his creditors;
when his mother, elder sister, and younger brother brought him home, they bound him in chains.
The Brahmin’s son then spoke to the creditors, saying:
"Your Excellency, it will be of no benefit to keep me bound for the rest of my life.
It would be better to release me so that I may go to King Śatānīka and beg for goods with which I might repay you."
The ruler ordered him to depart.
At that time, a foreign country raised an army and captured King Sāhvada.
Upon hearing this, the king thought to himself:
"Human life is brief and inevitably returns to impermanence.
In my youth, I delighted in practicing generosity."
Out of loving patience and without intent to cause harm, I do not wish to oppose or resist that kingdom again.
Why is this? It is simply because there is no need for further preparation.
Do not be afraid. Simply prepare yourself to go out and welcome him, pay him homage with reverence, and serve him;
let him receive my commands so that he may surpass me.
The ministers said to the king, "An enemy has entered our borders; why do you not prepare for defense?
The king remained silent and did not respond.
This was repeated three times.
The king said,
"There is no need to refuse or oppose."
As I previously stated,
the ministers received the command.
The King said, "Excellent!"
"Each of you shall settle in your own homes; be careful not to cause disturbance.
At midnight, the king removed his seal and insignia and departed in silence.
Upon entering his own kingdom, he immediately assumed the royal throne.
He immediately issued a proclamation to search for Sāṃkṛtyāyana,
offering a very heavy reward.
The king left the capital and traveled more than five hundred li until he saw a son of a brāhmaṇa in the distance.
The two met, and the king asked,
"Where do you intend to go now?"
He replied,
"I wish to go to Sāvatthī.
I lost my father when I was young."
His family was extremely impoverished;
he used his mother, sister, and brother as collateral for a loan.
"I wish to beg for alms to ransom him,
so that I may also save myself.
The king said:
I am Sāhvada. There was a king of another country who desired my kingdom;
not wishing to cause him harm, I have therefore avoided him.
The Brahmin’s son fell to the ground and wept bitterly,
unable to restrain himself.
The king then exhorted and consoled him, urging him to rise and saying that he need not weep any longer.
"What you seek, I shall now grant to you.
The Brahmin's son said,
"Your Majesty has now lost your kingdom."
"What should I carry with me to provide for my begging?
The king then replied,
"That king has come here seeking you with a very high reward."
"You may now cut off my head and take it to him;
whatever he seeks shall be obtained.
Thereupon, the Brahmin’s son spoke this verse:
In this world, those who kill their parents fall into hell when their lives end;
if you were now to harm the King, the sin would be no different.
I truly cannot bear to inflict evil upon the Great King.
"I would rather let my life end this very moment than ever harbor a rebellious thought against King Śatānīka.
The king then spoke again to the son of the brahmin:
"If you do not wish to take my head,
you may simply cut off my nose and ears and send them;
they will no longer be fit for the king."
The son of the brahmin said, "I also cannot bear it.
The king said:
"It would also be acceptable to bind him and send him away. The son of the Brahmin said,
"I know that the king will not cause him any harm."
Thereupon, the king and the son of the brahmin accompanied each other back home.
When they were more than twenty li from the capital,
the king said:
"You may bind me. The Brahmin's son then bound the king;
the people of the entire kingdom—men and women, old and young—did not fail to weep, their grief breaking them apart.
Deeply grieving for his parents, he went before the palace gate.
The ministers immediately entered and addressed the king, saying:
"The Sāvadha whom we previously recruited has already been bound by the son of a brahmin and brought here;
he is now at the palace gate.
The king then spoke.
He was then immediately brought forward.
When all the ministers and subjects saw King Sāhvada,
there was not one who did not move aside from their place and weep.
The king of men in that kalpa also shed tears and asked his ministers,
"Why are you all weeping?"
The ministers said,
"We have seen King Sāhvada renounce his kingdom and give it to the king."
Furthermore, he gave his own body as an offering to the son of a Brahmin;
because he did not regret what he had done, he weeps.
When the king of that eon heard each of his ministers and subjects speak thus, [he was moved].
He even fell to the ground and wept so bitterly that he could not restrain himself.
He then asked the Brahmin’s son,
"How did you originally obtain this kingship?"
The Brahmin’s son replied to the king,
“I am indeed impoverished;
I have used my mother, sister, and brother as collateral for a loan.”
Having heard that King Śibi was exceedingly fond of practicing charity,
they traveled from afar with the desire to beg for alms so as to redeem their mother and sister and save themselves.
On the way, they encountered him and exchanged greetings.
King Śatadhanu spoke to me, saying,
"I am now relinquishing my kingdom to another king;
do not beg it from me."
At that time, I was overwhelmed by grief and bitter despair.
Then King Sāhvada instructed me to cut off his head and bring it to him.
At that time, I did not dare.
Furthermore, he ordered me to cut off my nose and ears and send them to him;
I again refused to do so.
They then took him together back to the king and bound him to be sent away.
The full account of what was asked, from beginning to end, was exactly as such.
Thus it was with that king who plundered people.
Upon hearing what the son of the brahmin had said,
he immediately fell to the ground in tears,
speaking as the words had been spoken.
He issued a command to his ministers:
"Quickly untie the king's bonds, bathe him, dress him in robes, and restore his seals of office;
let him be reinstated as king immediately, ascending the throne and governing the kingdom as before."
Thereupon, that king knelt with his hands joined in reverence and praised him,
speaking in verse:
"When I was in my own kingdom, I heard from afar of the Great King's virtues."
Now I have come here and behold the Honored One, who surpasses all that I had heard;
his majesty is the result of accumulated merit, like a mountain of pure gold,
and his power is so firm that none can shake him.
Now I behold the conduct of Your Majesty, which is peerless in this world.
I pray that you restore the kingdom to me as its minister, and grant me back my own domain.
May I return to my native land and perform the rites of a subject in your service.
"I no longer dare to be arrogant; I serve the king as if he were a venerable deva or a Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"The King Sāhvada at that time was none other than myself."
The king of that country was Śāriputra;
the son of the brahmin was Devadatta.
They brought my six pāramitās to fulfillment.
The fulfillment of the thirty-two marks and the ten powers, as well as all other meritorious qualities,
are entirely due to the kindness of Devadatta;
Devadatta is my true spiritual friend.
He was also a good teacher who brought forth the *Buddhabhāṣita-Ṣaṭpāramitā-dānapati-carita-sūtra*.

The King said,
"Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot resolve my doubts.
Mañjuśrī said:
The Benevolent One said, "It can be seen through the causal conditions of the mind.
The King replied,
"The Buddha cannot be seen by means of the arising of the mind."
That there is no birth-and-death and that one is liberated through upholding [this teaching]—these two matters constitute Buddhahood.
My doubts could not be resolved even by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Why is this?
If someone were to say:
"Is it possible to defile empty space with dust?
If there is someone who says this...
Mañjuśrī said, "Can one remove the defilements of space through meditative concentration?
The King replied, "One cannot. Mañjuśrī said:
The Buddha knows that all phenomena are like empty space.
Why is this? Because they are detached from their fundamental source.
Furthermore, he did not perceive that any dharmas have a fundamental basis.
If there were anyone who could explain this, even the King’s doubts would not be something that Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could resolve.
At that moment, the King immediately attained the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, he said:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have resolved my doubts."
Mañjuśrī said, "This constitutes a great doubt. Since all dharmas that are spoken of have no fundamental basis, from what could doubt arise?
The King said:
"Having received this great kindness, I have recovered slightly.
Now that my life is at its end, I do not grieve that I shall not reach Nirvāṇa.
Mañjuśrī said:
Yet that which the King hopes for has no basis. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are fundamentally nirvāṇa, they are without arising.
The king then rose from his seat,
took a cotton cloth worth hundreds of thousands of millions, and wrapped it around Mañjuśrī’s body;
yet Mañjuśrī’s body did not appear.
The cotton cloth remained suspended in mid-air.
Only the sound of the speech was heard, but its form was not seen; yet hearing it was as if seeing it.
The King himself saw this and, having witnessed how all phenomena appear, he became free from doubt.
A voice in the air said, "That which the king sees shall be given to him.
He then gave him a piece of fine cotton cloth (*karpāsa*).
Next sat a bodhisattva named Prāptottarapraṇidhāna.
The king again took this cotton cloth and wished to offer it;
having received it, he spoke these words of aspiration:
"I seek liberation and nirvana."
I do not receive anything from this,
nor do I receive what belongs to ordinary people. Why is that?
Ordinary people are those who do not accept [the teaching] because they have worldly affairs,
nor do they seek to become arhats or pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding those who receive and give,
there is no duality of mind in the receiver,
nor is there any duality of mind in the giver.
Therefore it is said that what he received surpassed even liberation.
The King then wished to place his robe upon the Bodhisattva,
but he suddenly vanished and could no longer be found.
One hears only their voice but does not see their form. They say,
"I shall manifest a body and give you my robe."
In this manner, one after another, he gave him garments, yet none of them appeared;
even the beds, tables, and seating places all vanished from sight,
and he heard only his voice.
He said, "I shall give you the robes that appear here.
Even so, the five hundred śrāvakas all refused to accept them.
The king pondered this deeply.
"The assembly of bodhisattvas and bhikṣus has all perished;
to whom should I give my robes?
I shall give them to the Great Lady of the Inner Palace."
At that time, the lady also did not appear;
the king, having attained samādhi,
no longer perceived any forms.
Nor does one see women, nor does one see men,
nor even walls, trees, houses, or cities.
There still remains a residual thought, namely:
"My body, its various forms, and consciousness have all ceased."
Furthermore, one hears this sound:
"Just as one who has various perceptions should personally examine their own doubts,
so too it is with all dharmas when one perceives them through the lens of doubt."
He then took the robe back, intending to put it on himself, but he could not see his own body or mind;
he spoke of these signs of forgetfulness, though the text does not record them in full. Mañjuśrī asked:
"Have you ever heard the Buddha say that those who commit the crimes of immediate retribution shall enter the Great Niraya hell?"
The king said, "I have heard.
Do you know for yourself that you shall enter hell?
The king replied:
"Is there any dharma that, when attained by a Buddha, causes one to be born in heaven or enter niraya?
Is there any dharma that brings peace and security, leading one to reach nirvāṇa?
Mañjuśrī replied, "No, O King. The King said:
I know that all phenomena are empty.
Why is this? From the hells to the heavens above, even states of peace and security are likewise entirely empty.
All dharmas are indestructible;
therefore, one enters the Dharma-body.
Within the Dharma-body, there are neither heavens nor the human realm, nor the hells, the animal realm, nor the realm of hungry ghosts (preta).
"World-Ruler, having purified all the heinous crimes, you have attained this patience.
The King said,
"All dharmas are entirely pure and free from any defilement."

When these words were spoken, he quickly attained the patience of faith (*kṣānti*). This is excerpted from the lower fascicle of the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* and the second and third fascicles of the *Samādhi-vikrāmiṇa*.
8. King Mahāprabha First Produces the Mind of Enlightenment. King Mahāprabha first produced the mind of enlightenment. 8. Ānanda Knows the Thoughts of the Assembly.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions did you first resolve to attain the Way?
The Buddha said:
In the distant past, many eons ago,
there was a great king in this Jambudvīpa named Mahāprabha.
Possessing merit and intelligence,
he became close friends with the kings of the border regions,
who repeatedly presented him with the treasures most prized in their lands.
At that time, the king of that country hunted and captured two elephants,
as white as crystal, with seven limbs touching the ground,
adorned with various jewels— the most precious treasures in the world.
He dispatched a messenger to escort it.
Upon seeing the elephant, King Prabhāsa was filled with joy and entrusted it to the elephant trainer, Sañjaya.
Sañjaya received the imperial decree and,
before long, having been brought into compliance,
went to inform the king, saying:
"The elephant is now tamed;
I pray that Your Majesty will observe its trial.
The king then issued an order to his ministers to observe and test the elephant.
When the great assembly had gathered,
the King first mounted his elephant and went out from the city for recreation;
the elephant’s breath was fierce and powerful.
He saw a herd of elephants at a lotus pond;
they pursued a female elephant and eventually reached a deep forest,
where the king's body was wounded and blood flowed.
Reflecting that he was certain to die,
he grasped a branch of a tree with his hand; as the elephant departed and the king remained behind,
he descended from the tree and sat upon the ground, experiencing great anguish.
The elephant trainer prostrated himself and said,
"I pray that Your Majesty do not grieve;
the elephant's lustful mind has ceased, and he is now weary of and disgusted by impurity."
Sōshimi returned home after eating in this manner.
The King then told him,
"I shall no longer employ you."
The elephant subsequently returned;
the elephant trainer informed the king,
"The elephant has now come back."
The king said,
"I have no need for you, nor do I have need for the elephant.
Sañjaya addressed the king:
"If Your Majesty does not require it,
I only pray that you will observe my method for taming elephants.
The King then granted his consent.
He immediately had the master fashion seven iron balls and heat them until they were glowing red.
Having done so, he thought to himself,
"If the elephant swallows these balls, it will certainly die."
Later, the king may feel regret and say:
"Great King,
this precious white elephant is obtained only by a wheel-turning monarch."
"Now there is but a minor transgression; you should not suffer such loss.
The King, his anger intense, declared, "Depart far away!"
The elephant trainer said to the elephant,
"Swallow this iron ball;
if you do not swallow it, I shall split your brain with an iron hook."
The elephant understood his intention:
"I would rather die swallowing this hot iron ball than submit.
He knelt before the king, shedding tears and looking toward him for rescue.
The king, filled with rage, looked slowly at Sañjaya and asked the elephant, "Why did you not swallow the pill?
At that moment, the elephant took the pill, placed it in its mouth, and swallowed it;
once it had entered its belly, it was scorched and consumed by fire, passing straight through until the elephant died.
The ball fell to the ground, still red.
When the king saw this, he felt remorse and immediately informed Sañjaya.
"You have tamed the elephant to such an extent;
why then were you unable to restrain it in the forest?
At that time, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven knew that King Prabhāsa was destined to resolve upon bodhicitta.
He immediately ordered the elephant trainer to kneel and reply to the king, saying:
"I am only able to train the body, not the mind;
only the Buddha is able to train the mind."
The king asked:
"What is the Buddha's caste?
What is his clan and birth?"
Answer: Two kinds of lineage give rise to it: first, wisdom;
second, great compassion.
One diligently practices the six matters, namely the six pāramitās;
having fully perfected both merit and wisdom, one is complete.
He was titled "Buddha.
Upon hearing this, the king leaped for joy;
he immediately rose, bathed, changed into new clothes, and prostrated himself toward the four directions.
Raising a heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings, he burned incense and made this vow:
"May all my merits be dedicated to the Buddha-way;
having disciplined my own mind, I shall likewise subdue all sentient beings."
"If there is any benefit to be gained for those in hell, I shall enter this very hell;
I will never abandon the mind of enlightenment.
Having made this vow, he—
The earth shook in six ways;
amidst the mountains, the great oceans, and the void of space, there arose spontaneously the sound of music.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
At that time, the white elephant who swallowed the iron balls was Nanda;
the elephant trainer was Śāriputra;
and the Radiant King was my own self.

At that time, I saw the taming of the elephant; this concludes the third fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, beginning from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment. 9. The Story of King Bahudatta, the Brahmin Puṇyavardhana, and the Crown Prince Puṇyavardhana’s Service to the Buddha and the Two Teachers’ Contest in Arts.

In the past, there was a king. His name was Bahudatta. He had a son named Puṇyavardhana. [The story continues with] the two teachers competing in their arts before the Buddha, and how the Crown Prince Puṇyavardhana served them. [The narrative begins: Once upon a time, there was a king. His name was Bahudatta. He had a son named Puṇyavardhana. At that time, there were two teachers who were skilled in various arts and incantations. One was named Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa, and the other was named Puṇyavardhana. They lived together in the same village. Both were well-versed in the five branches of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*). Their fame spread far and wide, reaching all directions. Hearing of their renown, King Bahudatta summoned them to his palace to serve him. The king provided them with every necessity, treating them with great respect. After some time, the king thought to himself: "These two men are both highly skilled in the arts. I must test them to see whose mastery is superior. He then commanded his ministers to prepare a vast arena for a contest of skill. When the preparations were complete, he invited the two teachers to compete. The first teacher, Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa, performed a great feat of magic, causing a great rain to fall and a violent wind to blow. The second teacher, Puṇyavardhana, then manifested a great cloud and sent down a torrential rain, which extinguished the fire [created by the first]. Seeing this, the king was amazed and asked Puṇyavardhana what he desired. Puṇyavardhana replied: "I wish only to serve the Buddha and propagate the Dharma. The king granted his request. Puṇyavardhana then went forth to serve the Buddha, while Śroṇa Koṭīviṃśa remained in the world as a layman. This is the story of King Bahudatta, the Brahmin Puṇyavardhana, and the Crown Prince Puṇyavardhana’s service to the Buddha and the two teachers’ contest in arts. The ninth chapter ends here.
The king was named Bahudatta;
the crown prince was named Puṇyavardhana.
The king venerated the six teachers.
His son served the Buddha;
at that time, there were no śramaṇas in the world,
so he alone, as a layman (avadātavasana), served as his preceptor.
Five hundred non-Buddhist practitioners, jealous of his reputation and virtue,
addressed the king, saying:
"The affairs of state and the two religious laws cause the mind to be divided."
"I vow that I and the Teacher of the Buddha shall each manifest extraordinary powers;
whoever is inferior shall become a slave to the other.
The King approved of this.
The heretic and the Master set a date for their agreement,
stipulating that they would each demonstrate their skills before the King.
The Brahmin, being skilled in archery, immediately departed for the mountains.
Five hundred men each shot a large deer;
they all pierced its left eye and brought it back to perform acrobatic feats with its horns.
Meanwhile, the worthy one entered the mountains and meditated on the Buddha with refined concentration.
Seeking divine assistance to manifest the Great Way,
a deer of five colors leaped forth from the earth;
filled with joy, he took it back home.
The non-Buddhist practitioners learned of this;
they waited for the worthy one to go out and went to his wife, saying:
Your husband has left the household life to become a śramaṇa;
he sits here among these deer and has brought ruin to your family’s traditions.
Upon hearing this, the wife became enraged and gave the deer away as alms.
When the wise man returned home and did not see the deer,
he immediately asked where it was.
The wife said,
"This inauspicious object has now been lost. Her husband was deeply distressed and filled with anxiety.
He returned once more to the mountains and repented with utmost sincerity.
Immediately, a divine moon-jewel suddenly emerged from the earth;
he then took this jewel and observed the movements of the Brahmin as he went about his business.
He went to her gate to hawk his extraordinary wares.
The Brahmin’s wife said,
"My household also possesses a strange object that can be compared with yours."
He immediately produced a five-colored deer.
The worthy one then said,
"The King has sent me with this deer."
"If you steal it now, your crime will be unfathomable.
The wife immediately returned it.
When the day for the trial arrived...
The brahmins each sent a deer, but all had their left eyes wounded; being both filthy and foul-smelling, the king lamented them greatly.
Then the Worthy One arrived to present a divine deer, carrying the divine Moon-Bright Jewel (Candraprabha-maṇi) into the king’s palace.
The two objects flew upward together, sporting like shooting stars and flashing like lightning;
the entire palace marveled at this marvel.
Five hundred Brahmins [were present].
Realizing that his skills and arts were inferior,
he was immediately pressed into service as a slave,
and his wife became a maidservant.
