During the heat of the summer, he stayed atop a high tower,
seated upon a couch of the seven precious gems,
while young attendants massaged him and anointed his body with ox-head sandalwood incense.
The maidservant wore many bracelets on her arms, which brushed against King Māndhātṛ’s body.
At that time, the sound of the bracelets filled his ears, and the king was greatly distressed by it;
he therefore instructed her to remove the bracelets one by one.
Only a single bracelet remained silent and made no sound.
The King then realized:
"The many affairs and many afflictions of the state, its subjects, and the court ladies are likewise like this."
Immediately, becoming free from desire, he dwelt alone in contemplation and attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
His hair and beard fell away naturally, and he was clothed in robes that appeared spontaneously.
Departing from the pavilion, he left the household life by means of his own supernormal powers and entered the mountains.
Such are the causes and conditions for a pratyekabuddha of middling capacity.
There are those who aspire to become pratyekabuddhas and plant these roots of goodness.
At that time, there was no Buddha in the world. Having fully matured his roots of goodness,
he grew weary of the world, left the household life, and attained the Way.
From the *Pratyekabuddha-niṣkramaṇa-dhyāna-samādhi-sūtra*, Scroll Two.
The King of the Yuezhi Constructs Thirty-two Stupas and Attains Arhatship. The King of the Yuezhi constructs thirty-two stupas and attains the path of an arhat. (February) The King of the Yuezhi.
Desiring to seek the Buddha-way, he constructed thirty-two stupas as objects of veneration;
he completed each one up to the thirty-first.
At that time, an evil man offended the king.
The king’s mind turned back;
thinking, "How can such an evil person be saved?",
he immediately changed his heart, renounced birth and death, and turned toward nirvana.
He constructed the thirty-second stupa in order to seek liberation.
Through these causes and conditions, he attained the path of an Arhat.
For this reason, the name of this monastery is Pratimokṣa (which in the language of Liang means "liberation"). From that time until now, less than two hundred years have passed.
This monastery still exists;
I have also seen it mentioned in the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*. 3.

King Mahākapphiṇa Conquers Śrāvastī, Meets the Buddha, and Attains the Way. Regarding "King Mahākapphiṇa Conquers Śrāvastī, Meets the Buddha, and Attains the Way": The king of Śrāvastī was named Prasenajit.
At that time, there was a country in the south named Suvarṇabhūmi;
its king was named Kapphiṇa.
The crown prince was named Mahāgavinda.
When his father passed away, the prince ascended the throne.
By nature, he was intelligent and courageous.
He ruled over thirty-six thousand small kingdoms;
his prestige and majesty resounded afar, such that none failed to submit.
Nevertheless, he maintained no communication with the Central Kingdoms.
Later, a merchant arrived in the Golden Land and presented four pieces of fine cotton cloth to the king.
The king asked the merchant:
"This object is excellent; from where does it originate?
He replied, "It originates from the Middle Kingdom."
The king asked again,
"What is the name of that central kingdom?
He replied:
It is named Rājagṛha;
it is also called Śrāvastī.
The king asked again:
"For what reason does the King of China not come to offer tribute to me?
He replied again,
"Each rules over his own territory, and their prestige and fame are equal."
"Therefore, he has not come.
The king reflected to himself,
"I must now exert my power to compel him to submit."
He asked the merchants again,
"Among the various kings of the Middle Kingdom, which one is the greatest?
They replied:
The King of Śrāvastī was the foremost;
he immediately dispatched an envoy to the kingdom of Śrāvastī,
carrying a letter to present and instructing him in its principles, providing the king with a detailed and comprehensive account.
King Prasenajit said,
"My majesty extends throughout Jambudvīpa;
upon what do you rely that you have cut off my messengers?"
I have therefore now dispatched an envoy to communicate with you.
Seven days hence, you shall meet with me.
If it is not so, I shall mobilize my army to destroy your kingdom.
When King Prasenajit heard this, he was deeply alarmed and immediately went to the Buddha to report the matter in detail.
The Buddha said to the king:
He returned and said to the messenger,
"I have no other great king. The king then respectfully followed the Buddha's teaching.
He addressed the messenger, saying,
"In this world there is a holy king;
he is currently staying nearby."
"You may go to the border and deliver your king's message.
The messenger then proceeded to the Jetavana.
At that time, the World-Honored One—
He transformed his own body into that of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin),
fully equipped with the seven treasures and their attendants,
and sent him forward to enter the conjured city.
Upon seeing the Great King, he was filled with great alarm and trepidation, so he gave him a letter.
When the King of Transformation received the letter, he stepped upon it with his foot and addressed the messenger, saying:
"I am the Great King who presides over the four realms.
You, my king, being obstinate and deluded, have dared to defy and reject me.
Return to your kingdom at once and proclaim my instructions."
On the day the news of his arrival reached him, he hurried to come and pay his respects.
Hearing it while lying down, he would rise;
hearing it while sitting, he would stand up.
The deadline is set for seven days; no delay is permitted.
Should anyone dare violate this decree, the punishment shall not be subject to petition.
Upon your return to your own country, report all that you have heard and seen in detail to the King of the Earth.
Upon receiving this inquiry, the king deeply reproached himself.
He intended to lead his retinue of subordinate chieftains to pay court to the Great King, but as he had not yet set out on the road,
he first dispatched a messenger to inform the Great King, saying:
"Of the thirty-six thousand kings under my command,
shall I take all of them with me,
or shall I take only half?"
The Great King sent back a reply:
"I grant that half may remain; bring only half with you.
At that time, King Suvarṇabhūmi led eighteen thousand minor kings and arrived simultaneously.
Having seen the Transformation King and completed his prostrations,
he thought to himself:
"Although the Great King's physical appearance surpasses my own..."
His strength was certainly no match for it.
At that time, the Transformation King commanded his minister in charge of the army to give him a bow.
However, the King of the Golden Land could not even lift it with his hands.
The Transformation King took it back and drew the bow with his finger;
he then held it out again and commanded [the king] to pull it.
However, the King of the Golden Land was utterly unable to draw it.
The transformed king took it up again and plucked its string;
the trichiliocosm was shaken throughout.
Furthermore, he took an arrow, bent his bow, and shot.
After leaving his hand, it transformed into five arrows.
From all their arrowheads issued forth light,
and upon each tip of that light was a lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel.
Upon each and every flower, there was a universal monarch (cakravartin),
fully endowed with the seven treasures, who emitted a brilliant light that universally illuminated the trichiliocosm.
There are no sentient beings among the five destinies who do not rely upon and benefit from this.
Those within the realms of the devas, upon seeing his radiance and hearing his preaching of the Dharma,
find their bodies and minds purified, and there are those who resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Furthermore, there are those who abide in the stage of non-retrogression;
among the sentient beings of the human realm, there are those who attain the first, second, or third paths;
and there are those who leave the household life, enter the essential path, and attain arhatship.
There were those who gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment,
attaining the stage of non-retrogression in numbers beyond measure;
and sentient beings from the three miserable realms were freed from suffering and reborn among humans and devas.
At that time, King Mahākapphiṇa and the various minor kings of Suvarṇabhūmi,
seeing this divine transformation, were filled with faith and submission in their hearts.
They were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye;
eighteen thousand minor kings all did likewise at once.
In a mere moment, the Buddha withdrew his supernormal power and returned to his original form.
Surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus,
King Suvarṇabhūmi and his retinue sought ordination;
their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, and the saṃghāṭī robes appeared upon their bodies.
Reflecting upon the Sublime Dharma, one attains Arhatship; from the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Seven. 4.

King Guṇamati Protects the Dharma-Preacher Who Loses His Life for the Sake of the Buddha’s Disciples. Regarding King Guṇamati Protecting the Dharma-Preacher Who Loses His Life for the Sake of the Buddha’s Disciples: In the distant past, many eons ago.
In this city of Kuśinagara, a Buddha appeared in the world named Ānandavardhana.
Having remained in the world for immeasurable eons, he brought immeasurable sentient beings to liberation.
Thereafter, he entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.
After the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, his bequeathed Dharma remained in the world for immeasurable billions of years;
it was only forty years later that the Buddha-dharma was extinguished.
There was a precept-observing bhikṣu named Jue-de (Jñānaguna),
who was surrounded by a great multitude of disciples and followers; he was able to roar the lion’s roar and extensively expound the sūtras.
He established a rule that the bhikṣus were not permitted to keep slaves, oxen, sheep, or other such improper things.
At that time, many bhikṣus who had violated the precepts heard this proclamation and all gave rise to malicious thoughts.
They brandished swords and staves to intimidate this Dharma Master.
At that time, there was a king named Yude (Possessing Virtue).
Having heard this matter,
for the sake of protecting the Dharma, he immediately went to where the preacher of the Dharma was and [confronted] those evil bhikṣus who had broken the precepts.
They fought most fiercely,
enabling the Dharma-preacher to escape harm;
at that time, the king was wounded, with sores covering his entire body.
Bodhiśrī immediately praised the king, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You, O King, are now truly a protector of the True Dharma."
"In a future age, this body shall become an immeasurable vessel for the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma at that time,
the king’s heart was filled with great joy, and he passed away immediately.
He will be born in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha as his foremost disciple.
At that time, the king, along with his retinue,
subjects, and kinsmen, will engage in battle.
Those who rejoice in this shall all never regress from the mind of enlightenment;
at the end of their lives, they will all be reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha.
After his life has ended, the bhikṣu Jñānaguṇa will likewise be reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha as the second disciple among the assembly of śrāvakas.
If there is a time when the True Dharma is about to perish,
one should uphold and protect it in this manner;
the king at that time was none other than myself.
The monk who preached the Dharma was Kāśyapa Buddha; this is from the third fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. 5.
The King of Merit-Adornment Invites the Buddha to Attain the Way: The King of Merit-Adornment Invites the Buddha to Attain the Way. At that time, the King of Merit-Adornment...
Having heard the Buddha recite these verses and witnessed his miraculous transformations,

Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin immediately entered meditative concentration and manifested such signs as these;
the great trichiliocosm shook.
From the space above, flowers, incense, silken canopies, banners and streamers, music, exquisite foods and drinks, necklaces, garments,

Sentient beings attained what they had never experienced before and were all greatly filled with joy.
At that time, from the earth spirits up to the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven,

This great bodhisattva may be named Ākāśagarbha. Why is this?

The Buddha then confirmed this.

“World-Honored One,

When one has left the household life, they are not stingy and do not give rise to mental distress.
The king abdicated his throne in favor of his son, Kalyāṇabuddhi,

Having left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma,

At that time, King Śubhamati...
He who governs the country with the Dharma has no cause for resentment;

Krakucchanda Tathāgata was he;
the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin was none other than the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.

It was named Landā.
The land was fertile and rich, and the people were pure and faithful.
Ruler and ministers, fathers and sons, exhorted one another to follow the Way.
After the king ascended the throne,
both the clergy and the laity became increasingly degenerate, and governance grew unjust.
He oppressed the common people and executed the innocent at will.
When order is disrupted by chaos, calamities respond with untimely rains;
the five grains do not flourish, and various monsters appear.
This ultimately leads to desolation and ruin, bringing about the fear of imminent destruction.
More than five hundred people served heterodox paths;
furthermore, they sacrificed to demonic spirits, with those above and below imitating one another like grass bending in the wind.
The common people delighted in chaos and vied with one another in committing villainy and treachery.
The strong oppressed the weak, injuring and killing each other in turn;
they plundered the wealth of others, acting contrary to the Way and principle.
The ruler and his ministers were intoxicated with debauchery, committing adultery with the wives of others;
their delusions increased daily, and drought exceeded three years.
Despite repeated prayers from beginning to end, not a drop of rain was obtained.
The various masters addressed the king, saying:
"Now a great sacrifice shall be performed.
One should employ seven young boys, ten white oxen, and ten white horses, and burn them as offerings to worship the gods."
Nevertheless, it was possible to obtain rain.
The king immediately made the necessary preparations;
throughout the kingdom, people of all ranks were filled with anxiety and agitation.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"In the kingdom of Rāḍha, the land is desolate and the people suffer in toil.
There are three hundred million people who should attain liberation through you."
"You may go to convert them.
Maudgalyāyana went there and preached the Dharma to explain their minds,
yet among the people of the country, not a single one initially accepted it.
Maudgalyāyana transformed himself into the body of a great ghost-spirit,
several tens of zhang in height.
He sat at the city gate and called out in a loud voice for the king and his close ministers to come forth.
The ruler and his ministers were filled with alarm and confusion, fearing they would not survive.
The king immediately led his senior ministers to prostrate themselves and state their plea,
praying only for their lives.
The deity spoke to the king, saying:
“Seek out immediately a minister who is disloyal and a son who is unfilial;
I wish to eat them. The King then conducted an investigation.
He replied, "There is none.
The spirit spoke again to the king, saying,
"Quickly seek out the thief!"
Those who are lewd and dissolute,
and those who engage in double-tongued speech and harsh words—
I wish to devour them.
The king immediately interrogated him,
and he again replied that there was none.
The spirit spoke to the king once more, saying:
"I am urgently seeking someone who drinks wine;
I wish to eat him. The king immediately investigated the matter.
He replied again, "There is none.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana manifested his true body once more and went to converse with the spirits and deities.
When the King saw Maudgalyāyana,
he prostrated himself with his head at the monk's feet and earnestly entreated him to explain the great deity.
Maudgalyāyana said to the King:
"What does this deity seek?
The king replied,
"I wish to eat wicked people."
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"In this kingdom, are there people of such a kind?
The king replied, "There are none."
He requested again for the spirit to be dispatched,
saying, "I shall devote my life to taking refuge in you, O man of the Way.
Maudgalyāyana then spoke to the Great Spirit, saying:
Among the people of this country, there is no one such as you seek.
You should pardon their offenses;
should there be any who offend again, [then deal with them].
"You may come again to eat it.
The deity immediately granted his request and vanished in an instant.
The king, along with his ministers and subjects,
immediately bowed their heads together in thanks, entreating to take refuge;
Maudgalyāyana then addressed them, saying:
If Your Majesty wishes to take refuge,
you should first take refuge in the Buddha yourself.
The King then asked about the Buddha’s qualities.
Maudgalyāyana said, "The Dharma taught by the Buddha, who is uniquely honored throughout the three realms, has been heard by three thousand śrāvakas.
The King said,
"I am now fortunate indeed to have obtained this extraordinary teaching."
He then addressed Maudgalyāyana,
saying, "I wish to invite the Buddha to accept my reverent Dharma-exhortation, which I shall practice and uphold for the rest of my life.
Maudgalyāyana said to the king:
If one can truly achieve this through faith,
their merit will be immeasurable;
they need only maintain a pure mind and keep the Buddha in mind.
The king immediately followed these instructions, bathing and observing the fast.
He bowed his head toward the land of the Buddha from afar in salutation and said,
"Out of ignorance and delusion, I have mistakenly stood above my people."
I have failed to cleanse my heart and lead others;
that the land has been left desolate and waste is my own fault.
I only pray that the Celestial Honored One will shed his radiance and descend upon us.
He caused all the common people to obtain inexhaustible blessings.
Before they had yet reached a distance of one hundred li, the Buddha and the bhikṣus traveled through the air in advance.
Five-colored lotus flowers supported his feet from below.
The various devas followed as attendants, welcoming him along the road with precious canopies and flowered parasols.
They played a multitude of famous musical instruments, filling the air to its limits.
Beholding the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, which illuminated heaven and earth,
the king and his ministers prostrated themselves at his feet.
They then spread canopies and curtains across the four main roads, sweeping and sprinkling them until they were pure and clean.
The Buddha sat upon a natural lion throne,
which was entirely covered with celestial silken hangings and cushions.
The king personally poured out the food and drink and served the water for washing.
When the incantations and prayers were finished,
the Buddha then expounded the essentials of the Four Noble Truths— suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
The king immediately rejoiced and requested to receive the five precepts.
Having untied his bonds and removed his defilements, he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
At that time, the five hundred non-Buddhist practitioners whom the king served requested to become bhikṣus.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent.
He stroked their hair with his hand and placed his *kāṣāya* robes upon their bodies;
seven days later, they all attained the state of Arhat.
The people in the assembly attained the stage of Srotāpanna;
some received the five precepts and diligently practiced the ten wholesome deeds,
taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
They observed the six fasts of the month and the three fasts of the year,
encouraging one another to follow this as a constant practice.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"What karmic connection did this king and his people have with Maudgalyāyana in their past lives?"
The Buddha said,
"In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha,
Maudgalyāyana was a lay follower (upāsaka)."
Though dwelling in poverty and destitution, he faithfully observed the precepts and guarded his mind without transgression.
While gathering flowers in the mountains, he saw a *śimśapā* tree;
just as he was about to climb the tree to gather the blossoms, [he encountered the Buddha].
Unaware that there was a honeycomb ahead,
several thousand bees were startled and scattered as they pursued him.
He immediately thought to himself:

"If I attain the Way, I shall deliver you all. Those who attained the Way today were all bees at that time. From the *Lánda Wáng Jīng* (Sūtra of King Lánda). 7. Universal Peace King Converts the Four Kings; They Hear the Dharma and Attain the Way. Seven: Once there were five kings. Each ruled over his own kingdom, and none knew of the others' existence. One day, a sage appeared and said to them, "You five kings each rule over a realm, yet you do not know one another. This is a great pity. You should go forth together to seek the Way. The five kings then set out together. On the way, they encountered a great river. The sage said, "I will ferry you across. When they had reached midstream, the sage suddenly vanished.

The five kings were terrified and cried out, "We have been deceived! At that moment, the sage reappeared and said, "Do not fear. I am a transformation of the Buddha. Because you harbored doubts, you did not see me until now. Now listen to my words: 'The five aggregates are empty and false; the six sense bases are likewise unreal. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; only the unconditioned is true. Upon hearing this, the five kings immediately attained the Way. The sage then transformed back into his original form and departed. The five kings returned to their respective kingdoms and governed with righteousness. Their subjects lived in peace and prosperity, and all attained the Way. Thus it is said: "If one hears the Dharma with a sincere heart, one shall surely attain the Way. This is called the story of Universal Peace King converting the four kings, who heard the Dharma and attained the Way. Seven. End.
The neighboring kingdoms were close allies, frequently visiting one another;
their greatest ruler was named Puhuan (Universal Peace),
who practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva.
The other four minor kings were constantly practicing unwholesome conduct;
the Great King took pity on them,
summoned them to the palace hall, and enjoyed himself together with them.
This continued for seven days.
When the full seven days had passed, throughout the day and night,
the minor king addressed the great king, saying:
"The affairs of state are many; please allow me to return home.
The Great King saw him off, and once they had reached the road, he spoke to the minor kings.
Each spoke of what they delighted in. One king replied:
"In the third month of spring, when the trees are in full bloom, I delight in sporting in the wilds."
The first king replied again:
"May I always be a king,
surrounded on all sides by saddled horses, fine attire, officials, and subjects."
Brilliant and resplendent, as the bells and drums were struck, all who passed by or came along on the road turned their eyes toward him.
Another king said,
"May my wife and children be peerlessly handsome."
They enjoyed themselves together, reaching the height of pleasure and satisfaction.
Then one king spoke again,
saying, "May my parents live forever."
Friends, brothers, and wives were gathered in rows;
fine clothes and delicious food were provided to indulge their bodies and mouths,
while they enjoyed themselves together with zithers and green robes.
They both asked the Great King, "What is it that you desire? The Great King replied,

"I desire that which is neither born nor dies, neither suffers nor is afflicted, neither hungry nor thirsty, neither cold nor hot, and wherein existence and non-existence are both mastered with sovereignty."
The four kings all said,
"For such happiness as this, there must be an enlightened teacher.
The Great King replied:
"My teacher is titled 'Buddha.
He resides nearby at the Jetavana Vihāra.
All the kings, filled with joy, have gone together to visit the World-Honored One."
The Great King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now that I have obtained this human form, I am dull-witted and lacking in wisdom; I am merely deeply attached to worldly pleasures and do not understand the nature of sin and merit."
"I pray that the Buddha will explain the Truth of Suffering for the sake of his disciples.
The Buddha said,
"Listen well, all of you."
I shall now explain this for you.
When human beings live in this world, various sufferings cut into their very flesh.
To speak briefly, there are eight types of suffering.
Life is suffering.
When a person dies, they do not know toward which realm their spirit is heading;
before reaching a place of birth, they universally assume the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Upon reaching the twenty-first day,
when the parents are in union, the consciousness descends to receive conception in the womb.
During the first week, it is like thin curd.
In the second week, it is like thick curd;
in the third week, it is like solidified butter;
in the fourth week, it is like a piece of flesh.
When the five *kalala* have been perfected and the subtle wind enters the womb,
it blows through the body, causing the six sense organs to unfold.
It remains within the mother’s womb, situated below the raw viscera (*āma-koṣṭha*) and above the cooked viscera (*pakva-koṣṭha*).
When the mother ate a single grain of hot food,
her body felt as if it had been plunged into boiling water;
when she drank a single cup of cold water, [she felt as if she were being doused with ice].
It is also like cold ice cutting into one's body;
when the mother is full,
her body is so constricted that the pain is beyond description.
When the mother is hungry,
the bird within her womb likewise suffers as if it were hanging upside down, enduring immeasurable pain.
When the full term has reached its end and she is about to give birth, [the suffering continues].
With its head toward the birth canal,
it emerges with great difficulty as if squeezed between two rocks, falling onto the grass;
its body is so delicate and soft that when the grass touches it, it feels like walking upon swords and blades, causing it to suddenly lose its voice and let out a great cry.
"Is this suffering? "It is suffering.
Second is the suffering of old age.
The parents raised and nurtured them until they reached adulthood;
when hungry, they were left utterly famished, and when full, they were left utterly satiated,
with no moderation whatsoever.
Gradually reaching old age, the hair turns white and the teeth fall out;
the vision becomes dim and the hearing dull.
Vigor departs and decay arrives; the skin slackens and the face wrinkles.
The hundred joints ache with pain, making every step an extreme hardship;
sitting or rising involves groaning, sorrow, grief, and affliction.
As consciousness fades and perishes, one immediately passes away.
"The days of my life are hastening to their end; as I speak these words, tears flow from me, and I require assistance to rise from my seat. Is this not suffering?
He replied, "It is indeed suffering."
Third is the suffering of illness.
The body is composed of the harmonious combination of earth, water, fire, and wind;
if even one of these four elements becomes unbalanced, one hundred and one illnesses arise.
When the four great elements are out of harmony, four hundred and four diseases arise simultaneously.
When the earth element is disturbed, the entire body is in pain;
when the water element is disturbed, the entire body becomes swollen and distended.
When the fire element is disturbed, the entire body suffers from feverish heat;
when the wind element is disturbed, the entire body becomes rigid and stiff, with pain in all the joints as if being flogged with a staff;
as the four elements advance and recede, the hands and feet become useless.
Their vital energy was utterly exhausted, such that they required assistance to sit or rise;
their mouths were parched and lips withered, their sinews snapped and noses cracked;
their eyes could no longer perceive forms, and their ears could no longer hear sounds.
Impure fluids flow from his body as he lies upon them;
harboring bitter anguish in his heart, he speaks with constant lamentation.
His six kin stand by his side, watching him day and night without ceasing for even a moment.
"Sweet food and drink, upon entering the mouth, all become bitter. Is this not suffering?
He replied, "It is indeed suffering."
Fourth is the suffering of death.
At the time of a person's death, the four hundred and four illnesses arise simultaneously;
the four elements seek to disperse, and the soul-spirit is unsettled.
At the time of death, the "sword-wind" (*śastravāyu*) dissolves the physical form, causing pain in every part of the body.
Cold sweat flows forth, and both hands feel only empty space.
Family members, both inside and outside the home, stand at one's side.
Grief, sorrow, and lamentation pierce to the very marrow of the bones, such that one cannot bear it.
The wind departs and the breath disperses; the fire is extinguished and the body grows cold; the soul has departed.
The body lies straight and rigid, no longer possessing any consciousness.
Within ten days, the flesh rotted and blood flowed; it became bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling, such that one could not even approach it.
He abandoned it in the wilderness, where flocks of birds devoured the flesh until it was gone, leaving behind withered bones and a skull scattered in different places.
"Is this suffering? "It is truly suffering," he replied.
"This is the suffering of separation from those one loves."
The members of the household—those within and without, brothers, wives, and children—were once bound by mutual affection;
yet in a single day they were ruined and lost.

Plundered and robbed by others, they were scattered in all directions: the father to the east, the son to the west, the mother to the south, and the daughter to the north, no longer remaining in one place.
When people become slaves, each feels sorrow at heart;
they call out inwardly as their breath is severed, left in utter darkness with no prospect of ever seeing one another again. Is this not suffering?
The answer is: Truly it is suffering.
There are six kinds of suffering: the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
for instance, when a household possesses wealth and property, they expend them in pursuit of official rank.
Hoping for wealth and status, he sought them without ceasing;
eventually, he obtained them and was appointed to a frontier post.
Before long, however, he greedily seized the property of the people.
When one is slandered by others and suddenly finds oneself in trouble,
being brought in a caged cart with immeasurable suffering and anxiety, not knowing whether life or death will come on what day—
this is indeed suffering.
The answer is: Truly it is suffering.
This is the suffering of association with the seven types of those one hates.
Worldly people, being shallow and vulgar, dwell amidst desire and contend over matters that are not urgent.
They continued to kill and harm one another until they became great enemies;
each fled from the other, seeking concealment but finding no place to hide.
Each sharpened his sword and arrows, slung his bow over his shoulder, and took up his staff.
They encountered each other on a narrow path where bows were drawn and arrows fixed upon trees;
with two blades facing one another, they did not know who would emerge victorious.
At that moment, their fear was immeasurable.
"Is this suffering? He replied, "It is truly suffering. [These are] the eight types of suffering:
sorrow, lamentation, distress, and pain.
In this human life, even a hundred years is long; those with short lifespans perish in the womb.
Even if one should live a full hundred years, half is spent in the night, and the remainder is further diminished.
For fifty years,
he was intoxicated by wine and afflicted by disease, unable to function as a human being;
during his youth, he was so foolish that for fifteen years he did not know the rules of propriety.
I am over eighty years old, aged, dull-witted, and lacking wisdom.
My ears are deaf and my eyes are dim; I no longer possess the capacity for the Dharma.
The world is about to fall into chaos, with droughts, fires, and heavy frosts such that the seeds sown in the fields will not ripen.
Within the household, both inside and out, there are many ailments and pains.
In managing one's livelihood, there is a fondness for loss; officials have imposed various levies, and one is imprisoned in a jail with no known date of release.
Brothers and sons have traveled far away and have not yet returned.
His family lived in poverty and cold, lacking both food and clothing;
his neighboring villages and hamlets could not provide for the communal sacrifices;
when a family member died, there was nothing with which to prepare the funeral rites.
In springtime, when sowing and planting, there are no oxen for plowing.
On festival days, we gather together; we ought to rejoice and face one another with shared sorrow. Is this not suffering?
He replied, "It is truly suffering.
At that time, the five kings and several million people in the assembly,
upon hearing this teaching on the Truth of Suffering, had their minds opened and attained awakening.
He immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Now, observing the palace as one would view a foul latrine, he found nothing in it to delight him;
he then renounced his royal throne, entrusted it to his younger brother, and left home to practice the Way.
Practicing all meritorious virtues daily without weariness, from the *Pañcarājaka-sūtra*. 8.

The Brahmin King who Renounced His Royal Stipend and Attained the Way through Almsgiving; the Brahmin King who Renounced His Royal Stipend and Attained the Way through Almsgiving, [in] the Kingdom of Tāmaṭa. Eight.
There was a Brahmin king who,
having renounced his royal stipend, devoted himself extensively to heterodox paths.
One day, the king suddenly gave rise to a virtuous mind and desired to practice great giving.
It was like the custom of certain brahmins who accumulated treasures as high as mountains; when anyone came to beg, they were told to take whatever they wished for themselves,
yet even after taking handfuls by the pound day after day, the accumulation did not diminish.
The Buddha, knowing that this king’s past merit made him ready for deliverance,
transformed himself into a brahmin and went to his kingdom.
The king came out to meet him;
having paid his respects and inquired after his well-being, he said, "What do you seek? Do not hesitate or feel any doubt. The brahmin replied:
"I have come from afar wishing to beg for precious jewels to build a house.
The king said, "Excellent!
Take as much as you wish, even a heavy handful."
The brahmin took a handful of rice, walked seven paces,
and returned to place it back in its original spot.
The king asked:
"Why do you not take it?
The brahmin replied,
"This is merely sufficient to build a hut."
Furthermore, when taking a wife, both [the man and the woman] must be sufficient for use; for this reason, he did not take one.
The King said, "Take another three handfuls."
The brahmin immediately took it up,
walked seven steps, and then returned to place it back in its original spot.
The king asked the brahmin:
"Why is it so? He replied, "This is sufficient to take a wife."
Furthermore, he possesses no fields, slaves, oxen, or horses;
even when calculated, his resources are insufficient.
For this reason, he has stilled his worldly ambitions.
The king said,
"Take another seven handfuls.
The brahmin immediately took them.
He walked seven steps and then returned to place them back in their original position.
The king asked,
"For what reason did you do this again?"
The brahmin replied,
"If there are sons or daughters,
there will be the expenses for their marriages and the associated auspicious or inauspicious rites."
"Calculating that it would not suffice for my needs, I did not take it.
The King said,
"Take all the accumulated treasures and offer them to me."
The brahmin accepted it and departed;
the king, greatly wondering at this,
questioned him again regarding his intention.
The brahmin replied,
"I have always lived by begging for alms. Reflecting deeply,
I realize that the human life spent in this world is but brief."
All things are impermanent; morning and evening are difficult to preserve.
As causes and conditions weigh heavily upon one, sorrow and suffering deepen day by day. To accumulate treasures as vast as mountains does not benefit oneself;
the schemes and plots born of greed result only in fruitless toil.
"It would be better to quiet the mind and seek the Way of non-action;
therefore, I do not accept it. With these words, the King’s mind was opened and liberated.
"I pray that you will grant me your enlightened teaching.
Thereupon, the brahmin manifested the radiant marks of a Buddha and leaped into the air, remaining suspended there.
He spoke these verses for them:
"Though one were to acquire a hoard of precious jewels so vast they reach the heavens,
and fill the entire world in this manner, it would not equal the essential point of seeing the Path."
The unwholesome appears as wholesome; that which is craving resembles the absence of craving;
and that which is suffering has the appearance of pleasure—the King sees these, yet the madman does not grow weary of them.
The Buddha’s light shone afar across heaven and earth.
Hearing this verse, they leaped for joy with great delight;
the king and his ministers immediately received the five precepts.
Attaining the Path of the Srotāpanna, from the *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga), Volume 16. 9.
King Mada hears the Dharma from an Arhat and attains the Way; King Mada hears the Dharma from an Arhat and attains the Way. Chapter Nine: The King of the Nine Realms.
His name was Mada.
He mobilized an army of several million selected men for a campaign of conquest.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had attained the path of an arhat.
He entered the kingdom to beg for alms,
but was arrested and taken to the royal palace.
The king ordered him to tend the state horses.
He practiced austerities for seven days.
The king came in person to observe him.
When the bhikṣu saw the king, he [thought]:
He leaped lightly into the air and hovered there, manifesting his majestic spiritual power.
The king was struck with terror; he prostrated himself, striking his head in repentance, and said, "I am truly foolish, failing to distinguish between the true and the false."
He interrogated those both inside and outside [the palace], asking who had commanded the divine being to perform this deed,
saying, "Now there must be someone to be punished by execution.
The bhikṣu informed the king.
"It is not the fault of the king or the people of the country.
Since my past lives, I have practiced the Way and constantly made offerings to my teachers.
At that time, I prepared a drink for my teacher."
The teacher said to me,
"First wash your hands, and only then shall you drink.
With a foolish mind, I thought to myself:
The Master also does not keep official horses.
For what reason did you not wash your hands beforehand?
The Master then said to me:
"How can you now think lightly of this, which will be heavy in its consequences?
Upon hearing these words, I became sorrowful and anxious.
The teacher perceived my state of mind.
He then thought:
"I shall surely enter parinirvāṇa;
why should I cause people distress?"
That very night, during the third watch,
the Master entered parinirvāṇa.
From long ago until now, we have each undergone birth and death again and again.
Now, because of this, he undergoes the retribution for his past misdeeds.
He shall tend horses for seven days.
Indeed, good and evil deeds invariably bring about calamity or fortune, just as a shadow follows a form.
When the king heard the bhikṣu’s discourse on sin and merit, his mind was awakened and he rejoiced; he requested permission to take refuge in this divine man.
The bhikṣu replied:
"You, my lord, should take refuge in the Buddha;
the Buddha is the teacher of the three realms for both you,
O King, and the people of the land."
They all followed the bhikṣu out to where the Buddha was,
prostrated themselves in salutation, received the five precepts,
and became upāsakas.
The Buddha then manifested his physical marks and sublime features, with majestic spiritual power illuminating heaven and earth, for the sake of the king and the people of the land;
he further preached to them the impermanence, suffering, and emptiness [of all phenomena].
At that time, the king attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The people of the kingdom all received the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions;
they took refuge in the Triple Gem and observed the fasts month after month.
Considered a standard teaching from the *Mādāngarāja-sūtra*. 10.

King Gandhara Abandons External Practices and Internally Attains the Path of Srotāpanna. Regarding the time when King Gandhara abandoned external practices and internally attained the path of Srotāpanna: At that time, there was a king.
He was named Gandha.
He served the Brahmins while dwelling in the mountains;
there were many fruit trees, which woodcutters destroyed.
Then the brahmin took him before the king and reported his misconduct,
stating that he had destroyed the fruit trees and requesting that the king punish and execute him; the king held the brahmin in high esteem and attended to his service.
They were immediately slaughtered.
Not long thereafter,
there was an ox that ate people's rice.
The owner then beat the ox until one horn was broken;
blood flowed down its face and the pain was unbearable.
The ox went directly to the king's presence and spoke to him.
"I have truly committed no offense in eating a small amount of rice from people;
now you have beaten my horns to pieces.
Your Majesty understands the speech of birds and beasts."
He said to the ox,
"I shall treat you and then kill you.
The ox replied:
"Though this man has been killed, it does not stop my pain;
I only wish to exhort you that henceforth you do not cause suffering to others.
The king was then moved by these words.
"I serve the brahmins;
it is they who sit under fruit trees and command me to kill people, not this ox."
He then called out to the brahmin and asked,
"What merit is there in following this path now?
The brahmin replied:
"One may thereby ward off calamities, bring about blessings, and attain wealth, nobility, and long life.
The King asked again,
"Can one thereby escape from birth and death?"
He replied,
"One cannot escape from birth and death.
The king then went to where the Buddha was.
Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage to the Buddha and said:
"I have heard that the Way of the Buddha is most supreme;
it transforms all under heaven, and those delivered by it are countless."
"May I receive the words of the Dharma to reform myself.
The Buddha then conferred upon the king the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions,
and explained to him that all things in heaven and earth, among humans and beings, are subject to birth and none escape death.
Through practicing generosity and maintaining the precepts, one obtains blessings in the present life.
For those who cultivate patience, diligence, mental conduct, and wisdom, their merit is immeasurable;
in future lives they may be reborn in the heavens or even become a Cakravartin King.
One may attain the unconditioned path that transcends the world.
As the Buddha manifested his physical marks, signs, majestic power, and radiant glory,
the king’s mind was filled with joy and attained liberation.
He attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Seven days later, his life came to an end, and he was reborn in the heavens. (From the *Gandhārava-rāja-sūtra*).
11. King Puhua Meets the Buddha and Attains the Way. Regarding King Puhua of the country of Yan who met the Buddha and attained the Way:
there was once a king of the country of Yan named Puhua.
Personally upholding the Buddha-dharma, he has never been partial or unjust.
He is always compassionate and merciful;
yet, the ignorant people within his realm do not know the Triple Gem.
Whenever he observed the fasts and ascended to high places to gaze upon the landscape,
he would invariably return with his head and face bowed in prostration as a mark of reverence.
The ministers and subjects of the kingdom marveled at the King’s behavior in this regard.
They deliberated among themselves, saying:
"The King occupies the most honored position among the myriad people;
far and near, all revere and submit to him, and all follow his lead."
With what intent did he wish to humiliate the majestic deportment by prostrating himself with his head to the ground?
The ministers wished to remonstrate but dared not do so.
Not long after the king had departed from the palace with several thousand officials and commoners, they encountered a wandering mendicant.
The King descended from his carriage and set aside his parasol;
his retinue performed a prostration before him,
and he then returned with them.
The preparations for the meal were consequently not completed;
the ministers remonstrated, saying,
"Your Majesty is most exalted."
"Why should you, a mendicant on the road, prostrate yourself with your head to the ground?
Of all things in the world, the head and face are most precious;
moreover, as a king, you are not like others."
The King commanded his ministers to seek the head of a deceased person as well as the heads of the six domestic animals.
The ministers searched everywhere; it was only after many days that they finally found them.
The king said,
"Sell it in the marketplace.
His ministers sold it.
"The heads of oxen, horses, pigs, and sheep have all been sold,
but the human head has not yet been sold.
The king said:
Whether noble or base, they were sold away;
if they did not sell, they were forced to beg from others. Thus it continued day after day, yet they could not sell, and there was no one to take them as beggars;
their heads all became swollen and foul-smelling.
The king then became greatly incensed and said to his ministers,
"You say this."
"A human head is most precious and must not be defiled or insulted.
Why is it that this human head is being begged for and yet no one takes it?
He then ordered his carriage to be prepared and set out for the vast wilderness, intending to question [the being there].
The ministers trembled with awe as they went outside the city walls.
He addressed the ministers, saying,
"Do you perhaps remember the time of my late sovereign?"
"Is there a young boy who constantly carries an umbrella?
The minister replied, "I know him indeed.
The King said:
"Where is this child now? He replied,
"He has been dead for seventeen years."
The king asked,
"What is this child like as a person— how is he in terms of good and evil?
They replied:
"Your servants have often observed him serving the former king;
he maintained himself with purity, fasting, reverence, and sincerity, and spoke nothing that was not in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus the King addressed his ministers."
"Now, if you were to see the clothes this child wore while he was alive,
would you recognize them?
The ministers replied:
"Although it has been a long time, I still recognize it myself.
Your Majesty, have the clothes of the small child who previously went missing brought here," he said.
"Is this not so? The ministers replied, "It is so.
The king said:
"If you were now to see this child's body, would you recognize it?
The ministers and subordinates remained silent for a long while before responding, saying:
I myself feared that my own ignorance and blindness would prevent me from recognizing it immediately.
When the practitioner I had previously seen arrived,
the King was filled with great joy.
Furthermore, when he was a practitioner of the Way, he offered his head for sale, yet no one would take it.
Now I wish to show you its beginning and end;
fortunately, we have met.
"I pray that you will provide guidance.
The practitioner then spoke for the sake of the ministers and subordinates:
"The King was originally a young boy who held a parasol during the time of the former king."
He constantly followed the former king,
observing the precepts and fasts, practicing the True Dharma, maintaining purity of mind, and refraining from all evils. Subsequently,
after passing away from that life, he was reborn as a prince.
"That we have now attained such noble and honorable status is entirely due to our past practice of fasting and observing the precepts.
Among the ministers, both high and low, there was not one who did not say in unison:
'We are fortunate to have encountered and beheld this man of the Way.'"
"May you take pity on this foolish and deluded one and grant me the status of your disciple.
The practitioner told the ministers and citizens,
"I have a Great Master."
He should then accept the inquiry.
The ministers replied,
"We pray that for the remainder of our lives, we may receive these words of the Dharma."
The practitioner said,
"My teacher's name is Buddha;
he is able to fly through the air, and his head is radiant with light."
He manifested his body in myriad forms through various transformations;
he walked alone throughout the three realms with no one equal to him.
His disciples were pure and all became śramaṇas.
The teachings he imparts for the sake of liberation are never in vain.
The ministers then addressed the practitioner, asking,
"Is it possible to have an audience with the Buddha?"
"How far is it from here?
The practitioner replied,
"Very well."
He said, "I shall inform the World-Honored One.
Traveling more than six thousand li,
the practitioner immediately flew to Śrāvastī.
He reported this in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Tomorrow you shall arrive at the kingdom of Fu-yen. When they were about to reach it, he manifested his majestic spiritual power.
The king and his ministers, carrying flowers and incense, went out of the city to welcome the Buddha.

Beholding the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, joy and trepidation welled up within them simultaneously; they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to pay him homage and addressed the Buddha, saying:
I am deeply grateful that the World-Honored One,
together with the assembly of monks, has condescended to travel so far to this land;
the King has provided offerings with his whole heart.
With his own hands, he served the water for washing and performed the ritual of consecration;
when the prayer was finished,
the Buddha smiled, and light of five colors issued from his mouth.
Ānanda said, "The Buddha does not smile without cause.
He replied:
In the past, during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha,
the king was the son of a great clan family;
his father made offerings to the Triple Gem.
The father commanded his son to pass on the incense.
At that time, there was an attendant who,
in his heart, held the son in low esteem and did not give him the incense.
"Sin and merit respond like echoes, briefly summoning the retribution of service.
Because he served the Dharma without fail, he has now become a king.
If I attain the Way, I shall deliver this man."
By understanding the meaning of the fundamental and the derivative, one immediately attains the stage of Srotāpanna.
The people of the kingdom all received the five precepts and practiced the ten wholesome paths; this is from the *Pudada Wang Jing* (Sutra of King Puda).
*Jīnglǜ yìxiàng* (Distinguishing Phenomena in the Sūtras and Vinaya), Scroll 27;

13. King Much Wisdom Feigns Madness to Escape Calamity. 1. Hengxing Feidiao was killed by a treacherous minister; his spirit returned as a king.
Hengxing Feidiao was killed by a treacherous minister; his spirit returned as a king. Once, King Bimbisāra...
There was a high minister who,
having committed an offense, was banished to the Southern Mountains, a thousand *li* from the capital.
Since ancient times, there had been no place where people were not familiar with the five grains.
When the great minister arrived there,
the spring waters flowed freely and the five grains ripened in abundance.
Those from the various kingdoms of the four quarters who were suffering from hunger and cold came to this place.
Within a few years, there were three or four thousand households.
To those who arrived, he granted fields so that they might gain a livelihood.
Among them were three elders, various senior householders, and those of advanced age.
They deliberated together on the fact that the state was without a ruler.
Because he himself lacked a chief minister, they went to the residence of a high minister and appointed him as king.
The minister replied to the elder,
"If you would have me as king,
it must be according to the law of all kings."
The ministers on the left and right, the civil and military officers,
and those from high and low who present tribute, as well as those who provide women for the palace, open up royal estates, or pay taxes in grain and silk, shall follow the laws of the common people.
The elders of the various states said:
"So be it; we shall obey your command.
They followed the king's law and immediately installed him as king.
He appointed his ministers;
men of both civil and military rank, high and low,
were mobilized to build city walls, construct dwellings, and erect palaces and towers.
The people were so afflicted by bitter suffering that they could no longer endure it;
they all conceived thoughts of plotting against the king.
A group of treacherous ministers then took the king out on a hunt.
Thirty or forty *li* from the city,
they sought the king in a wilderness marsh intending to kill him.
The king asked those around him:
"For what reason do you kill me?
They replied in unison,
"The people long for abundance and joy, and they serve Your Majesty with propriety."
The people, distressed by hardship, contemplate rebellion; they would ruin their own households to seek the welfare of the state.
The King addressed them, saying:
"It is you who act for yourselves; it was not my original intent."
"May the gods and spirits bear witness to my wrongful execution.
Grant me the fulfillment of one vow, and I shall die without regret.
Thereupon, he made this aspiration:
"In the beginning, I reclaimed the wasteland and cleared the soil to nourish the people;
all who came were brought to life, and their wealth and joy were boundless.
They themselves raised me up to be their king."
"According to the records, these various nations have together committed this act, yet now they turn against me and kill me.
I have truly harbored no ill will toward these people.
If I am to die, I vow to become a rākṣasa."
"I shall enter my former body again to take revenge for this enmity.
Thereupon, he strangled him to death, abandoned the corpse, and departed.
Three days later, the king's spirit returned to his body.
He called himself Āravā.
He immediately rose and entered the palace,
where he killed the new king, along with the ladies of the harem and the treacherous ministers around him.
Desiring to kill everyone,
the three elders of the kingdom bound themselves with straw ropes and came forward to confess their crimes to the rākṣasa.
"This is the doing of treacherous ministers;
it is not something that ordinary people could possibly have known.
We beg for your originality and forgiveness, and pray that you will return to govern the state."
He said, "I am a rākṣasa.
When engaging with humans for food and drink, I must consume human flesh.
Rākṣasas are quick-tempered and do not consider difficulties when they are provoked."
The Three Elders said,
"Since this state belongs to the King, it should be as previously arranged; however,
regarding the food and drink required, we shall establish a proper order of precedence."
The state elders went out together to proclaim to the people:
"From this point forward,
each household shall send forth one young child."
He was born to serve as food;
he consumed three or four thousand households of rākṣasa kings,
with only one household remaining that were disciples of the Buddha.
While living at home, he diligently observed the Buddha’s five precepts.
The virtuous man, both great and small, was filled with anguish and wept;
from afar, he turned toward Vulture Peak and paid homage to the Buddha.
He repented and reproached himself.
The Buddha, seeing his suffering with his eye of the Way,
spoke these words of his own accord:
Because this child was destined to deliver countless people,
he then flew alone to the gate of the rākṣasa and manifested a transformative radiance that illuminated the interior of his palace.
When the rākṣasa saw the light, he suspected it was some extraordinary person;
he immediately went out to see the Buddha and, conceiving a malicious intent,
desired to approach and seize the Buddha, but the light pierced his eyes.
Carrying mountains and vomiting fire, they were all transformed into dust.
Only after becoming exhausted from this prolonged struggle did they submit and convert.
They invited the Buddha to enter and sit, bowing their heads to the ground in prostration.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he listened with single-minded devotion;
he immediately received the five precepts and became an upāsaka.
Meanwhile, the village official, pressing him for food, seized the boy and took him back.
The family members wailed and followed along the road;
countless onlookers were moved to grief.
The official took the child and held the food before the rākṣasa.
The rākṣasa held the child up with his hand,
knelt on one knee, and addressed the Buddha.
The people of the country then took turns offering their children as food.
"I have now received the five precepts from the Buddha and may no longer eat human flesh.
I beg to offer this child as a gift to the Buddha to serve as his attendant."
The Buddha accepted it for him.
He preached the Dharma and offered prayers of blessing.
The rākṣasa was filled with joy and attained the stage of srotāpanna.
The Buddha placed the child in his almsbowl,
carried him out through the palace gate, and returned him to his parents, saying to them:
"Quickly nourish this child and do not grieve further.
When the multitude saw the Buddha, there was none who was not struck with wonder, exclaiming, "What deity is this? What merit does this child possess?"
He alone rescued them;
he snatched back from the rākṣasa those who were being devoured and returned them to their parents.
The Buddha then spoke this verse:
The virtue of precepts is to be relied upon; the retribution of merit always follows oneself.
Seeing the Dharma, one becomes a leader among men, and in the end remains far from the three evil realms.
Through heedfulness in the precepts, one eliminates suffering and fear; the retribution of merit makes one honored throughout the three realms.
"Demons, dragons, and the harms of evil poisons cannot afflict those who possess the precepts.
All who behold the Buddha’s light or images become disciples of the Buddha.
Hearing these verses, they rejoice and all attain the stages of the Path. — From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Five.

2. Moved by the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one attains the stage of Srotāpanna. Moved by the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one attains the stage of Srotāpanna. Part Two: In the city of Śrāvastī, there were two merchants.
One of them thought to himself:
The Buddha’s body is sixteen feet tall, with a complexion like purple-gold.
Upon his crown is a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), and the radiance from his neck and back is so majestic as to be beyond words.
The Buddha is like an emperor, and the śramaṇas are like loyal ministers.
The Buddha set forth the clear Dharma, and the śramaṇa recited and proclaimed this King of Verses;
thus he knew that the Buddha was worthy of veneration.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, gazed upon him intently.
The person’s heart was filled with joy as if he had obtained a treasure.
He thought to himself:
"The Buddha is like the ox, and his disciples are like the cart."
Just as that ox-drawn carriage turns toward the east, west, south,
or north, so it is with the Buddha.
Knowing that those who harbor evil thoughts will surely incur calamity, the Buddha regards them with deep compassion and pity.
That man’s heart was evil, so the two of them departed together.
Upon reaching a pavilion thirty *li* away, they stayed overnight and purchased wine to drink,
while discussing and settling the complexities of their legal disputes.
As for those with wholesome thoughts,
the Four Heavenly Kings dispatch benevolent deities to protect them;
as for those with poisonous thoughts, [the same applies].
The ghosts and spirits of Mount Tai caused the wine to enter his belly;
it was as if fire were burning his body.
He emerged from the pavilion and lay exposed to the elements, rolling about until he fell into a carriage rut.
At dawn, a merchant’s caravan of five hundred chariots passed over it.
A companion saw this and said,
"I am now ruined."
Upon returning to his country, he was suspected of having taken the goods and departed;
thus, he deemed it unrighteous and abandoned both his person and his wealth to leave.

for all forms of affection must inevitably end in separation.
"Whatever is born must inevitably perish.

There was a brahmin of great lineage named Yajñadatta,

There was a maidservant named Yellow Head who constantly guarded the Malla garden.

"I would rather take this rice and give it as an offering to that śramaṇa;

At that time, the maidservant Huangtou immediately went forward and entered the Malla Garden.

He immediately turned his carriage around, entered the garden on foot,
and was seen from a distance by Yellow-Head (Pāṇḍuka), who recognized that it was Prasenajit coming.
His gait and movements were not those of an ordinary person;
he immediately went forward to welcome him, saying, "Welcome, Great Being; please be seated here."
He immediately removed a garment and spread it out for the king to sit upon.
Yellow-Head asked,
"May I inquire whether you require water to wash your feet?"
The king said, "So be it.
He immediately took water and gave it to the king,

He asked the king again,
"Would you like to wash your face?
and immediately gave water to the king once more for washing his face.
He asked the king again,
"Would you like to drink?
Thereupon, he went to the pond and washed his hands once more.
He took a fine lotus leaf, filled it with water, and offered it to the king.
He then asked the king,
"I wonder if you would like to lie down and rest?"
He then removed another garment and spread it for the king.
Having seen that the king was lying down,
he knelt before him and massaged his feet and other limbs.
She relieved the king’s fatigue.
Her hair was yellow and her body was like that of a celestial being—delicate, soft, and exquisite.

He thought to himself:
"It is truly marvelous that this girl is so intelligent;

The king then asked,

She replied:
"I am a maidservant of the house of Yaśodā;
I was assigned by my master to guard this garden.

The king’s various ministers followed the tracks of the king’s chariot to the park,

The king said,

He replied, "This is a maidservant; how can she be your wife?
The king said:
"There is no suffering;
let us simply discuss the price.
The Brahmin said:
If one were to discuss its value,
it would be worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold;

"I now offer this to Your Majesty.
The King said, "Not so."
"I shall take her as my wife;
why do you not give me the price?
He then produced one hundred thousand taels of gold.
He received the brahmin and immediately escorted him into the palace,

Because she had previously been in the Mallikā Garden, he immediately prophesied that she would become the Lady Mallikā.

She further thought:

By these causes and conditions, she has now been spared from slavery and enjoys such happiness. [End of] Volume Thirteen of the First Division of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
7. King Subhadra Makes a Vow to Consecrate the Buddha. Long ago, there was a Buddha.
He was titled Shiwu (Beginningless).
At that time, there was a king named Haoxin (Good Faith).

He planted a nyagrodha tree and,
beneath it, prepared a sandalwood seat for the Buddha.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
If the king does not see the Buddha,
he shall regard the nyagrodha tree as the Buddha-tree;
seeing it shall be as seeing the Buddha.
Day after day he went to sit beneath a tree;
at his usual place of sitting, he imagined hearing the instructions and admonitions.
The king had a maidservant.
His name was Kulu; he constantly attended upon the king.
Out of jealousy, the queen hired a Brahmin to cast a spell to kill the Bodhi tree.
At the house of a certain brahmin,
on the seventh night of the fourth month, he took the brain of a large poisonous snake from the southern mountains and smeared it upon a tree;
the tree immediately withered and died.
The king was immediately overcome with grief and could not restrain himself;
at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month, when the morning star appeared, he took perfumed water of five colors and gathered flowers to pour over this tree.
He was immediately reborn once more.
The king then made this aspiration:
"May the birth of all Buddhas of the ten directions always take place on this very day."
The day on which I attained the Way is this very day;
the day of my parinirvāṇa shall also be this very day.
From this time forth, the Buddhas shall appear in the world.

This represents husbands of later generations going away on journeys.
A wife commits adultery with another and consumes his wealth.
As for the sixth dream, a fox eats from a golden bed and golden vessels;
this signifies that in future generations, those who are currently lowly and base will become more honorable and noble.
Those who possess property are revered by all;
yet the descendants of dukes and marquises may become even more poor and lowly,
occupying the lowest seats and receiving food and drink last.
The seventh dream, in which a great ox returns to suckle from its young calf,
signifies that in future generations people will lack propriety and righteousness.
The mother acts as a procuress for her daughter, luring other men to have sexual intercourse with her;
she then demands wealth from them on behalf of her daughter to provide for herself,
yet remains devoid of any sense of shame.

The eighth dream was that four oxen came bellowing from the four directions, rushing toward one another as if about to fight; though they were on the verge of colliding, they did not know where the oxen had gone.
This refers to the emperors, high officials, and common people of future generations.
All lack a heart of utmost sincerity;
they deceive one another, and are characterized by folly and anger.
They do not revere Heaven and Earth, and for this reason, rain and moisture do not fall at their proper times.
The local officials and the people prayed for rain.
Clouds arose from the four directions, accompanied by the sound of thunder and lightning.
The officials and the people all said:
When it rains for but a brief moment, the clouds disperse and the rain ceases, so that it does not fall.
Why is this? Because the sovereign, high officials, and the people lack loyalty, integrity, benevolence, and compassion.
The ninth dream was that of a large pond whose center was turbid while its four edges were clear;
this signifies that in future generations, the central lands will be in turmoil and governance will be unjust,
such that the people will be unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward their elders.
The borderlands will be level and pure;
the people will live in harmony, filially obeying their two parents.
As for the tenth dream, that of a great mountain stream flowing bright red: [it signifies...]
In future generations, various nations will give rise to anger and strife, mobilizing armies and gathering multitudes to attack and subjugate one another.
They shall employ chariot troops, infantry, and cavalry,
engaging in mutual combat and killing one another in numbers beyond reckoning.
The dead man’s blood flowed along the road until it was bright red.
The king knelt down on his right knee and said,
"Having received the Buddha's teachings and precepts, my heart is immediately filled with joy."
Having paid homage to the Buddha,
he returned to his palace and stripped the chief consort and all the high ministers of their stipends and emoluments.
The *Sutra on the Ten Dreams of King Piliśāṇi*, in which he no longer believed in heterodox paths or Brahmins. 3.

The Wicked Young King Circumambulates the Stupa to Disperse the Bandits. In the kingdom of Zhimou, there was a king. For three months, the wicked young king circumambulated the stupa to disperse the bandits.
He was named King Wicked Youth (Duṣyanta).
There was no one in this world who did not submit to him.
His mother instructed the king, saying:
Even if you encounter the calamity of approaching death, take care not to circumambulate Buddhist temples counter-clockwise;
you must instead keep them to your right. Be careful not to violate this teaching of mine.
At that time, the wicked young king—
He mobilized a great army to attack the city of Pure Blood (Śuddhodana).
With his own hands he grasped a sword and slew three hundred million people.
Later, in battle, he was defeated.
Mounting his elephant, he galloped away while looking back at the Buddhist temple;
remembering his mother’s instructions, he turned the elephant to the right.
Seeing this, the enemy forces each scattered and took cover.
When the king saw that the bandits had retreated,
he immediately pursued them; having reached their original city, he captured the bandit king himself and then remembered the Buddha’s words.
"To take refuge in the Buddha is to rely on the most honored and supreme one, to whom none can equal.

Had I not circumambulated him clockwise, how could I have destroyed these bandits? This is from the sixteenth fascicle of the *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga), with a brief parallel found in the *Jiu za piyu jing* (Old Collection of Miscellaneous Parables).
4. King Āṭavika Attains Liberation through His Daughter-in-law. Four Buddhas were staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a king named Āṭavika.
He was named Fentuandan.
He greatly esteemed the Way and its Virtue,
providing daily meals for more than a thousand Daoist practitioners.
The king said to himself:
"My wisdom is peerless; I bind my belly with iron, fearing constantly that my wisdom might overflow."
Now, wishing to arrange a marriage for his son,
he asked his ministers,
"Is there anyone in the world whose wisdom is equal to mine?"
"If such a person exists,
I wish to take his daughter for my son; however,
there is no one such in the kingdom."
The king dispatched a messenger to seek him in other regions.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he asked the people there whether there was a Buddha.
The messenger said:
"Does the Buddha have a daughter?
He replied,
"The Way-man has no daughter."
The messenger said,
"Who is next? He replied:
Anāthapiṇḍika was virtuous and fond of the Way; he had a daughter who was foremost [among women].
The messenger asked, "In what way is she foremost?"
He replied:
"In the past, I contended with Prince Jeta over a garden and field, which I then offered to the Buddha.
Carrying hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of gold on elephants, I did not covet these heavy treasures, but set my mind solely upon doing good."
The messenger immediately went to the residence of Anāthapiṇḍada and returned to report to the king.
The king then hurried there to see him.
King Nala’s body was entirely without clothing;
he was naked, black, and ugly, appearing like a ghost.
Ānanda-bhṛtī asked him:
"What do you seek?
The king said,

Therefore, I have come to request your daughter for my son.
Ānanda-bhṛtya called him forward, seated him, and said,
"I shall inform the Buddha."
He reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Give it to him.
Ānanda-bhadrika said:
Fearing that he would kill his daughter,
[the father] said, "No," but the Buddha said,
"It is not so," and he then gave her to him.
The woman’s name was Samagha;
she shall deliver eighty thousand people in the land of Nang.
Ānanda-bhṛtya then again questioned the Buddha.
Her heart harbored resentment in truth;
she immediately returned and said to the King of Nala:
"I shall give my daughter to you."
The king immediately performed the rites of marriage and welcomed him back to his own country.
That night, the prince went to where Samajja was;
Samajja kicked the prince with his foot, knocking him to the ground.
Thus, for four or five days,
the Prince did not dare to go out again.
The King’s consort questioned him about this.
"Why do you not go?
The Prince remained silent.
The lady then went to where Triśaṅku was.
"I have taken a wife for my son, who is now to serve him.
For what reason has my son humiliated her? Samajjha replied:
The queen, the crown prince, and the people of the kingdom all had bodies like those of dogs, no different from common beasts.
The queen said to the king:
The King’s wisdom is peerless; he sought a son-in-law from afar,
yet he showed no fear or hesitation in humiliating my son and further reviled me face to face.
When the king heard this,
he immediately went to where Samajika was; however,
Samajika did not come out to pay his respects.
The king said,
"I have brought a new bride from afar;
is it right for you to insult my wife to her face and further humiliate my son?"
Samajja replied, "It is so. The king,
seeing that the people within his realm were all like dogs and cattle,
was greatly alarmed and said:
I have always feared that my wisdom might burst forth from my belly;
therefore, I bind it with iron.
Daily, I provide food for more than a thousand Daoist practitioners.
"Who could possibly equal me,
yet instead reviles me? Samajja replied:
Men and women, old and young, were naked and facing one another;
though they had cultivated merit, they were still to be treated with contempt.
The king went to the teacher’s gate and related these matters in detail.
The Master said,
"Ask him again and again;
be careful not to become angry."
The king then asked in return,
"In what way are the people of your kingdom superior? Samajja replied:
In our country, both men and women wear robes;
those of high and low station occupy different positions so that their bodies do not come into view of one another.
There is a person of great name called Buddha.
He transformed and taught many thousands of billions of people, causing them all to attain the Way.
He could enter fire without being burned and enter water without being drowned.
He was able to encompass the suns and moons of the three thousandfold world system and the heavens and earths of the twelve thousand worlds.
He knows the affairs of the three periods of time;
his body is endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
he has attained mastery in the Way and its virtue, and is venerated and visited by all the devas.
The king said,
"Can the Buddha indeed be seen?
Samajja replied, "Yes."
"It can be brought by inviting him from afar.
The King said,
"Excellent!"
"How should we proceed? Samajja replied, "Only you,
O King of Incense, should follow behind me."
The lady and the crown prince both followed me.
Then Samajina ascended the high terrace and addressed him, saying:
"The King of Rājagṛha has now first heard the name of the Tathāgata."
"May the Buddha accept the King's meal tomorrow.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana to instruct the bhikṣus accordingly.
Tomorrow, we shall all go to the kingdom of Samajja.
We will cause the king, his queen,
and the crown prince to observe the fast and purify themselves, burn incense, prepare mats, and arrange the necessary provisions for the meal.
He provided for and attended upon one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
Then Samajja immediately resided with the king’s consort and the crown prince in the central courtyard.
"Let the arhats come first; the Buddha will arrive later and put on his robes.
Be careful not to be startled or afraid; follow what I do.
Then the Buddha and his bhikṣus each manifested their own transformations.
Śāriputra manifested as a pair of white elephants;

and the great bhikṣus each transformed their bodies.
He manifested various displays;
at times, all the geese descended from above simultaneously,
causing the people of the kingdom of Nan to be greatly alarmed.
Samagama said, "Do not fear.
The Buddha was the very last to emerge from the water and fire."
Samudra first paid homage to the Buddha;
the king, his consort, and the crown prince likewise paid their respects.
The arhats then took their seats, arranged in order according to seniority.
The queen and crown prince of King Samavarta proceeded next to prepare the bathing water and the utensils for the meal.
The people of the kingdom marveled that the king had closed his gates.
Greatly incensed, each of them took up an axe, intending to hack down the palace gate.
The Buddha said,
"I desire only that all people perform good deeds."
He immediately caused the palace walls to transform into crystal, so that those inside and outside could see one another; the people then desisted and did not dare to hack at them again.
At that time, Piṇḍola was sitting on the mountain.
Suddenly departing for a land of hardship,
he pricked the ground with a needle,
causing the thread to remain connected to his garment.

the mountain followed behind him.
A woman in that country who was pregnant saw the mountain approaching and feared she would fall from it.

Pindola looked back;
the mountain was hurled back to its original location eight thousand li away.

yet now you have missed the appointed time and killed another person.
The gravity of taking human life is something I do not approve of."
"From this day forward, you must not follow me for even the duration of a meal.
You shall attain parinirvāṇa only when Maitreya Buddha appears.
Piṇḍola remained silent, filled with sorrow and distress.
The king said to the Buddha,

whoever is inferior shall throw himself into a well."
The Buddha said, "Very well.
If you fail three times, you shall be cast into a well.
The King replied, "So be it."
The Buddha asked,
"What do you do when reciting the sūtras?
The king replied:
