I crawled along until I was completely prostrate on the ground.
The Buddha said:
"When I recite the sūtras, I sit or walk back and forth.
If one were to recite the sūtras while crawling on all fours, that would be the way of a dog;
Your Majesty, you are not like that."
The king wished to throw himself into the well, but he gripped the ground with both hands and refused to enter.
The Buddha said, "Leave him be.
Thereupon, the king returned to his kingdom and practiced the Way of the Buddha.
Samagama then attended upon the king’s consort and the crown prince;
in the kingdom of Nanda, he converted eighty thousand people.
All attained the four fruits of the śrāvaka; from the *Sūtra on the Division of the King of Śrāvastī*.
5. King Ajjuna’s Faith Arising from the Buddha. Regarding King Ajjuna’s faith arising from the Buddha: At one time there was a king.
It is named A-zhi.
Its governed territory extends for one hundred thousand li,
and its inhabitants are numerous and flourishing.
The king was exceedingly violent and lacked understanding of the Dharma;
he invaded neighboring kingdoms and oppressed the virtuous and good,
causing suffering to all those neighboring lands.
The Buddha, together with the great assembly, traveled to that kingdom.
When Aśmaka heard of this,
he and his thirty-two sons— each of whom was physically brave and robust— raised an army with malicious intent.
A multitude of several million people gathered together;
they intended to intercept him on the great road and resist the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"King Ajātaśatru and his son will harbor evil intentions toward me and the great assembly tomorrow.
How shall you subdue them?"
When the great beings and devas smiled, heaven and earth shook.
The Buddha asked, "Why do you smile?
Ānanda replied:
"It was merely a joke, King Ajātaśatru.
The Buddha said, "Ajātaśatru is foolish; he has conceived this evil intent."
They cause the people to incur transgressions;
yet, having mobilized a great army and relying on the strength of their men and horses,
even if they were to fill the four quarters of the world, they could not move a single hair of mine.
How much more so for only several million people.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Command all the wise ones to go forth, each carrying an alms bowl."
"Tomorrow we shall take our meal from within the army of King Ajātaśatru.
The king’s father and son, along with their vast host of troops, will cause the spirits and deities to tremble.
At that time, the Buddha will stand before us and emit a great radiance."
As they crossed through the kingdom of A-zhi from within the army,
the king’s drums no longer sounded;
bows and crossbows were not drawn, and blades and weapons were not raised.
The elephants and horses stumbled, and the infantry’s sinews cramped;
heaven and earth became dark and gloomy, and the sun and moon lost their light.
The king and his sons—
They were all bewildered and lost their breath, prostrating themselves on the ground and fleeing.
The Buddha and the great assembly remained where they were, each taking a full bowl of rice and proceeding to the king’s kingdom.
The city gates opened of their own accord.
The Buddha proceeded to the royal palace, entered the hall, and sat down;
all was silent and without sound.
Eighty-one thousand seven hundred devas and humans each took their seats;
the palace expanded of its own accord, and naturally, high thrones appeared with jeweled canopies and lattices, while the five musical tones played spontaneously.
The king and his sons said to one another,
"The power of a king is not equal to the power of the Way and its Virtue.
The soldiers were struck with alarm and fear.
The princes said,
"We have now heard that the Buddha has entered and is already within the palace;
we should return to meet him."
The king said, "What face would I have to meet the Buddha again?
Above, I would be ashamed before the gods; below, I would bring shame upon the people."
The sons said, "Since the Buddha is compassionate and does not harm the feelings of others,
the King shall now withdraw his troops and return to the palace with calm composure."
He met with the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage, and stepped forward to offer his apologies.
The Buddha said, "You are base and lowly, ignorant and obscure; having studied little since youth, you do not understand propriety or righteousness, being comparable only to wolves and beasts."
Foolish and deluded, we have transgressed against the devas and humans.
The Great Sage does not deign to look upon this remote and minor kingdom;
yet now, having wronged the World-Honored One, you have come from afar to this humble land, where our ruler and ministers are in rebellion.
"I only pray that the Celestial Honored One will take pity on this one who lacks wisdom.
Having already bestowed such profound grace upon the people through your teaching,
the King then again placed his head and face upon the ground, joined his palms, and withdrew to stand aside."
The king’s thirty-two sons, the high officials, the hundred ministers, and the commoners and subjects all repented their transgressions,
reproached themselves, and turned their minds single-mindedly toward the Buddha.
The king saw that eight hundred and ten thousand beings— both gods and humans— were all seated in rows upon lion thrones.
Within the jeweled lattice pavilion, celestial music played spontaneously.
Recognizing the Buddha’s divine and wondrous power,
the king commanded the ladies of the harem and the court maidservants.
They all came forth to pay homage to the Buddha.
The King prepared a meal of a hundred flavors and offered it entirely to the Queen and her thirty-two sons.
Crawling on his knees, he washed the water and personally served the portions.
He distributed the food until everyone, from the highest to the lowest, was fully satisfied; all were reverent and composed, eating with single-minded joy.
When the meal was finished, the king bowed his head before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
Having received the grace of the Heaven-among-Heavens,
and by virtue of the thickness of my past merits and the assistance of my late father, I have attained a position above the common people.
O World-Honored One, Great Sage!
I lament for the people of my country; let them seek the precepts and observe them throughout their lives.
To govern the people with justice and impartiality, by what means should one act?
One should form alliances with neighboring states, abandoning evil and embracing the good.
"I pray that the Buddha will take heed.
The Buddha said,
"The King's invasion and conquest are neither righteous nor sought through proper means."
Longevity secures the altars of state.

Your Majesty should practice benevolence, trustworthiness, humanity, righteousness, compassion, filial piety, integrity, purity, magnanimity, gentleness, forbearance, generosity, and the nurturing of the people, covering them with protection as you would extend forgiveness to yourself.
If one carries out these matters,
the state and its altars may be preserved for a long time;
if these are absent, the state and its altars will be difficult to preserve.
The King said, "How should this be done?
I pray that you will deign to instruct me with compassion.
The Buddha said:
Sentient beings are pitiable and human life is precious;

The people and the crown prince regard him more highly than their own parents;
thus, all the myriad nations under heaven can be preserved,
not merely a single state alone.
Although the King possesses several million chariot troops and cavalry,
they are merely sufficient to resist a minor enemy.
When I was practicing the path of a Bodhisattva, I sat in meditation beneath a tree.
The Māra King, together with eighteen thousand ghostly spirits and soldiers,

By means of my supernatural power, I pressed the earth with the finger of my right hand.
Then heaven and earth shook violently, and all things were overturned;
they could no longer return to their original forms,
and the Māra King was subdued.
"Compared to the strength of millions of people,
how does it measure up against the strength of billions of ghosts and spirits?
The king said:
"It was truly because of my ignorance and lack of understanding.
The King then prostrated himself, offering repentance and requesting that his conduct be changed and made more rigorous.
The Buddha said:
With great compassion, I contemplate delivering all people throughout the ten directions so that they may all attain liberation.
May they quickly attain the Way of the Buddha; those not yet delivered, I shall deliver—not only for the sake of the king and his son.
The king repented once more and reproached himself,

The Buddha said, "O King, you should broaden your administration of justice, eliminate taxes and levies, extend kindness and trustworthiness, provide for the orphaned and solitary, frequently pardon prisoners, rescue those in distress, enrich the poor, and satisfy the hungry."
If the King is such a person, he may preserve his integrity from beginning to end.
The King, having resolved upon the mind of the Way, addressed his attendants and ministers, saying:

The thirty-two sons of the king said to one another:
To be born as one who acts without meaning,
and to die as a ghost who acts without meaning—

They all exclaimed, "Excellent indeed!
and together they went to the Buddha to recount their thoughts in detail.
The Buddha, knowing that their intentions had deeply entered the wisdom of the Way, [responded accordingly].
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, shaved off his hair and beard and became a śramaṇa; likewise,

the country attained abundant harvests,
and neighboring states, hearing of this, looked up to it with distant reverence.
From that time forth, the King governed the country with broad benevolence; there were no thieves or bandits.
Men and women respected one another, free from mutual lustful desire, and all were universally harmonious and virtuous.

The Buddha said:
"I seek the Way for the sake of humanity only to bring about their deliverance;

When you practitioners cultivate the Path, you should act as I have described in the *Azhiguowang jing* (Sūtra on the King of Aśmaka). VI.
The Request of King Udayana for Methods of Governance and Transformation. Regarding the six periods [of the day], King Udayana...
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, how many qualities must a king possess?"
Before long, external enemies will arise in competition;
failing to attain the practice of cultivation, they will die and enter the evil realms.
The Buddha spoke of ten dharmas.
What are the ten? First, the mind is not single-mindedly focused on its various tasks.
Second, it is greedily attached to morsel food, like a starving tiger.
Third, they are greedily attached to wine and meat and neglect the affairs of state.
Fourth, they delight in harboring anger and are beset by much sorrow and anxiety.
Fifth, they constantly practice folly and do not accept the admonitions of others.
Sixth, he acts according to his own strength and is capable of accomplishing whatever he intends.
Seventh, he constantly delights in killing living beings and oppressing the weak.
Eighth, he frequently dispatches military forces to invade the borders of other nations.
Ninth, they speak much but their words lack essential truth.
Tenth, they are not compassionate toward others.
If one accomplishes these [faults], one will not endure for long, as external enemies will arise in competition.
"If, after his life has ended, he should go to the three evil realms, his ill repute will spread far and wide.
The King asked,
"By accomplishing how many qualities can one remain long in this world without external enemies arising?"
If, after the end of life, one is reborn in a heavenly realm or a favorable state,
the Buddha spoke of ten dharmas by which one may long endure in the world without external enemies arising.
After the end of life, one is reborn in a good place in the heavens. What are the ten?
First, the mind is not confused regarding various karmic actions.
First, they are entirely equal in eliminating unwholesome conduct and drawing near to virtuous karma.
Second, the king does not become greedily attached to material food;
he sustains his life through equanimity and distinguishes himself by the categories of the precepts.
Third, not craving flavors or being addicted to alcohol;
seeing all faults and transgressions, one knows that the essential way out is true happiness.
Fourth, not being stingy or greedy, but delighting in practicing generosity and contemplating all karmic actions.
Fifth, possessing wisdom, one understands its meaning, constantly cultivates what is wholesome,
and eliminates what is unwholesome.
Sixth, one does not rely on one's own strength nor harbor self-important thoughts.
Whosoever among the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, ministers, or common people are intelligent and wise,
he explains the meaning clearly to them in response to their questions and provides instruction accordingly.
Seventh, he does not act with cruelty to harm the people;
rather, he observes their conduct and then inflicts punishment.
Eighth, he does not frequently dispatch troops to invade the borders of other kingdoms.
He is always in harmonious accord with all kings.
The nine essential truths he proclaims are neither redundant nor cumbersome;
he observes the speech of others before speaking on any matter himself.
Constantly harboring compassion for all ministers and subjects, and always attending to the affairs of state—
by accomplishing these ten dharmas, one shall endure long in the world without external enemies arising;
and when the body perishes and life ends, one will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavens above.
"Even after your life has ended, your fame shall spread far and wide, transmitted by gods and humans;
you should transform others through the equal Dharma and not through what is contrary to principle.
Then the King replied:
By transforming the people through such dharmas,
when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the good heavens.
As for those who practice non-dharma:
Upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, he will go to the three evil realms, and his ill repute will spread far and wide.

(From the *Ekottara Āgama*, Volume 39). 7. King Udayana, infatuated with a woman, shot an arrow at his chief queen, but it could not harm her. Seven nations sent beautiful women to present to King Udayana.

Even if there were many who suffered from famine,
the snake would feel no anger; yet,
if anyone emerged, it would immediately devour them.

one was named Mahā-tiao.

"The snake is a creature that harbors poison."

4. Queen Mallikā Observes the Fast. While the four Buddhas were staying in Śrāvastī, there was no one among the king or his ministers who did not look up to them with devotion. Queen Mallikā observed the fast.

At that time, there was a merchant named Pāli who,
together with five hundred other merchants, entered the sea to seek treasures.
Then the Sea God emerged and pushed back the water, asking Pāli:
"Is the seawater much?"
"Is it more water that was splashed? Pālitaka replied,
"It is more water that was splashed."
Though the waters of the ocean are vast, they cannot save one from hunger and thirst;
yet even a small amount of water can sustain the life of one parched with thirst.
The blessings one shall receive throughout successive lifetimes are beyond calculation.
The Sea God was filled with joy;
he immediately removed eight kinds of fragrant necklaces from his body,
adorned them with the seven treasures, and presented them to Pāli.
Pāli returned to his kingdom and presented this fragrant garland to King Prasenajit;
the king found it exceedingly rare and marvelous.
He then lined up all the ladies-in-waiting;
to whichever one was the most beautiful, he gave a fragrant garland.
Thus, sixty thousand ladies, fully adorned and prepared, went forth.
The king asked,
"Why has Queen Mallikā not come out?
The attendant replied:
Now, on the fifteenth day, he observes the Buddhist fast, wearing plain, unadorned clothing.
The king said,
"If you observe the fast now, would it not be a violation of my royal decree?"
Thus it happened three times.
Queen Mallikā emerged in plain dress,
yet among the multitude she was as radiant as the sun and moon, appearing twice as beautiful as usual.
The king’s mind was struck with awe and he questioned her with increased reverence, saying,
"What moral virtues do you possess that are so brilliantly extraordinary?
The lady replied to the king.
Reflecting upon myself, I consider my meager merit, which has resulted in this female form;
my emotional states and defilements accumulate like mountains day and night.
Human life is brief and fleeting, and I fear falling into the three miserable realms.
Therefore, from month to month and day to day, he has observed the Buddhist fasts;
by renouncing his attachments to follow the Way, he has received blessings in every lifetime.
Upon hearing this, the King was filled with joy.
She then gave him the fragrant garland,
but the lady declined it, saying,
"I am currently observing the fast; I ought not to wear this."
"You may give it to someone else.
The king said,
"I originally intended to give it to the victor."
"You are now most excellent.
Furthermore, you have received the Dharma-precepts and your resolve for the Way is exceptionally lofty;
it is for this reason that I associate with you."
"If you do not accept it, where shall I place it?
The lady replied,
"Great King, do not worry."
"I pray that Your Majesty will condescend to come with me to the Buddha’s dwelling.
By offering this fragrant garland to the World-Honored One and receiving his holy instructions, you shall gain the merit of many kalpas."
The King immediately granted his consent.
He then ordered his carriage to be prepared and went to where the Buddha was,
saying to the Buddha:
The Sea God presented this fragrant garland of *pāri* flowers;
among the sixty thousand ladies, there was none who did not covet it,
yet Queen Mallikā gave it away and did not take it for herself.
Maintaining the fast of the Buddha-Dharma with a mind free from greed and desire,
I respectfully offer this to the Buddhas;
I pray that you will graciously accept it.
"The disciples of the World-Honored One hold their minds so differently that they cannot be made uniform.
If one simply has faith such as this, how could there be no merit?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One accepted the fragrant garland.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Many precious flowers are fashioned into ornate *bùyáo* hairpins; The fragrance produced by the vast accumulation of merit becomes even more excellent.
Like the rare and fragrant blossoms of wondrous grasses, Their scent wafts forth even against the wind."
The Way is spread near at hand; the virtuous person’s fragrance pervades everywhere.
Though sandalwood has much scent and the blue lotus is fragrant, though these are said to be true [fragrances], they do not compare to the flower-scent of the precepts.
The scent of the precepts cannot be called trivial; it is the true fragrance of upholding the precepts.

Reaching the supreme state, perfected in the observance of precepts, practicing without negligence, and liberated through meditative concentration—may you forever leave the path of Māra behind. (From the *Dharmapada*, Volume 2, Chapter 5:
"The Wife of King Udayana Learns the Path and is Reborn in Heaven") The Wife of King Udayana Learns the Path and is Reborn in Heaven: In the kingdom of Pañcāla, there was a king named Udayana.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he left the household life to practice the Way.
Having encountered Śākyamuni, he attained the fruits of the Path.
His country was prosperous and wealthy, and its people were numerous and flourishing.
The king had twenty thousand consorts.
The first consort was named Candraprabhā (Moonlight).
Her appearance was upright and graceful, and the king loved and respected her deeply.
Before half a year had passed, signs appeared that the lady was about to die,
and the king was filled with profound grief and sorrow.
Candraprabha questioned him,
and the king said,
"Your life is about to end."
"It is precisely because of the separation from those one loves that there is sorrow. Yue Ming replied,
"In life there is death."
According to the constant ways of the world,
why should you alone be so distressed?
If you would honorably consider this, simply permit him to leave the household life.
"O King, permit him to enter the Way.
If he leaves the household life, even if he does not yet achieve the Way, he will certainly be reborn in the heavens.
If he is reborn in the heavens, he shall return to my place."
"I grant you permission to leave the household life.
Candraprabhā then consented to her vow and summoned a bhikṣuṇī.
He immediately renounced the five desires.
However, many people came to inquire after his well-being, pay their respects, and make offerings, which hindered his spiritual practice;
for this reason, he traveled through various kingdoms.
From the day he went forth, six months having elapsed,
he maintained the precepts with purity, grew weary of the world,
and attained the path of an Anāgāmin.
After leaving that village, he was immediately reborn in the Form Heaven;
there, observing his past causes and conditions, he realized he had a commitment to the king and wished to fulfill his original vow.
Observing that the king was submerged in the five desires, stubborn and difficult to transform,
[the Bodhisattva] realized that by simply approaching him directly, he could not be inspired;
it would be appropriate to subdue him through intimidation and pressure.
He then transformed himself into a great rākṣasa;
his body hair bristled as he brandished a five-foot sword and,
while the king was sleeping at night, he hovered in the air not far from him.
The king was greatly terrified.
[The deity] then spoke to the king, saying:
"Though you have thousands upon thousands of troops,"
"Now it belongs solely to me; I have no autonomy.
Since the time of death has already arrived, by what means can I save myself?
The king then replied:
The deity said: "I have no other causes or conditions; I simply maintain the wholesome deeds I have performed in the past.
By cultivating a pure mind, I am born in a good realm."
"This is the most reliable [reason], and there is no other principle [to be considered]. The king then asked,
"What deity are you that causes me such fear?"
The deity replied,
"I am Lady Candraprabhā. Having been released by the King,
I went forth as a renunciant, contemplated the state of detachment from desire, and was reborn in the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu)."
Now you have come to fulfill our appointment.
The king said,
"Although you speak thus, I still do not believe you."
"Only when you restore your original form will I believe you.
The deity immediately transformed back into his former shape,
standing there with his garments and ornaments just as they were before.
As the king’s lustful mind arose, he immediately went forward intending to seize her.
Candraprabhā then ascended into the void and preached the Dharma to the king, saying:
"This body is impermanent; it cannot be preserved for even the snap of a finger."
It is like the morning dew that vanishes at sunrise.
Do not merely contemplate impermanence while remaining greedily attached to this body.
Does Your Majesty not see?
The flourishing bloom of youth is swallowed and extinguished by old age;
the sense faculties decay and fail,
and the eyesight grows dim.
The ears no longer hear clearly;
the body is ruined and decayed, no longer capable of anything.
It is like wine that has fermented: one may extract the pure essence, but the dregs are of no value.
This body, now aged, has nothing left to desire or delight in;
there is only death remaining.
Since this body is subject to birth and death, it is ever accompanied by impermanence.
Your Majesty, do you not see that those in the womb, the infant, the youth, and the adult all die?
This body is precarious and fragile; the thief of death constantly follows it.
The body and mind are ablaze with nothing but manifold sufferings:
the mind possesses the three poisons, while the body experiences cold, heat, hunger, and thirst;
yet one does not give rise to revulsion, but remains greedily attached to this body.
The palace ladies, handmaidens, beautiful forms, and the five desires;
the state’s wealth, wife, and children—none of these are mine.
At the time of death, not a single one will follow me.
If you would abandon even your own body, how much more so other things?
Yet you are mired in the five desires, circling through birth and death without knowing the way out.
Your Majesty is a man of wisdom; why do you not feel weary of and renounce this world to leave the household life and seek the Way?
The King, with a virtuous mind, granted permission for him to leave the household life.
Moonlight further exhorted him, saying:
"I shall leave the household life to seek the wondrous Dharma; having received it, I will practice it, remaining diligent and energetic day and night without slackening."
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.
The king then abdicated the throne to the crown prince and renounced the five desires.
He joined Kātyāyana to leave the household life and pursue the Way;
at that time, people remarked that because he had renounced such heavy honors and profit,
he was seeking the true and correct Path.
Many officials, subjects, and people came to provide offerings, pay their respects, and inquire after his well-being as he was cultivating the path of practice.
Thereupon, he traveled on until he reached the kingdom of Magadha,
where the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the state of an Arhat.
Carrying his clay alms-bowl, he entered the city of Rājagṛha.
Having obtained leftover rice through alms, he returned to the forest and sat down to eat.
King Bimbisāra went out on a tour and arrived at the forest.
He greeted him, saying,
"Formerly you were a king, entering and exiting with honor and a retinue;
now you are a beggar, walking alone to beg for food."
"How could this be something to rejoice in?
Return to your former life as a layman and rule half the kingdom.
The practitioner replied:
"I am a great king with many settlements.
For what reason now would I abandon the great for the small? This is not fitting for me.
King Bimbisāra said:
"In the past, you consumed the finest delicacies served in precious vessels;
is it not now difficult for you to hold an earthen bowl and beg for leftover, stale food?
In the past, you were a king’s valiant warrior, attended by guards."
"Are you not afraid to be alone today?
Formerly, you resided within the deep palace, where the exquisite beauty of consorts and maids filled your eyes and delighted your ears;
you sat upon jeweled couches spread with fine silks."
"Sleeping and sitting alone today in the forest and wilds, with nothing but grass for bedding— is this not suffering?
He replied,
"I am now content and have no craving or attachment."
King Bimbisāra said,
"You are truly pitiable.
He replied:
"You are pitiable, but you are not I. Why is this?
You are entangled by the five desires and driven by affection, such that you lack self-mastery."
"I am now happy and my mind is free from hindrance.
Having heard this, King Bimbisāra immediately departed. [This concludes the excerpt from the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka*. 6.

The Queen of the Great King and a Wise Man Build a Monastery Together with the King. Once upon a time, there was a man. The Queen of the Great King and a wise man together with the king built a monastery. [End of section.]
He saw a Buddhist temple and desired to build one; however,
he lacked sufficient funds.
He made a vow to enter the sea to obtain even more gold and jewels,
thinking, "I shall build a monastery that is the foremost in the kingdom.
Having obtained the gold and silver, he returned and reflected deeply once again.
Who can agree to build a monastery together?
The king often says,
"I wish to build a monastery and a stupa."
Now, as this had never been done before,
he presented a precious jewel to the king.
The king was delighted and asked:
"Where did you obtain this?
The worthy one replied,
"I wished to build a monastery, but as I could not accomplish it alone, [I obtained it]."
"Having entered the sea and obtained treasures, I shall establish a monastery;
that I have now returned safely is my first benefit,
and that I have acquired gold and jewels is my second benefit."
My mind is free from greed and attachment; establishing monasteries and dwellings is my third benefit.
Relying upon the merit of these three benefits, I now wish to build a monastery, yet I lack the manpower and labor.
"Therefore, I have come to inform Your Majesty.
The King said,
"I too possess three benefits."
"To build a temple and stupa is my first benefit; to become a king, the supreme among men, is my second benefit;
for the four quarters to submit to me is my third benefit."
"I shall build a monastery together with you.
The king summoned his five hundred consorts and gave them the pearls;
all five hundred consorts adorned themselves and each desired to possess the pearls.
Only the chief queen alone did not adorn herself with ornaments.
When the king asked why,
she replied that there were likewise three advantages.
Therefore, I have become the king’s consort;
being honored by the entire palace is my first benefit.
That I have given birth to a son who shall be the crown prince is my second benefit.
"To always delight in the Way of the sutras and desire to build Buddhist temples and monasteries—this is my third benefit.
The King said, "Excellent!
and gave him the jewel.
The Chief Lady contributed one hundred thousand taels of gold to assist the King in establishing the temple.
The King built a temple for the wise men of the kingdom measuring one thousand paces in breadth,
all of which was inlaid and carved with gold and silver.
The king said,
"Only we three possess such merit.
Do not the people within my kingdom receive this as well?"
He dispatched messengers through the streets and neighborhoods to proclaim:
"Whoever possesses great goodness shall obtain immeasurable merit.
There was a poor woman who lived in a single small hut, begging for food and clothing.
Upon hearing this, he reproached himself, thinking,
"Because I failed to practice generosity in my past lives, I have now fallen into such poverty.
He untied his own cloth skirt, threw it toward the center for the messenger, and offered the skirt to assist the king.
"My body is naked and I have no clothes to wear.
When the king heard this, he was struck with wonder that such a virtuous mind could exist;
he immediately ordered him to be brought before him.
The messenger said,
"This woman has no clothes to wear.
The king then commanded five hundred ladies-in-waiting.
He took one robe from each and gave them to her, saying,
"Go quickly to welcome and receive him.
When the king saw her, he immediately prostrated before her and appointed her as his second consort.
He caused the *Daśa-vastuka-avadāna-sūtra* (The Sutra of Ten Chapters of Parables), scroll four, to be brought forth from the palace.
*Sūtra-lakṣaṇa-vibhaṅga* (Distinguishing Characteristics of Sutras and Vinaya), scroll thirty;
*Sūtra-lakṣaṇa-vibhaṅga*, scroll thirty-one: Section on Princes of Various Kingdoms Who Excelled in Practicing the Bodhisattva Path.
Compiled by the Liang dynasty śramaṇas Sengmin, Baoshang, and others.

Section One: The Section on Princes Who Practiced the Bodhisattva Path in Various Kingdoms (31). First: Prince of King Gandhaśrī Throws Himself to a Starving Tiger; His Bones Are Used to Erect a Stūpa.

1. Dharmagandha burned his own body for the Dharma, whereupon the fire pit was transformed into a lotus pond. 2. Renru (Kṣāntivādin) had his body killed by his father. 3. Zhizhi offered his flesh and blood to a sick bhikṣu. 4. Yueguang (Candraprabha) broke his own body to draw out blood and marrow to save a patient. 5. Xuchantide cut his own flesh to provide sustenance for his parents' lives. 6. Sudāna was fond of giving; he gave away his white elephant to others and was subsequently exiled to the mountains. 7. Jīvaka was born to a courtesan; he renounced his kingdom to become a physician. 8. The Crown Prince of King Gandhāśrī threw himself before a starving tigress; his remains were used to erect a stupa. The Crown Prince of King Gandhāśrī threw himself before a starving tigress; his remains were used to erect a stupa. First, the Crown Prince of King Gandhāśrī: 1. The Crown Prince of King Gandhāśrī threw himself before a starving tigress; his remains were used to erect a stupa. First, the Crown Prince of King Gandhāśrī.
Disliking worldly splendor, he dwelt in seclusion among the mountains and marshes.
At that time, there was a starving tigress at the bottom of a deep valley who had recently given birth to seven cubs; it happened that snow began to fall from the heavens.
The tigress had been carrying her cub for three days without being able to seek food.

Fearing that the cub would die of cold, she remained there guarding it from hunger; though the snow fell incessantly, both mother and child were so famished and exhausted that their lives could not last much longer.
As the mother was already driven by hunger and intended to devour her own son,
the seers said, "Who is able to sacrifice their body to rescue this one?"
The Prince said, "Excellent! My wish has been fulfilled.
He went to the edge of the cliff and looked down toward the valley below.
Seeing a tigress embracing her cubs, covered by the snow, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion.
Standing still upon the mountain peak, he entered meditative absorption in silence and immediately attained the pure patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
He perceived events from incalculable past kalpas, and the future was likewise;
he then returned and informed his teacher and five hundred fellow students:
"I now wish to sacrifice my body; I pray that each of you will rejoice in this."
The teacher said, "Your study of the Way has been brief and your insight is not yet broad.
Why do you suddenly resolve to sacrifice your beloved body?
The Prince replied:
In the past, I made a vow that I should sacrifice a thousand bodies.
Previously, I have already sacrificed nine hundred and ninety-nine bodies;
today’s sacrifice completes the full number of one thousand, and for this reason, I give them up.
"I pray that the Master will rejoice in this.
The Master said, "Your aspiration is lofty and sublime; you shall surely attain the Way first. Do not let me be left behind again."
The Prince took his leave of his teacher and departed.
The teacher, along with five hundred divine seers, wept until their eyes were full as they escorted the Prince to the edge of a mountain precipice.
At that time, there was an elder named Pūraṇa.
He led five hundred male and female attendants, carrying offerings, up the mountain.
Seeing the Prince sacrifice his body, they were overcome with grief and wept;
they also followed the Prince to the edge of the mountain cliff.
In the presence of the multitude, the Prince made this great vow:
"I now relinquish my body to save the lives of these beings;
by all the merit therein, may I swiftly attain Bodhi."
I have attained the adamantine body—the unconditioned Dharma-body of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
I shall deliver those not yet delivered, liberate those not yet liberated, and bring peace to those not yet at peace.
My present body, however, is impermanent, subject to suffering and affliction, and a collection of manifold poisons.
This body is impure, with its nine orifices constantly overflowing; it is bitten and stung by the four great poisonous snakes of the elements.
It is pursued, wounded, and mangled by five bandits with drawn swords.
Such a body as this knows no gratitude for the offerings of delicious foods and the pleasures of the five senses.
After this life ends, there will be no karmic reward for one's kindness,
and one will fall into hell to undergo immeasurable suffering.
As for this human body, it should only be made to suffer and not granted pleasure.
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"Now, with my flesh and blood, I shall save that starving tigress;
let the remaining relics be my bones."
After my parents pass away, they shall surely have a stupa erected for them.

May it cause all sentient beings whose various physical ailments and sufferings—due to the causes and conditions of past karma—cannot be cured by decoctions, medicines, acupuncture, or moxibustion, to find relief.
Come to my stupa and make offerings with a sincere heart;
according to the severity of the illness, it shall surely be cured within no more than one hundred days.
If this is true and not false, may the various devas send down rain of fragrant flowers.
In response to his voice, a rain of *māndārava* flowers fell and the earth trembled everywhere.
The Prince immediately untied his deerskin garment to wrap around his head and threw himself before the tiger.
The tigress obtained the Bodhisattva’s flesh,
and both mother and son survived.
At that time, the people on the edge of the cliff beheld the Prince from afar.
Devoured by tigers, their bones and flesh were strewn in disarray;
they wailed and shrieked with such intensity that the sound shook the mountains.
Some beat their breasts and threw themselves down, rolling upon the ground.
Some were engaged in meditative reflection,
while others prostrated themselves in repentance;
there were also the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, as well as Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the Four Great Kings.
Tens of millions of deities from the sun and moon realms all resolved their minds upon unexcelled bodhi;
they performed music and dance, burned incense, and scattered flowers as offerings to the Prince.
And he uttered these words:
"Excellent, Mahāsattva! Before long, you shall sit at the site of enlightenment."
The five hundred rishis all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path;
the Great Master, the Immortal, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The lady sent provisions for them.
He saw only robes, parasols, alms bowls, staffs, and water jars within the stone chamber.
He questioned the sages everywhere,
who were gathered in groups of ten, fifteen, or five, weeping toward one another.
Upon arriving at the Great Master’s quarters,
he saw only the Immortal Master sitting with his hand supporting his cheek, his eyes brimming with tears, groaning as he sat.
He questioned those surrounding him, but none were willing to respond.
The messenger was terrified;
he immediately offered food and drink to the various rishis and fled back to the lady to recount the matter in detail.
The lady said:
"Alas! My son is dead! He beat his breast and cried out loudly, then ran to the king.
Upon hearing this, the king was overcome with grief and confusion.
The ministers remonstrated with the king,
saying, "The crown prince is in the mountains;
we pray that Your Majesty will rest for a while."
The king, along with his queen, consorts, court ladies, ministers, officials, and subjects, fled up the mountain.
The elder Purāṇa came forward to inform the king:
"Yesterday, the prince cast himself down from the cliff, offering his flesh as food for the tigers."
Now, with only the bones remaining scattered upon the ground, they all went together to the site of the corpse.
The King, the Queen, the concubines, the court ladies, the ministers, and the officials and commoners raised their voices in mournful wailing, shaking the mountains and valleys.
The king and his consort prostrated themselves over the prince’s corpse; their hearts and livers were as if severed, and they fainted, losing consciousness.
The consort leaned forward, supporting his head and smoothing the crown prince’s hair, saying:
"I would rather my own body be ground into dust than that my husband should suddenly perish like this."
At that time, the ministers said to the king:
"The Crown Prince has vowed to practice giving in order to deliver all sentient beings;
he cannot be robbed or seized by the impermanent demon of death."
Furthermore, while the remains have not yet become putrid or rotten, one should arrange offerings.
Then, having collected the skeletal remains and brought them out from the mouth of the mountain valley,
one should pile sandalwood incense fuel upon level ground.
They used fragrant *sū* oil for the cremation.
Having collected the relics, they erected a stupa made of the seven precious substances.
At that time, the prince was none other than myself.
The royal father was my current father, Śuddhodana;
the lady was my mother, Māyā;
and the consort was Gopī, who is now Yaśodharā.
The one who performed the cremation was Ānanda.
The great master of the immortals on the mountain was Maitreya. [This is from] the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Throwing Himself into the Fire to Feed a Starving Tiger*.
2. Dharmakāśyapa Burns His Body for the Dharma: The Pit of Fire Transformed into a Lotus Pond. Part Two: Once upon a time in Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Brahmadeva.
The king had a crown prince named Dharmagada who deeply delighted in the True Dharma.
Śakra, having transformed himself into a brāhmaṇa, said:
"I am able to preach the Dharma.
The Prince prostrated at his feet in reverence and requested to hear it.
The Brahmin said:
I have studied for a long time;
why do you wish to hear it so abruptly?
If you can disregard your own life and limb, as well as your wife and children, [then you may hear it].
"To those who enter a great pit of fire to offer me worship,
I shall indeed grant the Dharma.
The Prince acted exactly according to these words.
They prepared a great fire pit.
The king, along with his queen and court ladies,
went to the palace to persuade the brahmin.
"I beg you to grant me the kingdom, the city, my wife,
and myself as attendants, so that the prince may not be cast into this fire. The Brahmin said:
"I shall not coerce you; let it be according to your will.
However, for one such as this, I do not preach the Dharma.
The King then issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom that seven days hence the Prince would cremate himself.
If you wish to see him, come early on that day;
let the nobles and commoners of the entire kingdom assemble at once,
and with earnest entreaties and expressions of grief, make your request as previously described.
The Prince said to the multitude:
"Throughout the long course of birth and death, I have lost my body countless times.
Among human beings, out of greed, we have repeatedly slaughtered one another."
When their lifespan in the heavens comes to an end, they suffer the grief and pain of losing their desires.
In the hells, they are scorched and boiled, cut and flayed by knives, and subjected to the Ash River and Sword Trees, with agony piercing to the very marrow of their bones.
Among the hungry ghosts, a hundred poisons bore into their bodies.
The retribution-body of an animal provides food for the mouths of others by grazing on grass and bearing heavy burdens;
it maintains this life and body through manifold sufferings in vain,
never having cultivated a virtuous mind for the sake of the Dharma.
Now you cast off this foul and impure form to seek purity and excellence;
why do you wish to see me pushed back?
Having attained the Way of the Buddha, I bestow upon you the fivefold Dharma-body.
The Prince then stood upon the fire pit.
The Brahmin said:
"Always practice a mind of compassion, And eliminate thoughts of anger and malice."
With great compassion, one takes pity on sentient beings and sheds tears of sympathy;
practicing the mind of great joy, one protects those who have attained the Dharma as if they were oneself—
this is what accords with the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Upon hearing this, the Prince immediately desired to throw himself into the fire.
At that moment, Śakra and Brahmā each seized one of his hands and cautioned him, saying:
All living beings within Jambudvīpa rely upon the Prince’s kindness;
there is none who does not find their place through him.
Now, if you cast yourself into the fire, the world will lose its father. Why do you wish to perish and abandon all?
The Prince replied,
"Do not obstruct my aspiration for the unsurpassed Way;
I shall cast my body into the fire pit."
Heaven and earth shook violently;
the various devas in the void simultaneously wailed, their tears falling like torrential rain.
At that moment, the pit of blazing fire was transformed into a pond of flowers.
The Prince sat upon a lotus pedestal,
and the various devas rained down flowers until they reached his knees.
The Brahma King was none other than Śuddhodana.

The mother was the present Lady Māyā; the Prince was the present World-Honored One. (From the *Xiányújīng*, Scroll One). 3. Endurance as a Father Slaying His Own Body. During the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin: [The story continues: At that time, there was a king who had three sons. The eldest son was named Śibi, the middle son was named Śakra, and the youngest son was named Viśvantara. Later, the king fell ill and died. The two younger brothers, desiring the throne, conspired to kill their elder brother. Śibi, out of compassion for his younger brothers, did not wish to harm them. He thought to himself: "If I do not yield the throne to my younger brothers, they will surely kill me. It would be better for me to give them the kingdom myself. Having thought this, he yielded the throne to his younger brothers. Subsequently, the two younger brothers, having obtained the throne, became arrogant and cruel. "Where will you be reborn after your life ends?

I was born in Jambudvīpa as the crown prince of a great king;

"I shall certainly lead you into the various treasure stores and give you whatever you desire;

"I have no need for any other miscellaneous jewels."
"I only wish to obtain the precious jewel upon the Great King's head;

He immediately went to see his father.
The father was filled with immeasurable great compassion, joy,

"If you have pity on me, you should give it to me;

"I have only this single jewel, which I always wear as a head ornament.
The people of Jambudvīpa are of meager merit and lowly; they should not see it.

For this reason, I have traveled far across hardships and braved death to come here;

I wish to fulfill their aspirations with this wish-fulfilling jewel.
Thereafter, he taught and transformed them through the causes and conditions of the Buddha-way.
The Dragon King gave him the pearl and made this covenant:

"When you have passed away, you must return it to me.
He replied, "I respectfully obey Your Majesty's word."
The Bodhisattva obtained the jewel and flew up into the void; in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, he arrived in Jambudvīpa.

Filled with joy and exultation, he embraced him and asked,
"What have you obtained? He replied:
He obtained a wish-fulfilling jewel and asked,

He said, "It is inside this corner of the robe.

"It lies in his divine virtue, not in its size."
He addressed his parents, saying:

Tomorrow at the clear dawn, let a long wooden pole be erected as a standard, and place a pearl upon its top."
At that time, the Bodhisattva made this vow:

At that time, dark clouds spread everywhere, raining down various kinds of precious objects, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions;

Such as these are called the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence arising from generosity. This concludes the twelfth fascicle of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra.

He was well-acquainted with the signs of passable and impassable roads,

The guide replied,
"I dare not disobey.

within the great ocean, obstacles are manifold.

He further spoke these words:
"This jewel is exceedingly heavy;

Do not load too heavily onto your boats, lest they sink and fail to reach their destination;
do not take too little, for the roads are so remote that it would not suffice to compensate for your toil.
Having finished packing, he took leave of the others.
And he spoke these words:
"You all may now return in peace and security;

The Prince and his blind guide proceeded forward by turns;
after traveling for seven days, the water reached up to their knees.
Proceeding further for another seven days, the water reached up to his neck.
Traveling forward for yet another seven days, he crossed by swimming and arrived at the place of jewels.
The guide asked him:
"What kind of ground is this?
The prince replied,

The Guide said, "In the four directions there should be white mountains; have you seen them yet?
The Prince replied.

From the mountain, proceeding further for another seven [leagues], there were exclusively blue lotuses.
Proceeding again for seven [leagues], the ground was entirely covered with red lotuses.

"All my wealth and possessions are now completely exhausted.

"I have now obtained the wish-fulfilling jewel of the Dragon King.

seeking life but unable to find it, seeking death but unable to find it.
Gradually proceeding forward, he arrived at the kingdom of Rṣivadana.

"Why did you go out privately without telling me? Where did you go, and from where have you returned?"
The wife said,
"I did not act privately.
The husband said, "Whether it was private or not, who would know of your actions?"
The wife made this oath:
"If I have acted privately [with another], may both your eyes remain blind for all time;
if it is not so, may one of your eyes be restored to its former state."
Having made this vow, it became level and full as before, its brilliant light clear and penetrating.
The wife said,
"Do you believe me?"
The good friend smiled and said,
"My wife says you do not recognize the kindness of her nurture."
"I am the daughter of a great king,
while you are but a lowly man; yet I have served you with all my heart,
and you have shown me no trust."
The son-in-law said, "Do you recognize me?
She replied, "I know you; you are a beggar."
The husband said, "It is not so.
I am Prince Kalyāṇamitra, the son of the King of Vārāṇasī.
His wife said:
"You great fool, how can you utter such words?
The Prince of the King of Vārāṇasī has entered the sea and has not yet returned;
I do not believe your current falsehood."
The good friend said, "Since my birth, I have never spoken a falsehood.
His wife said,
"Between the false and the true, who is to be believed?"
The son-in-law said:
"If I deceive you, may one of my eyes never heal;
if I speak the truth, may one of my eyes be restored as it was before, so that you may see."
Immediately, his eyes became as radiant and vibrant as they had been originally, without any difference;
Prince Sudhana’s two eyes were restored, his countenance became upright and handsome, and his exquisite complexion was transcendent.
The woman saw him and was filled with joy,
as if she were being gazed upon by a sage or a holy one, her eyes never turning away from his body for even a moment.
She immediately entered the palace and said to her father, the King:
"The man who is now my husband is none other than Prince Sudhana.
The king said, "Foolish woman!
Since Sudhana has not yet returned, how can you call this beggar 'Prince'?"
The woman said, "No.
If you do not believe me, you may go and see for yourself.
The king immediately went to look.
Consciousness is a virtuous friend.
Thereupon, filled with fear, he spoke these words:
"O King of Vārāṇasī!"
Upon hearing this, he felt no small amount of resentment toward me.
He immediately came forward to apologize to Prince Shōtoku, saying, "I truly did not know.
The Prince said:
"May there be no suffering for me;
let this be bestowed upon this cowherd.
The king then immediately provided him with gold, silver, precious jewels, clothing, and food and drink.
Along with the five hundred oxen that were released,
the man rejoiced and praised me beyond measure;
yet, I have not yet repaid even a small portion of his kindness.
I thus raised my voice and proclaimed:
"The rewards for secret giving are manifest and vast beyond measure.
Those in the great assembly who heard this all conceived the intention to practice generosity.
Before the Good Friend had gone out to sea, he had raised a white goose;
it was always with him in his clothing, food, drink, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
The lady spoke to this goose, saying:
"When the Prince was alive, he was always with you;
now that life and death are yet to be distinguished, do you have no feeling of gratitude for the Prince?
The goose then cried out piteously, weeping with tears as it replied:
Desiring to find the Prince,
the lady herself wrote a letter, tied it to the neck of a wild goose,
and ascended into the void, flying away.
He flew to the great ocean but could not find him;
proceeding by stages, he arrived at the kingdom of Rishabha,
where he saw his good friend from afar before the palace.
The geese went toward him, crying out with both sorrow and joy.
The Prince then took his mother’s letter, bowed his head in reverence, broke the seal, and read it;
he immediately learned that his parents were weeping day and night, longing for him in remembrance.
The Crown Prince’s two eyes had become blind.
The Prince wrote by hand a letter detailing these matters and tied it to the neck of a wild goose, which returned to Vārāṇasī.
Upon receiving the letter, his parents were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, praising him beyond measure.
Having learned that the Prince had been tormented by his evil companions and robbed of his precious jewels,
his parents bound the evil companions with cangues and fetters and cast them into prison.
They then dispatched a messenger to inform King Liśāva.
"Why do you now obstruct the Prince and cause me such grief and suffering?
King Lichchhavi was struck with terror;
he immediately dressed the Prince in his finery and escorted him to the border.
He dispatched a messenger to inform [the king],
who then gave his daughter as a wife to him and sent him back to his own country.
His parents then mounted a great elephant named Mahānāman.
They performed music as courtesans, swept and sprinkled the ground, burned incense, and hung silk banners and canopies to go out and welcome the Prince from afar.
When the men, women, and couples of the kingdom’s populace heard that the Prince was returning, they all came out to receive him with honor.
The Prince went forward to pay obeisance to his parents, but their eyes were so dim they could not see him.
Reaching out with their hands to feel for him, they said, "Are you our good friend? We do not recognize you; we have been filled with such grief and suffering because of you."

"Where is my evil friend?"
The king said,
"He is currently in prison.
The crown prince said:
"I pray that you release my evil friend so that we may meet. Thus he requested three times.
The king, unable to refuse him, ordered him to be released.
[The friend] immediately went forward to embrace him, consoling him with kind words and gentle inquiries after his well-being.
"You have undergone extreme toil and hardship carrying my precious jewel; where is it now?
He asked this three times, and only then did [the other] reply.
In that land, the prince recovered the precious jewel;
he went before his parents, knelt down, burned various exquisite incenses, and made this vow:
"This jewel is a wish-fulfilling gem;

They will immediately recover and see their son with joy."
On the morning of the fifteenth day of the month,
the Prince bathed himself thoroughly, donned fresh and clean robes, and burned exquisite precious incense.
Standing upon a high tower, he held a censer in his hand and prostrated himself with his head and face touching the ground before the mani-jewel.
He made this vow, saying:
"For the sake of all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa,
I shall endure this great suffering to seek this precious jewel."
At that time, a great wind arose from the east,
blowing away the clouds and mist so that all became bright and pure.
Furthermore, all the filth and impurities of Jambudvīpa— feces, urine, ash, dust, weeds, and brush— were swept away by the clear breeze until everything was rendered clean.
By the majestic power of the jewel,
throughout Jambudvīpa,
there fell a rain of naturally ripened, non-glutinous rice.
Fragrant, sweet, soft, and fine, endowed with perfect color and flavor,
the water filled the ditches and channels, accumulating up to the knees; next,

Later, when King Candracchattra passed away, [the prince] succeeded him and ascended the throne.
The evil friend said,
"I live by begging for alms.
The king said:
"Guard my neck and I will give you food.
The king fell asleep again;
[the man] drew his sword, intending to sever the king's head, but the head fell off by itself.

The father at that time was none other than the present King Śuddhodana;
the mother was the present Lady Māyā;

The daughter of King Candra was Gopī; the Good Friend was I myself.

This is from the fourth fascicle of the *Bao’en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), and it also appears in the second fascicle of the *Xiányú jīng* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish); the two accounts are largely the same with minor differences.

3. Changsheng Desires to Avenge His Father’s Vengeance and Later Regains His Kingdom; Changsheng Desires to Avenge His Father’s Vengeance and Later Regains His Kingdom. Long ago, there was a Bodhisattva who was the king of a great kingdom. He desired to avenge his father’s vengeance, and later he regained his kingdom. Part Three. Once upon a time, there was a Bodhisattva who served as the king of a great nation.
His name was Chángshòu (Long-life).
The king had a crown prince named Chángshēng (Long-living).
The king governed with rectitude, so that the suffering of swords and staves was not inflicted upon the officials or the people.
Wind and rain came at their proper seasons, and the five grains were abundant.
There was a neighboring king.
He established himself through violent and harmful conduct and failed to practice correct governance, so that the people fell into poverty.
He said to his ministers, "I have heard that King Jīvaka is exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, yet lacks military preparedness; I wish to seize his kingdom."
The minister said, "Very well.
He then raised an army for an offensive.
King Jīvarāja addressed his ministers, saying:
"He covets my wealth;
if we were to engage him in battle, he would surely harm my people.
Now, to contend for a kingdom by killing its citizens is something I cannot bear."
The ministers did not comply;
they raised an army and went beyond the borders to meet and resist him.
The King and the Crown Prince then scaled the city walls and went into hiding.
King Greed entered the kingdom and offered a reward of ten million coins and one thousand *kārṣāpaṇas* for whoever could find a means to attain long life.
Later, as the king was traveling along the road,
he came upon a tree and encountered a brāhmaṇa, whom he asked where he had come from.
He replied,
"I am a poor mendicant who,
having heard that King Dīrghāyu delights in giving, has come from afar to beg."
The king thought silently to himself.
Having lost his kingdom,
he shed tears and said:
"I am indeed the king. Since I have met with such a fate, there is no one to succeed me.
The two men wept.
The king said,
"I have heard that the new king seeks me with great urgency.
If you take my head to him, you will surely receive a generous reward."
The brahmin said,
"I am of meager merit and do not dare accept your command.
The king said:
"You have come from afar to meet me at a time of exhaustion.
In the life of man, death is inevitable;
I pray you grant me this—why do you refuse?"
He replied,
"How could I bear to kill you?
If you truly wish to bestow this gift upon me, I pray that you will accompany me back to my country."
Thereupon, they returned together and arrived at the city gate.
The king ordered him to be bound and presented before King Lobha (Greed).
King Lobha immediately rewarded him with gold coins and sent him back on his way.
As he sought to burn and kill Jīvaka at the crossroads,
the inhabitants of the cities, towns, fields, and wilds cried out to Heaven.
When the Crown Prince heard this, he was deeply moved.
As he emerged before his father, his heart was filled with bitter grief.
Fearing that his son might seek revenge for their enmity,
the father looked up to heaven and sighed, saying:
"This death is what I desire. I wish to be a filial son so that your father may die without regret; do not seek revenge.
Changsheng could not bear to see his father die, so he returned to the mountains.
After the king had died, Changsheng thought to himself:
"My father was profoundly sincere in his benevolence and righteousness, never wavering even unto death.
This greedy king is shameless, failing to distinguish between good and evil."
"I cannot endure that my father was unjustly killed.
If I do not kill him, I shall never live in peace.
He then went out to hire himself as a laborer for a high minister; the minister lent him some vegetables to cultivate, and the vegetables grew excellently.
The minister questioned the park superintendent, who replied,
"I have borrowed one man who is extremely diligent and capable."
The minister called Changsheng and asked him,
"Are you able to prepare food and drink?
He replied, "I am able."
Later, he invited the king to partake of delicious food and drink.
When the king asked who had prepared it,
he replied, "A laborer."
The king immediately summoned him back to the palace and ordered him to prepare food and drink.
Later, the king asked him,
"Are you able to study the art of war?"
He replied, "It is most convenient.
The king had him attend upon his person and addressed him, saying:
"I have an enemy whom I constantly fear encountering.
Now, relying upon you, I seek your assistance to prepare for him.
He replied, "So be it."
"I shall exert my strength and offer my life for the sake of Your Majesty.
On a later day, the king asked,
"Do you enjoy hunting?"
He replied, "Your servant has loved hunting since his youth.
Thereupon, the King ordered his attendants outside to prepare the carriage, and he set out together with Changsheng for a hunt.
Upon entering the mountain forest, they immediately saw a wild beast.
The King and Changsheng galloped after it,
plunging deeper into the remote mountains until they lost their way for three days.
Eventually, they became exhausted by hunger.
The king dismounted from his horse, untied his sword, and handed it to Changsheng, saying, "I am utterly weary;
you sit here while I rest my head upon your knees and lie down."
Changsheng drew his sword, intending to kill King Tan,
but remembering his father’s command, he sheathed it and desisted.
He did this three times.
The king was startled awake and asked Changsheng,
"In my dream, I saw that Prince Changshou intended to come and harm me.
Changsheng replied:
"In this matter, it is merely a powerful ghost that has come to terrify you.
Finally, he said, "I shall pardon your killing.
Changsheng replied:
"I am the crown prince of King Dīrghāyu, and I have come here intending to kill you, Great King.
As my father was dying, he earnestly entreated me not to seek revenge against the king.
Reflecting upon my father’s instruction, I cast my sword to the ground to follow his command."
"Even so, I still fear that on a later day I may become deluded and lose my way.
I pray that Your Majesty will put me to death this very moment.
The King then repented, saying:
I am a cruel and rebellious man who cannot distinguish between good and evil; yet,
O worthy son, your father practiced benevolence with such steadfastness that he did not waver even unto death.
I was so greedy and cruel that I was not aware of it at first;
today my life rests in your hands,
yet you still harbor benevolence.
I recall only my father’s words;
how could I possibly harm you? Truly moved by your profound kindness, I am filled with gratitude.
"Now that I wish to return to my kingdom, by which path shall I go?
Changsheng said, "I know the direct route;
it is because you were previously lost, O King, that you now wish to take revenge for your father's enmity."
They then emerged from the forest together and saw their own troops.
The king returned to his native country and restored the kingdom to the prince, whereupon they bound themselves with a brotherly oath never to invade or seize one another's lands.
They further exchanged gifts and supported each other in times of urgent distress.
The King of Long Life was myself;
the Crown Prince was Ānanda;
and the Greedy King was Devadatta. This is from the *Rājavamśa-sūtra*.
4. The Story of the Prince of Cāraṅga Named Virūpa who Lost His Queen and Regained Her through the Application of Wisdom. Once upon a time, there was a king of Cāraṅga named Virūpa.
The Queen Consort had passed away without issue;
the King lamented this deeply and issued a decree, saying:
"You must return to your own lineage to seek the means of obtaining an heir.
The consort wept and took her leave;
she vowed to sacrifice her life, casting herself down from mountain crags and retiring to the forests and marshes.
Śakra was moved and said,
"This queen was my elder sister in a former life;
now, having no heir, she has cast her body from a perilous mountain height."
Filled with sorrow and pitying him,
she suddenly descended and,
placing fruit in a vessel, handed it to him, saying:
"Sister, since you have swallowed this fruit, you will surely have a holy heir who shall become a World Hero.
If the King has any doubts, show him the vessel."
"This is the supreme, clear manifestation of the divine vessel of the Heavenly King.
Later, as she looked up at the heavens and swallowed the fruit, it suddenly vanished; she immediately felt her body grow heavy.

When the moon was full, he gave birth to a son.
