Consequently, the King took a daughter of a neighboring state as his consort.
His name was Candraprabha; he was upright, elegant, and possessed every worldly excellence.
He had seven younger brothers, who were likewise beautiful and handsome.
Later, the Queen feared that King Candraprabha would disapprove of the Prince’s appearance;
she feigned this excuse:
"According to our country's ancient custom, members of a household do not see one another during the day."
"Consider this a matter of great importance.
Your Consort must not lose her dignity.
She replied:
"I respectfully accept.
I dare not disregard your noble instruction.
From that time forward, the Crown Prince never again showed any sign of distinction in his comings and goings.
I reflected deeply that my own kingdom was at enmity with seven other states, contending for power without a moment of peace, while the myriad people sighed in lamentation.
"I shall employ expedient means to bring them security," I thought to myself.
Thus, I pondered within my heart:
"My body is exceedingly humble; when my consort beholds it, she will surely depart.
My mother wishes to behold my consort’s countenance once.
The Empress said:
The woman’s appearance was ugly, while the consort’s countenance was radiant and beautiful.
The Crown Prince repeated his refusal,
but the Queen, taking pity on him, took the consort along to observe her.
The Prince feigned being a cowherd.
When the Consort saw him, she said,
"This cowherd is ugly."
The successor said,
"This was the herdsman of the former king; hereafter,
you shall observe the celestial signs."
The consort beheld him once more and, suspecting him, said:
"Whenever I travel, I invariably behold this man; could he be the Prince?"
The consort said,
"I wish to behold the radiant countenance of the Crown Prince.
The Queen then contrived a plan and sent her younger brother out for a stroll.
The Crown Prince was accompanied by his officials and attendants;
when the Consort saw this, her heart felt a slight joy.
Later, he entered the garden again.
The Crown Prince climbed the tree and threw a fruit at his back;
the Consort said,
"This is certain proof that he is the Crown Prince."
At night, while she was sleeping, he silently illuminated her with fire to observe her appearance; terrified, he fled back home.
The queen and concubines were indignant and said, "How can you allow the consort to return?"
He replied, "The Consort’s departure is the foundation for the peace of the world; the people will ultimately find rest with their kin.
He bowed and took his leave, then sought her out until he reached the land of the Consort.
Yang worked as a hired laborer for a potter making ceramic vessels;
he also entered the city to work as a hired dyer;
and he served as a hired groom for a high minister to keep his horses in good condition.
Furthermore, the Grand Cook was appointed to supervise all the delicacies and soups for entry into the inner palace.
The King had eight daughters who all took delight in this task, yet Candraprabhā did not look upon them.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, marveled and said:
The Bodhisattva’s sorrowful concern for sentient beings has reached this point;
I shall employ skillful means to assist him.
I shall transform the seven hostile kingdoms into moonlight and provide a letter from the hand of my father, the King.
He gave his daughter, Candraprabhā, in marriage to him.
Seven kingdoms established ceremonial rites and sent representatives to escort him to the kingdom for the wedding.
They all said:
He took as his bride the king’s daughter, named Candraprabhā;
their legal dispute became so protracted that each produced a written document.
Their resentment was expressed with one voice, saying:
"We shall exterminate your descendants;
we are resolute in this."
When the envoy returned with the letter, everyone unanimously rebuked him, saying:
"By giving one of your daughters to seven states, you have incurred their enmity;
the Qi army is now mobilizing in great force, and we realize that your loss of the state lies precisely in this."
Upon hearing this, the king was struck with fear and said, "This calamity is about to arrive; it has been summoned by my own past actions.
He then addressed Candraprabha, saying:
As you have become a consort to a man, whether your husband is wise or foolish, auspicious or inauspicious, handsome or ugly—all these stem from past karma (*sukṛta*); who can alter them?

Yet, failing to maintain constancy and single-minded devotion, and failing to exhaustively practice filial piety and reverence, you returned to your country with meager wisdom; thus has this calamity come upon you.
"I shall now divide this body of mine into seven parts to offer as a tribute to the seven kings.
Candraprabha wept and said,
"I pray you grant me the space of a mere moment of life."
"I shall seek out men of wisdom; there must be one capable of repelling the threat posed by the seven states.
The King then issued a proclamation, saying:
"Who among you can ward off this calamity?"
His wife was nurtured by moonlight and raised with primal blessings.
The Prince said, "Construct a high tower quickly; I am able to ward off this calamity."
The visualization was accomplished.
The Prince feigned illness, stumbling and collapsing to the ground;
only when borne by Candraprabha could he then repel the enemy.
Candraprabha, terrified that he would be slaughtered, supported Puṣkarasārin as they ascended the tower.
The Prince cried out in a loud voice,
and the sound of his words reverberated far across the seven kingdoms.
If one were to use the lion’s roar as a metaphor for the greatness of the Buddha's teaching,
then the people should be gathered through the Way of Benevolence;
yet now, as anger arises with intensity, calamity becomes manifest.
When calamity manifests, the person perishes and the state falls;
is this not due to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)?
Among the seven kingdoms, there was no great master who did not fall prostrate in trembling.
After a short while, he revived and wished to return to his own land.
The Prince addressed the King, saying, "In matters of marriage, there is no one more suitable than the various kings.
Why not bestow your seven daughters upon those seven princes?"
The son-in-law serves as a protective screen for the King, bringing about great peace;
the ministers and the people find rest,
and the parents obtain nourishment.
The king said, "Excellent! This music is truly great.
He then commanded the seven kings to give their daughters in marriage to him.
The eight sons-in-law paid their respects, and the sovereign and his ministers were filled with joy.
The King, along with his subjects, finally learned that these were the former husbands of Prince Candraprabha.
He then selected excellent ministers and warriors to accompany them, and each returned to his own kingdom.
The nine kingdoms were harmonious and peaceful, and the myriad people danced for joy.
They all sighed in unison, saying:

"Heaven has bestowed upon us a sage authority that transcends the perception of ordinary men; virtue has gathered and merit has been perfected, resulting in a state of tranquil peace beyond reproach."
After he had been in his country for several years, the Great King passed away.
The Crown Prince ascended the throne and issued a general amnesty for all crimes.
He then instructed the myriad people through the five precepts, the six perfections, the eightfold fast, and the ten wholesome actions.
Calamities and misfortunes shall all cease; the nation will be abundant and the people peaceful; the Great Transformation will spread, and all shall revere the Triple Gem.
Virtue will flourish and blessings will converge, and all illnesses shall be extinguished.
The reason for this is as follows:
When the Bodhisattva was formerly at home, he was plowing together with his wife and told her to go fetch food.
While waiting for his wife’s return, he saw her walking along with a Pratyekabuddha;
as she did not arrive for a long time, doubt arose within him.
Filled with rage, he seized a hoe, intending to strike him;
however, upon seeing his wife dividing her own food to offer it to the śramaṇa,
he withdrew and stood with palms joined in reverence.
When the śramaṇa had finished eating, he lifted his bowl into the air; radiance blazed forth brilliantly as he flew away.
The groom felt remorse and shame, thinking that his wife possessed such virtue that she had brought about the arrival of this venerable one.
"I am deeply foolish and shall surely suffer the consequences.
He then said to his wife,
"The merit from your offerings, you and I shall share together."
They ate the remaining rice together, and thus there was no further need for it.
When their lives came to an end, each was reborn into a royal family;
the wife possessed the grace of pure compassion.
He was handsome from birth.
Because his son-in-law was first angry and later compassionate, he was initially ugly and subsequently beautiful.
The Crown Prince was myself.
The wife was Gopī; the father-king was King Śuddhodana;
and the mother was my own mother, Māyādevī.
The Heavenly Lord Śakra was Maitreya.
Regarding the *Cālakya-rāja-sūtra*, it says that from lifetime to lifetime, the Bodhisattva was concerned for sentient beings and rescued them from the mire of suffering.

Fifth: Mupoke (Mukhapaṭa) did not speak while he was buried, but after being buried, he spoke and attained the practice of the Way. This concerns the crown prince of the King of Vārāṇasī during the five periods.
His name was Mupo.
He was of peerless beauty and possessed the ability to remember his past lives across countless kalpas.
He perceived all things—good and evil, long life and early death, beauty and ugliness—with complete knowledge and vision.
At the age of thirteen, he remained silent with his mouth closed.
He was the king’s only son, beloved by the entire nation, and destined to succeed to the throne.
He did not speak of hunger or cold; he was tranquil and simple, his mind like withered wood.
Though he possessed ears and eyes, he gave no heed to seeing or hearing;
though his wisdom and deliberation were far-reaching, they were as if he had no will or intention.
He was like one who is blind and deaf, unable to distinguish east from west;
his appearance was like that of a dull-witted fool, no different from a commoner.
His father was filled with anxiety and suffered greatly from this distress.
Deeply ashamed that his neighboring country might look down upon and mock him,
he summoned the brahmins of the kingdom and asked them,
"For what reason is this child unable to speak?"
The Brahmins said, "Although this child has a handsome face and features, he harbors inauspicious intent within.
He desires to harm his parents and bring about the ruin of the state and the extinction of the clan; this will happen before long."
Those who no longer bear children are all hindered by this wicked child; it is fitting that you bury it alive.
Thus, Your Majesty’s person may be fully preserved, the state secured, and the lineage stabilized;
thereafter, you shall again be able to give birth to a noble son.
Otherwise, it would be extremely perilous.
The king, believing the mad and foolish words to be true, was immediately overcome with grief;
he could find no peace whether sitting or rising, he did not attend to music or entertainment, and he found no pleasure in fine clothes or delicacies.
He then consulted with the elders and great ministers; some said to cast him away into the deep mountains, while others said to sink him in deep waters.
One minister spoke:
Simply construct a deep pit with side entrances like chambers;
provide him with provisions and attend him with five servants.
He placed him inside and followed his instructions wherever he went;
the king immediately complied with him.
The prince was moved by grief and lamented his foolish delusion.
His mother, out of pity and love, was broken by grief and said, "My son’s fate is meager; he has met with such calamity.
Weeping and lamenting, she had no choice but to reluctantly let him go.
They took all the clothes, necklaces, and jeweled ornaments belonging to the prince and sent them with him;
while the servants remained outside,
they proceeded together to dig a pit, though the digging was not yet finished.
Mupò remained alone in the carriage, reflecting deeply within himself,
speaking to his own heart and mouth:
"The king and the people all say that I am truly a fool and mute."
Therefore, I did not speak of abandoning worldly ties to settle the body, avoid vexations, and rescue the spirit from suffering;
yet now, I am instead endangered by the mad and the deceitful.
Having lost my life, I shall fall into the same state as those people.
He then silently took the necklace and jewels for himself and departed;
the people there were unaware that Mupai had taken the items and left.
At that time, Mupai immediately went to the water’s edge,
purified herself by bathing, anointed her body with incense,
and took all her garments, coverlets, and necklaces to put them on.
Arriving at the place where the pit was being dug, he asked,
"What is this pit being made for?
The servant replied:
The king had a crown prince named Mupò (Mūkapāla).
He was mute, deaf, and mentally dull; at the age of thirteen, he was unable to speak.
We dug a pit and intended to bury him alive.
The Prince replied, "I am Māṇavaka.
The people were struck with terror and fled;
they looked upon the chariot, but he was nowhere to be seen.
Returning to the site of the pit, he observed it with intense scrutiny; the sounds of speech had ceased, yet there was a different sound—a radiance like that of the moon, rarely heard in the world.
Those walking to his left and right halted their steps, and those sitting rose to their feet.
The flying birds and running beasts all gathered together and prostrated themselves before the Prince to listen to his words.
He spoke again, saying:
"Observe my hands and feet; examine my physical form."
How could the masses believe this mad deception and allow themselves to be buried by their own views?
They composed eloquent words, causing those around them to be struck with alarm;
they all prostrated themselves, knocking their heads to the ground, seeking mercy and pardon.
The Prince said,
"Now that I have been cast out, it is not fitting for me to return.
The servant immediately galloped back to inform the King.
Upon hearing this, the king was moved by both grief and joy;
he immediately set out with his consort in a carriage to welcome them.
Before the king had yet arrived, Mupai thought to himself:
While he was practicing the Way,
Śakra transformed himself into a garden tree of incomparable bliss.
From afar, the King saw the Prince sitting beneath the tree.
When Mupò saw the king, he immediately rose to welcome him.
The king paid his respects to him, and Mupò then addressed the Great King, requesting him to take his seat.
The king heard the voice and tone of the prince’s speech.
His majestic spiritual power was immeasurable, shaking heaven and earth, and was utterly peerless;
they were then filled with great joy and circumambulated Mopai before returning together to their country.
Mumingu said, "I request to decline my seat while you occupy the position and govern the state.
Mupo replied, "It must not be so."
Out of shame and weariness for the manifold sufferings, sorrows, and poisons of hell,
I reflect that in the past I was once a king named Kṣaṇika.
He governed the state according to the laws and practiced all manner of goodness.
For twenty-five years, neither the whip nor the staff was employed, weapons were not set forth, and there were none held in prison.
He bestowed kindness and practiced benevolence, his grace and virtue flowing everywhere; he rescued the destitute and the obstructed, having no greed or stinginess.
Although they perform these practices, they still commit minor offenses and ultimately fall into hell for over sixty thousand years.
There, they are boiled, roasted, flayed, and torn apart; the agony is so cruel it is unbearable.
They seek death but cannot find it, and their existence is one of utter despondency.
At that time, although my parents possessed great wealth and high status and enjoyed boundless happiness,
how could they have known that I was undergoing such severe torment in that hell?
"How could they possibly come to share in my suffering?
The reason I fell into this state of sin is that in the past, when I was a king ruling over a small kingdom,
my nature was exceedingly compassionate and benevolent, and my moral discipline was so lofty that my laws and decrees were not strict."
All the minor kings, regarding him with contempt, deliberated together:
"Now this Great King is both gentle and weak;
his majesty and strategy do not restrain others, and his virtue is insufficient to govern a great kingdom. We ought to punish and depose him."
He immediately raised his troops and came to invade the great kingdom.
At that time, the king momentarily reflected and sent him exquisite treasures and wealth as gifts;
furthermore, he pacified him by appointing him to high office with generous stipends, providing him with care and consolation.
He immediately returned to his own country.
Not long after this, he came again to attack and punish him on numerous occasions, not just once.
The ministers of the great kingdom then addressed the Great King, saying:
The various minor officials of the state are foolish, ignorant, and devoid of righteousness;
disregarding the consequences of their transgressions, they repeatedly act with insolence and arrogance,
plotting murder and committing acts of rebellion against their sovereign.
"The people have been thrown into a state of alarm and unrest, and their defensive preparations will not cease; you ought to execute them to eliminate this scourge.
The King said, "As the parents of the people, I must strive for benevolent transformation."
Forgiving oneself while nurturing all things, risking one's own life to save the multitude—
regarding others as if they were infants, he takes pity on their lack of understanding and guides them gradually, unable to bear inflicting harm upon them. Thus,
the King universally loves the lives of all beings and never inflicts execution or punishment.
The ministers of the great kingdom could not bear to do this repeatedly;
however, the subordinate cities and small kingdoms were easily provoked to anger and disregarded the difficulties,
raising armies to invade and slaughtering the people.
The Great King shed tears of rain;
he observed a period of mourning for the deceased people of the various kingdoms as if they were his own sons, his compassion being boundless.
When the minor kings saw that the Great King’s heart was so compassionate and mindful of the people, they were moved.
They were all immediately subdued and subsequently came to submit.
"Your Majesty, you intend to prepare a grand feast of rare delicacies; for this, it will be necessary to slaughter oxen, sheep, and the six domestic animals to provide the various flavors.
I venture to inform Your Majesty of this first."
Although the king’s heart was compassionate, he could not help himself;
his head was pressed down, and because of this, he incurred such grievous suffering.

With every thought, his mind trembled violently and his body grew cold and clammy as he recalled the various fortunes and misfortunes, safety and peril, successes and failures that had occurred throughout his past lives.
Fearing that he might again encounter [misfortune], I hope to remain in silent seclusion,
so as to escape defilement, emerge from the dust of worldly toil,
bid eternal farewell to the mundane world, and avoid further calamities.
I then further thought: "If I close my mouth and remain silent, I fear the King will bury me alive.
I dread that at a later time I might again incur this calamity and enter hell from which there is no period of escape."
It was because I did not wish for the King to incur sin that I spoke again.
Guard your mind; do not take pleasure in being king.
The people of this world are as fleeting and insubstantial as a dream.
The joy and entertainment of one's household last but a moment;
calculating the span of life, it is but brief, while anxieties and fears endure for a long time.
Pleasure is little, suffering is much, and the myriad forms of affliction are beyond count.
Therefore, the wise regard national wealth,
treasures, and the bonds of affection as burdens,
and manifold desires as dust.
If I were to become king, I would surely again succumb to arrogance and indulgence, greedily seeking pleasure and satisfaction,
thereby causing the people distress and anxiety;
this would be a great calamity for the world.
Now I wish to cast them aside, to turn back the current and exhaust the source, to rescue and deliver those who have not yet crossed over.
Life in this world is like a temporary lodging; there is not a single thing upon which one can rely.
Not coveting wealth or nobility, nor valuing precious jewels;
casting aside worldly glory and contemplating the Great Way,
they soar high and travel far, withdrawing themselves from the world.
The father king said, "You are a wise man; you should not act so hastily. Mopai replied:
"I have heard that father and son were born only to abandon one another;
that their very flesh and blood have been severed is a most grievous transgression.
To receive me with such hardship would only increase your toil and vexation in vain."
The father, beholding his firm resolve,
was utterly bewildered and at a loss for words with which to reply; he then said:
Just as you practiced various virtues when you were a king in a previous life,
even though the loss of wealth was minor and not worth remembering,
you still underwent such diligent suffering for your transgressions.
Now, as I govern the state, I do not uphold the laws and regulations.
Having failed to perform even the slightest good, I have instead committed these transgressions and errors.
My conduct is purely perilous; how can my offenses be described? They are beyond measure.
He then released the Prince, permitting him to go forth and study the Way.
Thereupon, the Prince abandoned his kingdom and relinquished his kingship, no longer attending to worldly affairs.
With single-minded devotion and focused diligence, he contemplated the Way and cultivated virtue; through the accumulation of merit and achievement, he has eventually reached his present state.
The one who yearned for the remains was my own body;
the father-king was Śuddhodana;
and the mother was Māyā.
The physiognomist was Devadatta;
the attendants were Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the other four, as recorded in the *Taizi Mupo Jing* (Sutra of Prince Mūkaputra).
6. The Sacrifice of the Body by Prince Sattva. Long ago, there was a king named Mahāratha.
Through his practice of virtuous conduct, the kingdom was free from enemies.
The king had three sons;
the eldest was named Mahāpanada.
Next was named Mahādeva, and his younger brother was named Mahāsattva.
Together they went out for a stroll and reached a bamboo grove, where they dismounted to rest.
Proceeding further, he saw a tigress who had recently given birth seven days prior; she was surrounded by her seven cubs,
emaciated by hunger and exhaustion, her body so wasted that her life was on the verge of ending.
The first prince said, "How strange!
This tiger has failed to find food;
driven by hunger, she will surely return to devour her own cubs."
The third prince asked,
"What does this tigress usually eat?
The first prince replied:
They ate the warm flesh and blood.
The third prince said,
"Who can provide food for this tiger?"
The second prince said, "Our remaining lifespan is but brief; if others were to come seeking [our help], we certainly would not be able to save them.
Who could possibly disregard their own body and life?"
The first prince said,
"There is nothing more difficult to relinquish than one's own body.
The third prince said:
Their wisdom is meager while their greed and attachment are profound;
unable to relinquish their bodies, they are struck with terror upon hearing this.
Only the Great Beings harbor compassion within their hearts.
"To sacrifice this body and life for the benefit of others is not difficult.
Having all harbored such anxious thoughts, they departed after gazing at him intently.
Then the third prince thought to himself:
"The time has come for me to relinquish this body.
Since ancient times, I have cast this body away in vain, accomplishing nothing at all,
while constantly guarding my house, home, and clothing."
One provides various foods and drinks to nourish them so that they lack for nothing;
yet, instead of recognizing such kindness, they respond with resentment and harm.
In the end, all things return to impermanence, and thus there is no benefit whatsoever.
This body is as loathsome as a thief and like a walking latrine.
Now, this body of mine serves as a great bridge over the ocean of birth and death,
amidst immeasurable abscesses, ulcers, diseases, and hundreds of thousands of terrors.
Excrement, urine, sinews, blood, skin, and marrow are all interconnected and sustained together;
I shall now renounce them in order to seek the quiescent, unsurpassed nirvana and the immeasurable merits of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Fully accomplishing the subtle and wondrous Dharma-body,
he brings all manner of Dharma-joy to sentient beings;
yet he fears that his two elder brothers will create obstacles for him.
He then said to his elder brother,
"You may return to your dwelling with your retinue.
The Sattva returned to where the tigress was.
He stripped off all his garments and hung them upon a bamboo pole.
Thinking, "For the sake of the wisdom of Bodhi, I shall forever leave the three realms of existence," he then cast his body down and lay before a starving tigress.
The tiger was unable to devour him.
[The man] pierced its neck with dry bamboo and threw himself down from a height; the earth shook violently, and the sun lost its brilliance.
Heavenly rain fell of various flowers and manifold exquisite fragrances,
and from the sky there issued praise, saying: "How unprecedented!"
The tiger then licked the blood and gradually became able to eat the flesh;
as it grew stronger from the power of its food, only the bones remained. (From the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Volume Four).
7. Prince Oṣadhiprabha Relieves the Sick. Prince Oṣadhiprabha Relieves the Sick.
In the past, during a kalpa when the people of Jambudvīpa were afflicted by disease, a universal plague broke out and everyone suffered from illness.
At that time, there was a king of Jambudvīpa named Mahīsena,
who ruled over eighty-four thousand great cities.
Possessing sovereign power and majesty,
since the Chief Queen became pregnant,
all those whose hands she touched were cured of their illnesses.
When the moon was full, she gave birth to a son.
As soon as he was born, he spoke, saying,
"I am able to cure diseases."
Furthermore, at the time of his birth,
all the devas and spirits within Jambudvīpa proclaimed together:
"The one now born as the king is truly a medicine for mankind."
Because this sound flows and resounds everywhere, he is named "Human Medicine" (Manuṣyabhaiṣajya).
At that time, they brought sick people to show to this prince;
thus, various patients arrived.
If a prince touches them with his hand or with his body, they are immediately healed and restored to peace and happiness.
In this manner, Prince Manuṣyabhaiṣajya treated diseases for a thousand years.
Afterwards, his life came to an end.
When various sick people heard that he had died,
they grieved and wept, crying out, "Who will now deliver us from our sickness, pain, and affliction?"
The various sick people said,
"Where has Prince Manuṣyabhaiṣajya burned his body?
Having learned where he was, they went to the place of his cremation.
He extracted his bones and ground them into powder, which he applied to their bodies, and they were all immediately healed.
After his bones were exhausted, he went to the place where he was to burn his body, and there too everyone was healed.
I am that Prince of Human Medicine; this is from the lower fascicle of the *Bodhisattvapitaka Sūtra*.

8. There was a prince who, having heard of his past lives, was terrified and sought refuge by returning to the Buddha. There was a prince who, having heard of his past lives, was terrified and sought refuge by returning to the Buddha. (8) There was a prince who wished to know his past lives.
He then asked the Buddha about this.
The Buddha said, "It is not necessary to know it; it only causes people to suffer in grief."
The prince wished to know [this] for the sake of his former lives.
Thus it was asked up to three times.
The Buddha then conferred upon him the precepts so that he might know his past existences.
Thereupon, the prince examined his own situation;
at fifteen, he was due to die, and his grief was beyond words.
When he reached the age of fifteen, he then died.
The royal family buried him and planted cypress trees, which grew large;
their roots descended deep into the earth, striking directly upon his heart.
His consciousness remained within his body, and as he watched, he saw the cypress roots sprouting.
It pierced my heart straight through, penetrating its very core.
Thereupon, emerging from the roots among the cypress leaves, he saw a sheep coming again.
He thought to himself:
"This sheep eats cypress; it will surely harm me as well.
When the sheep came to graze, [the poison] was within its belly.
They emerge from sheep dung and cling to it;
according to the *Yuánjiā lù* (Gardeners’ Records), they are gathered to manure leeks,
whereupon they dwell among the leek leaves.
The Queen Mother craved leeks;
she issued an order to the outside to have some sent.
A gardener, holding a knife, was about to cut some leeks when [the Buddha appeared].
Fearing he might be harmed by a blade,
his grief and anxiety over every matter were beyond description.
The gardener cut a bundle of leeks and sent them to the royal palace.
Within a bundle of leeks,
the royal household obtained some leeks and ate them;
as the leeks entered the belly, they developed into offspring.
When the moon was full, he was born;
as he grew to adulthood, he again recognized his past lives and went to the Buddha’s dwelling, saying:
"I shall no longer use my knowledge of past lives,
for it causes me grief and anxiety.
I now return this knowledge of past lives to the Buddha."
The Buddha said to the prince,
"At that time, I did not wish to give it to you;
yet you desired to obtain it."
Then he repented; this may be found in the eighth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* (Miscellaneous Parables Sutra).
9. The Prince Abhaya’s Study of Medicine under Jīvaka. In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a young girl.
Her name was Vārāvatī. The king issued an edict to establish a brothel for her,
where anyone who stayed with her would receive two hundred taels of gold every day and night.
People from the four quarters gathered to gaze upon her, finding her exceedingly beautiful.
At that time, there was a prince of King Bimbisāra named Abhaya;
he stayed the night with this courtesan and subsequently became pregnant.
At that time, the courtesan commanded her gatekeeper,
saying, "If anyone comes seeking to see me, tell them that I am ill. Later,
when the months were complete, she gave birth to a son.
His countenance was handsome and upright.
At that time, the courtesan wrapped the child in white cloth and commanded her maidservant to discard him in the alleyway.
King Abhaya saw this and asked those nearby, "What is this?
They replied:
"This is a child. He was asked,
"Is it alive or dead?"
He replied, "He is alive.
The man had him carried back to his house and entrusted him to a wet nurse to be raised.
He immediately gave him the name Jīvaka Kumāra.
Later, as he gradually grew up,
the prince took a liking to him and called out to him, saying:
If you wish to remain long in the royal household,
yet possess no talent or skill,
you shall not be permitted to consume the king’s provisions in vain.
"You may learn a craft.
He replied, "So be it," and immediately followed a physician from the country of Takṣaśilā.
His clan name was Ātreya and his personal name was Piṅgala.
After seven years had passed, he addressed his teacher, saying:
"What shall I study? he asked.
Then the teacher gave him a basket and tools for digging grass, saying, "You may go to the country of Takṣaśilā."
He searched for medicinal herbs over an area of one yojana,
and brought back those that were not actually medicines.
At that time, the youth Jīvaka...
Just as when one has followed the teacher’s instructions to their conclusion, there is nothing among the grasses,
trees, and all other objects that one perceives which cannot be identified as a medicine;
one is well able to discern and know the appropriate application for each, such that there is nothing that is not medicinal.
He returned and reported this to his teacher.
The teacher replied, "You may go now; your mastery of the medical arts is complete."
"I am the foremost in Jambudvīpa.
After my death, you shall next succeed me;
return to the city of Bhagavat."
The wife of a great elder in the city had suffered from chronic headaches for twelve years;
although treated by many physicians, she could not be cured.
Upon hearing this,
Jīvaka went to his house and said to the gatekeeper,
"Inform the elder for me."
A physician was standing outside the gate.
The gatekeeper informed the elder, and the elder’s wife asked: "Who is there?"
"What does his appearance and form resemble?
He replied, "He is a youth."
He thought to himself:
"Even the elderly and experienced physicians could not cure him;
how much less so those who are young?"
Since there was no harm done, he called her in.
Then Jīvaka went to the householder’s wife and immediately took excellent medicine, which he boiled with ghee.
The physician poured [the medicine] into the nose and mouth of the elder’s wife;
both phlegm and saliva came out together,
which his attendants caught in a vessel.
Sū then collected it, spat it out,
and discarded it elsewhere.
At that time, Jīvaka said:
"If he is so stingy as to begrudge even this small amount of impure ghee,
how could he possibly repay me?
The householder's wife replied.
"It is not easy to maintain a household;
what benefit is there in discarding it?
It can be used for lighting fires, therefore I have collected it."
"You need only treat the illness; why worry about such things?
Later, when the illness was cured, the householder's wife—
He gave him four hundred thousand taels of gold,
along with male and female slaves, oxen, and horses.
Jīvaka returned to Rājagṛha and arrived at the gate of Prince Abhaya.
The king summoned him in and he related the preceding circumstances in detail to the prince,
offering all the goods he had obtained as a tribute. The prince said:

This is the account of Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya’s first treatment of a disease from the third fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Since the narrative details differ from those in the *Jīqíyù* (Jīvaka), both versions have been preserved.
*Jīnglǜ yìxiàng*, Scroll 32; *Jīnglǜ yìxiàng*, Scroll 33.
Section on the Princes of Various Kingdoms Who Studied the Path of the Śrāvakas.
Compiled by the Liang dynasty śramaṇas Sengmin, Baochang, and others.

3. Section on the Princes of Various Kingdoms Who Studied the Path of the Śrāvakas (33) 1. Jūlinru awakens to the impermanence of the world and attains the path of an Arhat. 2. Dīrghaśikha leaves the household life and attains the path of an Arhat. 3.

Jeta renounces the five precepts, practices the ten wholesome deeds, invites the Buddha to hear the Dharma, and attains the first fruit of the path. 4. Prince Kunāla loses his physical eye and gains the wisdom-eye. 5. Various princes ask the Buddha about those who have already left the household life; the Buddha explains what they have undergone, and they all awaken to the Way. 6. Prince Vaiśravaṇa plants roots of merit so firmly that they can never be moved. 1. Jūlinru awakens to the impermanence of the world and attains the path of an Arhat. There was once a king.
He was named Brahmadatta.
He made offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha,
attending every fast-day ceremony.
The king would frequently lead his retinue to visit the Buddha.
Whenever the Buddha preached the Dharma,
the king would always listen to the sutras with joy and reverence.
The Crown Prince was named Junlinru.
With a sincere mind and diligent effort, he realized that the world is impermanent;
seeing that nothing is born without dying, he did not crave the splendors of his time.
He addressed the king, saying, "A Buddha appears in the world but rarely; the Dharma and Vinaya are difficult to hear.
I beg to become a śramaṇa. The king immediately granted his request.
Junlinru then took his leave of the king and went to the Buddha’s dwelling,
where he requested to become a bhikṣu.
The Buddha then stroked his head with his hand.
His hair fell off naturally and the *kāṣāya* robe clothed his body.
He upheld the heavy precepts and practiced with diligent effort,
never wearying by day or night for three months.
He immediately attained arhatship; however,
at that time, the king did not know he had already realized the Way,
for he saw him enduring hardship by eating coarse vegetables.
Whenever he went to make offerings, he was different from the other monks;
his mind was not the same,
and he would frequently say to them:
"In our kingdom, there are all manner of rare delicacies made of the seven precious gems and sweet dishes beyond measure.
Why do you take pleasure in becoming a śramaṇa?
Jūnlín Rú then immediately leaped up lightly and ascended into the air.
He flew through the air, manifested transformations, divided his body into many parts, and entered and exited without obstruction.
When the King saw this, sorrow and joy welled up within him simultaneously; he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and paid homage to Gunaratna.
The Buddha commanded the Brahmin Sunetra to explain for the king the Dharma of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and the Four Noble Truths.
The king immediately attained understanding and realized the stage of Srotāpanna. This account is extracted from the *Brahmadatta-rāja-sūtra*.

2. Tiṣya’s Renunciation and Attainment of Arhatship. Regarding Tiṣya’s renunciation and attainment of arhatship: when King Aśoka first ascended the throne, he established his younger brother Tiṣya [as crown prince]. The *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states that he was named Vitasoka, while the *Qiyao jing* (Saptaratna-sūtra) records his name as Shanrong (Good Appearance). When he was a crown prince, he heard the Buddha preach the Dharma and subsequently renounced the world to become a śramaṇa. He practiced the path with great diligence and attained arhatship. At that time, King Aśoka, having heard that his younger brother had become a śramaṇa, dispatched messengers to summon him back. Tiṣya replied, "I have already renounced the world; I am no longer a member of the royal family. The king then sent a second messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall destroy your monastery. Tiṣya replied, "Even if you were to destroy a hundred monasteries, it would be of no consequence. However, if you were to destroy even a single person's faith, it would be a grievous matter. The king then sent a third messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall cut off your head. Tiṣya replied, "If you cut off my head, I shall simply take another birth; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a fourth messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall burn your monastery to the ground. Tiṣya replied, "If you burn my monastery, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a fifth messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill you. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill me, I shall simply be reborn again; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a sixth messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all your fellow practitioners. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill my fellow practitioners, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a seventh messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill you and all your fellow practitioners. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill me and all my fellow practitioners, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill you, your fellow practitioners, and all the monks in this country. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the monks in this country, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill you, your fellow practitioners, all the monks in this country, and all the people of Jambudvīpa. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the people of Jambudvīpa, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the people of Jambudvīpa and all the people of the four continents. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the people of the four continents, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the people of the four continents and all the people of the three thousand great thousandfold worlds. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the people of the three thousand great thousandfold worlds, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the people of the three thousand great thousandfold worlds and all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the Buddhas of the ten directions, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm and all the dharmas of the three times. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the dharmas of the three times, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the dharmas of the three times and all the emptinesses of the ten directions. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the emptinesses of the ten directions, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the emptinesses of the ten directions and all the non-emptinesses of the ten directions. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the non-emptinesses of the ten directions, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the non-emptinesses of the ten directions and all the dharmas of the three times. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the dharmas of the three times, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the dharmas of the three times and all the dharmas of the ten directions. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the dharmas of the ten directions, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the dharmas of the ten directions and all the dharmas of the three times. Tiṣya replied, "If you kill all the dharmas of the three times, I shall simply go elsewhere to practice the Way; there is nothing to fear. The king then sent a final messenger, saying, "If you do not return, I shall kill all the dharmas of the three times and all the dharmas of the ten directions. "If anyone can obtain the head of a Nirgrantha,
I shall give them one gold coin.
Vitashuka had been ill for many days while staying at the cattle-pen.

"You shall certainly receive a gold reward.
Thereupon, he drew his sword and went forth.
Vitasoka then reflected to himself:
Seeing that there was no way to escape the retribution of his karma,
he immediately met his death;
yet, carrying his head to the king, he sought gold.
The king, filled with doubt, questioned his physician and attendants.
They replied, "This is the head of Vitashoka.
The king fainted and remained unconscious for a long time.
The minister said to the king,
"One who is free from outflows does not extinguish this suffering.
Great King, you should bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings."
The king followed his words and issued a proclamation that no one should ever again kill any Nirgrantha.
The bhikṣus became doubtful and questioned Upagupta.
"What karma did Vitashuka create in the past to receive this retribution now?
He replied,
"In a past age, there was a hunter who killed many deer."
In a great forest there was a spring.
At that time, this hunter spread out a net and set snares with ropes by the water's edge, killing many deer.
At that time, before the Buddha had appeared in the world,
there was a pratyekabuddha who was eating by the water's edge.
Having finished his meal, he washed himself and returned to sit beneath a tree.
At that time, having smelled the fragrance of the pratyekabuddha, the herd of deer did not go to the water's edge.
Seeing that the deer did not come, the hunter sat waiting;
he then followed their tracks to the place where the pratyekabuddha was.
He thought to himself,
"It is because of this man that the deer do not come.
He then immediately killed the pratyekabuddha with a knife.
The hunter of old was none other than Vidhūṣaka;
because he killed various deer, he now suffers much from illness and pain.
Furthermore, because he killed a pratyekabuddha, he has remained constantly in hell for countless years.
For five hundred lifetimes, he has undergone various sufferings and afflictions;
in every birth within the human realm, he was constantly killed by others.
This is now his final retribution.
Although he had attained arhatship, he was still harmed by others.
Having gone forth in the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha,
he delighted in practicing generosity.
He constantly exhorted and transformed others to make offerings to the Sangha.
There was a stupa for a Buddha’s hair and nail clippings,
which he honored with incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and various kinds of music.
By the retribution of these karmic deeds, he was born into a great clan.
For one hundred thousand years, he constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Furthermore, he made this vow:
By these karmic conditions, he attained arhatship. From the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*, Volume Three. 3.

Prince Jeta Abandons the Five Precepts, Practices the Ten Wholesome Paths, Invites the Buddha to Hear the Dharma, and Attains the First Fruit of the Path. Prince Jeta abandons the five precepts, practices the ten wholesome paths, invites the Buddha to hear the Dharma, and attains the first fruit of the path. Third: Prince Jeta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, I received the five precepts;
however, the precept against alcohol was difficult to maintain, and I feared falling into transgression.
Now, I wish to relinquish the five precepts and receive the ten wholesome dharmas."
The Buddha asked,
"When you drank wine, what evil was there?
He replied:
The powerful and influential men of the country frequently led one another out,
bringing wine and food to enjoy themselves together;
thus they attained joy and amusement, and harbored no further ill will.
"Upon obtaining wine, one should mindfully recollect the precepts and refrain from evil.
The Buddha said,
"If a person can act as you do, what evil could there be in drinking wine for the rest of one's life?"
A practitioner who acts in this manner will accordingly generate merit and incur no fault.
Generally, there are two kinds of wholesome conduct for a person:
the first is that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Second is the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Tainted wholesome states lead to the pleasures of humans and devas;
untainted wholesome states transcend the suffering of birth and death.
Regarding the retribution of nirvana:
if a person drinks alcohol but does not give rise to evil karma,
they will receive a wholesome retribution due to the causal conditions of their virtuous mind.
"What fault is there in your upholding of the five precepts?
In the city of Śrāvastī, there were various noble kṣatriya princes who,
due to a minor dispute, eventually came to a great enmity."
Each side plotted together and raised armies to attack one another.
Both families were the preeminent heroes of their respective kingdoms,
and they were all further related by kinship, making them impossible to arrest or detain.
They engage in chaotic combat and do not follow reasoned counsel;
I am deeply concerned about this.
Furthermore, I thought to myself:
Formerly, there was a high minister of the late kings named Tivara.
Relying on his noble lineage, wealth, and power,
he treated [the Buddha] with contempt and insolence, even mocking him with physical gestures.
At that time, filled with rage, he truly desired to exterminate them.
He reported the matter to his father,
but his father would not listen.
Bearing poison in my heart and harboring resentment, there is nothing that can be done;
I am so distressed and emaciated by grief that I cannot eat or drink.
When the Empress Dowager saw me in such sorrow and suffering, [she asked what was wrong].
Though admonished in various ways, his mind remained undeterred;
he then sought fine wine and urged me to drink.
At that time, I addressed my mother, saying:
"Our ancestors have handed down the practice of worshipping Nārāyaṇa.
If we were to drink wine now, we fear the deity would surely be incensed,
and the brahmins would surely impose punishment upon us."
During the stillness of night,
the mother secretly opened the palace gate without letting anyone know;
though she was pressed repeatedly, she finally yielded and complied.
Having drunk the wine, he forgot his sorrows and resentments;
he summoned the palace women to perform music and entertainment for twenty-one days,
through which he found relief.
Having reflected thus,
he immediately commanded his loyal ministers to prepare fine wine and various delicacies.
He summoned his various ministers and assembled them in the royal hall.
A loyal minister prepared a lapis lazuli bowl with a capacity of three sheng.
The king first poured out one bowl;
each person prepared one bowl of ambrosial, wondrous medicine.
Afterwards, they discussed state affairs while simultaneously performing as a troupe of entertainers.
When those people received the wine and heard the music, their hearts were filled with joy; they forgot their enmity and became carefree, free from sorrow.
The king then took up his cup and said to the gentlemen:
When a gentleman cultivates virtue, it is transmitted through successive generations;
in following the holy teachings, one must not err.
Why, sirs, do you engage in such angry contention over a trivial matter?
"If you do not accept this, we fear the ancestral shrines of the state will perish.
Therefore, we earnestly entreat you to please desist.
Thus did the ministers address the king.
I respectfully receive this weighty command and dare not disobey it;
this is due to the merit of the *Huapijing* (Peaceful Wine Sutra), as recorded in the lower fascicle of the *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya-sūtra*.
4. Kunāla loses his physical eyes but gains the wisdom-eye. Regarding Kunāla losing his physical eyes and gaining the wisdom-eye: King Aśoka had four queens.
Her name was Padmāvatī (in the Liang language, "Hibiscus Flower"), and she gave birth to a son whose physical form and features were upright and handsome, with eyes that were preeminent;
there was no one who saw him who did not love and delight in him.
The palace attendants informed the king that the queen had given birth to a son;
the king was greatly delighted.

Therefore, this child was named Dharmapālita—*Dharma* meaning "Dharma" in the language of Liang, and *Pālita* meaning "increased" in the language of Liang. He then took the child and showed him to King Aśoka.
When the king saw him, he was filled with joy and spoke this verse:
My son’s eyes are upright and majestic, Created by merit,
their radiance is most brilliant; Like the *utpala* flower,
with these meritorious eyes, He adorns one side of his face.
His countenance was upright and handsome, like the full moon in autumn.
When Kunāla had grown up, his father took a queen for him;
the queen’s name was Ujjayinī, which in the language of Liang means "Golden," and Mālā, which in the language of Liang means "Garland of Flowers. At that time, King Aśoka—
He took Kuṇāla to the Kukkuta Monastery.
In that monastery was a senior elder (*sthavira*), an arhat possessing the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), named Yaśas.
At that time, Yaśas saw Kuṇāla, who was soon to lose his sight;
he immediately addressed the king, saying:
Therefore, he did not allow Guṇāra to perform his own work.
At that time, King Aśoka said to Guṇāra,
"Venerable one, reflect upon what you have done."
"You should follow him.
Then Kunāla prostrated at the feet of Yaśas and said:
"Venerable sir, please instruct me in what I should do.
Yaśas replied, "The eye is not permanent; you should contemplate this."
Then he spoke in verse:
“O Kauṇḍinya, you have constantly contemplated the eye as impermanent, a mass of suffering, disease, and manifold afflictions;
yet the foolish worldling, through inversion, gives rise to transgression because of it.”
At that time, Kuṇāla sat alone in a quiet place within the palace and reflected that the sense bases,
such as the eye, are suffering and impermanent.
At that moment, King Aśoka’s principal queen—
Named Viśākhā, she went to Kuṇāla’s dwelling and saw him sitting alone;
because she gazed at his eyes, a lustful mind arose within her.
He embraced her with his arms and spoke this verse:
"By the fire of the power of love, I am now being consumed by my own heart."
"Just as fire consumes fuel, you must fulfill my wish.
Kuṇāla covered his ears and spoke this verse:
"Now, for my mother—this is unrighteous attachment. She ought to abandon it and leave the gateway to the evil realms.
Her mother’s heart was filled with anger and resentment, and she spoke again in verse:
"Affection has gone to your place, yet you have no affection;
since your mind possesses evil, it shall soon perish in an instant. Kunāla said:
I would rather die now than give rise to an impure thought;
if an evil mind should arise, one loses the wholesome dharmas of humans and devas.

The Princess’s Contemplation of Impermanence upon Seeing Bubbles on the Water. Once, long ago, there was a princess of a king.
She was beloved by the king and never left his sight.

when the woman saw these water bubbles, her heart was filled with great affection and reverence for them.
The woman said to the king,
"I wish to have water bubbles to serve as a flower garland for my head.
The king said to the woman:
"Now, a bubble upon the water cannot be grasped;
how could it be taken to make a flower garland?
The woman said:
"If I do not obtain her, I shall take my own life.
When the king heard the girl's words,
he told the master craftsman:
"You are all masters of marvelous skill; there is nothing you do not understand.

If you do not, I shall have you all executed."
He replied,
"We are not capable of taking bubbles to make a garland.
Then an old craftsman said:
"I am able to take up the bubble.
The King was greatly delighted and immediately said to his daughter:

you should go yourself and personally supervise him.
Following the king's words, the woman went outside to observe.
Then the old artisan said to the princess,
"I am not accustomed to distinguishing the quality of water-bubbles.
I pray that you, Princess, will personally select the bubbles yourself, and I shall fashion them into a garland."
The woman then sought to grasp the bubbles, but as soon as they reached her hands, they burst and could not be captured.
In this manner, she spent the entire day without ever obtaining a bubble.
Exhausted and weary, the woman finally abandoned her search and departed.
The woman said to the king, "Bubbles are hollow and false; they cannot endure for long.
I pray that Your Majesty will fashion for me a crown of purple-gold."
Throughout the day and throughout the night, they never wither.
Bubbles upon the water deceive the human eye;

The human body is illusory, with little pleasure and much suffering.
The nature of things subject to decay cannot endure for long;
they undergo transformation and change, remaining in this world for but a brief moment, like a bubble upon the water.
