first their hair and nails fall away, then as the flesh cooks and separates from the bone, the boiling heat blows the bones out.
Once outside, the wind blows upon them, and they immediately regain their human form.
He took his own flesh and ate it.
Continuing further on his way, he saw a great tree surrounded by many insects that were biting and sucking its trunk, branches, and leaves.
There was not even a space as small as the tip of a needle left empty;
it resounded with great cries, vibrating like the sounds of hell.
Furthermore, he saw a man.
All around were various malevolent spirits with animal heads,
holding bows and crossbows from which they discharged three poisoned arrows each, all with flaming tips,
vying with one another to shoot him.
Their bodies were all scorched and burning.
Furthermore, he saw a great mountain with swords and blades fixed beneath it, and there he saw a man.
Swords, halberds, blades, and spears were hurled down from above to strike and pierce his body;
yet he immediately withdrew them, pulled them out, and set them back upright in their original places,
coming and going without ceasing.
Previously, he saw the Mountain of Bones,
seven hundred yojanas high;
Maudgalyāyana preached the Dharma for him upon that mountain.
The wife of a great caravan leader in the city of Śrāvastī was deeply beloved by her husband; yet,
wishing to enter the great ocean, he could not bear to part from her.
He was about to set out upon the sea.
His wife held up a mirror for him to look at his face;
he saw that he was handsome.
Having thus given rise to arrogance and deep-seated attachment,
they encountered a large tortoise that trampled their boat,
causing it to sink into the sea; everyone died.
All five hundred merchants died;
the ocean would not accept their corpses,
so the yakṣas and rākṣasas cast them out onto the shore.
According to their desires and thoughts, they die and are reborn as insects;
having cast off these insect bodies, they fall into the great hells.
In Śrāvastī, a female lay disciple’s maidservant invited a bhikṣu.
For ninety days during the summer retreat, he provided offerings and support.
A maidservant was sent to deliver the food;
when she reached a secluded spot, she would select the finest portions for herself to eat.
She gave the remainder to a bhikṣu.
When the mistress woke up and questioned her,
the maidservant answered.
"If I were to eat first, it would cause me to eat my own flesh in life after life.
Now, having first received this 'flower-retribution,' I shall later fall into hell.
The various insects on the great tree are biting and devouring me, emitting a great and terrible sound."
This bhikṣu, the administrator of affairs named Śaila,
used the property of the Saṃgha— such as flowers, fruits, and food—
to send them to laypeople.
Having received this retribution in the form of flowers,
they will later fall into hell as various insects that devour trees.
This is the person who obtained the object.
As for the one who raised a loud cry and wept as arrows pierced his body,
this person was a great hunter in a previous life.
Because they harmed many birds and beasts, they undergo this bitter suffering as retribution for those sins.
When their lives end here, they fall into the Great Hell.
As for those who cast themselves down from great mountains onto swords and blades:
This was a great and valiant warrior in the city of Rājagṛha.
Because of his fierce courage, he stood at the vanguard of the front lines;
because he had harmed and taken the lives of beings with swords, blades, spears, and shields, he has received this retribution.
There was a king named Dharmabhadra who practiced generosity,
maintained the precepts, and was compassionate, never harming the lives of living beings.
He governed the country with righteous laws for a full twenty years.
While he was gambling with others, at that time a man killed someone. The ministers addressed the king, saying: [The man who killed has been caught].
He replied, "I shall act according to the laws of the land," and immediately executed him in accordance with the Vinaya.
When the king had finished his play, he asked,
"Where is the criminal?
The minister replied, "He has already been executed."
Upon hearing this, the king wept and said,
"The seven treasures shall all remain here while I alone enter hell.
He immediately abdicated the throne and entered the mountains to dwell in self-restraint.
At the end of his life, he was reborn as a makara fish seven hundred yojanas in length.
The king and his ministers, relying on their power, had oppressed and exploited the common people.
When his life ended, he was reborn as a great makara fish.
As the worms on his body crawled about and scratched themselves against Mount Sphaṭika, they were crushed to death;
the blood flowed for a hundred *li*, turning everything crimson.
He ought to fall into the great hell.
At that time, the fish sleeps for a hundred years before awakening;
upon awakening, it is overcome by great hunger and thirst.
Even if one were to open their mouth, the seawater would flow in like a great river in full flood.
There were five hundred merchants who had gone to sea to gather treasures;
they encountered a situation where their ship was heading straight for the mouth of a fish.
The merchant called out, "Namo Buddha.
Upon hearing this, the fish closed its mouth,
and the merchant was saved.
The fish, its life ending from hunger, was reborn in the city of Rājagṛha.
A yakṣa took its body and placed it on this seashore.
At that time, the king was none other than you.
"Killing people is like [killing] fish.
Bhitika understood impermanence through his own mouth and grew weary of the world;
having exhausted all fetters, he attained the fruit of Arhatship. (From the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Seven).

5. Sudatta Attains Enlightenment upon Seeing the Buddha Amidst Difficulties. In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder named Sudatta. When he encountered the Buddha amidst difficulties, he attained realization of the Way. There was a great elder in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
The *Xiányújīng* (Sutra on the Wise and the Foolish) concerning Sudatta begins by stating:
"The four divisions of the Vinaya all call him a *gṛhapati* (householder); because he constantly provided alms to the solitary and the beggars, people took this as his title."
Previously, he possessed landed estates in the city of Rājagṛha.

Every year he would travel there; according to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Śāriputra-mūla-abhidharma-śāstra*, it is said that for the sake of his son and daughter-in-law, he went to the city of Rājagṛha and stayed in the house of the elder Ghoṣila. According to the *Mūla-vastu*, it is said: [text continues].
Kalandaka. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states that Sandhāna rose at night to sweep and repair his house and prepare various delicacies.
Sudatta questioned him,
and he replied,
"In the city of Kapilavastu, there is a son of the Śākya clan."
His name was Siddhārtha,
and his clan was Gautama.
Not long after his birth, physiognomists examined him.
He was destined to become a wheel-turning monarch,
yet his heart had no desire for it;
he renounced it and went forth into homelessness.
Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through self-awakening without a teacher,
he is called a Buddha because his mind is impartial toward all sentient beings;
he has clearly accepted my invitation.
He asked again,
"Where are you now? He replied:
In the Karanda Bamboo Grove Monastery, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that as Śūradatta was single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha and all his meritorious virtues in the Śītavana cemetery,
a great radiance suddenly appeared.
Following the light, he emerged and arrived at the city gate of Śikhā;
by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the gate opened spontaneously. The *Four-Part Vinaya* states that as he exited through the gate, there was a celestial shrine on the road.
Sudatta paid his respects and immediately returned to the darkness;
his heart was filled with terror,
and he wished to turn back toward the city gate.
A great deity addressed Sudatta, saying, "Virtuous one,
upon seeing the Buddha, you shall obtain excellent benefit."
The merit obtained throughout the entirety of Jambudvīpa is not equal to the merit of one who resolves to take a single step toward the presence of the Tathāgata. Sudatta asked:
"Who are you? He replied, "I am the son of the Brahmin Śraddhālinga.
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: "I am the deity Sīha; I was your spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in the past."
Because in the past I saw Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana prostrating and rejoiced,
I cast off my body and was reborn as a son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North.
He was solely intent on knowing how to protect this city. This is largely consistent with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. How much more so when one sees the Tathāgata, pays homage, and makes offerings?
Sudatta paid homage to the Buddha, and the Buddha preached the Dharma to him according to his needs.

The *Sūtra on Attaining the Path of Srotāpanna and Exiting Great Nirvāṇa*, fascicle twenty-seven; furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle twenty; and the four divisions of the *Vinaya* concerning the *Mahāvastu* (or *Madhyama Āgama*) are all largely the same with minor differences.

6. After Sudatta had relieved the seven poor people from their destitution, they obtained food and offered it together to the Buddha and the Sangha; consequently, his storehouses became spontaneously full. Regarding the six elders, after Sudatta had relieved the seven poor people, the latter’s poverty was most extreme.
In a heap of refuse, he found a wooden measure;
it was actually sandalwood.
He took it to the market and sold it.
He obtained four *dǒu* of rice and said to his wife, "Cook one *dǒu* together;
I shall go to seek some vegetables."
At that time, the Buddha thought to himself:
"I must deliver Sudatta so that his merit may be renewed.
Just as he had done so, the rice was fully cooked.
Śāriputra went there.
When the woman saw him,
she was filled with joy and cast an entire peck of rice and boiled grain into his alms bowl.
He cooked another peck of rice.
Maudgalyāyana went there again,
and the man likewise joyfully gave it to him.
He boiled another peck of rice.
Kāśyapa went there again,
and he gave it to him once more.
There was exactly one *dou* remaining;
he then cooked it until it was ready,
and the Tathāgata went there in person.
The wife thought to herself:
"There is no one who will provide even food for every other day."
Now that this rice exists,
the Tathāgata has personally looked upon it;
could there not be one whose transgressions are exhausted and merit is born?
He offered a full peck of cooked rice entirely to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then uttered a blessing:
"From this day forward, your transgressions shall be extinguished and merit shall arise."
Sudatta soon returned home.
Fearing his anger, his wife asked him:
"Now that the Buddha has arrived, as well as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana,
and Kāśyapa— all have come to seek alms.
Should we give them food or not?"
The answer is: "I shall give it.
A field of merit is difficult to encounter;
if someone comes to seek from you, this constitutes meeting with such a field."
The wife said,
"I have already given away all four pecks of rice as alms.
Her husband was greatly delighted.
There remained some rice gruel, which the husband and wife drank together.
After a short while, they wandered about,
[and found] precious treasures, granaries, and stores of grain and silk in every room.
It was naturally and truly full,
just as it had been in the past when he was wealthy.
Sudatta leaped for joy.
Knowing that the Buddha took pity on him, he further invited the Buddha and the Sangha for offerings until the vessel was empty.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the fruit of the Path (srotāpatti). This is from the *Za piyu jing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables), lower fascicle.

7. Unshakable by the Most Victorious Mara’s Temptations. Having heard the sublime Dharma, the seven most excellent elders attained the pure Dharma-eye, with all dust and defilements vanished, right there on their seats.
Having received the three refuges and become a lay follower (*upāsaka*),
he vowed not to kill for as long as his life lasted.
Not long after the Buddha had departed, [he passed away].
The evil Māra Pāpīyān transformed himself into the form of a Buddha, complete with the primary and secondary marks,
and came to the house of the elder.
The elder thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata has just departed; why has he returned so quickly?
The counterfeit Buddha replied, "I thought the elder was a man of high talent and broad wisdom, capable of discerning and criticizing the essential points."
"Listen attentively, householder.
You are deluded and lacking in wisdom;
the Four Noble Truths that I previously taught were not, in fact, the ultimate truths."
"This is a perversion,
practiced by the non-Buddhists.
The elder immediately realized this for himself.
He immediately replied to him, saying:
"Stop, stop! Do not speak.
I have attained the eye of wisdom and abide on the firm ground."
Even if you were to manifest a thousand million bodies through transformation,
I would not retreat.
Why should the light of a firefly compete with the brilliance of the sun?
The householder Kāṣṭhakuṇḍika wished to rival Mount Sumeru;
owls, vultures, crows, magpies, and garuḍas all flew together.
Pāpīyān felt ashamed and departed with his body. This is from the *Sūtra on the Most Victorious Householder Receiving the Benediction*.
8. Shenri prepared poisoned rice and a pit of fire for the Buddha, but they both spontaneously transformed and vanished. At that time, in the kingdom of Rājagṛha...
There was a householder of the four castes named Shenri;
his wealth and property were exceedingly vast.
His gold, silver, and precious jewels were beyond measure.
Shenri served other practitioners of the Way,
but he alone did not serve the Buddha.
All the various heterodox practitioners were filled with jealousy.
They deliberated together and said,
"The Buddha is now revered by the king, his ministers, the elders, the officials, and the common people."
Yet we alone are not held in high regard by him.
The Buddha himself has often said that he knows the matters of the past, future, and present.
Knowing what others are thinking,
he thought, "I should now test whether this is indeed so."
Shenri said, "How should we test him?
The heterodox practitioners replied:
He requested that the Buddha take the poison and place it within the rice;
he then dug a pit five *zhang* deep inside the gate,
placed fire within it, and covered the top with a thin layer of earth.
He caused the Buddha to come down from above;
yet if he had known that the invitation would not be accepted, he would not have invited him, but because he did not know this, he invited him.
Shenri replied, "I accept," and immediately went to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Very well."
The heterodox practitioners said:
"Since we already have nothing further to know,
we should simply dig into the earth."
Shenri had a son named Chanlufa,
who was sixteen years old.
Having attained mastery over past lives and being well-trained in the Buddha-way, he was able to know the affairs of the past, future, and present.
He addressed his father, saying,
"The Buddha already knows this."
Do not follow the words of evil people and cast yourself into boiling water or fire.
Shenri did not believe this;
he dug a pit, lit a fire, and placed poisoned food within it.
He addressed the bhikṣus,
"Follow behind me.
The Buddha then set out upon the path.
He then emitted light and shadows, causing the entire house of Śreṇika to turn entirely golden.
At that time, Caṇḍāla Dharma spoke to his father, saying,
"The Buddha has now arisen and is proceeding toward the path."
The ten directions were all as bright as the sun.
When the Buddha reached the city gate,
he stepped upon the threshold with his feet.
As soon as he raised [his hand] within the great city, it shook violently;
the sick were immediately healed,
and stringed instruments such as the *konghou* resounded spontaneously without being struck.
When the Buddha arrived at the gate of Shenri,
a fire pit five zhang deep was transformed into a bathing pool,
in the midst of which lotus flowers grew.
Each flower has a thousand petals.
From every lotus flower trodden upon by the disciples,
a hundred flowers sprout forth.
They all walked upon lotus flowers.
When Shenri saw the fire transformed into a pond with lotuses growing within it,
he was struck with great fear and terror.
Prostrating with his head to the ground, he spoke with sincerity:
"I have now prepared this meal for the Buddha, but I have placed poison within it all.
I pray that you will grant me leave to cook it again."
The Buddha said,
"There is no need to cook again.
Bring the meal containing the poisoned food and eat it."
The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus:
"Do not eat for now;
you shall eat only after I have given you instruction."
The Buddha then spoke a mantra, saying:
"In the world there are generally three poisons:
the first is lustful greed."
The second is hatred;
the third is delusion.
Since the Buddha is free from these three poisons, he does not engage in them.
For one who possesses the sutras and the Dharma with utmost sincerity,
even poison will not take effect;
if food is poisoned, it will all naturally dissipate on its own.
The Buddha said, "All shall eat.
Shenri bowed his head to the ground in prostration at the Buddha’s feet and said,
"I have been most irreverent."
Having used the words of evil people,
he wished to seek compassion from the World-Honored One and repent for his transgressions.
The Buddha then preached a sutra for him.
Attaining the Path of the Srotāpanna; excerpted from the *Shenritou Benjing* (The Original Scripture of Shenritou).

9. Bianyi Invites the Buddha and the Sangha. There were two beggars, one dead and one a king; Bianyi invited the Buddha and the Sangha. [In] the ninth [chapter], in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was the son of an elder.
His name was Bianyi (Discerning Intent).
Upon hearing the Buddha’s exposition of the fifty essential matters,
he attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
Five hundred sons of elder householders attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Bianyi said: "I only pray that the World-Honored One and the great assembly..."
"Tomorrow at noon, he will personally humble himself to our house for a meal.
The Buddha and the great assembly went to his house for the meal; before the blessing had been recited, [the food was served].
There was a beggar who went from seat to seat begging for alms;
no one dared to give him anything, and he returned with nothing at all.
Leaving in a state of anger,
he immediately gave rise to an evil thought: "These śramaṇas..."
He is self-indulgent, foolish, and deluded;
what path of cultivation could he possibly have?
When the poor beg from him, he has no intention of giving.
"If I become king,
I shall crush his head with the iron-rimmed wheels of my chariot.
Having said this, he departed.
When the Buddha had finished his prayer of blessing,
another beggar came and begged for food from the assembly.
He gave them each some;
having received the food and drink, they departed with joy.
Thereupon, he thought to himself:
"These śramaṇas possess a heart of compassion;
I shall serve as king to provide offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha for as long as seven days."
Having said, "I shall not repay the kindness of your present relief from hunger and thirst," he departed.
The two beggars then wandered about, seeking alms.
He arrived in that country and lay down by the side of the road amidst the deep grass.
At that time, the ruler of that country suddenly passed away without an heir.
A physiognomist declared:
The recordkeeper said, "A man of low station shall become king.
Then the ministers, officials, and their thousands of carriages and tens of thousands of riders traveled along the borders of the kingdom.
From afar, they beheld a cloud-like canopy upon the grass.
The physiognomist said,
"Among them is a divine person," and he immediately found the beggar.
When the ministers paid their respects,
the beggar was struck with astonishment and said to himself,
"I am low-born; I am not of royal lineage."
They all said,
"One should bathe with fragrant water and don the king's robes."
As Prabhāsa, adorned with radiant marks, entered the city with his retinue,
a beggar of evil intent lay sleeping in deep grass, unaware of him.
A carriage ran over and severed his head;
this is from the *Bianyi jing* (Sūtra on Resolving the Intent). 10. Dharmaruci’s Previous Life as a Great Fish. Once upon a time, there was an elder.
The one named Dharmaruci inquired after [the Buddha's] health.
The Buddha said, "Dharmaruci."
"It has been a very long time since we last met; it is only now that we have been able to see one another.
Someone asked this, and the Buddha replied:
In the past, incalculable eons ago,
there was a Buddha in the world named Dīpaṃkara.
At that time, I was a brahmin named Chao-shu. At that time,
there was the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
Just as he was about to enter the city,
I encountered him midway;
I loosened my hair and spread it upon the mud so that the Buddha might step across it.
The Buddha then gave this prediction:
"Your courage is such as this;
after incalculable kalpas (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa), you shall attain Buddhahood."
At that time, you gave rise to a mind of anger and said,
"This person is no different from an animal," and then walked over his hair as you passed by.
Since beginningless incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
they have constantly fallen among the animals;
furthermore, they dwell within the great ocean.
He became a makara fish,
seven thousand yojanas in length.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants.
They boarded a ship and entered the sea to gather treasures.
When they encountered a great fish that swallowed the ship and was on the verge of drawing them into its mouth,
the five hundred people each invoked the name of the deity they served.
Then the merchant leader spoke to the multitude, saying:
"In this world there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni;
there is none superior to him for rescuing people from peril and distress."
"We call upon your name, hoping to attain liberation.
Thereupon, they all called out in unison.
Hearing the Buddha’s name, the fundamental consciousness of the fish remained intact.
He then reflected to himself:
"The Buddha Śākyamuni has already appeared in the world;
why am I still here among these fish?"
He immediately submerged himself in the water,
and the five hundred merchants returned in safety.
At that moment, the fish leaped from its body onto the sandy bank.
Having neither drunk nor eaten for two full weeks, his life came to an end;
he was reborn as a son in the family of a *śreṣṭhin*, named Dharmaruci.
"He has now come to meet me;
that is why he spoke of 'long ago.
When Guṇavīra heard this account from beginning to end,"
He immediately went to the seashore to search for his old corpse.
Seeing the bones of a large fish with its skin and flesh already gone, he walked along the ribs and reflected, saying:
"This is my former corpse.
He then scattered flowers over his former corpse and immediately departed.
Suddenly, the *Chū-fen-bie-gong-de-jing* (Sutra on the Manifestation of Merit), Scroll Four, was completed.

11. The Stingy Elder Who Went to Sea; His Wife Gave Silk to the Buddha; All the Merchants Died and Only He Alone Survived. In the past, there was a man who was immensely wealthy yet extremely stingy. He went out to sea, and his wife gave silk to the Buddha. All the merchants died, and only he alone survived. (11) Formerly, there was a man of great wealth who was miserly.
His wife loved the Dharma and wished to practice giving, yet she did not dare.
When her husband was about to set out for sea,
she first surrounded their house with three layers of iron caltrops.
The woman was obstructed by them and could not escape;
she single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name,
whereupon all the iron gates and barriers transformed into goose feathers.
He took one roll of silk and entrusted it to someone to offer to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted it and recited the blessing.
Meanwhile, the husband was at sea with five hundred companions.
They were devoured by ghosts,
leaving only her husband.
The ghosts said to one another:
This man’s wife serves the Buddha;
he must not be approached.
His companions have all died, yet he alone has returned with treasures.
He asked his wife what had happened,
and she told him everything in detail.
The two of them were filled with joy.
He immediately invited the Buddha and the Sangha to hold a feast and thereby attained the Way; this is from the first fascicle of the *Za piyu jing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables), chapter 12:

"Vīradatta Invites the Buddha and the Sangha for a Meal and His Treasury Spontaneously Becomes Full. Twelve: In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a great elder. Vīradatta invited the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal, and his treasury spontaneously became full. Chapter Twelve: In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a great elder.
Named Śūradatta, he possessed immeasurable wealth and placed his faith in the Way and its Virtue.
He made a vow that on the eighth day of the twelfth month every year, he would invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
The descendants of the householder practiced this without ceasing until his death;
when he was about to pass away,
he instructed his sons not to let it fall into disuse.
The boy's name was Vīradatta.
Later, as their wealth gradually diminished, when the time for offerings arrived, they had nothing with which to provide them; thus, they were filled with sorrow and distress, finding no joy.
The Buddha sent Maudgalyāyana to inquire, saying, "Your father wishes to offer a monthly feast; what plan do you intend to employ?
He replied:
I only pray that the World-Honored One will not neglect or abandon me;
please deign to look upon me on the eighth day.
He took his wife to her maternal home and pawned one hundred taels of gold to provide the offerings.
The Buddha went with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty monks to the house and sat down.
After they had finished eating the pure food served by the attendants and returned,
at midnight that very night, the various ancient treasuries became spontaneously filled with precious objects.
The husband and wife saw this;
they were both joyful and fearful,
apprehensive that an official might question them.
He immediately went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Set your mind at ease and use it freely; do not harbor any doubts or difficulties."
"You have practiced faith and did not disobey your father's instructions;
having heard the path of giving and wisdom, you are fulfilled with the seven riches. This is from the third fascicle of the *Dharmapada*. 13.

Vāseṭṭha, who was stained by desire and endangered his life, was rescued by Maudgalyāyana. When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, Vāseṭṭha was so deeply immersed in lust that he placed his own life in peril; he was subsequently saved by Maudgalyāyana. (13) [End of Section] 13. The Buddha was in the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
There was a prominent elder named Śrījit,
whose great wealth overflowed in abundance.
The wife gave birth to a son whose appearance was magnificent and exquisite.
She invited a master to perform a divination, who marveled at the son’s merit and virtue, and asked:
"What auspicious signs have occurred since she conceived this child?
The elder replied,
"Her mother has been mute and dull in speech."
Having conceived this son, who was eloquent and skillful in speech,
they named him Vāseṭṭha;
when he had grown up, he went about traveling and sightseeing.
Seeing a girl from the family of a Nara-artist,
his mind became stained with attachment and he desired to marry her;
he returned to inform his parents, expressing his wish for them to seek her hand in marriage for him.
The parents replied, "Your status is so vastly different that you are no match for one another; how can we arrange a marriage?
The son addressed them again with earnest words:
"Do not inquire about his lineage; speak only of his character.
I pray you seek one for me, and if it does not accord with my wishes, I shall take my own life.
His parents complied with this request.
They entered into marriage.
The son, infatuated by her beauty, felt no shame in performing base tasks;
he would immediately go to her house.
He had already mastered all the arts of performance.
At that time, the king assembled many *naṭas* for various spectacles.
It was then the turn of the elder’s son to appear and perform the feat of running along a high rope.
The king did not see him and again commanded him to go up;
his strength gradually failed, and he was about to fall midway.
His heart was filled with terror and he had no refuge;
Maudgalyāyana, soaring through the air, addressed him, saying:
"If you would preserve your life today, it would be better for you to leave the household life and study the Way."
"Would you rather fall to the ground than marry that woman?
He replied, "I would rather save myself; I have no need for the woman."
Maudgalyāyana immediately manifested level ground so that his body and head were restored;
overjoyed beyond measure,
he followed after Maudgalyāyana.
He went to the World-Honored One to pay homage and make offerings.
At that time, the Buddha extensively expounded the sublime discourse;
his mind was opened and liberated, and he immediately attained the first fruit of the path.
Seeking to leave the household life, he requested it from the World-Honored One, who granted his permission.
His hair and beard fell away naturally, and the dharma robes appeared upon his body.
Devoting himself to meditative contemplation with single-minded diligence, he attained the state of an Arhat.
The Buddha said:
"In a past age, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī,
there was a great elder."
When he first had a son born to him, he was of incomparable beauty.
A man came from the sea carrying a bird's egg and presented it to the elder;
the elder accepted it.
After a short time,
the egg split open and a fledgling emerged,
its feathers glossy and radiant.
The elder accepted it and gave it to his son to play with.
The son mounted the back of the bird and flew about to observe the sights.
He heard that the king of another country was performing a *nara* (human) spectacle.
He rode upon a bird to that place;
the bird perched atop a tree,
and by chance seeing the princess, its heart was immediately filled with lustful attachment.
She dispatched a messenger to convey her feelings,
whereupon she engaged in sexual union with him;
this was discovered by the king.
They pursued, captured, and bound him, intending to execute him.
The son of the elder said,
"Gentlemen, why do you trouble yourselves to kill me?"
"Listen to me; I shall climb this tree and throw myself to my death.
When the people gave their consent, he climbed the tree, mounted the bird, and flew off into the void.
He obtained an extension of his lifespan.
The son of the elder at that time was none other than the present Vāseṭṭhi;
the princess was none other than the present courtesan.
The bird at that time was none other than Maudgalyāyana.
In a past life, he was distressed by delusion regarding forms and was saved by a bird;
now, when he was on the verge of death, he was likewise delivered.
By means of Maudgalyāyana, they were able to emerge in safety. *The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume Thirteen. 14.

The Elder’s Newly Born Son Immediately Recognizes His Past Causes and Seeks His Mother to Invite the Buddha; Sweetness Descends of Its Own Accord. In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder. A son was born to him, and immediately upon birth, he recognized his past causes and conditions. He sought out his mother and requested that she invite the Buddha, whereupon a sweet flavor descended of its own accord. (Section 14) In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder.
A son was born, whose eyes were upright and handsome; as soon as he was born,
he was able to speak and asked his parents:
"Are the World-Honored One, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the others still in the world?
His parents replied, "They are.
Seeing that he was able to speak, they realized he was not a non-human spirit.
He immediately went to question the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"This child possesses the marks [of a great man]."
The parents were filled with joy.
The son addressed them again, saying,
"I only pray that you will invite the Buddha and the Sangha."
He replied, "I have not provided any offerings at all.
The son then addressed him again, saying:
He merely swept and sprinkled the hall, adorned the couches and mats,
and set out three high seats; then,
food of a hundred flavors spontaneously filled the hall.
Furthermore, my mother from a former life still exists;
she resides in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
I pray that you will show her your favor in return.
The parents dispatched messengers riding elephants to welcome him,
providing three high seats:
one intended for the Tathāgata.
One was his father,
and the other was his mother from a previous life.
Once the Buddha and the assembly of monks had entered her house, [the two women]...
Sweet-tasting rice and food descended spontaneously in manifold abundance.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and the entire family, both great and small, all attained the first fruit [of the path]. (From the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Volume One).

15. Anāthapiṇḍada’s Seven Sons Receive the Precepts for the Sake of Wealth, Hear the Dharma, and Are Freed from Defilement. Regarding Anāthapiṇḍada’s seven sons in the city of Śrāvastī, they received the precepts for the sake of wealth, heard the Dharma, and were freed from defilement. (15) Anāthapiṇḍada in the city of Śrāvastī.
The seven sons lacked sincere faith;
they did not uphold the five precepts toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. The elder Anāthapiṇḍada said:
"I shall grant you a thousand taels of gold.
You all should take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the five precepts.
When the seven sons heard this, they...
They then desired to take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the five precepts.
Their father bestowed upon each of them one thousand taels of gold,
and they all went together to the place where the World-Honored One was.
He reported this in full to the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One?
Do those seven sons possess any merit, goodness, or virtuous qualities?"
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, householder!
You bring great benefit to sentient beings and peace and security to gods and humans."
Regarding those seven sons who were endowed with these various roots of goodness and merit,
I shall now describe the karmic fruits they obtained.
In the north, there is a country.
The city is named Śaila-guhā;
the land is fertile and abundant, and its population is flourishing.
Therein lies the Irapatara treasury.
Countless hundreds of thousands of pieces of gold, silver,
and precious jewels were spent from among the seven treasuries of the people of Gandhāra,
according to whatever they desired.
Neither this great treasure-store of Elapatra nor seven thousand units of gold—
multiplied by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or even countless times—
can ever equal the merit obtained by your seven sons.
The World-Honored One was preaching the subtle and wonderful Dharma to Anāthapiṇḍada. Thereupon,
[Anāthapiṇḍada] rose from his seat and addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"I pray that you will accept my invitation."
And [he invited] the community of bhikṣus,
wishing to provide them with ambrosial food and drink for the sake of his seven sons.
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing the proper time,
he entered the city of Śrāvastī, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him.
They went to the house of Anāthapiṇḍada and all took their seats.
The elder and his son paid homage to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One preached the Dharma, and they immediately attained right view.
He replied, "It is so.
The seven sons of the elder prepared delicious food and drink and offered it to the Buddha and the bhikṣus.
When the meal was finished, the bowl was set aside.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to the seven sons,
and each of them, while still seated, was cleansed of all defilements and impurities.
Free from blemish, he attained the arising of the Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma, he was without doubt and without hesitation. [From] the *Anāthapiṇḍika’s Transformation of His Seven Sons Sūtra*.

he burned it to charcoal in order to sell it quickly. 19. 1. The Flowing Water [King] saved ten thousand fish.
The Elder’s Son Jalavāhana, who saved ten thousand fish,
governed all sentient beings and alleviated their immeasurable sufferings and ailments within the kingdom of King Divyendraprabha.

because the illness had been eliminated, he performed many meritorious deeds,
speaking as follows:
Excellent, householder!
You are able to benefit sentient beings by granting them immeasurable life;
you must surely be a bodhisattva who understands all medicinal prescriptions.
Then the elder, together with his two sons, Water-Space and Water-Treasury,

until finally they arrived at a vast, empty marshland.
He saw tigers, wolves, dogs, and various birds and beasts all fleeing away in one direction;
the elder pursued them and observed until he came upon a pond.
The water in that pond had dried up. Seeing the many fish within it,
he gave rise to a heart of great compassion.
At that time, a tree spirit manifested half of her body and spoke these words:
"O Great Son of Good Family!"
"These fish are pitiable; you should give them water.
For this reason, I name you 'Flowing Water' (Śrotasvāha).
You should now act in accordance with your name to establish its reality."
Then the son of the householder asked the tree deity,
"How many fish heads are there?
The tree deity replied:
When ten thousand [years] were fully completed,
his great compassion increased;
at that time, this empty pond was scorched by the sun.
Only a small amount of water remained;
these ten thousand fish were on the verge of death,
writhing and twisting in all four directions.
Seeing this elder, they conceived a sense of reliance upon him;
wherever the elder went, they followed after him,
gazing at him with eyes that never for a moment left his presence.
At that time, the elder rushed in all four directions;
though he searched everywhere for water, he could find none.
Seeing a large tree, he immediately took its branches and leaves.
He returned to the edge of the pond to provide shade for him.
He then further investigated where the water in the pond originally came from;
he went out and searched thoroughly in all four directions, but could not find it.
Not knowing where the water was,
he ran even faster and saw a great river named Jāyodaka.
There were certain evil men who, for the sake of catching these fish, dammed up the water at a steep and precipitous point upstream so that it could not flow downstream.
The elder explained this circumstance to the king.
I only pray that Your Majesty will lend me twenty great elephants,
so that I may carry water to save the lives of those fish,
just as I have preserved the lives of these various sick people.
The King commanded his ministers to provide [the supplies] with great haste.
"You may now go yourself to the elephant stable and select as you wish whatever will benefit sentient beings.
At that time, Flowing Water and his two sons—
He borrowed twenty elephants and leather bags,
went quickly to the riverbank to fill them with water, and had the elephants carry it back;
thus the water was completely restored to its original state.
At that time, the son of the elder walked along the four sides of the pond as if strolling;
the fish also followed him, moving along the bank.
Then the son of the elder thought again:
"This fish must be tormented by the fire of hunger and wishes to seek food and drink from me;
I shall now give it to him."
Then the elder’s son said to his son,
"Take one of the elephants that possesses the greatest strength and go quickly home."
All edible things are the portion for one's parents to drink and eat,
as well as the portion for one's wife, children, servants, and slaves.
Having loaded all the gathered goods onto the elephants,
they returned with great speed.
At that time, the two sons went to their home.
He informed his grandfather of the aforementioned matters,
gathered whatever edible items were available in the house,
placed them upon the elephant's back, and returned swiftly to his father’s location at the empty marsh and pond.
At that time, when the elder’s son saw his child return,
his heart was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation;
he took food and drink from his side.
Having scattered it into the pond as food for the fish,
he then reflected to himself:
"I have now been able to provide food for these fish."
May they be fully satisfied.
In future ages, you shall provide them with the food of the Dharma.
It has been heard that in the past, in a secluded place, there was a bhikṣu who recited the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
That sutra states:
"If there are sentient beings who, at the time of their death,
are able to hear the name of the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī."
They were immediately reborn in the heavens.
I shall now, for these ten thousand fish,
explain the profound twelve links of dependent origination.
One should also recite the name of the Buddha Ratnashrī and then enter the water,
speaking these words:
Homage to the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī of the past.
In times long gone, while practicing the bodhisattva path,
he made this vow:
If there are sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who hear my name at the time of their death,
may they immediately attain rebirth in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Furthermore, he explained this profound and wondrous Dharma to these fish—
namely, the twelve links of dependent origination—
and having spoken this teaching, he continued.
They immediately returned home together.
Later, at another time, the son of that elder was gathered with guests;
having become intoxicated, he lay down to sleep.
At that time, the earth suddenly shook violently.
Then, ten thousand fish died on the same day and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Having been born there, they reflected as follows:
"By what wholesome karma have we been born among the gods?
they asked one another.
"Previously, while we were within Jambudvīpa..."
We fell among the animals and received the bodies of fish.
The Elder Srotodhara gave us water and food,
and for our sake he expounded the twelve links of dependent origination.
We also recited the name of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava.
By these causes and conditions, we have been born in this heaven.
We shall now repay his kindness by making offerings to him.
At that time, the son of the elder was sleeping while lying exposed on the upper floor of the mansion.
Those ten thousand devaputras placed ten thousand celestial, exquisite pearl necklaces at his head.
Again, ten thousand were placed at the side of his feet;
again, ten thousand were placed at the side of his right flank;
and again, ten thousand were placed at the side of his left flank.
Mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers rained down, accumulating to the height of the knees.
Various celestial musical instruments produced exquisite sounds,
and all those in Jambudvīpa who were asleep were awakened.
The elder’s son, Srotodhara, also awakened from his sleep.
Those ten thousand devaputras then soared and traveled through the air above,
while within the kingdom of King Devasabha, celestial lotuses of exquisite beauty rained down everywhere.
These sons of the gods returned once more to their original location at the pond in the empty marsh,
where they again rained down celestial flowers;
then, they vanished from that place and returned to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He enjoyed the five celestial desires at his own will and ease.
When that night had passed,
King Divyaprabha, the Sovereign of Heaven, [arose].
He questioned the ministers,
"For what reason did such a pure and wondrous auspicious sign manifest last night?
The ministers replied:
"Great King, you should know that the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven rained down forty thousand pearl necklaces and incalculable māndārava flowers upon the house of the Elder’s son, Sudāna."
The king immediately informed his minister,
saying, "You may go to that householder's home and summon him to come.
He then went to that house and proclaimed the king's command.
At that time, the elder went to the king's presence.
The king asked the elder,
"For what reason have you manifested such auspicious signs?"
The son of the householder said,
"I know for certain that the lives of these ten thousand fish have already ended."
Then the Great King said,
"Now you must dispatch someone to verify this matter.
Thereupon, Shrotasvatī immediately sent his son to the location of that pond.
He looked to determine for certain whether those fish were dead or alive.
At that time, his son went toward that pond and saw that there were many mahāmandārava flowers within it.
They piled them up into a heap,
and all the fish within it died.
He returned and said to his father:
All those fish had already passed away.
At that time, Shrotas again went to the king's presence;
those ten thousand fish had all died.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy.
Then the World-Honored One said to the goddess Bhadraśrī:
"The son of a merchant, Jalavāhana, was none other than my own self in that time."
The eldest son, Water-Space (Vāriākāśa), was Rāhula;
the second son, Water-Treasury (Vārigarbha), is now Ānanda;
and those ten thousand fish were these ten thousand devaputras.
Therefore, I now bestow upon him this prediction of enlightenment.
The tree spirit who manifested half her body at that time is none other than you yourself. (From the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Volume Four)
2. Jyotiṣka’s Body Born Among Humans Receiving Celestial Retribution. Once upon a time, there was an elder.
His name was Jyotiṣka.
His storehouses were overflowing with gold and silver;
his male and female servants were arranged in rows, and he lacked for nothing.
There was a white cotton hand-towel hanging by the edge of a pond;
when a celestial wind arose, it blew it before the king’s palace.
The ministers gathered to deliberate and sought divination to determine its cause.
All the ministers said,
"The kingdom is about to flourish, for Heaven has bestowed upon us this white cotton cloth.
The minister Jyotiṣka remained silent and spoke no word.
The king asked,
"Why do you remain silent? Ti-ga replied:
I dare not deceive Your Majesty.
This is a towel for wiping the body from my household,
which was hanging by the side of the pond.
A celestial wind arose and blew it before the palace;
several days later,
flowers of nine colors appeared, as large as chariot wheels.
Furthermore, it was encountered when a celestial wind blew it before the king’s palace.
The king again consulted with his ministers regarding divination and inquiry,
and Tiṅga replied:
"This is merely withered and fallen flowers from my household garden that have been blown here by the wind.
The King asked Tiṅga,
"Is your household such as this?"
"I wish to lead two hundred thousand troops to your residence to visit you.
Tiṅga replied, "I pray that Your Majesty will follow me at once."
The King immediately led a multitude of two hundred thousand people to the house of Jyotiṣka and entered directly through the southern gate.
There were thirty youths of upright and handsome countenance.
The king asked Jyotiṣka,
"Are these the sons and grandsons of your family?"
He replied,
"He is a gatekeeper slave from my household.
He then proceeded to the middle chamber.
There were twenty young maidens of upright and handsome appearance.
The king asked,
"Are these women from your household?"
Ti-ga replied, "She is a maidservant who guards the gatehouse for this minister's family.
She has arrived at his door."
The walls were made of white silver and the ground of crystal.
When the king saw the flowing water, he suspected he could not proceed further.
Jyotiṣka then led the king forward to the doorway.
A bed was made of gold and a stand of white jade.
Sudarśanā’s wife possessed one hundred and twenty sets of precious silver and gold curtains and canopies, peerless in their elegance.
She prostrated herself before the king, tears falling from her eyes.
The king asked,
"What did your wife see in me that caused tears to fall from her eyes?
He replied:
The king’s robes were filled with the smoke [of burning fat], and for this reason tears fell.
The king said,
"The common people are burning fat."
The feudal lords burn wax;
the Son of Heaven burns lac.
In both cases, there is no smoke.
"Why have you shed tears? Jyotiṣka replied,
"In my family there is one..."
The divine pearl of the bright moon is suspended in the hall;
day and night it remains unchanged, requiring no light from fire.
The king is the king among smoke;
therefore, he merely smells the odor.
[This occurred] before the hall of Jyotiṣka’s house.
There were twelve stories of high towers;
he led the king to the top, where,
looking toward the east, he forgot the west.
Gazing south, he forgot the north;
all was hushed and silent.
The King thought for a moment that it might be bearable for a short while longer.
He went to the flowing springs and bathing pools in the rear garden,
where he ate various fruits and melons to his heart's content, enjoying their sweet flavors;
it was truly delightful, and this continued for as long as one month.
The minister addressed the king, saying,
"It is time to return to the kingdom.
Thereupon, Jyotiṣka bestowed upon him gold, silver, rare treasures, and fine silks and brocades.
Two hundred thousand people, along with their horses and carriages, returned to the kingdom all at once.
The king immediately assembled his ministers and marveled at the reason for this,
saying, "Jyotiṣka was my minister."
"The women's quarters are far more excessive than mine;
I wish to destroy them.
May I take them or not?"
The ministers all said,
"It would be appropriate to take him.
The king immediately led four hundred thousand followers, beating bells and sounding drums, to surround the house of Devadatta.
He destroyed walls of a hundred layers.
Within the gate of the city of Ti-ga stood a mighty warrior who,
grasping a golden staff in his hand, confronted a host of four hundred thousand.
At that time, they all collapsed together and lay on the ground, unable to rise.
The Tīrthika, riding a flying cloud-chariot in the midst of the void, asked them:
"O people, when you arrived here, for what reason did you lie on the ground and not rise?"
The people answered as they had done above. Jyotiṣka asked,
"Do you wish to attain it?"
Everyone said they wished to obtain it.
Sudatta then cast forth his great divine eye and looked out once;
the assembly of four hundred thousand people all rose up at the same time.
Upon returning to his own country,
the king immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Jyotiṣka.
Together they went to the Buddha's dwelling and asked:
"Bhagavān, Jyotiṣka was my minister. What meritorious deeds did he perform in his previous life?"
"The house of this woman is far superior to mine," the Buddha replied.
"This is due to the merit of Śrīgupta’s generosity."
Seeing the delights of the heavens,
five hundred caravan leaders led their merchants,
carrying precious treasures, and fled into the empty mountains.
He encountered a sick practitioner and provided him with a thatched hut, thick bedding and mats,
water, broth, cooking utensils, and grain.
He provided him with lamps and candles;
at that time, he prayed for the offerings of heaven,
and now he has obtained such a karmic fruit as this.
The Buddha said,
"Those who gave alms at that time were none other than the husband and wife Jyotiṣka and his wife in the present."
The sick man at that time was my own self in this present life;
all five hundred merchants attained the path of Arhatship. This is recorded in the *Sūtra of Jyotiṣka*.
3. The Householder Capable of Raining Jewels from His Hand. The householder capable of raining jewels from his hand:
Long ago, in the kingdom of King Aśoka, there was a householder who made offerings to twenty thousand bhikṣus.
He requested to remain for one more year.
His fame reached the king,
who summoned him for an audience.
"I have heard that you are very wealthy;
what do you possess in its entirety?
He replied:
In truth, there was nothing at all.
The king did not believe him,
so he detained the householder Kāla and dispatched men to inspect his home.
He saw that at its entrance were seven layers of residences and halls,
all made of the seven treasures,
surpassing even the palaces of a victorious king.
The women were also superior;
however, as they had no grain, silk, or money,
they returned and informed the king, and his mind gradually began to change.
The householder immediately smiled.
The king asked, "Why do you smile?
He replied:
The king did not believe him.

the king then sent him back.

An elder bhikṣu entered samādhi and saw objects extending for four hundred yojanas, which he then brought to mind.
Seeing this elder,

and scattered them from atop the upper three stories of the stupa toward the four directions.

He who has now obtained this natural treasure is this very person.
The King, having heard this, extensively cultivated meritorious deeds;
this is the first fascicle of the *Dṛṣṭānta-paryāya-sūtra*. 4. The Householder Kāla gives food to a bird so that a pearl may emerge from its belly. Once, there was a householder named Kāla.
He was intelligent and widely learned, possessing wealth in the billions.

where he had planted many trees that grew so luxuriantly they reached toward the heavens.

entering at dawn and emerging at dusk,

The elder, possessing great wisdom and skillful means, devised a plan.

The bird, having eaten its fill, vomited up pearls that covered the ground.
The elder obtained them and consequently became immensely wealthy. (From the *Avadāna-sūtra*, Scroll Seven).

He was proficient in writing, arithmetic, and the interpretation of texts; he distinguished between gold, silver, pearls, and shells, as well as currency, furs, and fields.
He understood everything regarding shopkeeping and marketplaces, and when asked about the annual yield, he could calculate exactly how much produce each would require.
He replied,
"One thousand gold coins per year.
The householder said:
"In this present age of famine, I have hired five hundred men.
When their term is complete, they shall return the children to me. [The man replied:
"I simply cannot give them away; these must be used as they are urgently needed."
I now give it to you;
have him sit at the stall.

10. The Elder Resolves upon Bodhicitta and Leads the Poor to Obtain Precious Jewels. Long ago, there was an elder. He resolved his mind upon bodhicitta and led various impoverished people to obtain precious jewels. Ten. In the past, there was an elder.
He resolved his mind upon the Bodhisattva path and gathered five hundred impoverished people,
providing them with clothing and provisions.
Having entered the sea to gather treasures, they stayed overnight on a great mountain.
While the others were dazed and dull-witted, only the elder sat alone,
maintaining constant vigilance.
At night, he saw a person emerge from the slope of the mountain;
his radiance was extraordinary and his countenance was upright and handsome,
yet his mouth resembled that of a pig, and he amused himself with music and dance.
As he was wandering by the side of the mountain, an elder asked him, "Who are you?"
Hearing the voice, he cried out in astonishment, "I am a man who has received great merit; how have I come to dwell here?
The elder asked him:
Question: "Your physical form is upright and handsome; why is it that your mouth alone is so? Answer:
"Because I have committed the fault of verbal transgression, I am constantly prone to leaking secrets."
The celestial being asked, "Who are you?
He replied:
"I am an elder of this kingdom.
Out of concern for the poor and destitute, and desiring to bring them peace and security, I have led these people into the ocean to gather treasures,
intending to transport these riches to benefit Jambudvīpa."
The deva said, "Could you not be this bodhisattva?
The elder replied:
I have resolved upon the mind of a bodhisattva to rescue and relieve all those afflicted by the diseases of lust, anger, and ignorance;
among all who have not yet crossed over, I shall be their deliverer.
The deva said, "Excellent!

He then escorted [the man] to the place where the treasures were, loaded them onto his carriage once more, and returned. This concludes the fifth fascicle of the Ten Fascicle *Piyū-jīng* (Sutra of Parables).

11. Later, when the elder was poor, he took up gold to provide as an offering for plowing; he encountered a thousand cauldrons, which he used without them being exhausted. Thus ends the eleventh story. Formerly, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was an elder.
He was originally very wealthy.
After his parents passed away,
he constantly made offerings to several practitioners of the Way.
Within a few years, his family fell into poverty and could obtain nothing more;
he became consumed by grief and anguish as he contemplated making merit for his parents.
The wife said to her husband:
"It would be better for us to endure hardship for a single lifetime so that we may later attain long-term liberation,
rather than sending our parents far away to obtain immeasurable merit."
The elder said, "So be it.
Take two hundred taels of gold from me on credit;
when the work is finished and the gold is exhausted, settle the payment."
Having obtained gold, she gave it all away and then went to work as a laborer.
She sent her husband to plow the fields while she herself cooked in the kitchen.
While plowing, she found a large stone that resembled a millstone cover.
Upon opening his eyes, he saw a thousand cauldrons of gold;
he immediately covered them back up and did not return to eat.
The elder sent his wife to bring food to her husband.
The man then took up the gold and returned to his own home,
saying, "I shall weigh the gold and return it tomorrow.
The host and his wife then went back to their quarters.

Furthermore, it was used for making offerings on behalf of parents for seven generations, never being exhausted throughout one's entire life; this constitutes the first fascicle of the *Daśādhyāya-avadāna-sūtra*.

12. The Wife of the Elder Gandharva Taken by the King. Twelve: In ancient times, there was a king. His wife, the elder Gandharva’s consort, was seized by the king. (End of Fascicle One). 12. The Wife of the Elder Gandharva Taken by the King. Twelve: In ancient times, there was a king.
Greedy for lustful beauty, he acted without moral restraint;
whenever he heard of a beautiful woman, he would immediately go to seize her by force.
The entire kingdom suffered from this.
There was an elder whose wealth was incalculable and who was of lofty talent and broad erudition;
his wife was of upright and beautiful countenance.
The ministers informed the king;
upon hearing this, the king’s heart was moved, and he dispatched messengers to forcibly seize her.
Her husband was filled with grief and distress.
He then abandoned his home and family to become a śramaṇa;
from his mouth issued a fragrant scent that perfumed forty li,
and his entire body was permeated with the fragrance of sandalwood.
The king saw that the man had no children or descendants,
so he confiscated all his family property.
The king established his wife as the principal consort.
Within the kingdom, exquisite lotuses grew—
blue, yellow, red, and white— extremely large, fragrant, and pure.
The king respectfully took the flowers from his consort and gave them to her first.
Upon receiving the flowers, the consort was moved by even greater sorrow.
The king asked:
You are now the mother of a kingdom;
we respect one another and shall not be parted.
What could be improper in this?
"Are you truly not happy?
The lady replied,
"I dare not say I am not happy."
"I only thought that the fragrance of my former husband’s body and mouth surpassed these many flowers.
Secretly reflecting on our old affection, I could not help but feel sorrow.
The King did not believe her words, so he sent for her to be summoned.
The former husband had already attained arhatship;
by means of his supernormal powers, he flew through the air, and a multitude of fragrances issued from his body, pervading the entire kingdom.
The king sent for him to bathe and then rubbed and polished his body again.
The fragrance of his body became even more intense.
The king tested this by questioning the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
In the past, there was a poor man who,
destitute and without means of livelihood, sustained himself by selling firewood.
He had gathered his wood and was on his way back before he had yet reached the city gate.
The city gates were already closed.
Outside the gate was a monastery where a monk was reciting sutras at night;
the man, seeking lodging, sat down and listened to the recitation.
He burned incense and offered praises until dawn.

Because of this, for five hundred lifetimes he did not fall into the evil realms, but was constantly reborn in the heavens with his body and speech fragrant and pure. (From the *Daśa-varga-avadāna-sūtra*, Scroll Four).

13. The Wife of the Householder’s Pregnancy and Her Fragrant Breath. The wife of a householder became pregnant, and her breath was fragrant. Thirteen: In the past, there was a householder whose wife became pregnant. Her breath was fragrant.
A fragrant scent issued from his mouth, filling the entire kingdom.
King Ajātaśatru dispatched messengers to search for him and found him at the house of the elder.
He questioned the elder,
who answered in full detail.
The messenger then informed the king.
The King was greatly delighted and summoned the elder, saying:
"If you give birth to a son, you shall bring him to me to be given as a husband to my daughter.
Subsequently, a daughter was born, and a garment of gold thread appeared spontaneously upon her body.
The mother marveled at how it was removed;
as soon as she gave birth, another layer appeared and returned to her body.
She then went to question the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a poor household.
The wife went out and encountered rain."
He saw an old śramaṇa, a pratyekabuddha, who had fallen prostrate on the ground;
his knee was injured and blood was flowing.
He immediately helped the śramaṇa up and washed away the blood.
Her blood flowed from her own torn garment, which she used to bind her wounded knee.
Although this woman had not yet formally received the essential teachings of the Dharma,
she was always fond of praising the Buddha-way.
After dying and being reborn in the second heaven,
his lifespan ended and he descended to be born here;
therefore, there were naturally appearing garments.
*The Sutra of Ten Volumes of Parables*, Volume One, "Good Fragrance Emitted from the Mouth.
14. Birth in the Howling Hell Due to Stinginess with Wealth. In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a wealthy elder.
When he passed away, having no son,
all his wealth and property were confiscated by the government.
During his lifetime, he had consumed coarse and poor food, wore tattered and worn-out clothing, and used tree leaves as a canopy.
The Buddha said:
"Though one may attain a position of great power, if one does not nourish oneself,
nor nourish one's children, nor provide for one's parents, [it is of no avail]."
"He did not associate with friends nor give alms to śramaṇas;
today, at the end of his life, he has entered the Tīraka Hell.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
In the past, he gave food as an offering to a pratyekabuddha;
having given it, he felt regret in his heart and said,
"I should not have given this to a slave."
He then became a shaven-headed śramaṇa.
By virtue of this wholesome karmic retribution,
he was reborn seven times as a deva and seven times as a human, always attaining noble and eminent status.
Due to this mind of remorse, such is the karmic retribution:
he does not eat fine food, nor does he wear fine clothing,
and he no longer craves the five sensual desires.
King Prasenajit: One Should Diligently Practice with Vigor and Eliminate Laziness; The Sūtra on the Elder’s Death Without an Heir. 15.
Reborn in Heaven by Giving a Rock for Beating Clothes to Others and Erecting a Stūpa. Fifteenth: There was an elder who wished to erect a stūpa and monastery.
The timber was all prepared;
only one stone was lacking to serve as a base for the pillar.
There was an elder who,
although he did not follow the Buddha, nevertheless knew that there is merit;
he then offered a stone for pounding clothes from his home to him.
The temple was thus completed.
When that man who had donated the stone passed away,
he was immediately reborn in the second heaven within a palace made of the seven treasures.
The jade maidens served as attendants, and food and clothing appeared spontaneously.
After a long period such as this, the kingdom was destroyed;
no one maintained it, and the monasteries were completely ruined.
There was only a single stone buried in the earth;
as the people were plowing, the stone obstructed their plow,
and they resolved to dig it up.
The lord of the stone, a celestial being, felt his heart tremble with agitation;
observing with his divine eye that a man was digging at the stone,
he thought to himself:
"Because of this stone, I have attained the merit to be reborn in heaven.
Now that people have taken it away, will my merit not be exhausted?
Having said this, he descended and transformed himself into an ordinary man, standing before the person digging for the stone.
He asked, "Do you wish to take this stone away?
The man replied:
"I wish to plow this field, but I have encountered a stone that obstructs the plow; therefore, I wish to remove it.
The deva asked, "If you were to plow this ground, you would only obtain several tens of *hu* of grain."
The deity said,
"Do not take this stone;
I shall give you five hundred taels of gold."
The man asked, "Could it be that you are a spirit?
He replied:
"I am a celestial being.
He then resumed his celestial form and said to the man,
"I was originally a person of this very land."
"In my previous life, I gave this stone to a practitioner to establish a temple.
By virtue of this merit, I was reborn in the heavens where I enjoy natural abundance.
Just now, the celestial palace shook, and I wondered at its cause."
"I have come because I observed you.
This stone is the very root of my merit; do not take it."
Upon hearing this, the man said,
"This was originally something I did not know;
this is a shrine and temple of the divine spirits."
The heavenly beings and humans, regarding him as a field of merit, did not dare to offend him. When the deity returned to heaven, he reflected:
"If this deity merely gave this stone and obtained such merit, I should establish even more stupas and monasteries."

He immediately began the construction and restored the stupa as it was before. From the *Fubao jing* (Sutra on the Retribution of Merit), there also emerges the first fascicle of the ten-fascicle *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Parables).

16. The Story of the Three Sons of Sudatta Believing Only When They Were in Extremity. Sixteen: Formerly, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had three sons. When they reached the point of utter destitution, they finally came to believe. 16. The Story of the Three Sons of Sudatta Believing Only When They Were in Extremity. Sixteen: Formerly, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had three sons.
They all turn their backs on the right and head toward the perverse, becoming intoxicated by wine and debauched by women;
they gallop about hunting and indulge in games of chance and gambling,
abandoning light for darkness, and day by day they become mad and foolish.
The father pitied and mourned him;
out of compassionate sympathy, he instructed and exhorted him, pointing out the consequences of fortune and calamity every single day.
Yet the son alone remained unyielding, and his dissipation grew ever more extreme.
The father then clothed him in grass from the sprouts and fed him with beans and wheat;
later, he regretted his actions.
The father said:
"Because you committed unwholesome deeds, you have incurred calamity in this present life and suffer such extreme distress.
How much more so, then, for the agony of being burned and boiled in hell—who could possibly save you?
The son bowed his head and said:
Led astray by evil friends, he became deluded and habituated to such ways;
like a pig dwelling in a latrine, he was unaware of its stench.
From this day forth, I shall restrain my person and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
The father said, "Very well.
If you purify your heart and uphold the five precepts of the Buddha without violating them for the rest of your life,
I shall give you fifty million gold pieces every year."
"Threefold self-refuge, thirty million times.
The son replied, "Yes;
having already received the Honored One's instruction."
He immediately ordered him to bathe and brought him to the Buddha’s presence.
There, he prostrated himself, received the precepts, and withdrew to cultivate virtue.
He purified his resolve and relieved the destitute and impoverished.
His benevolence reached all sentient beings and his state was praised for its virtue by scholars;
his fame equaled that of the ancient sages. He produced the *Sūtra on Teaching Sons*.
17. Sudāna Kills His Younger Brother Out of Greed for Wealth. Once, in the city of Rājagṛha...
There was an elder named Sudāna, who was immensely wealthy and possessed great riches.
His son was named Sumati.
After his father passed away,
his younger brother was named Suyasasmati.
The elder brother did not share the inheritance with his younger brother and intended to kill him.
He said to his brother:
They went together to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to engage in discussion;
he then took his younger brother by the hand, led him up to the edge of a precipice,
pushed him over, and crushed him with a boulder.
He then passed away.
The one named Sudāna was none other than my true father, the Pure King;
at that time, the one named Sumati was myself.
The one who was Śreyas is now Devadatta. (From the *Ciyiqixingjing*, Scroll Lower). 18. Regarding Likhita:
the seventh son-in-law of Likhita gave birth to thirty eggs; from each egg emerged a male child. Eighteen of these became kings of the Paiśācikas.
There was a high minister named Ligimi,
who took a wife for his seventh son.
He then married the daughter of King Prasenajit’s younger brother, named Dharmadinnā.
This woman was intelligent, sharp-witted, and possessed many virtues and arts;
after ten months of pregnancy, she gave birth to thirty eggs.
From the egg emerged a boy,
whose physical form was exceptionally distinguished and whose courage and strength were peerless;
the power of one man exceeded that of a thousand men.
The Parents’ Affection and the Entire Nation’s Veneration; from the *Xianyu jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish), Volume Ten.
19. The Foolish Son Who Sells Incense Slowly and Burns It to Charcoal to Seek a Quick Sale. Nineteen: There was a wealthy elder.
The son born was foolish.
When he embarked on a sea voyage for trade, he loaded only with agarwood;
the wood was both exquisite and precious.
Purchasers were rare;
it remained stagnant for a long time without being sold.
His companions returned to their home country, but he alone could not bear to depart.
Fearing that he would lose his companions,
he surveyed the market and saw that the sale of charcoal was the swiftest.
He immediately burned incense to make charcoal, hoping to obtain it quickly.
When the crowd saw this,
they all reproached and ridiculed him together,
saying, "This great madman may take a long time to sell his incense, but the price he obtains will not be small."
Now, what can be obtained by burning [something] into charcoal? From the *Baiju poyu jing* (Sūtra of One Hundred Parables), Volume One.
From the *Jinglü yixiang* (Diverse Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya), Volume Thirty-six.
