3. An upāsaka serves as a kitchen official for a king; coerced into committing murder, he points to a lion to manifest the truth.
1. An upāsaka was tested by Māra; 2. Four faithful laymen gave their daughters in marriage to families that served ghosts; 3.
Five faithful laymen began to practice with vigor and did not slacken, yet later they felt shame and remorse, so that the ghosts could no longer harm them; 4.

A faithful layman, at the point of death, felt such love for his wife that after he died, he became a worm in her nose; 5. Bakula maintained the precepts and obtained the retribution of five immunities from death.
1. Eighth: One who maintains the precepts and recites the sūtras while continuously making offerings cannot be harmed by ghosts. 2. Ninth:

One who holds fast to the Buddha’s precepts and seeks their restoration will have the various ghosts in their mouth exit and strike their own bodies [in remorse]. 3. Tenth: A person who does not believe in the retribution of sin and merit may be seized by a ghost in a dream;

if they subsequently receive the precepts, they will live for a hundred years. 4. Eleventh: In a household where six members cut off their mouths [to eat less] to give to the Sangha, they will all equally enjoy wealth and happiness.
12. There was a person who, while traveling on a road, encountered three transformed beings practicing diligent effort. 13.
There was a person whose life ended and who, ten days later, returned to life to recount what he had seen during his journey. 14. 1. The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa entered the sea and saw the hells.
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa entered the sea and saw the hells. 1. In the country of Aśmaka-Avaṇtī.
There was a village king named Śreṣṭhin.
Among them was a very wealthy householder.
Though his wealth and treasures were abundant, he alone had no son;
despite seeking one from various deities, he could not obtain one.
When the time for a son arrived, the wife became aware that she was pregnant.
This woman possesses four uncommon knowledges due to her sharp faculties:
first, she knows what men find attractive;
second, she knows what men do not find attractive.
Third, she knew the time of her conception;
fourth, she knew from whom she had obtained it,
and she informed the householder.
The householder was filled with joy.
When the month was full, he gave birth to a son whose ears were adorned with golden rings;
the boy was so handsome that all who saw him were filled with delight.
He assembled the brahmins and said to them,
"This child truly possesses merit, fortune, and majestic power."
He was given two names:
because he had left the household life in a previous existence, he was named Śramaṇa Karṇika.
It was not something made by worldly hands and was worth one hundred million;
he was given the name Śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa and provided with the five kinds of sustenance.
First, the mother who nurtures the body;
second, the mother who removes impurities;
third, the nursing mother.
Fourth is the Auspicious Mother;
fifth is the Playful Mother.
By the power of this child's merit, he grows up quickly and matures.
He was then taught writing, arithmetic, calculation, and seals;
he became well-versed in the prices and qualities of various goods, both high and low.
This was a place where kings, villagers, and traveling merchants gathered.
At that time, people from the four directions came to the village and asked,
"Who in this place possesses good virtue such that we may entrust our words to them? Please show us who can inform us of what is beneficial or harmful."
The people pointed out the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa to them,
and those merchants immediately went to him and he received them as his guests.
Seeing his great majesty and power,
those merchants thought to themselves:
"If he acts as the caravan leader and leads many people into the sea, we will surely return in safety."
The people said,
"Śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa,
why do you not enter the great ocean?"
He replied,
"What would I do by entering the great ocean?
It is full of many terrors."
"Of a hundred thousand people who depart, only one returns"—
this is the exhortation of those merchant travelers.
What kind of person would rely on others for their livelihood?
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, having received their instructions with faith, wished to depart.
Upon reaching his parents' home, he took leave of them, intending to enter the sea.
At that time, his parents recounted various terrifying matters, hoping to cause him to change his mind and turn back so as to restrain him from leaving.
At that time, he did not follow his parents' words.
His parents said to a nobleman, "Help me to detain Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
Then, the high officials, elders, and householders all assisted in detaining him.
He would by no means comply.
His parents, recognizing that his resolve was firm, permitted him to depart.
Thereupon, he mounted an elephant, shook a bell, and traveled throughout the villages to proclaim his message.
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa wished to enter the great ocean.
I acted as the caravan leader and asked, "Who wishes to go with me?
This man possessed such merit that five hundred merchants all joyfully followed him.
On the day the boat was launched into the water, one rope was cut.
On the seventh day, they encountered the *iler* wind—Liang’s gloss explains this as a favorable wind—and the seventh rope was cut.
The boat proceeded faster than an arrow and reached the Jewel Island directly.
He said to the merchants,
"Load the ship with treasure, but do not let it be too heavy.
When you encounter the *Iler* wind, the ship will travel faster than an arrow."
Returning to Jambudvīpa toward the village of the Sārthavāha King,
there were two paths.
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said to the merchants:
"By which route do you wish to go?
Everyone replied,
"It would be best to go by land."
Staying overnight in a desolate marsh,
he said to the merchants,
"I have heard that bandits are coming to plunder the caravans."
If he were to kill the caravan leader first,
then the merchants would achieve nothing;
if he did not kill the caravan leader, [the same would follow].
"If I rely on the power of money or my own physical strength,
or if I rely on the power of others, I will certainly be able to catch the thief;
I shall stay overnight elsewhere."
"When you leave, you must call for me. The others agreed.
Then, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa drove his donkey and went to stay overnight in another place.
At midnight, these merchants set out;
though they woke one another, they did not call for Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
Later in the night, there was a great wind and rain.
When Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa realized that there was no response to his calls,
he immediately galloped along a road thick with dust. Amidst the wind and rain sweeping across the landscape,
he followed the tracks by looking up at the donkey’s scent as it moved forward.
Extremely hungry, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa proceeded forward and saw a city.
Thinking he would obtain food, he stood at the city gate;
following this thought, he cried out in a loud voice:
As they were eating,
hundreds of thousands of hungry ghosts emerged and all said:
"What food do you have, and who gave it to you? "I have no food," Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied.
"I was traveling and became so exhausted with hunger that I thought only of obtaining some food."
Because he uttered these words, "I have no food," the hungry ghosts said,
"This is a city of hungry ghosts."
"Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of years, we have heard the sound of the meal being announced only today.
Because we failed to practice generosity and were full of stinginess, we fell into this realm of hungry ghosts."
"Where do you wish to go?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied,
"I wish to go to the village of the Saṃbhararāja."
The ghost said,
"Go by this path. Thereupon,
he proceeded forward and again saw another city.
He recited the mantra over the water as before.
After traveling for a short distance, he again saw a tree named Pāra.
They stayed overnight below;
shaking the trees, they ate the fine leaves themselves and gave the coarse ones to the donkey.
Thus it was at the close of day.
Immediately, a bed appeared from which a man and a woman emerged;
they were handsome and well-proportioned, wearing celestial jewel crowns, and they took pleasure together.
Then, this thought arose:
I should not look at others' private affairs in this manner; thus,
when the night had passed and day was coming, [he spoke].
Immediately, the bed vanished and a dog came and devoured the man’s flesh until only the bones remained.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself,
"What conduct did this man perform in the past that he now receives such retribution?"
"The night is good and the day is bad;
I shall wait to question him.
When night arrived, there was yet another fine bed.
While the man and woman were amusing themselves,
he went immediately to question them.
The man said:
"Do you recognize that butcher named So-and-so from the merchant town of Āśmaka-Avanti?
There was an elder, Kātyāyana,
who used to come and go to my house."
I constantly provided him with food, drink, clothing, and medicine.
He would always say to me:
"Do not commit evil deeds, lest you suffer great misery hereafter."
I replied at that time:
"Since previous lifetimes, this has been my occupation.
If I do not practice it now, how shall I support myself?"
Candana spoke again:
"In committing this evil, was it more during the day or more at night?
I replied: "More during the day."
He then said to me,
"If you receive the five precepts at night, you may obtain some slight merit.
I immediately accepted them from him.
Now one receives this retribution.
After traveling for no long time, one again sees two trees named *pāla*.
They dwell there, staying overnight and eating leaves as before.
During the day, men and women come together to amuse themselves;
at dusk, the women all vanish from their beds.
A centipede emerged and devoured the flesh of this man until only the bones remained.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked: "What was that?"
"What practice did you perform to obtain this retribution now?
The man replied,
"In the kingdom of Āśmaka-Avantī..."
"In the village of the Sārthavāha King,
a certain man committed adultery with another's wife.
There was an elder, Kātyāyana, who used to come and go to my house."
He instructed me, saying,
"Do not commit evil deeds, lest you receive bitter retribution later. I replied:
"Since I am unable to restrain myself, what can be done?
He spoke to me again, saying:
'At what time did you become particularly excessive in this matter?'"
I said that the night was long. Kātyāyana then said to me,
"One may obtain slight merit by receiving the five precepts during the day."
Because I followed those words, I have obtained this retribution.
Furthermore, I see a grove of trees and a pond of pure water;
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa bathes and drinks his donkey therein.
Beside this pond was a hall adorned with various jewels;
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa looked up and immediately had this thought:
"I am so hungry and thirsty that I am on the verge of death; where should I go?
He then immediately ascended the hall and recited verses from the Buddhist sutras.
"Hunger is the foremost illness; conditioned existence is the foremost suffering.
Knowing the reality of phenomena thus, Nirvana is the supreme bliss.
[He] saw a woman sitting upon an ivory couch.
At the feet of the bed were bound two hungry ghosts;
the woman recognized Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa and,
having greeted him, spoke.
"Śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, have you not suffered from exhaustion, thirst, or hunger on the road?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied,
"Noble lady, I begged for food."
The woman said, "I will give it to you both,
provided you do not give it to these two hungry ghosts.
She then gave them water to wash their hands and food to eat.
Because this woman wished for Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa to understand this causal connection, she stepped slightly outside the hall.
At that time, two hungry ghosts extended their hands and said,
"Give us one mouthful."
"Give me half a mouthful;
my belly is as hungry as if it were being burned by fire.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was fond of giving, so he gave him one mouthful from each of his own portions.
It turned into pus and blood; though much was swallowed, it was all spat back out, full of stench and filth.
The woman said, "I told you not to give it to him."
"Why did you give it to him? Eḷeyya said, "Sisters."
"I gave it because I did not know.
At that time, another woman came and said,
'Noble lady.'"
"Give me food.
The woman said,
"Eat what you usually eat."
Having spoken these words,
three extraordinary cauldrons immediately appeared, their boiling brine bubbling over.
This woman stripped off her clothes and entered the cauldron, where her skin and flesh were completely dissolved.
Only when a cold wind blows upon their marrow do they emerge from the cauldron and return to life;
they put on their clothes and eat the putrid flesh,
and having finished eating, they depart.
Furthermore, another woman came and said,
"Noble sir, give me food."
The woman said,
"Eat your usual food.
Having finished speaking these words, [she vanished].
The woman transformed into a black ewe and began eating grass.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said to the woman,
"What is this matter?"
The woman said,
"Do you know the village of the merchant leader in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avanti?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied, "I know it."
"The ghost that bound the bedpost at my head is my husband, the layman [Name].
The one that bound the bedpost at my feet is..."
"This is my son.
The Elder Kātyāyana used to come and go from my house,
receiving from me offerings of robes, medicine, and other necessities."
These two people spoke angrily to me, saying,
"We have suffered great hardship in our search for it,
yet you have given it away to another; you have merely exhausted yourself in vain."
Because of this stinginess and greed, and because he did not rejoice in giving, he fell among the hungry ghosts.
Due to his karma of harsh speech, the food given to him turned into pus and blood.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said:
"Why does this woman eat her own flesh?
The woman replied,
"She is my son's wife."
I gave it to others to take away;
some ate it themselves, while others gave it to others to eat.
I went to search for it.
He replied,
"I neither eat it myself nor give it to others.
If I were to eat it myself or give it to others,"
"Because she was eating my own flesh, I ate my own flesh.
This second woman was my servant;
I made her pound and grind."
Whether one eats it oneself or gives it to another,
if questioned, one says:
"I did not eat it myself, nor did I give it to another."
"If I had eaten it myself or given it to others, I would have been reborn as a sheep to eat grass in a future life.
By reason of this, I am now a ewe eating grass.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said:
"What practice did you perform?
The woman replied,
"I have committed a minor transgression, and as a result, I was born here."
I shall not remain long; I am to be reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
You should go for my sake to the village of the Sārthavāha king and say this to my daughter: [text continues]
I have seen your parents, your elder brother’s wife, and your maidservant;
only your mother alone enjoys blessings,
while the others undergo suffering.
"Your mother spoke to you because of me:
'Do not commit evil deeds, lest you suffer many painful retributions in future lives.
If you do not believe these words of your mother,"
"In such-and-such a place there is a storehouse containing great wealth.
Take it and perform meritorious deeds for me,
making offerings to the assembly of monks and to Kātyāyana."
The remnants were sufficient for his own livelihood.
He asked Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa,
"Do you wish to depart?"
He replied, "I wish to go.
The woman said,
"Close your eyes while you sleep."
In a short while, they arrived at the settlement of the caravan leader.
These merchants arrived first, and the people there asked them: "Have you [seen him]?"
"Did you see the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa?
He replied,
"I lost him at sea."
The entire town wept as if they had lost their own parents.
When Ayiravata heard this, he thought:
"If they were to see me now, they would surely be disturbed once more; there is no need for me to return."
Gradually arriving at the girl's house,
they exchanged greetings;
the mother then spoke to the girl.
The woman said,
"Hey, man! You are a deluded and mad person."
"My parents practiced generosity and performed meritorious deeds; they must have been reborn in heaven upon their death.
Why then are they among the hungry ghosts?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa then spoke to the woman, saying:
Your mother said,
"There is a storehouse in such-and-such a place containing a great deal of money and goods;
have it brought out for you to use as offerings."
Upon hearing this, the woman opened the treasury and obtained a great amount of wealth;
she was thereby able to give rise to faith and acted according to her mother’s instructions.
He requested Kātyāyana to follow him and preach the Dharma.
Thereupon, while still seated, he attained the pure and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena and gained fearlessness.
He paid homage to Kātyāyana and said:
"Venerable Sir,
I take refuge in the Triple Gem and become a lay follower (upāsaka).
I wish to go forth in this most excellent Dharma and receive full ordination."
Kātyāyana asked, "Have your parents permitted you to leave the household life?
He replied, "They have not yet permitted it."
Kātyāyana said, "In my family,
if my parents do not permit it, one cannot leave the household life to receive full ordination.
He then returned home and paid obeisance to his parents.
Previously, because of their grief and suffering, they had both lost their sight.
Upon hearing that Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had returned safely from the great ocean,
they wept with a mixture of sorrow and joy, and their eyes immediately regained their vision.
After five or six days had passed,
he said to his parents,
"Please allow me to leave the household life."
The parents said,
"We originally sought you with our whole heart and made a vow to have you.
Because we were filled with grief and anxiety over the news of your death while you were at sea, our eyes went blind."
Now that you have returned, I am filled with great joy and my eyes are opened to see.
You have truly been born anew;
by accepting my words, you shall be honoring me.
"How much longer can my life endure?
If we could complete our full lifespans without leaving the household life, I would have no regrets even in death."
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied, "Yes. (From the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*, Volume Four). 2.

The Upāsaka Observing the Precepts and the Ghost Who Took His Flowers in His Place. Regarding the second [story], "The Upāsaka Observing the Precepts and the Ghost Who Took His Flowers in His Place": Once upon a time, there was an upāsaka.
He was living as a sojourner in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
His wife’s physical beauty was renowned throughout the entire country;
friends wished to see her, but she would never consent to show herself.
People reported this to the king.
The king thought longingly of seeing him but did not know by what means it might be possible.
A minister then addressed him, saying:
"The husband and wife together observe the five precepts and make offerings to the Daoist master, serving him with their own hands.
You, Your Majesty, should feign being a Daoist and go to their gate carrying an alms bowl;
you will surely be able to see them."
He immediately followed the minister’s words;
assuming a different appearance and attire, he secretly arrived at her home.
When the wife saw the practitioner, she bowed her head and face in salutation.
Having observed her closely, the king returned and said to his ministers, "This woman is truly beautiful; she has entered my heart.
I do not know from where she could have come."
The ministers said:
"Although this man is a conceited scholar, he ought to have an audience with the King.
That he does not come out of arrogance can be considered an offense."
More than a thousand *li* from the city of Śrāvastī,
there is a great pond in which five-colored lotuses grow;
it is said that three dangers exist there.
Vipers, ghosts, spirits, and fierce beasts—
those whose offenses merit death are sent to gather flowers there,
and they immediately perish upon arrival.
The king then called out to him and asked, "What kind of person are you? He bowed twice and replied, "I am a subject of Your Majesty.
The king said:
"Why do they not come?
He replied, "It is simply because they are too ignorant to reach it."
Knowing himself to be guilty,
the king said,
"As punishment, you shall go to the pond to fetch lotuses and return within seven days."
"If you fail to arrive by the appointed time, I shall punish you severely.
Having received these instructions, he took his leave and returned to inform his wife in full detail.
The wife said to her husband:
"Your current transgression arises from my beauty.
You should recognize the Buddha’s clear teaching: within the three realms there is no refuge; only the precepts can be relied upon."
On the day you set out on the journey, keep the Three Honored Ones in mind and recite the Ten Wholesome Precepts aloud without forgetting them for even a moment.
If you do not return, I shall leave the household life to find joy in the precepts and will not pass through two more men.
Having provided her husband with provisions and taking his leave to proceed on his journey,
he traveled halfway when he encountered a man-eating demon who asked him:
Someone replied, "He is a disciple of the Buddha.
The ghost said:
Those who have committed offenses have been sent to us under the pretext of gathering flowers; yet,
O worthy one, you have indeed committed an offense.
Being slandered by evil people,
he answered the ghost, saying,
"Human life is difficult to obtain; it depends solely upon the Great Deity."
The ghost said,
"You are a disciple of the Buddha and furthermore are without fault; I shall not harm you."
"There are two further difficulties remaining; I fear you cannot escape them—what shall we do?
The ghost spoke again, saying, "I will take your place to fetch the flowers so as to save your life."
"May I obtain immeasurable merit throughout the long night.
The spirit then departed immediately,
but returned a moment later.
Five-colored beautiful flowers were given to the worthy man;
the worthy man was so overcome with weight that he could not lift them.
The ghosts then took the flowers and supported the worthy man.
In the time it takes to bend and extend one’s arm, they had already arrived at the palace gate.
Having taken their leave and departed,
the worthy man approached the gate and announced himself.
The king marveled at the swiftness of his return and questioned him thoroughly about the beginning and end of the matter;
he then related the facts exactly as they were.
The King was greatly shocked and ashamed, saying,
"A ghost lacks human righteousness and harms sentient beings;
yet now that it has saved a virtuous person, I am the one who lacks righteousness."
Failing to distinguish between good and evil, he was no different from a malevolent spirit;
he immediately reproached himself for his transgressions, prostrated himself in homage, and took refuge, saying,
"I pray that you will accept me as your disciple."
Having received the five precepts and extensively practiced the six perfections,
the nation attained great peace.
The virtuous couple further intensified their diligent cultivation.
The Sūtra of Parables on Attaining Non-retrogression, Volume Five. 3.
The Upāsaka Who Was Forced to Kill for the King’s Kitchen Staff and Pointed Out the Lion Upāsaka. Three hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.
The king served the heavenly deities by performing a great sacrificial rite, for which he employed one hundred each of oxen, sheep, pigs, dogs, and chickens,
all of whom he ordered his kitchen officials to slaughter.
Then the cook said,
"I have received the Buddha's precepts and may not kill living beings.
The kitchen supervisor became greatly enraged and informed the king to punish him.
The king said,
"Those who disobey my command shall die. The cook replied:
"I am a disciple of the Buddha who upholds the five precepts.
It would be better for me to kill my own body than to violate the Buddha's teaching by taking the life of another.
If I were to follow the King's command and commit murder,"
After dying and entering hell, once their retribution for their offenses is exhausted, they emerge, yet they shall always have short lifespans.
Those who die while upholding the precepts will be reborn immediately in the heavens; there, the blessings and joys of heaven will be spontaneously fulfilled according to their wishes.
"Even if I were to die now, I would leave this human body and receive a celestial form.
For this reason, I do not kill.
The king said:
I grant you seven days;
I shall have an elephant trample you to death.
If you do not die, [then I shall spare you].
"What you say is true.
After seven days, the king will see that this upāsaka’s body is like the body of a Buddha;
he shall then drive five hundred elephants to trample him to death."
The upāsaka raised his five fingers according to the Buddha’s teaching,
which transformed into five mountains;
from within each mountain, a lion emerged.
Upon seeing the lion, the elephant crouched on the ground in terror,
just as when the Buddha was alive and the king had faith in him at that time.
He then discontinued the ancestral sacrifices and immediately received the five precepts of the Buddha from this man.
Both the officials and the common people, both within and without, likewise received the Dharma.
He then served as the National Preceptor and produced the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Six.
4. The Upāsaka Tested by Māra. There was once an upāsaka.
Accompanying a large group of merchants on a long journey for trade,
they encountered freezing snow.
Traveling by night, they lost their companions and took shelter in a stone cave.
At that time, a mountain deity transformed herself into the likeness of a woman and came to test him, saying:
"White snow covers heaven and earth; birds and beasts are all hidden away."
"I alone have nothing to rely upon;
I only pray that you will take pity on me.
The upāsaka covered his ears with both hands and said:
Shameless and wicked people speak such impure words;
you are one whom we do not wish to see or hear, even as water drowns or fire burns.
You have no desire for a wife.
How much more so for committing sexual misconduct!
Sensual desire is shallow and trivial, while great suffering is profound and terrifying.
When the mountain deity heard this, he was moved.
Holding [the text] with both hands, he presented it to the attendants and emerged. This concludes the seventeenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

5. A Lay Devotee Marries His Daughter to a Family that Worships Demons; Five Upāsakas Marry Their Daughters to Worldly People. A lay devotee marries his daughter to a family that worships demons; five upāsakas marry their daughters to worldly people.
When she was about to be sent away,
her parents wished to revoke her precepts,
but the girl said:
What is the forfeiture of precepts?
One's parents say:
"According to the law, we shall give our daughter in marriage to a worldly man."
"It is like throwing gold into cow dung;
what further use would there be for precepts?
The woman said.
It is like a person traveling far through a vast desert where no people dwell;
they should increase their provisions for the journey.
A family that serves spirits fears that a spirit might perhaps find an opportunity against them.
One should further maintain the precepts so that one's resolve becomes firm and steadfast.
It is like gold found within cow dung;
once washed clean, it may be used as desired.
"How could it possibly be the same as cow dung?
His parents were moved by these words and gave him a Buddha image.
The woman placed it in a solemn vessel and paid homage to the vessel morning and evening.
Her husband asked:
The wife replied,
"This Buddha can cause one's hair not to turn white and keep one's complexion always beautiful.
Her husband then made offerings together with her.
Later, they were reborn together in heaven and did not again undergo the three miserable realms; this is from the fifth fascicle of the *Daśa-varga-avadāna-sūtra*. 6.

The Lay Practitioner Shi Jingjin (Beginning Diligence) Who Did Not Slacken, and Whom the Ghost of Shame and Remorse Could Not Harm. Sixth: Once there was a lay practitioner named Shi Jingjin. He had begun his diligent practice and had not yet slackened. Later, he gave rise to shame and remorse, and a ghost could not harm him. The lay practitioner Shi Jingjin, who had begun his diligent practice and had not yet slackened, later gave rise to shame and remorse, and a ghost could not harm him. Sixth: In the past, there was a lay practitioner.
When he first received the precepts, his diligence was peerless;
later, as he grew old and infirm, he became estranged from the assembly of the virtuous.
Dwelling alone in mountain fastnesses, his resolve further declined.
Neglecting his fields and gardens, he forgot the Buddha and abandoned the Dharma,
becoming once again an ordinary person.
Within that mountain lived a brahmin ascetic.
Thirsty and seeking a drink,
he was preoccupied with his fieldwork and had no one to give him any.
The brahmin, harboring resentment, departed in this state of grievance.
The brahmin was able to raise the dead and command spirits and deities.
He immediately summoned the spirit of slaughter and commanded him, saying, "That man has insulted me; go and kill him."
A *arhat* dwelling in the mountains who knew of this went to the farmer's house.
Upon seeing the *śramaṇa*, the farmer joyfully prostrated himself and provided him with a single meal.
The śramaṇa said:
"This evening, light your lamps early, diligently take the three refuges, and recite the verse on guarding the mouth and restraining the mind.
Cultivate thoughts of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, so that they may long abide in peace and security."
After the śramaṇa had departed, the host followed his instructions;
he became proficient in mindfulness of the Buddha and the recitation of the precepts, never neglecting them.
When the murderous spirit arrived at dawn, it watched for a slight lapse in his conduct, intending to kill him.
Beholding his compassionate heart, one would not kill him even without cause.
Even if ghosts, spirits, or humans command oneself to kill him, or if he desires to kill himself,
he possesses a virtue that makes him inviolable.
"It was only right that he should have been killed.
When the ghost grew angry at being killed and sought to harm the brahmin,
the Arhat shielded him with his supernatural power.
He caused the ghosts to become invisible;
the farmer awakened to the Way,
and the Brahmin was restored to life.
The ghost was thus unable to incur the sin of killing;
the farming family immediately received the Three Refuges and recited the Buddha's name without ceasing.
The *Sūtra on the Fall of a Lay Disciple* (Upāsaka-patana-sūtra) contains the entirety of one fascicle; it also includes the fifth fascicle of the ten-fascicle *Avadāna-sūtra*. 7.

The Faithful Layman Who, at the Point of Death, Was Reborn as a Worm in His Wife’s Nose Due to Mutual Attachment. There was once a faithful layman (*upāsaka*). As he approached his death, he and his wife were filled with mutual attachment; consequently, he was reborn as a worm in the nose of his wife. [This is the seventh account.]
Maintaining the precepts with diligent and tireless effort,
there was a śramaṇa who had already cast off the heavy burden;
birth and death were forever ended, and he attained supernormal powers.
He was a close friend of theirs.
At that time, the lay devotee suddenly fell gravely ill;
though medical treatment did not cure him, his wife was overcome with great sorrow and suffering.
She said to her husband,
"As husband and wife, you alone are suffering.
By what means can we share this illness so that it may be lightened?"
"If you, my lord, should pass away, upon what shall I rely?
My children will be left orphaned; whom else shall they have to depend on?
Hearing this, the husband felt even deeper affection and longing.
As his great life-force was about to reach its end, he died immediately;
his soul and spirit returned at once into the wife's nostril and transformed into an insect.
The woman wept loudly and could not restrain herself.
At that time, the practitioner went to see the woman,
wishing to exhort and console her so that she might cast off her grief and sorrow.
When the woman saw the practitioner approaching, her grief and distress intensified all the more.
"Alas," she cried, "how could it be that my husband, the Upādhyāya, has already died?
At that moment, a worm emerged from her nasal mucus and suddenly fell to the ground.
The woman was immediately filled with shame and intended to crush him with her foot.
The practitioner said to her, "Stop, stop! Do not kill!"
"This is your husband who has transformed himself into this insect.
The wife said, "He is a practitioner of the Way;
my husband reveres the sutras and maintains the precepts with a diligence that is difficult to equal."
"For what reason did you die and transform into this form?
The practitioner replied,
"Because I gave rise to excessive attachment in a past life, I have now been born as an insect."
The practitioner of the Way preached the sutras for the insects.
You have applied yourself with diligence to honoring the sutras and upholding the precepts; by the merit thereof, you ought to be reborn in heaven and behold the Buddhas.
Yet, you remain seated here due to thoughts of affection, attachment, and longing.
Upon falling among these insects,
one should feel shame; when the insects hear this, they understand its meaning.
She immediately reproached herself, and shortly thereafter her life ended;

she was reborn in heaven. Because she had given away the householder’s goods, this became known as the *Biqiuzhishiwuguoweifunizhongchong jing* (Sutra on Becoming a Nose-Worm for a Wife Due to Giving Away a Householder’s Goods).
8. Bakula Attained Five Immortal Rewards for Observing One Precept. Bakula attained five rewards of immortality for observing one precept. Long ago, there was a man.
He had only one son,
named Bakula, who was then seven years of age.
When his wife passed away, he took another as his consort.
She harbored malice toward the son of his former wife and steamed rice cakes in a steamer.
When the boy asked his mother for some, she [refused].
The mother took him and placed him inside a steamer;
she covered his head with a large jar, intending to kill the child.
While in the steamer, the child ate the steamed rice and did not die.
Later, she was again placed upon a heated iron griddle;
though she ate the parched grain from the griddle, she did not consider it a calamity.
Afterwards, she went to the riverbank to wash her clothes.
It was cast into deep water and swallowed by a fish;
seven days passed.
The father invited the assembly of monks and established a great assembly for them.
Having purchased a fish, he loaded it onto a cart and returned home.
When he was about to cut open the belly of the fish,
his son said:
"Proceed slowly and do not injure the child's head.
This child previously received the precept against killing;
he has now attained the five kinds of immortality," as stated in the *Apituo jing* (Sūtra of Parables).

9. Upholding the precepts, reciting the sūtras, and maintaining the continuity of light offerings—ghosts cannot harm one who upholds the precepts, recites the sūtras, and maintains the continuity of light offerings. Nine: In the past, there were five brothers.
The father instructed him to observe the precepts,
but the eldest son alone was unwilling to do so.
He took five coins and went to a physiognomist to seek [his fortune].
The physiognomist said,
"He shall live to be a hundred years old and attain great wealth and nobility.
He further said, "Yet he is certainly destined for evil."
He spoke again, saying,
"I do not approve. Thirteen days from now, you shall die."
The man, struck with great terror, said:
"This is not something that can be treated by any ordinary teacher of the world;
only the Buddha possesses the foreknowledge of what has not yet occurred."
"He is currently at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
you may go there and ask him.
Thereupon, he went immediately to question the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"You have a karmic enemy from a previous life who intends to come and seize you.
If you wish to escape him, [you must do as follows]."
"You shall attain liberation only by upholding the five precepts.
Return home and prepare more oil and wicks to burn them; after thirteen days have passed, you will receive the precepts and light lamps to continue the illumination."
Throughout the day and throughout the night, he recited the sutras and verses,
saying "Namo Buddha," taking refuge in the Buddha, never ceasing for a moment.
After thirteen days had passed, he was naturally liberated.
That very night, two ghosts went there together to kill him;
one ghost stayed a hundred paces away.
He sent a ghost to go and kill him,
but [the ghost] saw the bright light of the lamp and heard only the sound of him calling out, "Namo Buddha! I take refuge in the Buddha!"
He did not dare to go forward and speak a single word to the ghost, saying:
"This person cannot be recovered;
he merely calls out 'Namo Buddha' and takes refuge in the Buddha."
"I loathe hearing this sound; it causes me a headache.
Thereupon, the two demons held each other and ran away, no longer approaching him.
From that time forward, he attained long-lasting peace and security. This is an essential matter from among the various sūtras.
10. Seizing and Seeking to Return the Buddha’s Precepts: Various Demons Emerge from the Mouth and Strike His Body. Ten. Formerly, in the kingdom of Kālaṇa...
There was a son of a brahmin named Dhāraṇa,
who received the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts and did not transgress them in any way.
Having long maintained his grasp [of these views], he later traveled to another country.
Upon seeing people killing, stealing, or committing adultery, he would greedily crave such acts;
upon seeing people's likes and dislikes, he would immediately pass judgment on them.
Whenever he saw someone drinking alcohol, he would immediately desire to pursue them;
not for a single moment was he steady,
and he thought to himself:
He regretted having received the precepts and vowed to return them to the Buddha.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was and said,
"Since receiving the five precepts, I have been subject to many prohibitions and am unable to follow my own will."
"The Buddha-Dharma is so revered that it is not something an ordinary person like myself can attend to with due respect; may I now depart?
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
Before his words had even ceased,
natural spirits and ghosts appeared from within his mouth,
wielding iron mallets to strike and seize his head.
Furthermore, there are spirits who strip them of their clothes and hook out their tongues;
there are female demonesses who cut off their genitals with knives;
and there are spirits who pour molten copper into their mouths.
In front, behind, to the left, and to the right, there were various ghosts and spirits who vied with one another to come and tear him apart,
taking his flesh and blood to devour it.
Furthermore, there is a spontaneous fire that burns their bodies;
they seek life but cannot find it, and they seek death but cannot find it.
Various ghosts seize them urgently, not allowing them to move.
The Buddha saw him and asked,
"Why do you now hold your mouth shut and remain unable to speak,
merely beating yourself with your own hands?"
The Buddha, by means of his majestic spiritual power, rescued the elder.
When the various kṣetrapāla kings and ghost generals saw the World-Honored One,
they each stood to one side.
Thereupon, he regained consciousness.
He immediately rose, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and said to the Buddha:
"In my body, there are five thieves."
"You have dragged me into the three evil realms;
because of my desires, I committed transgressions and betrayed what I had received.
I pray that the Buddha will have compassion for me."
From this day forward, I shall reform my past ways and cultivate the future by reverently receiving and upholding the Dharma of the Precepts:
observing the six fast days each month and the three long periods of fasting each year,
burning incense, scattering flowers, and hanging various banners and canopies.
"I shall serve the Triple Gem and dare not transgress again.
The Buddha said,
"What you have now spoken is truly great goodness."

"If you see with your own eyes that one commits a transgression oneself and receives its retribution oneself, rather than having it bestowed by Heaven," as stated in the third fascicle of the *Mahā-abhiṣeka Sūtra*.

11. Regarding those who do not believe in sin and merit: A dream-demon seizes them and causes them to receive the precepts; subsequently, their lifespan reaches one hundred years. (Repeated) Eleven. In ancient times, people did not believe in sin and merit.
He was already fifty years old when he dreamed that a demon of slaughter came to seize him;
upon waking from his sleep, he was filled with terror and sought out a master to interpret the dream.
The Master cast the divination stalks and declared:
"A murderous ghost surely intends to harm you; it will not exceed ten days.
If you wish to ward this off,"
From now on, within ten days, by receiving the five precepts of the Buddha,
burning incense, lighting lamps, and hanging silk banners and canopies,
and by placing faith and taking refuge in the Triple Gem, one may avoid this death.
Thereupon, relying on this teaching, he devoted his mind to faith and practice.
When the demon arrived at his door, it saw him performing meritorious deeds and was unable to cause him harm;
the demon then fled away.

The family was destitute;
they sustained their lives solely by gathering various wild vegetables.
Having prepared a soup, it was just now finished cooking.
Outside, as a practitioner of the Way was coming out after begging for alms, he saw a śramaṇa;
his parents then said,
"We shall give him a portion."
The sons and grandsons each gave their respective portions to her,
yielding to their mother so that she might eat.
The six of them simultaneously resolved to each abstain from food for one day.

I only regret that my family was poor and lacked the means for excellent offerings; yet by virtue of this merit, I have been born among gods and humans, always enjoying peace and security, and possessing abundant wealth.
This is because our initial resolve was equal.
Throughout successive lifetimes they have shared karmic causes and conditions;
now, meeting once again,
parents and children, great and small, all simultaneously uphold the five precepts.

A Man on a Journey Encounters Three Who Manifested Transformations and Practiced Diligence. Thirteen: There was a man traveling on a road who encountered three [beings] who manifested transformations and practiced diligence.
Seeing a dead person by the side of the road,
a spirit whipped him with a staff.
A traveler said:
"This person is already dead; why do you whip him?
The spirit said, "He was my former body."
From the day of their birth, they were unfilial toward their parents and disloyal toward their sovereign;
they failed to revere the Triple Gem and did not follow the words of their teachers.
"Now you have caused me to suffer according to my transgressions;
the pain is beyond words.
Out of anger, you have lashed me with a whip."
Advancing a short distance further,
he again saw a dead man.
A celestial being descended from above.
He scattered flowers over the corpse and rubbed it with his hands.
A traveler asked him,
"I observe that you appear to be a celestial being."
"Why is Māṣa a dead man? He replied,
"Because he was my former body."
From the day of his birth, he was filial toward his parents;
he served his sovereign with loyalty and integrity,
and he venerated the Triple Gem.
That I have received my teacher’s instruction and been enabled to attain rebirth in heaven is entirely due to the kindness of my former body.
Therefore, I have come to repay him with this.
Proceed a little further,
and you will see another celestial being.
Her robes were fresh, fine, well-fitting, fragrant, and pure.
As she was picking and eating sour jujubes by the side of the road,
a traveler asked her:
"Beholding you, I thought you were a deva;
why then do you eat sour jujubes?
The deva replied:
While I was in the world, I served my parents with filial piety,
attended to my sovereign with loyalty and integrity, and honored the Triple Gem;
I performed various kinds of meritorious deeds.
It was only that he did not like to give sweetmeats to his guests;
now, as a celestial being, his constant food is insufficient,
and for this reason he eats sour jujubes.
When the practitioner saw these three transformations in a single day,
he immediately returned to uphold the five precepts and cultivate the ten wholesome actions;
he was filial toward his parents and loyal and trustworthy in serving his ruler.
14. Showing the matters essential from various sūtras regarding how transgressions and blessings follow a person through successive lives:

There was a person who, ten days after his death, returned to life and recounted what he had experienced and seen; there was another who, ten days after his death, returned to life and recounted what he had experienced and seen. Furthermore, there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who, having previously been a non-Buddhist practitioner weary of suffering, performed prayers and sacrifices.
Relinquishing all attachments, one enters the Dharma, upholds the precepts with diligence,
zealously recites the sutras, delights in giving, maintains patience in mind,
and always possesses a heart of loving-kindness.
When his life was suddenly cut short and he was on the verge of death, he instructed his parents, saying,
"If my illness does not end in death within seven days, do not bury me.
Suddenly appearing as if dead, the corpse remained for eight days.
The relatives all said,
"We must hastily prepare the coffining.
His parents said:
"I shall not become bloated or foul-smelling, but will remain for ten days.
As he spoke these words, his eyes opened;
yet he was still unable to move.
The parents rejoiced and waited until the tenth day,
when the child suddenly sat up by himself and was able to speak well.
They asked him where he had come from and what he had seen.
He replied,
"There came officials and soldiers who led me to a great city.
Within the city was a prison."
The prison is pitch black, with iron walls on all four sides.
The city gates are entirely made of glowing, red-hot iron.
Within the prison, the bodies of those bound there sit amidst the flames.
Above and below, the hells burn with blue smoke rising upward.
Some people there cut their flesh with knives and eat it.
The King of Hell asked me:
"What kind of person are you?
For what offense and for what reason have you come here?
Herein we punish those who commit the five heinous crimes, those who are unfilial toward their parents, and those who are disloyal and untrustworthy toward their sovereign."
He replied,
"In my youth, I was deluded by evil people and served the foolishness of non-Buddhist paths."
Furthermore, they drink alcohol and kill living beings to sacrifice to Heaven and Earth;
moreover, they seek profit in the marketplace,
using measures and weights to enrich themselves.
Later, I encountered a virtuous teacher who drew me into the Buddha-way;
there I beheld śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way.
He conferred upon me the five precepts and instructed me to practice the ten wholesome deeds. From that time until today,
I have not committed any further evil.
Looking up, I relied upon the Illustrious King’s compassion for my inadequacy;
I then bowed my head to the ground.
The King immediately rose, joined his palms, and said to me:
"Stop, stop!
A person of pure faith should not act in such a manner.
Please, sit with me."
He summoned an official and questioned him, saying:
"This is a disciple of the Unsurpassed, Right, and True One.
All of you should attain deliverance through this person."
When that person's own lifespan is exhausted,
only then will they die;
their soul and spirit will then follow on.
If he were to be reborn in the heavens, the celestial deities would have welcomed him;
if he were to be reborn among humans, those among humans would have welcomed him.
How could you bring this man here?
"He has entered this place of the five heinous crimes.
The official replied to the king,
"In this world, there are many such people."
They do not fear the laws of kings;
they do not fear the four seasons;
they are not constrained by the five elements.
Heaven, earth, ghosts, and spirits roam across the world;
one must not fail to inquire of them.
There is a teacher named a śramaṇa.
Having shaved his hair and wearing coarse, shabby clothing,

From the various Śakras, Brahmās, and Moon-and-Sun Kings above,

those who honor and revere this person shall obtain immeasurable merit.

The Buddha, with great compassion, protects all that crawls and flies;
even the heavenly deities, earth spirits, ghosts, and dragons all revere him.
How could he be constrained by royal omens, the four seasons, or the five elements?
"The Buddha's grace is like the four seas; it cannot be measured.

If a person has entered the True Dharma,"

Without distinguishing between the true and the false,

Falling from the high place, he suddenly revived;

2. When Anāthapiṇḍada invited the Buddha with a sincere heart, everything was spontaneously prepared within his park. [The same occurred] when the two [kings] of the city of Vaiśālī invited him with a sincere heart.
There was a woman named Āvaṃhārī who,
hearing that the Buddha had come to travel through the land, rejoiced immeasurably.
Together with five hundred women, she went to where the Buddha was.
Upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, her mind attained awakening.
She then invited the Buddha for a meal.
At that time, there were also five hundred sons of elders in the city who likewise invited the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
Having accepted the invitation for the following day from Avantīputra,
the sons of the elders then spoke to Avantīputra, saying:
"The Most Honored Buddha has come to convert our country;
I should be the first to offer him food.
You must cease your offerings for now."
The woman said,
"Do not use your power and strength to oppress the weak.
If you would grant me four wishes, I shall yield to you."
First, may my mind preserve its goodness without wavering;
second, may my life be preserved so that it does not perish;
third, may my wealth and possessions not diminish.
"Fourth, cause the Buddha to dwell long in this country.
The elder said, "Excellent!
You are now able to realize impermanence."
"The aspirations we all hope for are not something I am capable of accomplishing;
allow me first to feed the Buddha.
Among them was a youth who felt ashamed to be left behind.
He remained obstinate and would not relent.

He then sent messengers to seek out various goods from Holi.
He obtained nothing at all;
yet the various foods within the storehouse were spontaneously replenished.
Only firewood and charcoal were lacking.
He soaked white cotton cloth in oil to serve as a substitute.

and he made this petition before the Buddha.
He immediately dispatched a parrot to announce that the meal was prepared;
when the elder shot at it,

He reached the place where the Buddha was,
flying there and calling out to the Buddha— the One Blessed with Multitudes— and the Sangha.
As his feet stepped upon the city gate, heaven and earth shook.
Five hundred elders,
Āṭavaka, and the women, having seen and heard this matter,
attained the Dharma-eye and received and upheld the five precepts. (From the *Zhongbenqijing*, Scroll Lower)

3. The Story of the Daughter Sumanā Giving Birth to Ten Eggs, Which Developed into Ten Sons, Along with Their Past Causes and Conditions. In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a householder named Sudatta.
There was a young daughter recently born,
named Sumanā, whose countenance and features were most exquisite.
Her father, out of affection and love for her,
took her to the Buddha’s dwelling;
upon seeing the Buddha, the girl’s heart was filled with redoubled joy and exultation.
"I wish to obtain fine incense to smear upon the Buddha’s dwelling.
In that woman's hand there was a *piṇḍapātra* (alms-bowl);
the Buddha requested it from her.
She then gave it to the Buddha;
he wrote a letter on it with incense and gave it back to her.
The girl returned to the city with her father and went about searching for a buyer.
Whatever the Buddha required, she would carry it to the Jeta Grove and grind it with her own hands;
she did this every day in this manner.
At that time, the King of Takṣaśilā dispatched one of his sons as an envoy to Śrāvastī to travel about and observe extensively;
he further went to the vihāra and saw the maiden Sumanā.
He then took her as his wife.
Subsequently, she became pregnant and gave birth to ten eggs.
After the eggs opened, ten sons emerged.
His physical appearance was handsome and his prowess extraordinary;
however, he took pleasure in hunting,
which his mother forbade him to do.
The sons said to their mother,
"Hunting is our greatest pleasure.
Their mother tried to dissuade them, but they regarded her as an object of resentment.
The mother spoke again, saying:
"It is because I love you that I have restrained you;
had I harbored hatred for you, I would never have said such words."
"The sin of taking life leads to rebirth in hell;
for incalculable kalpas, by what means could one find liberation?
The sons said to their mother:
Having personally set out his own mind, he heard it from another.
His mother spoke again, saying,
"I have heard it from the Buddha."
The child asked his mother again,
"Who is the Buddha? I pray that you will explain this fully to me."
The mother said to her sons:
"In the kingdom of Kapilavastu, the son of King Śuddhodana,
having grown weary of old age, sickness, and death, left the home life to study the Way and attained the unsurpassed fruit."
His body was sixteen feet tall, and with the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, his far-reaching vision encompassed all things without limit.
When his sons petitioned their mother to go and visit the Buddha,
she immediately granted her permission.
They went to the Jeta Grove to pay their respects to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them,
and all ten of them simultaneously attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
He then sought to leave the household life.
The Buddha granted him permission to follow the Way;
his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the dharma robes appeared upon his body.
Through diligent effort in this great enterprise,

Question: We wish to hear the method for extinguishing transgressions.

thus he departed. [This concludes] the seventh chapter, "A Woman Pregnant Wishes to Leave Home," from the lower fascicle of the *Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra*.

It was from this that the ascetic Brahmins further arose.
After the bhikṣu had bathed, his body was covered with many sores that were being bitten by flies and bees;
he immediately smeared white ashes over the sores here and there and covered his body with a water-soaked cloth.
At that time, those who saw him said, "This is the Way;
one should study this dharma.
It was from this that the ash-smearing Brahmins originated.
A bhikṣu kindled a fire to cauterize his ulcer;
as the pain of the ulcer became increasingly unbearable,
he threw himself from a cliff to take his own life.
At that time, some who saw him said,
"This bhikṣu formerly wore fine robes;
now he is like this."
How could they have abandoned the wholesome dharmas and,
with correct knowledge, concluded that throwing oneself from a cliff was the path to liberation?
It was from this that the practices of throwing oneself from cliffs and worshipping fire originated.
In this manner, there are ninety-six such types;
all arise because of the various forms and categories of these bhikṣus,
giving rise to manifold false conceptions.
Each gives rise to a view;
it is like a country where people look at one another and conceive coarse perceptions.
Once coarse perceptions have arisen, they each kill one another;
the same applies to the emergence of heterodox views. This is from the fourth fascicle of the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*.
