Clinging greedily to gain and offerings, they proclaimed themselves uniquely exalted.
Upon hearing that a Buddha had appeared in the world, whose divine virtues surpassed those of men,
they gathered together and made a solemn oath.
"We ought to deliberate with one mind;
only by not contradicting one another's words can we prevail.
They then dispatched one person to go and observe the Tathāgata.
It was as if a person could never look upon them enough;
he returned and informed the six teachers.
"Gautama’s countenance is rare in this world; his majestic power and radiant light surpass those of the sun and moon.
As I see it, there is nothing with which he can be compared.
Then the six men thought again:
Since this person is born of royal lineage,
it is only natural that he should be handsome;
why should it be considered strange?
Now let us send another person to observe whether he is free from agitation or if he is restless; upon his return,
report back to the six teachers.
"Gautama is among the assembly like a king of beasts;
he has no fear or difficulty.
Then the six men thought again:
Fools, desiring further experience,
crave that radiance;
this is their constant practice.
What is there to find strange in this?

Having emerged from the royal palace, she has been entertained day and night by sixty thousand court ladies; without having yet undergone formal instruction, she was sent again to listen [to the teachings].
Thinking that there might be some underlying principle as with ordinary people,
they immediately dispatched one person of clear understanding to observe what the Buddha had said;
he returned and reported to the six men.
What he taught reached back to antiquity and understood the present;
his foresight was boundless and his retrospective vision infinite.
He discerned meanings and analyzed principles with such clarity that matters were never redundant or cumbersome.
The six teachers further thought to themselves:
"In this world, there are many people whose eloquence is swift and clever, and who can please the hearts of others;
yet, the underlying principle is not something that cannot be investigated."
He sent them out again to observe whether the people,
upon hearing his teaching, listened in tranquil silence or in a state of confusion.
They returned and reported this to the six teachers.
The flavor revealed by Gautama is like nectar;
the multitude look up to him with thirst and listen without ever being satiated.
The six men thought again:
The assembled people will inevitably disperse after a long time from the beginning;
therefore, send another person of superior character to go and observe whether the principles are profound or shallow.
They returned and reported to the six teachers:
"What Gautama has manifested is like an ocean without shore;
what we have seen is like water in a cow's hoofprint."
Now, I alone wish to go there and seek to become his disciple.
Let the messengers from before and those from behind each escort me together to the place where the Tathāgata resides.
Furthermore, countless sentient beings arrived, vying with one another.
The Buddha spoke in verse, saying:
"Having attained the most perfect enlightenment for oneself, One remains unstained by any phenomena."
The All-Knowing One is fearless; he is self-enlightened without a teacher or protector.
When the disciples of the Six Teachers heard the Buddha recite these verses, those whose minds were firm immediately sought the Way.
One whose mind was hesitant returned and reported to the Master, saying:
"He who is uniquely honored throughout the three realms and presides over the ten directions is truly without equal."
"You should each disperse and seek your own safety.
Since I have neither teacher nor protector, and am likewise alone without a companion, I shall accumulate merit until I attain Buddhahood;
by myself, I will penetrate the Holy Path. Thus he spoke when he emerged from the "Sutra on the Six Teachers' Oath."
3. The Six Teachers and the Buddha’s Disciples Compete in Spiritual Power. The King of the Three Realms was named Bahusuta;
his crown prince was named Puṇyavardhana.
The King served the Six Teachers,
while his son followed the Way of the Buddha;
what they adhered to was not the same.
At that time, there were no śramaṇas in the world;
he alone was a layperson (avadātavasana) who served as their teacher and leader.
Five hundred followers of external paths (tīrthika) became jealous of his reputation and virtue.
He then addressed the king, saying,
"The affairs of state and the two religious traditions cause a person to lack single-mindedness.
I pray that you and the Teacher of the Buddha-way each manifest your extraordinary virtues."
"If you do not prevail, you shall be forfeited as a slave.
The King agreed to this.
The non-Buddhists and this master then set a date for the contest.
It was agreed that they should first test their respective skills and arts before the King to reach a mutual understanding;
the brahmins were all skilled in archery and charioteering.
They immediately proceeded into the mountains.
Each of the five hundred men shot at a deer;
all of them pierced the left eye, and the deer came forward with their antlers as a display of skill.
The worthy one also entered the mountains to contemplate the Buddha with focused mindfulness, seeking the assistance of his majestic spiritual power to manifest the Great Way.
Immediately, a fawn of five colors suddenly emerged from the earth.
He joyfully took it back with him.
The non-Buddhists learned of this and waited for the worthy one to go out.
He went to her house and said to his wife with deceptive words,
"Your husband wishes to renounce his home to become a wandering ascetic."
"However, by sitting upon this deer, you shall destroy your family.
When the wife heard this,
she became enraged and gave the deer away as a gift.
When the worthy man returned home, he did not see his deer.
He asked his wife,
"That inauspicious creature has now been lost."
Filled with profound sorrow and anxiety,
he returned to the mountains and repented with utmost sincerity.
Immediately, a divine moon-jewel suddenly emerged from the earth.
He then took this jewel and went to see the brahmin,
arriving at his gate to sell this extraordinary object.
The brahmin’s wife said:
"In my house, there is also a remarkable object that may be compared with yours.
He then brought forth the *mṛgaśiras* (deer-head) gem.
The worthy one then addressed the king:
"I have been entrusted with this fawn;
if you were to steal it now, your crime would be unfathomable.
Terrified, the wife returned it to him.
When the time for the trial arrived, the brahmins each presented a dead deer; all had their left eyes injured, being both filthy and foul-smelling.
The King loathed them greatly.
The wise man led the divine deer forward and presented the bright pearl to the royal palace;
both objects soared and frolicked, shimmering like falling stars and flashing like lightning.
Gong Qi challenged them;
the five hundred Brahmins, realizing that their own arts and skills could not compete,
immediately surrendered themselves as slaves.
The wives were all made into maidservants; this concludes the eighth fascicle of the *Daśādhyāya-avadāna-sūtra*. 4.

Displaying one’s own extraordinary prowess by girding one’s loins, pressing out one’s belly, and carrying fire upon the head. Regarding "Displaying one’s own extraordinary prowess by girding one’s loins, pressing out one’s belly, and carrying fire upon the head": in South India there was a master of debate.
With copper razors scraping his belly and a fire burning upon his head,
he entered the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, people asked him,
"For what reason are you like this? He replied:
"I am so full of wisdom that I fear my belly will burst.
I wish to wear fire to illuminate the darkness.
At that time, people said to him:
"O foolish Brahmin,
when the sun illuminates the world, why do you say it is dark? He replied:
You do not know that there are two kinds of darkness:
the first is that which lacks the sun, moon, fire, or lamps.
Second, they are foolish and lack the light of wisdom.
Furthermore, people say:
"You have not yet seen the bhikṣu Gautama Śākyaputra."
"How could I dare utter such words in reply?
It was as if one who had been conversing in the darkness saw the sun rise.
At that time, the people within the city immediately called out to the Śākya son, the bhikṣu Hāṭaka.
Desiring to engage in debate with him,
Hāṭaka heard of this; his heart filled with sorrow, he entered the city.
On the way, he saw two rams fighting together.
That very day he took this as an omen: one ram was a brahmin.
"The single sheep is myself;
as for 'I,' it is not as good [as it seems].
Thus, I become even more sorrowful and anxious."
Proceeding further, he again saw two oxen fighting together,
and he thought to himself:
"One ox is a brāhmaṇa."
"One ox is mine," he said,
but this was still not enough.
He then went to the front gate.
He again saw two men wrestling,
and he thought to himself once more:
"This, too, is not as good."
As he was about to enter the place of debate,
he saw a man carrying a full water jar,
which immediately broke.
Again he thought to himself:
"I have seen various inauspicious omens;
I have no choice but to enter this house."
Seeing this brahmin, he recognized from the expressions of his eyes and mouth that he was not his equal;
after sitting for a brief moment, he [proceeded].
The people then said,
"Let us debate together.
He replied:
I am currently slightly unwell;
I must wait until tomorrow before returning to my lodging. (From the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Second Recension, Volume Three). 5.
The Story of the People of Jihonika Regarding the Crow and the Peacock. Regarding the People of Jihonika Concerning the Crow and the Peacock: Five. In a past life.
There was a great kingdom located in the northern frontier region,
known as Jñānamāyā.
The illusory man of wisdom took the crow with him and arrived at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra; however,
such crows did not exist within the borders of that country.
Nor were there any other species of wondrous birds.
When the people of the time saw the crows,
they rejoiced and leaped for joy.
They made offerings and served him with food, fruit,
and melons, tending to his needs;
crows from distant lands all gathered there in numbers beyond counting.
The entire kingdom universally honored him beyond measure.
Later, at another time, a merchant arrived from another country bringing a peacock.
When the multitude saw its exceptionally magnificent plumage and its grand, elegant gait—unprecedented in their experience—they were struck with wonder.
Hearing their voices, his heart leaped with joy;
he abandoned all affection for the crows and came to cherish the peacocks.
All the provisions formerly used to nourish the crows were now offered to the peacocks.
Having paid homage and taken refuge,
all the crows vanished, their whereabouts unknown.
At that time, a celestial being spoke this verse:
Before the sunlight was seen, the lamp alone provided light;
when the birds were first observed, they drank from the water and ate the sweet fruits and melons.
Now that all these things are fully present, it is as if the sun has risen from among the trees.
The crows lost their offerings; seeing the distinction between the honored and the lowly, Ānanda spoke in verse:
"If the Buddha had not appeared in the world, the brahmin would have received the offerings."
The Buddha who now possesses the perfect voice was I myself, the peacock who lost his offerings to the heterodox teachers.
The crows were those various external heterodox teachers.
The "Deva" refers to Ānanda; this is extracted from the *Mayūra-jātaka-sūtra*. 6.

Pūraṇa Kāśyapa Competes with the Buddha in the Way and Fails, Then Commits Suicide. Six: Formerly, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a Brahmin teacher. Pūraṇa Kāśyapa competed with the Buddha in the Way and, being unsuccessful, committed suicide. Six. Formerly, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a Brahmin teacher.
His name was Pūraṇa Kāśyapa;
he was accompanied by five hundred disciples,
and there were none among the king or the people who did not pay him homage and serve him.
When the Buddha first attained the Way,
he traveled with his disciples from Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī;
his physical marks were resplendent, and his teachings were pure and sublime.
Among the king, the ladies of the inner court, and all the people of the realm, there was none who did not revere him.
Kāśyapa, filled with jealousy and wishing to disparage the World-Honored One,
said to King Prasenajit:
"We elders were the former teachers and ancient masters of this land.
This śramaṇa Gautama appeared later;
though he seeks the Way, he truly possesses no divine sanctity."
"But the King has abandoned me; now I wish to compete with the Buddha.
Whichever of us excels in the Way and its Virtue shall be honored by the King.
The King said, "Very well."
The king reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Excellent.
Set a period of seven days for a contest of supernatural transformations."
The king established two high seats on a level, expansive, and auspicious site to the east of the city.
The king, his ministers, and the great assembly gathered like clouds.
Desiring to observe the two men contesting their paths,
Kāśyapa and his disciples arrived first at the site of the seat and climbed up the ladder;
so too did the divine king Pañcaśikha.
Seeing their falsehood and jealousy,
he immediately raised a great wind that blew their sitting mats and overturned their banners and streamers.
Sand, gravel, and stones flew up and rained down,
so that the eyes could not see;
yet the World-Honored One sat upon his high seat, majestic and unmoving.
The Buddha and the great assembly approached with dignified decorum;
they suddenly ascended toward their high seats,
and all the monks sat down in silence in their respective places.
The king and his ministers, increasing their reverence, prostrated themselves and said:
"We pray that you will bestow your divine transformation to suppress false views,
and cause the people of the nation to clearly believe in the correct and true."
The World-Honored One suddenly vanished from his seat and ascended into the void,
emitting a great radiance that disappeared in the east and appeared in the west, and likewise in all four directions.
Water and fire issued from his body, alternating between upper and lower;
he sat and lay in mid-air, performing twelve transformations;
and having made his body vanish, he reappeared upon his seat.
Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits offered flowers and incense;
the sound of their praises shook heaven and earth.
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa realized for himself that he possessed no true Way.
With heads bowed in shame and fear, they did not dare to lift their eyes.
The Vajrapāṇi held his vajra, from the tip of which flames issued forth, brandishing it toward Kāśyapa.
When asked why he did not manifest transformations,
Kāśyapa fell down in terror and fled;
his five hundred disciples scattered in all directions in a frantic rush.
The World-Honored One’s majestic countenance was entirely free from joy or sorrow;
he returned to the Jeta Grove,
while the king and his ministers withdrew with joyful farewells.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa and his disciples departed, having suffered this humiliation.
On the way, they encountered an elderly female lay follower (upāsikā) named Maṇi.
He reviled them, saying: "You lot,
a pack of fools, do not measure your own worth,
yet you wish to compete with the Buddha in the display of spiritual arts."
They are crazed, foolish, deceitful, and devoid of shame;
they need not even maintain such faces while walking through the world.
Kāśyapa felt ashamed of his disciples.
He went to the riverbank and deceived his disciples, saying,
"I shall now cast myself into the water and will surely be reborn in the Brahma Heaven;
if I do not return, it will be for my own happiness."
His disciples waited for him but he did not return;
they deliberated among themselves, saying,
"The Master has surely ascended to heaven."
"What is appropriate for me to do?
I shall each throw myself into the water, hoping to follow my teacher;
yet, dragged by their own transgressions, they all fall into hell."
On a later day, when the king heard of these matters,
he was greatly astonished and marveled at them. He went to the Buddha’s dwelling and said to the Buddha,
"For what reason has the master Kāśyapa and his disciples come to such a state?"
The Buddha told the king:
"Kāśyapa and his disciples have two grave offenses.
The first is that their three poisons are raging, yet they claim to have attained the Way."
Second, slandering the Tathāgata while desiring to serve him with reverence.
By these two transgressions, one ought to fall into hell;
driven by the weight of such calamity and retribution, one causes oneself to drown in the river.
When the body dies and the spirit departs, one undergoes immeasurable suffering.
In the past, there were two monkey kings,
each presiding over five hundred monkeys.
One king gave rise to a mind of jealousy;
wishing to kill the other king and plotting to rule alone,
he went forth to fight him.
In their repeated battles, they were no match for him;
filled with shame and humiliation,
they retreated and went to the edge of the great ocean, to a secluded inlet of the sea.
There was a great mass of foam,
blown together by the wind into a pile hundreds of *zhang* high;
the foolish monkey king took it to be the Snowy Mountains.
He spoke to the group, saying,
"I have long heard that within the ocean there is a Snowy Mountain (Himavat),
where one may enjoy happiness and satisfy the palate with sweet fruits at will."
"Today I shall go first to observe it myself.
If you truly find it pleasant, you will not be able to return;
if you do not find it pleasant, I shall return and tell you."
Thereupon, he climbed the tree and leaped with all his might,
plunging into the midst of the gathered foam and drowning at the bottom of the sea; the others,
finding it strange that he did not emerge, [searched for him].
This refers to the one who must have been greatly joyful;
each time he threw [the monkeys] into the water, they were cut off and drowned in the crowd. The envious monkey king was Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.

The group of followers refers to the five hundred disciples of Pūraṇa; this is taken from the fourth fascicle of the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, where the accounts of the noble and the foolish are presented in both detailed and abbreviated forms, and are not included here.

7. The Seer Kṣānti Cultivated Patience and Loving-kindness While Being Mutilated by King Kali. The Seer Kṣānti cultivated patience and loving-kindness while being mutilated by King Kali. Seven: The Seer Kṣānti was in a great forest.
He practiced patience and cultivated loving-kindness.
At that time, King Kali, accompanied by his court ladies, entered the forest for recreation.
Having finished their meal, they sat down.
While King Wǎo was sleeping lightly,
the various court ladies were gathering flowers among the groves when they saw this seer.
Having paid respectful homage, they stood to one side.
At that time, the seer preached various discourses on loving-kindness and patience to the ladies-in-waiting;
his words were so exquisite that those who heard them never grew weary.
After a long time he did not leave.
King Kali, waking up and not seeing his court ladies,
drew his sword and pursued them.
Standing before the rishi,
his arrogance and envy flourishing, he glared with eyes wide with rage, brandished his sword,
and questioned the rishi.
"What are you doing? The rishi replied,
"I am currently practicing patience and cultivating loving-kindness here."
The king said,
"I shall now test you;
I will cut off your ears and nose with a sharp sword and sever your hands and feet."
"If you do not become angry, I shall know that you have cultivated patience.
The rishi said, "As you wish.
The king then drew his sword and cut off his ears and nose, and severed his hands and feet.
He then asked him,
"Is your mind moving?
He replied:
"I cultivate loving-kindness and patience, so my mind remains unmoved.
The king said, "You are but a single person here; you possess no power."
"Though you speak with your mouth, who would believe that you do not move?
At that time, the rishi immediately made this vow:
"If I have truly cultivated loving-kindness and patience..."
"The blood shall become milk.
Immediately, the blood transformed into milk.
The king was greatly astonished and delighted.
He took the women away.
At that time, the nāgas and devas of the forest caused thunder and lightning to strike this rishi;
the king was fatally harmed and perished without returning to his palace. (From the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Volume 4).

8. The Scribe of the Conch-Script: Wind and Rain Cannot Injure It. In the past, there was a rishi. This rishi of the conch-script created characters that wind and rain could not blow away or invade. Long ago, there was a rishi.
He was named Śaṅkhapāla, endowed with perfect diligence;
yet, though he lived as a householder, he did not practice the holy life (brahmacarya). Some spoke thus:
Just as that conch-shell pattern possesses pure lines,
yet while residing at home it is not well-purified;
the conch-shell pattern forms written characters.
Wind and rain cannot dampen or destroy it;
while dwelling in the secular world, one cultivates pure conduct as if one were an Anāgāmin.
Surrounded by his household and kinsmen—
is this not the practice of purity?
The inconceivable realm of supernormal powers is described in the sixth fascicle of the *Vasumitra-sūtra*.
9. The Story of the Four Rishis Attaining the Path. When the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha preaching the True Dharma, the minds of all the Nirgranthas were filled with grief and distress.
On Mount Līyi there were five hundred rishis.
A messenger sent by the Nirgranthas said,
"There is a Buddha here."
Claiming for themselves that they have attained the Way and possess the foremost supernatural transformations,
they say that none can equal them and thus exalt themselves. We pray that you,
Great Masters, [will address this].
He humbled himself to come and assist me;
yet, in discussing the ultimate essentials of the Way, he proceeded to disparage it,
thereby causing the fame and achievements of various masters to become even more prominent.
He replied, "Very well.
Let us first dispatch four men to challenge Gautama.
Then the Nirgranthas issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom.
"Seven days from now, four Buddhas shall enter the kingdom to deliver sentient beings.
When that day arrived,
the four men manifested supernatural transformations before his eyes.
They came from the air, each entering through one side of the city.
When the people saw them, they thought they were the true Buddha.
The Nirgranthas sent a messenger to inform the Buddha.
"You may come to discourse on the Way.
The Buddha said,
"You should go at mealtime."
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said,
"Gautama is likely not his equal;
he has feigned not coming forward."
The assembly all agreed that this was so.
The Buddha then caused fire to arise in the sky,
coming from the western direction.
The four men flew southward, and the fire followed them from the south.
As the heat intensified from all four directions, the four men were struck with terror and collapsed prostrate upon the ground.
The Buddha was present in a cool place;
immediately seeking the coolness, he came before the Buddha,
and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him.
They all became śramaṇas and attained the path of arhatship.
When the Buddha entered the city,
the people of the city said:
At dawn, four Buddhas appeared in the void.
The Buddha spoke,
pointing to his left and right.
These are the four arhats mentioned in the fifth fascicle of the *Daśa-varga-avadāna-sūtra*. 10.
The Seer Losing His Supernormal Powers and Being Born into an Evil Realm: This is like the case of the seer Udraka.
Having attained the five supernormal powers,
he flew to the king’s palace to eat.
The king’s chief consort, according to the laws of that country, [acted as follows].
He prostrated at his feet in salutation;
as soon as the lady’s hand touched him, he lost his supernatural powers.
He then requested a chariot from the king.
He mounted his carriage and departed, returning to his original dwelling.
Entering among the forest trees, he sought the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) again;
with single-minded devotion, he was on the verge of attaining them.
However, a bird on the tree cried out urgently, distracting his mind.
Leaving the tree, he went to the water's edge to seek concentration,
but again heard the sound of fish fighting and agitating the water.
This man, failing to attain meditative concentration,
immediately gave rise to anger, thinking:
"I shall slaughter all the fish and birds."
After a long time, this person attains concentration through reflection and is reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. There,
when his lifespan comes to an end, he passes away.
In his next life, he was reborn as a flying weasel that killed various fish and birds;
having committed immeasurable sins, he fell into the evil realms. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 17).
11. When the various seers saw or heard the forms and sounds of women, they all lost their supernatural powers. Thus ends the eleventh [chapter]: King Udayana.
He took his palace ladies and court maids to the forest of Udupavata; having removed all men,
he enjoyed himself with the five kinds of music together with women alone.
The sound was pure and exquisite as various famous incenses were burned. At that time,
some of the court ladies danced while naked.
At that time, five hundred rishis were passing through that place.
Upon seeing forms, hearing sounds, and smelling fragrances, those rishis lost their supernormal powers (ṛddhi),
just as wingless birds fall into a forest.
The king asked, "Who are you? The sages replied:
"I am a seer. The king asked again,
"Have you attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
He replied, "I have not.
He asked again,
"Have you attained the first dhyāna?"
He replied,
"I once possessed it, but have now lost it.
At that, the king spoke in anger:
A person possessed by desire, seeing my palace attendants, thought it utterly improper;
he then drew a sharp sword and severed the hands and feet of five hundred rishis. Excerpted from the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume Thirty-three.
12. Pāṇikhāta, son of King Janaka, conceived a lustful desire for a woman; later, he gave rise to an evil thought and fell into the Avīci hell. (Twelve) Udārāyaṇa, son of Māṭhara.
There was a king who constantly provided him with food. Whenever it was time for his meal, [the king would provide it].
By the power of his supernormal faculties, he flew through the air and arrived at the royal palace.
The king immediately came forward to welcome him, embraced him, and seated him upon a golden couch;
he then provided him with offerings of the flavors enjoyed by the various seers.
Then, having finished his meal, that rishi set aside his utensils,
rinsed his mouth, recited verses of blessing, and departed through the air.
Some time later, this king...
Because of affairs of state, he had to go elsewhere;
there was no one to attend to the rishi.
The rishi was of an impatient nature.
"Perhaps they will give rise to anger and curse me;
perhaps they will lose their royal throne or even take my life.
He then questioned his daughter.
"If the rishi comes, according to my usual practice, will you be able to provide him with offerings?
The girl replied, "I can.
Then the king strictly instructed his daughter to serve him with all her heart.
Thereupon he set out and attended to the affairs of state.
On the following day at mealtime, a rishi flew in from the air.
The princess, in accordance with royal custom,
personally rose to meet him, embraced him, and seated him upon a golden couch;
the princess’s body was delicate and soft.
The rishi touched the woman and lost his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
Having finished eating,
he removed the vessels, rinsed his mouth, and recited verses for the benediction.
Wishing to fly, he was unable to do so.
At that time, there was a pleasure grove within the royal palace;
he entered it and intended to cultivate his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Hearing the sounds of elephants, horses, and chariots, he was unable to practice.
At that time, the people within the city constantly thought to themselves:
"If only the Great Seer would walk upon the ground."
"We shall be able to approach and pay homage at his feet.
The seer was intelligent, wise, and skilled in expedient means;
he spoke to the princess, saying:
"Announce now to the people within the city:
'Today the Great Seer shall depart from the royal palace on foot.
You, the people, must perform all that is required to be done.'"
Then, at her command, the king’s daughter immediately issued a proclamation:
"The streets and thoroughfares shall be cleared and purified, free from tiles, rubble, filth, and excrement."
Banners were hung, incense was burned, and various kinds of flowers were scattered;
all were exquisitely adorned and pure.
Not far from the city, the place was as level as a sage’s stride.
He entered among the trees and groves, desiring to cultivate the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*).
However, hearing the cries of the various birds, he was unable to achieve his cultivation.
He then abandoned the trees and groves and went once more to the riverbank.
Intending to cultivate the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) through his original practice,
he again heard the sound of fish and turtles turning about in the water,
and thus was unable to cultivate them.
He then ascended the mountain and reflected thus:
"The reason I have now fallen away from the wholesome dharmas is entirely due to sentient beings.
Whatever wholesome dharmas and pure practices I possess—"
"May I become such a being that I am able to harm all beings seen in the world— those who move on land, those who fly, and those who dwell in water—
so that none may escape me."
Having made this evil vow, he saw himself departing from the desire realm of the eighth stage to be born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He opened the gate of ambrosia, the garden of tranquility.
For eighty thousand kalpas he dwelt in the bliss of seclusion;
once his karmic retribution was exhausted,
he returned to this world to the Tāpasa-vana Dharmāraṇya hermitage.
He became a winged tanuki,
with a body fifty yojanas wide and each of his two wings fifty yojanas wide.
Its body measures one hundred and fifty yojanas;
with this massive form, it slaughters beings of the air, water, and land,
none of whom can escape.
Upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, he was reborn in the Avīci Hell. [Excerpted from the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 33. 13.

Ti-pa-yan-na (Devadatta) gave rise to craving upon hearing the sound of the śi-ji (śṛgāla). 13. Devadatta gave rise to craving upon hearing the sound of the śi-ji. Thirteen: Before the Buddhas had appeared in the world...
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, used to go regularly to the hermitage of the seer Tīpayaṇa to listen to the Dharma.
On one occasion, as he was mounting his jewel-adorned chariot intending to visit the seer,
Śarabha thought to himself:
Now Śakra, having abandoned me to go to other celestial maidens,
immediately concealed his form and ascended his chariot;
unaware, he drew near to the place where the rishi was.
Looking back, he saw them and asked,
"For what reason have you come?"
"The immortal does not wish to see a woman with his own eyes;
you may return to the palace.
Sheizhi did not wish to go.
Śakra struck him with a lotus stalk.
Śepa apologized to Śakra with the soft and beautiful voice of a woman.
When the rishi heard this, [he was moved].
Desire and love arose, and his spiral locks fell away. The Ear-Consciousness then departed; [this concludes] the third volume of the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*. 14.

The Snow Mountain Seer and the Tiger Engage in Sexual Intercourse and Give Birth to Twelve Sons. 14. In the past, there was a seer on the Snow Mountains. The Snow Mountain Seer and the Tiger engaged in sexual intercourse and gave birth to twelve sons. Long ago, there was a seer on the Snow Mountains.
He was named Bhārgava;
though he practiced loving-kindness while subsisting on fruits and roots,
he was unable to eliminate the fetters of the various afflictions.
At that time, there was a tigress dwelling in that place.
She engaged in sexual intercourse with him and subsequently became pregnant.
When the months were fulfilled, she came to the hermitage and gave birth to twelve sons.
The rishi, out of compassion, took them up, bathed them, and nourished them.
The tigress mother, out of love and affection, suckled and raised them according to their needs.
The rishi gave each of them a name.
The first was named Kega;
the second, Bābhaga; and the third, Vṛka.
The fourth is named Siṃha;
the fifth is named Bhāra-bhāra;
the sixth is named Brahmadatta.
The seventh is named Pāda-bhājana;
the eighth is named Brāhmaṇa;
the ninth is named Subhakṣa.
Tenth is named Evil Nature;
eleventh is named Lion’s Burden;
twelfth is named Vigorous Striding.
At the age of seven, he was already able to eat roots, flowers, and fruits.
When both his parents passed away, the son’s heart was filled with grief and distress;
he looked up to heaven and wailed, having no one to turn to for refuge.
The tree deity said,
"Cease your wailing for now. You all should,
throughout the six periods of day and night, bathe yourselves with purity and, facing the void, worship with a sincere heart and seek the compassion of Brahmā."
Brahmā heard this and said:
"I shall go to your place and destroy your darkness of ignorance;
I shall bestow upon you the light of wisdom and shall make offerings to you."
He practiced according to the teachings for twelve years.
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra Devendra, and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
together with their countless retinues, all came to make offerings.
He addressed the youths, saying,
"For what reason have you practiced diligent asceticism for twelve years?
What do you seek by making offerings to me?"
They all said:
"We only pray that the Great Being will bestow wisdom upon us.
Now, my recognition of the various karmas of good and evil, as well as the experiences of suffering and pleasure, is derived from the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*.

There was a rishi named Bāhuka who had attained the five supernormal powers.
At that time, he was honored and served by the king.
Possessing supernatural powers, he traveled back and forth between the royal palace by means of flight.
The king then made offerings to him, providing all things necessary for his peace and comfort.
The king personally held the seer’s matted hair in his hands as he walked,
and with his own hands he served a hundred varieties of food and drink,
continuing this for many years.
At that time, the king was occupied with state affairs.
The king had a daughter who was so beautiful and exquisite that she was a rarity in the world.
The king held her in great esteem.
Before the girl had even stepped out the door,
the king said to her:
"I serve this seer with utmost devotion and dare not let my mind stray from him.
Now that I am traveling far away, you must provide for him;
treat him as if I were still here."
Then that rishi descended from the air into the palace;
when the princess saw him coming,
she received him with her hands and seated him upon a throne.
Upon touching the woman's body, which was soft and supple, he immediately conceived a lustful thought.
As his craving and desire flourished, he instantly lost his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
Although he contemplated and practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) in order to recover that power, he was unable to regain it.
He walked out of the palace.
At that time, countless people all gathered to watch him.
When the King had finished his walk and returned, he heard that [the prince] had fallen into the bonds of affection and could no longer fly.
At night, the king went alone and in secret to the palace;
he went to see the seer, bowed his head at his feet,
and spoke in verse:
"I have heard that the Great Brahmāṇa was originally different [from others];
how did he come to practice eating and drinking? By what cause did he cultivate lustful desires?
Vajrapāṇi replied:
"I am indeed such, O Great King, as the Noble One has heard. The King said:
"Even if one should give rise to a mind of desire, one cannot subdue the fundamental nature.
Bala-kṣepa replied: "It is so."
Upon hearing the King’s words today, he immediately renounced his sensual desires;
the rishi felt shame and remorse, chastising himself until he regained his supernormal powers through diligent effort throughout the night.
The seer at that time was Śāriputra;
the king at that time was myself. This is from the *Sūtra on the Seer Phalguna*. 16.

The One-Horned Seer, Whose Mind Was Stained by Worldly Desire, Was Mounted by a Courtesan. Regarding the One-Horned Seer, whose mind was stained by worldly desire, and who was mounted by a courtesan: At that time, there was a seer in the mountains of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
In the middle month of autumn,
while urinating into a washing basin,
he saw deer mating, and his lustful mind was immediately aroused.
The semen flowed into a pool, and a deer drank it.
Immediately she conceived;
when the months were full, she gave birth to a son who was largely like a human being.
He had a single horn on his head and his feet resembled those of a deer.
When it was time for the deer to give birth, she went before the hermitage of the rishi, gave birth to her offspring,
entrusted the child to the rishi, and departed.
When the rishi emerged and saw this fawn,
he reflected upon his past causes and conditions and recognized it as his own son;
he took it and raised it.
When he reached adulthood,
he applied himself diligently to his studies and mastered eighteen kinds of great sūtras.
Furthermore, he practiced seated meditation;
by cultivating the four immeasurable minds, he attained the five supernormal powers.
At one time, he went up a mountain.
It happened that it was raining heavily and the ground was slippery;
his feet were unsteady and he stumbled, injuring his foot.
He then became greatly enraged.
He cast a spell to prevent rain;
through the spiritual power of the rishi, all the nāgas, spirits, and deities likewise brought about drought.
Because it did not rain, the grain and fruits failed to grow.
The people were impoverished and had no further means of survival.
King Bārāṇasī was filled with sorrow and distress,
and he commanded his high officials to assemble for a council regarding the matter of rain.
The wise ones deliberated, saying:
"I have heard that there was once a one-horned rishi who,
having injured his foot while climbing a mountain, uttered a curse in anger so that it would not rain for twelve years."
The king immediately issued a proclamation:
"If there is anyone who can cause the seer to lose his five supernatural powers and become my subject,
I shall grant him half of the kingdom to rule."
In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a courtesan named Śāntā,
who was both beautiful and immensely wealthy.
She came to respond to the king's recruitment.
The courtesan said, "If this is the man, I can ruin him. Having spoken these words, she departed.
He took a golden tray and filled it with fine treasures,
then said to the king,
"I shall ride upon this immortal (ṛṣi) and come."
The courtesan immediately sought five hundred carriages to carry five hundred beautiful women,
and five hundred deer-drawn carts laden with various kinds of joy-pills.
They all blended various medicinal herbs together and took diverse,
potent, fine wines; their complexions and flavors were like water,
and they wore garments of tree bark as they moved among the forest trees.
He resembled a seer;
he built a grass hut beside a seer’s dwelling and lived there.
A seer, while wandering, saw him at one corner of the hut.
The women all brought forth exquisite flowers and wonderful incense to make offerings to the rishi.
The rishi was filled with joy.
The women addressed the rishi with gracious words and respectful greetings.
Upon entering the chamber, he sat upon well-prepared bedding;
he provided fine, pure wine as his ritual water and offered *mṛdvīkā* fruits as his melons.
Having finished eating and drinking his fill,
he said to the women,
"Since my birth, I have never before obtained such fruit and water as this."
The women said,
"Because we practiced virtue with single-minded devotion, the devas granted us this wish, and we have obtained this fruit-water.
The rishi asked the women:
"Why is your complexion so full and radiant?
He replied,
"I constantly eat these excellent fruits and drink this fine water."
The seer said,
"Why do you not dwell here? He replied:
He remained there for a while.
The woman called him to bathe together;
when her hand, soft as silk, touched him, he was moved.
His mind being moved, he immediately fell into lustful desire and lost his supernatural powers.
Heaven then sent down a great rain for seven days and seven nights.
He caused them to enjoy food and drink for seven days until the wine and provisions were all exhausted; thereafter,
they subsisted on water, wood, and fruit.
The flavor was not delicious,
so he asked for the previous portion.
The man replied, "It has already been finished."
"Now we shall gather it together;
there is a place not far from here where it can be obtained.
The rishi said:
"As you wish.
Not far from leaving the city together,
the girl lay down on the ground and said:
"I am utterly unable to proceed any further," he said.
The rishi replied,
"If you cannot go, then mount upon my neck."
"I shall carry you.
The woman first sent a messenger to inform the king:
"Your Majesty may come out for a moment to observe my skill and wisdom."
The king saw this and asked,
"By what means was this accomplished?
The woman replied, "Through the power of skillful means, nothing further can be done."
He was made to dwell within the city, where he was provided with excellent offerings and shown great respect;

The Account of the Dreams of the Brahmachari Ratnasāgara. Regarding the account of the dreams of the Brahmachari Ratnasāgara: there was a Brahmachari named Ratnasāgara.
He addressed the Buddha,
saying, "I pray that the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus will accept my offerings of the four requisites for a full seven years."
The Tathāgata granted his permission.
Later, the brahmin thought to himself:
"I have now caused hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta."
However, I do not know what the aspiration of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is;
whether it be that of a human king, a celestial king, a śrāvaka, or a pratyekabuddha,
it is for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
If I shall certainly attain the path of Buddhahood in a future life,
then while I am lying down at night, the various devas, Māras, Brahmās, and World-Honored Buddhas shall manifest themselves to me in a dream;
within my sleep, I shall see a brilliant light.
He immediately beheld the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions;
each of them reached out from afar and bestowed a lotus flower upon him.
These flowers were subtle and wondrous, and upon each flower pedestal he saw the image of a solar disc.
Upon each solar disk was a canopy made of the seven precious gems;
from each solar disk sixty billion rays of light issued forth,
all of which entered the mouth of the brahmin.
He saw his own light filling a thousand yojanas,
as pure as a clear mirror, and within his abdomen he saw sixty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.
He sat cross-legged in meditative absorption upon a lotus flower.
Furthermore, he saw the filaments of the sun surrounding his body,
and from within the various flowers, various musical instruments emerged.
Furthermore, he saw that king with blood flowing and staining his body as he ran about in the four directions;
his face and head resembled those of a pig, and he was devouring various kinds of insects.
Sitting beneath an eranda tree,
immeasurable sentient beings came to devour his body until only a skeleton remained.
Taking birth again and again is likewise thus. Furthermore,
he saw various princes who had manifested faces like those of pigs, elephants, water buffaloes, lions, foxes, wolves, tigers, leopards, and monkeys.
With their bodies stained with blood, they all devour sentient beings.
Seated beneath an eranda tree,
there were again immeasurable sentient beings.
They come to devour his body until the skeletal remains are separated;
the repeated taking of bodies is likewise thus.
Or one may see a prince adorned with a necklace of sumana flowers,
riding in a small, dilapidated carriage drawn by water buffaloes.
He galloped southward along an improper path.
Then he saw the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, and Mahābrahmā approaching his location,
and they addressed the brahmin, saying:
"Of all the lotuses now surrounding you on every side,
you should first take one flower and give it to the Wheel-turning King,
and give one flower to each of the princes."
The remaining flowers and the minor kings were then given to your son,
and they were all distributed to the other people as well.
Suddenly he awoke and recalled all the things he had seen in his dream;
he understood that the noble king’s aspiration was base and that he took pleasure in birth and death.
Furthermore, knowing that these princes have resolved their minds [on awakening],
yet seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas, I dreamt that they wore garlands made of sumanā flowers and rode ox-carts on an uneven path, galloping southward.
For what reason have I seen these Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, in my dream?
It is because I previously taught and exhorted immeasurable sentient beings within Jambudvīpa.
He resolved his mind on Bodhi in order to cause all beings to dwell securely in the three bases of merit.

He invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, and for seven full years he provided them with everything necessary for their well-being. This is from the *Sūtra of the Brahmacārin Ratnottara Inviting the Tathāgata*.
3. The Brahmin Sūṅkha Resolves His Grief upon Hearing the Dharma. The Brahmin Sūṅkha resolves his grief upon hearing the Dharma. Third:

This is not merely a reversal of sorrow.
In the past, the land of Jambudvīpa had five rulers.

"Are you content?
