4. The Brahmin Māgandiya Takes His Daughter as a Wife for the Buddha. Regarding the Brahmin Māgandiya taking his daughter as a wife for the Buddha: Long ago, there was a Brahmin named Māgandiya.
A daughter was born who was exceptionally beautiful.
Although kings, crown princes, ministers, and elders came to request her hand in marriage, they could not obtain her.
She then beheld the Buddha’s golden body and its thirty-two marks.
He then thought to himself,
"I shall give my daughter to such a person as this," and upon returning home, he said to his wife:
"Now that I have obtained a son-in-law who surpasses my daughter," she thought,
and she immediately adorned her daughter with various precious necklaces and ornaments,
and led her out of the city.
The mother saw that the patterns on the Buddha’s footprint appeared clearly and distinctly,
and she said to her father,
"How can you know that one born from emptiness will ultimately never obtain a husband?"
The wife spoke in verse:
"The lustful man drags his heels; the angry man walks with toes curled;
the deluded man stumbles over the ground. These are the tracks of those who honor gods and humans."
The father said,
"Fools bring suffering because of women.
He then took his daughter to the place where the Buddha was.
Holding his arm with his left hand and a flask in his right,
he addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I now offer this woman to you as a wife."
When the woman saw the Buddha’s form, her lustful mind became fixated upon him,
and the fire of passion blazed within her heart.
The Buddha then spoke this verse:
I have seen the three daughters of Māra, yet I do not even desire illicit lust;
now, I would rather embrace excrement and urine. Even the touch of my feet is not permitted. [From] the *Chuyou jing* (Sūtra on the Departure from Meaning), Volume 5.

The Brahmin Who Lost His Son Begs Yama for Life, Then Visits the Buddha and Attains the Way. Long ago, there was a Brahmin who left home at a young age to study. He lost his son and went to the realm of King Yama to beg for his life. Having visited the Buddha, he attained the Way. (Part Five) In the past, there was a Brahmin who left home while still young to pursue his studies.
When he reached the age of sixty and was unable to attain the Way,
according to the Dharma, he should return home,
take a wife, and become a lay devotee (gṛhapati).
He gave birth to a son who was handsome and lovely;
when he reached the age of seven, he suddenly fell gravely ill.
When his life ended, a brahmin felt such compassion for him that he lay prostrate over the corpse until he fainted and then revived;
his kinsmen admonished and entreated him, forcibly taking the body away to perform the funeral rites and burying it outside the city.
The brahmin thought to himself,
"My weeping now will be of no benefit.
It would be better to go to King Yama and beg for my son's life."
Having bathed, observed the fast, and taken up flowers and incense,
he departed from his home and inquired of people wherever he went.
"Where is the realm governed by King Yama located?
He traveled forward for several thousand li until he reached a deep mountain.
There he saw various brahmins and questioned them as he had before.
He replied,
"What do you seek by asking about the realm governed by King Yama?
He answered:
"I have a son who recently passed away.
I wish to go to the abode of King Yama to beg for my son's life.
The Brahmin, pitying his foolishness, [spoke].
He then addressed him, saying:
"The realm where King Yama rules is not a place that can be reached by those who are still living.
I shall show you the way."
One should proceed from here westward for more than four hundred *li*.
There is a great river within which lies a city;
this is the city where the celestial deity halts while touring the world.
King Yama constantly inspects this city on the fourth day of every month; if you observe the fast and maintain the precepts when you go there, you will surely see him, and he will depart with joy.
Upon reaching the middle of that river, you will see a magnificent city with palaces and dwellings.
Just as in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
a brahmin went to the gate,
burned incense, stood on tiptoe, and offered prayers for a son.
King Yama commanded his gatekeeper to admit him.
The Brahmin addressed him, saying,
"I have recently fathered a son whom I wish to provide for my old age."
"He who raised me for seven years has recently passed away.
I only pray that Your Majesty will show mercy and grant alms to restore my son's life.
The King replied, "Very well."
"Your son is currently playing in the eastern garden;
go there yourself and bring him back.
He immediately went and saw his son.
While playing with the other children, he came forward, embraced him, and wept, saying:
"Day and night I have thought of you; eating and sleeping have been no pleasure to me."
"Do you not at all consider the hardships endured by your parents?
The child called out to him in opposition and rebuked him, saying, "You foolish, senile old man! You do not understand the principles of reason."
One who stays but for a brief moment is called a son;
do not speak much in vain—
it would be better to depart early.
"Now we already have our own parents here.
The brahmin departed in dejection, weeping,
and immediately thought to himself:
"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama knows the way of the transformations of human souls and spirits.
I shall go and question him.
He then returned to the Buddha's presence, prostrated himself, and paid homage.
He related the matter from beginning to end to the Buddha, saying,
"Truly, this is my son who refuses to return.
He calls me a foolish and senile old man."
To treat another as one's son for a mere moment while harboring no father-son affection at all—
by what cause is it so?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"You are truly deluded.
When a person dies, the spirit departs and immediately receives another form."
"Parents, wives, and children dwell together through the convergence of causes and conditions;
they are like guests who scatter upon rising.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin attained sudden and clear understanding, prostrated himself, and surrendered his person."
"I wish to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said, "Excellent.
His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the dharma robes were upon his body.
He immediately became a bhikṣu.
On that very seat, he attained the path of arhatship. [From] the *Dharmapada*, Chapter Four: "The Path of Practice. 6.
The Brahmin’s Deceitful Gift to a Bhikṣu: One Verse Capable of Consuming the Brahmin’s Deceitful Gift. Sixth: Once there was a brahmin.
Possessing wealth and learning, he did not believe in the Right Path.
Whenever he debated with śramaṇas, he was defeated;
every time he heard that śramaṇas consumed the offerings of the faithful, he could not bring himself to practice with diligence.
"After death, I shall be reborn as an ox or a horse to repay my debt to the donor's family.
He then secretly devised a plan to provide a meal,
intending to take [the reward] in a future life.
He was ordered to manage his livelihood.
By nature stingy and greedy, he suddenly went to a monastery.
There were five hundred practitioners in the monastery, and he invited them all.
He increased his reverence and prepared a sumptuous meal, surpassing that of others,
intending to obtain five hundred oxen and horses.
One of the senior monks had already attained the four paths and become an Arhat.
Knowing his thoughts, he then called the *karmadāna* and commanded the bhikṣus: "Everyone must concentrate their minds;
when one person recites a single verse, you shall all together pay him respectful homage."
The Elder said, "The debt has already been repaid in full;
you shall no longer obtain oxen or horses."
The brahmin was astonished and said, "This practitioner is divine and holy; he has anticipated my thoughts.
Thereupon, the Elder informed all the bhikṣus in detail.
Once you have received the food,
recite a single Dharma phrase with a mind of loving-kindness while mindful of the Path;
then you will be able to digest even Mount Sumeru.
"How much more so for this small meal!
The brahmin felt profound shame and remorse;
thereupon, [the Buddha] preached the Dharma for him, extensively expounding the essential meaning.

With his mind opened, he received the Way and immediately realized the traces of the Path; this is an essential matter from among the various sutras. 7. The Brahmin Offers Honey from His Alms Bowl to the Buddha;

the Food Does Not Diminish as He Gives to the Beings in the Water. Once upon a time, there was a Brahmin. [The Brahmin offered honey from his alms bowl to the Buddha; the food did not diminish as he gave it to the beings in the water. Seven. Once upon a time, there was a Brahmin.
Fearing that he might not see the Buddha, he stealthily entered another’s house.
The Great Sage, taking pity on him, appeared before his eyes;
though he wished to flee and hide, he was unable to move.
He came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for him, and joy arose in his heart.
Having taken refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha and received the precepts, he circumambulated the Buddha and departed.
He then took his alms-bowl, filled it to the brim with honey,
and holding it up with both hands, desired to offer it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"Take this bowl of honey and distribute it among the Saṃgha. Then,
with that single bowl of honey, both the Buddha and the Saṃgha were fully satisfied.
The bowl was full as before.
He immediately offered it back to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
He was caught in a vast, immeasurable current of great water.
The brahmin asked again why this was so,
and the Buddha said:
All the insects, snails, soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, fish, and turtles within the water were fully satisfied by its flavor.
Having received these instructions, the brahmin [departed].
The World-Honored One smiled joyfully, emitting rays of five-colored light.
Ascending as far as the Brahma Heaven, it universally illuminated the five realms of existence;
it then circled the body three times and conferred the prediction of enlightenment upon the Bodhisattva, its light entering through the crown of his head.
When bestowing the prediction of enlightenment for a Pratyekabuddha, the light enters through the mouth;
when bestowing the prediction of enlightenment for a Śrāvaka, the light enters through the arms;
when teaching the blessings of rebirth in the heavens, the light enters through the navel.
It is taught that when bestowing a human body, the light enters through the knees;
when teaching of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, the light enters through the feet.
Ānanda rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
The Buddha does not smile without cause;
when he smiles, there is always a meaning behind it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see the brahmin offering honey to the Buddha?
He replied, "Indeed I do.
"This brahmin, in a future age..."
For twenty kalpas he will not fall into the evil realms;
after twenty kalpas have passed, he shall attain the state of a pratyekabuddha named Madhuvṛṣṭi.
The bhikṣus said,
"By means of a single bowl of honey given to this brahmin, he has attained the state of a pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
Thus, it was not only in this present life that the brahmin was so;
in his past lives as well, it was likewise.
In the past, there was a brahmin who dwelt in solitude and silence.
He saw a divine seer.
Someone said, "This seer here is excellent, auspicious, and beyond compare."
"You should go and receive [the teaching].
Someone replied, "What is the use of seeing this? It is merely a means for nourishing the body."
There was a rishi possessing the five supernatural powers who,
perceiving what [the king] was thinking in his mind,
immediately leaped from among the trees and rose into the air.
He stood before the man;
seeing him, he leaped for joy and immediately filled his bowl to the brim with honey and offered it to him.
Having accepted it, the rishi flew into the void.
By virtue of this merit from the offering, he later became a king named Madhuvṛddha.
"Ruling the country according to the True Dharma, he passed away and was reborn in heaven.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"If you wish to know who the rishi with the five supernormal powers was at that time,"
I was that very person at that time;
the brahmin of that time is now this brahmin.
At that time, he bestowed honey as a gift, bestowing upon the devas and humans the merit thereof.
Because of this, he also made offerings to the Buddha in the present life;
later, he attained the state of a pratyekabuddha and produced the *Madhuvāsiṣṭhasūtra*. 8.

The Brahmin who traveled far to study encountered five who were ungrateful. There was once a Brahmin who traveled far to study and encountered five [people] who lacked reciprocity. There were eight such Brahmins.
While in Rājagṛha,
he heard that the people of Śrāvastī were largely filial and supportive, upholding the sutras, practicing the Way, and making offerings to the Triple Gem.
Desiring to pursue his studies, he went there at once to seek instruction.
Not far from his native land,
he saw two father and son plowing the earth and sowing seeds.
At that moment, a venomous snake emerged and bit the son to death.
The father continued plowing without ceasing and did not look back.
When the brahmin questioned him,
the plowman asked in return.
"Where have you come from?
The brahmin replied,
"I have come from Rājagṛha."
"Having heard that the people of this country are largely filial and devoted to serving the Triple Gem, I have come here to study. Who was your father?
He replied, "He was my son."
He asked, "Why does this young man not grieve, but instead returns to plowing and planting?
The man replied, "In the life of man there is death; in the formation of things there is decay."
It is not something that can be remedied by grief, lamentation, or weeping.
Even if you do not eat or drink, what benefit would that bring to the deceased?
When you enter the city, please go to my house and speak on my behalf.
"My son has already died;
do not bring food for two people anymore.
The brahmin thought to himself in secret:
People lack constancy;
though her child lay dead upon the ground,
she remained calm and free from grief, returning instead to seek food.
He entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to the house of a farmer.
Seeing the mother of a dead child, he said to her:
"Your son has already died."
The father said,
"Bring only the food provisions for one person.
His wife said:
Just as a traveler comes to stay,
arriving without difficulty and departing without lingering,
so it is with this child.
Life after life one comes of one's own accord, and death likewise departs alone;
it is not within my power to advance or retreat.
One follows according to one's original karma, pursued by the destiny of one's rebirth.
He spoke again to his elder sister,
and she too gave him a parable on impermanence.
Then the brahmin spoke to his wife.
Her husband had already died.
The wife spoke a parable for the brahmin and also addressed the servant boy.
"The master has already died," the servant said, "and he also spoke this parable.
When the brahmin heard this, [he was moved].
My heart was moved and my vision grew dim, such that I could not distinguish east from west.
Hearing that in this country people practice filial piety and serve the Triple Gem, I have come here to study;
yet, I have not yet cultivated any virtuous intent.
Seeing that there was no reciprocity and only the fruitless exhaustion of body and mind,
he asked the practitioner again, "Where is the Buddha?
The practitioner replied:
He was currently staying nearby at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The brahmin went straight to the Buddha’s location,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
He was filled with sorrow and distress,
and with his head bowed, remained silent without saying a word.
The Buddha knew his thoughts.
The Brahmin asked,
"Why are you not joyful?
The Brahmin replied:
"It is because my original vow has been thwarted that I am sorrowful.
The Buddha asked again,
"In what way?"
He answered with the facts as they were.
The Buddha said, "It is not so;
it is not as you have said."
These five persons are the most resilient;
knowing that life is impermanent and cannot be altered by grief,
they remain self-composed and thus free from sorrow.
Worldly people do not recognize impermanence;
they lament and weep, unable to sever their attachments.
It is like a person whose body has contracted a fever.
Unaware of their own state, they speak with bewildered delusion.
When the skilled physician gives them medicine,
their fever is immediately dispelled and cured, and they no longer speak falsely.
Worldly people are intoxicated by the fever of sorrow, grief, and delusion, unable to liberate themselves.
If they personally realize impermanence, they will no longer grieve,
just as one who has recovered from a fever.
"These five men are all capable of attaining realization through the Way.
Upon hearing these words, the brahmin immediately reproached himself:
"I am foolish and ignorant; I do not understand the Great Meaning."
Now, having heard the Buddha’s words, it was as if one born blind had regained their sight and seen light in the darkness.
He immediately received the five precepts, prostrated himself, and withdrew; thus ends the *Wu wu fan fu jing*.
9. Four Brahmin brothers pass away on the same day. Four Brahmin brothers pass away on the same day. (9) Four Brahmin brothers.
Each attained the five supernormal powers.
Seven days hence, their lives would all come to an end;
they then deliberated among themselves, saying:
By the power of the five supernatural faculties, they can overturn heaven and earth;
with their hands they can touch the sun and moon, move mountains, and arrest flowing rivers—
there is nothing they cannot do.
"It would be better indeed to be unable to avoid this confrontation with death.
Another person said,
"I shall enter the great ocean."
It does not appear above nor reach the bottom;
it dwells precisely in the middle.
How could the ghost of impermanence know my location?
One person said,
"I shall enter into Mount Sumeru and cause its exterior to merge back together so that no boundary appears."
"How could the ghost of impermanence know my whereabouts?
Another person said,
"I shall ascend lightly and hide within the void of space."
"The ghost of impermanence knows not where I dwell.
Another person said,
"I shall hide myself within the great marketplace."
"The Ghost of Impermanence seeks out one person at a time; why must he seek me?
Having finished this discussion, the four men took leave of the king together.
"Our remaining lifespan is but seven days.
We now wish to flee for our lives,
hoping to escape and return to visit our kin."
"May you alone continue to advance in virtue.
Having said this, they parted ways.
When the seven-day period had ended, each of them passed away.
It was like fruit ripening and falling.
The market supervisor informed the king:
"A certain brahmin has suddenly died in the marketplace."
The king then awoke and said,
"Of the four men who avoided confrontation, one has already died;
how can the remaining three possibly escape alone?"
The king immediately prepared his carriage and went to where the Buddha was.
Having paid homage, he withdrew to sit at one side and said:
"Recently there was a brahmin..."
The four brothers each attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Knowing their lives were coming to an end, they all fled together.
I wonder whether you can now escape this fate?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"There are four things with which a person cannot be separated.
First, while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one must inevitably undergo rebirth."
Second, those who are born cannot avoid aging;
third, those who age cannot avoid illness;
fourth, those who are ill cannot avoid death. (From the *Dharmapada*, Volume Three).

10. The Brahmin Abandons His Handsome Wife on a Tree for a Lowly Slave Girl; Regret Is of No Avail. There was a lay follower of pure faith who abandoned his handsome wife on a tree out of attachment to a lowly slave girl; he later regretted this, but it was of no avail. This is the tenth [case].
His wife was upright and possessed peerless majesty;
her eloquence and skill in speech were such that she was respected by all.
Yet her husband did not hold her in high regard, nor did he take pleasure in seeing her.
She instead showed affection toward her servants.
When the wife perceived her husband's true feelings, she said to him:
"You do not rejoice in me;
I wish to be permitted to leave the household life.
Her husband then granted her permission.
She immediately left the household life to become a bhikṣuṇī.
Practicing with diligence day and night,
before long she attained the state of an arhat.
Subsequently, when the woman whom the lay devotee (upāsaka) revered passed away,
the lay devotee called for the bhikṣuṇī to return [to him],
but she resolutely refused.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the Buddha,
recounting the matter from beginning to end.
The Buddha said:
In a previous life, this lay devotee already insulted and humiliated this person of virtue.
This woman possesses extraordinary resolve,
yet this man has constantly sought to corrupt and disrupt her.
Having already entered the Great Path, he wished to destroy it again,
but he was unable to do so.
The Buddha said:
In a past age, there was a brahmin woman named Padmā,
whose beauty was peerless in the world.
The brahmin was displeased;
he had a beloved maidservant,
and he acted according to her words.
Leaving his wife in the mountains,
he climbed an *utpala* tree, selected the ripe fruits,
and discarded the unripe ones for her.
The wife asked,
"Why do you alone eat the ripe fruits while discarding the unripe ones for others?"
The husband said,
"You may climb the tree.
The wife immediately climbed the tree.
He took thorns and brambles and surrounded the tree on all four sides,
intending to prevent the man from descending even if he were to die;
at that time, the king was out hunting.
Seeing that the woman was of exquisite beauty, he immediately asked her, "Who are you?"
The wife related the matter from beginning to end.
The king thought to himself:
"This brahmin is foolish and ignorant; he is no man at all."
He immediately cleared away the thorns and briars,
loaded her onto a carriage, and returned to the palace where he established her as his queen.
She possessed many artistic skills and was peerless in wisdom and eloquence.
Furthermore, she was skilled at the game of *chūbó*.
Women from far and near came to play with her, yet the Queen always emerged victorious; none were able to match her.
The brahmin was skilled at games of chance and board games;
hearing from afar that the queen had won,
he thought to himself:
"This is my former wife; she is no other person.
She intends to go before the King to display her artistic skills.
When the Queen heard this, she recognized from the appearance of the brahmin that he was indeed her former husband.
The King revealed it to him.
From afar, he tested him with a game of dice.
The Queen then answered in verse:
The brahmin felt shame and resentment in his heart;
he immediately reproached himself, but his remorse came too late to avail him.
The brahmin of that time was none other than this present lay devotee.
The wife at that time was none other than his present wife;
the king of that country was myself. [From the *Fufu jing* (Sūtra on the Husband and Wife)]. 11.
The Brahmin Couple Who Lost Their Lives While Gathering Flowers: The Buddha Explains Their Past Deeds. There was once a Brahmin whose wealth was immeasurable.
He had an only son, twenty years of age,
who had recently taken a wife;
it had not yet been seven days.
In the aforementioned three months of spring,
the husband and wife went together to the rear garden to play.
There was a pear tree there, tall and large, with beautiful blossoms.
The wife desired to obtain it, but there was no one to gather it for her.
Knowing his wife's intention, the husband immediately climbed the tree and plucked a single flower.
Furthermore, he desired two more;
as he climbed the tree, a branch broke and he fell to the ground, dying.
Both the large and small [members of the retinue] rushed in haste toward the place where their child was.
He cried out to heaven and wailed, collapsing and then reviving;
his countless kinsmen all shared in his grief.
Hearing of it, their hearts were wounded; seeing him, they were filled with sorrow.
The parents lamented to Heaven, saying that it did not protect them;
once the funeral rites were completed,
they returned home, weeping so profusely that they could not restrain themselves.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One,
out of compassion for their ignorance, went to inquire after them.
Both the elder and the younger saw the Buddha.
Filled with grief, he related his hardships in detail.
The Buddha said to the elder, "Cease your lamentation and listen to the Dharma: all things are impermanent and cannot be preserved for long."
"Once born, there is death; merit and demerit follow one another.
This child has been weeping for him in three places;
his grief and despair are so overwhelming that they are difficult to endure."
"In the end, whose child is one?
Who is truly a kinsman?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
Life is like fruit upon a flower, ever fearing it will fall;
all that is born possesses suffering—who can attain immortality?
From the beginning one delights in desire, yet through lust one enters into this fragile existence.
Receiving a physical form, life is like a flash of lightning; day and night it flows on, difficult to stop.
This body is a thing destined for death, yet the spirit is formless.
Through the laws of karma, it causes the dead to be born again; thus, neither sin nor merit can ever perish.
"From beginning to end, this is not for a single lifetime;
following from ignorance and craving for a long time, one creates for oneself suffering and pleasure. When the body dies, the spirit does not perish.
Upon hearing these verses, the elder understood their meaning and forgot his grief.
Kneeling for a long time, he addressed the Buddha:
"What transgressions or offenses did this child commit in his past lives,
that such a full and magnificent lifespan should have been cut short by an untimely death?"
"I only pray that you will explain the offenses committed in my past conduct.
The Buddha said,
"In the past, there was a young child."
Holding a bow and arrows, he entered the divine tree to play.
Nearby, three men were watching the sparrows in the tree;
the boy wished to shoot them.
The three men urged him, saying,
"If you can hit the mark, you will be hailed by the world as a hero.
The boy, pleased with the prospect, drew his bow and shot at it.
The sparrow died immediately.
The three men laughed together, rejoiced at having helped it, and each departed on their own way.
Thus they passed through countless kalpas of birth and death.
Wherever they encounter one another and assemble together, they receive their retribution.
Of those three people, one possesses merit and is now in the heavens;
another has been born in the ocean as a transformation-born dragon king.
The one person today is the elder himself.
This child was previously born in the heavens as a son of a deva;
when his life there ended, he descended to become the elder’s son.
Falling from the tree, his life ended, and he was immediately reborn in the ocean as a son of the nāgas born by transformation.
On the very day of his birth, the King of the Garuḍas seized him to devour him.
Today, the lamentation and weeping in these three places—how can it even be described?
Because they had rejoiced in his assistance in a previous life, these three people repaid him with weeping and tears. [From] the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Five, Chapter 12:
"The Brahmin Śilabhadra Kills a Woman and Slanders the Buddha. Chapter Twelve: At that time, the king, ministers, and people of Śrāvastī—
He honored and made fourfold offerings to the World-Honored One,
abandoning the brahmin.
The brahmins deliberated together.
I shall seek out a beautiful woman, kill her, and bury her among the trees,
so that Gautama’s evil reputation may spread far and wide,
and he may suffer the consequences for how he treated me.
They then went together and urgently instructed the woman Hǎoshǒu, saying,
"From this day forward, you must go to the Buddha morning and evening so that the myriad people may see and know of it.
The young girl accepted their instructions.
He then killed him and buried him among the trees.
The brahmin then gathered his followers and went to the gate of the royal palace,
crying out in grievance and lamentation.
Among those women, I shall become one who is uniquely and most beautiful,
with a flower-like complexion peerless in the world, whose place of birth and death is unknown.
The king asked him,
"Where do you usually go?
He replied:
"Let us go to the presence of Gautama.
The king said,
"One should seek it from him."
The messenger arrived at the Jeta Grove,
exhumed the woman's corpse, placed it upon a bed,
and went through the streets proclaiming his grievances.
The śramaṇa Gautama always proclaims that his virtue of precepts is vast, universal,
and unsurpassed; how can he now privately consort with a woman and furthermore kill her to conceal it?
"What kind of Dharma and precepts do they have?
At that time, as the bhikṣus entered the city to beg for alms,
the people reviled them, saying:
Such are the offenses committed by these śramaṇas;
they ought to receive food and clothing.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu took an empty vessel and went out of the city.
He returned and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu,
"I shall not have been subjected to this slander for more than seven days."
At that time, the daughter of Yama heard within the city that the bhikṣus had returned with empty bowls after seeking alms;
she went to where the Buddha was and prostrated herself, touching her head to the ground in salutation.
With palms joined, he said to the Buddha,
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept a meal at my home for seven days.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Enter the city with the assembly of monks through the streets and alleys,
and speak these verses, saying:"
Constantly deceiving and falling into perverted darkness, one speaks of committing acts against the body yet does not incur grave offenses;
through dark conduct, one must inevitably experience sorrow and suffering for oneself.
At this time, Yama [prepared] a meal for the Buddha and the Sangha. (From the *Yizu jing*, Scroll One).
*Jinglü yìxiàng*, Fascicle 40; *Jinglü yìxiàng*, Fascicle 41:
Section on Brahmins, compiled by the Liang dynasty śramaṇas Sengmin, Baochang, and others.
3. Section on Brāhmaṇas (41) I. Dhanika’s Body Incurs Various Sins II. Agnidatta, while in the womb, enables his mother to engage in debate III.
Kevaddha pledges his body as collateral for money to provide a meal for the Buddha and the Sangha; Śakra assists him, reaching even to the King IV.
An old beggar brāhmaṇa recites a verse of the Buddha; his son returns to provide him with offerings.
1. Sañjaya, who learned archery and obtained a wife; 2. Five brāhmaṇas who offered their daughter in marriage as a gift to the Buddha and received a prediction of their future enlightenment;

3. Six brāhmaṇas who offered cakes to the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and attained the Way; 4. The brāhmaṇa Udraka Rāmaputra, who became angry and lost his disciples, was reborn as a malevolent dragon and was subsequently subdued by the Buddha;
5. A brāhmaṇa who entered meditative absorption for more than three hundred years; 6. A brāhmaṇa... [text fragment].
The Brahmin’s daughter-in-law had faith and saw the retribution that followed: eleven Brahmins understood the Buddha’s intent;
ten Brahmins observed the one-day fast (upoṣadha) incompletely and were reborn as tree spirits able to produce food and drink to provide for hungry beings;
twelve Brahmins swallowed gold coins as their sustenance, and when their bodies perished, people took them [as relics] to perform meritorious acts, whereby they immediately attained [rebirth].
13. The Path of the Stream-Enterer (*Srotāpanna*): A Brahmin gives birth to a beautiful daughter; the Buddha says she is not pleasing. 14. The Fire-Garlanded One (*Jvālāmālī*):
He forms a virtuous friendship with a potter’s son, and they together encourage one another in faith. 15. The Brahmin’s Wife: She serves the Buddha and is troubled by her husband;
she throws herself into a river which then dries up, whereupon her husband finally awakens to the truth. 16. 1. Dhanika: He personally attains all [merits].
Regarding the body of the sinner Dāniṣṭha obtaining various punishments:
within the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a brahmin named Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja;
his wife was hideous and ugly, with both eyes a piercing blue.
The seven daughters had no sons.
She was a poor woman and a destitute wife, her appearance wretched;
she would scold others and, when women came to beg from her, she would glare at them with tears streaming down her face.
In a field where the grain was ripe, he borrowed an ox from another and led it to trample the crops in a marsh; having lost it there,
the brahmin sat down and reflected to himself.
"What sin have I committed that I am so tormented by my wife and have also lost another's cow?
Exhausted from searching, I happened upon this forest."
Encountering the Tathāgata,
he observed him and gave rise to this thought:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is now most peaceful and happy."
Free from the afflictions of selfhood,
the Buddha, knowing his mind,
spoke to him, saying:
"It is as you have thought," the Buddha told him.
"Do you wish to leave the household life?"
He then addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One,
it would be most fitting for you to grant my humble wish. The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu! As he spoke,
his hair and beard fell away of their own accord,
and the garments he wore were transformed into saffron robes.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him,
and he attained the state of an Arhat.
The Buddha then said to Ānanda:
In the past, there was a king named Aparājitamukha (in the language of Liang, "Upright"),
who transformed sentient beings through the Way.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Dhanika whose family was destitute and poor,
possessing only a small amount of ripened grain.
He borrowed an ox, used it to till the fields, and drove it back to its owner.
Having forgotten to inform his host of the entrustment,
the owner, upon seeing it, claimed that its use was not yet finished.
Furthermore, the two parties did not settle their dispute and instead abandoned it.
The owner of the ox took Dhanika to the king to seek a definitive resolution.
As they were leaving, they encountered the king’s horse running loose.
He called out to Chandaka, saying, "Stop my horse.
Reaching down, he found a stone and took it up to hurl it;
it struck his foot and immediately broke it.
Next, he proceeded toward the water but did not know where to cross.
He encountered a woodworker who had a wooden adze clamped in his mouth; with his robe hitched up, he was about to leap across.
Then Dhanika asked that man, "Where can one cross?
The man replied immediately with the location.
As his mouth was already open, a wood-chopping axe fell into the water.
Oppressed by his creditors and further afflicted by hunger and thirst,
he begged for a little white wine from a tavern.
He went to bed to drink it,
unaware that a young child was lying beneath him;
he pressed down on the child's abdomen until it burst open.
He went to the side of a wall;
contemplating his fear of the sin,
he threw himself over the wall.
Below was a weaver; as soon as [the snake] fell upon him, he died.
Then the weaver’s son caught it again.
They then took him together with the crowd to the king.
At that time, the creditors brought him before the king, saying, "He killed my father."
At that time, the owner of the oxen came forward and said to the king,
"This man borrowed oxen from me;
they have not been returned, so please hand him over."
"What has been lost cannot be compensated for.
The king asked, "For what reason? Dhanika replied:
I truly borrowed the ox and returned it immediately;
the owner saw it as well.
Although he did not verbally hand it over, the ox was at his gate.
The king said to that man,
"Both of you are at fault;
it was because Dhanika would not give it to you."
"You shall have your tongue cut out,
because you saw the ox and did not restrain yourself;
you shall have your eyes gouged out."
That man addressed the king, saying, "I beg you to spare this ox; I take no pleasure in gouging out its eyes or cutting off its tongue.
The king immediately granted permission for a reconciliation.
The groom spoke again, "He,
being devoid of the Way, broke my horse's leg.
The King then asked:
"This royal horse has suddenly broken its leg.
He knelt and addressed the king, saying,
"A creditor has brought me here along the road."
That man called out to me to stop the king’s horse;
I reached down, picked up a stone, and threw it,
but by mistake, I broke the horse’s leg.
The king said,
"Because you called out to him, your tongue shall be cut off;
because he struck the horse, his hand shall be cut off."
The groom informed the king,
requesting that they each reconcile.
The carpenter then spoke:
"Dantika has lost my adze.
The king said to the carpenter,
"Because you called him by that name, you shall have your tongue cut off."
The proper etiquette for carrying objects is to use one's hands;
since you have been carrying it in your mouth,
two of your teeth shall be broken.
The carpenter said to the king, "Please spare me my adze and axe rather than inflict this punishment.
Then the mother of the wine-seller again pleaded with the king, "It is a wrongful execution; please spare my son."
Kneeling, he addressed the king, saying,
"I am oppressed by hunger and thirst;
I beg for a small amount of wine to drink."
"I did not expect to find a small child lying beneath my clothes.
May Your Majesty examine this.
The King addressed the woman.
"You run a tavern where many customers congregate;
why have you laid your child down in the seating area?
Both actions are at fault."
"Your son is already dead.
We shall give Dhanika to you as a son-in-law;
only when he has restored your son to life will we release him to go."
The woman bowed her head and said,
"Please allow us to reconcile;
I have no need for a husband."

Agnidatta, while in the womb, enabled his mother to engage in debate. Regarding "Agnidatta, while in the womb, enabled his mother to engage in debate": in the city of Pāṭaliputra, there was a Brahmin.

and the physiognomist replied:

The people said, "You have no money.

When you have searched everywhere and cannot obtain them,
return and tell your wife."
The wife spoke again, saying,
"Go to the house of the elder Vatsa-mitra and borrow from him."
He went at once to request a loan, saying, "I shall repay it in seven days;
if I do not return it, both my person and my wife shall become your slaves.

At that time, the cock was being cooked in an iron cauldron,

"You may manifest a high and spacious lecture hall so that the Buddha and the Sangha may sit and partake of their meal.

adorned with embroidered patterns.
Holding an incense burner in his hand, he burned various famous incenses,

when a gentle breeze stirred them, the sound of the bells was heard from afar.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha heard of this and questioned his ministers.
The ministers replied, saying:
This is because the brahmin Kukkuṭa cooked food for the Buddha and the Saṅgha in an iron cauldron using gośīrṣa sandalwood;
it was from this that such a fragrance arose.

"Who has done this now?

"I did not even know the name of this jewel, much less see it.

Now, having received the Buddha’s grace, I behold such a sight.

The king continued:

"Tomorrow, having accepted the invitation, we shall assemble here in this lecture hall.

Carrying a chicken head and exquisite garments,
and holding a fragrant incense burner in his hand,

"Now is the very time;
the meal is prepared."
"May you deign to grace us with your presence.
Surrounded by the Buddha and the Saṃgha, he proceeded to the lecture hall and took his seat; the monks then sat down in order.
At that time, the king, having prepared his carriage and surrounded by his ministers, went to the place where Kiki was.
There were various kinds of sweet foods and drinks, each numbering one hundred varieties.
He urged Kiki to offer this meal to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. This account of the people of Rājagṛha inviting the Buddha follows the sutra.
4. The Elder Brahmin Recites a Single Verse of the Buddha and His Sons Return to Serve Him. At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city of Śrāvastī.

elderly and of mature faculties,

That staff is most excellent; it is not for you to part from love and affection.
It protects me from the wicked bull and brings safety to dangerous ground;

"I now take this most excellent robe and go before the World-Honored One to inquire after his well-being and say to the Buddha:

The Sūtra on the Buddha Teaching the Elder Brahmin with Verses to Inspire Joy. 5.

7. A Brahmin Offers Cakes to the Buddha, Hears the Dharma, and Attains the Path. There was once a Brahmin who offered cakes to the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and attained the Path. This constitutes the seventh [account] of a Brahmin.
He asked his wife,
"There are provisions in our house;
I do not wish to provide offerings for the śramaṇa Gautama along with my companions."
The wife said, "There is.
He then took it with him and went there,
where he encountered the king, his ministers, kṣatriyas, brahmins, and the lords of eighteen great villages seated together.
The brahmin did not dare to step forward, thinking to himself:
"The Buddha is omniscient; he must surely know my thoughts."
The Buddha called out from afar to summon him and asked,
"What is in the vessel?
He replied, "It is a cake."
The Buddha said,
"You may distribute it to the community of monks.
He replied, "It is too little to reach everyone."
The Buddha said,
"If you simply give it to others,
even after one round, it will still not diminish."
Even after three repetitions, it was not yet diminished.
The Buddha knew his thoughts and preached the Dharma accordingly, whereby he attained the stage of Srotāpanna. (Cited from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 29; also cited from fascicle 6).
8. The Brahmin Bāḍhi, having lost his disciples through anger, was reborn as a malevolent dragon and was subdued by the Buddha. Regarding the eighth [case]: Long ago there was a Dragon King.
His name was Baladhi.
His disposition was violent and cruel;
he frequently brought death upon the people through wind, rain, thunderbolts, and hail.
Birds, beasts, and wriggling insects have died in incalculable numbers.
There were ten thousand venerable arhats who deliberated together:
"If one kills a single person, the retribution for falling into hell for an entire kalpa will not yet be exhausted."
Now this dragon harms sentient beings; having failed to reproach him before or after his transgressions,
I fear he will be difficult to transform.
"It would be fortunate indeed if we were to go together and advise him to desist.
At that time, the Buddha knew this and praised them, saying, "Excellent!"
At that time, ten thousand arhats set out together.
The dragon unleashed wind, rain, thunder, and lightning bolts.
The ten thousand people were struck with terror and prostrated themselves as they retreated.
At that time, the Buddha was on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Together with ten thousand bodhisattvas and ten thousand arhats, he went to the place where the dragon was.
The dragon then became enraged.
During violent winds, torrential rain, thunder, hail,
and lightning, he would discharge a single hailstone that would cover a wall forty zhang square.
If it reached the ground, it would sink four feet deep.
They intended to harm the Buddha and the Sangha of Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Arhats perceived the calamitous transformation wrought by the dragon.
Each harboring fear, they approached and took refuge near the Buddha.
When the dragon himself saw that the hailstones had transformed into flower canopies,
he thought to himself:
"I shall coil my body firmly into a ball forty zhang long,
intending to hurl it at the Buddha and the assembly of monks.
Immediately, he threw himself down, yet he was unable to reach his target.
Raising his head and opening his eyes, he gazed intently and beheld the Buddha;
suspecting him to be a most sublime and unsurpassed divine being,
the small dragons then all threw themselves down, yet remained utterly unmoved.
At that time, the Dragon King’s life came to an end and he was reborn as a deva;
the other minor dragons likewise all ended their lives and became sons of gods.
They all descended and stood by the side of the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you know from where this deva has come?
He replied, "I am not equal to that."
The Buddha said,
"Those nāgas who previously gave rise to malicious intent have now prostrated themselves upon the ground;

When his life ended, he was reborn in heaven; this is who that person was.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the deva and all the sons of heaven conceived the aspiration for supreme, impartial liberation.

9. A Brahmin Enters Samādhi for Over Three Hundred Years. Once upon a time, there was a Brahmin who took no pleasure in worldly affairs. He entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and remained therein for over three hundred years.
He lived in seclusion among the mountains, single-mindedly contemplating the Way.
He entered into meditative concentration for over three hundred years;
dust and soil covered his body, and grasses and trees grew upon his frame.
At the foot of the mountain lived several hundred Brahmins who maintained wives and children;
both young and old together gathered firewood by climbing trees,
breaking off withered branches and tree roots.
When the tree on the forehead of the Brahmin trembled,

Seeing the wood-gatherer, he questioned him.
"Who are you? He replied, "I am a brahmin."

He replied, "They are my wife and children."
The Brahmin laughed and said,

his parents were greatly incensed.
This means they broke into my house.

He intended to let all the people of the world see it together. At that time,

"I am also like this;
this old woman has obtained a great fruit of retribution."
This was due to the excellence of the Tathāgata’s field of merit.
At that time, the brahmin’s mind opened and his understanding was clarified; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he repented before the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the first fruit of the path.
He immediately raised his voice and addressed the multitude, saying, "The gate of ambrosia is open; why do you not come forth?
He then requested that the brahmins contribute gold coins as alms.
They welcomed the Buddha and made offerings to him.
The Brahmin king, together with his ministers and subjects, took refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma.
Both the men and women within the city attained pure faith. (From the *Puyao jing*, Scroll Five).

12. A Brahmin who observed the fast incompletely was reborn as a tree deity capable of producing food and drink to bestow upon hungry beings. A Brahmin who observed the fast incompletely was reborn as a tree deity capable of producing food and drink to bestow upon hungry beings. (12) Long ago, there was an elder named Sudatta.
He invited the Buddha and the Sangha to hold a grand assembly.
On the way, he encountered a man carrying a jar of curd;
seeing a Brahmin, he asked him to take it back for him.
Upon arriving, he saw the Buddha and the Sangha; filled with joy, he stayed there.
He listened to the sutras and observed the fast until evening, at which point he returned home.
His wife found this very strange.
He also did not eat until evening, when they pressured him to eat;
because he did not complete the rules of the fast, his life ended,
and his spirit was reborn as a tree deity in a great marsh in the country of Uttara.
At that time, there were five hundred scholars who intended to go to a divine pool at a triple shrine to bathe in hopes of attaining immortality; however,
their provisions were exhausted and they had no water or drink.
Having thus become exhausted,
they looked toward that tree from afar, imagining it to be a spring of water;
yet when they all reached the foot of the tree, there was no spring or water at all.
They were on the verge of great distress,
so they raised their voices together to implore the tree deity for mercy, praying for his protection of their lives.
The tree deity immediately manifested his upper body.
Raising his right hand,
he naturally produced food of a hundred flavors;
from his hand, he offered honeyed nectar, complete with every variety.
Everyone was fully satiated.
Then the five hundred people deliberated among themselves, saying,
"We wish to go to the divine pool to bathe and seek immortality."
"How could this majestic path of the immortals not be superior?
He then asked the tree deity,
"What meritorious deeds did you perform such that your holy virtue is thus?"
The tree spirit replied,
"In the past, I saw the Buddha at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī,
observing the eightfold fast."
Because he was defeated by his wife and failed to complete the ritual of the fast,
his spirit should have been reborn in heaven.
At that time, five hundred people immediately together received and upheld the precepts of the fasting ritual.
The subsequent attainment of the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) is the essential matter among all the sūtras.

13. The Brahmin Couple Who Swallowed Gold Coins for Food: Upon the Dissolution of Their Bodies, Others Took [the Remains] as Merit and Immediately Attained the Path. 13. Formerly, there was a Brahmin. [The couple] swallowed gold coins for food; when their bodies perished, others took [the remains] as an act of merit and immediately attained the traces of the Path (*mārga*). 13. Formerly, there was a Brahmin.
The husband and wife had no son,
yet their wealth was immeasurable.
As their lives were drawing to a close, they said to one another:
Each person should swallow coins as provisions for their journey.
According to the customs of that country,
when someone dies they are not buried, but merely placed beneath a tree.
Each swallowed fifty gold coins and died;
their bodies rotted away and the coins emerged.
A wise man of the country saw this as he was walking by.
Moved by compassion, he shed tears, grieving for his stinginess and greed;
he took [the man] to perform meritorious deeds on his behalf,
inviting the Buddha and the Sangha, and prepared offerings with all his heart.
Holding the food before the Buddha, they called out his name and made a prayer of aspiration.
At that moment, the stingy husband and wife,
who had been suffering the torments of hungry ghosts, were immediately reborn in the heavens.
He prepared a vast merit-making feast and invited the fourfold assembly.
At that time, those who had been reborn in the heavens, having attained the divine eye, knew that he was performing meritorious deeds;
they descended from heaven and transformed themselves into youths to assist the donor.
The Buddha said,
"This youth in the kitchen is a true donor. Upon his arrival,
I preached the Dharma to him, and he immediately attained the fruit of the Path."
The wise also attain the traces of the Path.
The assembly rejoiced, and all attained birth in heaven; this is from the *Sutra on the Fruit of the Vow for Overnight Abiding*.

14. The Brahmin Gives Birth to a Beautiful Daughter; the Buddha Says He Does Not Like It. Regarding the Brahmin who gave birth to a beautiful daughter, the Buddha said he did not like it. Fourteenth. During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was a certain Brahmin.
She gave birth to two daughters, both of whom were exceptionally beautiful. Consequently,
she hung up a piece of gold for ninety days to recruit anyone capable of making her daughters appear ugly.
He was about to give him gold,
yet in the end no one came forward to accept the offer. As he was approaching the Buddha’s dwelling, [he encountered the Buddha].
The Buddha then rebuked him, saying, "This woman is entirely ugly; she possesses not a single point of beauty.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This woman is beautiful, yet the Buddha says she is ugly.
How can she not be beautiful?
The Buddha said:
It is excellent when the human eye does not gaze upon forms;
the same applies to the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.
It is excellent when the body does not cling to tactile sensations.
Not stealing the wealth of others with one's hands and body is to be a good hand;
not committing such an act is what is truly excellent.
With the eyes one sees forms, with the ears one hears sounds, and with the nose one smells fragrances.
The body delights in smoothness and softness;
the hands delight in stealing the wealth of others.
Such things as these are all not good. (From the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*).

15. Agnidaṇḍin and Ghaṭīkāra as Spiritual Friends, Exhorting One Another in Faith. Agnidaṇḍin and Ghaṭīkāra as Spiritual Friends, Exhorting One Another in Faith. Fifteenth: Long ago, in the city of Kalandaka.
There was a brahmin who served as the royal astrologer and was the foremost in the kingdom.
He had a son whose head was naturally adorned with a wreath of fire;
he was named accordingly.
His physical form was upright and possessed thirty marks.
There was a potter named Nandipāla.
He had been a close friend with Agnikhandin since childhood, and they held mutual respect and affection for one another.
The potter’s son was diligent, courageous, compassionate, and filial;
he served his parents, both of whom were blind, without ever failing to provide for their needs.
Although he was a potter, his hands did not dig the earth;
he took only broken walls, crumbling riverbanks, and molehills to mix and fashion into vessels.
If there were any who wished to buy them, [he would sell them].
They placed grains, wheat, hemp, and beans on the ground and took the vessels;
from the outset, they did not haggle over prices,
nor did they accept gold, silver, wealth, or silk.
They merely took grain and rice to offer as sustenance.
The vihāra where Kāśyapa Tathāgata resided was not far from the city of Vārāṇasī.
Accompanied by twenty thousand great bhikṣus,
all of whom were arhats,
he spoke to Huhaiyu Huoman, saying:
"We have seen the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
Agniketu replied,
"What is the use of seeing this mendicant?"
"He is merely a shaven-headed man;
what Way does he possess?
The Buddha-way is difficult to attain."
This was repeated three times.
Then Huhui spoke again to Huiman, saying,
"Shall we go together to the water to bathe?"
Jyotiṣka replied, "So be it," and they went together to the water to bathe.
Rakṣita raised his right hand and pointed from afar, saying:
"The Kāśyapa Vihāra is not far from here;
we may go there together for a brief visit. Jvālāmālin replied:
Seeing this, Pāṭaliyā took hold of Aggikabhāradvāja’s robe and pulled him;
Aggikabhāradvāja stripped off his garment and fled.
Hugong then seized him by the head and pulled him along, saying, "Let us go together for one more visit to see the Buddha.
According to the laws of that country, it was forbidden to seize someone by the head; the penalty for such an act was execution by beheading.
Jvālamālī, overcome with fear, thought to himself:
"Will the potter seize my head and kill me? Rakṣita said:
"I shall die;
death will never let me go.
I must certainly cause you to see the Buddha."
Huo-man thought to himself,
"There must surely be some good news.
He then ordered this man to seize the other by force, even at the risk of death.
Jvalanaprabha said,
"Release my head and I will follow your son.
He then immediately tied his hair back and put on his robes.
They went together to visit Kāśyapa Buddha.
Hu-xi addressed the Buddha, saying,
"This Fire-Wreath was my close friend since childhood."
However, he did not yet recognize or place faith in the Triple Gem;
may the World-Honored One enlighten and transform him.
When the youth Agnikundala beheld the Buddha’s marks and signs of excellence, [he was moved].
He thought to himself:
"The marks and signs recorded in the scriptures are all present,
with the sole exception of two things."
At that time, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa extended his broad and long tongue to cover his face,
his uṣṇīṣa, and both ears seven times over.
He licked his head, withdrew his tongue into his mouth,
and emitted a radiant light that illuminated the great trichiliocosm,
eclipsing the brilliance of the sun and moon and extending as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
The light returned and circled his body seven times before entering through the crown of his head.
By the power of his supernormal faculties, he manifested the hidden organ of a stallion so that Fire-Wreath alone could see it.
Others did not see him;
only the youth Agniskandha beheld the Buddha’s thirty-two marks in their entirety.
He leaped for joy with such exuberance that he could not contain himself.
The Tathāgata Kāśyapa taught the bodhisattva’s abandonment of merit to the youth Agniśikha.
What is this abandonment of the bodhisattva’s merit?
The Dharma-body acts where there is no action;
it speaks where there is nothing to be spoken;
it contemplates where there is nothing to be contemplated.
"These are the three evil deeds of a bodhisattva.
Then, Jvālamālī prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said, "I now repent;
I pray that the Buddha will accept my confession."
"From this day forward, we shall not dare to transgress again.
This was repeated three times.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata accepted it by remaining silent.
The youth Jvālāmālin and the youth Raticitrasena both prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took their leave,
and departed. Jvālāmālin said:
"You have brought about loss rather than gain.
I take no pleasure in seeing your face,
nor do I take pleasure in hearing your name."
Rakṣita replied, "For what reason is this so?
Jvālamālī said:
"You have long ago heard the profound Dharma from the Buddha;
how can you remain at home? Hu Xi replied:
"My parents are aged and both are blind.
How could I leave home to practice the religious life while supporting my two parents?
If I were to leave home, my parents would surely pass away."
"For this reason, you are unable to leave the household life.
Fire-Top said to Joyful Protector,
"From Kāśyapa Buddha, I heard of the bodhisattva practice regarding the karmic retribution for the three evil conditions."
"I no longer take pleasure in the household life;
I wish to return from here to the Buddha's presence to seek ordination as a bhikṣu. Hu Xi replied:
"Excellent, Agniveśya!
Have you attained the power of contemplation?
You may now return at once."
The reason for this is that a Buddha is difficult to encounter in the world.
The youth Agniśikha then embraced and protected Huǐxǐ (Ratnākara),
circumambulated him three times, and with palms joined in reverence, said in thanks:
If I should happen to have any transgressions of body, speech, or mind that exceed yours,
I pray you will grant me your forgiveness.
If you would instruct me in the true and correct Great Way, I shall follow.
Thereupon, Jyotiṣka spoke these verses in praise:
"You are my virtuous friend, A Dharma-friend free from all craving.
You have guided me upon the right path; Such a friend is praised by the Buddhas."
Having spoken these verses,
he circumambulated Rucirā three times, returned to the vihāra,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Would you rather enter the Way and receive the full precepts?
He then ordained Huaman and conferred upon him the full ordination.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
At that time, the youth Agniśikha was none other than myself;
the father of Agniśikha was my present father, King Śuddhodana;
and it was Rāhula who repeatedly exhorted me to leave the household life.
This is to act as a false spiritual friend on the path.
Previously, I spoke ill of Guhagupta, saying,
"What kind of path does the shaven-headed śramaṇa Kāśyapa Buddha have?"
