He served the non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika),
while his wife served the Buddha.
She spoke to her husband, saying:
"Please allow me to become a servant to the Buddha,
hanging banners and canopies, burning incense, and lighting lamps.
Her husband would not permit it.
He then made a banner and hung it inside the house,
prostrating toward it morning and evening.
His son-in-law slaughtered oxen and sheep and summoned a ritual master to perform the rites.
The Master arrived at his gate and said,
"In your residence there are Buddhist banners and canopies;
I did not dare to enter."
He immediately went inside to question his wife;
having searched for it, he found the banner and beat his wife in anger.
The woman immediately threw herself into the river.
Her heart was so deeply moved that it touched the divine;
the river water receded until it was exhausted, and naturally, a canopy of the seven precious jewels appeared above her.
Upon seeing this auspicious omen, the son-in-law realized that the Buddha was worthy of veneration.
He immediately abandoned the non-Buddhist paths and devoted himself to the Great Dharma.
(Cited from the *Apadāna-sūtra*; *Jīnglǜ yìxiàng*, Scroll 41).
*Jīnglù yìxiàng*, Scroll 42, Section on Laypeople (*Gūshìbù*), Compiled by the Liang Dynasty Śramaṇas Sengmin, Baochang, and others. Section 1:
Laypeople (*Gūshìbù*) (42). [Case 1] Māṭhara: Increasing Wealth and Food, Hearing the Dharma and Attaining Enlightenment; [Case 2] Ugra: Seeing the Buddha.

1. One who was intoxicated became sober of his own accord; one who received the precepts gave away his wife to another; two who were fish gained wealth as a karmic condition; three—the *ācārya* brothers—obtained wealth through the Dharma and never lost it; four—the son of a lay devotee, Mahāmati—sought a bright pearl; five—Mṛḍaka’s wealth and food increased of their own accord, and upon hearing the Dharma, he attained realization. Mṛḍaka’s wealth and food increased of their own accord, and upon hearing the Dharma, he attained realization. First: In the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a great householder.
His name was Maṇḍavya; he followed the Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, possessed abundant treasures and great power, and provided for all people according to their every wish.
In his granary there was a hole as large as a chariot axle.
Grain emerged spontaneously.
His wife prepared rice from eight pecks and fed it to the soldiers of the four divisions and those who came from the four quarters.
Because he ate, it was never exhausted.
That son gave a thousand taels of gold to the four divisions of his army as well as to beggars from the four quarters;
it was spent according to their wishes and remained inexhaustible.
The daughter-in-law applied a single packet of incense [to the ground],
and the fourfold army as well as the beggars coming from the four directions were satisfied according to their desires;
yet the incense was not exhausted.
The slave plowed seven furrows each day with a single plow,
yielding an abundance of rice;
his maidservant used eight pecks of grain.
He provided food for the four divisions of his army and fodder for the horses;
the horses did not finish their rations.
Within the household, they all disputed over it, each speaking for themselves.
"I am Puṇyabala. Māndhātṛ approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and departed. From the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Four.
It says:
"By whose power?
The Buddha said,
"It is by the power of you all together."
Long ago, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a weaver.
The weaver had a wife and a son; the son also had a wife.
He had one male slave and one female slave.
At one time, they were eating together when a pratyekabuddha came to beg for food;
each wished to set aside their own portion to give it to him.
The Pratyekabuddha said,
"You have all already renounced with virtuous minds;
you may each take a small portion."
"It is not enough for you,
but it is sufficient for me.
They then departed together with him.
After the Pratyekabuddha had finished eating, he manifested various supernatural transformations in the air and then departed;
the weaver and his family members relinquished their lives.

Having been born in the heavens of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, he transmigrated through these seven realms in succession; with his remaining merit, he was then born here.
When Māndhātṛ heard this, he said:
He immediately invited the Buddha and the Sangha to practice boundless giving,
saying, "Whatever you require, at whatever time, and in whatever quantity, please take from me.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept.
He informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to accept it according to your own inclination."
Later, when the bhikṣus traveled and sought provisions,
they sent messengers carrying gold and silver to follow their route;
having acquired much wealth along the way, they brought it back to the elder.
The elder said:
"I have already relinquished it; it should not be taken back. This is from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* contains the full text for both cases. 2.

When Ugra saw the Buddha, his intoxication was naturally cleared away; he received the precepts and gave his wife as an offering to others. Regarding Ugra seeing the Buddha, his intoxication was naturally cleared away, he received the precepts, and gave his wife as an offering to others: Ugra was intoxicated and surrounded by court ladies.
In the Great Forest at Vaiśālī,
he saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting among the trees,
upright and sublime, with his faculties and mind stilled in meditative concentration.
His radiance was like a mass of gold.
Having seen this, his intoxication was dispelled;
he approached the World-Honored One and sat to one side.
The Buddha explained the Four Noble Truths for him;
having attained the state of fearlessness,
he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet.
"I take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Having become a lay follower (upāsaka), I shall observe the five precepts.
Returning to his own place, he addressed his kinsmen, saying:
"You should know this now:
I have received the precepts from the World-Honored One;
if you so desire, you may practice giving and cultivate merit."
"If you do not wish to stay, you may each return to your own kin;
I shall release you. Then the senior queen said:
The son followed the World-Honored One and received the precepts for the rest of his life.
There was a certain man who intended to take me as his wife;
at that time, the householder summoned that man.
Taking the lady’s right hand with his left hand and holding a golden water-pitcher, he said to that man:
"I give this most excellent lady to you as your wife."
That man was terrified, his hair standing on end,
and said to Ugga: "Householder, do you not wish to kill me?"
He replied, "No. I have practiced the holy life under the Buddha for as long as I live;
therefore, I give my principal wife to you."
"Never again shall he change his mind or regret [this]," as recorded in the ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
3. The Story of the Fish-Body Attaining Wealth. Regarding the story of the fish-body attaining wealth: Long ago, there was a family of great renown.
He was always fond of practicing generosity.
Later, he gave birth to a son who had no hands or feet.
His physical form resembled that of a fish;
he was named Yushen (Fish-Body).
After his parents passed away, he inherited and maintained the family estate.
While he was lying down in his chamber, there was no one to see him.
At that time, there was a strong man who looked up toward the King’s kitchen for food.
Constantly harboring a sense of hunger and deprivation,
he alone hauled sixteen carts of firewood to sell for his own sustenance.
Furthermore, he had never made offerings before;
he went to these four castes to seek what he lacked.
Then, in his fish body, he requested an audience with them.
He revealed his physical form.
The Malla thought to himself,
"Such is my strength!"
"It would be better for you to be a person without hands or feet than to go to where the Buddha is and ask about your doubts.
The Buddha said:
In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
the fish-bodied being and this king went together to offer food to the Buddha;
at that time, you were poor and assisted him in his service.
The fish, equipped with all its parts, followed the King's path and said to him:
"Today I have business; we cannot travel together."
The practitioner who, when his hands and feet were being severed without hesitation,
was none other than the present King;
the one who did not speak out was the fish.
At that time, the assistant was none other than yourself.
The strongman attained awakening and immediately became a śramaṇa.
Attaining the Path of Arhatship; excerpted from the *Old Pi-yu Jing* (Sūtra of Old Parables), Volume One.

4. The Brothers Śāri Obtain Wealth through the Dharma and Never Lose It. The Brothers Śāri Obtain Wealth through the Dharma and Never Lose It. Part Four: Formerly, within the city of Śilākṣa, there were three householders.
The first was named Jali;
the second, Pūrṇamāsa; and the third, Vāpana.
These three men were biological brothers.
They possessed abundant wealth, treasures, elephants, horses, and the seven precious gems. There was also a brahmin.
The Naga Erāvaṇa observed the fast,
hoping for wealth and status;
the Naga then manifested his form and spoke to the Brahmin.
"Why do you now undergo such diligent hardship?
Why do you abstain from grain, eliminate flavors, and observe these fasts here?
What is it that you seek?"
The brahmin said,
"I hope for great wealth.
The nāga said:
I have two names: the first is Ilāpatra,
and the second is Asaṃtuṣṭa-vitta.
"Since you are named 'Insatiable,' why do you still come to me for a request?
The brahmin said:
If he were not gracious, [the king] would immediately meet his end.
The dragon brought forth fine purple-gold to repay him.
At the city gate, there was a wealthy and eminent elder.
"He comes from India.
Give him gold, and he will seek wealth for you.
When the elder saw him, he spoke to him.
Conceal it so that no one sees it.
Inform his five relatives;
while they enjoy food and drink in merriment, he hides the gold within the treasury.
The miscellaneous goods within the storehouse all returned to the earth and went back to that dragon's treasury;
the same occurred for the wealth and possessions of the seven households on either side.
When the three householders heard this,
they said to one another,
"The wealth acquired by our three families through the Dharma has not been obtained unjustly."
He squandered what had been seized from the five families;
when the people of the country heard of this, they regarded it as mere boastful talk and gathered together at the three houses.
He asked the layman,
"When you offer wealth according to the Dharma so that it does not become excessive or lost,
what do you take as proof?"
At that time, the three householders each brought out ten *jin* of gold,
divided it into six portions,
and took it with them along with the people and the owners of the lost property from the seven households.
He went to Longquan (Dragon Spring) and cast gold into the water;
the water immediately surged and boiled like the broth in a cauldron.
The Dragon King was struck with alarm and fear.
He immediately dispatched the dragon girl to retrieve the gold and return it;
having offered his thanks, the messenger returned.
That which is obtained through the Dharma is accomplished through principle.
In the end, they will never be plundered by the five families who deceive them regarding their treasures and wealth, as described in the *Bimbasāra-sūtra* concerning the seven families. 5.
The Story of the Householder’s Son Mahāmati Seeking the Moon-Bright Jewel. Once upon a time, there was a kingdom.
The name of the land was Joyful and Free from Sorrow;
the king was named Vast Compassion and Pity.
In that kingdom there was a householder.
His name was Mahā-dāna;
his wife’s name was Caṇḍā,
and they had one son.
His physical form was upright and handsome, with few equals in the world;
upon falling to the ground, he spoke immediately,
making a vow and saying:
"I shall practice giving throughout the world to rescue and relieve those who are orphaned, solitary, or impoverished;
I shall provide for and protect them so that they may attain peace and security.
Because of this, his parents named him Da-i (Great Resolve).
Seeing his extraordinary appearance, which was unlike that of any human,
he feared he might be a deva, a nāga, or a spirit,
and wished to perform a divination to inquire about him.
He understood the general meaning of this and replied,
"I am a human being; I am not a deva, a nāga, a spirit, or a ghost."
I merely contemplate those among the people of the world who are in distress and poverty,
wishing only to protect and care for them.
This is the intent I express.
He then ceased speaking altogether.
When he reached the age of seventeen, he addressed his parents, saying,
"I wish to practice giving to those in suffering so that they may attain peace and security."
The parents thought to themselves,
"When our son was first born, he already made this vow," and they spoke to him, saying:
"My wealth is countless; I bestow it as I please, without restriction.
Da Yi replied, "Although my parents' wealth is vast, it is still insufficient for my needs."
"I shall only enter the sea to gather treasures in order to provide for and bestow upon the people of the world.
He spoke thus many times,
and his parents finally gave their consent.
In general, he traveled by sea to other countries.
In one of those countries, there was a brāhmaṇa whose wealth was immeasurable.
Seeing that Da-yi’s countenance was radiant and his features were upright and handsome,
he was greatly pleased with him and said,
"I hold you in high esteem."
"I now have a young daughter whom I wish to offer to you;
I pray that you will remain here. Da-yi replied:
"I have left my home to enter the sea to gather the seven treasures;
I do not yet dare to grant you permission.
You must first wait until I have returned."
Thereupon, they proceeded to gather treasures.
They immediately dispatched people to carry the treasures back to their own country.
Continuing further, they reached the edge of the sea to seek out extraordinary objects.
Suddenly he saw a great tree,
eighty yojanas in height and breadth;
Mahāmati then climbed the tree and from afar beheld a city of silver.
The palaces and halls were all made of white silver;
celestial maidens attended at their sides, and music arose spontaneously.
A venomous snake coiled itself three times around the city.
Upon seeing Da Yi, he raised his head; Da Yi thought to himself, "Those who are harmed by poison do so because they lack a benevolent heart.
He then sat down and reflected within himself.
In a short while, the snake immediately lowered its head and fell asleep.
Da Yi wished to enter the city,
so the gatekeeper went inside and informed the king, saying:
There was a worthy man outside who wished to see the king;
the king himself went out to meet him and spoke with joy.
"I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will remain here for a period of three months so that I may extend my offerings.
He replied, "I am traveling to gather treasures; it is not appropriate for me to stay long."
The king replied,
"I do not attend to state affairs;
I only wish for you to remain."
The king’s general intention was thus satisfied; he immediately provided clothing,
food and drink, music, and bedding.
When the ninety days had finally concluded,
Da Yi took his leave of the king, wishing to depart.
The king then took precious and rare seven-jeweled treasures, desiring to present them as gifts to him.
The general meaning is this:
"I do not make much use of these seven treasures;
however, I have heard that the King possesses a single 'bright moon' pearl."
He desired to seek it out.
The king said,
"I do not begrudge this pearl."
I only fear that the roads will be perilous and difficult to traverse on one's own.
The general meaning is this:
when fortune accompanies a person, they do not dread hardships and dangers.
The King said:
"This jewel has the power to follow its master's wishes for a distance of twenty li.
I shall provide for my disciple so that he may receive offerings."
It has surpassed even today.
With this thought, Da-yi accepted the pearl and departed.
Then, Da-yi continued forward and saw a golden city.
The palaces and halls were all made of gold;
the trees of the seven treasures produced music spontaneously,
and the celestial maidens serving as attendants were twice as numerous as before.
Furthermore, there were venomous snakes coiled six times around the city.
When the snakes saw Da Yi, they raised their heads to look at him;
he then sat down again and composed his mind.
The snake again lay low.
Da-yi (Mahāmati) desired to enter the city,
whereupon the gatekeeper immediately went in and informed the king.
The king immediately went out to meet him and invited him to come forward.
He spoke to him, saying, "Please stay;
for three months at once, I shall extend my offerings to you."
The general gist of the matter was thus concluded.
The King treated him as before,
and after sixty days had passed, he took his leave.
He addressed the king, saying:
"I have heard that Your Majesty possesses a bright moon pearl;
I pray that you will grant it to me as a gift."
The king answered as before.
Within forty *li*, precious treasures pursued him,
which he then presented as offerings.
"O Benevolent One, when you later attain the Way,
I pray that you will take me as your disciple;
may my supernatural powers be peerless."
Having obtained the opportunity to perform offerings exceeding those of today,
he accepted the pearls and departed.
Da-yi then continued his journey forward once more.
Furthermore, he saw a city of crystal;
its palaces, towers, and halls were in every respect as described before,
and there was likewise a venomous snake.
He circumambulated the city nine times and lay down to sleep with his head bowed.
The king went out to meet him and requested that he remain for three months.
The Great Being remained there.
The king again offered him his utmost hospitality,
providing food, drink, clothing, and music.
After forty days had passed, he took his leave and said to the king,
"I have heard that Your Majesty possesses a bright moon pearl."
"I pray that you will grant me this as a favor.
The king then replied,
"This pearl contains treasures extending sixty li."
I shall naturally follow you and present this to the Emperor. If you,
O Benevolent One, should later attain the Way, [I shall do so].
I wish to become your disciple;
my wisdom shall be peerless,
and I shall offer you even greater worship than I do today.
He then accepted the jewel and departed.
As he proceeded further, he again saw a city of lapis lazuli,
where he likewise encountered a venomous snake.
He circumambulated the city twelve times and lay down to sleep with his head bowed.
The King invited him to stay for three months,
and Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented to remain.
The king personally provided him with offerings of food, drink, clothing, and music to entertain him.
After twenty days had passed, he took his leave and addressed the king, saying:
"I have heard that Your Majesty possesses a bright moon pearl;
may it be granted to me as a favor.
The King said:
This pearl is worth eighty *li* of precious treasures; I offer it to you,
so that when you attain the Way in the future, [I may likewise receive its benefit].
May I become your disciple;
with a pure mind, may my offerings exceed those of today,
so that I may long attain wisdom.
The Great Being accepted the jewel and departed,
thinking to himself:
"I originally came here seeking treasure."
"Now that my wishes have been fulfilled, I shall return from here.
He then followed the old path, intending to return to his native land,
and traveled across the great ocean.
The various divine kings then deliberated together, saying,
"Although there are many rare and famous treasures within our ocean,
there are no pearls such as these."
He then issued a command to the Sea God to seize the pearl by force.
The God immediately transformed himself into a human being and met with Mahāmati,
asking him:
"I have heard that you have obtained some extraordinary objects.
Might I borrow them for a moment to see them?
Da Yi then extended his hand and showed him the four pearls.
The Sea God then shook his hand, causing the pearl to fall into the water.
Da Yi thought to himself,
"The King has spoken to me of the Way."
"This jewel is difficult to preserve; by good fortune I have already obtained it.
Now that it has been seized by this son, it would not be right.
He then addressed the Sea God, saying:
"I have come through great hardship and traversed dangerous obstacles to obtain this jewel;
you, on the contrary, have seized it from me.
Do not now refuse to return it."
"I shall drain the waters of the sea to their very end. The Sea God, knowing his resolve, asked him:
"Your ambition is most extraordinary.
The depth of the sea is three million three hundred and sixty thousand yojanas."
Its breadth is boundless;
how can it be exhausted?
It is like the sun, which never falls to the earth.
Just as a great wind cannot be grasped or bound,
even the sun might be made to fall to the ground,
and the wind might be grasped and bound.
"The waters of the great ocean cannot be drawn out until they are exhausted.
Da Yi replied with a smile, saying,
"I have been reflecting to myself:"
Throughout successive lives, from birth to death and through repeated destruction,
the bones accumulated exceed Mount Sumeru in height,
and the blood shed flows as five great rivers.
The four seas are not sufficient to serve as a metaphor for this;
I still wish to sever the very root of birth and death.
Yet, how could this small sea be anything but drainable?
In the past, when making offerings to the Buddhas, I made this vow:
"May my resolve and conduct be courageous in the Way, so that whatever I turn toward shall encounter no difficulty;
even if Mount Sumeru were moved and the great ocean exhausted, I shall never retreat."
He then focused his mind with single-minded intent and used a vessel to bale out the seawater.
Moved by the power of his sincerity,
the Four Heavenly Kings came to assist Da Yi.
When two-thirds of the water had been drawn out,
the various kings of the gods within the ocean were all greatly struck with terror and deliberated together, saying:
"It is no small matter that we do not now return this pearl.
Once the water is exhausted and the mud is exposed, it will destroy our palace.
Thereupon, the Sea God brought forth various treasures and gave them to Mahāmati.
In general, he did not accept them. He said,
"I have no need for such people."
"He merely wishes to obtain my pearl;
once he has returned it to me, he will never cause me further trouble.
The sea deity, perceiving his earnest intent, immediately brought forth the pearl and returned it to him.
Having obtained the jewel, he married a Brahmin woman and returned to his own country, where he bestowed great alms at his pleasure.
From that time forward, there were no longer any who suffered from hunger, cold, or poverty within his realm.
The officials and people of the four quarters all abandoned their former rulers and, carrying their infants on their backs,
returned to him out of benevolence.
Thus, through years of such giving, his grace extended far and wide.
All creatures that fly, crawl, or wriggle receive its moisture;
thereafter, when their lives end, they may ascend to become Śakra, the Lord of Devas,
or descend to become a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) who traverses the air.
By accumulating merit, one attains Buddhahood for oneself;
that one is preeminent within the triple world is entirely due to past practices and is not spontaneous.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The one named Great Intention was my own self.
The householder Mahādhana at that time is now the present King Śuddhodana."
The mother Candā of that time is the present Queen Māyā;
the King of the Joyful and Sorrowless Country of that time is Mahākāśyapa;
and the Brahmin woman of that time is Gopī.
The father of the girl at that time was Maitreya;
the king of the silver city was Ānanda;
and the king of the golden city was Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The king of the city of crystal at that time was Śāriputra;
the king of the city of lapis lazuli was Sūda;
and the fourth heavenly king who assisted Mahāmati in bailing out the ocean was Udra.
The one who at that time seized the jewel was none other than Devadatta.
The four gatekeepers of the city were none other than Subhadra, Pṛthivībandhu, Svāgata, and Kolita.
The poisonous snakes that encircled the four walls of the city were none other than the four ministers, including Kokālika and Sandhāna.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"By what merit does one obtain the four bright moon-jewels, with all manner of treasures following them?
The Buddha said:
In the past, during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin,
Dàyì once constructed a stūpa for the Buddha out of the four precious substances;
he made offerings to the Triple Gem and observed the fast for seven days.
At that time, there were five hundred people who simultaneously built monasteries together;
some hung silk banners and lit lamps.
Some burned incense and scattered flowers;
some made offerings to the community of bhikṣus;
and some recited the sūtras and expounded the Way.
Now all have come together for the assembly;
this is the *Dachiyi jing* (Sutra of Great Meaning).

His name was Pāri.
Together with five hundred men, he entered the sea to seek jewels.
At that time, the Sea God emerged and scooped up some water in his cupped hands.
He asked Pāli, "Which is more:
the water of the great ocean or the water held in my cupped hands? Pāli replied:
A handful of water is more.
Why is this? Although the waters of the ocean are vast, they are of no benefit for immediate use.
Although one cannot save those people from their hunger and thirst,
if one scoops up even a small amount of water and, upon encountering a thirsty person, gives it to them to sustain their life,
the blessings one shall receive throughout successive lifetimes will be beyond measure.
The Sea God, filled with joy, praised him, saying, "Excellent!
He then removed from his own person eight kinds of fragrant garlands adorned with the seven treasures and gave them to Pāli.
The Sea God escorted him;
An Sheng traveled safely back and forth until he reached the kingdom of Śrāvastī,
where he presented this fragrant necklace to King Prasenajit.
He fully explained the circumstances of his arrival, wishing to be granted acceptance.
The king, regarding the fragrant garland as a rare and marvelous gift,
immediately summoned all his consorts and had them stand in a row before him.
To whichever woman was the most excellent, he gave a fragrant garland.
Then sixty thousand ladies, fully adorned, came forth.
The King asked:
"Why has Lady Mallikā not come out?
The attendant replied, "Today is the fifteenth day; she observes the Buddhist fast and wears plain, unadorned clothing."
For this reason, he did not come out.
The king then became enraged and sent someone to summon him, saying,
"If you are observing the fast now, you should not disregard the king's command."
Thus it was repeated three times.
Queen Mallikā came forth dressed in plain garments,
yet she shone among the multitude like the sun and the moon.
He was twice as excellent as usual.
The king’s mind was struck with awe, and he increased his reverence, asking:
"What virtue or realization do you possess that makes you so brilliantly different?"
The lady said to the king,
"I reflect upon my own meager merit;
having received this female form, my disposition and appearance are defiled."
Day and night, mountains of lives are piled up, yet human life is brief;
fearing a fall into the three miserable realms,
I therefore observe the Buddhist fast every month.
"Relinquishing what you cherish to follow the Way, you shall receive blessings in every lifetime.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and gave him a fragrant garland.
Queen Mallikā replied,
"I am currently observing the fast and should not wear this;
you may give it to someone else."
The king said,
"I originally intended to give [this] to the most excellent;
you are now the most excellent."
Furthermore, you who honor the Dharma and observe the fast possess an exceptionally lofty aspiration for the Way;
this is why we associate with one another. If you do not accept [this], where shall I place you?
The lady replied, "Great King,
do not be anxious. I pray that Your Majesty will deign to accompany me to the presence of the Buddha."
With these fragrant necklaces, I offer them to the World-Honored One and receive his holy instructions;
this shall be the merit for successive kalpas.
The king immediately granted his consent.
He then ordered his carriage to be prepared and proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling.
Prostrating himself on the ground, he withdrew to take his place upon the royal throne.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"The sea deity Xiangyingboli presented this [garland],
and among the sixty thousand ladies, there was none who did not covet it."
Lady Mallikā gave it away but did not take it for herself;
upholding the Buddha-dharma and observing the precepts with a mind free from greed,
she respectfully offered it to the Buddha.
I pray that you will graciously accept this.
It is difficult for the disciples of the World-Honored One to maintain their resolve;
they must simply believe in this way.
"How could there be merit?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept this fragrant garland.
The Buddha spoke in verse, saying:
Abundantly crafting precious flowers and weaving *bu-yao* pendants, one produces ever more exquisite forms through the accumulation of the fragrance of virtue.
Like rare grasses and fragrant blossoms that do not waft against the wind,
yet whose scent is perceived when one draws near, the virtuous person’s pervasive fragrance is indeed the truth.

*The Sutra of Similes from the Dhammapada*, Fascicle Two: "Seeking Goodly and Seeking Evil," "Gathering Jewels," and "The Tree of Famine Produces What is Needed. Regarding "Seeking Goodly and Seeking Evil," "Gathering Jewels," and "The Tree of Famine Producing What is Needed": Long ago, in Jambudvīpa...
There was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a caravan leader named Mahānāman.
His wife became pregnant;
naturally, she possessed a benevolent and virtuous disposition and a gentle nature.
When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son.
His physical form was upright and handsome;
his parents loved and cherished him,
providing him with exquisite meals.
He invited his relatives and various physiognomists to enjoy themselves together;
he then took the child in his arms to show him to the assembly and established a name for him.
The physiognomist asked,
"What auspicious signs accompanied this child's conception?
The father replied:
The mother who conceived him was naturally virtuous;
the physiognomist named her Suprabhā.
She nurtured and raised him with great care, excelling in the accumulation of all virtues and showing compassion for all sentient beings.
Thereafter she conceived,
and when her term was full, she gave birth to a son whose physical form was hideous.
The physiognomist asked,
"What signs or omens accompanied the conception of this child?
She replied:
The mother who conceived him was naturally depraved and wicked;
the physiognomist named him Akṣa (Evil-Seeker).
As he grew up on milk and nourishment, he took great pleasure in committing evil deeds.
Constantly harboring greedy thoughts and a jealous disposition,
as they each grew older,
they went together into the sea to seek precious treasures.
Each had five hundred attendants.
The road was long and arduous, and they ran short of provisions midway;
after seven days had passed, they were not far from death.
At that time, Shanqiu and the merchants all together prayed with sincere hearts to the various deities, desiring to cross over the perilous desert of hunger; then,
from within the empty wilderness, they saw a tree in the distance.
The branches and twigs were lush and verdant;
he immediately approached them and found a spring there.
Śubhānveṣin and the entire assembly together entreated him with compassion.
The tree deity manifested her form and said to them,
"Cut off one branch, and what you require shall emerge."
The people were filled with joy;
they then cut off one branch, from which a delicious drink flowed out,
and they cut off a second branch, from which various foods emerged, complete with a hundred flavors.
Together they received [the offerings] and each was fully satisfied.
When the third branch was struck, various exquisite garments were produced, complete in every variety.
When the fourth branch was struck, all manner of precious objects were produced, fully provided in their entirety.
The pack animals were all fully loaded and everything required was completely prepared.
When the one who sought [the goods] wickedly arrived later,
the multitude obtained their full satisfaction just as before.
He then thought to himself:
"If these branches of this tree can produce such various excellent things,
how much more so its roots!"
"I shall now go to cut it down;
it will suffice to obtain things of the utmost excellence and beauty that will delight people. And he had it felled.
To seek good through evil words—
how can we wish to cut down this tree, which has sustained our remaining lives through its bounty during our hunger and exhaustion?
Evil-seeking immediately dug up its roots;
Good-seeking was so moved and pained that he could not bear to see it,
so he led the assembly back home.
Once the felling of the tree was completed,
five hundred rākṣasas seized this wicked seeker and all the merchants and devoured them;
their wealth and goods were lost.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The one who sought [the jewel] well was my very self in this life;
the father was King Śuddhodana."
The mother was none other than Māyā;
the one who sought evil was Devadatta.
In the past, I constantly encountered him and always instructed him in the wholesome Dharma.
Yet he did not employ it;
on the contrary, he treated me with enmity. (From the *Xiányújīng*, Scroll 9).
3. The Lion with Wisdom Escapes the Rākṣasa and the Rākṣasī. In Jambudvīpa, there were many merchants.
They joined together and entered the sea to gather treasures;
they encountered a swirling wave and a malignant wind that wrecked their great ship,
and there were other people as well.
Boarding a dilapidated ship, they were driven by the wind and cast adrift until they fell into the realm of the rākṣasīs.
The rākṣasīs, whose countenances were beautiful and upright, came forward to meet the merchants and said,
"There is much treasure here."
"Priceless bright pearls may be taken at will.
We have no husbands and you have no wife or concubines;
you may stay here and enjoy yourself together with us."
Later, having obtained a favorable wind and good companions, he returned home.
You gentlemen should know that if one sees [this], it is auspicious.
"Those who encounter such a person must be careful not to follow him.
At that time, among the merchants, there was one wise man who said:
"What these women say must not be followed.
He immediately proceeded along a left-hand path for several li,
when he heard from within a city the cries of tens of millions of people calling out in lamentation.
"How did he abandon Jambudvīpa and pass away here?
The merchant approached the city and observed it from all sides;
he saw that the city was surrounded by walls of cast iron, and there were no gates or openings for entering or exiting.
Not far from the city was a śirīṣa tree.
He went there and climbed the tree, where he saw many tens of millions of people inside the city.
From a distance, he asked the people within the city:
"What is he doing? Is he calling out for his parents and brothers?
The people in the city replied:
We entered the sea to gather precious treasures, but were driven astray by the winds.
Furthermore, we were deceived by rākṣasīs and imprisoned within a fortified city.
Previously, five hundred men were gradually taken and killed.
"There are now two hundred and fifty people here.
Do not address this woman as a human;
she is merely a rākṣasī demon."
The man climbed down from the tree and spoke to his companions,
advising them to return home and seek skillful means:
"What do you intend to do today?"
The crowd replied,
"Why did you not question him further last night?
That man possesses considerable skillful means and stratagems."
"Have the multitude and my own self returned home in safety?
The wise man replied,
"I shall rise this very evening and go to inquire further."
While the woman of the Virgo constellation was asleep, she rose furtively and climbed a tree.
She asked the people within the city, "Do you have any skillful means?
You all, as well as my own person, [are in peril]."
"Will we be able to return to Jambudvīpa?
The people within the city replied,
"We have conceived the thought that we wish to return."
This iron city has been transformed into multiple layers that cannot be destroyed.
Those who die each day have no way to escape.
Only you, an outsider, possess a slight expedient means.
They may attain liberation and return to their own lands.
On the fifteenth day at dawn, a horse-king will come from Uttarakuru to this realm.
Dwelling atop the high mountain peak,
the king called out himself:
"Who wishes to return to the land of Jambudvīpa?"
"If you all hear the sound of the horse,
go together to pay your respects and request to return to your own land.
The man then related his circumstances in detail to his companions.
The crowd replied,
"May we go now? He answered, "Yes."
"It will take fifteen days to reach the Horse-King; only then can you depart.
Before many days had passed, the Horse-King arrived.
Having heard this, the merchants went to the Horse King and said,
"We all wish to return to our own country."
"I pray that you will receive me.
The Horse King replied,
"Listen with wise minds to what I shall say."
Those who each desire to return home to their native lands will,
if their minds are focused and upright, succeed in returning;
if their minds are not focused and upright, they shall not return.
These women, cradling their sons and daughters,
pursued behind you, wailing and crying out;
among them, many gave rise to hearts of attachment and longing.
"Even if it were upon my back, it still could not depart.
If you can abandon affection and love,
with a correct mind and single intent, free from all attachment."
"If you grasp a single hair of mine with a sincere heart, you shall be able to return home.
At that time, each of the women said to her husband,
"Truly, you may abandon this lowly body of mine."
"Why do you abandon your children?
First, have your children go to embrace their father's neck,
weeping and crying out."
"Abandoning us, where do you wish to go?
Those whose hearts and minds are attached shall not return;
there is only the Greatly Wise One, the Lion."
They returned safely.
At that time, the rākṣasī took her son and daughter and went to pursue the lion.
She informed the village:
"The one with the body of a lion is my husband;
we have fathered sons and daughters together."
Having abandoned me and fled, I do not know where they have gone.
When the people heard this, they asked Siṃha,
"Observe your wife."
"His physical nature and countenance are most exquisite among men;
how can you abandon these children who are so pitiable?
The Lion replied:
"This is no human being, but a rākṣasa demon.
He has gone to the islands of the sea and slaughtered and devoured merchants beyond counting.
My companions, numbering several hundred, are confined within an iron city."
"I alone have fortunately been spared;
now this female demon pursues me from behind,
intending to harm me, and I fear I shall not escape."
He proceeded further on his way and returned to his own country;
yet the ghost continued to pursue him from behind until it reached that land.
The ogress went and informed the king:
"I have become husband and wife with the lion,
and we have fathered these children."
Later, hoping to gain his strength, he did not expect to be permanently abandoned this day.
The king summoned Siṃha and questioned him regarding the facts of the matter;
Siṃha reported all that had occurred above in detail to the king.
The king said to Sīha,
"Even if you do not need it yourself,
you may bring it to me. Sīha replied:
"This is truly not a human, but a rākṣasa demon.
He is full of transgressions; do not harbor resentment toward him later.
He then spoke again to his ministers and attendants.
"This demon has arrived here specifically to cause harm.
If Your Majesty now refuses to believe this and wishes to bring him into the inner palace,
it will not be long before both the King and the inner court are utterly consumed by ashes."
The king, filled with indignation, said to the Lion:
"The beauty of this woman is like that of a celestial jade maiden;
for what reason do you still call her a rākṣasī demoness?"
"Come out quickly so that I may see for myself.
The king took the female ghost into the palace and stayed there for one night.
The next day, at mealtime, the palace gates did not open.
The ministers deliberated together:
"Because the king has recently taken a wife and his mind is preoccupied with sensual pleasure, he does not open his ears.
Then Siṃha said:
"It would be better to come and deliberate. It is because the King, the Queen,
and all the court ladies have surely been devoured by the rākṣasa that the gate remains closed."
He immediately provided a ladder and climbed over the wall into the interior.
There he saw the skeletons of dead people filling several rooms.
The ministers rebuked Siṃha, saying:
"By sitting upright with you and bringing this rākṣasa ghost,
the king has been killed, the kingdom lost, and the palace destroyed.
What do you intend to do?"
The Lion replied, "I have already made an agreement with you; do not harbor resentment later.
Why do you all continue to reproach and enumerate my faults?"
The ministers and the people came before Siṃha and said,
"The king has now passed away and there is no heir to the throne.
We pray only that you, Siṃha, will ascend the royal throne and govern the people."
The lion declared: "If you wish to elevate me as king, you must follow my instructions;
though our forms differ, let our voices be one in acclaiming 'Excellent!'"
The king addressed his ministers, saying,
"We must assemble our troops together and enter the sea to launch an attack,
slaying the rākṣasas, both male and female, so that none remain."
Afterward, they broke open an iron city and brought out the people within.
It was the established custom of that region that if even one person failed to serve the Buddha, they were to be sent to the west of the mountains to be given to the ghosts to devour.
From that time onward, the Buddha-dharma flourished and countless beings attained the Way.
Therefore it is said:
"All those who have faith in the Buddha—such sentient beings as these—who attain peace and security and return [to their homes], do so entirely because of the Horse King."
Furthermore, it is the constant custom in that land that when a king fathers sons—
whether ten, or a hundred, or even up to an incalculable number— [he performs the following].
He left his home life entirely to practice the Way and recite the Buddhist scriptures;
he mastered all three collections (Tripitaka),
yet later returned to lay life and ceased his religious practice.
Ascending the royal throne:

generally, those who have not mastered the scriptures and do not perform the required rites may not ascend the royal throne; this is recorded in the *Chengshijing* (Sūtra on Succession to the Throne).

4. Mili Attains Joy by Observing the Fast; Tadamu Burns His Head. In the past, there were five hundred merchants. Mili attained joy by observing the fast, while Tadamu burned his own head. [End of section].
Ekākṣarī-miliṇa was the most venerable among them.
Five hundred people boarded a ship together and entered the sea.
A makara fish struck and shattered his boat;
five hundred people all died,
while Miliyan survived by clinging to a plank.
While at the Nimiṃdhara mountain,
he walked back and forth from east to west to ward off the fish;
there, he saw a small path.
He entered and beheld a silver city;
its trees reached toward the heavens,
and among them were bathing pools.
The city was square and its surrounding grounds were encircled by moats.
Four women emerged from within the city;
they were as exquisite in appearance as jade.
The women went out together to welcome Miliyan, saying,
"We are truly distressed; we offer our deepest congratulations on your arrival."
We have long observed your signs of greed;
you ought to serve this virtuous man.
This silver city now belongs to you.
Within the city, the trees were fortunate enough to reach the heavens.
There were canals, bathing pools, pleasure gardens, and dwellings.
Within the city was a palace made of the seven treasures.
It is named Lomaṇa.
Its palaces are made of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva.
We four shall provide for its service.
Sleep late and rise early, keeping the instructions and admonitions in mind;
this will suffice,
and there is no need to go before him in person.
Milián then entered the city with the four women and ascended the palace of the seven treasures,
where they indulged themselves to their heart's content day after day for more than a thousand years within this city.
Later, Miliyan thought to herself:
"These four women do not wish for me to go and appear before another man.
What is their intention?"
Miliàn waited until the four women were fast asleep;
he rose furtively, descended from the palace, and departed the city, proceeding forward until he saw a golden wall in the distance.
The trees, bathing pools, and all other matters were as before.
There were eight women;
their physical beauty and the words they spoke were all as described previously.
Miliyan enjoyed himself to his heart's content with the eight women for several thousand years.
Later, Miliyan reflected and became suspicious of these eight women.
"I do not wish for you to go further to another's side.
What was his intention?
Miliyan waited for the eight women while they were napping during the day.
He rose secretly and proceeded forward.
From afar he beheld a city of crystal;
its trees, bathing pools, and all other features were exactly as before.
Sixteen women came out from the city to welcome him and spoke as before.
Miliyan then took pleasure with the sixteen women to his heart's content for several thousand years.
Milián departed again and beheld a city of lapis lazuli;
the circumstances were also as before.
Thirty-two women came out from the city to welcome him.
Miliyan enjoyed himself with the woman to his heart's content for several thousand years.
Later, he went out of the city and proceeded forward,
where he saw from afar an iron city.
Having encountered no one to greet him,
Miliyan entered the city gate,
where a spirit questioned him.
While Miliyan was practicing the Way,
he personally witnessed a man in the city named Ji Yin.
"A glowing iron wheel rolls upon my head because I entered various cities and sat there without ever feeling satisfied."
Miliyanian, Loman-dian,
Xiemo-dian, Lamo-dian, and Yan-yudan-dian shed tears and spoke.
"Why have I entered this? Miliyan said to the ghost of the Iron-Cast City, "I have entered this burning iron wheel which rolls over my head; when shall I ever be released from it?"
The ghost replied,
"Only when someone like you comes shall you be released.
The Buddha said:
An iron wheel rolled across Mīlaṇa’s head;
only after sixty billion years did he finally escape it.
Mīlaṇa was none other than myself.
Before he sought the Way, while in a state of ignorance,
he bathed, put on new clothes, and stepped upon his mother’s head with his feet;
for this reason, his head burned for one day.
Because his heart remained joyful even during the eightfold fast of the four months,
he obtained a city of four treasures— gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli—
and lived for many thousands of myriads of years.
For this reason, people in the world do not grow weary of the five desires until death;
they desire what they long for and are unfilial toward their parents and teachers.
A chariot wheel trampled him; it was just like the case of Miliyan. This appears in the *Miliyan Sūtra* and also in the *Fubao Jing*. 5.

Upasena’s Brother-in-law Regrets Becoming a Monk, Shoots His Brother, and the Arrow Returns to Harm Himself. In the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there was a merchant. His brother-in-law, having regretted his decision to become a monk, shot and killed his own brother; the arrow, however, turned back and harmed him. Upasena’s brother-in-law later regretted becoming a monk, shot his brother, and the arrow returned to harm himself. Five. [End of section]. In the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there was a merchant.
The two brothers lived together in one place.
The elder brother sought the daughter of an elder for his wife,
but the girl was young and not yet of age to be given in marriage.
The elder brother traveled far with a group of merchants to another country;
after many years had passed, he remained delayed and did not return.
When the daughter reached marriageable age, she spoke to her younger brother.
"Your elder brother has traveled far and perished there, never to return.
You should now take my daughter.
Her younger brother replied:
"How could such a thing be?
The elder spoke thus repeatedly.
His younger brother’s resolve remained firm and never wavered, so the elder deceitfully forged a letter from afar.
He entrusted the matter to some merchants and told them that his elder brother had died,
further informing them, saying,
"Your brother has already passed away."
"What will you do? After his younger brother had married the girl and some time had passed,
she became pregnant.
When the elder brother returned from afar,
the younger brother, harboring fear in his heart, fled to Śrāvastī;
thus wandering from place to place, he arrived before the Buddha.
He sought to leave the household life,
and the Buddha immediately granted his permission;
he then became a śramaṇa named Upasena.
Having upheld the practice of the Vinaya, he attained arhatship.
His elder brother, knowing of his resentment,
intended to kill him and went to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
He immediately issued a heavy recruitment notice with a reward of five hundred taels of gold.
Those who responded to the call advanced together;
seeing his younger brother sitting in meditation, a sudden thought of compassion arose within him.
"How can I kill this bhikṣu?
If I do not kill him, he will take away my gold.
Desiring to shoot the bhikṣu, he instead struck his own elder brother.
His elder brother, harboring resentment and indignation, met his end suddenly and was reborn in the form of a venomous snake,
appearing within the pivot-hole of this practitioner’s door.
As he opened and closed the door,
his body was struck and he died;
he then made a vow to become a small venomous insect once more.
Relying on the dwelling of a practitioner,
[a snake] fell from beneath the roof onto the head of a bhikṣu;
its venom was so fierce and virulent that he immediately passed away.
He addressed Śāriputra:
"In the distant past, there was a pratyekabuddha who appeared in the world and dwelt in the mountain forests."
At that time, there was a hunter who constantly captured birds and beasts,
employing various stratagems and lying in wait in hopes of catching them.
The Pratyekabuddha startled the birds and beasts so that the hunter could not catch them.
He then, harboring malice, shot a poisonous arrow at the pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the pratyekabuddha...
Out of compassion for this man and wishing to cause him to repent and reform,
he manifested his supernormal powers.
At that time, the hunter’s heart was filled with reverence and admiration.
Terrified, he returned in sincerity to confess his transgression.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted his repentance;
however, the poison took effect and he died.
When that person’s life ends, they will fall into hell.
Once they emerge from hell,
they will frequently die from poison for five hundred lifetimes.
"Having attained the path of Arhatship by today, he was still bitten by a venomous insect and died. (From the *Xiányújīng*, Scroll 10). 6.
The Merchant Leader Burns His Arm to Rescue the Caravan. Once, in Jambudvīpa... [The Merchant Leader burns his arm to rescue the merchants. 6. Formerly, in Jambudvīpa...
Five hundred merchants were traveling together through a vast wilderness along a perilous path;
they passed through the hollow of a great mountain that was utterly pitch-black.
At that time, the merchants were bewildered and despondent with grief;
fearing they would lose their wealth and being terrified by the many bandits in this place, they were filled with dread.
With one mind, they turned toward heaven and earth, the sun and moon, the mountains and seas, and all the deities,
weeping and entreating them with piteous cries.
At that time, the Sārthavāha,
out of compassion for the merchants,
said to them, "Do not be afraid."
"I shall act as a great illuminator for you.
At that time, the caravan leader immediately wrapped his two arms with white cotton cloth and poured ghee over them.
Nevertheless, using it as a torch,
he led the merchants and after seven days they finally passed beyond this darkness.
At that time, the merchants were moved by his kindness and honored him with immeasurable reverence;
each attained peace and security, their joy beyond measure.
At that time, I was that caravan leader.
The various merchants are these five hundred bhikṣus today; this is from the sixth fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*. 7.

The Sārthavāha Wishes to Purchase the Five Precepts, but the Rākṣasa Cannot Overcome Him. The Sārthavāha Wishes to Purchase the Five Precepts, but the Rākṣasa Cannot Overcome Him. Seventh: In the past, there was a sārthavāha.
Having heard that there were even more extraordinary treasures in foreign lands,
he wished to go there to seek his livelihood;
however, between the two countries lay the peril of rākṣasas.
It was impossible to pass through.
As the caravan leader was traveling along, he saw at the western gate of the market a practitioner of the Way sitting on an empty bed, proclaiming that he was selling the five precepts.
The Sārthavāha asked, "What are the five precepts?
He replied, "They are formless and upright."
Receiving it orally and upholding it in mind,
one will later attain birth in the heavens;
in this world, one will be able to repel the calamities of rākṣasa demons.
The merchant wished to purchase it and asked,
"How much do you ask for it?
He replied, "One thousand gold coins."
He immediately conferred the five precepts upon him,
and having finished, said:
"Go to a foreign country and stand upon its border."
"If a rākṣasa comes, you need only say to him:
'I am a disciple of Śākyamuni who observes the five precepts.
" After a short while, the Sārthavāha arrived at the border between the two countries.
He saw a rākṣasa,
one zhang and three chi tall,
with a head as yellow as a yāng fruit.
Their eyes were like red spots;
their entire bodies were covered in scales and shells;
they opened and closed their mouths alternately, like fish gurgling with their gills.
Reaching up to catch the flying swallows and treading upon the ground until it sank to his knees,
with blood flowing from his heated mouth,
the multitude of several thousand people seized the Sārthavāha directly.
He spoke these words:
"I am a disciple of Śākyamuni who observes the five precepts.
When the rākṣasa heard this, he was never willing to release him.
The merchant struck it with both fists,
but his hands sank into its scales and could not be pulled out;
he then kicked it on the head with his foot.
He struck and pulled again, yet he could not emerge;
his five limbs were submerged within the scales and shells,
and only his back was able to move.
The rākṣasa said:
"Your body, along with your hands and feet, are all simultaneously bound;
you must simply go to your death—why do you leap and struggle further?"
The merchant’s resolve remained firm;
he said to the rākṣasa:
"Though my body and my hands and feet are all bound at once,"
"Control your mind as one would iron or stone; you shall never be slain by me, Rākṣasa.
The Rākṣasa spoke again to the Sārthavāha:
"I am the king among ghosts, possessing great strength and vigor."
"Since time immemorial, we have eaten you all; they cannot even be numbered.
You should simply go and face death; why do you speak such words of self-comfort?
The caravan leader has intentionally provoked us with insults and rage."
He thought to himself:
"Throughout my cycles through the three realms,
this body has never once been given as alms to a beggar."
"I shall now give this to him so that this rākṣasa may be satisfied for one meal.
He then said:
This foul and stinking body of mine, which I have long desired to cast off,
has now provided an opportunity for the rākṣasa; I shall give it all as a gift,
seeking the Mahāyāna and aspiring to achieve the fruit of omniscience.
The rākṣasa was intelligent and understood the caravan leader’s words;
he immediately felt a sense of shame.
He released the *sārthavāha* and, kneeling with palms joined, addressed him in gratitude, saying:
"You are a teacher who delivers beings; you are a rarity within the three realms."
Aiming to seek the Mahāyāna, one shall before long attain Buddhahood;
therefore, I take refuge and bow my head in prostration,
repenting before the rākṣasa.
In the end, they escorted the Sārthavāha to a foreign land,
where he acquired a great quantity of rare treasures,
and then sent him back home.

He cultivated great merit and subsequently attained the traces of the Way. This is recorded in the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* (Miscellaneous Parables Sutra), where it largely agrees with the preceding account, though there are slight differences;
therefore, both versions are preserved here. 8. The Merchant and the Crane Beget Sons, and the Sons All Attain the Way. Eight: Animals and humans comprise all four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
Question: How is it known that among humans there are those born from eggs?
Answer: [As follows:]
As it has been said:
on the continent of Jambudvīpa,

He obtained two cranes;

subsequently, two eggs were produced.
The eggs gradually grew warm and matured.

How is it known that among humans there are those born from moisture?
The answer is:
as it is stated in the sūtras.
King Bhavāgraja, the Venerable Cāra,
and the Venerable Upacāra.
The maiden Rāhula asked:
"How is it known that there are beings born by transformation among humans?"
The answer is:
they are the humans at the beginning of a kalpa.

From the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 14, concerning those born from eggs and those born from moisture who are included within the realm of animals.

9. A Group of Merchants Suffering from Hunger and Thirst; Eight Flavored Waters Descend from Between the Fingers of a Deva. Regarding the ninth [section]: "A Group of Merchants Suffering from Hunger and Thirst; Eight Flavored Waters Descend from Between the Fingers of a Deva. Long ago, there was a guide.
He traveled together with five hundred merchants on a trading journey until they reached a vast wilderness where there was absolutely no water or drink.
Exhausted by extreme hunger and thirst, they searched in all four directions.
Climbing to a high place and looking afar, they saw trees and thought there must be water;
they all ran toward it together.
Upon arriving at the sight of the tree,
they saw that grass grew all around it and the ground was clean;
they all joined together in digging there.
At that time, a celestial being saw the Teacher from afar;
in the time it takes to stretch out an arm, he arrived at his side and,
perched upon a tree, extended his right hand.
From between his five fingers, eight kinds of sweet and delicious water flowed forth,
never exhausting,
so that all were fully satisfied. (From the *Daśādhyāya-avadāna-sūtra*, Scroll Three).

The merchant drove eight oxen and arrived at the northern kingdom of Kuntala.
There was yet another merchant there.
While they were together in a marsh tending cattle,
a Licchavi captured a nāga maiden;
he pierced her nose and led her away.
When the merchant saw this,
he immediately gave rise to a mind of compassion and asked the Licchavi:
"What do you intend to do with this?
he asked. He replied, "I wish to kill and eat it."
The merchant said, "Do not kill it;
I will give you one ox in exchange so that you may release it. The hunter was unwilling to agree.
"Up to eight oxen," he said.
"In the local dialect, it means: 'Now, for your sake, I shall release them.'"
He immediately took eight oxen and released them, letting the dragon girl go.
At that time, the merchant thought again:
"This is a wicked man; I fear he will pursue me further to capture her once more."
He immediately followed him to observe his destination,
arriving at the edge of a pond where the dragon had transformed himself into human form.
He said to the merchant, "The deity has granted me my life; now I wish to repay his kindness.
You may enter the palace with me."
"You must repay the grace of the devas.
The merchants replied,
"You dragons are by nature impetuous, prone to anger, and fickle."
"Perhaps he can kill me.
He replied, "The man before me has bound me."
"I have the power to kill him; however,
because he has merely undertaken the *poṣadha* observance,
he is entirely devoid of any intent to kill."
How much more so now that the deva has granted me my life;
how could I possibly harm him?
Please stay here for a moment.
I entered first to prepare the room;
by the Dragon Gate, I saw two dragons tied together in one place,
and I asked them:
"For what purpose? He replied,
"This dragon girl observes the dharma of fasting for three days during the half-month."
"My brothers were guarding this dragon girl,
but because we were not firm, she was obtained by the Licchavis;
for this reason, we have been bound."
I only pray that Your Majesty will show me mercy and command them to release me.
If this dragon girl asks what kind of food she should eat,
you should request the food of the human world in Jambudvīpa.
Once the dragon girl had finished preparing everything,
she immediately called him in and seated him upon a precious couch and cushions.
The dragon girl said,
"O Deva, what kind of food do you wish to eat now?
He replied:
When he desired food from among the humans of Jambudvīpa,
he immediately brought down various kinds of food and asked the nāga girl:
"Why is this man bound?
The nāga girl replied, "He has committed an offense against me; I wish to kill him."
The merchant said,
"Do not kill him. [The other replied,] "If you do not, I shall certainly kill him."
The merchant said,
"I shall eat only if you release him.
He replied:
"You must not simply release him.
He shall be punished with six months of banishment among human beings.
The merchant asked:
"Do you have such adornments as to be permitted to observe the poṣadha?
He replied,
"In our dragon dharma, there are five things that are painful."
What are the five?
They are the dragons that arise and the dragons that slumber.
The dragon when lustful;
the dragon when angry;
three times during half a day.
His skin and flesh fell to the ground, and his body was scorched by the hot sand.
He asked again, "What do you seek?"
He replied,
"I wish to seek rebirth among human beings.
[The other] asked, "Now that you have already obtained a human body, what should you seek?"
He replied,
"It is difficult to obtain the going forth.
He asked again.
"To whom should one go for ordination?
He replied,
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is currently in Śrāvastī."
"Those who have not yet been liberated shall be liberated.
You may go forth into homelessness.
He then said:
"I wish to return home.
The nāga girl then gave him eight pieces of gold,
saying, "This is nāga-gold."
This shall suffice for your parents;
these words will serve your kinsmen for the rest of their lives without end.
Now, close your eyes.
He immediately used his supernormal powers to transport him back to his own country.
His traveling companions arrived first and spoke to his family, saying:
He entered the dragon palace.
His parents believed their son was already dead,
and his kinsmen and relatives gathered in one place, wailing and weeping in grief.
At that time, the herdsmen and those gathering firewood and grass,
having seen him, returned first to their homes and said,
"So-and-so has come back."
Upon hearing this, his family members were filled with great joy.
They went out to welcome him home, and once he had entered, they held a birth celebration for him.
During the celebration, they presented eight pieces of gold to his parents.
"This is nāga-gold;
once cut, it grows back again.
It may be used for as long as one lives. (From the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll 33).
11. The Merchant Bound by a Rākṣasa. There was once a merchant leader who, taking a company of merchants, entered a perilous and difficult region.
He encountered a rākṣasa demon, who blocked him with his hand and said, "Stop!
Do not move! I will not allow you to go."
The merchant leader immediately struck him with his right fist;
the fist stuck fast to the ghost and could not be pulled away.
He then struck him again with his left fist.
Nor can it be avoided;
he kicks it with his right foot,
and the result is likewise the same.
He struck it with his head, and his head immediately returned to its place.
The ghost asked: "Why did you do this?"
"What do you intend to do now?
Has your mind found rest?
He replied, "Although I am bound by these five matters..."
"The mind will never cease;
I shall strike you with the power of diligence.
At that time, the ghost thought:
"This person possesses immense courage and strength," he said.
"With such great power of diligence, you shall certainly not rest."
"Now I release you to go," as recorded in the sixteenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

12. The Merchant Who Gathers Jewels and Saves a Dying Man. There was a merchant leader who gathered jewels. 12. There was a merchant leader who gathered jewels and saved a dying man. There was a merchant leader.
His name was Kṣema;
he entered the sea to retrieve great treasures and returned safely.
He possessed eighty billion maṇi jewels,
each worth ten billion taels of gold;
he gave these many precious objects to a single beggar.
Not entering their homes, he returned once more to the sea.
After entering the sea, he obtained double the amount of precious treasures.
After eighty years had passed, he returned to his own country.
As he was about to enter the city, he saw a criminal who had been executed;
the executioners bound him and beat the drum of ill omen.
As they were being led through the streets and alleys to the place of execution to be subjected to the death penalty,
those who were to die encountered Kṣemaka.
He spoke these words:
"O merchant leader,
save me from the death penalty!"
"He has granted me my life.
This great donor is a virtuous and excellent man.
Having heard this, Kṛtaka spoke to those who were about to die.
"O man! I now grant you fearlessness;
I shall save you from the death penalty."
He went immediately to where the executioner was.
To each person there, he gave a mani jewel worth one hundred million taels of gold,
saying, "Wait here for a moment."
"I shall now return to the presence of the King.
At that time, Kṛtaka quickly went to the King's location and said:
"Great King,
I wish to purchase this man's life with excellent treasures.
The King replied:
"Kṛtaka! This person’s transgression is unforgivable and cannot be bought.
If you must buy him, give me everything you possess."
Only by sacrificing my own life in their stead can they be liberated.
Kṣemaka was filled with joy, thinking, "I have attained great benefit; my wishes are fulfilled."
"If you can save this person, it will satisfy my wishes.
He then took all the wealth and property belonging to his household, as well as the rare treasures obtained from the great ocean—
immeasurable thousands of billions of gold, silver, and precious objects.
They all brought [the items] to the king and said to the Great King:
"Please release this man;
all that we possess is now displayed here."
He said to the executioner,
"Kill Kṣemaka. The executioner then bound Kṣemaka and led him to the place of execution.
He raised a sword with his right hand, intending to strike Kṣemaka,
but his arm would not come down.
Stricken with wonder and terror, he immediately informed the king.
He looked for himself.
Upon hearing these words,
the king immediately took up a sword, intending to kill Kṣemaka.
As he raised his sword, both hands fell to the ground; he suffered great agony and died while crying out.
At that time, Kṛtaka was none other than myself.
At that time, the king was Devadatta. This is recorded in the lower fascicle of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra*.

13. Two Merchants Gathering Jewels: The Greedy Perish, the Upright Remain Safe. Once, in the past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago. There were two merchants gathering jewels; the greedy one perished, while the upright one remained safe. (Thirteen) Once, in the past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago.
There were two groups of merchants, each numbering five hundred men,
in Vārāṇasī; having gathered their capital and provisions, they prepared their ships to cross the sea.
Having untied the moorings and hoisted the sails, he rode directly with the wind and arrived at the Jewel Island,
where there were exquisite maidens and nothing that was not present.
A certain caravan leader said,
"We have come here through great hardship for the sake of our wealth;
we should remain here and enjoy ourselves."
The second caravan leader said,
"Although there are many treasures here, we should not remain for long.
At that time, a celestial maiden felt compassion for this group.
Then, speaking from mid-air to the multitude, he said:
"Although it is pleasant here, it is not fit for long-term residence;
seven days hence, this land shall submerge."
Having finished speaking, she vanished.
Furthermore, there was a female demon who wished to cause the merchants to perish right there;
she announced from the air:
"You need not prepare your carriages to return.
There is no water here; even if there were water, how could these many jewels, these women, and these five kinds of music exist?"
"All that was said the day before yesterday was false.
Having spoken thus, he vanished.
The first merchant leader then commanded his followers:
"You all must not depart; do not believe the words of the previous caravan leader.
The second caravan leader returned and addressed his group:
"You all must not be greedy; quickly prepare and repair the ship."
What I said the day before yesterday was sincere and not false.
If the water does not arrive, you may amuse yourself here and then return leisurely;
if the water is certain to come, prepare yourselves with solemnity and then depart.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Seven days from now, just as the heavenly voice previously spoke,
the earth will be filled with water."
The second caravan leader immediately led his followers onto the ship.
The first caravan leader, however, had not yet prepared himself;
when the water arrived, he donned armor and weapons and engaged in combat with them.
The second merchant, standing upon the ship, pierced the foot of the first merchant with a spear;
it passed straight through, and he immediately died.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
Do you know who that first caravan leader was? It was Devadatta.
The second caravan leader was none other than myself.
And those five hundred merchants at that time were these five hundred disciples of Devadatta today.
The second group of five hundred merchants were the present five hundred arhats;
the first heavenly maiden was Śāriputra;
and the second heavenly maiden was the present bhikṣu named Pūrṇacandra, who was formerly a disciple of a brahmin. (From the *Udānavarga-vyākhyāna-sūtra*, Volume One).

14. A merchant harmed his companions and took the precious treasures for himself; out of great compassion, [the Buddha] killed this wicked man. When the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was a merchant, he harmed his companions and took the precious treasures for himself; out of great compassion, [the Buddha] killed this wicked man. (14) At the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
There were five hundred merchants who had entered the sea to seek treasures.
One among them, harboring a malicious intent, thought to himself:
"I shall now kill all these merchants and take the precious treasures for myself alone."
At that time, there was a great guide in Jambudvīpa named Mahākāruṇika.
While he was asleep in a dream, the Sea Deity spoke to him.
Among the caravan was a thief who wished to kill his five hundred companions and seize the treasures for himself alone,
even if it meant that when the deed was discovered, he would fall into hell.
"Now, O benevolent guide, you must employ skillful means so that the merchants do not die and the bandits do not incur guilt.
The guide reflected thus for seven days.
"There is no other expedient;
we must simply kill this wicked man.
When they spoke thus to the merchants, they all became enraged and said, "We shall kill him together."
Both will fall into the evil realms.
Even if I alone were to kill him,
I would have to undergo the retribution for my sin.
I would rather endure suffering for hundreds of thousands of kalpas myself than allow these merchants to be universally harmed,
and cause even a single thief to fall into hell.
The Buddha first preached the Dharma for him,
causing his heart to become joyful and exultant as he fell asleep.
The Buddha said:
The Great Compassionate Guide, like a great merchant, gave rise to great compassion and, through skillful means, eliminated this one thief.
After his life ended, he was reborn in the twelfth heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
At that time, the one of Great Compassion was none other than myself.
By means of this skillful expedient, I transcended birth and death for a thousand kalpas.
As for the five hundred merchants on the same ship—
