They boarded a ship and entered the sea.
There they encountered a makara fish that raised its head and opened its mouth, intending to devour living beings.
At that time, the sun was low and there was little wind, yet the ship moved as swiftly as an arrow.
The caravan leader said to the multitude, "The ship is moving too fast; we should lower the sails.
As he spoke, they lowered them accordingly.
The ship moved faster and faster, and it could not be stopped.
The caravan leader asked those on the upper deck, "What do you see?"
I see two suns rising above;
below are white mountains,
and in between are black mountains.
The caravan leader was startled and said, "This is a great fish; what shall we do?
We have now fallen into dire straits together with you."
"Once one has entered the belly of this fish, there is no possibility of survival.
Each of you must single-mindedly seek [deliverance] according to that which you serve.
Thereupon, the multitude each followed what they worshipped.
With single-minded devotion, he sought deliverance from this calamity;
the more earnest his supplication, the faster the boat moved.
In an instant, it could not stop and was about to enter the mouth of the fish.
Thereupon, the caravan leader addressed the people, saying,
"I have a great deity whose name is Buddha.
Each of you should abandon the deities you have hitherto worshipped and with one mind invoke his name."
At that time, the five hundred people together raised their voices and cried out, "Namo Buddha!
Hearing the name of the Buddha,
the fish reflected within itself, saying:
"Today there is once again a Buddha in the world;
how could I bear to harm sentient beings?
Thereupon, he immediately closed his mouth.
The waters all flowed backward, enabling them to reach distant fish.
Five hundred merchants gave rise to wholesome thoughts and all attained liberation. From the *Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables*, Volume Six.

16. A merchant, pressured by a friend, drank wine and violated his precepts; though his parents banished him to a distant land, he was still feared by ghosts. A merchant, pressured by a friend, drank wine and violated his precepts; though his parents banished him to a distant land, he was still feared by ghosts—this is the sixteenth case. There was a man from a certain district.
Everyone there observed the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions;
within the jurisdiction of the district, there was no one who brewed wine.
Among them was the son of a prominent family.
Desiring to travel abroad for trade,
his parents spoke to him as he set out on the road:
"Be diligent in upholding the five precepts and practice the ten virtuous deeds."
"Be careful not to drink alcohol and violate the grave precepts of the Buddha.
While traveling in another country, he encountered former fellow students;
filled with joy, he returned home, brought out grape wine, and wished to drink it together with them.
He replied:
"In my country, we uphold the Buddha's precepts and none dare to transgress them.
Furthermore, I take leave of my parents; though it is joyful that we part after a long separation from our respective vows and now meet again with one heart, [I must depart]."
"It would be improper for me to violate the precepts or disobey my teacher's instruction.
The host replied, "I and you share the same teacher; by virtue of that grace, we are as brothers."
"My own parents are indeed your parents.
When parents drink together, how could one possibly go against this?
If I were in your house, I would certainly follow your parents."
Having no other choice, he then drank it from him.
When the matter was concluded, he returned home and informed his parents;
his parents replied:
"You have disobeyed my instructions and furthermore violated the precepts.
This is the gradual onset of disordering the Dharma;
you are no filial son. Do not speak of this."
He then took the goods he had obtained and drove him out of the country.
Having been expelled by his kinsmen for violating the precepts,
the son went to another country and stayed at an inn.
The master served three ghosts and spirits who could assume human forms,
eat and drink with people, and converse with them.
Years have passed since these matters began, and our wealth has been entirely exhausted;
meanwhile, illnesses, deaths, and funerals have occurred incessantly within our household.
We have discussed this together in private.
The ghosts knew the man's thoughts.
They deliberated together, saying,
"This man's wealth and property have been completely exhausted."
"He has never been of benefit to us;
now we are weary of him.
We should seek out precious jewels and give them to him."
He then went and stole fine jewels from the royal treasury of another king and placed them within his garden, saying,
"You have served me for many years with great diligence and toil."
"I now wish to bestow blessings upon you so that you may attain abundance.
The host replied,
"I receive the great grace of the deity."
The ghost said, "In your garden there is gold and silver; you may go and take it.
The host was delighted.
Entering the garden, he saw objects which he carried back to his house;
he offered his thanks for the favor received and intended to provide a meal the following day.
I pray that you will deign to visit us;
all preparations have been made.
The spirits and deities have already arrived at our gate.
Seeing people from Śrāvastī in the host’s house,
he fled in haste. The host called out after him as he pursued.
Having already looked down,
why do you abandon it and depart?
The spirit said:
"You are a venerable guest in my home; how could I venture forward?
Again and again he fled in alarm.
The host reflected:
"There is no one else in my house; it is only this person.
Having spoken thus, he immediately rose and completed his respectful offerings.
He questioned him, saying,
"What merit do you possess that the deity I serve flees from you?
The guest explained in detail the merits of the Buddha, the five precepts, and the ten wholesome actions.
Although he has indeed violated the precept against alcohol and been driven away by his relatives,
because he still observes the remaining four precepts, he is protected by celestial deities;
thus, you, O spirit, do not dare to confront him.
The host said, "I wish to uphold the five precepts. Consequently,
he received the three refuges and the five precepts from the guest.
With single-minded diligence, he did not dare to be indolent.
He asked, "Is it possible to see the Buddha wherever he may be?
The guest replied:
In the Jeta Grove at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī,
the host went there with single-minded devotion and passed through a pavilion.
Inside, there was a woman.
She was indeed a demoness who devoured human women.
As the journey grew long and the day drew toward dusk,
he took her as his lodging for the night.
The woman replied,
"Be careful not to linger here;
you should go on quickly."
The man asked, "For what reason do you have this intention?
The woman replied:
"I have already told you; why do you ask again?
The man thought to himself:
"Previously, when the people of Śrāvastī observed even four of the Buddha's precepts, my spirit was still struck with awe."
I have already received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts;
my mind is free from indolence.
What, then, is there to fear?
He then stayed the night there himself.
At that time, a man-eating ghost, having witnessed the majestic power of his observance of the precepts, departed forty *li* from the pavilion and did not return for one night.
The next day, upon entering for an audience, he saw the bones and skeletons of people devoured by ghosts scattered in utter disorder.
His heart was filled with terror and remorse, and he withdrew.
He reflected to himself:
"I have sufficient food and clothing in my own country;
it was in vain that I was converted by this man,
who said the Buddha was in Śrāvastī."
Having seen nothing marvelous, he instead beheld skeletons scattered about.
"It would be better to take this woman back to our native land and live together as before," he thought,
and immediately turned back.
Because he sought to stay overnight with the woman once more,
the woman asked the man,
"Why have you returned?"
He replied,
"I have returned simply because my plan for travel was not successful.
He then stayed there for one more night.
The woman said, "You shall die.
My husband is a man-eating ghost;
he will arrive before long."
"You must leave this place immediately.
The man did not believe her and remained, refusing to go;
thus he became bewildered, and his lustful thoughts arose once more.
No longer believing in the Buddha, the Three Refuges, or the Five Precepts,
the heavenly deity departed immediately and the ghost was able to return.
The woman feared that the ghost would devour this man.
He hid it inside a jar.
When the ghost smelled the scent of human flesh, he said to the woman,
"Have you obtained some meat?"
"I wish to eat it.
His wife said,
"If I do not go out, how can I obtain meat?"
The wife asked the ghost,
"Why did you not return home yesterday?
The ghost replied:
"Because of what you have done, you have harbored a noble guest and caused me to be driven out.
At these words, the man within the jar became even more terrified.
He no longer recognized the Three Refuges.
His wife asked,
"Why have you failed to obtain meat?"
The ghost said,
"Precisely because you have harbored disciples of the Buddha,
the celestial deities have driven me out forty li away."
Having slept in the open air, he remained trembling with fear and was not at ease even now; therefore, he could not obtain meat.
His wife then asked her husband, "What are the Buddha's precepts?"
The ghost said, "I am extremely hungry and in great distress; bring me flesh without asking such questions.
This is the unsurpassed, true, and correct precept."
"It is not something I dare to speak of," she said.
"The wife's words—
speak of them for me."
"I shall give you meat," [he said].
As a class of ghosts, they are greedy and cruel, and their desire for food knows no end.
His wife pressed him with questions.
Taking advantage of the occasion, he preached the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts to her.
When the ghost first spoke the first precept, the woman immediately accepted it;
by the time she reached the fifth precept, she held it firmly in mind and recited it aloud.
The man recognized the five precepts within the jar and received them accordingly. Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, knowing that the hearts of these two had taken refuge in the Buddha,
immediately dispatched fifty benevolent deities to protect them both.
The ghost then fled.
When the next day arrived,
the wife questioned the man.
"Am I afraid?
He replied, "I am greatly afraid.
It is by the grace of your benevolence."
The woman realized that it was the Buddha;
she said to her husband, "It was a man.
Why did he return yesterday?"
He replied, "I saw the skeletons of those who have recently died and those who died long ago scattered about; because I was terrified, I returned.
His wife said:
"Bones are what I have discarded.
I was originally a daughter of a noble family.
I was abducted by a ghost who took me as his wife."
In my misery and desperation, I had no means of escape.
Now, having received your benevolence,
I have been able to hear the Buddha's precepts and am freed from this state as a hungry ghost.
He spoke again, saying,
"Virtuous one, where do you wish to go?
The man replied:
"I wish to go to Śrāvastī to see the Buddha.
His wife said, "Excellent!
I shall follow you, worthy sir, to see the Buddha."
They then proceeded together until they encountered four hundred and ninety-eight people.
They exchanged greetings with them, asking,
"Virtuous ones, from where have you come, and where do you intend to go?"
He replied,
"We have come from the presence of the Buddha.
He then asked:
"You have already been able to see the Buddha; why then do you depart?
They replied, "The Buddha’s spoken sutras left our minds in a state of bewilderment; we still do not understand them, so he has sent us back to our own country."
The two sages related the matter from beginning to end.
Because ghosts fear those of high conduct who observe the precepts,
their minds were opened and they both returned together to see the Buddha.
The Buddha saw him from afar and smiled;
five-colored lights issued forth from his mouth.
Ānanda knelt down for a long time.
The Buddha does not smile without cause; he will surely have something to say.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Do you see these four hundred and ninety-eight people?"
"These people have now found their original teacher;
all who come to see the Buddha shall attain the Way.
At that time, five hundred people came to where the Buddha was and listened to the sutra with single-minded devotion.
Their minds opened and their intentions were liberated;
they all became śramaṇas and attained the path of arhatship.
Furthermore, these two individuals were the former teachers of the four hundred and ninety-eight people.
Those who seek the essentials of the Way must obtain their original teacher and virtuous friends;
only then will they attain understanding, emerge from the precepts, and eliminate calamities. *Jie xiao zai jing*.

38. 1. Bhadra invited the Buddha by means of a conjured city; when he saw the Buddha, he wished to extinguish the conjuration, yet he could not. Bhadra invited [the Buddha] by means of a conjured city.
When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he could not manifest himself alone within the city of Rājagṛha.
There was a magician there named Bhadra (translated as "Renxian" in Chinese).

He was clearly proficient in the scriptures and thoroughly understood all arts and techniques; he was skillful, clever, and versatile, delighting in his fame which spread far and wide, such that none among the people of Magadha could surpass him.
The people of the land, both great and small, received instruction from him.
When Bhadrayaśas beheld the World-Honored One’s physical form, which was majestic and sublime,
he conceived the desire to test him.
He then indicated that he wished to invite the Buddha, thinking: "If he knows my intention, he will surely not accept the invitation;
but if he does not know it, he will certainly accept without doubt."
The Buddha, knowing his intention and desiring to deliver him,
accepted it in silence.
Bhadrapāla said:
The Buddha, though possessing supernormal wisdom, did not perceive my intention;
he entered the city of Rājagṛha and,
in a pure location, manifested a lecture hall by means of his transformative power.
Hanging silk banners and flowered canopies,
beneath each and every tree,
he prepared lion seats for the bhikṣus.
Within the lecture hall,
he specially prepared a lion throne for the Tathāgata,
four zhang and nine chi in height.
When he had prepared a meal of a hundred flavors,
the Four Heavenly Kings and Śakra, Lord of Devas,
together with thirty-two thousand devas, addressed Renxian, saying:
Having truly attained excellent benefit,
he invited the Tathāgata to his lecture hall for offerings;
I shall assist him by providing whatever he lacks.
He immediately manifested a palace and hall like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Buddha, together with the bodhisattvas and the bhikṣus, went to that lecture hall.
There they saw the seat prepared for the Buddha upon which he sat.
Śakra also saw the Tathāgata seated upon the adorned throne he had constructed.
Bhadrapāla listened to what the Buddha taught;
having cast aside his pride, he prostrated his head at the Buddha’s feet.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will forgive my transgressions;
I wish to cease my transformative manifestations."
The Buddha caused him not to change his mind, and further preached for him the *Sūtra on the Emergence of the Worthy and Wise Māyā-puruṣa from All Dharmas Being Like Illusions and Transformations*.
2. Ānanda-bhadrika: The Well of Ānanda-bhadrika Produces Precious Jewels; Ānanda-bhadrika: The Well Produces Precious Jewels (Part Two). Ānanda-bhadrika.
He lived beneath Mount Erlian and was immensely wealthy,
possessing precious treasures;
merchants from all directions came to him to borrow money.
Those who went as beggars never failed to receive alms.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants whose sea vessel was wrecked and whose precious treasures were all lost.
Not a few had died, while others had survived by clinging to wooden planks;
they all went to Ānanda-Bhaṭṭi,
where the host provided them with food.
The host drew water from the well and found a precious casket and a chest;
each bore an inscription with names and surnames.
When the merchants had finished eating, they were all filled with grief.
The host asked for the reason,
and they replied,
"Our companions number five hundred."
While traveling together at sea, their ship capsized and sank;
not a few died, while he managed to survive by clinging to a small plank.
"I have lost my precious treasure and am grieving for my companion;
yet now I see this casket of jewels found in the well,
all of which belongs to me— I do not know how it came to be here."
The host said,
"If you all conduct your livelihood through trade and commerce with a sincere heart, you will not fail."
It was merely because you did not apply yourself with a sincere heart that you failed; since countless kalpas past,
I have never failed to be sincere, nor have I ever deceived or encroached upon others.

Previously, on three occasions when he participated in the Eight Precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), he heard the words of the recited sutras;
with his divine eye (divyacakṣus) never blinking, he chanted and remembered them without forgetting.
Yet, this worthy man was upright and straightforward.
A skilled thief stole another's property without being noticed before his eyes.
The king lost a pearl and summoned his ministers to deliberate upon the matter.
The minister replied to the king, saying,
"I have heard that there is one who is virtuous and upright, yet extremely capable at stealing.
Your Majesty has commanded me to arrest him for interrogation, hoping to obtain his word that he did not steal."
Since the King possesses the Way, how could he wrong others?
He then summoned his ministers to deliberate together.
One minister spoke, saying:
"You should employ a stratagem to first subdue him;
then, having placed heavy shackles upon him and paraded him through the marketplace with a proclamation of his execution, give him wine to intoxicate him.
Once he is drunk, remove the shackles and place him in the hall, where the courtesans shall perform music."
The King commanded the female entertainers:
"When the noble and upright one asks you while intoxicated, you must answer him thus."
"This is heaven, and I am a celestial maiden.
You should serve by my side;
it was because you stole the king’s jewel during your previous life that you were born here."
The king then complied with this.
Having heard it, the virtuous and upright man departed, thinking silently to himself:
"I have heard the words of the Sūtra."
"The divine eye does not blink, yet this woman blinks her eyes.
Furthermore, having stolen the jewels, I ought to enter hell;
will the King not expose me and make me his head?"
"Even though I spoke,
I attained birth in heaven because I did not steal the jewel," the courtesan reported to the king.
Daoxian spoke bluntly,
and the king laughed heartily, saying,
"This young man certainly did not steal my pearls."
He immediately released him to go,
bestowing upon him gold and jewels once more,
even though this man was indeed a thief of the pearls.
Reciting a single verse can exempt one from sin and grant deliverance; this is from the *Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables*. 4.

Cīra Releases a Turtle and Later Saves Its Life During a Great Flood. Once, there was a man named Cīra. He released a turtle, and later, encountering a great flood, he saved its life once again. 4. Formerly, there was a man named Cīra.
Seeing a man selling a turtle, he felt pity for it in his heart and wept toward the turtle.
The seller of the turtle said:
"Why do you weep toward the turtle? Cīra replied,
"I cannot bear to see it."
The man who was selling turtles laughed heartily and said,
"You are merely deluded and mad.
He replied:
I thought of this tortoise and requested to buy it from you.
The owner said,
"The tortoise is worth one million."
Cilāta then took him home.
After exhausting all his sons and grandsons, he obtained eight hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Cilāta said:
"My money is exhausted; there is nowhere else to seek it.
The turtle-seller said, "Since your money is spent, you may work for me in the fields to complete the payment for its value."
Cilā replied, "Yes," and placed the tortoise upon his cart to cast it into the pond;
once there, the tortoise was able to speak.
Soon there will be a great flood; you should climb a tree and call out to one another.
On the following day, the floodwaters will rise greatly and the people will all perish.
Cilā climbed the tree and called out to the tortoise.
The turtle then approached;
Ci-lo sat upon the turtle's back and traveled several li forward.
He saw a woman on a drifting raft, gasping for breath and about to die.
She then begged Cīra for passage.
Cīra informed the turtle.
This person was pitiable, so he begged for the turtle and carried it away.
The turtle said,
"When you go back, please carry me along again."
After traveling ten li,
he saw a seller of turtles whose clothes were caught on a log in the current.
He approached the seller with compassion, wishing to have him transport them across.
The turtle said, "I am already heavy;
I fear that I will surely become utterly exhausted and unable to cross by myself.
Be careful not to carry me."
Cira said, "It is pitiable that this current error should be recorded.
Cira then recorded it again.
After traveling several tens of li,
he saw several sheng of moths streaming over a log bridge.
Cila again informed the turtle to carry them.
When they arrived at the kingdom of Cina-keta,
the woman then offered gold to Cira.
The turtle-seller said:
"This tortoise was originally sold by me.
Now that you have obtained the gold, you ought to return it to me.
Cīra would not give it back.
The seller of turtles went to the king of that country of Kheka and said,
"Cīra has stolen a man's wife and is selling her;
he has now brought gold and silver here to this kingdom."
The King of Rājagṛha immediately summoned the executioner Cīrā and ordered him to behead him.
When the executioner reported this matter to the king and was about to take up his pen to write it down,
moths kept alighting upon the pen so that he could not form a single character.
When the king heard this, he asked Cīra,
"What meritorious qualities do you possess?
Cīra answered him in full detail.
The King executed the turtle-seller; this is from the *Ānanda-xian-bian-jing* (Sutra on Ānanda Manifesting Miracles).
Five thousand laborers painted [the image] and obtained gold, yet they were sued by their wives for holding a feast. [This occurred in] the city of Puṣkarāvatī in the five regions of the Yuezhi.
There was a painter named Cchanna who traveled back and forth to the eastern land of Dakṣiṇāpatha.
The guest spent twelve years painting it.
Having obtained thirty taels of gold, he took them back to his own country.
There, he encountered a community of monks whose faith was pure and clear.
He then asked the karmadāna,
"How much wealth is required for this assembly to obtain food for one day?
He replied:
Thirty taels of gold may be used;
let the painter be entrusted to the *karmadāna* to provide for a single meal.
"I shall come tomorrow.
He returned home empty-handed.
His wife asked him.
"What did you obtain in twelve years?
He replied,
"I obtained thirty taels of gold."
Having already planted the field of merit and entrusted it to the Sangha for the performance of a memorial assembly,
the wife bound her husband and delivered him to the authorities.
He related the aforementioned matter in full.
The official asked,
"Why did you not give it to your wife and children, but instead beg it from others?"
The painter replied,
"In my previous lives, I lacked merit and was poor, constantly enduring hardship.
Now that I have encountered the assembly of monks, who are a most excellent field of merit."
If one does not plant roots of goodness again, one will be poor in future lives;
such poverty and suffering will continue in succession without a time of liberation.
Therefore, one should give to the Sangha as a whole.
The judge, who was an upāsaka, immediately removed his jeweled necklace,
gave away the horse he was riding, and offered the village as well to the painter,
saying to him:
"You have given to the Sangha,
yet the Sangha has not yet eaten;
this is like a grain seed that has already sprouted before it has been sown."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, scroll eleven, states that the great fruit [of rebirth] appears later.
6. Regarding the consciousness returning to rub against the bones of the former body: Long ago, there was a man.
After death, his spirit returned to the side of his old bones and rubbed them.
When people asked him,
"You are already dead," he replied:
"Why do you use this parched human bone?
The spirit replied,
"This was my own body."

By refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech; and by being free from envy, ill will, and delusion, one will be reborn in the heavens after death.
One's wishes are spontaneously fulfilled with boundless happiness;
for this reason, one cherishes it deeply. (From the *Old Collection of Miscellaneous Parables*, Scroll 7).
7. The Carpenter and the Painter Deceive Each Other. Long ago, in Northern India...
There was a skilled craftsman who fashioned a wooden woman,
so peerlessly beautiful that her clothing, girdle, and ornaments were no different from those of a worldly woman.
It could come and go and was capable of serving wine and attending to guests;
its only incapacity was speech.
At that time, there was a painter from South India.
He was also skilled at painting.
When the master craftsman heard of this,
he prepared fine food and drink and invited the painter.
He then had the wooden woman serve wine and carry food;
from dawn until night,
the painter did not realize it was a wooden figure, believing her to be a real woman.
His lustful mind was so intense that he could not forget her;
by then, the sun had already set,
and the carpenter entered to stay the night.
He kept the painter there and had this wooden woman stand in attendance by his side,
then spoke to the guest, saying:
"Therefore, let us keep this girl so that we may sleep together.
Once the host had entered,
the wooden woman stood by the lamp.
The guest immediately called out to her,
but the woman did not come;
the guest then stepped forward and pulled her.
Only then did he realize it was wood,
and he felt ashamed, thinking,
"The host has deceived me."
"I shall repay him.
Thereupon, the painter again employed a stratagem;
he immediately painted his own likeness upon the wall.
The clothing he wore was no different from his own body.
He tied a rope around his neck so that it appeared as though he had been strangled, and he drew an image of a rope and placed it upon his mouth and beak.
Having done this, he closed the door and entered beneath the bed himself.
At dawn, the master came out and saw that the door was not yet open;
he immediately looked inside and saw only the image of a guest who had been hanged on the wall.
The master was struck with great terror and thought he had truly died;
he immediately broke through the door and entered, cutting the rope with a knife.
Thereupon, the painter emerged from beneath the bed.
The carpenter was deeply ashamed.
The painter then said,
"You have been able to deceive me."
"I am capable of deceiving you;
as guest and host, our mutual obligations are now fulfilled and we shall not betray one another.
The two men, believing him to be deluded, [accepted his words].
The Fourth Volume of the *Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables on Leaving Home to Practice the Way by Abandoning All Loved Ones*. 8.
The King’s Illness Cured and the Physician Receiving an Extraordinary Reward from the King. 8. There was once a king of a country.
His body was afflicted by a grave illness that did not subside for twelve years;
none of the great physicians were able to cure him.
At that time, a small frontier kingdom was subject to a great king.
There was a physician there who was highly skilled in treating illnesses.
The king immediately summoned him and ordered him to treat his own ailment.
Before long, he was granted a reduction in his sentence.
The king then thought of how to repay this teacher’s kindness and dispatched a messenger to proclaim an edict throughout that country.
Since this master has been appointed to the task, he ought to be rewarded.
Elephants, horses, chariots, cattle, sheep, fields, houses, male and female servants, laborers, and all manner of ornamental articles should be granted to him.
That minor king respectfully proclaimed the imperial decree.
While the Master was by the king's side, no one spoke;
the Master then reflected.
"I have exerted great effort in treating the King's illness;
I do not yet know whether the King will reward me or not.
After several more days had passed, the King’s condition improved further.
The master requested leave to return to his own country,
and the king granted his request;
he provided him with a weak horse and dilapidated riding gear.
The Master laughed heartily, saying, "I regret that although I possessed great skill in treating the King's illness,
the King failed to recognize my kindness."
"You did not attend to me,
leaving me to depart empty-handed.
As I follow my path, I lament with sorrow, harboring this as a lifelong regret."
Upon arriving in his own country, he saw a herd of elephants and asked the elephant keeper,
"Whose elephants are these?"
The elephant cub replied,
"This is my teacher-elephant.
He asked the elephant cub again:
"From whom did my teacher obtain this elephant calf?
He replied,
"My teacher cured the Great King's illness, and he was restored to health."
This is the reward obtained through merit.
Proceeding a short distance further,
he saw a herd of horses, cattle, and sheep.
He asked, "Whose property is this?
The shepherd replied:
"Master, you have granted me permission;
let us proceed a little further.
He saw his original house, with its lofty halls and multi-storied pavilions, appearing vastly different from his former residence.
He asked his disciples,
"Whose house is this?
The disciples replied:
"This is the dwelling of such-and-such a teacher.
He then entered the inner chamber and saw his wife,
her appearance full and joyful, wearing robes of precious jewels.
Finding this strange, he asked,
"Whose wife is this?
A person came forward and replied.
"This is the wife of Master So-and-so;
she has come from seeing the elephants and horses,
and has now entered the house."
They all knew that this was obtained as a reward for the merit of treating the king’s illness;
they then immediately felt regret for their own past actions.
This concludes the fourth fascicle of the *Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables* (*Zāpíyùjīng*) concerning the effort spent treating the king’s illness.
9. Breaking the Fast and Yet Attaining Birth in Heaven. Once, there was a householder who prepared a great sacrificial altar and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
At that time, there was a man selling curd.
The host invited him to eat,
encouraged him to observe the fast, and urged him to listen to the sutras.
When he returned at dusk,
his wife said to him,
"I have not eaten since this morning; I have been waiting for you until now."
One who violates the fast destroys its merit;
yet even the merit of half a fast will cause one to be born in the heavens for seven lifetimes,
and when born among humans, one will always obtain natural abundance.
By observing the fast for one day, one will naturally receive provisions sufficient for six million years.
Furthermore, there are five blessings:
first, one will have little illness.
Second, physical and mental tranquility;
third, little sexual desire;
fourth, little sleep.

The sun was already nearing its zenith,
yet the family’s midday meal had not arrived;
the practitioner, having lost his way, reached the site of the field.
He requested alms for his midday meal.
The plowman replied, "Yes," adding, "I have a small favor to ask; you must stay awhile."
The family meal was delayed until late.
The practitioner said,
"Since the food has not yet arrived, I still wish to rinse my mouth."
The plowman untied his waistband and gave him one harītakī fruit;
the practitioner accepted it and ate it.
He then offered a coin as a religious gift (*dakṣiṇā*) to the practitioner.
The practitioner said,
"If your mind is capable of being moved, there is no need for further recompense.
I wish to confer upon you the five precepts."
"Are you able to receive them?
He replied,
"As a lay disciple, I find it difficult to fully observe the five precepts."
He merely undertook the vow of non-killing.
When his life came to an end, he was reborn into the household of a royal minister.
The queen, leading her retinue, arrived at the banks of the flowing water.
While performing music with song and dance, she held her child by the water;
she lost her grip and he fell into the water, whereupon a fish swallowed him.
Remaining in the fish's belly for seven days, he experienced neither hunger nor thirst.
Following the current downstream for over a thousand *li*,
he entered the borders of a lower kingdom where people caught fish and traded them in the market.
At that time, the ruler of the lower kingdom sent someone to purchase fish from the market.
As he was returning to the city and preparing to scale the fish with a knife,
the child within his womb cried out,
"Proceed slowly; do not harm me!"
Upon cutting open the fish's intestines, he saw a small boy, peerless in his exquisite beauty; the entire kingdom rejoiced.
When the sovereign of the upper realm heard of this, he said:
"This must surely be my son.
He sent a messenger to demand him back.
The ruler of the subordinate state replied:
A fish in its belly had received a divine gift,
which I was unwilling to give up;
the two states disputed over it until the matter reached the Great State.
The Great King ruled:
"If this child is not born in the Upper Country, how could he be obtained by the Lower Country?
If the Lower Country does not obtain this child," [the Upper Country shall keep him].
In which upper kingdom should they be sought?
These two have a karmic affinity with you two kingdoms.
In the interim, a palace may be constructed to house this child together;
let him be named the Crown Prince of Two Kingdoms,
and let him remain therein according to this decree.
Following the ritual for a crown prince,
the Buddha spoke to his disciples:
"The plowman of the past."

Giving a single coin as alms to a practitioner of the Way, one immediately obtains the status of a crown prince in two kingdoms. From the *Za puyi jing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables), Chapter 11: "Offerings to Śramaṇas—The Manner in Which Rewards Differ According to the Goodness or Evil of One's Intentions. 11. Offerings to Śramaṇas—The Manner in Which Rewards Differ According to the Goodness or Evil of One's Intentions. In the past, there was a practitioner of the Way who was lame in his feet. He lived by begging for food from door to door. Whenever he encountered someone, he would say: "I am a poor man; I have no wealth or property. I beg for a single coin to offer as alms to a śramaṇa. At that time, there was a wealthy man who heard this. He thought to himself: "This man is truly sincere and possesses a heart of goodness. I shall give him ten coins. The lame practitioner received them and immediately went to a monastery to offer them to a śramaṇa. The wealthy man followed behind him and asked, "Did you obtain what you sought? The practitioner replied, "I have indeed obtained it. The wealthy man said, "I gave you ten coins; why did you only offer one to the śramaṇa? The practitioner answered, "I intended to give all ten, but I feared that if I offered so much, the śramaṇa might not be able to consume it all. Therefore, I offered only one coin and kept the remaining nine for myself. The wealthy man thought: "This man’s intentions are pure and his heart is good. Although he only offered one coin, his merit is vast. He then took out another ten coins and gave them to the practitioner. The practitioner again went to the monastery and offered these ten coins to the śramaṇa. The wealthy man followed once more and asked, "Did you obtain what you sought? The practitioner replied, "I have indeed obtained it. The wealthy man said, "I gave you twenty coins; why did you only offer ten to the śramaṇa? The practitioner answered, "I intended to give all twenty, but I feared that if I offered so much, the śramaṇa might not be able to consume it all. Therefore, I offered only ten coins and kept the remaining ten for myself. The wealthy man thought: "This man’s intentions are even more pure and his heart is even better. The second man replied, "That phoenix is a creature of the heavens and does not dwell among humans. It will surely fly away at dawn; how can you rely upon it? Then a cormorant also came and perched on the tree. The first man said, "This cormorant is a creature of the water; it will surely remain here. We should rely upon it. The second man said, "This cormorant is a bird of ill omen; it will surely cause us harm. How can you rely upon it? Before long, the phoenix flew away, and the cormorant remained. The first man, relying on the phoenix, was carried away by the current and perished. The second man, relying on the cormorant, was saved and reached the shore. The Buddha said to the monks: "At that time, the man who relied on the phoenix was myself. Because I did not rely on the cormorant, I perished. The man who relied on the cormorant was Śāriputra. Because he did not rely on the phoenix, he attained deliverance. The Buddha further said: "In the future, there will be those who seek the Way but rely on heterodox teachers. They will be like the man who relied on the phoenix and perished. Those who rely on the true Dharma and attain deliverance will be like the man who relied on the cormorant and reached the shore. Thus the Buddha spoke. This is called the seventeenth parable.
Living creatures took refuge on a mound to avoid it.
Just as they were about to be submerged,
suddenly a phoenix appeared.
Upon reaching the wise one, they took refuge in his wings;
thus they ascended to high ground and escaped the calamity of the waters.
As for those others who had not yet departed:
Suddenly seeing a cormorant, he immediately took refuge in its feathers;
the cormorant then entered deep water, and they both perished together in the drowning.
(From the *Za pīyù jīng*, Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables).
18. Some purchase wisdom and thereby escape great calamity; some purchase wisdom and thereby escape great calamity. 18. Once upon a time, there was a man who was poor and destitute.
While returning to his country after making a living by entering the sea to gather treasures,
he encountered a spiritual friend who said:
"I have long been poor, yet now I have obtained these goods."
"It will suffice for my own satisfaction.
If my mother cannot do so,
I shall abandon her and depart from this dwelling."
"If that wife will not do,
I intend to seek another," he said.
His friend replied:
In this vicinity, people of great wisdom abound throughout the city;
you may go there to purchase wisdom for no more than a thousand taels of gold.
"I shall personally explain the Dharma of wisdom to you.
That person, acting according to these words,
entered the village where the Buddha resided.
He questioned others about this in detail,
and they replied:
"As for that which you doubt,"
He walked forward seven paces and then walked back seven paces;
this was repeated three times, whereupon wisdom arose spontaneously within him.
That man returned home that night.
Seeing his mother sleeping with his wife,
he thought she was another man's woman;
he drew his sword, intending to kill her.
Do not conceal what is within your mind.
Instead, let the great lamp of wisdom shine afar upon your contemplation;
purchase this wisdom in the morning.
Thus he vacillated three times;
his mother then became enlightened,
and the man sighed, saying:
This is truly wisdom.
How could it be worth only a thousand taels of gold?
He immediately gave him another three thousand taels of gold and produced the fourth fascicle of the *Daśādhyāya-avadāna-sūtra* (Ten-Fascicle Avadāna Sūtra).
19. Someone Spreads the Rumor of a Ghost to Avoid Harm. Once, in the past, there was a man traveling through the mountains who encountered a man-eating ghost.
He seized [the man] intending to eat him.
The man begged for mercy, saying,
"Please allow me a brief moment to ask about one matter."
He then saw that he had been eaten, yet he felt no resentment.
The ghost believed the man’s words as a matter of sincerity and granted him whatever he desired.
He then asked the ghost:
"For what reason is your face, feet, knees, and belly white,
while all other parts are entirely black?"
The ghost replied, "As for my nature as a being,
I am malevolent and crave the essence of the sun;
I can travel when my back is turned to the sun, but I cannot face it."
For this reason it was so.
That man ran toward the sun;
the ghost could only harbor empty resentment, unable to catch him. (From the *Daśa-varga-avadāna-sūtra*, Scroll 4).
20. There was once a man who, being detested by two wives, met his death because of them. Long ago, there was a certain man who [served] two masters.
Two wives went to visit the junior wife.
The junior wife said, "I am young."
"My husband is old;
I do not wish to remain here.
You may go to my senior wife's place to make your home."
Her husband plucked out his white hair and went straight to the place of the eldest wife.
The eldest wife said to him:
"I am old and my hair has turned white;
your hair is black, so you should go.
Thereupon, she plucked out his black hair and made it white.
He did not stop doing this,
until his head was eventually completely bald.
His two wives detested him for it.
They then each departed and sat in grief until they died.
In a past life, they had been dogs in a monastery.
There was one temple to the east of the stream and one temple to the west.
When they heard the sound of the *gandī* being struck, the dog would go there and obtain food.
On a later day, the two temples struck their bells simultaneously.
The dog floated on the water, wishing to cross over.
Just as it was about to reach the western temple, it feared the food at the eastern temple would be better;
as it turned toward the east, it again feared the food at the western temple would be better.
Thus, from drowning in the waters of doubt, there emerge ten volumes of the *Avadāna-sūtra*. 21. A man sought the water of the immortals from afar;

the master, with an evil heart, made him climb a tree and obtain the elixir of the immortals. 21. Once upon a time, there was a man who traveled a great distance to seek the water of the immortals. The master harbored ill intent and compelled him to climb a tree, whereby he obtained the elixir of the immortals. Twenty-one. In the past, there was a certain person.
Having heard that there was "Immortal Water" in a foreign land, by entering which one could attain immortality,
he traveled to that foreign land and stayed overnight with another.
The host asked the guest:
"Where do you wish to go? he asked. He replied, "I wish to study the arts of the immortals.
The host harbored ill will toward him.
He said to the guest,
"I have a tree of the immortals;
if you can work for me with diligence for one year, [I shall give it to you]."
"I shall provide you with provisions; why trouble yourself by traveling so far?
The guest said, "That is most excellent.
For a year he worked diligently, never showing even the slightest trace of resentment.
When the year had come to an end,
the host, whose original intention was to deceive him,
found that there were no immortal trees.
Upon arriving at the mountain, he pointed to a tree on the edge of a cliff and said, "This is the Immortal Tree.
You must climb to its top.
He called out, "Fly! and [the other] flew away, casting himself down, in response to the sound.
The guest’s heart was most sincere;
he immediately soared from this tree into the void and thereby attained the Way of the Immortals.
The protagonist saw me and caused me to die;
how could he have awakened to the attainment of immortality?
He held this tree in such deep affection that he spoke of it as being sacred.
After a short while,
father and son went together to the foot of a tree; the son yielded to his father,
requesting that he ascend first.
The son then called out, "Father, you may fly.
The father immediately attempted to fly,
but fell upon a rocky cliff.
The *Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables* (*Zapiyu jing*), Volume 22:
"A Man Employs a Ghost to Gain Wealth, Then Later Kills His Son. Twenty-second. Once upon a time, there was a man.
In the marketplace, he was selling the Vaiyāghra ghost.
Those who wished to buy the ghost asked how much it cost.
The master of the ghost replied:
[He gave] two hundred taels of gold.
[The other] said:
"What extraordinary or strange thing does this ghost possess?"
He then asked for the gold that belonged to Er.
[The other] said, "This ghost performs every kind of labor; there is no task it will not do."
It is calculated that one day's work shall equal that of a hundred men.
There is only one illness;
it is fitting to provide for its prevention beforehand.
Question: What kind of illness is this?
Answer: It is when this ghost desires to make [the person] perform labor.
Day and night they are made to labor,
never allowed to rest;
if there is no one to work, they will even turn back to harm their master.
The host looked at Jin and intended to send him home;
he ordered him to work the fields.
When the field work was finished, he then made him perform carpentry.
When the carpentry was finished, he again ordered the ground to be leveled;
building houses, operating mortars and mills, and cooking fires never ceased.
Within a few years, he attained great wealth.
The host had business and was about to travel as a guest;
having forgotten to give instructions, the ghost again intended to act, but there was no order to it.
It took the host’s child, placed him inside a cauldron, lit a fire, and boiled him.
When he returned to his master, the son had already become thoroughly matured.
Stricken with grief and remorse, knowing what more could be said, he departed.

From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter 23: "A Rich Man Reprimanded by the King for His Expenditures; Upon the King’s Inquiry, He Attains Awakening. Twenty-three: Once there was a wealthy man. A rich man was reprimanded by the king for his expenditures; upon the king’s inquiry, he attained awakening. (23) In the past, there was a wealthy man.
The King ordered a detailed inventory to be made,
which was immediately drafted:
"In such-and-such a year, [a sum of] several tens of millions was used to construct a Buddha image."
A certain amount was used for the sūtras and assemblies of the fasting ceremony,
and another amount was provided for the relief of the poor and the elderly;
there are currently eighty-nine million remaining.
He presented the list to the king.
The king became greatly incensed and asked,
"Why have you already used the items you presented?"
The wealthy man replied,
"That which has already been used is the most precious treasure;
because it provides spiritual sustenance to others, I present it to you."
Wealth that has not yet been put to use is shared among five families;
this is not merely my own view.
I venture to set it forth in detail.
The king then attained awakening.
"Virtue is to be relied upon" is from the *Apadāna-sūtra* (Piyūhasūtra). 24.

A man was punished for his crime by having five *jin* of flesh cut from him; a man was punished for his crime by having five *jin* of flesh cut from him. Twenty-fourth: Long ago, there was a man who committed a crime against the king.
The king became greatly enraged and furious;
he sent men to cut five *jin* of flesh from his back and loins,
and placed it beneath his palace.
This person cried out in agony until it reached the King.
The King asked, "What is the meaning of this?
He replied:
"In truth, it was not my fault.
The King felt ashamed and remorseful,
and issued an edict requesting one hundred jin of meat.
He continued to groan as before.
The king said, "I have just replaced it with a hundred jin; why do you cry out so loudly?"
The ministers replied,
"We have not seen such a law;
what benefit would a thousand *kṣāra* bring to its pain?"
If a person’s only son has died and another gives him a hundred [pieces of gold],
can that person not think of his son? (From the *Bai ju biyu jing*, Scroll Three).
25. There were two people who made a mutual vow that their children in the womb would be married to one another; there were two people who became mutual friends.
The wives each became pregnant and made a mutual vow:
"If we give birth to children, whether male or female, let them marry one another."
After they were separated, one family gave birth to a son and the other to a daughter.
The father of the boy died early, and when the boy grew up, he had not yet married.
While traveling to sell miscellaneous goods, he happened to arrive at the girl's house.
The father-in-law asked the son where he had come from,
where he resided, and the names of his parents;
the son answered him fully.
When the Duke heard this, he was greatly alarmed and said to his son,
"When your father was alive, he entered into a prenatal marriage with me."
"I have constantly sought you, yet we have not known one another;
as a maiden, I have not yet dared to marry.
Thus spoke the man.
"I do not know the woman at all.
The Duke said, "Your Excellency asks about those who are close to her."
The man returned and questioned the wet nurse, who confirmed it was indeed so.
When the man arrived at the woman’s house,
he saw on the road that the water in the ditch was flowing.
He entered a skull, yet it was never filled.
Fearing this, the boy moved forward again and saw the fruit of a tree ripening;
he wished to pick and eat it.
The child cried out, "Save me! Save me!
Terrified, he ran away in haste and fell to the ground.
When he arrived at the woman's house,
a dog came forward on its knees and licked his two feet.
From within the dog’s belly, a pup came running forward, barking and howling.
Desiring to bite and devour him, she struck him down on the ground; only after a long time did he revive.
His mother came out and related the matter to her son in detail.
The Duke was greatly astonished by this and went in to tell his daughter.
His daughter replied to him, saying, "I saw on the road a skull into which water from a ditch flowed, yet it was never filled.
This signifies that in future generations there will be one who collects the wealth, treasures, and precious goods of the whole world."
No matter how much was provided to him, he could never be satisfied.
Seeing the fruit on a tree ripe for picking, he desired to take and eat it;
however, the fruit cried out, "Take me! Take me! as he reached for it.
In later generations, people sought only their eldest daughters;
yet the younger daughters would say, "Why do you not seek me? Why do you not seek me?"
The dog knelt upright in reverse and licked its two feet.
A puppy within the dog’s belly howled and came forward, wishing to bite him.
People of later generations spoke of this among themselves.
Their mouths are like greasy fat, but their hearts are like awls and knives;
their mouths appear full and satisfied while inwardly they plot and scheme—
all for the sake of future generations, not for the present.
He immediately gave his daughter in marriage to the man, thus fulfilling his original wish. This concludes the eighth fascicle of the *Daśa-varga-avadāna-sūtra*.

26. The Two Sons of a Great Family: The Elder Son Loses His Wealth and is Reminded of It; the Younger Son Acquires Wealth and Commits an Offense. 26. Once, there was a man of great family who had two sons. The elder son lost his wealth and was reminded of it, while the younger son acquired wealth and committed an offense. 26. In the past, there was a man of great family who had two sons.
Each was given two million coins to trade with merchants.
The eldest son squandered it all on gambling;
his clothes and bedding were ruined, and upon returning, he informed his father.
The father said,
"I have you alone;
what is the use of wealth?"
He provided him with clothing, bedding, food,
and drink, and comforted him well.
The young son returned home and addressed his father.
He obtained a profit of two million.
His father said,
"Bring the account book here."
They compared the accounts together and found a discrepancy of several thousand [units].
They then bound and beat him;
this was done three times.
He collected six million in interest,
yet upon returning it, he was immediately beaten. Thus,
the crown prince’s three transactions resulted in a loss of six million.
He remained in another country and did not return.
He associated with disreputable people and spoke to them, saying:
"My father has one casket each of gold, silver, and white pearls,
which are at the head of the large bed.
When you return, tell my father this."
"I have not foolishly lost my wealth;
I have not yet dared to return it.
You may kill my father whenever you find the opportunity and take the goods away."
It may be used in common.
This man went to his house and met with his father,
recounting the words of his son.
Hearing this, the father wept and said,
"What use are material wealth and possessions?
Why has my son not come?"
While eating and breathing, he wept with a choked voice.
The guest said,
"A gentleman does not practice unfiliality by spending money to commit evil."
All at once they were completely exhausted.
This led me to come here to kill you and take your gold and silver.
Yet, I saw that you treated me with great kindness, mindful of your son.
"This has moved my heart.
His father said, "My young son is still foolish; you must go and welcome him."
"I say to you, my son:
go and return with the money early.
For what reason do you utter such foolish words?"
He further made robes and gave them to him.
The Master said,
"My young disciple has repaid his debt."

Each person received five million and some change.
If one wished to give a single coin to another person,
it would have been considered unfair.
He wished to divide it,
but the matter was not so;
at that time, the śramaṇa was on his alms-round.
The three people spoke together, saying, "Giving to the śramaṇas is most excellent," and they held it with their hands and gave it to him.
The śramaṇa then offered a prayer of blessing.
This shall cause you to obtain blessings in both this life and future lives;
together you shall be born in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, each attaining great wealth.
One of you shall preside over a mountain where gold is mined.
One person was in charge of plowing fields to extract gold;
another was in charge of drawing gold from within the water.
This was due to the merit they had received from practicing generosity in previous lives.
When the king heard this,
he thought, "The people and things of my kingdom all belong to me.
He then led his men and soldiers to the mountain to gather them.
The gold transformed into stone.
Then he went to another house’s land and plowed it up to retrieve the gold.
The gold turned into earth.
Again, he went to a well in another house and drew up the gold;
the gold turned into tiles.
None of them could obtain it.
The king asked the Buddha,
"These three men have each paid gold as my fee."
When they went to retrieve it, it had all been transformed and could not be found as gold.
[The king asked,] "What merit did this man possess in his previous lives that he has now attained such fortune?
The Buddha explained it in detail.
This is not the property of the king;

The Poor Man Who Attained Wealth by Making Offerings to the Sangha. Twenty-eight: Once there was a poor family that made offerings to a practitioner of the Way.
After one year, he departed.
He took a bronze bottle and asked the host, saying,
"This bottle was struck by a deity."
"Whatever you seek from the mouth of this jar shall be obtained.
Do not ask for the king;
otherwise, the jar will break."
The family subsequently became immensely wealthy;
forgetting the practitioner’s injunction,
they invited the king.
The king asked for the reason for his wealth,
and he answered the king truthfully.
The king then seized the jar.
The family fell into further poverty and distress;
only then did they remember the practitioner and went out in all directions until they found him.
They spoke to him truthfully, saying: [the rest of the narrative].
The practitioner said,
"I must have this jar;
I beg you for a basin to hold these forest stones."
Carrying [the request], he went to the king’s gate to seek the jar.
Upon reaching the king’s gate, he cried out for the jar in a loud voice.
When the king heard this, he was greatly incensed.
He dispatched several dozen men intending to seize him;
as they emerged from the forest, the wind blew stones across the sky.
The king’s messengers were struck by these wooden logs and stones until their heads were shattered, yet within a moment, a thousand men emerged.
The wind's force had scattered the corpses so that they blocked the gate;
the king was terrified and trembled,
seeking to have his jar returned.
That person obtained the jar,
and his family became exceedingly wealthy once more;
he extensively performed meritorious deeds.
"Dying and Attaining Birth in Heaven" from the *Zāpíyùjīng* (Miscellaneous Avadāna Sūtra). 29.
"The Poor Man Who Finds a Hidden Treasure and Is Punished by the King. Twenty-nine: The Buddha and Ānanda entered the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, it rained heavily.
The water drenched the hidden storehouses, causing various treasures to emerge.
The Buddha said, "It is like a venomous snake."
Ānanda said, "A venomous snake.
Hearing this, a wheat-gatherer at the foot of the mountain thought to himself,
"I have never seen a śramaṇa who is a venomous snake."
He immediately went to see the object;
taking a carriage and a clothing bag, he brought them into his house,
manifesting an air of wealth and nobility as he constructed a new, grand residence.
A jealous person said to the king:
"Previously there was a poor and lowly man who suddenly displayed signs of wealth;
this man must surely have obtained a great treasure-trove."
The king immediately summoned him for questioning.
He replied that he had not obtained it.
The king then issued an order to interrogate and punish him.
This person remembers the Buddha and Ānanda, regarding them as a venomous serpent;
who would fail to speak of obtaining the treasure-trove?
One should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha.
The King spoke thus: "The Buddha calls it a poisonous snake;
Ānanda calls it a venomous snake."
The king immediately summoned him and questioned him. The man replied,
"Great King."
"If you grant me safety, I shall speak the truth.
The king consented,
and he related the aforementioned matter in detail.
"What can you possibly do with my body?
You shall surely devour my life.
The King has offered a reward of five hundred gold coins."

30. The Poor Man Who Bought an Axe and Did Not Recognize It as a Treasure. Thirty: Once there was an old man, poor, destitute, and alone.
The family had no means of its own livelihood;
by chance, they encountered a single axe in the market,
which was the finest of all precious jewels.
Not recognizing it,
he took it to chop down the trunk and sell it to sustain his meager livelihood;
he used his axe until he had nearly finished cutting it down.
He encountered a foreign merchant of great means,
known as a *sārthavāha*.
Upon seeing him, he recognized him by his axe.
He then asked his husband,
"Will you sell this axe?
The husband replied.
"I rely on this axe for my livelihood; I will not sell it.
The merchant again said, "I will give you a hundred bolts of silk; why will you not sell it?"
The official did not agree to the terms.
The merchant spoke again, saying,
"I will give you two hundred horses."
The lord then became despondent and unhappy.
The Sārthavāha spoke again, saying,
"If you find it insufficient, I shall increase it."
"Why do you not rejoice?
he asked, and gave him five hundred horses.
The Duke then wept aloud.
The merchant again said, "The silk is insufficient;
it shall be supplemented. Why do you weep?"
The Duke said, "I do not regret that the silk was insufficient; I regret only my own foolishness.
This axe was originally one foot and a half long."
He broke through the ground until only five inches remained;
he still obtained five hundred bolts of silk,
which was his only regret.
The merchant chief spoke again:
"Do not harbor any lingering regret;
I shall now give you a thousand bolts of silk."

Even if one were to tear up the ticket and carry it away, firewood and flames would burn it until it is completely transformed into precious jewels; this is an essential matter from among the various sūtras.
31. The Poor Old Couple and Their Laziness Throughout the Three Periods. Thirty-first: In the early morning, the World-Honored One entered the city of Śrāvastī.
As the Venerable Ānanda was departing,
there were an elderly couple;
they were advanced in years with mature faculties, their backs bent like hooks.
They went to a place where refuse was being burned at the head of a village lane;
there they squatted together facing the fire like old cranes,
gazing at one another with lustful intent.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you see that husband and wife?
Ānanda replied:
"So it is," the Buddha said.
"These two elderly husband and wife..."
If, during the prime of youth and vigor,
he had diligently sought wealth, he would have become the foremost wealthy man in the city of Śrāvastī; if, however,
he had left the household life to study the Way and practiced with diligence, he would have attained arhatship.
During the second stage of his life, when he was in the prime of his vigor,
if he had diligently sought wealth, he would have become the second wealthiest person in the city of Śrāvastī;
if he had left the household life to study the Path, he would have attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
If, during middle age, he had diligently sought wealth,
he would have become the third wealthiest person in the city of Śrāvastī;
if he had left the household life to study the Path, he would have attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Now, on this day, my years are advanced and my faculties have matured;
I possess neither wealth nor skillful means,
and am no longer capable.
Though he sought wealth and riches with great effort,
he was still unable to attain the state that transcends humanity.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] spoke to him in verse:
Because one does not practice the holy life, one fails to obtain the wealth of youth;
reflecting on matters of the past, one lies upon the ground like a bent bow—
because one did not practice the holy life, one fails to obtain the wealth of youth.
"Just like an old crane that dies guarding an empty pond," as stated in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*,
fascicle 5 (also fascicle 42), and the *Sūtra on the Three Times Passing Away*.
32. The Poor Man Who Broke His Vow to the Tree Spirit Was Killed by a Tree Branch. Thirty-second: In the kingdom of Vaiśālī, there was a householder (gṛhapati).
Having completed the offerings and recitations of praise to the Buddha,
they requested to hear the meaning of the Dharma.
The Buddha smiled, and light from his mouth circled his body three times before returning to enter through the crown of his head.
Ānanda asked for the reason,
and the Buddha said,
"In that land there are five hundred people."
Having entered the sea to gather treasures, he set sail to return;
passing through deep mountains, he halted for the night as dusk fell.
Having prepared his provisions in advance, he set out early the next morning.
Four hundred and ninety-nine people all departed;
one person remained lying fast asleep and lost his companions.
Yet they encountered snow and rain from heaven;
losing their way, they were brought to exhaustion and distress in the mountains, weeping and crying out to Heaven.
There was a deity of a sandalwood tree who said to the destitute man,
"You may stay here."
They provided him with food and clothing from their own resources,
saying, "You may leave when spring arrives.
The destitute man remained there for three months.
He addressed the tree deity, saying,
"Having received your kindness, I have been spared my life;
yet I have not yet offered even a small token of gratitude."
I look back and see that my two parents are currently in their native land;
I truly long to see them and pray that you will grant me leave to depart.
The tree deity said, "Excellent.
Give him a golden cake.
It is not far from here."
"You shall obtain a kingdom and city;
you may then return to your own native village.
As the poor man was about to depart, he addressed the tree deity, saying:
"This tree is fragrant and pure, a rarity in this world.
Now that you have come from afar, I wish for you to know its name.
The deity said:
"There is no need to ask.
The destitute man spoke again:
"I have relied on the shade of this tree for three full months."
"Now you must distance yourself from feelings of resentment.
When you reach your own country, you should proclaim and cultivate gratitude.
Then the deity spoke:
There is a tree named *candana*.
Its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves cure a hundred ailments of humans;
its fragrance is perceived from afar, and people seek it out with such greed that they do not even need to ask for it.
When the destitute man arrived at the kingdom,
his relatives both inside and outside the court joyfully congratulated and comforted him.
Later, the king fell ill with a headache.
Prayers and sacrifices offered to the deities of heaven, earth, mountains, and waters could not alleviate the ailment.
A renowned physician examined him and declared that only with *candana* sandalwood could the disease be cured.
The king immediately sought it among the common people, but none possessed it.
He then issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom:
"Whoever obtains sandalwood incense shall be enfeoffed as a marquis, and his wife shall be my younger daughter."
At that time, the poor man, hearing that the reward for his service was substantial, said,
"I know the location of the sandalwood."
The king then ordered an attendant to lead the destitute man to go and cut it down.
They went directly to the location of the tree.
Upon seeing the tree, the messenger noted that it was massive and straight.
Its branches and twigs were lush and its flowers and fruits resplendent;
such a sight was rarely seen by people, and their hearts could not bear to cut it down.
Yet, to not cut it down would be to disobey the king’s command.
The illness did not subside or heal.
As he felled it, his heart felt a deep, throbbing ache;
he hesitated and lingered, not knowing what to do.
The tree spirit spoke from mid-air, saying,
"Then cut it down;
however, leave only its root."
Once the felling is complete, smear it with human blood and cover it with liver and intestines;
the tree will then grow of its own accord.
It returned to its former state.
Having heard these words from the deity,
the messenger immediately ordered men to cut it down.
The destitute man was staying by the side of a tree.
A branch of the tree snapped against the ground and crushed him to death.
The messengers deliberated together.
They slaughtered the destitute man and took his liver and blood.
As the deity had commanded, the tree immediately grew back.
They loaded the felled trees onto carts and returned with them to the kingdom.
The physician then administered the medicine,
and the king’s illness was cured;
the entire kingdom rejoiced.
The king commanded the people of the kingdom:
"All those who are ill shall come to the palace gate;
the king will go out and provide them with fragrant medicines."
All illnesses were healed;
the King’s person was healthy and at ease, and the common people were free from disease.
The entire nation rejoiced, leading to a state of great peace, as recorded in the *Candanavṛkṣa Sūtra*.

33. A man encountered an elephant while traveling through a deep valley; as he was falling, the heavens sent down sweet dew, and he subsequently ascended to heaven. Once, in the past, there was a man walking through a vast wilderness. As he was pursued by an elephant and fell into a deep valley, the heavens sent down sweet dew, whereby he attained rebirth in the heavens. Thirty-three [times]. Once, in the past, there was a man walking through a vast wilderness.
He saw a black elephant and thought to himself,
"This elephant will surely come and harm me."
"I shall kill him," [the man thought].
The elephant also thought to itself,
"This person will surely kill me."
"I shall distress him.
The man then abandoned him and departed.
The elephant pursued him from behind.
After running forward for several li, he fell into a deep valley.
The valley was bottomless;
he immediately grasped the roots of a tree on the bank.
Its shape was like a finger;
following its root downward,
it hung suspended by the riverbank.
An elephant at the top of a ravine tried to reach it with its trunk;
whether it was about to reach it or not,
he looked down and saw the bottom, which consisted only of thorns and brambles, while two rats were gnawing together at the base of the tree.
Furthermore, three black snakes emerged with their heads bared, intending to bite him;
moreover, mosquitoes and gadflies came to sting his eyes.
The man thought to himself:
"Today I am dying.
I look up to Heaven seeking rescue;
my voice is mournful and my emotion is sincere."
Heaven sent down drops of sweet dew into his mouth.
When he had received one drop, two mice departed;
when he had received two drops, a venomous snake left him.
If one obtains three drops, the black elephant returns of its own accord;
if one obtains four drops, mosquitoes and gadflies are eliminated;
if one obtains five drops, deep valleys level themselves out, and one emerges upon level ground.
The *Dṛṣṭānta-sūtra*, Volume Seven, translated by the Celestial Being for the purpose of conversion and intended for return to the heavens.

34. Five Hundred Young Boys Gather Sand to Build Stūpas and are Reborn in Heaven. Five hundred young boys joined together as companions. They gathered sand to construct stūpas, and upon the end of their lives, they were reborn in heaven. (34) Five hundred young boys formed a group of friends.
Day after day they played together by the river,
gathering sand to build stupas and each claiming their stupa was the finest.
Although they possessed virtuous hearts, the merit from their past lives was meager.
At that time, it rained heavily and the river waters surged, sweeping them away and drowning them.
The Buddha told the multitude,
"The five hundred youths have been reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven."
They all together resolved their minds to practice the bodhisattva path.
The Buddha emitted a radiance that enabled their parents to see where their sons were located.
From afar, the Buddha called out to the five hundred young boys, saying, "Come here!"
Immediately, they all arrived and remained suspended in mid-air;
scattering flowers before the Buddha, they bowed their heads in prostration and said,
"We have received the grace of the World-Honored One."
"Though your bodies perish, you shall behold Maitreya.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
You have made a firm resolve to know the Way and the Ultimate Truth, and you have established stupas and monasteries."
By this cause, they were born in heaven and had an audience with Maitreya, receiving his instruction on the Dharma.
The Buddha preached the sutra for them, and they all rejoiced, establishing themselves in the stage of non-retrogression.
Each addressed their parents, saying, "Do not grieve or suffer any longer."
Exerting themselves with vigor, they cultivated themselves through the Dharma.
Both parents gave rise to the aspiration for the Way;
they prostrated at his feet and circumambulated the Buddha three times.

When the King’s consort requested her hair in exchange for a thousand ounces of gold, she refused to give it.

Knowing her distress was extreme, the consort gave her only five hundred taels of gold.
