which is likewise situated among the ten precious mountains.
Therein, there is no Buddha-dharma, nor sun, moon, or stars.
By the power of his past generosity,
he now dwells in a palace of the seven treasures and possesses an exceedingly long lifespan.
This king was originally among human beings.
There was a great elder who constructed a stūpa for the Buddha;
this kinnara offered a single pillar for it, thereby completing the temple.
Furthermore, by giving pure food to artisans, one will,
at the end of one's life, become the deity of the breast situated between two mountains.
Formerly, when he was among humans, he was a great elder who possessed immeasurable wealth.
Once, there was a śramaṇa begging for food,
and his wife held up a bowl of rice and gave it as an offering.
He then became greatly incensed and said,
"What beggar is this who gazes upon my wife?
I shall cause this man's hands and feet to be severed!"
After his life ended, he received this hideous form;
for eighty-four kalpas, he was constantly without hands or feet.
Whenever the devas held banquets, he always shared turns with the gandharvas to move between the upper and lower realms.
When the gods wished to perform music,
filth flowed from beneath his armpits;
he then ascended to heaven by himself.
There was a kinnara named Tūruṃga who sang of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) in praise of the World-Honored One.
At that time, Mount Sumeru and all the forest trees shook violently.
Kāśyapa could not remain settled in his seat,
and the hearts of the five hundred rishis became intoxicated with madness.
Losing his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*), he fell to the ground at once; this is recorded in the *Bodhisattvagati-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
4. Miscellaneous Ghosts and Spirits: The four types of ghosts and spirits are all named after their respective abodes: first, those who receive the retribution of hungry ghosts (*preta*);
second, ghosts who sell wine, who speak to their masters and command them to retrieve gold and silver from corpses in lakes; third, those with golden beds.
1. A naked woman put on clothes; 2. Fire broke out; 3. Two ghosts carried a corpse away; 4. Hands, feet, head, and ribs were pulled out;
5. They exchanged forms with humans; 6. Their appearances changed while their minds remained fixed; 7. Meeting the Buddha, they attained the Way; 8.
Five-colored divine fingers flowed as nectar, providing sustenance for all beings to supply those on the path; 9. The evil Piśāca ghost who devoured people met the Buddha and attained awakening.
1. The seven sons of Hārītī first devoured people; the Buddha hid her child, and only then did she undergo conversion. 2.
The yakṣa Kumbhakarṇa invited the Buddha to provide him with a dwelling and lamps. 3. The Māra King harassed Maudgalyāyana; [the Buddha] spoke of his former life as a Māra’s deed. 4.
A ghost who possessed the power of knowing others' minds harmed a woman who was his enemy. 5. Pāpīyān harassed Mañjuśrī with persistent persistence. 6. Twelve.
13. A hungry ghost asks Maudgalyāyana about the cause of his suffering. 14. Thirteen evil ghosts see the form of Śakra gradually becoming ugly and diminished.
15. Ghosts whip their own former corpses. 1. All spirits and gods derive their names from their respective abodes;
all spirits and gods derive their names from their respective abodes. First, there are four great deities of the elements: the first is Earth.
Second is water;
third is wind; fourth is fire.
The Earth Deity thought to herself,
"The earth has no water, fire, or wind.
The Buddha said:
Within the earth element there are water, fire, and wind;
it is simply because the earth is predominant that it receives its name.
It is exactly the same for the deities of water, fire, and wind.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them,
and they all received the five precepts to become upāsikās.
As for the houses and dwellings where all the people resided, [the Buddha transformed them into jeweled palaces].
There are spirits and deities everywhere; there is no place that is empty.
Whether it be the streets, lanes, alleys, butcher shops, marketplaces, or the various mountains and burial mounds—there are spirits and deities in all of them;
not a single spot is devoid of them.

All ghosts and spirits are named according to that upon which they depend; as the *Loutan jing* states: "There are ghosts and spirits on trees seven feet high with a circumference of one foot. When a person is first born, there are always ghosts and spirits who follow them to provide protection."
When a person is about to die, the ghosts seize their vital essence (*ojas*).
A person who has committed the ten unwholesome deeds, whether there be a hundred or a thousand such people, is protected by a single deity.
This is just as a king employs hundreds of thousands of men to guard a single minister. (From the *Dīrgha Āgama*, Scroll 20).

2. The Retribution of Hungry Ghosts. Regarding the retribution of hungry ghosts: if there are sentient beings born among the hungry ghosts, because they are constantly hungry and thirsty, their eyes are sunken and their hair is long.
They run frantically east and west, eating only vomit, fat, flesh, pus, blood, excrement, urine, mucus, saliva, and the leftover dregs of wash-water.
Their lifespan lasts for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of years;
they have never even heard the names of sauces or water,
and even if they were to see them with their own eyes, they would rush toward them in haste.
It transforms into fierce flames, pus, and blood;
sometimes it does not change at all, and many people wielding weapons prevent one from proceeding;
or when it rains in summer, it reaches the body and turns into fire—this is called an evil retribution.
Along the banks of the Ganges River there were five hundred hungry ghosts (*preta*).
For immeasurable years, they had not seen water at all.
Although they reached the riverbank, they saw nothing but flowing fire.
Driven by hunger and thirst, they raised their voices and wailed.
The hungry ghosts addressed the Buddha:
"We are so hungry and thirsty that our lives will not last much longer.
The Buddha said,
"The waters of the Ganges flow."
The ghost said,
"Where the Tathāgata sees water, I always see fire.
The Buddha said:
"Having removed your perversion so that you may see the water," he spoke at length on the faults of stinginess and greed.
The hungry ghost said:
"I have been thirsty for a long time; although I hear these words of the Dharma, they do not enter my mind at all.
First, let me enter the river and drink as much as I desire.
By the power of the Buddha, he was immediately able to drink the water.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all resolved to attain bodhicitta.
They cast off their forms as hungry ghosts;
some of these hungry ghosts had been constantly burned by fire.
Just as at the end of an eon, fires break out from the mountains;
some are emaciated and run about frantically with disheveled hair covering their bodies,
while others stand by latrines and privies, waiting and seeking after impurities.
There are some who constantly seek the afterbirth blood of women in labor to drink;
their bodies resemble scorched trees and their throats are like needles.
Even if they were given water to drink, they would not be satiated for a thousand years.
Some break their own heads to take out the brains and lick them;
others have forms like black mountains with iron chains binding their necks,
as they strike their heads in supplication for mercy and take refuge in the wardens of hell.
There are those who, in previous lives, were malicious in speech and habitually addressed others with coarse words;
because all people detested them and viewed them as enemies, they fell among the hungry ghosts due to this transgression.
Thus, one undergoes immeasurable suffering as retribution for such sins before emerging into the Great Wisdom of Nirvāṇa. [From] *The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Chapter 3.

[Regarding] "The Ghost Selling Wine Speaks to His Master, Commanding Him to Retrieve the Gold and Silver of a Dead Person from the Lake": Third, there was a man whose occupation was selling wine. A ghost, while selling wine, spoke to his master, commanding him to go into the lake and retrieve the gold and silver of a deceased person. There were three people who made their living by selling wine.
A ghost appeared and, while drinking wine for which he had not yet been paid, said to the host:
"Tomorrow there will be a man carrying flowers, dressed in upper and lower white garments with a blue sash."
Within the binding cloth are a thousand catties of gold and silver.
When you were bathing in the lake, you died and they did not come out.
Go and retrieve the gold and silver; you will have no further cause for worry.
The next day, the host waited in attendance.
He saw a man enter the water to bathe, come ashore to put on his clothes, wash his feet, and then suddenly fall to the ground and die.
The wine-maker went there, recovered the gold and silver, and obtained it all according to the amount.
On a later day, the ghost came.
The host prepared food and brought out wine, saying to the deity:
"I saw a person dressed in clothes who was about to leave, and then he died."
"Why do you not kill him in the water so that he may reach dry land?
The ghost replied,
"I cannot kill a person who is ill."
"I know only when the life-span of human beings is decaying.
The Master said,
"Among the gods above and the spirits below..."
He knows the lifespan of others and whether their merit and demerit have reached its end or not;
he cannot sustain life, nor can he take life;
he cannot cause people to become wealthy or noble, nor poor or lowly.
It is merely that he wishes to cause people to commit evil and violate the precept against killing;

taking advantage of their decline and exhaustion, he goes to disturb them, speaking of calamities and blessings to lead people to establish shrines and offer sacrifices to him. (From the *Daśa-varga-avadāna-sūtra*, Scroll Six).
4. A golden bed, a naked woman, clothing, and fire; a golden bed, a naked woman, clothing, and fire. There were four kings of the Kāśī kingdom named Brahmadatta.
At that time, he went out on a hunting expedition into the wilderness.
Seeing a house—according to the *Puying jing* (Sutra on the Merit of Offerings), it was by a mountain at the foot of a tree—he went toward it.
Inside was a woman.
From the time she began seeking food and drink, there was nothing she sought that she could not obtain.
The king invited her to meet him;
at that time, the woman was entirely naked.
The king took off his garment and gave it to her; as soon as she put it on, it fit perfectly.
This happened three times.
The king then questioned the woman about this.
The woman replied,
"In the past, I was the wife of a king.
That king provided meals for śramaṇas and further bestowed robes upon them."

At that time, I remonstrated with him, saying: "A meal alone is sufficient for almsgiving; there is no further need for clothing. The *Fubao jing* (Sūtra on the Retribution of Merit) states that because one cuts off and gives [a portion of one's body] to a śramaṇa, one consequently undergoes this retribution.
If Your Majesty wishes for me to be able to wear clothes, [then you must act accordingly].
"Make robes for me and first offer them to śramaṇas and those learned in the scriptures.
The king sought śramaṇas but could not find any;
he then said, "They may be offered to virtuous ones who observe the five precepts."
The wise man offered this blessing:
"May the maiden on the golden bed obtain immeasurable merit and be clothed in royal garments.
The king then asked the woman:
"What deity are you?
She replied,
"I am superior to humans."
Because they are inferior and do not reach the heavens, they remain within the realm of ghosts and spirits.
After casting off this life, they shall be reborn in the first heaven above. (Cited from the *Apadāna-sūtra* and the *Puṇyavipāka-sūtra*).

5. Two Ghosts Carry a Corpse, Pull Out Hands, Feet, Head, and Ribs, and Exchange Them with a Person; Their Forms Are Changed, Their Minds Are Transformed, and Meeting the Buddha, They Attain the Way. In the past, a man was traveling far away and stayed alone in an empty house. Two ghosts carried a corpse there and pulled out its hands, feet, head, and ribs, exchanging them with those of the man. Their physical forms were thus changed, and their minds were transformed. Encountering the Buddha, they attained the Way. (Note: The numbering "5" at the beginning of the entry appears to be a section marker from the source text.)
In the middle of the night, a ghost came carrying a dead person and placed it before him.
Another ghost followed after, chasing him and shouting in anger:
"That dead person is my property! How dare you carry it away!"
The first ghost said, "This is my property;
I brought it myself. The second ghost said, "This is a dead person; I truly carried him here."
The two ghosts each seized one foot and one hand, contending for them.
The front ghost said, "There is a person here; we may question him."
The ghost then asked,
"Who brought this dead person here?
The man reflected.
These two ghosts possess great power;
whether one speaks the truth or lies, neither can escape death.
Thus he spoke.
The front ghost brought it along,
while the back ghost became greatly enraged;
he seized the man's hand, pulled it out, and placed it on the ground.
The ghost before him took one arm of the dead man and grafted it on;
it immediately became as such.
Both arms, both legs, the head, the ribs, and the entire body were all replaced.
Thereupon, the two ghosts together devoured the human body they had exchanged,
wiped their mouths, and departed.
The man reflected:
"With my own physical body,
I saw with my own eyes two ghosts devouring my parents' flesh;
now this body of mine is entirely the flesh of others."
"I am now certainly possessed of a body, or am I without a body?
Having traveled to a Buddhist stūpa, he questioned the bhikṣus and related the aforementioned matter in detail.
The bhikṣus said:
"From the very beginning, there has always been no self;
it is only because of the combination of the four great elements that we conceive of it as 'my body.'"
He is no different from who you were in your former life and who you are now.
Monks, ordain him into the Path.
The twelfth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* on attaining Arhatship concludes here. 6.

The Golden-Haired Deity’s Finger Flows with Ambrosia and Provides Sustenance for Travelers. There was once a spirit who possessed a golden-haired finger that flowed with ambrosia, providing all manner of provisions to travelers. There was one such spirit.
His body is immense and his hands are golden;
from his five fingers, nectar constantly flows.
Whatever a traveler may require, [it is provided].
Food, drink, and all necessities of life were provided from his finger, given to him at will.
Maudgalyāyana asked:
"Who are you, O deva?
Your merit, reward, and extraordinary virtues are such as these.
"I am not a king of the gods; I am Brahmā, the King of Gods."
"I am a spirit. I dwell in a great city of a certain country,
and have come here for the purpose of wandering about and sightseeing."
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"What wholesome deeds did you perform to obtain such a reward?
He replied:
In that land, there was a great city named Rāvaṇa.
In the past, I lived there as a poor woman,
weaving bags of woolen thread and selling them to support myself.
As his resources dwindled and his house fell into ruin,
he eventually went out onto the main road and took up residence near the home of a wealthy and generous elder who lived by weaving thread. He supported himself by weaving threads.
When the sun was about to reach its zenith,
if there were śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who,
carrying alms bowls, went begging for food.
He asked me, "Where is the house of such-and-such an elder?
My mind was truthful and free from any falsehood.
Rejoicing, he raised his hand and pointed toward his house, saying, "Go to that place;
the time is passing, so do not seek elsewhere. [Thus ends] the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra*.

7. The Piśāca demon who devoured people encountered the Buddha and attained awakening. The Piśāca demon who devoured people encountered the Buddha and attained awakening. In the realm of the seven Vajjis, there was a demon.
The *Vaiśravaṇasevita-sūtra* states that Ālāpa was extremely violent;
he slaughtered countless commoners,
averaging several dozen people every day.
They all gathered together and spoke thus:
"We should avoid this country and travel far away to another realm.
When the ghost knew their thoughts, he spoke to those people, saying:
"Do not leave this place for other lands;
you shall never escape my hands.
If you bring one person to me as an offering every day, I will no longer trouble you."
At that time, the people of Vṛji were taking one person each day to sacrifice to that evil spirit;
this demon devoured human bones until they filled the streams and valleys.
At that time, there was the son of a householder named Sujāta,
who lived there possessing abundant wealth and many treasures;
his son was named Nandana.
"He has but one son; there is this restriction:
the boy Nāyula must make an offering to this spirit."
When the parents had finished bathing this child and dressed him in fine clothes, they went to the place where the ghost was;
they wailed and cried out in numbers beyond reckoning.
He spoke thus: "May all the spirits and earth-deities bear witness together:
I pray that you protect this one son of mine, so that he may be delivered from danger."
Śakra-devānām-indra and Brahmā-devaputra;
the śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgatas who have exhausted their outflows and attained arhatship, as well as pratyekabuddhas;
and even the Tathāgata himself, the most honored, supreme, and excellent field of merit.
There is none who can surpass the Tathāgata;
you should examine this.
May the Tathāgata illuminate this utmost sincerity.
Having entrusted the child to the spirit, he withdrew and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his divine eye and divine ear of far-reaching hearing and vision,
used his power of supernatural travel to go to the north of the Snowy Mountains.
He entered the abode of the pretas and sat cross-legged.
At that time, the young boy arrived at the abode of the pretas and saw from afar the Tathāgata’s radiance, brilliantly resplendent.
His body was adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics;
yet, with a heart of joy directed toward the Tathāgata,
he said, "May this evil ghost eat me as it pleases."
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Nanda, it is as you have said.
I am now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Therefore, I have come to rescue you and to subdue this ghost.
Nāyula was filled with joy and prostrated himself, touching his head to the Buddha’s feet.
Then the World-Honored One expounded the sublime Dharma to him.
Immediately upon that seat, all defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma, he took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of noble ones, and received the five precepts.
The evil spirit returned to its original place and saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting upright and motionless.
Thereupon, they give rise to wrath and anger,
raining down thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts, or raining down swords and blades;
yet before these have even fallen to the ground—
The Tathāgata has manifested a blue utpala lotus, and he has further sent down various supernatural powers to descend upon it accordingly.
The śramaṇa’s body hair does not even quiver; I shall now go to inquire about this profound meaning.
"If you cannot repay me, I shall seize your two feet and hurl you across the southern sea.
The Buddha said,
"Whether human or non-human, none shall be able to seize my two feet and hurl me across the southern sea."
"Ask whatever you wish.
Then the ghost asked:
"What are these 'old practices,' 'new practices,' and 'the practice of cessation'?"
The World-Honored One said:
"You should know that the eye is a conditioned formation (*saṃskāra*).
That which was created in the past as a condition for illness has now become a formation."
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these are past formations.

That which is created by the body, speech, and mind in this present life—namely, three of the body, four of speech, and three of the mind—this is new formation. One should know that past formations have been extinguished.
No longer arising and no longer performing formations,
one is able to take these formations such that they are forever non-arising and forever extinguished without remainder;
this is called the cessation of formations.
The ghost said to the Buddha, "I am now extremely hungry; give me back my young child.
The World-Honored One replied:
In the past, when I was a bodhisattva,
there was a dove that sought refuge with me; I did not begrudge even my own body and life in order to save that dove from its peril,
let alone now that I have already become a Tathāgata.
I can give up this child for you to devour.
You were once a śramaṇa during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha;
you cultivated the holy life, but later you violated the precepts.
Thus this evil ghost was born.
At that time, the evil ghost, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power,
immediately recalled the various karmic actions he had performed in the past.
He immediately went to where the World-Honored One was,
prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet,
and said: "I have now been foolish and deluded, unable to distinguish the true from the false."
Thereupon, he gave rise to this mind directed toward the Tathāgata, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my repentance.
Thus he did so three or four times.
The World-Honored One said,
"I grant you permission to repent.
I shall preach the sublime Dharma for you."
Then that evil spirit held up several thousand taels of gold in his hands and offered them to the World-Honored One,
saying, "I now offer these mountain valleys to the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept it from me.
The World-Honored One then accepted it and spoke this verse:
By giving garden fruits with purity, by constructing wooden bridges and building great ships,
and by providing various means of sustenance without sloth day or night, one obtains immeasurable merit.
"Having accomplished the Dharma, its meaning, and the precepts, one is reborn in the heavens after death.
The ghost asked, "What further teaching is there?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Cast off your original form, don the three dharma robes, and become a śramaṇa.
Enter the city of Vṛji and go everywhere to issue this command:
'The Tathāgata has appeared in the world; he delivers those who have not yet been delivered.'"
He causes them to attain liberation;
he is the most honored, the most supreme, the excellent and blessed field of merit.
Now he delivers the youth Nandopandara.
"And having subdued the evil spirit Viśa,
you all may go there to receive his transformation.
At that time, the spirit Viśa was in the kingdom of Vṛji.
He uttered these words.
At that time, the elder Sujāta,
having heard this speech, was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself.
Leading a multitude of eighty-four thousand people, he went to where the World-Honored One was. This concludes the eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

8. The Mother of Ghosts (*Hārītī*) First Ate People; the Buddha Concealed Her Son and She Was Then Converted. In the past, there was a woman who first ate people. The Buddha concealed her son, and she was subsequently converted. Long ago, there was a mother who...
She has many children,
who are by nature evil and devoid of compassion;
they delight in stealing the children of others to kill and devour them.
The family of the deceased child did not know who had taken it;
they wept and wailed as they walked through the alleys in this manner, not just once.
Whenever Ānanda went out, he would encounter them weeping and crying.
Having returned, they deliberated together and grieved for the family that had lost its son.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked them:
"What was the assembly discussing?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
"Just now, while going on almsround, I saw people weeping."
When questioned, they all said,
"Our children have died, and we do not know where their corpses are.
The Buddha then spoke to Ānanda.
The one who steals children in this country is no ordinary person;
she is Hariti, the Mother of Ghosts,
who has now been born as a human and delights in stealing the children of others.
This mother has a thousand sons:
five hundred sons are in the heavens,
and five hundred sons are in the human world.
The thousand sons were all kings of ghosts;
each king was followed by tens of thousands of ghosts.
Thus, these five hundred ghost-kings harassed the devas in the heavens.
Five hundred kumbhāṇḍa kings were harassing the sovereign and the people in the world;
even the gods could do nothing about these five hundred kumbhāṇḍa kings. Ānanda said:
"The Mother of Demons resides within this kingdom;
would it not be possible to issue a command that she cease stealing people's children?
The Buddha said, "Excellent."
Ānanda said, "By what skillful means?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
Upon arriving at his mother's location, once she had gone out,
he gathered her children and placed them within the vihāra;
immediately thereafter, [the mother] went to scout for them, found ten or so children, and fled into the vihāra.
When his mother came, he did not see her; thinking she was another's child, he did not dare kill her again.
He went about searching for his son, but could not find him anywhere.
Thus he wandered along the roads weeping for ten days.
The mother then beat her own breast and threw herself to the ground, looking up to heaven and crying out loudly; she no longer took food or drink.
The Buddha sent a śramaṇa to inquire after her, and she immediately replied to the śramaṇa, saying:
"I weep only because my many children have perished.
The śramaṇa spoke again:
"Do you wish to obtain children?"
He replied, "I wish to have him.
The śramaṇa said,
"If you truly wish to have him, you may go and ask the Buddha whether you can obtain your son."
Upon hearing these words,
the mother was filled with joy and her mind was liberated; she then proceeded to where the Buddha was and paid him homage.
The Buddha then asked his mother,
"Why are you weeping?
His mother replied:
"Because my son has perished," he said.
The Buddha asked,
"Have you abandoned your son?"
"To where did you go to lose your son?
The mother remained silent.
This was repeated three times.
The mother, knowing that her son had committed an evil deed by stealing,
immediately rose and paid homage,
saying, "It was because I was foolish."
The Buddha asked again:
"Do you have a son whom you love so much that you do not let him leave your side?
I too have a son whom I wish to keep by my side whenever we sit or rise."
The Buddha asked again:
"You have a son whom you know and love;
why do you go every day to steal the children of others?"
Others have children whom they love just as you do;
families who have lost their children also practice the Way by weeping just as you do.
Yet you, on the contrary, steal others' children and kill them to eat.
"After death, you shall enter the Tai Shan hell.
Would you rather have your son back?
The mother immediately prostrated herself, her head touching the ground.
"I pray that the Buddha will have compassion for me.
The Buddha said,
"If your son were here, would you not be able to repent on your own?"
"If you can repent for yourself, I shall return your son.
The mother said,
"I am able to repent."
The Buddha said,
"If you are able to repent, how should you repent?
The mother replied:
"One who hears the Buddha's teachings and observes his precepts should follow the Buddha's words.
The Buddha returned and said to his son,
"It is indeed as you have said."
He conferred upon him the five precepts.
"You have a thousand sons; I shall name them all for you.
Five hundred sons are in the heavens."
Your five hundred sons remain in the world,
harassing the devas and humans;
your son acts as a king of ghosts, leading tens of thousands of spirits.
In this way, they were beyond counting.
Some invoked the spirits of trees, the spirits of the earth, the spirits of water, as well as those of ships,
carts, houses, darkness, dreams, waking terrors, and various other strange deities.
Thus, by falsely claiming that they cause others to perform sacrifices,
they slaughter and cook living beings for food; rather than being able to protect or sustain human life,
they only increase their transgressions.
This foolish person did not realize that poverty resulted from their own past thoughts and actions.
When the Mother of Ghosts heard the Buddha’s teaching,
she repented with single-minded devotion.
He immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna and,
kneeling with his right knee on the ground, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha will have compassion for me."
I wish to dwell beside the Buddha’s vihāra;
I wish to summon my thousand sons;
I wish to cause them to enter into a covenant with the Buddha.
"I wish to repay the kindness of those in the heavens above and the humans below.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
It is most virtuous that you possess such an intention."
The Buddha said,
"Stop right there by the side of the Buddha's vihāra.
Then, among the people of that country, those who were childless—
"Whoever comes to seek a child, I shall grant them one according to their own wishes.
I shall command my son to go and protect such people,
so that he may no longer harass them recklessly."
Those who wish to seek a boon from Hārītī should address her by the name Potalaka-maṇibhadra;
her elder sister’s name is Jvalanā.
In the heavens above and the worlds below, all spirits and their subjects belong to Maṇibhadra.
Within the four seas, all who live by ship or carriage and possess property belong to Maṇibhadra.
Maṇibhadra entered into a solemn covenant with the Buddha and received the precepts.
He protects the person’s wealth and property.
If the master of the house is about to give birth, he should go to rescue her. *The Sutra of the Mother of Ghosts* (Guizimu jing), Chapter 9:
"The Yakṣa Kucumāra Invites the Buddha to Provide a Chamber and Lamp-Light. At the ninth watch, the yakṣa ghost Kucumāra invited the Buddha to provide a chamber and lamp-light.
He approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the yakṣa Kūṭadanta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,"
"I now request that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly,
spend this night here.
The World-Honored One remained silent.
At that time, Kṛmīlā manifested five hundred multi-storied pavilions, along with bedding, couches, and stools;
she provided five hundred sets of mats and pillows for each,
and further manifested five hundred lamps.
"Absence of Smoke and Flames," from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Volume 49. 10.

Māra Harasses Maudgalyāyana and He Speaks of His Former Life as a Demon King; Māra Harasses Maudgalyāyana and He Speaks of His Former Life as a Demon King (10). At that time, Maudgalyāyana was walking in meditation during the darkness of night.
The evil Māra transformed himself into a shadow and entered Maudgalyāyana’s belly.
Maudgalyāyana entered samādhi to investigate its origin and immediately spoke to the evil Māra.
Come out, come out!
Do not harass the disciples of the Buddha,
lest you suffer for a long night.
The Māra thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa has never even seen me, yet he has recklessly fabricated a falsehood."
"Even if his teacher does not yet know me,
how much less so his disciple.
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"I further knew what was in your mind;
Mara, you were already terrified that I had perceived you.
You immediately transformed your entire body so that it appeared before me."
Maudgalyāyana told Māra:
"In a past age, during the time of Krakucchanda Buddha,
I was once a Māra."
She was named Minghen (Dark Resentment).
I have an elder sister named Yankhei (Dark Black).
"You have become my son;
by this I know you are my sister's son.
At that time, the Buddha appeared in the world.
He had two disciples:
the first was named Hongyin,
and the second was named Zhixiang.
For what reason is he named "Great Sound"?
Because while dwelling in the Brahma Heaven, he utters a sound with a cough that is heard throughout the trichiliocosm.
The one who knew thoughts dwelt alone in a secluded place,
sitting beneath a tree on the mountain in meditative absorption (*samādhi-samāpatti*). As cowherds and shepherds carrying firewood and grass passed by,
they spoke to one another, saying:
After he had passed away, they cremated him together [with his disciples].
This account of Maudgalyāyana’s emergence from samādhi to enter the city for alms and his encounter with the evil Māra is also found in the twenty-seventh fascicle of the Madhyama Āgama.
11. A Ghost Obtains the Power of Mind-Reading and Harms an Enemy Woman; A Ghost Obtains the Power of Mind-Reading and Harms an Enemy Woman, Number Eleven.
Once there was a woman who was possessed by a hungry ghost (*preta*).
He then used a spell to question the ghost, saying,
"Why do you harass other women?
The ghost replied:
"This woman is my enemy; for five hundred lifetimes she has constantly killed me,
and I likewise [have killed her] for five hundred lifetimes."
I shall sever his life-force;
however, if he can relinquish his heart of old enmity,
I too can relinquish mine.
At that time, the woman spoke these words:
"I have now abandoned my hostile mind.
Although the ghost observed that the woman spoke with her mouth of having abandoned it, [he did not yet believe her].
Yet his mind did not waver;
he immediately took his life. This is extracted from the eighth fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
12. Māra Pāpīyān Harasses Mañjuśrī. Māra Pāpīyān Harasses Mañjuśrī. 12. Māra Sets Out a Feast Offering.
He manifested as forty thousand bhikṣus,
wearing soiled and tattered robes and holding broken alms bowls;
their chests and backs were entirely exposed, and their countenances were hideous.
Lame, crippled, wattle-necked, and hunchbacked, their hearts filled with anxiety,
they received various kinds of food;
Mañjuśrī caused the bowls of all these emanated beings to remain perpetually full.
As he was about to take a morsel of food into his mouth, it became stuck so that he could not swallow it.
His body grew restless and he naturally fell to the ground.
He asked Māra, "Bhikṣu, for what reason do you not eat?"
Māra said, "He is about to die.
Mañjuśrī replied:
How could a person who is free from poison ever again practice defilement or poison?
One who possesses lust, anger, and delusion is what constitutes poison.
Therefore, I preach the Dharma for them, saying, "I am free from this poison."
Five hundred devas who had followed Māra resolved their minds on *bodhicitta*.
[From] the *Mañjuśrī-vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ratnagarbha-sūtra*, Scroll Lower, Chapter 13:
"The Pretas Ask Maudgalyāyana the Causes for Their Suffering. Chapter 13: The Pretas Ask Maudgalyāyana the Causes for Their Suffering. Maudgalyāyana arrived at the banks of the Ganges.
He saw a multitude of five hundred hungry ghosts approaching the water,
where a water-guarding ghost was driving them away with an iron staff so that they could not draw near.
Thereupon, the ghosts went directly to Maudgalyāyana.
They paid homage at Maudgalyāyana’s feet and each asked about their transgressions.
One ghost said,
"Since I received this body, I have constantly suffered from heat and thirst."
Having previously heard that the waters of the Ganges were clear and cool,
he joyfully approached it, only for the boiling heat to destroy his body;
he then tried drinking a single mouthful.
"The five viscera are scorched and putrid, their stench unbearable.
By what causes and conditions has he incurred such retribution?
Maudgalyāyana said:
In your previous lives, you were a physiognomist who judged the fortune and misfortune of others;
your assessments were mostly false and rarely true.
Whether disparaging others or praising them,
they claim their own words are authentic and discerning to move the hearts of people;
through deception, delusion, and fraud, they seek wealth and profit.
Deluded sentient beings lose their wish-fulfilling things.
Again, another ghost said:
"I am constantly devoured by large dogs with sharp, reddish-white fangs that eat my flesh until only my bones remain."
The wind comes and blows upon it;
the flesh is gradually restored,
and the dog returns to devour it again.
"What is the cause of this suffering?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life,
you served as the master of a celestial shrine."
"You constantly taught sentient beings to slaughter sheep to offer their blood as sacrifice to the heavens,
and you yourself ate their flesh;
therefore, today you must repay this with flesh."
Again, another ghost said:
"I always have excrement covering my entire body; I also eat it."
"What is the cause of this offense?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In a previous life, you were a brāhmaṇa."
Malicious and unbelieving,
he took a bowl from a mendicant monk who was begging for food, filled it with excrement, placed rice on top, and gave it to the monk.
The monk took it back and ate the rice with his hand.
He defiled his hands with excrement;
for this reason, he undergoes such suffering today.
Yet another ghost said:
My belly is as vast as a large jar,
yet my throat, hands, and feet are as thin as needles; thus,
I am unable to consume food or drink.
"For what reason is this suffering?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In a previous life, you were a village headman."
Relying on their own wealth and nobility,
they indulge excessively in food and drink, treating others with contempt and disdain;
they seize the food and drink of others, leaving sentient beings hungry and distressed.
Again, another ghost said:
"I constantly go toward the latrine, desiring to eat excrement;
yet there is a great throng of ghosts who seize staffs and drive me away, so that I cannot approach the toilet."
"His body is rotting from within, stinking, and he is famished and destitute.
For what reason is he like this?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
In a previous life, you served as the master of a Buddhist monastery (*stūpa*).
While various laypeople provided offerings for the assembly of monks and prepared the necessary food and utensils,
you provided coarse provisions for the visiting monks.
The slender ones ate it themselves.
Again, another ghost said,
"My body is entirely covered with tongues that have grown."
An axe comes to cut off his tongue;
it is severed and then grows back again, and this continues without end.
For what reason does this occur?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In a previous life, you were a practitioner of the Way.
The community of monks appointed you to prepare honey syrup."
A lump of rock honey was so large that it was difficult to consume;
he hacked at it with an axe and,
with a thieving mind, ate a single mouthful.
For this reason, his tongue was cut off again.
Furthermore, another ghost said:
"I always have seven red-hot iron balls that enter directly into my mouth."
Entering their bellies, the five viscera are scorched and rotted;
they emerge only to enter again.
For what reason do they undergo this retribution?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In a previous life, you were a śrāmaṇera.
While walking with melon seeds in hand, you arrived at the place of your teacher."
Out of respect for his teacher, he showed partiality and gave him seven more [fruits] than the actual number.
Furthermore, another ghost said:
"There are always two hot iron wheels."
Beneath both my armpits,
as I turn my body, it is scorched and withered.
For what reason is this so?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In a previous life,
you made cakes for the community of monks."
With a thieving mind, he took two banners and tucked them under both his armpits.
Then another hungry ghost said,
"My ball is as large as a jar."
When walking, he carried it upon his shoulder;
when standing, he sat upon it, suffering pain with every movement.
For what reason was this so?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In a previous life, you served as a market official and habitually gave out with light scales and small measures."
They take using heavy scales and large measures;
they constantly desire great profit for themselves by exploiting and encroaching upon others.
Furthermore, another ghost said:
I always have eyes upon my two shoulders and a mouth and nose upon my chest;
I am perpetually without a head.
"For what reason is this so?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous lives, you constantly served as an executioner."
"Disciple, when you kill a criminal,
you must always maintain a joyful mind as you bind him with a rope, tie the knots, and pull."
Again, another ghost said:
"I always have hot iron needles that enter and exit my body; I suffer misery beyond all measure."
"For what reason is it so?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In a previous life, you were a horse trainer."
Or he may become a trainer of elephants.
When a horse is difficult to control,
you shall prick its feet with an iron needle.
On another occasion, when the ox was slow, he also pricked it with a needle.
Again, another ghost said,
"Fire constantly issues from my body, burning me and causing me great distress."
"For what reason is this so?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In a previous life, you were the queen of a king."
There was another consort whom the king favored greatly;
she constantly harbored jealousy and sought an opportunity to cause him harm.
It happened that the king had risen from his sleep and departed.
At that time, while his beloved consort was still sleeping and had not yet risen from bed to dress herself,
he conceived a wicked thought; coinciding with the moment she was making cakes,
he took hot sesame oil and poured it directly onto her belly.
Their bellies rot and they die immediately.
Again, another ghost said:
"There is always a whirlwind that spins my body around."
Unable to move freely as they please from place to place,
their minds are constantly distressed and oppressed.
For what reason is this so?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In your previous lives, you were frequently a diviner;
at times you spoke the truth, and at times you spoke falsely."
The minds of people are deluded and cannot act as they wish.
Furthermore, another ghost said:
"My body is always like a lump of flesh."
Lacking feet, eyes, ears, noses, and so forth,
they are constantly devoured by insects and birds;
their suffering from transgression is unbearable.
"For what reason? [He] replied, "In a previous life,
you constantly gave others medicine to cause them to miscarry their fetuses."
Another ghost further said:
"There is always a hot iron cage that ensnares my body."
"Burning with feverish heat and filled with anguish,
for what reason do you undergo this?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"In a previous life, you constantly used nets to capture fish and birds.
Furthermore, another ghost said,
"I used objects to cover and conceal my head."
Furthermore, they are constantly afraid that someone will come to kill them;
their minds are perpetually terrified and filled with unbearable dread.
For what reason is this so?
He replied, "In your previous lives,
you committed sexual misconduct with the wives of others and were constantly afraid of being seen by people;
you feared that their husbands would seize you, bind you, beat you, or kill you."
Or they fear being executed by the laws of the state in the marketplace;
their terror continues without end. Then, another ghost asked:
I have received this body,
upon whose shoulders there is always a copper vessel filled with molten copper;
holding a ladle in my hand, I take it and pour it over my own head.
Their entire bodies were scorched and withered;
thus they suffered for countless and immeasurable eons.
What crime or fault did they commit?
He replied, "In a previous life,
you left the household life to pursue the Way and served as a monastic official in charge of food and drink."
He secretly hid a jar of ghee elsewhere;
when visiting practitioners of the Way arrived, he did not give it to them.
After they had departed, he took out the ghee and gave it to the resident monks.
"This ghee is the property of the Saṃgha of the four quarters; everyone has an equal share in it.
Although this person concealed it, even though the distribution was not equal, for this reason he incurs this offense. This is from the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra*.
14. When the evil spirits saw that Śakra’s form was somewhat ugly, they vanished. Thus ends the fourteenth [section]. Śakra-devānām-indra was in the Hall of Universal Assembly.
He enjoyed himself in mutual pleasure with the jade maidens.
At that time, a certain son of heaven addressed Śakra, saying:
"Goyiṅ, you should know."
"Now there is an evil spirit upon my honored seat.
Now that the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are filled with extreme wrath, this spirit has become exceptionally handsome, its countenance surpassing that of ordinary beings.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
"This ghost must be a divine and wondrous spirit.
He went to the place where the ghost was located, not far away,
and announced his own name.
"I am Śakra Devānām Indra, the lord of the devas.
The evil spirits have become increasingly hideous and loathsome.
Thus it was gradually extinguished and emerged [as recorded] in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Volume 27.
15. A Ghost Returns to Whip Its Own Corpse. Once, in a foreign land, there was a man who died;
his spirit returned and whipped its own corpse.
A bystander asked, "This person is already dead; why do you whip him again?
He replied:
"This was my former body;
it committed evil for me.
It saw the sutras and precepts but did not read them."
They commit theft and fraud; they violate the wives of others;
they are unfilial toward their parents and siblings;
and they are stingy with wealth, refusing to practice generosity.
"Now that I am dying, it causes me to fall into the evil realms, where the diligent suffering and piercing pain are beyond description.
For this reason, I have come to lash him. — From the *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Similes).

Section on Miscellaneous Beasts and Animals (47). 1. The Lion. First: The Lion King Attempts to Give Up His Life for a Monkey. Second:
The Lion King Possesses Eleven Superior Qualities. Third: The Lion Dies from Choking While Eating an Elephant; the Woodpecker Pulls It Out and He Revives.
1. Later, he forgot his gratitude; 2. the three lion cubs were killed by a hunter and were reborn together in the house of a *śreṣṭhin*, where they attained the Way;
3. the Lion King fell into a well and was rescued by a jackal; 4. the Lion and the Tiger were betrayed by the double-tongued jackal, who caused them to split apart and lose their lives;
5. the Lion and twelve other animals successively taught one another; 6. [The seventh item follows as indicated in the source numbering.]
1. The Lion King Wishing to Sacrifice His Life for a Monkey.
Once upon a time, there was a lion king.
Dwelling in a cave deep in the mountains,
he constantly thought to himself:
"I am the king among all beasts."
His power enabled him to see and protect all the beasts.
In the mountains there were two monkeys who had together fathered two young ones.
Then the two monkeys asked the lion king:
"If you, O King, can protect all animals,
we now entrust our two children to you."
"I wish to go elsewhere to seek food and drink.
The lion king then granted him permission.
The monkey left his two children as a trust and departed immediately.
At that time, there was a king of vultures in the mountains named Li-jian (利見).
While the lion king was asleep, [the vulture...]
Even though he seized the two young monkeys and stayed in a precarious place,
the lion king immediately woke up and spoke to the vulture:
"I now earnestly entreat you: please release him for me; do not let him break his word and cause me shame.
The King of Vultures replied:
"I am able to fly through the air; I pass through your realm without fear."
"If you wish to protect your two children, for my sake you should sacrifice your body.
The lion replied:
"I shall now protect my two children; I will cast away my body like withered grass."
Having recited this verse— "How can one who guards their own body yet speaks falsely be called a practitioner?"—
he immediately went to a high place, intending to cast off his body.
The King of Vultures spoke again:
"Because he was able to sacrifice his own body, He shall receive unsurpassed bliss.
I give you back, little monkey; I pray that the King does not harm himself. —From the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Volume Three.
2. The Lion King has eleven superior qualities. The Lion King has eleven superior qualities: second, the Lion King is born and dwells in deep mountain valleys.
His cheeks were square and his jawbones prominent; his body was fleshy and well-filled.
His head was large and his eyes long; his eyebrows were high and broad.
His mouth and nose were deep and square, and his teeth were even and sharp.
His tongue protrudes, red and white; his two ears are high and prominent.
His spine is long and his waist is slender, with no protruding belly.
He has six tusks, a long tail, and a mane of glossy, lustrous hair.
Knowing full well his own strength, fangs, and sharp claws,
he plants his four feet firmly upon the ground, dwells securely in his rocky cave, and, lashing his tail, lets out a roar.
Should anyone possess such characteristics as these:
One should know that when the true lion king emerges from his den at dawn, stretches his body and yawns,
surveys the four directions, and lets out a thunderous roar.
It was for eleven reasons:
first, to destroy one who is not actually a lion but falsely pretends to be a lion;
second, to test his own physical strength.
Third, he orders that the dwelling place be purified.
Fourth, he causes his son to know the location.
Fifth, he ensures that the group has no feelings of fear.
Sixth, those who are asleep shall awaken.
Seventh, no beasts will dare to be heedless.
Eighth, all beasts will come to seek refuge and depend upon him.
Ninth, taming the great fragrant elephant;
tenth, addressing his sons;
eleventh, adorning his retinue.
Whenever they hear the lion’s roar,
aquatic creatures remain hidden in the depths,
and land-dwelling animals retreat to their burrows.
Flying high, he fell;
the fragrant elephant in the stable shook itself, snapped its chains, and fled in terror,
dropping dung like a jackal.
Although one may study the lion for as many as a hundred or a thousand years,
one will ultimately never be able to let out the lion’s roar; yet,
if a lion cub is born and reaches only three years of age, it can immediately roar with a thunderous cry.
On the path to Mount Gandhamādana there were lions;
birds and wild beasts had ceased their tracks and did not venture to look upon it. All animals—
The Lion as Supreme: The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 25; also from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. 3.

The Lion Who Ate an Elephant and Died from a Throat Obstruction; the Wood-Wren Who Saved Him and Was Later Forgotten. After the lion ate an elephant and died from a throat obstruction, the wood-wren pulled out the bone and he was restored to life, yet later he forgot the bird's kindness. The Three Buddhas told Maudgalyāyana: [the story continues].
The Bodhisattva Yongzhi was once a lion king during the time of the Buddha Guangming; at that time,
I was a brahmin practicing pure conduct.
At that time, the lion king stood motionless in eight postures during the early morning;
shaking his body, he let out a great thunderous roar,
causing the running beasts to crouch in fear and the flying birds to fall from the sky.
Only then did he rise.
He traversed the wilderness, mountains, and marshes throughout his domain, searching for herds of wild animals;
he encountered an elephant king, whom he killed and ate.
When the spleen-bone became stuck in his throat and he died only to revive, he told the wood-wagtail:
"Help me extract this bone.
Later, when you find food, you shall repay my kindness."
Upon hearing this, the woodpecker entered its mouth and pulled out the bone with all its might,
whereupon it was able to depart. Later that day, when the lion king went out to seek food and slaughtered many beasts,
the woodpecker remained by his side and asked for a small favor, but the lion did not grant it.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"At that time, the lion king replied to the woodpecker with this verse:"
I am the Lion King; killing is my ancestral profession.
I devour flesh and drink blood; this is my constant meal.
Since you failed to measure yourself, you have escaped my fangs and emerged from the peril.
"Having escaped from my mouth, how could this kindness ever be forgotten?
At that time, the wood-sparrow again spoke this verse.
He replied to the lion cub:
"Though I am but a small bird, I recognize kindness and do not spare my life for it;
yet since Your Majesty does not acknowledge this kindness, I myself shall honor the weight of my own vow."
"If you could be slightly more generous and bestow even a small measure of grace upon me,
I would have no regrets even unto death and would not dare to offer any criticism.
At that time, the Lion King did not repay his kindness at all.
They abandoned him and departed.
The wooden sparrow thought to itself:
"My kindness was most profound, yet I have instead been treated with contempt."
We shall now pursue you and wait for an opportunity to seize you.
One who fails to repay kindness will never move through this world;
wherever you may be, we shall never part from you.
At that time, the lion king again slaughtered a herd of beasts and ate them at his pleasure.
Once satiated, he fell asleep, free from all fear.
Then, that woodpecker flew toward the lion.
He raised his head and exerted all his strength and power to peck at one eye until it was destroyed.
The lion started in alarm and looked around left and right, but saw no other beasts;
he saw only the woodpecker remaining alone upon the tree.
Then the lion king said to the woodpecker,
"Why have you now destroyed my eyes?
At that time, the woodpecker replied to him with a verse:
Failing to recognize the weight of this kindness, you have instead conceived a heart of malice;
now that I have spared you one eye, how could you ever forget this grace?
Though you are the king among beasts, your conduct is devoid of constancy.
From this point on, each took their leave; do not create further conditions for conflict.
The Lion King was the present-day Vīrajñāna Bodhisattva.
The wood-sparrow was the present-day Maudgalyāyana. (Excerpted from the ninth fascicle of the *Bodhisattvālaṃkāra Sūtra*).

5. The Lion King Falls into a Well and is Rescued by a Jackal. In a past life, not far from the foot of the Snowy Mountains, there was a lion king who fell into a well and was rescued by a jackal. (Fifth)
There was a lion, king of beasts,
who was the lord of five hundred lions.
In later years, this lion king became old, sickly, emaciated, and his eyes grew dim.
While he was walking ahead of the lions, he fell into an empty well.
All five hundred lions abandoned him and departed.
At that time, a jackal saw the lion king.
He thought to himself:
"The reason I have obtained this peaceful dwelling in the forest and am so well-satisfied with flesh is due to the lion king.
Now that he has fallen into such a dire situation, how shall I repay his kindness?"
At that time, there was a channel of flowing water by the side of this well.
The jackal then said,
"I shall divert the water with my feet."
As the water entered the full well, a lion emerged floating upon it.
Then this forest deity spoke these verses:
Though one's own body may be strong and vigorous, one should take weakness as a friend;
even a small jackal can save [one]. The Lion King was in a well.
The Buddha said: "The Lion King was my own self."
The five hundred lions were the bhikṣus; the jackal was Ānanda.
(From the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-kṣudraka*, Fascicle 1).
6. The Lions and Tigers as Good Friends; the Jackal with Divisive Speech Loses His Life by Splitting Their Bodies. Sixth: In a past life, beneath the Snowy Mountains, there were two beasts.
One was named Fine-Maned Lion and the other Fine-Fanged Tiger;
they were good friends who would close their eyes and lick one another.
These two beasts always obtain and eat soft, fine meat.
Not far from them, there was a two-tongued jackal who thought to himself:
I went to the side of the two animals and said,
"I shall act as your third companion;
allow me to enter."
The lion and the tiger said, "As you wish.
The jackal engaged in slanderous speech and grew fat by eating the remains of the two beasts' carcasses.
He then had this thought:
This fine-haired lion and this fine-toothed tiger act as virtuous friends to one another, cherishing each other with mutual affection;
they close their eyes to lick one another and constantly devour choice meat.
"If I cannot escape at this time, I shall certainly be devoured by him.
I will first employ skillful means to cause his mind to become detached from me.
She then spoke to the lion:
"The tiger harbors ill will toward you, O lion;
that he devours [his prey] is entirely due to my power.
The lion said:
"How can this be known?
The two-tongued jackal replied,
"O Tiger, when you see him tomorrow, you shall know it to be an evil omen if he closes his eyes and licks your fur."
He went and said to the tiger:
"The lion harbors ill will toward you,
saying that whatever is eaten is solely through his power."
The tiger asked,
"How can this be known? He replied:
"When I see you tomorrow, I shall know it as an evil omen if you close your eyes and lick my fur.
Between these two companions,
the tiger conceived a sense of fear.
Therefore, he went first to Siṃha and said,
"Have you conceived an evil mind toward me?
Siṃha replied:
"Who spoke these words? He replied,
"A two-tongued jackal."
Haomao asked again,
"Have you also conceived an evil thought toward me?
The tiger replied, "No."
The tiger said to the lion,
"If you possess such evil speech as this, you cannot be my virtuous friend.
The one with beautiful fur replied:
This sly jackal of double-tongued speech spoke these words:
"Why do you not take pleasure in dwelling with me?
He then uttered this verse:
If one trusts such an evil person, one will quickly be separated from them;
one will harbor sorrow and grief, and resentment will not leave the mind.
One who acts as a true spiritual friend does not allow others' words to cause difficulty.
Those who lack faith and wish to eliminate it— if they believe in the separation of others,
they will be devoured by them; those who lack faith in divisive speech,
they instead bring about reconciliation and speak what they harbor toward one another.
With a pure mind and gentle speech, one should act as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
harmonizing like water and milk; yet this wretched little insect,
from birth its nature has been evil— having but one head and two tongues.
Having verified the facts regarding the tiger and the lion, [the text] records that they together seized the jackal and tore it into two parts.

This appears in the *Ten-Recitation Vinaya* (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*), Part Three; again, it appears in the ninth fascicle of the same, with identical wording; it also appears in the sixth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*; and it also appears in the *Sūtra on the Jackal’s Divisive Speech*, which is largely the same.

These twelve animals constantly travel within Jambudvīpa day and night;

Day and night, one beast was constantly sent forth to wander and teach,
while the remaining eleven beasts remained settled in the cultivation of loving-kindness;

On the first day of the seventh month, the mice first go abroad;

In this manner, proceeding in sequence until the thirteenth day,
the mouse again began its journey;
and so it continued through the entire twelfth month, and likewise for twelve years.
Therefore, this land possesses many merits;
even beasts and animals can be transformed through its teachings.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas from other directions—
One should always pay respectful homage to this Buddha-world.
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who wish to behold these twelve animals, [they should do so].
If one desires to attain great wisdom, great meditative concentration, and great supernormal powers;
if one desires to receive all existing scriptures;
and if one desires to increase wholesome dharmas.
This person should fashion a mountain out of white clay,
seven feet in length and breadth and twelve feet in height,
anointing it with various fragrances and gilding it with thin gold leaf.
Its four sides shall be twenty feet in circumference.
The *campaka* flowers to be scattered should be placed in copper vessels.
Various kinds of non-seasonal juices should be set out on the four sides.
Maintaining pure precepts, bathing three times a day,
and with reverence and faith in the Triple Gem,
one should stand exactly three *zhang* to the east of the mountain.
Recite this mantra while remaining for fifteen days;
on a mountain peak, one shall see the image of the new moon.
At that time, one will know how to perceive the twelve animals.
Having seen them, one’s aspirations will be fulfilled according to one’s wishes;
they may also be attained by practicing asceticism.
With one's own eyes, one beholds these twelve animals, who are all bodhisattvas.
Sometimes manifesting as celestial beings, sometimes as spirits, or as the forms of birds and beasts,
he wanders through Jambudvīpa to teach and transform such various sentient beings.
Whether appearing as humans or devas, he tames and transforms sentient beings accordingly.
This is not difficult. To tame sentient beings who are like elephants is truly difficult. [From] the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Volume 24. 2. The Elephant:

The Second Elephant King Makes Offerings to the Buddha. I. The Elephant King Makes Offerings to the Buddha. The Buddha was traveling alone, seeking a place of quietude and seclusion. At that time, there was a noble elephant king named Sunivāsin (Well-Abiding). He was a precious elephant belonging to a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). When the elephant cub was born, it lost its mother and was raised by a rishi. The elephant, the monkey, and the jīvañjīvaka bird were all mutually respectful. [End of Section] 1. The Elephant King Makes Offerings to the Buddha. The Buddha was traveling alone, desiring to seek tranquility.
He arrived at the country of Kośala and stayed beneath a precious tree in the Pāriyātra-sālavana forest.
At that time, there was a herd of five hundred elephants,
with the elephant king always walking at the rear.
Constantly obtaining only turbid water and withered grass,
he grew weary of his herd and came alone beneath a tree.
From afar, he saw the Buddha.
He used his trunk to pull up grass and trample the ground to level it;
he used his trunk to take up water and sprinkle it to settle the dust, then spread the grass to serve as a seat.
Bending his knees, he invited the Buddha to sit.
He made offerings for three months.
The Buddha, knowing the elephant's intention,
immediately accepted his invitation.
And he spoke in verse:
"Alone and virtuous, free from sorrow, Like an elephant in the wild wilderness, Delighting in the training of the precepts— What need has one for companions?
—Thus spoke the Elephant King at that time.
She took a fine lotus root, washed it clean,
and offered it to the World-Honored One.
Thus ends the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

2. The Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita as the Jewel of the Wheel-Turning King. There was an elephant king named Supratiṣṭhita. He served as the jewel of the wheel-turning king. II.1. There was an elephant king called Supratiṣṭhita.
The body is pure white with seven parts level and even;
it has the power of flight,
a crimson head, and body hair of variegated colors.
With six tusks, slender and elegant,
he has eight thousand elephant kings as his retinue and dwells beneath a śāla tree on Mount Gandhamādana.
The King of Śāla Trees has eight thousand bathing pools,
each fifty yojanas in length and breadth;
their waters are cool and refreshing, and they are surrounded by moats made of the seven treasures.
Flowers of five colors were gathered within the pond.
When the Elephant King thought of entering the pond, eight thousand elephants arrived in response to his thought.
Some held parasols and fans.
Some acted as precursors, chanting praises;
some elephant kings washed their tails, backs, thighs, and feet;
and some plucked flower roots to give to the king for his food.
Some gathered flowers and scattered them over the King;
eight thousand elephants likewise bathed, frolicked together,
and relieved themselves of urine and excrement.
The various yakṣas and ghosts moved [the elephant] outside the mountain forest. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there is a palace of the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita at Lake Anavatapta.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states:

Beside Mount Gandhamādana there were eighty-four thousand white elephants; the lowest among those ridden by Śakra Devendra was the one called Elephant-Treasure (hastiratna), which a Wheel-turning Sage King (cakravartin) would ride.
Within Mount Kāñcanapārśva, there are eighty thousand rock caves where eighty thousand elephants dwell and rest;
their bodies are pure white in color.
Its head is variegated in color, and its mouth has large fangs;
the gaps between its teeth are filled with gold. This is recorded in the eighteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, as well as in the *Ekottara Āgama* and the *Loutan Jing*.
3. A young elephant was born and lost its mother, being raised by a rishi. A young elephant was born and lost its mother, being raised by a rishi. Long ago, in a past age.
There was a solitary elephant living in seclusion who gave birth to a single cub;
not long after it had fallen to the ground, [the mother died].
His mother passed away.
Not far from that place was a dwelling of a seer possessed of majestic spiritual power.
Endowed with merit and harboring great compassion,
he saw from afar that the mother elephant had passed away and her calf could only just lift its feet.
Unable to support himself while traveling abroad in the East and West,
he was immediately escorted back to his residence and provided with fruit for food and drink.
At that time, the elephant cub was gentle,
kind, virtuous, and possessed of exquisite merit;
he delighted in the principles of righteousness.
Having attained peace and security, free from all anxiety and affliction,
the rishi thereafter slept and rose in the same place;
his body grew increasingly tall, and his hair and fur became bright and lustrous.
He then offered water and gruel to the rishi, as well as his choice fruits and melons,
before eating himself.
The rishi, moved by compassion, observed his virtuous conduct and cherished him like a son, gazing upon him without weariness.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately gave rise to this thought:
"This rishi’s mind is now fixed upon the elephant calf; his longing for it is insatiable.
I should now cause him to feel a different kind of sorrow."
At that time, Śakra manifested a trial by causing the elephant calf to suddenly die on the ground, its blood flowing and spilling.
When the seer saw the elephant calf dead, he was filled with grief and wept.
Other rishis heard of this and came to admonish and console him,
but they could not dispel his grief.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was dwelling in the void.
He spoke a verse for the sake of the rishi.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, restored the elephant calf to life.
The rishi was greatly delighted.
The seer and elder was this very person;
the deceased elephant calf was his disciple;
and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was myself. Thus it is stated in the *Buddhabhāṣitaśrāvakamaraṇadoṣasūtra*.

4. The Elephant, the Monkey, and the Cakravāka Bird as Friends. Regarding the elephant, the monkey, and the cakravāka bird being friends together: in a past life, there were three friends—an elephant, a monkey, and a cakravāka bird (*jīvañjīvaka*).
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle 27, they lived together in a single nyagrodha tree. Today we call this bird the *diántuó* (cakravāka). They dwelt together in that one nyagrodha tree.
They said to one another,
"Since we all depend upon this same tree, we should treat each other with respect.
Then the monkey and the francolin bird asked the elephant:
"Do you remember how long ago this occurred?
The elephant replied, "I remember when I was small; this tree reached up to my belly."
The elephant and the lapwing questioned the monkey.
The monkey replied, "I remember when I was small, this tree reached up to my hands and head. (The *Saṃghāṭī-vinaya* says: "He urinated on this tree. The elephant said to the monkey: [text fragment].
"You are older than I.
The elephant and the monkey both questioned the partridge,
and the partridge said:
"I recall that on the right side of the Snowy Mountains there was a great nyagrodha tree.
After eating its fruit and coming here, it immediately took root and grew into this very tree.
Thus they spoke to one another.
The francolin had lived for many years.
The elephant placed the monkey upon its head,
and the monkey placed the francolin upon its shoulder.
They traveled together through the human world,
from village to village and from town to town.
He often spoke this verse:
"If a person can embrace the Dharma And always respect their elders,
They will enjoy renown in the present life And be reborn in a good realm in the future."
At that time, the francolin partridge preached this Dharma.
All people followed his instructions, and the teaching spread.
You have all gone forth as monastics within my Dharma.
"You should further show mutual respect.
In this way, the Buddha-dharma will spread.
From this day forward, I permit you to pay respects, prostrate, welcome, and inquire after one another's welfare according to seniority."
At that time, the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s instruction.

The bhikṣus, arranged according to their seniority, paid respectful homage. [End of] Volume Three of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Also from the seventh fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the sixth section on the "Seven Dharmas."
3. The Horse: Chapter Three, Part One. The Brahmacārin Horse King as a Wheel-Turning King’s Jewel. There was a horse king named Brahmacārin. He served as the jewel of a wheel-turning monarch.
The palace resides on Mount Candraprabha within the island of the great ocean.
It has eight thousand horses as its retinue.
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, [these appear].
Taking the smallest one to serve as the Horse-Treasure (*aśvaratna*) for the king’s carriage, it was presented from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 4.

**The Great Ox Sold and Escaping to Approach the Tathāgata: The Buddha Explains Past Causes Leading to Rebirth in Heaven.** 1. There was a man from a distant land. [The following sections follow: - The Great Ox Sold and Escaping to Approach the Tathāgata: The Buddha Explains Past Causes Leading to Rebirth in Heaven. - A Water-Buffalo King Endures the Insult of a Monkey. - Two Bulls Compete in Strength and Pulling Loads. - The Householder’s Ox Speaks of His Own Previous Life: Having Borrowed One Thousand Coins, He Was Reborn as an Ox Three Times Without Repaying Them. **1. The Great Ox Sold and Escaping to Approach the Tathāgata: The Buddha Explains Past Causes Leading to Rebirth in Heaven.** There was a man from a distant land. [Text continues.]
He sold a large ox—
plump, vigorous, and strong—
to a person from the city of Śrāvastī.
The city-dwellers purchased him intending to kill him.
While he was at the city gate, he encountered the Buddha.
From afar, the ox beheld the Buddha.
With a heart of mingled grief and joy,
he broke his shackles and fled, such that no one could restrain him;
he went straight toward the Tathāgata and bowed down before his two feet.
Crying out in lamentation with tears streaming from his mouth, he spoke these words himself:
