her tears flowing freely as she did so.
He spoke these verses separately:
"This morning I walked and met with misfortune; by error I fell into the hands of a hunter.
This very moment I am to be butchered and sliced; my body shall be crushed and turned to rotting pulp."
"I remember how you came seeking my compassion; now you must return to face death.
Pity you, who were orphaned so young! Strive to survive on your own.
Having spoken thus, the mother deer departed and left her.
The two children wailed with piteous tears, longing for her;
they followed after her, collapsing and rising again.
Their mother turned back and commanded them, saying:
"Go back and do not come here.
Do not let mother and child perish together;
my heart grieves at the thought of our deaths."
"You do not yet realize that all things in this world are impermanent and subject to separation.
My own fate is meager and I have been without protection since you were born;
why harbor such grief, for it only serves to increase your suffering?"
"One must simply establish one's resolve and dedicate one's life.
Thereupon, the mother spoke these verses again for her son:
"In my previous lives I was driven by craving; now I have come, yet still hold fast to this body out of attachment."
All those born in the world must die; none escape this ultimate affliction.
By restraining the mind and abandoning greed, one thereafter attains great peace and security.
To speak with faith regarding death is never to deceive oneself in life.
The son, still grieving and longing, cried out as he searched for him,
wandering back and forth until he reached the place where the corpse lay.
There he sought him everywhere, east and west.
Then he saw a hunter lying beneath a tree;
the mother deer stood still and spoke a verse to awaken him, saying:
The deer previously released has now returned to face death;
you have bestowed such grace upon this lowly beast that it may bid farewell to its two young ones.
As you prepare to depart, show me water and grass, and for my sake, speak of the suffering of impermanence.
"May ten thousand perish without a lingering regret; mindful of your kindness, I dare not betray you.
At this, the hunter suddenly awoke from his dream in a startle.
The deer once again knelt before him.
He spoke again in verse:
"Having been released by you before my eyes, His virtue is weightier than heaven and earth;
Though a lowly beast, he is covered by your compassion, And out of faith, he comes to face death."
Feeling that the benevolent grace is difficult to forget, I dare not disobey your command;
though I have returned to repay you, I still cannot fully exhaust my record of gratitude.
When the hunter saw the deer, he was moved by its profound faith and its death for the sake of righteousness.
His will and integrity were of crimson sincerity, and his compassionate conduct gave rise to loyalty.
When he was released in accordance with a divine sign, he cast aside his life to fulfill his vow;
mother and son, bound by grief and longing, sought one another until they met.
Moved by compassion and pity,
he bowed his head in apology and said:
"The heavenly deities and the spirits possess such wondrous faith and righteousness."
My heart trembles with fear; how could I dare commit such a rebellious injury?
It would be better to take my own wretched life than to bring harm upon my wife and children.
How could I bear to direct even a hair’s breadth of thought toward the Divine Spirit?
The hunter immediately released the deer, allowing them to depart.
Mother and child, filled with both sorrow and joy, uttered their plaintive cries;
they then offered verses of thanks to the hunter.
Born into the lowly state of an animal in this world, he ought to be sent to the kitchen to be slaughtered and cooked immediately;
yet, out of broad benevolence, the Son of Heaven declined to harm his two sons,
valuing compassion and cherishing all living things, so that they were again granted pardon and release.
His accumulated merit was immeasurable, beyond what could be fully described by word of mouth;
the hunter reported it all to the King,
and the people of the land came to know it all.
All were moved to feel compassion and faith;
the benevolence displayed in his hunting surpassed that of ordinary righteousness,
such that everyone could not help but sigh with solemn admiration.
To stop the killing of the hunt, the deer returned to their groups and howled to their companions; they gathered together, each finding peace in its own place.
The Buddha said:
The deer at that time was my own self;
the two sons were Rāhula and Maudgalyāyana;
and the king at that time was Śāriputra.
The hunter Ānanda is mentioned in the *Mṛgajā-sūtra*.
2. The Deer King who, when captured, sacrificed his own body to save the herd of deer. Long ago, a king went out on a hunting expedition.
He constructed a trap with moats to capture herds of deer.
At that time, a deer king leading several hundred million deer came to graze on the delicious grass and entered the enclosure.
The guards closed the gates and went to inform the king.
The king was greatly delighted.
The deer king immediately understood this and thought to himself,
"The reason this herd of deer has come is solely because of my own person."
He devised a plan to save the lives of the multitude;
he immediately lay his body crosswise across the moat so that the herd of deer could trample over his back and escape.
His foot was so severely wounded that the skin and flesh were completely destroyed,
leaving only bone; yet,
enduring the pain, he rescued them, and they all managed to escape.
The deer king stepped onto the shore and looked in all four directions;
there was but a single deer who did not know how to seek escape.
The deer king called out to it, and it came forth and emerged.
Thereupon the king of deer’s life ended and he fell into the moat. [From] the *Daśa-varga-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Eight.

8. Mṛga-mṛga, Part Eight. 1. Mṛga Deer Skins His Hide to Save the Hunter’s Life. Mṛga Deer Skins His Hide to Save the Hunter’s Life, Number One. Once the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha.
His body was afflicted by a wind disorder,
so Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, prepared a medicinal ghee using thirty-two ingredients.
He consumed thirty-two *liang* every day.
At that time, Devadatta constantly harbored jealousy;
his mind was puffed up with pride, and he aspired to be equal to the Buddha.
The physician also applied medicinal ointments to his various channels and veins;
his physical strength became feeble, and he groaned in bitter distress.
The World-Honored One, out of compassion, stroked his head with his hand.
When the medicine was digested and the illness removed, [the king] observed and recognized it as the Buddha’s hand.
He said, "Siddhārtha has mastered other arts that the world does not yet employ; he shall further study the way of medicine."
The Buddha said,
"Devadatta has harbored unwholesome intentions not only today.
Long ago, in Jambudvīpa, there was a city named Vārāṇasī."
The king was named Brahmadatta;
he was cruel and devoid of compassion.
He dreamed of a beast.
The hair on his body was golden in color, with the tips of the hairs emitting golden light.
He immediately summoned a hunter and told him everything about his dream.
"You all must search for and capture it.
If you obtain its skin, I shall grant you a heavy reward;
if you do not, I shall exterminate your clans."
At that time, the hunters, distressed and bewildered, gathered together to deliberate and plan.
They agreed to recruit one person to go and search for him, promising:
"If you do not return with good news, we shall also provide goods for your wife and children."
The man thought to himself,
"I must cast aside my life and proceed.
He then set out across the perilous terrain.
After a long time, his body grew frail;
the weather was hot and humid, stifling him as if he were dying.
In deep distress, he spoke:
"Who possesses the compassion to save my life?
There was a wild beast named Mṛga whose body hair was golden;
having heard this, he felt profound pity.
His body entered the cold spring, whereupon [the man] came forward to wrap him in his arms;
though small, he still possessed strength and led him to the water's edge to bathe him, and gathered fruit for him to eat.
Once his body had recovered,
he thought to himself:
"Now I see that this king of beasts is truly seeking me."
However, as I was on the verge of death, I relied upon him to save my life.
Having not yet repaid his kindness, with what heart could I harm him?
If I do not obtain [the fruit of my merit], [it will be lost].
"Those hunters will surely be executed.
Thinking this, he was moved by compassion.
Mṛgāra asked him, "Why are you not happy?"
He answered according to what was in his mind, speaking in the Mleccha tongue:
"Do not worry about this; my skin is easy to obtain."
Throughout countless lifetimes, I have never performed meritorious deeds;
now, by offering my own skin, I shall save the lives of those multitudes.
Whatever merit may be gained from this, [let it be for their benefit].
"Simply flay the skin; do not take its life.
I shall give it to you and will never have cause for regret.
The hunter then flayed the skin.
Ming-ta immediately made this vow:
"I now offer my skin to this person to save their precious life."
He took these merits and bestowed them upon those sentient beings,
vowing to attain the Buddha-way to universally deliver all;
having made this vow, the three thousandfold world-system shook in six ways.
After the skin has been flayed and the flesh of the body removed, leaving it naked and with blood flowing and dripping,
eighty thousand species of flies and ants gather upon its body and devour it all at once.
At that time, as he was about to enter the hole, he feared being harmed;
enduring the pain, he steadied himself and remained motionless, dying therein.
At that time, those flies and ants that had eaten [the flesh] died and were reborn in heaven.
The hunter carried the hide to the king;
when the king saw it, he marveled at its excellence and constantly spread it out to lie upon.
Their bodies and minds were peaceful, secure, and joyful.
The one named Vemacitra was my very self at that time; King Brahmadatta was Devadatta.
"When I first attained Buddhahood and began to turn the Wheel of Dharma, eighty thousand worms [attained realization];
the eighty thousand devas above who attained the Way are recorded in the third fascicle of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* (Xianyu jing)."

9. The Wild Fox, Chapter Nine, Number One: The Wild Fox Who Begged Food from a Lion, Grew Fat, and Was Afterwards Eaten by the Lion. A certain wild fox went to a lion to beg for food. Having grown fat from what he received, he was later eaten by the lion. Once, there was a wild fox who went to a lion to beg for food.
Whenever he obtained leftovers, he went there and ate them without ceasing.
It happened that a lion was hungry and had not yet found food;
he called out to the wild fox, who sniffed him and then swallowed him whole.
Before he died, he called out from his throat,
saying, "Master, save me!
The Lion thought to himself:
"I have been nourishing you with your thick fur; you should keep it for your own needs.
Why do you further claim to have produced ten fascicles of the *Avadāna-śataka* (Piyu jing)? 10.

The Wolf Who Obtained the Power to Know Others' Minds and Harm His Enemy’s Daughter and Infant. Part One of the Eighth Division: The Wolf Who Obtained the Power to Know Others' Minds and Harm His Enemy’s Daughter and Infant. There was a woman who placed her infant in a certain spot."
The wolf carried the child away and fled.
People who were pursuing it caught up with it and said to it,
"For what reason are you now carrying another's child away?"
The wolf replied,
"The mother of this child is my enemy;
for five hundred lifetimes, she has constantly devoured my children."
I, too, have constantly killed my own sons for five hundred lifetimes.
If he can relinquish his heart of old enmity,
I, too, can relinquish mine.
At that time, the people said to the boy’s mother,
“You should abandon your heart of enmity.
The boy’s mother replied:
"I have now abandoned him," the wolf said,
observing the mother of the child;
though her mouth spoke of abandonment, her heart did not let go.
[He] harmed [them] and departed. Excerpted from the *Abhidharma* (*Vibhāṣā*), fascicle twenty-eight. 11. The Monkey. Chapter Eleven:

The Monkey and the Four Beasts Forming Karmic Connections with a Brahmin; One Monkey Offering Honey from a Bowl to the Buddha; Two Monkeys Serving as Teachers for Five Hundred Seers; Three: Five Hundred Monkeys Imitating Arhats by Building a Stūpa; Four: A Monkey Learning Meditation, Falling from a Tree, and Reborn in Heaven; Five: A Monkey Sporting with a Maidservant. 1. The Monkey and the Four Beasts Forming Karmic Connections with a Brahmin. The monkey and the four beasts formed karmic connections with a Brahmin. Once, there was a Brahmin one hundred and twenty years of age.
In his youth, he did not marry and remained free from lustful excesses.
He dwelt in deep mountains, making his hut of thatch and his mat of wild weeds; he sustained himself on fruits and melons.
He did not accumulate wealth or treasures;
when the king sent messengers to summon him, he would not go,
remaining upright and inactive for more than several thousand years, sporting with birds and beasts.
There are four kinds of beasts:
the first is named the fox;
the second is the macaque.
Third, otters; fourth, rabbits.
These four animals listened to the discourse on the Dharma and the recitation of the precepts given by the practitioner.
Thus, after a long time had passed,
all the fruits and melons he ate were completely exhausted.
Later, the practitioner wished to depart.
These four great beasts were sorrowful and unhappy;
they deliberated together, saying,
"Let us each seek offerings for ourselves."
The monkey took sweet fruit and came to offer it to the practitioner.
The fox also sought food and obtained a bag of rice and flour, which he brought to offer to the practitioner.
The otter entered the water, caught a large fish, and came to offer it to the practitioner.
The rabbit thought to himself,
"With what shall I make an offering to this man of the Way?
He reflected further.
"You should instead offer your own body as an offering.
He then went to gather brushwood to kindle a fire and produce charcoal,
returning to inform the practitioner, saying:
"Now I am somewhat feeble;
please make charcoal of me and cast me into the fire,
so that I may place my body upon the Way-farer."
The fire was not lit. The Daoist,
moved by his benevolence and righteousness,
took pity on him and stopped.
The brahmin at that time was the Buddha Dihaṅga;
the rabbit was myself;
and the monkey was Śāriputra.
The fox was Ānanda; the otter was Maudgalyāyana. (From the *Old Piyujing*, Scroll Lower). 2.
The Monkey Offers Honey from a Bowl to the Buddha. The monkey offered honey from a bowl to the Buddha. The two Buddhas [and] the various bhikṣus.
Having accepted the invitation of the Brahmin Śreṣṭhin,
he returned to Gṛdhrakūṭa and washed his utensils by the riverbank.
In the Āmra grove there was a monkey who,
while wandering, saw a tree that had no bees but contained ripe honey.
He approached Ānanda and requested his almsbowl.
Ānanda would not give it.
The Buddha said, "Just give it.
Having obtained the bowl, the monkey—according to the *Miśrakābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*—sought out honey to fill the Buddha’s bowl and offered it to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One did not accept it, as he required the water to be purified;
the monkey, not understanding,
thought there were insects in it.
Upon reaching the water’s edge, he washed his alms bowl;

as the water overflowed with honey, he held it up and returned it to the Buddha. The *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish* says, "He washed away the red insects," while the *Mahīśāsaka Vinaya* states, "Seeing the insects, he set it aside."
The Buddha again distributed the monks until they were all fully accounted for.
The monkey, filled with joy, leaped and danced backward, fell into a pit, and died;
he became the child in the womb of his teacher’s wife.
Later, he was born as a male with upright features; according to the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya,
he was subsequently born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and later born again in the human realm.
When he attained the path of Arhatship, the Buddha said:
"In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
there was a young śramaṇa."
Seeing an arhat leap across the Jing River,
he said to an ordinary bhikṣu,
"Your leaping speed is like that of a monkey."
In the final five hundred years of the age, he was constantly reborn as a monkey; this appears in the twelfth fascicle of the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish).
It also appears in the tenth fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, and it also appears in the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
3. The Monkey as Teacher of Five Hundred Sages; the Monkey as Teacher of Five Hundred Sages (III). Three Tathāgatas entered parinirvāṇa in the kingdom of Mathurā.
One hundred years later, on Mount Urumuṇḍa...
On one side were five hundred pratyekabuddhas;
on another side were five hundred rishis;
and on yet another side were five hundred monkeys.
The monkey leader went among the pratyekabuddhas; seeing the various pratyekabuddhas,
he gave rise to a heart of joy and took flowers and fruits from the trees to offer to them.
He prostrated and sat at the end of the assembly of monks,
doing so every day in this manner.
Subsequently, all those pratyekabuddhas entered nirvana.
The monkey made offerings as before;
seeing that the pratyekabuddhas would not accept them,
he then pulled at their robes and grasped their feet, yet they remained unmoved.
The monkey reflected,
"They have all died," and wept in bitter grief and distress.
They proceeded again to the place where five hundred sages were;
they all entered among the thorns,
and the monkey likewise entered.
The seer went again to the ash and dust;
the monkey also went to the ash and dust.
The seer scorched his body with the five heats.
The monkey was likewise treated thus:
the seer reached out his hand and hung himself from the tree,
whereupon the monkey pushed his hand away, causing him to fall to the ground.
He constantly instructed the various seers through the four modes of deportment;
having thus instructed them,
he sat upright among the seers and practiced meditative concentration.
He spoke to the sages, saying,
"All of you should sit in this manner.
Then the five hundred sages sat down for meditation accordingly.
These sages teach the Dharma without a teacher;
by contemplating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
they realize and attain the path of the pratyekabuddha.
They all thought to themselves,
"We have attained the Noble Path because of this monkey," and they immediately made offerings of fragrant flowers, food, and drink to the monkey.
When the monkey’s life ended, its body was cremated with fragrant wood.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"This monkey was none other than Upagupta."
Within the evil realms, he shall bring benefit to many sentient beings.
More than a hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this superior matter shall occur. (From the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*, Scroll Six).

4. Five Hundred Monkeys Imitate the Arhats by Building a Stūpa for the Buddha. Once, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, five hundred monkeys imitated the Arhats by building a stūpa for the Buddha. 4. Formerly, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Rājagṛha...
He dispatched an arhat named Sumana,
who took the Buddha’s hair and nail-clippings to the Southern Mountains of the kingdom of Kaśmīra to construct a Buddhist stūpa.
Five hundred arhats constantly resided within that monastery.
Morning and evening, he burned incense and circumambulated the stupa to pay his respects.
At that time, there were five hundred monkeys on that mountain who saw the practitioner making offerings at the stupa and temple.
Even if we were to go together to the edge of a deep ravine,
carry stones upon our backs to construct a Buddhist stupa,
erect wooden poles as flagstaffs, and tie tattered banners to their tops.
Morning and evening they performed prostrations just like practitioners of the Way.
At that time, the mountain waters suddenly surged,
and five hundred monkeys were swept away and drowned all at once.
Their spirits were immediately reborn in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There, the palaces of the seven treasures, clothing, and food appeared spontaneously;
each thought to themselves:
From where did he come to be born in the heavens?
He then used his divine eye to see his own original form:
the body of a monkey.
In the past, while assisting various practitioners in playfully constructing stupas and temples,
although my body was submerged and drowned, my spirit attained rebirth in heaven.
Now I shall descend to repay the kindness of my former corpse.
Each took their attendants, flowers, incense, and musical instruments, and approached the former corpse;
they scattered flowers, burned incense, and circumambulated it seven times.
At that time, there were five hundred brahmins in the mountains.
The non-Buddhist practitioners held heterodox views and did not believe in sin or merit.
Seeing the devas and humans scattering flowers and performing music around the corpse of the monkey, they were astonished and asked: "Why do you do this?"
"The splendor and majesty of the various devas are so immense;
for what reason do you humble yourself to make offerings to this corpse?
The devas and humans replied:
"This corpse was our former body.
Having fully recounted their past lives, they said,
"By means of this slight merit, we have been born in the heavens."
I now scatter flowers to repay the kindness of my former body.
If even playing at building a stupa or temple can yield such merit,
how much more so if one were to serve the Buddha with a sincere heart?
His virtue is beyond comparison.
You all hold false views and do not believe in the true and correct;
though you toil and suffer for a hundred kalpas, you shall gain nothing at all.
"It would be better for us to go together to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to pay homage, serve, and make offerings, so that we may obtain limitless merit.
Thereupon, they all joyfully went together to the Buddha’s dwelling.
Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they scattered flowers as an offering.
The devas and humans addressed the Buddha, saying,
"We were recently monkeys; by the grace of the World-Honored One, we have [attained this]."
"I have attained rebirth in the heavens;
yet, regretting that I did not see the Buddha, I now come to take refuge in him myself.
He addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
"What transgressions did we commit in our previous lives to receive the body of a monkey?
Although we built stūpas and temples, our bodies were swept away by the flood.
The Buddha told the devas and humans:
It does not arise from emptiness.
In a past age, there were five hundred young brahmins who traveled together into the mountains seeking the way of the immortals.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa on the mountain.
Desiring to plaster the vihāra on the mountain with mud, he went down the valley to fetch water; his body was so light it was as if he were flying.
Five hundred brahmins, conceiving feelings of jealousy, laughed at him in unison.
"Now this śramaṇa moves up and down with such rapid agility as a monkey;
what is there to marvel at?
He continues thus without ceasing to draw water."
Not long after he first entered the mountains and waters, he drowned.
The Buddha told the devas and humans:
"At that time, I was the śramaṇa Upāśānta."
The five hundred young brahmins were none other than these five hundred monkeys.
Having committed offenses in jest, they now experience their retribution in this body.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"Committing evil in jest, one receives retribution with wailing and weeping. Upon hearing these words of the Buddha, five hundred devas immediately attained the fruit of the Path (srotāpatti).
Five hundred brahmins heard of the retribution for sins and merits.
And they sighed to themselves, saying,
"We have studied the arts of the immortals for many years,
yet we have not received their fruit."
"It would have been better for me to have performed meritorious acts through playful laughter like a monkey and thereby attained birth in the heavens.
The Buddha’s virtue is truly sublime.
I prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and pray to become his disciple."
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu.
He immediately became a śramaṇa; through diligent effort, he attained the Way. (From the *Dharmapada*, Volume One).

5. A Monkey Learns Meditation, Falls from a Tree, Dies, and Is Reborn in Heaven. Once, in the past, there was a practitioner of the Way. A monkey learned meditation; it fell from a tree and died, thereby attaining rebirth in heaven. Once, in the past, there was a practitioner of the Way.
He sat in meditation and recited the sutras beneath a tree.
A macaque on a tree above him imitated him;
unaware, it fell from the tree and died.

12. The Twelfth: The Hare (Śaśaka) 1. The Hare King Follows a Recluse, Throws Himself into a Mass of Fire, and is Born in Tuṣita Heaven. Once upon a time, there was a hare king who roamed in the mountains.
Together with his followers, he ate fruit and drank water.
He practiced the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity,
and instructed all his kin and retinue to be entirely harmonious and gentle, refraining from all evil deeds.
Having finally been liberated from this body and attained a human form,
they were able to receive the teachings of the Way.
At that time, their kinsmen and attendants rejoiced.
Obediently following the instructions, I did not dare disobey his command.
There was a rishi dwelling among the forest trees,
who ate fruit and drank water while practicing the path alone.
Never indulging in idle wandering, he established the four Brahma-vihāras—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. He recited the sūtras and remained mindful of the Way;
his voice was fluent and clear, and its tone was so harmonious and elegant that all who heard it were filled with joy.
At that time, the hare king went near him and listened to his recitation of the sutras;
his heart leaped with joy within him, and he never grew weary of it.
Together with his retinue, he brought fruits and melons to offer as alms to the practitioner.
In this manner, days accumulated and months and years passed.
Then, as the winter cold arrived,
the seer wished to return to the human world.
When the hare king saw this, he was filled with sorrow and distress;
harboring feelings of longing and regret, he did not wish for her to leave.
He asked, "Where are you going?"
Meeting here day after day, we find delight;
forgetting hunger and thirst as if relying upon our parents,
we pray that you will remain and not depart.
The seer replied, "I possess the four great elements; you must carefully protect them.
Now that winter has arrived and the fruits and vegetables are exhausted."
The mountains and waters were frozen, and there were no caves where he could dwell;
therefore, wishing to depart and rely upon human habitation,
he went on almsround for food and stayed temporarily in a monastery.
"When this winter cold has passed, we shall come together again;
do not be despondent.
The rabbit king replied:
"We, your kinsmen, shall go forth to seek the fruit [of our labor].
Whether from far or near, we shall recruit and search for it to provide you with everything you need.
We pray that you will deign to lower your dignity and, out of compassion, grant us your aid."
If I were to abandon my grief and attachment, I might not preserve my life;
even if there are no offerings available today,
I shall offer my own body to the Great Teacher.
When the practitioner saw this, he was moved to deep compassion and pity,
wondering with utmost sincerity what could be done for him.
Before the immortal’s fire-altar, there were live coals.
The rabbit king thought to himself, "It is for my sake that this man of the Way remains silent. He then raised his body and threw himself into the fire.
As the flames grew fiercely intense, the man of the Way sought to rescue him.
Having passed away shortly thereafter, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
His physical form possessed preeminent merit and his majestic spiritual power was most sublime.
When the rishi saw him, he [was struck with wonder].
For the sake of the Way and virtue, he did not spare his own body or life;
out of compassion and pity for them, he also reproached himself,
abstaining from grain and refusing to eat.
Immediately thereafter, his spirit transmigrated to the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Buddha said:
"The rabbit king at that time was none other than myself."
The "Sage" refers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha; this is the third and fourth fascicles of the *Jātakasūtra*, and it also appears in the *Śaśarājasūtra*.

Emaciated by hunger and thirst,
he waited within his burrow for a mouse to emerge;
when a young mouse came out, he swiftly seized and swallowed it.
The mouselet’s body was small, so it entered his belly while he was alive;
it devoured his internal organs,
leaving the cat or wildcat in a state of bewildered distress as he ran frantically hither and thither.
Thus he eventually came to his death.
This foolish mendicant was unskilled in guarding his body and mind when he beheld women.

14. The Fourteenth [Section]: The Rat. 1. The Rat Saves the Life of the Licchavis. First: The Buddha said:
Kalandaka is the name of a mountain mouse.
At that time, the King of Vaiśālī,
taking his court ladies with him, entered the mountain to amuse himself.
At that time, the king grew weary and fell asleep beneath a tree.
The female musicians scattered to the left and right to play about.
At that moment, there was a large venomous snake within a hollow in the tree.
Smelling the king's breath of alcohol, the snake intended to sting him.
A rat on the tree came down from above and, by its cries, alerted the king;
the snake immediately retreated and retracted itself.
After the king had awakened, he fell back asleep.
The snake came out once more,
and the mouse called out again, descending to wake the king.
The king arose and saw a great venomous snake;
immediately he was seized with terror,
but when he sought his female musicians, they were nowhere to be seen.
The king thought to himself,
"I have now been saved by the kindness of this mouse."
Reflecting that he wished to repay [his debt],
there was a village at the foot of the mountain;
he immediately summoned those from the village.
"From this day forward, let my entire allotment of provisions be dedicated to the mice.
Because of these mice, let this village be named Kalandaka.
At that time, there was an elder in the village.
There were forty billion gold coins;
the King immediately conferred upon him the rank of Elder (Śreṣṭhin).
Because of this village’s name, he was called the Elder Kalandaka. (From the *Sūtra-vibhāṣā* of the *Suvarṇabhāsottama-sūtra*, Volume Six).
2. A Mouse Steals the Ghee from a Tall Vessel. Once, in the house of an elder, there was a jar of ghee on a high storied building, which was not securely covered.
A mouse entered the jar of ghee and ate it day and night;
its body grew large until the ghee was completely consumed,
and the mouse filled the jar, appearing in color just like the ghee.
Someone was buying ghee.
At that time, the elder took the ghee and placed it over a fire;
the mouse inside the jar then died within the jar.
It further transforms into ghee,
which is sold to buyers;
as they measure it out by pints and pecks, the bones sink to the bottom.

They all previously possessed a mind of great generosity, soaring with pride upon the void;
yet they were plagued by suffering and affliction, their minds abounding in anger and arrogance.
Born among these birds,

these manifest in ten thousand transformations, capable of accomplishing anything whatsoever.

3. The Third Section on the Wild Geese (Hamsa) 1. The Golden-Winged Goose Still Cherishes His Wife and Children of a Previous Life; He Gives Them One Hair of Gold Each Day. On the bank of the Monkey River (Markaṭahradatīrtha) in Vaiśālī, there was a garlic garden.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was not far from the garden.
The owner of the garden asked her:
“Does the *ayya* require garlic?
The bhikṣuṇīs then gave it to the śrāmaṇerīs and śikṣamāṇās,
who went repeatedly to request more garlic.
Consequently, they were all completely exhausted.
The owner abandoned his garden and departed.
The Buddha then recounted this Jātaka tale.
In the past, there was a brahmin who was one hundred and twenty years old; his physical form was emaciated and frail,
yet his wife was incomparably beautiful.
He fathered many sons and daughters;
this brahmin fixed his mind upon his wife and their children,
never letting go of them.
Because his attachment was so profound,
when his life came to an end, he was reborn among the geese;
the feathers of his body were entirely golden in color.
Due to the causes and conditions of past merit, he naturally remembered his former lives.
He thought, "By what means can I support these children so that they do not suffer from poverty?
Day after day he would return, leaving behind a single feather each evening before departing.
Seeing this, the children did not understand the underlying causes and conditions,
and they immediately deliberated together, saying,
"We would rather wait for him when he comes."
Using skillful means, he grasped them and extracted all the golden feathers.
Just as he had planned, he plucked out every golden feather;
yet, once the feathers were gone, white feathers grew in their place.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that brahmin was who died and became a goose at that time,
could he have been anyone else?"
The owner of the garden was none other than this person; the beautiful woman was the bhikṣuṇī;
and the man and woman were the śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs, as recorded in the third fascicle of the second division of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
2. Five hundred geese were killed by a hunter; having heard the Buddha-dharma, they were reborn in heaven and attained the Way. Two Buddhas were in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Within a forested marsh,
he was expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of the various devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly.
At that time, there were five hundred wild geese traveling in a flock through the air.
Hearing the Buddha’s voice, he felt deep love and joy, and as he circled about intending to descend,
the hunter spread his net and the goose fell into it.
Killed by the hunter, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Sitting upon his parents' laps like an eight-year-old child,
his exquisite beauty was peerless and his radiance like a mountain of gold;
he then thought to himself:
"What is the cause for my birth here?
he wondered, and immediately recognized it as the karmic fruition of his past-life devotion to the Dharma.
He then took the flowers with him and descended to Jambudvīpa.
He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Having been born in the Sublime Heaven by virtue of hearing the sound of the Dharma,
I pray that you will grant me further instruction."
The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths.
Having attained the stage of Srotāpanna, he immediately returned to the heavens. (From the *Xiányújīng*, Scroll 13).

At that time, there was a heavy fall of rain and snow.
A certain person had lost his way and was in dire straits, suffering great hardship;
hunger and cold came upon him together, and his life hung by a thread.
The pigeon flew away seeking fire;
for its sake, [the man] gathered wood and lit it.
Once it was ablaze, he threw his own body into the flames.
The gift to this hungry person is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven. 2.
A pigeon pursued by a hawk finds peace upon encountering the shadow of the Buddha, yet trembles again in the shadow of a disciple. Two Buddhas were walking at sundown in the Jeta Grove.
As Śāriputra was following him,
a hawk pursued a pigeon;
the pigeon flew to the Buddha’s side.
The Buddha’s shadow covered it;
the pigeon’s body became peaceful and its fear was immediately dispelled, so that it no longer made a sound.
Later, Śāriputra’s shadow arrived.
The pigeon then made a sound, trembling with fear as before.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Both the Buddha and my own person are free from the three poisons."
When the Buddha’s shadow covered the pigeon, the pigeon was not afraid;
when my shadow covered the pigeon, it trembled as before.
The Buddha said:
"Because you possess the habitual tendencies of the three poisons, observe this pigeon:
through how many lifetimes in its past causes and conditions has it been a pigeon?
Śāriputra immediately entered the *pūrvanivāsajñāna-samādhi* (the samādhi of knowledge of former existences).
Observing this pigeon,
I see that for eighty thousand great kalpas he has constantly been in the body of a pigeon;
beyond that point in the past, I am unable to see.
The Buddha said,
"If you cannot fully know the past,
try to observe when this pigeon shall be liberated."
Śāriputra immediately entered the Samādhi of the Knowledge of Vows and beheld that this pigeon had not been released from its pigeon body for eighty thousand great kalpas.
This was due to ignorance.
Throughout great kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he constantly took the body of a pigeon. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven.
6. The Pheasant, Part Six. 1. The Pheasant Saves the Forest from Fire. Once, in the past, a wild fire burned through a forest.
In the forest there was a pheasant that,
exerting its own strength, flew into the woods;
it sprinkled water upon the forest, toiling back and forth without regarding the exhaustion as suffering.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came and asked him,
"What are you doing? He replied:
I have rescued this forest out of compassion for sentient beings.
This forest is a place of vast, cool, and pleasant shade where my own kind and all my kinsmen rely upon and look up to me.
"I possess physical strength; why should I be indolent and fail to rescue them?
The Heavenly Emperor asked, "How long must you continue in such diligent application?"
The pheasant said,
"I shall die as my appointed time.
The Lord of Heaven said:
"Who can bear witness for you?
He then made a vow of his own:
"If my heart is most sincere and my faith is not false, may the fire be extinguished of its own accord."
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, knowing the pheasant’s great vow, immediately extinguished the fire;
from beginning to end, it remained ever-lush and was not burned by the flames. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Volume 16).

7. The Seventh Chapter on Crows. Regarding the four crow-messengers dispatched by King Ikṣvāku to the kingdom of Śāketa: first, a red-faced crow was a close friend of a monkey; second, a crow and a rooster mated and together produced an offspring; third, a crow and a fox alternately praised one another. 1. Regarding the four crow-messengers dispatched by King Ikṣvāku to the kingdom of Śāketa: King Prasenajit had four great ministers.
He was appointed as general.
Assembling the four divisions of his army, he intended to attack a small kingdom.
When the four ministers saw the Buddha, they prostrated themselves at his feet.
The World-Honored One questioned them,
"Where have you all gone?
They answered him in full detail regarding the matter.
"Our bodies have been established for the sake of this king in many ways, yet we constantly fear for our lives as he now intends to launch a military expedition.
The World-Honored One praised them, saying,
"Excellent, worthy ones!"
This constitutes repaying kindness with reciprocity.
It was not only for the sake of this king in the present life;
in a past life, it was likewise in the kingdom of Śāketa.
A multitude of crows came and assembled, settling in that country.
The king of the crows was named Ikṣvāku,
and he ruled over eighty thousand crows.
The king of the crows had a wife named Jūlinī.
When she became pregnant, her cravings for food grew intense, and she spoke with sincerity to the king:
"My body has begun to swell slightly; I desire something that is wholesome and soft."
"The deer king can only survive by eating meat; otherwise, he will die.
Thereupon, the crow king, hearing his voice, gathered the assembly of crows and said, "You all must go to the kingdom of Śāketa."
In the kingdom of Śāketa, there was a great deer king named Sūkṣma;
[the king] desired to obtain its meat.
The four crows volunteered,
saying, "We are capable of this;
we shall not spare our own lives or vitality, but will accomplish this task."
At that time, four crows repeatedly came to the place of assembly.
When the prince of the kingdom saw the crows, he was terrified;
he fled back and informed the king.
"I have seen four black birds of such appearance repeatedly coming to the Deer Park.
The King immediately ordered his men to capture them."
A fowler set up a snare as a skillful means to catch crows;
he immediately captured them alive and presented them to the king.
The king questioned the four crows and reviled them.
"Why have you come here so frequently,
violating my domain?
The crow replied:
"Indeed, O Heavenly King, this is not what I desire.
There is a king named Anvaya;
his wife has conceived."
Desiring to obtain the meat of a fine, gentle deer,
the king sent him forth;
he received his lord’s command and departed.
At that time, the king was struck with astonishment and marveled at this;
having personally received the royal command to devise such a stratagem,
he felt that sacrificing his life was truly beyond his reach.
If one seeks this reciprocity among ordinary people of the world,
it is already difficult to find even those who receive the instructions of their lords and parents;
how much more so, then, among birds and beasts?
The King addressed the crows: "I now pardon your offense; come forth with the honey and prepare the scriptures. This is also known as the *Sūtra of the Crow King of the Country of Kusā*.

2. The Red-Billed Crow and the Monkey as Friends. The Red-Billed Crow and the Monkey were close friends. Long ago, there was a crow named Kukī—Kukī means "red-beaked" in the local language—who lived among the thickets. He nested in the trees and raised his young there.
At that time, Kakuda was on intimate terms with a monkey.
In the midst of a thicket of trees there was a venomous snake,
which waited for him to be away from home.
He devoured the son of Kuki until nothing remained.
Kuki, having lost his son, wailed and cried out in grief, not knowing where he was;
he then reflected deeply within himself.
He learned that the monkey had been devoured by a snake.
When the monkey returned, he saw him and asked what had happened.
He replied:
"The snake has devoured my children until none remain.
The monkey said,
"I shall take revenge upon it."
At that time, a venomous snake was moving along.
A monkey came forward and circled it;
the snake grew angry and coiled itself around the monkey.
The monkey seized him by the head and dragged him to a stone,
where he rubbed him until he was wounded and died;
then he cast him away and returned.
The *Sūtra of the Crowing Crow* (Kukī-yud-yot-chik-chwi-o-yu-gyeong).
3. The Crow and the Hen Produce One Offspring Together. Regarding the crow and the hen producing one offspring together: In a past life, three times over... [text fragment ends].
There was a flock of chickens living in a thicket.
A wildcat preyed upon them until only a single hen remained.
A crow came and sheltered her, and together they produced one chick.
When the child made a sound, the crow spoke this verse:
"This child is not mine; Born from the union of a wild father and a village mother, He is neither crow nor chicken."
If one wishes to learn the cry of the father, it is produced by the mother;
If one wishes to learn the call of the mother, its father is a crow.
To learn the crow’s cry like that of a cock, And to learn the cock’s sound like that of a crow—this is impossible.
If a black hen were to study both [techniques], neither would succeed.
(From the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume 24).
Long ago, in times past...
There was a eunuch who passed away;
he was discarded among the *cūta* trees,
where malevolent foxes and crows [gathered].
They came together to eat the meat and praised one another.
The crow said:
Your body is like a lion; your head is like that of a *kumāra* (youthful sage).
Among the deer you are the king; how beautiful you are, like a fine flower!
The fox said:
Who is the Honored One upon the tree? His wisdom is foremost;
his brilliance illuminates the ten directions like a mass of purple-golden gold.
At that time, the Great Seer dwelt in seclusion.
"Purifying one's conduct is the path.
Hearing this, he spoke a verse in question:
"I have long observed what you do; your actions constitute double-tongued speech."
Hiding yourself among the trees, you eat the flesh of a dead eunuch;
you base and lowly creature, you call yourself a superior man!
O crow, speak!
The Lion and the Peacock: Why do they not eat bird flesh? [Why] do you shave your head and beg for alms in succession? *The Sūtra on the Fox, the Crow, and the Owl*, Part 3:

Grain-robbers (1 item); 7. Worms in fermented liquids (1 item); 8. Lice (1 item). **1. Dragons** **First: Birth, Abiding, and Sustenance** 1. The Dragon King Sāgara is protected by five hundred spirits. 2. His retinue was small at first but later became numerous. 3. A dragon who observes the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*) will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven even if he is flayed by humans. 4. The four Great Dragon Kings suffered from the *garuḍa* (golden-winged bird) and petitioned the Buddha. **First: Birth, Abiding, and Sustenance** There are four kinds of dragons. [End of fragment]
First, birth from an egg;
second, birth from a womb;
third, birth from moisture.
The fourth are those born by transformation.
They all previously possessed much anger and crooked, unupright minds;
having practiced great acts of giving, they now receive these forms.
The palace is made of the seven precious gems; where the palace stands, there appears the body of a garuḍa forty *li* in height,
with robes forty *li* in length and eighty *li* in width.
It weighed two and a half taels.
By his supernormal power, he transformed it into food and drink of a hundred flavors;
at the very last mouthful, it changed into a frog.
If one transforms their own retinue to inspire them toward the path of enlightenment,
and bestows dark-colored robes upon beggars such that all the nāgas each offer worship,
then sand shall not fall upon the body and one shall be freed from all afflictions; it is also said thus.
Transforming their bodies into snakes, vipers, and the like, they do not suffer from being eaten by frogs or *garuḍas*, nor do they become food for soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, fish, or turtles.

Regarding their "lump-food" (*kavaḍīkāhāra*), the *Loutan jing* (Lokasthāna-sūtra) states that dragons eat fish, turtles, and *tivyativila* large fish. Their bathing and clothing constitute their "food of smoothness" (*ślakṣṇāhāra*).
There is also marriage;
they form the union of yin and yang through physical contact.
Their lifespan is one kalpa.
There were some who decreased;
having escaped being eaten by the garuḍas,
there remained only sixteen kings.
First, Sāgara; second, Nanda; third, Upananda.
Fourth, Aṇavatapta; fifth, Caitraratha;
sixth, Sudarśana.
7. Ākhu; 8. Gāgula; 9. Gavila.
10. Aparā; 11. Gaṇu; 12. Gogaṇu.
Thirteen, Anavatapta;
fourteen, Supratiṣṭhita; fifteen, Uśanaga-pāṭha.

The Dragon King Sāgara protected by five hundred spirits; the Dragon King Sāgara protected by five hundred spirits—[this is] the second [section on] the Dragon King Sāgara.
He dwells at the bottom of the great ocean to the north of Mount Sumeru;
his palace is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
with walls made of the seven precious gems and arranged in seven tiers.
Its railings and lattices are magnificently adorned above;
in its groves and bathing pools, various birds sing in harmony;
its walls are of gold and its gates of silver.
The gates are two thousand four hundred li high and two thousand two hundred li wide;
they are beautifully adorned with colorful paintings.
It is constantly protected by five hundred spirits who can cause rain to fall according to one's heart's desire,
a power that even the host of dragons cannot match.
The deep pools where they dwell surge and flow into the ocean.
[This passage concerning] the blue lapis lazuli color appears in the *Loutan* (Ratnakūṭa) and *Huayan* (Avataṃsaka) sūtras.
3. Regarding the fact that the retinue was small at first and became large later: three dragon kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
Since the beginning of the kalpa, I have dwelt in the great ocean.
From the time of Krakucchanda Buddha until now,
those with wives and children in the great ocean have been very few.
Now, the retinue of the sea dragon is vast and numerous.
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"Those who have gone forth from home within the Buddha-dharma..."
Those who violate the precepts, commit transgressions, and do not abandon their broken discipline are mostly reborn among the nāgas;
those with direct insight do not fall into hell.
Beings of this kind, after the end of their lives, are all reborn among the nāgas.
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"In the time of Krakucchanda Buddha,
there were nine billion eight hundred million householders and renunciants."
Those who violated their prohibitions and precepts were all reborn among the nāgas.
During the time of Konāgamuni Buddha, eight billion people—
both householders and renunciants— [were likewise reborn there].
Having violated the precepts and indulged their own minds,
after the end of their lives they were all reborn among the nāgas during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Sixty-four billion householders and renunciants who violated the precepts were all reborn among the nāgas within my world.
Nine hundred and ninety billion householders, having engaged in strife,
contention, and the slandering of the sutras and precepts, shall die and be reborn among the dragons;
some have already been so reborn.
For this reason, the wives,
children, and retinues of the various nāgas within the great ocean are beyond calculation.
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be many wicked upāsakas.
Those who violate the prohibitions and precepts shall be reborn among the dragons, or fall into hell. *Sāgara-nāgarāja-sūtra*, Volume Two. 4.
Dragons who maintain the precepts until death without breaking them; dragons who maintain the precepts until death without breaking them, such as the four great powerful venomous dragons.
If he looked at a person with his eyes, the weak would die;
if he breathed upon a person with his breath, even the strong would die.
At that time, the dragon received the one-day precept (*upavāsa*).
Having gone forth, he entered among the forest trees to practice meditation.
After sitting for a long time, he became weary and fell asleep.
According to the nature of dragons, when they sleep, their form takes on the appearance of a snake.
It was variegated with the seven treasures.
Upon seeing it, the hunter was filled with wonder and joy, saying:
"This hide is rare and difficult to obtain."
"To present this to the King as an ornament for his boat— would that not be fitting?
He then pressed the man's head down with a staff and flayed his skin with a knife.
The dragon thought to himself:
"My power is capable of toppling a kingdom;
how could this tiny creature possibly trouble me?"
Now, because I uphold the precepts, I do not regard this body.
I shall follow the Buddha’s words and endure it myself;
closing my eyes, I will not look, and closing my breath, I will not exhale.
Out of compassion for this person,
he single-mindedly accepts being flayed for the sake of maintaining his precepts, without giving rise to a thought of regret.
Once his skin has been lost, his raw flesh lies upon the ground.
At that time, the sun was scorching hot, and as he lay writhing in the dust,
he saw a great body of water nearby. Upon seeing small insects coming to devour his body,
he did not dare move at all for the sake of maintaining his precepts.
He thought to himself:
"Now I shall give this body of mine to all these insects for the sake of the Buddha-way."
"Now, by giving flesh as a gift, one satisfies their body;
later, by giving the Dharma as a gift, one benefits their mind.
When the body withers and life ends, one is immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. — From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Volume 14.
5. The Four Great Dragon Kings, Afflicted by the Golden-Winged Bird, Entreat the Buddha. There were four great dragon kings afflicted by the golden-winged bird who entreated the Buddha.
Among them was one dragon king named Āśvāsa (Inhaling).
The second is named Great Inhaler;
the third is named Able to Encompass;
the fourth is named Immeasurable Color.
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"In this ocean there are countless species of nāgas.
There are four kinds of garuḍas that constantly feed upon these various nāgas of the sea."
"May the Buddha protect you so that you may attain peace and security, and harbor no sorrow or fear.
The World-Honored One removed his black robe and said to the Dragon King Sāgara,
"You should take this black robe of the Tathāgata."
He distributed [the relics] among all the nāgas so that they were spread everywhere;
even those who possessed but a single thread in the great ocean could not be harmed by the King of the Garuḍas.
The inconceivable and majestic virtues established by the Buddha are thus.
At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara took the Buddha’s robe and distributed it among the various dragon kings.
According to whatever was lacking—whether extensive or narrow, large or small—it was naturally provided;
yet his robes remained as they were, never being exhausted.
At that time, the Sea Dragon King addressed the various dragon kings:
One should revere this robe as one would revere the World-Honored One;
just as one makes offerings to the relics after his parinirvāṇa,
one should serve the World-Honored One with all manner of requisites.
Upon hearing what the Buddha had established, the four kings of the garuḍas were struck with alarm and fear;
they quickly went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet,
and asked, "For what reason, World-Honored One, have you taken away our food?"
The Buddha said:
"In total there are four kinds of nutriment,
which lead to three destinations."
What are the four?
First, setting nets to hunt birds and beasts, harming herds of livestock, and taking life and depriving them of their lives for the sake of food and drink.
Second, carrying weapons such as swords and spears to strike, pierce, oppress, and shoot, and plundering the wealth of others for the sake of food and drink.
The third is to obtain food through stinginess, greed, flattery, deceit, violation of prohibitions, wrong views, and craftiness.
The fourth is to claim to be a teacher when one is not,
or to claim to be the World-Honored One when one is not.
Following what is deviant, they call it correct;
those who are not of tranquil intent, they call tranquil;
those who are not pure, they call pure.
To claim to practice the holy life when one does not,
and to falsely represent oneself in order to obtain food—
these are the four kinds of food.
One will sit and head toward the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The Dharma I teach excludes these four kinds of food;
one should not use them to nourish the body at the expense of harming sentient beings.
"If you wish to protect yourself, you must protect others.
That which ought not to be done, take care never to do.
At that time, the four kings of the garuḍas—
Each, together with a thousand followers, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Today we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
We confess and repent for the transgressions and calamities we have previously committed."
From this day forward, I shall uphold the prohibitive precepts.
I grant the gift of fearlessness to all dragon kings and shall protect the True Dharma until the Buddha-dharma remains in the world.
From the Dharma of the Path to its ultimate extinction, not contradicting the Buddha’s teachings, [ends] the *Sāgara-nāgarāja-sūtra*, Volume Four.

2. The Two Snakes: The Second Story of the Two Poisonous Snakes Giving Gold to Hold a Feast and Being Reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; Each Snake’s Head and Tail Quarreling, and Death from the Tail; Two Snakes, a Tortoise, and a Frog Encountering Famine and Speaking to One Another. 1. The Poisonous Snake Giving Gold to Hold a Feast and Being Reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Once, in Jambudvīpa, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī.
Among them was one man who particularly loved gold;
he worked his body to the bone to seek it out and obtained seven jars of gold.
He was buried within the earth and never again provided with food or clothing;
he died of illness,
his craving being so profound.
He transformed himself into a venomous serpent that coiled around a golden jar;
after dying there, he was reborn and remained so for tens of thousands of years.
Later, through self-reflection, he suddenly attained awakening.
Just as he was receiving this evil retribution for his gold,
he should have abandoned it as a gift to a field of merit and sought a wholesome rebirth;
at that time, as he emerged onto the roadside, he saw a brahmin.
He then said,
"I have a jar of gold that I entrusted to you to offer to the assembly of monks.
If you do not do so for me, I shall kill you."
The brahmin said, "I can perform the divination for you.
He gave him gold, and the snake emerged.
He immediately took [the snake] and went to the monastery,
reporting the matter in full to the Sangha and expressing his intention to provide an offering for the serpent.
The Sangha granted permission.
He took the gold and entrusted it to the *karmadāna*.
The *karmadāna* then managed the arrangements as the day for the meal drew near.
The brahmin went to the place where the snake was with a small *aṅkuśa*;
seeing him, the snake rejoiced and immediately coiled itself upon the *aṅkuśa*.
The brahmin covered it with fine cotton cloth and carried it toward the monastery;
seeing him on the road, many people gave him wealth and escorted him to his home,
where they specifically set aside one day for him.
He invited the assembly of noble and holy monks to partake of a meal.
When the gathering was concluded,
he went before the monastery and stood in the street in front of the community of monks.
He ordered the brahmins to go and inspect them in succession,
while he himself, with a mind of faith, observed those receiving the food,
gazing intently without blinking.
When the business was concluded, the snake’s heart of reverence increased further, and it felt no sense of satiety.
After the monks had finished their meal, he preached the Dharma to them once more.
The snake then offered seven jars of gold, which the *karmadāna* took to serve as an offering.

3. The Snake, the Turtle, and the Frog Speak to One Another While Starving.
Once upon a time, there was a snake who, along with a frog and a turtle, lived together as close friends in a pond.
Thereafter, the water in the pond dried up completely.
Starving, destitute, and exhausted, they had no one to whom they could appeal.
At that time, the snake sent the tortoise to summon the frogs, saying:
If one encounters poverty and loses their original resolve, they do not contemplate the fundamental meaning but prioritize food.

The frog said: "Take my voice and tell it to the snake; the frog will never come to your side. From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Volume 12, Section 3: The Third [Section on] the Turtle, Part 1: The Blind Turtle Encounters the Hole in a Floating Log. [The Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus: "The blind turtle encounters the hole in a floating log... (One account).
It is like a blind turtle in the great ocean,
whose lifespan lasts for immeasurable kalpas,
that surfaces with its head exposed only once every hundred years.
Furthermore, there is a floating log with exactly one hole, drifting upon the ocean waves, driven east and west by the wind.
A blind turtle surfaces once every hundred years; it may happen that this turtle encounters the hole as it reaches the eastern side of the sea.
A floating log may drift to the western side of the ocean, and its deviations are likewise;
though it may stray or even encounter [the shore],
so too do ordinary beings drift upon the ocean of the five destinies.
To return again to a human body is even more difficult than this.

(From the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Volume 16). 4. Fish, Fish: Four Hundred Heads of Fish Captured by a Fisherman; Hearing Their Past Causes, the Fisherman Attains Enlightenment. 1. Three Fish Follow the Waves into a Small Stream; 2. The Strong Return, the Weak Are Bound. 2. One Hundred Heads of Fish Captured by a Fisherman; Hearing Their Past Causes, the Fisherman Attains Enlightenment. 1. The Buddha and His Bhikṣus.
He headed toward Vaiśālī and arrived at the River Lāvāṇaka.
On the riverbank were five hundred cowherds and five hundred fishermen.
The Buddha went a short distance from the river and sat down to rest.
At that time, a fisherman caught a fish in his net;
five hundred men pulled at it but could not get it out.
He again summoned a multitude of cowherds;
with a thousand men exerting their strength together,
they caught a great fish whose body had a hundred heads of various kinds.
Donkeys, horses, camels, tigers, wolves, pigs, dogs, monkeys, foxes, and other such creatures were there;
the multitude, greatly astonished, gathered together to watch them.
At that moment, the World-Honored One proceeded to where the fish were.
He then asked the fish,
"Are you Kapila? He asked this three times, and each time the fish replied, "I am."
He asked again,
"Where are those whom you have converted now?
He replied:
"He has fallen into the Avīci Hell. Ānanda asked,
"For what reason do you now call these hundred fish 'Kapilīs'?"
The Buddha said:
"During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
there was a brāhmaṇa who fathered a son."
His name was Kāpilīya (in the language of Liang, "Yellow Head").
He was intelligent and profoundly learned;
among his peers, he was foremost in erudition.
It was only that he was not like those other śramaṇas;
for when his father was nearing death, he earnestly instructed him, saying:
"Be careful never to engage in debate on the principles of the Dharma with the śramaṇa Kāśyapa."
Why is this? Because you, Śramaṇa Jñānagambhīra, will certainly not be his equal.
After her husband had passed away, his mother asked him:
"Originally you were brilliant and wise; is there now anyone who surpasses you?
He replied, "The śramaṇa is far superior to me."
The mother asked again,
"In what way is it superior? He replied,
"When one has doubts, one goes to question the Buddha, who is able to provide clarification and resolution."
"If he were to question me, I would not be able to answer.
His mother spoke again, saying,
"Why do you not study that dharma?"
He replied, "I respectfully wish to study that Dharma and become a śramaṇa.
But I am a layperson; by what means could I possibly study it?"
The mother spoke again, saying:
"Having feigned the life of a śramaṇa and mastered its training, you shall return to the household life.
Following her mother's instruction, he became a bhikṣu.
After a short time, he had read and recited the Tripitaka and thoroughly mastered its principles.
His mother asked him,
"Have you attained victory yet?"
He replied, "In terms of learning, excellence does not equal that of sitting in meditation.
How do we know this?"
When I question others, they are able to distinguish all things;
yet when they question me, I am unable to know.
For this reason, I am not equal to them.
The mother spoke again, saying:
"From this day forward, if you engage in conversation with him,
should he fail to respond at the proper time, you may then revile and insult him."
Kāpilī said, "A renunciant śramaṇa is beyond reproach;
why do you revile him?"
He replied,
"If you simply revile me, you shall surely prevail.
At that time, Kāpilī could not bear to disobey his mother.
On a later day, he debated the principles once more.
When they were defeated by his arguments, he immediately reviled them, saying:
"You fools are so devoid of discernment that you are worse than beasts!"
The heads of all the various beasts were used as comparisons for this;
such instances were not limited to one.
Because of this karmic retribution, he now receives the body of a fish with a hundred heads.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"When shall he be released from this fish body?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
Within this Bhadrakalpa, even though a thousand Buddhas have passed away, one is still not yet liberated.
At that time, Ānanda and the great multitude heard what the Buddha had spoken.
They all raised their voices together and spoke these words:
"One must be careful regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind.
At that time, there were fishermen, cowherds, and others.
At that time, they all simultaneously joined their palms toward the Buddha,
seeking to leave the household life and practice the pure conduct of brahmacarya.
The Buddha said, "Welcome."
His beard and hair fell off naturally and the Dharma robes appeared upon his body;
for him he preached the wondrous Dharma, and he became an Arhat—recorded in the tenth fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.

2. Three Fish Follow the Waves into a Small Stream: Two Strong Ones Escape, One Weak One Is Captured. Two strong ones escape, one weak one is captured. Suddenly, a great surge of waves from the South Sea surged forth and flooded the area.
Three great fish flowed into a small island stream and said to one another,
"We are in distress here, as long as the waters have not yet receded."
"It would be appropriate to swim upstream back toward the great ocean;
however, we are again obstructed by a water-island and cannot pass over it.
The first fish exerted all its strength, leaped over the island, and succeeded in crossing.
Next, the fish at Yufu relied on the grass to escape its pursuers;
however, the third fish, its strength completely exhausted,
was caught by a hunter.
The Buddha saw this and spoke in verse:
"This day has passed, and life accordingly diminishes, Like a fish in diminishing water; What joy is there in this? *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga), Volume 18.
5. The Fifth Section on the Frog. 1. The Frog Who Heard the Ambrosia, Died and Was Reborn in Heaven, Saw the Buddha, and Attained the Way. One: In Kālaka Lake there was a frog.
Having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma,
he immediately emerged from the pond and went beneath the roots of a grass plant.
At that time, there was a cowherd.
Seeing the great assembly surrounding [the Buddha] to listen to his preaching of the Dharma,
he went to where the Buddha was;
desiring to hear the Dharma, he pierced the ground with his staff.
He mistakenly put on a snail-shell head;
immediately upon his death, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
where he beheld various celestial maidens enjoying themselves amidst music and song.
He immediately reflected:
"I was previously an animal;
by what causes and conditions have I been born in this celestial palace?"
He immediately observed with his divine eye that they had previously listened to the Buddha preaching the Dharma by the side of a pond;
it was through this merit that they obtained this karmic retribution.
At that time, the deva Śambuka immediately mounted his celestial palace and went to where the Buddha was;
he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. This concludes the fourth fascicle of the *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā*.
6. Chapter Six: The Grain Thief 1. The Heavenly King Kanakavarṇa Rewards the Master of the Grain Once upon a time, there was a great household that harvested a thousand *hu* of grain.
They were buried in the ground;
when spring warmth arrived, they were unearthed to take the seeds,
but no grain was to be seen at all.
There was, however, a creature as large as a cow-dung basket;
it had neither hands nor feet, nor head nor eyes, being like a mass of dull, insentient flesh.
None of the master’s household members, whether great or small, failed to find it strange.
When he emerged onto level ground,
[the other] immediately asked, "Who are you?"
He said nothing at all,
but then pricked himself in one spot with an iron awl and said:
"If you wish to know my name, hold me up by the side of the great road;
there shall naturally be those who call me by my name.
Thereupon, he lifted it up and placed it by the roadside.
Within those three days, there was no one able to name it.
Next, there were several hundred yellow horse-drawn carriages;
their clothing and attendants were all yellow.
He stopped his carriage and called out, "Grain-thief! Why are you here?
He replied:
"Because I have eaten the grain of this man, he has detained me here.
After speaking for a very long time, he took his leave and departed.
The host then questioned the "grain-thief."
"Who was that just now?
He replied,
"It was the essence of gold and jewels."
He lived beneath a great tree more than three hundred paces to the west of here.
There was a hundred-stone jar filled with gold.
The host immediately took several dozen people to dig, and they found the jar of gold.
His family rejoiced and carried him home on a palanquin.
He prostrated himself before the grain-thief, saying,
"That I have obtained gold today is due to the great grace of Your Divinity."
"It would be better to remain attentive and together return to provide further offerings.
The Grain Thief said,
"Previously, when I ate your grain, I did not mention my surname or name."
I wish for you to obtain this golden reward;
now you must turn and bestow this merit upon the world.
You may not remain here any longer.
Having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished. [End of] the second fascicle of the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. 7. The Seventh Story of the Worms:

The Great Worm in the Pond and the Karmic Conditions of His Previous Life. In the southeastern corner of Rājagṛha, there was a pond. There was a great worm in that pond. Regarding the karmic conditions of this great worm’s previous life: [The story begins... In the southeastern corner of Rājagṛha city, there was a pond of water.
The ditches and canals within the city were filthy;
excrement and urine all flowed into them, and their stench was such that one could not approach them.
There was a great beast born within the swirling waters;
its body was several zhang long and it had neither hands nor feet,
yet it rolled, lowered itself, and raised itself as it played within the churning water.
Thousands of people were watching.
When Ānanda went to see them while begging for alms,
the insects immediately leaped about and surged like billowing waves.
He reported this in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha, together with the bhikṣus, went to the site of the pond.
When the multitude saw the Buddha, they were filled with joy.
Each of them thought to themselves:
"Today the Tathāgata shall explain the origins and end of the insects for this assembly to dispel their doubts; would that not be wonderful?"
The Buddha said:
"After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Vipaśyin,
there was a stūpa and monastery."
Five hundred bhikṣus passed through the monastery.
Upon seeing them, the monastery master was greatly delighted and invited them to remain for three months of offerings; the entire assembly accepted his invitation.
The abbot served the meal with his whole heart, leaving nothing out.
Later, five hundred merchants returning from the sea after gathering treasures passed by the stupa-temple.
There they saw five hundred bhikṣus diligently practicing the Path.
Each of them then gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and joyfully deliberated together:
"A field of merit is difficult to encounter; we should prepare a modest offering."
He then informed the abbot of the monastery. The abbot replied,
"I have invited [the monks] for three months, with five days remaining until the end."
Only then could it be prepared extensively.
The merchants said, "We must depart; we cannot wait until it is finished."
The five hundred merchants each gave up one jewel,
thereby obtaining five hundred maṇi jewels,
which they entrusted to the temple master.
He entrusted the temple master, saying,
"Use our pearls daily to provide offerings for the assembly of monks.
The bhikṣu replied, "So be it."
They all accepted them immediately.
Later, however, they conceived unwholesome thoughts,
plotting to seize them for themselves alone.
In the end, he did not provide the offerings.
The assembly of monks asked him, saying,
"The merchant who previously gave you the pearls ought to have been provided with offerings."
"And have you dispatched it?
The temple master replied,
"It was given to me as a gift."
"If you wish to take my excrement, I shall give it to you;
but if you do not depart immediately,
I will cut off your hands and feet and cast you into the cesspit."
The assembly, pitying his folly, departed silently, each to their own place. This concludes the fourth fascicle of the *Daśādhyāya-avadāna-sūtra*. 8. *Yūkā-yūkā*, the Eighth [Chapter]. 1.

On Lice Dwelling upon a Meditator and the Seasonal Intervals for Drinking Blood. Regarding lice dwelling upon a meditator and the seasonal intervals for drinking blood: Long ago in the distant past...
After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa,
during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there will be a bhikṣu who practices meditation alone in a forest,
constantly plagued by lice and nits.
Even though they had made an agreement that if he were to practice meditation,
she should remain silent and stay hidden in stillness, the louse acted most appropriately.
At a later time,
a louse from the soil came to the side of a flea and asked:
"Why is your body so plump and robust now?
The louse replied,
"The master upon whom I depend constantly practices meditative concentration."
"Teach me the proper timing for eating and drinking;
by practicing according to the Dharma, I shall become fresh and robust.
He spoke thus.
"I also wish to practice that dharma.
The louse said, "As you wish.
Upon hearing the scent of blood and flesh, the flea immediately began to devour it.
The bhikṣu was distressed;
he immediately removed his robes and burned them with fire.
This bhikṣu who practiced meditation was Kāśyapa Buddha.
The earth flea was Devadatta;
the louse was I myself. (From the *Bao'en jing*, scroll 4; *Jinglü yixiang*, scroll 48).
