his military forces were no match for the enemy.
Thereupon, he made a vow, wishing to become the lord of hell.
He was assisted by eighteen ministers who led a host of one million; they all had horns and ears on their heads, and were entirely filled with resentment and rage.
They made a vow together, saying:
"In the future, we shall assist in governing these sinful beings.
King Vaiśravaṇa is the present King Yama.
The eighteen individuals are the various minor kings;
the multitude of one million are the various *ābhangas*.

They serve under the Northern Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. The *Chujin Dizhu jing* (Sūtra on the Questions Concerning Hell) and the *Jingdu Sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Purification and Deliverance) state that they collectively govern one hundred and thirty-four hells.
2. King Yama Suffers at Three Times. Regarding King Yama suffering at three times: to the south of Jambudvīpa there is a great Vajra Mountain;
within it lies the palace of King Yama.
It is six thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. The *Diyu jing* (Sūtra on the Inquiry of the Hells) states:

"Residing within the intervals of the hells, there are cities three myriad *li* in length and breadth, composed of gold and silver. At three times during the day and night, great copper cauldrons spontaneously appear before them."
If the cauldron enters the palace,
the king sees it and, struck with fear,
abandons it and goes outside the palace.
If the cauldron is moved outside the palace while the king enters within,
there are great hell-wardens who lay the king upon the hot cauldron.
With iron hooks, their mouths are pried open and molten copper is poured inside;
from the throat down, there is nothing that is not scorched and rotted.
When the business was concluded, he returned to enjoy himself with his court ladies.
It was the same for those ministers who shared in his merit. (From the *Dīrgha Āgama*, Scroll 19).
3. King Yama Questions the Offenders. King Yama questions the offenders regarding the three existences and the three taints:
first, old age;
second, sickness.
Third, death:
if there are sentient beings who commit evil through the three types of action,
they shall fall into hell upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life.
The king asked,
"Have you been summoned by a celestial messenger?
The king said:
"Do you see the first messenger? Among human beings,
do you not see those whose hair has turned white, whose teeth have fallen out, and whose vision has grown dim?"
"Does this man, with his wrinkled skin, shriveled muscles, hunched back, and walking with a cane while groaning, exist?
"I see him," the sinner replied.
The King said:
"Why do you not reflect for yourself:
'I, too, shall become like this'?
The sinner said:
At that time, I was negligent and did not realize it myself.
The king said,
"Now I shall cause you to know the suffering of negligence."
"This is not the fault of your parents, brothers, the Lord of Devas, ancestors, acquaintances, servants, śramaṇas, or others.
You have committed evil yourself, and you must now experience its consequences.
He asked again, "Do you see the second messenger?"
In your former lives as a human being,
have you ever seen anyone who was so gravely ill that they lay upon their own excrement and urine in a foul-smelling place;
whose every joint ached with such pain that they shed tears and groaned, unable even to speak?
He replied, "I saw them.
The King asked, "Why did you not reflect upon the coming and going as the first messenger did? And did you notice the third messenger?"
Have you ever seen a person who has died, whose body has disintegrated and life has ended, with all the sense faculties forever extinguished,
the body straight and rigid like a withered tree, cast away in a cemetery to be devoured by birds and beasts?
The answer is: Having seen him come and go as previously described, he was handed over to the hell-wardens. The *Sanzhishi e jing* (Sutra on the Treatment of Evil Beings in the Three Times) states:
"Five messengers were dispatched and five questions were posed."

This refers to those who, due to the evil karma of their previous lives, undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death by entering the great hells; this is as described in the nineteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Loutan jing* (Sūtra of the Iron Cauldron), with slight variations.
4. The Names of the Eighteen Hells and Their Wardens; the Names of the Eighteen Hells and Their Wardens, and the Forty-eight Minor Kings.
First is Kāyana, the Overseer of Niraya.
Second, the Mountain of Knives for those who violate the scriptures;
third, the Boiling Sand for those who violate their life-span and the scriptures;
fourth, the Boiling Excrement for those who violate the scriptures.
Fifth, Kāśyapa, is the scripture of Black Ears;
sixth, Sāṭha is the scripture of the Fire Chariot;
seventh, Tāpa is said to be the scripture of the Boiling Cauldron.
8. Ayaḥkāraṇa presides over the Iron Bed;
9. Duḥkhānta presides over Mount Śālmalī; 10.
Śītoṣṇa [presides over the Cold Ice Hell, though the king's name is missing from the scripture]; 11. Vikara presides over the Flaying.
The twelfth, Jingtou, presides over domestic animals.
The thirteenth, Dibao, presides over weapons of war.
The fourteenth, Yi, presides over iron and grinding stones.
15. The Hell of the Head-pleasing Ice-Master;
16. The Iron Spike Hell (the name of the king is missing from the text); 17. The Body-Master of Maggots; 18.
The Contemplation of the Body Master of Molten Copper, as recorded in the *Diyu chuwen diyu jing* (Sutra on Questions Regarding the Hells).
5. The Names of the Thirty Hells and Their Wardens. Regarding the names of the thirty hells and their wardens:
first is King Samjīva, who presides over the great niraya of Avīci.
The second is King Pingwang of Jin,
who presides over the Black Rope (Kālasūtra) heavy prison.
The third is King Tudu.
The fourth is the Assistant of the Heavenly King;
he presides over and governs the Hell of Conjunction.
The fifth is the King of the Holy Capital (Śrīmad-rāja),
who presides over the Great Mountain Hell.
The sixth is the King of the Mysterious Capital (Guhya-rāja).
He presides over the Hell of the City of Fire.
The seventh is King Vighusta,
who presides over the Hell of the Sword-Tree Forest.
The eighth is King Wuyang,
who presides over the Howling Hell.
The ninth is King Pingyang.
He presides over the Eight Paths of Hell.
Tenth is King Dūyāṅ,
who oversees the Spiked Tree Hell.
Eleventh is King Eliminating Yang,
who presides over the Hell of Boiling Ashes.
Twelfth is King Relieving Suffering.
The Director of Justice presides over the Great Crying Hell and the Small Crying Hell.
Thirteenth is King Vistara-cārin,
who presides over the Great Avīci Hell.
14. King Gaodu presides over the Iron Chariot Hell. 15. King Gongyang.
It primarily governs the Iron Fire Hell.
The Sixteenth, King Píngjiě (Peaceful Liberation),
primarily governs the Boiling Excrement Hell.
Seventeenth is King Yang,
who presides over the Hell of Burning Grounds.
Eighteenth is King Pingqiu.
Dianzhi presides over the Mili hell;
Shiqiu, the King of Stones,
presides over the mountain-stone hell.
The twentieth is King Laṅgaya,
who presides over the Tuḥuṇa hell.
The twenty-first is King Duguān.
The Twenty-second, King Xuanxi, presides over the Niraya Hell and presides over the hell of flying insects.
Twenty-third is King Taiyi,
who presides over the Yang'e prison.
Twenty-fourth is King Heshi.
It primarily governs the Great Grinding Hell.
The twenty-fifth is King Coolness,
who primarily governs the Cold Snow Hell.
Twenty-sixth is King Without Origin,
who presides over the Iron Pestle Hell.
Twenty-seventh is King Political Governance.
He presides over the Iron Pillar Hell.
The Twenty-eighth is King Distant Height;
he presides over the Hell of Pus and Blood.
The twenty-ninth is King Dujin,
who presides over the Hell of Burning Stones; the thirtieth is King Yuandu,
who presides over the Hell of the Iron Wheel.
These constitute the thirty great and agonizing hells.
The divine spirits observe and record merits and transgressions without regard for rank or status;
they report them six times a month and review them four times a year.
On the four days of concealment, all eight *rājas* (auspicious days) are employed.
As for the *rāja* days, the Heavenly Kings conduct inspections to compare them with the various classes of heavenly subjects;
those with merit have their lifespans increased, while those with transgressions have their allotted years diminished.
The span of life is regulated so that even the finest hairs are not out of place;
yet the people are blind and ignorant, utterly unaware of this.
Failing to perform good deeds in advance, they are consigned to hell. *Chujingdu Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Purifying Deliverance).
6. The Five Officials Prohibit People from Committing Crimes. Regarding the five officials who prohibit people from committing crimes:
first, the Official of Freshness prohibits killing;
second, the Official of Water prohibits theft.
Third, the Iron Officials prohibit sexual misconduct;
fourth, the Earth Officials prohibit double-tongued speech;
fifth, the Heavenly Officials prohibit intoxicants. This is from the *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance).
7. Regarding the initial experience of birth in hell: to the east, south, west, and north of the ten cities of King Yama, various hells are arrayed.
Although there is the light of the sun and moon, they are neither bright nor pure.
Only the Black-Eared Hell (Kālakarnī-naraka) is not illuminated by its light.
When a person's life ends, their spirit is born into the intermediate state (antarābhava).
This intermediate state has already abandoned the aggregates of death but has not yet reached the aggregates of birth.
Those sinful beings, mounting their intermediate state bodies (*antarābhava*), enter the city of Niraya.
"Niraya City" is translated in the Liang language as "City of Entrustment and Bondage" (*ji-xi cheng*) or "City of Closure" (*bi cheng*). This is where all these sinful beings reside.
Before they have yet undergone their retribution, they gather together in this place.
Blown by the wind of skillfulness, they receive bodies large or small according to the lightness or heaviness of their karma;
blown by the foul wind, the forms of the offenders are brought to completion as coarse and hideous.

Each has its own person to come and meet them.
When a person is ill and about to die,
they see this person coming to meet them with their own eyes.
Those destined to be born in the heavens will be welcomed by devas bearing celestial garments and music.
Those destined to be born in other realms will see honored beings before their eyes who speak sublime words to them.
Those destined to fall into hell will see soldiers before their eyes, brandishing swords, shields, spears, halberds, and nooses, surrounding them.
What they see differs;
they cannot speak of it with their mouths,
yet each receives its retribution according to what they have done.
"Heaven is without partiality or excess;
it is impartial and straightforward, without duality.
It governs according to one's deeds through the Net of Heaven," as stated in the *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance).
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
When a person is about to die, they perceive the signs of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Those who have performed evil deeds see themselves suffering in the three miserable realms.
Some see Yama holding various weapons and leading them away in captivity;
others hear cries of suffering.
However, those who have performed wholesome deeds see such superior things as the celestial palaces of the devas, adorned with celestial maidens, and the joy of playful recreation.
9. The Messengers of the Eight Kings Examine Good and Evil on the Six Uposatha Days. The Messengers of the Eight Kings examine good and evil on the six Uposatha days. 9. The Eight Kings said:
This refers to the thirty-two ministers who guard Śakra,
the Four Great Kings of the Quarters, the Lords of Fate and the Registrars,
and the Five-hundred-armed King and the eight kings and their messengers.
They all emerged and spread out their fourfold canopies over the procession.
Furthermore, they encountered the Four Heavenly Kings reporting on the fifteenth and thirtieth days,
examining and verifying the conduct and the good or evil deeds of the people.
The King of Hell also dispatches his attendant ministers and minor kings;
they emerge simultaneously, and as soon as there is a transgressor, it is recorded.
This occurs prior to the eighth day of the fasting period.
If one commits an offense while the power of merit is strong, there is rescue and peace; there is no other means than to rely on the original source of merit for pardon.
If one commits the offense again on a subsequent day of fasting (upoṣadha), and the number of transgressions is great, it will diminish one's lifespan—a condition known as "death by exhaustion."
The years, months, days, and hours determine one's descent into hell.
Upon receiving the official document, the hell-wardens immediately dispatch their minions with the register of names to summon the deceased.
Yet these hell-wardens lack compassion; even when the day of death has not yet arrived, they still proceed to seize them.
If one forcibly urges others toward evil, their life will be brought to a premature end;
if one possesses much merit, their lifespan and allotted years will increase,
and the gods will dispatch benevolent deities to protect their person.
They are transferred from the hells to have their transgressions eradicated;
death is averted and rebirth is certain, followed by birth in the heavens. This is from the *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Purity).
10. Cold and Heat Hells, Borderlands Hells. Regarding the ten [types of hells], what are the cold and heat hells and the borderlands hells?
The answer is: they refer to the cold and heat hells and the borderlands hells.
There are immeasurable varieties.
Now, I shall briefly explain them.
As for the cold hells, they are the Reviling and the Howling.
They do not cease their wailing;
they do not call out.
There are these three signs of most terrible shrieking.
There are three types of those who cry out:
first, Arbuda; second, Nirarbuda.
Third, *āpāpa*. In the *Arbuda* hell, boils resembling abscesses arise within the frozen body.
In the *Nirarbuda* hell, the body is blown up and distended by wind.
In the *Ababa* hell, an extremely cold wind blows and strips away their skin and flesh until they fall off entirely;
all of them cry out in urgent distress.
These three hells can be understood [as described].
Those who do not understand the cries are:
first, the *aṭṭāṭṭahāsa*;
second, the *utpala*.
Regarding *aṭaḥ-aṭaḥ*: they are also blown by an extremely cold wind;
as their skin and flesh are stripped away, they cry out, "Aṭaḥ-aṭaḥ! Regarding *utpala*:
they are blown and stripped of their skin and flesh by an extremely great wind and cold, and iron leaves from within their bodies spontaneously wrap around them.
Like an *utpala* flower,
those who slander the noble ones fall into this hell;
they are the "Non-Crying" (*Araṭa*).
First, the kumuda;
second, the sugandhika;
third, the puṇḍarīka.
Fourth is the *Kāpota* hell.
An extremely cold wind blows, causing the body to swell;
one suffers and groans according to these four characteristics.
Because they slandered the noble ones and the sages, they fall into those four kinds of hells,
where at all times they undergo immeasurable suffering;
these are all the great cold hells.
Situated between the four continents,
they dwell at the base of the Cakravāḍa mountains,
looking upward while residing in total darkness.
The cold wind destroys the body;
it is burned by a great fire as if burning a grove of bamboo.
Their coughing and voices clash together;
furthermore, there are other sentient beings who undergo suffering therein,
all of whom revile and slander the noble ones and thus experience such torment.
As the Blessed One said in verse:
"In Nirarbuda there are one hundred thousand, And thirty-five in Arbuda;
These are the evil destinies and hells for those who revile the noble ones, Due to the evil intentions of speech and mind."
This is called the Cold Hell.
Question: What is the Hot Hell?
Answer: There is one primary presiding authority.
Second is the minor method of counteracting;
third is the method of counteracting without [a specific] focus. These three methods of counteracting refer to interrogation and flogging.
There are two types of those with owners: first, those who live by working;
second, those who wander.
Third is the Black Rope Hell.
As for the Reviving Hell,
its wardens use sharp knives and axes to flay, hack, and mince the sinful beings, just as one might cut and chop the tips of grass.
The skin and flesh dissolve away, yet because the conditions for their transgression have not been exhausted,
they are restored as before by a cold wind.
Furthermore, due to their evil karma, iron claws grow upon their hands, as sharp as knives.
Each gives rise to bonds of enmity and they further tear and mangle one another,
like cutting through bamboo or reeds;
because they die with hearts bound by resentment while hearing one another's voices, they are born here.
As for the Black Rope Hell (Kālasūtra),
the offenders are stretched out upon the ground;
they are marked with black lines and then hacked and severed along those lines.
Because they slaughtered sentient beings, they are born in that hell.
Furthermore, their bodies are bound with hot, red copper sheets,
so that their bones are shattered and their marrow flows.
Because they applied whips and staves to sentient beings and to those who have left the household life,
and because they did not practice diligently but instead greedily clung to robes offered out of faith, they are born therein;
there they suffer in extreme, profound darkness as if scorched by smoke.
They hang their bodies upside down and force them to inhale smoke;
this is because they have smoked out creatures that dwell in burrows.
These are those who travel through the earth hells.
Sentient beings who have committed offenses of the serial type are like those at a butcher’s stall;
their hands, feet, ears, noses, and heads are severed.
It is because they were originally butchers that they now undergo this suffering.
Furthermore, there is a ground of glowing iron upon which iron chariots are driven.
The hell-wardens mount them, staring with wide eyes and shouting "Chi-chi!
as they force [the beings] to run; because of the exhaustion from being driven like elephants or horses, they fall into this place.
One who commits adultery with another’s wife is driven up a sword-tree and naturally burned by fire, undergoing such suffering.
It is said that there are jailers who preside over the hells;
because of their past conduct, they are not burned by the fire.
The minor hells are those that preside over the hells of suffering:
first, Saṃjīva (Reviving); second, Kālasūtra (Black Thread);
third, Saṃghāta (Crushing). Regarding the Saṃghāta hell:
Sinful sentient beings, fearing the hell-wardens,
flee into the mountains by the hundreds of thousands; yet,
fire spontaneously arises before and behind them.
The two mountains close together as if grinding;
blood flows like a river and flesh and bone are completely crushed,
because they delight in grinding sentient beings.
Furthermore, they are burned by fire and pounded in a great iron mortar with a pestle;
though a hundred years pass, their lives do not end because of the conditions of their transgressions,
for they were killed by being pounded in the mortar like fleas, lice, and bugs.
As for the Hell of Great Wailing:
great iron mountains are ablaze with fire on all sides, leaving no place to pass;
the cruel hell-wardens are devoid of compassion.
Speaking with malice,
he asked, "Where do you wish to go?
and then struck his head with an iron pestle set ablaze.
It is because they have brought suffering upon the myriad people that they are born within this realm.
As for the Hell of Roasting,
great iron mountains have flames that strike against one another.
They scoop them up with iron shovels;
as they are scorched on all sides, one side becomes just cooked,
and the shovel naturally turns them over, flipping and inverting them.
Because they killed people by piercing them through with spears, they are born within this realm.
As for the Hell of No Deficiency (Avaṃcanā),
its iron ground is surrounded by blazing fire, extending for a hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
The four gates are like those of a city, covered above with thin copper plates from which flames blaze in continuous succession.
The various sinful beings are heaped there like firewood;
the flames pass through them without obstruction, scorching and rotting their bodies as they undergo unceasing suffering.
Having killed one's father, mother, and a *ṛṣi*,
harboring evil intent toward the Buddha so as to cause blood to flow,
and inciting strife among the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, because they have committed the ten unwholesome karmas with excessive intensity, they are born in this [intermediate] realm.
As for the peripheral hells,
they are located among houses, between waters, among mountains, and in wildernesses.
To undergo the retribution for evil karma alone is called the peripheral hells. This concludes the third fascicle, the Chapter on the Emergence of Garments. Section 11:

Between the Diamond Mountains, each of the eight great hells has sixteen minor hells. Between the Diamond Mountains, each of the eight great hells has sixteen minor hells. Outside the four continents of the ten thousand worlds, there are eighty thousand worlds surrounding them.
Beyond the eighty thousand worlds of the earth, there is again a great ocean.
Beyond the ocean, there is a great Vajra Mountain.

Beyond that mountain, there is another mountain also named Vajra; the *Loutan jing* (Kāṣāyaprabhāsa-sūtra) calls it the Great Iron Ring Mountains (*Mahācakravāḍa*). Between these two mountains, the majestic radiance of the sun and moon deities does not reach.
There are eight great hells:
the first is called Saṃjīva (Reviving),
and the second is called Kālasūtra (Black Thread).
The third is Crushing;
the fourth is Screaming;
the fifth is Great Screaming.
Sixth is the Hell of Burning and Roasting;
seventh is the Hell of Great Burning and Roasting;

eighth is the Hell of Uninterrupted Suffering (*Avīci*). As stated in the *Loutan jing* (Sūtra on the Iron Tower), there are differing texts, most of which are not recorded here. Among these hells is the first one.
Each has sixteen minor hells. The *Diyu jing* (Sūtra on Asking about Hells) states:
"Hells exist upon the earth.
Regarding the sixteen *saṃjñā*-hells:
First is the Hell of Black Sand;
second is the Hell of Boiling Excrement;
third is the Hell of Five Hundred Nails.
The fourth is hunger;
the fifth is thirst;
the sixth is a single bronze cauldron.
The seventh is many copper cauldrons;
the eighth is stone grinding mills;
the ninth is pus and blood.
Tenth is the Hell of Measuring Fire;
eleventh is the River of Ashes;
twelfth is the Iron Ball.
Thirteenth: Adzes and Axes;
Fourteenth: Jackals and Wolves;
Fifteenth: Sword Trees.
The sixteenth is the Cold Ice Hell.
The sentient beings therein have iron claws growing from their hands, with which they alternately strike one another in mutual rage and resentment.
They claw at one another with their talons until the flesh falls away at the touch of their hands;
they imagine themselves to be dead.
Furthermore, the sentient beings therein harbor thoughts of malice and harm toward one another.
Holding swords and blades in their hands, they strike and stab one another;
they flay, mince, and cut each other's bodies until they are shattered upon the ground,
and they say to one another, "We are dead."
A cold wind blew upon him, and he revived;
he said to himself, "I have now returned to life.
Having endured his punishment for a long time, he emerged from the Saṃjīva Hell.
In a state of frantic terror, they cry out for rescue, unaware that they have suddenly arrived at the Black Sand Hell.
A violent hot wind arises, blowing burning black sand onto their bodies;
it sears the skin and penetrates to the bone, causing flames to erupt from within their very flesh.
They are turned over and back again, their bodies scorched and seared until they are rotten;
yet because their retribution is not yet exhausted, they do not die.
After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Black Sands Hell and arrive at the Boiling Excrement Hell.
Boiling excrement and iron balls spontaneously appear before them.
The sinners are driven and coerced to embrace the iron balls, which burn their hands and bodies;
they are then further forced to grasp them and thrust them into their mouths.
From the throat to the abdomen, it passes straight through until nothing remains unscorched or unrotted.
There are iron-beaked insects that gnaw at the flesh and penetrate to the marrow, causing immeasurable bitter agony.
Though they undergo these punishments without end, they refuse to die.
Having long endured suffering, they emerge from the Hell of Boiling Excrement and arrive at the Hell of Iron Nails.
The wardens strike them down, laying them supine upon hot iron;
they stretch out their bodies and nail their hands and feet with iron spikes.
With five hundred nails driven completely through his body,
he wailed in bitter agony yet still did not die.
After suffering for a long time, he emerged from the Iron Nails Hell and arrived at the Hungry Ghosts Hell.
They are immediately thrown onto glowing hot iron and molten copper is poured into their mouths;
from the throat down to the abdomen, it passes straight through until nothing remains unscorched or unrotted.
Yet, because their remaining karma is not yet exhausted, they do not die.
Having long endured suffering, they emerge from the Hungry Hell and arrive at the Thirsty Hell.
They are immediately flung onto hot iron and a glowing iron ball is placed into their mouths;
it burns their lips and tongues, passing straight through until there is nothing that is not scorched and rotten, as they wail in bitter agony.

Having endured suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Kṣāranadī (Salt Water) Hell and arrive at the Tāmradroṇī (Copper Cauldron) Hell. There, the hell-wardens, with eyes blazing with rage, seize the sinners by their feet and cast them headlong into the cauldrons.
As the boiling broth surges and ebbs, the sinners swirl up and down within it.
As their bodies become putrid and decayed, ten thousand poisons converge upon them, yet they are not allowed to die.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge from one copper cauldron and enter the Hell of Many Copper Cauldrons.
There, the wardens seize the offenders by their feet and hurl them headlong into the cauldrons.
As the boiling water surges and swirls up and down, their entire bodies are mangled and decomposed;
they are then seized with iron hooks and placed into other cauldrons,
where they wail in grief and endure such bitter agony that they do not die.
Having long endured suffering, they emerge from the Many Copper Cauldrons and arrive at the Stone Grinding Hell.
They seize those offenders and throw them onto hot stones;
stretching out their hands and feet, they press their bodies down with great, scorching stones.
They are turned over and ground until their flesh and bones are crushed to pulp;
because the bitter poison and piercing pain are so intense, they do not die.
After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Stone Mill Hell and arrive at the Pus and Blood Hell.
Pus and blood boil and surge; within it, the sinners run hither and thither from east to west.
Their bodies, heads, and faces are scalded and ruined, and they are further made to eat that pus and blood.
Because they have thoroughly penetrated through the unbearable bitterness and poison below, they do not die;
having long endured suffering, they eventually emerge with pus and blood and arrive at the Fire Hell of Measured Heat.
There is a great mass of fire with blazing, fierce flames that drives and compels the offenders.
Holding an iron ladle, they measure out masses of fire;
their entire bodies are scorched by bitter, poisonous heat and pain,
and as they groan and wail, they are made not to die.
Having long endured suffering, they emerge from the Hell of Measuring Fire and arrive at the Hell of the Ash River.
It is five hundred yojanas in length, breadth, and depth.
The caustic ash-water surges and boils, its foul stench wafts and swirls, and the crashing of its circling waves produces a terrifying sound.
From the bottom to the top, iron spikes run crisscrossing.
On the banks of that river stands a forest of sword-trees,
whose branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all swords and blades.
The sinners enter the river, rising and falling with the waves;
they are overturned and submerged, as iron thorns pierce their bodies until they are permeated from within and without, and pus and blood flow out.
Because their sufferings are manifold, they are not allowed to die;
thus they emerge from the Ash River and reach the opposite bank,
where sharp swords cut and pierce their bodies, wounding and breaking them.
Furthermore, jackals and wolves come to bite the offenders, devouring their flesh raw.
When they run up the sword-trees, the blade-edges point downward;
when they descend from the sword-trees, the blade-edges point upward.
As they grasp with their hands, their hands snap off; as they tread with their feet, their feet are severed.
The skin and flesh fall away, leaving only white bones connected by sinews.
At that time, there are iron-beaked crows upon the sword-trees.
Crows peck at their heads and devour their brains; they wail in bitter agony so that they do not die.
They return to the Ash River, sinking with the waves, while iron spikes pierce their bodies in ten thousand ways of bitter torment.
The skin and flesh rot and decay, with pus and blood flowing out,
until only white bones remain floating on the surface.
When a cold wind blows, they immediately stand up.
Dragged by the pull of past karma, one arrives suddenly and unconsciously at the Iron Ball Hell.
There, hell-wardens drive hot iron balls into them;
their hands and feet are scorched and destroyed, and their entire bodies burst into flames.
Because ten thousand poisons arrive simultaneously, they are made not to die.
After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Iron Ball Hell and reach the Axe and Hatchet Hell.
There, the wardens seize these offenders and throw them onto glowing red iron.
With hot iron adzes and axes, they hack at their hands, feet, ears, noses, and bodies;
though they wail in bitter agony, they still do not die.
After enduring these punishments for a long time, they emerge from the Adze-and-Axe Hell and arrive at the Hell of Jackals and Wolves.
A pack of jackals and wolves vied with one another to gnaw and mangle him;
his flesh fell away, his bones were injured, and pus and blood flowed out.
He suffered ten thousand kinds of agony, yet was not allowed to die.
After having suffered for a long time, they emerge from the Śṛgāla-wolves and arrive at the Sword-tree Hell (Asipatravana).
Upon entering that forest of swords, a violent wind arises,
blowing the leaves of the sword-trees down upon their bodies.
Their heads, faces, and bodies are completely mangled and destroyed;
iron-beaked crows peck at their two eyes,
and they wail in agony so that they do not die.
Having endured suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from the Forest of Swords and arrive at the Hell of Cold Ice.
A great freezing wind blows upon their bodies;
their entire frames are frozen and wounded, and their skin and flesh fall away.
They cry out in bitter agony and only then do their lives end.
Their bodies have committed unwholesome deeds, and so too have their speech and minds.
Thus they fall into the Saṃjīva Hell, where terror makes the hair on their bodies stand on end.
The Black Rope Great Hell is surrounded on all sides by sixteen minor hells,
each measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Why is it named Black Rope?
Its various hell-wardens seize those sinners and throw them onto hot iron;
they stretch out their bodies and mark them straight with hot iron cords.
With a red-hot iron axe, they chase the victims along the path of the ropes and hack them into hundreds of thousands of pieces.
Furthermore, they mark them with iron cords and saw them apart.
Moreover, they hang them amidst countless intersecting lines of glowing iron cords.
The sinners are driven and forced to walk between the iron cords.

A violent, evil wind suddenly arises and blows against their bodies, piercing through the skin, penetrating the flesh, scorching the bones, and boiling the marrow; thus their suffering and torment are manifold.
Because their remaining karma is not yet exhausted, they do not die;
therefore, it is called the Black Rope Hell.
After suffering there for a long time, they emerge from the Black Rope Hell and arrive at the Black Sand Hell.
They shall remain there until the end of the寒冰 (Cold Ice) Hell before their lives finally conclude.
Those who harbor evil intentions toward their parents, the Buddha,
or the Śrāvakas will fall into the Black Rope Hell, where the suffering is beyond description.
Surrounding the Great Avīci Hell are sixteen minor hells,
each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Why is it called "The Pressing Together"?
There are two great rocky mountains facing each other;
when a person enters between them, [they are crushed].
The mountain naturally closes in to crush his body;
his flesh and bones are ground to pulp, and the mountain returns to its original place.
Endowed with ten thousand kinds of bitter suffering, he is thus made not to die.
Furthermore, there are great iron elephants with their entire bodies ablaze who come roaring and trampling upon the sinners,
rolling over them until their bodies are crushed to pieces and pus and blood flow forth.
They wail and shriek in grief so that they do not die.
Again, they seize the offenders and lay them upon a great stone, crushing them with another large stone.
Furthermore, they take the offenders and lay them on the ground, pounding them with iron pestles.
From the feet to the scalp, the flesh is crushed and mangled;
pus and blood flow out, and myriad poisons arrive together.
Because the remaining retribution has not yet been exhausted, they are not allowed to die; therefore, it is named "Pushing and Crushing."
Having endured suffering for a long time, they finally emerge and are driven onward to the Black Sand Hell,
continuing through to the Cold Ice Hell before their lives come to an end;
this occurs because they have committed the three types of evil karma and failed to cultivate the three types of wholesome conduct.
The suffering in the Crushing Hell (Pancatapanīya) is beyond description.
In the Great Hell of Wailing (Raurava),
there are sixteen minor hells.
Each is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
For what reason is it called the Hell of Screaming?
The hell-wardens seize the offenders and hurl them into large cauldrons.
Furthermore, they are placed within a great iron cauldron where boiling hot water surges and seethes,
cooking those sinners as they wail and cry out in bitter agony and distress.
Furthermore, they take those sinners and cast them upon the griddle, repeatedly broiling and frying them as they wail and shriek.
Because their remaining retribution is not yet exhausted, they are not allowed to die; therefore, this place is named "Wailing" (Raurava).
Having endured suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from Raurava and arrive at the Black Sand Hell;
only upon reaching the Cold Water Hell do their lives come to an end.
This is because they harbored malice and poison, committing various evil deeds.
They fall into the Raurava Hell and the Mahāraurava Great Hell,
which have sixteen minor hells.
What is called the Great Screaming Hell?
It is where those sinners are taken and placed inside a great iron cauldron,
and further set within an iron vat.
Boiling hot water surges and seethes as it cooks those sinners;
they are also cast upon great iron griddles,
where they are repeatedly scorched and simmered, wailing and crying out in bitter and acrid agony.
Because their remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, they do not die; this is called the Great Screaming Hell (*Mahāraurava*).
After suffering there for a long time, they emerge from the Great Screaming Hell and enter the Cold Ice Hell (*Himāraniraya*), whereupon their lives finally come to an end.
They cultivate various wrong views,
are dragged along by the net of craving,
and engage in base and ignoble conduct.
They fall into the Great Howling Hell and the Burning Hell,
which have sixteen minor hells.
Why is it called "Burning and Roasting"?
It is because various offenders are placed within an iron city;
that city is ablaze with fire, both inside and out glowing red, burning and roasting the offenders.
Furthermore, they are cast onto iron towers;
those towers are ablaze, glowing red both inside and out.
They are also thrown into great iron cauldrons.
The kiln fire blazes so fiercely that both the interior and exterior are glowing red;
it roasts and scorches the sinners until their skin and flesh are singed and putrefied, and myriad poisons assail them simultaneously.
Because their remaining retribution is not yet exhausted, they are made not to die.
Therefore, it is called the Hell of Burning and Roasting.
After suffering for a long time, one leaves the Hell of Burning and Roasting and proceeds to the Hell of Black Sand,
continuing through the various hells down to the Cold Ice Hell, and only then does one’s life there come to an end.
Because they practiced the act of burning and roasting, they fall into the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell,
where they suffer the torments of burning and roasting for a long night;
[and likewise] into the Mahāsaṃjīva (Great Reviving) Hell.
There are sixteen minor hells,
each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth;
all the sinners are placed within these iron cities.
That city blazes with fire, both inside and out, glowing crimson.
It scorches and roasts the sinners until their skin and flesh are charred and putrefied, and ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously.
There is a great pit of fire where the flames burn most fiercely.
On both banks of that pit there are great volcanic fires.
They seize those sinners, impale them on iron forks, and stand them upright amidst the flames; the intense fire burns and roasts them until their skin and flesh are scorched and rotten.
Because their remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, they do not die;
having long endured suffering, they emerge from the Great Burning Hell and proceed through the Black Sand Hell,
continuing even unto the Cold Ice Hell, only then passing away.
Abandoning wholesome fruits and karma for various evil deeds,
they fall into the Great Burning Hell and the Avīci Great Hell.
There are sixteen minor hells,
each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth; there,
they seize those sinners and flay their skin from their feet to the crown of their heads.
They then wrap the sinner’s body with that very hide;
he is placed upon a flaming iron wheel and made to tread upon hot iron ground,
where he is driven back and forth until his body is crushed and mangled.
The skin and flesh fall away and myriad poisons converge, yet they are not permitted to die.
Furthermore, an iron city arises with fire breaking out on all four sides;
the flames from the east reach the west, and the flames from the west reach the east.
It is likewise in the north, south, above, and below;
amidst the blazing flames and frantic turmoil, there is not a single empty space.
They run hither and thither, east and west, as their bodies are scorched and roasted until their skin and flesh are singed and putrefied.
Painful and bitter, ten thousand poisons arrive all at once;
the sinner remains within until, after a long time, the gate finally opens,
whereupon the various sinners rush toward it.
Flames burst forth from all the joints and limbs of his body;
he runs toward the gate, but the gate closes of its own accord.
Because his remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, he is not permitted to die.
Furthermore, among them, whatever the sinners behold with their eyes, they see only foul colors;
what they hear with their ears is only foul sounds; what they smell with their noses is only foul odors;
what they touch with their bodies is only painful sensations; and what they contemplate with their minds are only unwholesome dharmas.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, there is no moment that is not one of suffering;
therefore, it is named the Avīci Hell.
After enduring suffering for a long time, their lives come to an end.
Due to their grave offenses, they are reborn in the evil destinies,
even as far as the Cold Ice Hell (Arbuda),
only then passing away from that life.
For having committed grave offenses that produce karma leading to rebirth in the evil destinies, one falls into the Avīci Hell; the gravity of such sins is beyond description.
Within each of the eight great hells, there are sixteen minor hells.
12. Between the Vajra Mountains there are ten additional hells; between the two great Vajra Mountains there are twelve.
There is a great wind named Saṃkha;
if this wind were to blow upon the four continents and the eighty thousand continents,
it would cause the great earth and its mountains to rise ten *yojanas* above the ground.
Even if they reach a hundred *li* and fly through the air, they are all completely pulverized,
like a strong man grasping light chaff in his hand and scattering it into the sky;
this is because two great mountains obstruct this wind.
If this wind were to reach the four continents,
the streams, rivers, seas, and oceans within them would all be parched and dried up.
Furthermore, the winds from the mountain clefts are foul-smelling, impure, stinking, and acrid.
If they were to come to the four continents,
their smoke would cause all sentient beings to lose their sight;
furthermore, these two mountains provide great benefit.
This, too, is brought about by the retribution of the actions of sentient beings.
Furthermore, between the two mountains there are ten hells;
the first is named Thick Clouds (Ghanavāta).
The second is named Cloudless;
the third is named Ha-ha;
the fourth is named How Can It Be? (Nai-he).
The fifth is named Ewe’s Bleat;
the sixth is named Sugandhika;
the seventh is named Utpala.
The eighth is named Kuvalaya;
the ninth is named Puṇḍarīka;
the tenth is named Padma.
Why is it called "Thick Cloud"?
The spontaneously born bodies of the hell-beings are like thick clouds; therefore, it is named "Thick Cloud."
Why is it called "Cloudless" (Anabhraka)?
Because the bodies born of sentient beings are like lumps of flesh, it is therefore called "Cloudless.
Why is it called "Ha-ha"?
Because their pain is so acute that they all cry out "He-he," it is called He-he.
Why is it called Nai-he?
Sentient beings undergoing punishment experience such bitter and piercing agony that, having no refuge, they all cry out "Nai-he."
What is meant by "the bleating of sheep"?
Sentient beings undergoing punishment experience such piercing pain that they wish to raise their voices to speak, yet their tongues cannot move; thus their cries are like the bleating of sheep.
What is meant by "sūkaṇṭhika flowers"?
The hells are all black, like the color of a *sukandika* flower.
Why is it called the *utpala* flower?
The hells are all blue, like the color of an *utpala* flower.
Why is it called the *kumuda* flower?
Because the hells are all red, like the color of the *kumuda*.
Why is it called the *puṇḍarīka* flower?
The hells are all white like the *puṇḍarīka* flower.
What is meant by the *padma* flower?
The hells are all red, like the color of the *padma* flower.
It is like a basket with a capacity of sixty-four *hu* filled to the brim with sesame seeds.
Suppose there is a person who, every hundred years, removes a single seed.
In this manner, until the basket is completely emptied.
Having not yet finished undergoing punishment in the Ghanodadhi (Thick Cloud) Hell,
a lifespan of twenty Ghanodadhi Hells is equal to one lifespan in the Anabhraka (Cloudless) Hell.
Twenty lifespans in the Cloudless (Anabhraka) hell are equal to one lifespan in the Ha-ha hell;
twenty lifespans in the Ha-ha hell [are equal to one lifespan in the next hell].
The lifespan of one Nahe Hell is equal to the lifespan of twenty Nahe Hells;
the lifespan of one Yangming Hell is equal to the lifespan of one Nahe Hell.
Twenty lifespans in the Raurava (Twenty-Sheep-Crying) Hell are equal to one lifespan in the Śūkarikā (Pigsty) Hell.
Twenty lifespans in the Śūkarikā Hell [are equal to one lifespan in the next hell].
The lifespan of one Utpala hell is equal to twenty Utpala hells;
the lifespan of one Kumuda hell is equal to that [lifespan of twenty Utpala hells].
Twenty lifespans in the Kūṭaśālmalī hell are equal to one lifespan in the Puṇḍarīka hell;
twenty lifespans in the Puṇḍarīka hell [are equal to one lifespan in the next hell].
It is equal to the lifespan of one Padma hell;
just as twenty Padma lifespans are called one intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa),
so twenty intermediate kalpas are called one great kalpa (mahākalpa).
In the Padma Hell, the flames blaze with intense ferocity.
When the offenders are one hundred yojanas away from the fire,
the fire has already scorched them for sixty yojanas.
Both his ears were deaf so that he could hear nothing;
from fifty yojanas away both his eyes were blind so that he could see no more.
The bhikṣu Kokālika had already harbored an evil mind.

Having slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, their bodies were destroyed at the end of their lives and they fell into this Padma Hell; this is from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, where it corresponds to the *Loutan jing* (Kāṣṭha-saṃvartanī Sūtra), though with slight differences.

2. Section on the Hells (50): The Characteristics of the Various Sufferings Endured in the Avīci Hell, Part One. Each of the eighteen minor hells is surrounded by eighteen [subsidiary] hells. [The text discusses] the eighteen hells surrounding Avīci; the sixty-four hells illustrating the characteristics of suffering through their causes; and the five great hells illustrating the characteristics of the suffering endured. 1. Furthermore, it is said that there is no interval [between rebirths], and that fierce fires enter the heart, extending eight thousand yojanas in both length and breadth,
with sevenfold iron walls and seven-layered iron nets.
Below are eighteen compartments,
seven layers deep all around,
which are entirely forests of swords.
Furthermore, there are seven layers of sword-forests.
At the four corners are four great bronze dogs,
forty yojanas in length and breadth.
His eyes are like flashing lightning;
his fangs are like sword-trees;
his teeth are like mountains of knives.
Their tongues are like iron thorns;
all the hairs on their bodies are likewise ablaze with fierce fire,
emitting foul-smelling smoke.
There are eighteen hell-wardens whose mouths are like those of yakṣas;
from their sixty-four eyes, iron pellets scatter and fly forth.
The dog's fangs protrude four yojanas high;
from the tips of the fangs flows fire that burns and sears iron chariots,
while fire issues from the rims of their wheels.
Sharp blades, swords, and halberds burn the city of Avīci, making it as red as molten copper.
The hell-wardens have eight heads and sixty horns;
from their horns, fire erupts and blazes.
The fire transforms into copper, which further becomes sword-wheels;
these appear one after another amidst the flames,
filling the city of Avīci.
Within the city are seven iron pillars;
fire surges from them like boiling molten iron, erupting and gushing forth from the four gates.
Above them are eighteen cauldrons.
Boiling copper surged and overflowed, filling the city.
Between the two enclosures were eighty-four thousand iron pythons, great serpents that spat venomous fire,
their bodies covering the interior of the city.
That snake hissed like the thunder of heaven,
raining down five hundred great iron balls and five billion insects.
From eighty-four thousand mouths, streams of fire flow down like rain,
filling the city of Avīci.
When these worms descend, their fierce and blazing fires illuminate the area above the hell for eighty-four thousand yojanas.
It surges toward the great ocean and flows beneath Mount Wu-chiao, piercing the seabed with droplets as thick as axle-trees.
If there are those who kill their fathers, harm their mothers, or revile their six kin,
at the time of their death, bronze dogs will transform into eighteen chariots.
It resembles a precious canopy.
All the flames transform into jade maidens;
seeing them from afar, the sinner’s heart rejoices and he desires to go toward them.
When the wind-blade dissects him, the cold is so intense that he loses his voice.
"How wonderful it would be if a fine fire were placed upon my carriage; I would burn myself to death.
Having said this, he immediately passes away.
Seated in golden chariots and gazing upon jade maidens,
they all seize iron axes to hack and sever their own bodies;
in the time it takes to bend and extend an arm, they fall directly into the Avīci Hell.
From the upper partition to the lower partition, like a whirling wheel of fire,
their bodies fill the space within the partitions;
bronze dogs bark loudly as they gnaw on bones and suck out the marrow.
The hell-warden rākṣasa seizes a great axe and hacks [the victim], then impales him on a fork at the neck to make him stand up; flames erupt from his entire body, filling the Avīci Hell.
King Yama issues a loud proclamation:
You foolish person, a seed of hell!
While you were in the world,
you were unfilial toward your parents, perverse, arrogant, and unprincipled.
The place where you have now been born is called the Avīci Hell.
The hell-wardens then ascend from the lower tier to the upper tiers,
passing through eighty-four thousand tiers, traversing them with their bodies suspended until they reach the boundary of the iron net.
A single day and night there is equivalent to sixty small kalpas in Jambudvīpa;
when a full great kalpa has elapsed,
one commits the five heinous crimes.
At the time of death,
eighteen winds like iron chariots slice and sever his body;
because he is oppressed by heat, he utters these words:
"Would it not be joyful to sport beneath a great tree of exquisite color, fragrance, and coolness?
As this thought arose, eighty-four thousand forests of evil swords [vanished].
He transforms them into jeweled trees with lush flowers and fruit arranged in rows before him;
the great, blazing flames are transformed into lotus flowers.
The sinners, faster than a torrential rain, sit upon the lotus flowers.
Iron-beaked insects emerge from the flaming flowers, piercing the bones and entering the body,
writhing in agitation; all the sword-branches slice away the flesh and bone.
Immeasurable forests of knives descend from above,
and the eighteen types of suffering, such as the fire chariots and burning coals, all come to meet [the practitioner] at once.
When these signs appear, one falls into the depths of the earth.

From the lower partition upward, his body is like a blooming flower, filling the space; from the lower partition downward, the fire blazes fiercely, reaching up to the upper partition so that his body is entirely filled within it.
Because of the intense heat and distress, he opens his eyes wide and sticks out his tongue.
Billions of molten copper cauldrons and hundreds of thousands of razor-edged wheels descend from the sky,
entering at the neck and exiting through the feet;
all these sufferings exceed those previously described by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
Those who have committed the five heinous crimes shall suffer retribution for five kalpas.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who violate the four grave prohibitions, consume the offerings of the faithful in vain, slander the Dharma with false views, and fail to recognize cause and effect.
They abandon the study of Prajñāpāramitā and revile the Buddhas of the ten directions;
they steal the property of the Saṃgha, engage in lewdness and lack of morality,
and violate pure-natured bhikṣuṇīs who are like sisters or close kin.
Having committed various evil deeds,
when this person’s life comes to an end, such is the retribution for their sins.
The wind-blade dissects his body as he lies prostrate and restless, as if being whipped and beaten.
His mind becomes wild and distracted, giving rise to deluded thoughts of madness;
he sees his own house and its inhabitants, both men and women, great and small.
Everything there consists of impure things;
foul-smelling excrement and urine overflow outside.
The hell-wardens, who are rākṣasas, hold them aloft with great iron forks.
The Avīci Hell and its various forests of blades were transformed into jeweled trees and cool, refreshing ponds;
the flames were transformed into golden-leaved lotuses, and the iron-beaked insects were transformed into wild ducks and geese.
The sounds of suffering are like songs and chants;
hearing these, I shall wander therein and sit upon a lotus of fire.
The multitude vied with one another to divide the goods;
a dog devoured its heart in an instant.
Their bodies are like iron flowers and fill eighteen compartments.
These sinners pass through eighty-four thousand great kalpas and then enter the eighteen compartments in the eastern direction.
They shall suffer as described above;
it is likewise in the south, west, and north.
This applies to those who slander the Vaipulya sutras.
They have committed the five heinous crimes,
destroyed the Saṃgha,
and defiled bhikṣuṇīs.
Having severed all roots of goodness and being possessed of manifold transgressions, their bodies fill the Avīci Hell,
and their four limbs further fill the eighteen compartments within it.
This Avīci Hell burns only those sentient beings who belong to this class of hell-beings.
When the kalpa is about to end, the eastern gate opens,
and one sees outside the eastern gate.
Clear springs, flowing streams, flowering fruits, and forest trees all appear together.
These sinners, seeing from beneath the partition that the blazing fire has momentarily subsided,
rise from below and crawl forward on their bellies.
He climbed onto his body and reached the upper chamber,
where he grasped the wheel of blades;
at that moment, hot iron balls rained down from the void.
As he ran toward the eastern gate and reached its threshold,
the rākṣasa jailers seized him with iron forks and pierced his eyes from behind;
iron dogs bit into his heart, and he died in a state of fainting.
The southern, western, and northern gates were likewise so.

After half an eon had passed, each of the eighteen minor hells surrounding the Avīci hell was itself surrounded by eighteen hells; thus, there were two sets of eighteen minor hells encircling the Avīci hell.
There are eighteen minor hells.
Each of these minor hells has eighteen cold hells.
The eighteen dark hells, the eighteen minor hot hells,
and the eighteen sword-wheel hells.
The eighteen Sword-Wheel Hells;
the eighteen Fire-Train Hells;
and the eighteen Boiling Excrement Hells.
The eighteen hells of boiling cauldrons;
the eighteen hells of ash-rivers;
and five hundred billion hells of sword-forests.
Five hundred billion Śālmalī-forest hells;
five hundred billion Copper Pillar hells;
five hundred billion Iron Ball hells.
There are five hundred billion Iron Rimmed Hells,
eighteen Iron Cave Hells, and eighteen Iron Ball Hells.
The eighteen Spiked-Stone Hells,
the eighteen Copper-Drinking Hells,
and many other such hells.
From the Avīci Hell, one dies and is reborn within the Cold Ice [Hell];
from the Cold Ice Hell, one dies and is reborn in the Place of Darkness.
For eighty million years his eyes were unable to see;
he received the body of a great beast, crawling on his belly,
with all his senses darkened and obstructed, until he was devoured by foxes and wolves.
In subsequent lives, they were born as animals;
for five million lifetimes they took the forms of birds and beasts,
and then were reborn among human beings.
With their six sense faculties incomplete, they were poor and lowly;
after five hundred lifetimes, they were reborn as hungry ghosts.
Later, they encountered a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and gave rise to the bodhicitta.
As for the eighteen cold hells,
there are ice mountains in the eight directions,
with eighteen ridges between each mountain.
Furthermore, there are eighteen small ice mountains;
between these cold ice mountains are lotus flowers made of tiles,
eighteen yojanas in height.
Above is a wheel of ice,
twelve yojanas in length and breadth, equal in all dimensions,
falling from the sky like hailstones raining down.
When this person who has robbed, plundered, stripped, and slaughtered sentient beings through cold approaches the end of their life as a retribution for their sins,
all the winds of the blade transform into blazing hot fire.
The sinner thinks to himself, "Why do I not now lie upon the ice?
As he is thinking this,
the rakṣasa wardens, holding wheels of ice in their hands, arrive by treading through the air.
Upon seeing this, the sinner’s heart was filled with longing;
his breath ceased and his life ended, and he was reborn upon the Ice Mountain.
Once born there, he...
In the eighteen ice mountains, it is as if fanned by a fan;
all the cold ice enters through the pores,
filling every single compartment within the eighteen compartments.
It is split, torn, and shattered like a red lotus;
ice wheels above and below completely cover its body,
and the ice mountains from the eight directions close together all at once.
Having no other words to speak, they say only "A-ra.
At that time, the sinner immediately thinks to himself:
"When shall I be freed from this Cold Ice Hell and born into the Heat Fire Hell?"
At that time, there was an iron-beaked bird in the air;
it spat fire, broke through the ice, and pecked at the brain,
whereupon the sinner died immediately.
The hell-wardens again struck the ground with iron forks and shouted, "Live! Live!
At the sound, he immediately revived.
His body was ablaze with fierce flames, and he prayed that he might obtain the ice before him to extinguish this fire.
The hell-wardens further receive them with wheels of ice and place them within the hells.
In this manner, they pass through all eighteen compartments without exception.
Such is the lifespan in these cold hells, measured in years.
As for the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, eighty million years is equivalent to one day and night;
when their retribution is exhausted, they descend to be born into lowly,
impoverished, and ignoble circumstances, serving as slaves to others for fifty lifetimes.
Their clothing shall not cover their bodies and their food shall not suffice for their mouths.
Once these karmic retributions are exhausted,
they will encounter virtuous friends and resolve to attain bodhicitta.
As for the Hell of Dark Obscurity,
it consists of eighteen layers of black mountains and eighteen layers of black nets.
There are eighteen layers of iron beds and eighteen layers of iron curtains;
one mountain is eighty-four thousand yojanas high.
Each layer is also eighty-four thousand yojanas thick.
Between each layer, eighteen tiers of Cakravāḍa mountains stand like a forest of rākṣasas;
these mountains are dark and gloomy.
Stealing the lamps and light of the Buddha,
the Sangha, and one's parents and teachers;
slandering those who preach the Dharma.
They also disparage worldly masters of logic and debate;
showing no regard for the distinction between the honorable and the lowly, they lack a sense of shame.
Because of these transgressions, when their lives are about to end, [they suffer...]
The eyes possessed flashes of lightning, flickering and ceasing not.
He immediately thought:
"What sin do I have that I constantly see this fire?"
He immediately closed both eyes, unwilling to look upon them.
As his life was about to end,
the rākṣasa wardens of hell raised up a great iron bed and spread out a great iron wheel.
Like a great mass of clouds riding upon the void, they arrive;
formless yet possessing sound.
The sinner, desiring to depart, reaches the end of his life;
he sits upon an iron bed and falls into a place of pitch darkness,
where blades on wheels slice through his body from above and below.
There are great iron crows with long,
sharp beaks and talons that fly down from the mountains to peck at the offenders;
in their agonizing haste, they run about seeking light but find none.
Beneath your feet, caltrops pierce through the bones and penetrate to the marrow.
Thus, in terror, you shall pass five hundred million years, with days and nights as before.
That person’s head will strike against the various mountains of total darkness.
The brain flows out and emerges from the eyes.
The hell-wardens, who are rākṣasas, impale it with iron forks and place it back into the eye sockets.
Only when their retribution is exhausted do they emerge.
He becomes a person of poverty,
with eyes that roll and stare, blind and dark, seeing nothing;
or he is driven away by those afflicted with leprosy.
Such retribution for these sins lasts for five hundred lifetimes.
After this period has passed, one encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and gives rise to the bodhicitta.
As for the eighteen minor hot hells:
It is like the Avīci Hell,
with sevenfold walls and sevenfold iron rims,
adorned with immeasurable evils.
Because they did not follow their teacher’s instructions, they gave rise to malicious and rebellious thoughts;
they were ungrateful for his nurturing care, stole from the teacher, harmed the teacher,
defiled the teacher’s pure food, sat upon the teacher’s seat, and seized the teacher’s alms bowl to hide away its impurities.
They concocted various kinds of malicious poisons to drink for their teachers—
whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—
and committed all manner of unrighteous acts without any sense of shame or remorse.
When one strips images, destroys stupas, seizes the treasures of the Dharma,
and kills paternal uncles, aunts, parents, brothers, or sisters,
at the moment their life is about to end:
Eighteen hell-wardens each took up an iron fork and placed it within a separate compartment of the hell.
Like a great precious canopy, they rained down a fine mist;
the droplets were like flowers that entered the hearts of those suffering from the heat.
Seeing the rain was cool and refreshing, he immediately formed this thought:
"May I obtain a place beneath a canopy;
would it not be joyful for the cool rain to fall upon me?"
His breath ceased and his life ended;
in the space of a single instant, he was seated upon a forest of swords,
amidst ten billion sword-blades.
Blades all burst forth flames to burn and pierce their bodies;
a precious canopy in the air transforms into a wheel of fire,
descending from above to split their crowns straight through.
The body is shattered into thousands of fragments.
From above, showers of copper balls fall and enter through the pores.
The rakshasa jailers pierce the eyes of the offenders with great iron forks.
Alternatively, they may be pierced through the heart with iron arrows, fainting and dying;
yet in an instant they revive and sit upon a bed of swords,
where violent whirlwind gales blow them down into hell.
Then King Yama addressed him, saying:
"O inhabitant of hell, you have committed many evils;
you killed your teacher and slandered your teacher."
"The place where you have now been born is called the Avīci Hell of Severed Tongues.
You shall remain in this hell for three kalpas.
Having spoken these words, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
As for the Hell of the Blade-Wheel:
on all four sides are mountains of blades,
and between these mountains, blades are piled up like a wheel.
There are eight million billion extremely large sword-wheels that descend one after another like drops of rain;
they bring joy to those who cause suffering and kill sentient beings.
At the time of his death,
suffering from the ailment of upward-moving qi (hiccup), his heart became as hard as stone,
and he immediately made this vow:
"Would it not be a joy to obtain a sharp blade to excise these various afflictions?
At that time, the hell-warden took a wheel of blades upon his head, concealing it so as not to reveal it,
and approached the place of the offenders with humble speech and deferential words.
"I possess a sharp sword capable of excising grievous illness.
Upon hearing this, the sinner rejoices and thinks to himself,
"Only this is truly delightful."
When their breath ceases and their lives end, they are reborn upon the Blade-Wheel Mountain.
Like a drunken elephant running and falling into the midst of a mountain of blades,
at that moment the four mountains close together all at once.
Four kinds of blade-mountains slice and cut their bodies;
unable to bear it themselves, they faint and die.
The hell-wardens and rākṣasas then drive and crush the offenders.
They are made to ascend a mountain of blades until they reach the summit;
their feet are wounded by the blades all the way up to their hearts,
yet they crawl upward out of fear of the hell-wardens.
Once they have reached the summit of the mountain,
the hell-wardens seize all the trees with their hands;
while the victims are yet to die, iron dogs gnaw at their hearts, inflicting hundreds of kinds of agonizing suffering.
Iron insects devour the flesh until it is completely gone;
immediately thereafter, one cries out for life as iron wheels descend from the sky upon one's feet.
In a single day and night, there are sixty billion births and sixty billion deaths.
Such a multitude [of beings] is like the lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings, which is eighty million years.
Only when their retribution is exhausted do they emerge and fall among the animals.
For five hundred lifetimes he provided food for the mouths of the multitude;
for another five hundred lifetimes he took on lowly and base forms;
subsequently, encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he gave rise to the bodhicitta.
As for the Sword-Wheel Hell (Khaḍgacakraka-naraka),
it is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal on all sides.
It is filled with sword-trees, and as for the number of these trees:
Like rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds,
each sword-tree is forty yojanas high,
with eighty-four thousand sword-wheels for leaves.
Eighty-four thousand sword-wheels serve as its flowers;
eighty-four thousand sword-wheels serve as its fruits;
eighty-four thousand cauldrons of boiling copper serve as its branches.
Delighting in killing without satiety,
such a sinner, when facing the end of life,
encounters a great fever and immediately thinks to himself:
"Right now my body is sometimes hot and sometimes cold;
my entire frame is as rigid and hard as an iron anvil.
He then made this aspiration:
Having obtained the vajra-sword, they sever this affliction; the joy is beyond description.
At that time, the hell-wardens immediately transform their own bodies into the forms of one's parents, relatives, and friends.
Standing before that person, he said to him:
"I possess a secret dharma which, as you have contemplated, I shall bestow upon you.
The sinner replied: "I desire it with great urgency."
Their breath ceases and their lives end as they are born within the Sword-Flower Hell, having run like galloping horses.
Immeasurable swords and blades slice through their bones and tear through their flesh until they fall shattered like empty space.
Furthermore, there are iron crows.
Descending from the tree, they gouge out eyes and peck at ears;
there are great rākṣasas who seize iron axes in their hands and split open heads to extract the brains.
An iron dog comes to lick him; though he has already died, it proclaims him alive.
It drives him up a tree, and before he reaches the treetop, his body is shattered like dust.
In a single day and night, they kill themselves as many times as there are motes of dust, beyond all calculation.
Because of the sin of killing others, they undergo such calamities for eighty trillion years, being reborn among the animals.
Constantly bearing heavy burdens in life, they are further flayed of their skin at death;
after five hundred lifetimes, they are reborn among humans,
where they are impoverished, short-lived, and emaciated with many ailments.
After this period has passed, they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and resolve their minds on Bodhicitta.
As for those in the Hell of the Fire-Drawn Chariots,
there are individual copper cauldrons.
It is forty yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal on all sides,
filled with fire,
and beneath it are twelve wheels.
Above are nine thousand four fire-wheels.
Among them are sentient beings who have become disciples of the Buddha,
as well as those who serve the ninety-six kinds of Brahmā-devas.
Furthermore, when householders who deceive others, live by wrong livelihood, are sycophantic,
and commit evil deeds are about to die,
the wind-element first agitates them, and their bodies become as cold as ice.
He then had this thought:
"When shall I obtain a great mass of fierce fire,
so that by sitting within it, I may forever eliminate my cold ailment?"
Having formed this thought,
the rakṣasa hell-guardian transforms himself into a fire chariot like a golden lotus;
the hell-guardian sits upon it in the likeness of a young boy.
Holding white whisks in their hands, they arrive dancing and leaping.
The sinners become attached to them,
thinking, "If I were to sit upon these, the pleasure would be beyond description."
When their breath ceases and their lives end, they are placed upon a fire-chariot;
their limbs burst into flames and their bodies are scorched and scattered.
The hell-wardens cry out, "Be alive! and as soon as they respond, they are restored to life.
The fiery chariots run over his body eighteen times, crushing his body into dust.
Heaven rains boiling copper that douses his entire body, yet he immediately returns to life.
In this manner, he travels back and forth, ascending as far as the surface of the cauldron and descending into its depths.
Crushed by the fiery chariot for one day and one night, there are ninety billion deaths and ninety billion births.
When this person's retribution is exhausted, they will be born into a poor and lowly family and be made to serve others.
Bound to others and lacking autonomy,
he must repay his offerings before he can finally be liberated; yet,
by virtue of the merit from his previous wholesome mind of renunciation, he eventually attains release.
Encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he was taught the Dharma for him;
his mind opened and his understanding was realized, and he became an Arhat.
As for those in the Boishi (Boiling Excrement) Hell:
There are eighteen iron cities, eighty yojanas in extent.
Each iron city has eighteen partitions,
and within each partition, all four walls are lined with ten billion sword-trees.
The ground is like the edge of a blade;
the blade is three feet thick,
and upon that blade are hundreds of thousands of uncountable caltrops.
Between each of the thorny jili plants and sword-trees,
there arise countless iron insects;
each iron insect has hundreds of thousands of heads.
Each head has hundreds of thousands of beaks,
and at the tip of every beak there are hundreds of thousands of venomous snakes;
these snakes spit hot excrement from their mouths.
It boils like molten copper, filling the interior of an iron city;
above it are iron nets and iron crows,
[retribution] for having violated the eight precepts of the fast.
They defile the śrāmaṇerī and śikṣamāṇā precepts;
they defile the bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī precepts;
they defile the upāsaka and upāsikā precepts.
Likewise, all those among the seven classes of followers and others who defile the food of the Sangha, the food of their parents,
or food that has been stolen; those who eat before [others] or handle food with impure hands.
Furthermore, because the monastic administrators relied on their own status, they defiled the pure food of the Sangha;
and the disciples of the four assemblies sat upon the communal beds with impure bodies.
Having committed these *sthūlātyaya* offenses, they did not repent for a long time.

These many and immeasurable persons of impure and evil karma— those who have consumed the food of the Sangha in vain, sat among the assembly of monks, and participated in the *poṣadha* ceremony with the Sangha—
find their entire bodies emitting fragrance at the moment of death.
Just as when one cannot bear the presence of musk,
one thinks: "In what place might I not smell this fragrance?"
The hell-wardens manifest transformations like painted jars filled with excrement and filth;
they go to where the offenders are and touch them with their hands,
causing those offenders to give rise to feelings of attachment.
When their breath ceases and life ends, they fall into the Hell of Boiling Excrement.
Their bodies are mangled and decayed as swarms of worms devour them, gnawing through their bones and penetrating to their marrow.
Driven by the torment of thirst, they drink the hot, boiling excrement.
Vipers and maggots gnaw at the root of their tongue;
in a single day and night, they undergo ninety billion births and ninety billion deaths.
Only when their retribution is exhausted are they born into poor and lowly families, lacking any autonomy.
Even if they are born into the world, they will constantly encounter wicked kings and rulers who hold false views;
various kinds of evil matters will oppress their bodies,
and they will wear goiters, swellings, and malignant sores as their clothing.
Due to the wholesome causal conditions of having heard the Dharma in previous lives,
he encountered a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), left the household life to study the Path, and became an Arhat.
As for the eighteen cauldrons of boiling water in hell:
There are eighteen cauldrons,
each forty yojanas in length, breadth, and height,
filled with boiling iron within seven layers of iron mesh.
Five hundred rākṣasas beat upon great stones of charcoal,
causing the flames of the copper cauldrons to blaze up one after another;
for sixty days the fire could not be extinguished.
When twelve myriad years are full in Jambudvīpa,
the boiling cauldron surges upward and transforms into a wheel of fire,
which then returns into the cauldron.
They violate the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts by performing sacrifices involving the killing of living beings.
For the sake of eating meat, they burn mountains and forests, thereby harming sentient beings;
they devour living creatures raw and incinerate them with fire.
When such a person’s life is about to end, their body and mind become distressed and agitated;
they lose control over their excrement and urine, unable to restrain themselves.
Their body may feel as hot as boiling water or as cold as ice.
He then had this thought:
"Would it not be pleasant to obtain great warm water and enter it to bathe?
Thereupon, the rākṣasa hell-wardens transformed themselves into servants.
Holding a basin of boiling water in his hands, he went to where the offenders were;
as a feeling of affection and delight arose in his mind,
